Now, when sages compose treatises, they do so for three purposes: first, to establish the doctrine; second, to refute opposing views; and third, to benefit sentient beings. This treatise is composed for these three reasons. First, to establish the doctrine: it establishes the doctrine of the Mahāyāna by refuting those who hold erroneous views regarding the Mahāyāna. Second, to refute opposing views: it refutes the views of the Śrāvakas and others who hold erroneous views regarding the Mahāyāna. Third, to benefit sentient beings: it benefits sentient beings by causing them to abandon their afflictions and attain liberation. Furthermore, there are two types of treatises: those that primarily establish the doctrine and those that primarily refute opposing views. This treatise belongs to the latter category. Why? Because it primarily refutes the views of the Śrāvakas and others who hold erroneous views regarding the Mahāyāna. Moreover, there are two types of refutation: refutation through direct contradiction and refutation through logical inference. This treatise employs both methods. Why? Because it refutes the views of the Śrāvakas and others through direct contradiction, and it refutes the views of the Tīrthikas and others through logical inference. Third, Kātyāyana composed the Prajñaptipāda-śāstra.
The three treatises above were composed while the Buddha was still in the world; [the others] were composed during the first hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Devasarman composed the *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra* during the early part of the third century.
The Venerable Vasumitra composed the Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra and also composed the Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra.
At the end of the third century,
Kātyāyanīputra composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
The six preceding *pāda-śāstras* contain relatively few topical categories (*arthamukha*), whereas the single treatise,
the *Jñānaprasthāna*, contains many.
This dharma-gate is the most extensive.
Later masters of treatises, however,
maintain that six [factors] are sufficient.
The *Jñānaprasthāna* serves as the body [of the Abhidharma].
Subsequent masters of the treatises mostly rely upon the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
The Mahāvibhāṣā was composed based upon this;
untainted, pure wisdom is the true Abhidharma.
The treatise on tainted wisdom is not the true Abhidharma.
That which is called Abhidharma is so designated because it serves as a provision for the untainted.
It is also called Abhidharma.
Thus, the treatise says:
"These various [treatises on] wisdom..."
Because it is the equipment for that [Abhidharma], it is also called Abhidharma.
As for the term "equipment" (sambhāra):
First there is wisdom derived from scriptural instruction;
next, there is that which is acquired at birth;
and following the wisdom acquired at birth, there subsequently arises wisdom derived from hearing.

Following the wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā), the wisdom derived from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) subsequently arises; following the wisdom derived from reflection, the wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) is first produced;
and following the wisdom derived from cultivation, the untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā) arises.
Therefore, all treatises on wisdom are the provisions for pure wisdom. To explain the name of this dharma:
it is that which can maintain its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it is called "dharma.
For instance, the dharma of form has transformation and resistance as its intrinsic nature.
Because it can maintain this nature,
it is called "form-dharma" (rūpa-dharma).
This is one such example cited in brief.
Other dharmas are likewise.
There are two kinds of dharmas:
first, ultimate dharmas (paramārtha-dharma).
Regarding the two types of phenomena:
the ultimate phenomenon refers to nirvāṇa.
This is wholesome and eternal;
therefore, it is called supreme.
This is because it possesses substantial reality.
It is also called "meaning" (*artha*);
that is, it is the supreme meaning.
That which is the supreme meaning is called the "Dharma."
Therefore, it is called the "Dharma of Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha-dharma*);
this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Second, as for the "Dharma of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*):
It penetrates the four noble truths.
"Characteristic" (xiàng) refers to nature (xìng) and appearance (zhuàng).
Viewed from the perspective of its own essence, it is called "nature" (svabhāva); viewed from the perspective of other conditions, it is called "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa).
These are the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths.
Because it is the characteristic of dharmas,
it is called the "dharma-characteristic dharma. The term "dharma-characteristic" is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, meaning that the characteristic itself is the dharma.
"Facing" has two meanings.
The first is "directing toward," which refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*).
The first is directed toward nirvāṇa;
the second is contemplative observation,
namely, untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā).
Regarding the contemplation of the Four Truths:
the previous term "facing toward" refers to the cause facing toward the fruit.
The cause is pure wisdom;
the fruit is nirvana. The subsequent statement concerns contemplative observation:
it is the mind confronting its object.
The mind is pure wisdom;
the object is the Four Noble Truths. Pure wisdom free from outflows is merely its counterpart.
Because it is that which opposes,
yet it is not a dharma,
as it is not that which is opposed. Thus, it is called "Abhidharma" (the Dharma that opposes).
Because this is the counter-correlative of that dharma,
it is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Master Kuang said:
It is able to counteract its respective object;
thus, it is provisionally designated by the name "counteracting.
However, speaking according to the ultimate principle:
It is also called "dharma" because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since the dharma that serves as the object of reference is preeminent,
the name "dharma" is established for it first.
To speak according to the actual principle,
it is also called "counter" (pratipakṣa),
because it is that which is countered.
Based on this, the Abhidharma,
which encompasses both the subject and the object, consists of six types in total.
The first is the Abhidharma of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-abhidharma*).
This refers to pure wisdom.
Second is the Abhidharma that accords with practice,
which refers to the retinue of pure wisdom.
Third is the Abhidharma of skillful means,
which refers to the four types of contaminated wisdom.
Fourth is the Abhidharma of provisions.
This refers to the scriptural teachings.
Fifth, the Abhidharma of objects refers to the Four Noble Truths.
The sixth is the Abhidharma of the fruit,
which refers to nirvāṇa. The preceding four are capable of being "confronted" (abhi-mukha).
It is named Abhidharma.
The latter two [categories] that are confronted are what is named Abhidharma. Regarding this subject-object relationship, there are three interpretations for each.
Furthermore, regarding the term "able to counter" (*pratipakṣa*),
there are three interpretations.
First, that which is able to counter is called "counter."
That which is opposed is called "dharma.
Because it is the opposite of dharma,
it is named "Abhidharma" (Counter-Dharma).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).
Regarding the two categories of "counterparts" (*pratipakṣa*) and "non-counterparts" (*apratipakṣa*), that which is countered is termed "counterpart" (*abhidharma*).
That which is capable of confronting [the objects] is called Abhidharma; because there are dharmas to be confronted,
it is named Abhidharma.
This is a possessive compound (tatpuruṣa).
Because these three are capable of being opposed, they are called "opposites" (pratipakṣa); because they are opposites, they are also termed "dharmas."
Because it maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that which is "opposed" (*prati*) is itself the phenomenon (*dharma*);
thus, it is called *abhidharma*.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Within the dharmas being contrasted,
there are likewise three types of explanations.
According to Master Baoliang, both the counterpart and the speaker are mentioned; according to Master Sengbao,
only the counterpart is mentioned.
It is named Abhidharma. Regarding the etymological analysis of the term Abhidharma,
it is explained solely according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) interpretation.
This interpretation is excellent;
it perfectly accords with the treatise.
From here begins the second [section], the explanation of the name of the Piṭaka.
The treatise says: "The Abhidharma has already been explained.
Why is this treatise called the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma)?
The verse says:"
"Because it encompasses that ultimate truth and because it relies upon it, this is established as the name 'Abhidharmakośa'.
Commentary: The first phrase explains the "Treasury" (Kośa);
the second phrase explains the name.
Regarding the phrase "because it subsumes that ultimate truth and relies upon it," the Piṭaka is explained by way of two meanings:
first, because it subsumes that ultimate truth.
"Second, because it relies upon that [Abhidharma], it subsumes its ultimate meaning"— this refers to the *Abhidharmakośa*,
which contains the treasury of names.
This is what is meant by "this *Kośa*."
It encompasses those Abhidharma works,
such as the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and others,
which contain words of supreme meaning.
Therefore, it is called a "pitaka" (repository).
Being the repository of the Abhidharma,
it is named the "Abhidharmapiṭaka."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).
"Depending on that" means that the basis is called the "Treasury" (*piṭaka*).
That is to say, this *Abhidharmakośa* relies upon those treatises such as the *Prakaraṇapāda* and the *Jñānaprasthāna*,
from which it was derived.
Because it is that which serves as the basis, it is called a "piṭaka" (storehouse).
The *Jñānaprasthāna* and other such works are the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Now, this Abhidharmakośa is a treasury of the dharmas that possess resistance; therefore,
it is called the Treasury of Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośa).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound). This establishes the name *Abhidharmakośa*;
it serves as the conclusion.
Third, this clarifies the person who explains and the person who speaks the meaning.
The treatise says:
For what reason is the intention behind the *Abhidharma-praśna-vyākhyā* explained?
And who was the person who first spoke this *Abhidharma-praśna-vyākhyā*?
The verse says:
Apart from the discernment of dharmas, there is truly no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions;
because of these afflictions, the world drifts in the ocean of existence. For this reason, it is traditionally said that the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
Commentary: "Apart from the discernment of dharmas... means:
Up to the fourth phrase.
For this reason,
it is traditionally said by the Abhidharmikas:
"Explaining" clarifies the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*).
"Transmitting the Buddha's exposition of the Abhidharma" clarifies the person who expounded the treatise.
Therefore, the third phrase,
"Abhidharma" (the Treatise on Phenomena),
is stated to apply to both locations.
The discernment of dharmas is wisdom.
Wisdom is able to extinguish delusions;
it is the supreme skillful means.
If one is devoid of wisdom,
there is no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions.
It is due to these afflictions that sentient beings are tossed about within the ocean of birth and death in the three realms of existence.
Therefore, it is called Abhidharma (the "Higher Dharma"), because within the Abhidharma, wisdom (*prajñā*) is primarily elucidated.
Although the treatise also clarifies ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), these are not its primary focus. According to tradition, the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
taught the Abhidharma in scattered fragments here and there;
[it was later compiled] by Kātyāyanīputra and others.
They were compiled and established,
just like the Chapter on Impermanence and others compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
The above is the prose commentary on the *udāna* verses. As for *udāna*,
this term means "collected exposition" (*saṃgīti*),
or alternatively, "collected and dispersed."
To collect the meaning that has been explained and distribute it to sentient beings is called *udāna*.
As for the one called Dharmatrāta,
it is because he saves people through the Dharma.
This is the Venerable Dharmatrāta.
The Buddha taught the meaning of impermanence;
these were compiled as verses on impermanence,
continuing up to the compilation of the meaning of non-self.
This concludes the verses on non-self;
the preceding section explaining the introductory portion is finished. From here onwards:
This is the orthodox tradition of the Treatise on Illumination (*Abhidharmakośa*). Within it, there are two parts:
first, a general presentation of the essential framework.
Second, the detailed explanation of the essential nature.
First, regarding the presentation of the fundamental outline, the treatise asks: "What is dharma?"
It is called that which is discerned by it;
for this reason, the Buddha is said to have taught the Abhidharma.
The verse says:
Regarding tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena: with the exception of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena are called "tainted" because the outflows increase therein;
the untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena.
These are space and the two types of cessation. Among these, space is non-obstruction;

analytical cessation refers to disjunction. There is a distinct [cessation] for each object of bondage, which is the ultimate obstruction of that which is to arise; this is the acquisition of non-analytical cessation.
The commentary states: The first sentence provides a general heading;
the subsequent eleven sentences provide a detailed explanation.
Within this detailed explanation:
The first three phrases specifically explain contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*);
the latter eight phrases specifically explain uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
"Defiled and undefiled phenomena" is the heading;
it refers to all phenomena.
There are only two kinds:
first, those with outflows (sāsrava);
second, those without outflows (anāsrava).
"Except for the Path, all other conditioned phenomena" clarifies that their essence is contaminated (*sāsrava*).
"Except for the Path" means excluding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
There are four kinds of truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Of these, three—suffering, its origin, and the path—are [to be understood].
These are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Although the Path is conditioned,
it is an outflow-free phenomenon (*anāsravadharma*).
Now, to clarify that these are with outflows (*sāsrava*),
the Path (*mārga*) is excluded.
As for the remaining conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*):
This refers to the truths of suffering and its origin; because they are external to the truth of the path,
they are designated as "the remainder."
Therefore, the remaining conditioned phenomena are the truths of suffering and its origin;
those among them in which the outflows increase are [the objects of the outflows].
Regarding the meaning of "understanding the outflows" (*āsrava*):
"in that" refers to the aforementioned suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
"Outflows" (āsrava) refers to the afflictions (kleśa).
Because they leak out faults without end,
the afflictions are called "outflows."
Because the various outflows (āsrava) equally conform to and increase within those truths of suffering and its origin,
the truths of suffering and its origin are termed "with outflows" (sāsrava).
Because those outflows exist therein,
the treatise says:
"Among these, the various outflows..."

Because they increase equally and accordingly, the outflows (āsrava) mutually conform to and mutually increase within the phenomena associated with suffering and its origin, as well as within the objects of those phenomena.
They are called "equal" because their mutual power is equal. Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Although various outflows (āsrava) may arise taking the truths of cessation and the path as objects..."
And because they do not increase accordingly,
they are not outflows (*āsrava*).
This is the meaning of "not increasing accordingly."
This shall be explained in detail within the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Dispositions); therefore,
they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
This concludes [the section on] fetters.
Regarding the statement "the untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena," this is a detailed explanation of the untainted.
The Truth of the Path consists of conditioned and untainted phenomena.
As for the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena:
"Unconditioned" refers to the untainted (anāsrava).
"Namely, space and the two cessations" enumerates the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
The two types of cessation are analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Among these, "space" (*ākāśa*) is that which is unimpeded.
Explaining the essence of space:
"In this context" refers to among the three unconditioned phenomena briefly mentioned above.
Space has non-obstruction as its sole nature;
because it is unobstructed, matter moves within it. Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) refers to disjunction (visamyoga).
It brings forth the essence of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Cessation through deliberation has the nature of dissociation (*visamyoga*).
As for "bondage" (*saṃyojana*):
It is bondage.
There are two kinds of bondage:
first, the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*).
Second is the bondage of the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*). These two bondages are explained in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Dispositions).
This is not explained in detail here.
By severing these two fetters,
one realizes the unconditioned.
It is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "Deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*),
because it is by means of wisdom that one discriminates the Four Noble Truths.
Cessation is nirvāṇa;
non-arising is called cessation.
It is the cessation obtained through the power of discernment.
It is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is like calling a cart drawn by oxen an "ox-cart," where the intermediate term has been omitted.
Therefore, this statement was made.
"According to the distinctness of the objects of bondage" clarifies the number of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This means that because the substance of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is distinct for each respective object of bondage, it is as follows: for instance, within the three realms and nine stages,
there are nine grades of afflictions in each stage.
There are eighty-one grades [of afflictions].
One eliminates one grade of delusion and realizes one grade of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Up to the point of severing the eighty-first category [of afflictions],
one realizes the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of those eighty-one categories; therefore,
their entities are distinct from one another.
Furthermore, the treatise asks:
"Based on what meaning is it said that cessation has no similar class?"
Since the essence of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is manifold, it should possess homogeneous counterparts (*sabhāga*).
Based on what meaning is it said that cessation through deliberation has no homogeneous counterpart?
Because cessation itself lacks the nature of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it does not [act as one] for others either;
therefore, this statement was made.
It is not that there is no answer regarding the similarity of types.
As for the statement that, based on cessation, there is no sense of a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for itself,
this reveals that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) does not arise from a homogeneous cause.
"Nor does it give to others" means that cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also does not act as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for others.
Therefore, this statement was made.
The Sūtra makes this statement based on the principle that there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);
thus it says that cessation has no homogeneous [cause].
"It is not that there is no similar entity" indicates that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has multiple entities that are of the same kind.
It is the ultimate obstruction to what is to arise.
Regarding "attaining cessation not through deliberation separately," this explains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for the term "that which is to arise":
Regarding phenomena that are destined to arise in the future:
these phenomena destined to arise will come into being when the necessary conditions converge.
When conditions are lacking, [a phenomenon] does not arise; at the time it does not arise,
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
it obstructs dharmas that are about to arise,
causing them never to manifest again.
It is called "ultimate obstruction.
As for the term "attained separately," it refers to cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It possesses substantial reality;
within the state where conditions are absent,
a distinct acquisition arises.
Therefore, analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is not attained through analysis;
it is merely termed "non-analytical cessation" due to the absence of conditions.
The treatise says:
"For example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single form,
other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away."
Conditioned by those objects,
the five groups of consciousness and so forth abide in the future.
It is ultimately unarisen,
because it cannot take past objects as its cognitive domain due to the incompleteness of the conditions for such cognition.

Regarding the attainment of cessation through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the explanation is as follows: for example, when the eye and mental consciousness are focused exclusively on a single visible form,
the remaining [faculties] do not see or hear,
and the [objects of] visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles have fallen away into the past.
At the time when one is focused on a single form,
there should be a corresponding class of five consciousnesses that take as their objects those five sense-fields which have already passed away.
Because it is conditioned by the single object of form with right concentration,
the other five consciousnesses cannot arise;
these five consciousnesses have not yet arisen.
They are ultimately non-arising,
because the five objects have already passed away; thus,
the five consciousnesses take only the present as their object.
Because it is not appropriate for [the five consciousnesses] to take past objects as their conditions,
the future five consciousnesses attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the statement that "contact" and so forth grasp [objects] within the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*):
There are cases where that which is capable of being the object of cognition arises simultaneously with its cognizer;
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds,
whose objects are the mental factors (caitta) of those minds.
Among the five consciousnesses and so forth, within the mental consciousness there is also that which takes a simultaneous object;
this refers to the knowledge of others' minds.
By means of the knowledge of others' minds,
one takes only the present mind as its object;
it does not take mental factors as its object.
The knowledge of others' minds takes mental factors as its object, not the mind itself;
at the very moment it takes the mind as its object,
it takes the mental factors associated with that mind as its object.
One attains non-analytical cessation when,
while correctly taking mental factors as objects, one takes the mind of another as an object through the knowledge of others' minds.
The attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is explained here with respect to simultaneity;

this refers to the statement regarding the convergence of conditions. Furthermore, the treatise states: "Regarding the attainment of cessation in relation to dharmas, one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*)."
Or, regarding certain phenomena, one attains only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
that is to say, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.
Phenomena belonging to the past, present,
and future, being with outflows (sāsrava),
can only attain cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Because they are dharmas that have arisen in the past or present,
non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) cannot be attained with respect to them, or with respect to those dharmas.
One attains only non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
namely: dharmas that do not arise and untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).

Because they are unarisen, they attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not attain cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Or, with respect to all phenomena...
Both attain the two types of cessation;
that is to say, the non-arising of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
Because it does not arise, one attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
because it is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
One may also attain cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), or one may not attain either of the two cessations with respect to certain phenomena;
that is to say, all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
Dharmas of the past, present, and arising do not obtain analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) because they are untainted (anāsrava),
and because they are past, present, or arising.
Therefore, it also cannot be non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Following this second point,
there is a separate explanation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the differentiation of the various names of phenomena;
second, the elucidation of the essence of phenomena.
Within the section distinguishing alternative names, there are two parts:
first, explaining the alternative names for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*);
second, explaining the alternative names for contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, first to clarify the alternative names for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the treatise states:
"The previous statement that, with the exception of the Path, all remaining conditioned phenomena are called 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*)—what is meant by 'conditioned'?
The verse says:

Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena—namely, the five aggregates such as form and so forth—are also called "paths of the world," "bases of verbal expression," "possessing departure," and "possessing entities.
The commentary states: "Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena..."
The phrase "the five aggregates, namely form and so forth" designates conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) means "produced" (*kṛta*).
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are produced by a multitude of conditions;
therefore, they are called "existent" (*bhava*).
Because they are [produced] by those [conditions], they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). Question: Is it because the past and present are produced by a multitude of conditions?
It may be said that they are called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta).
Since the future has not yet been produced,
how can it be called conditioned?
Answer: Because they are of the nature of having been produced in the past and present, they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
It is like milk or like firewood.
When one drinks a child’s milk,
it may be called "milk";
even when not yet drunk, it is called "milk."

Because it belongs to the category of that which is being consumed, that which is currently burning is called fuel; that which has not yet burned is also called fuel because it belongs to the category of that which will be consumed.
"Form and so forth" refers to the inclusion of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
these are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "also the paths of the world, dependent on existence, with departure, with objects, and so forth," this correctly distinguishes its various synonyms. As for "also the paths of the world":
"world" refers to the three periods of time.
The path is itself the Dharma,
for it is that upon which the world relies;
that is to say, past dharmas.
This is what has already been practiced in the world;
this is the present dharma.
This is what is correctly practiced in the world.
Future phenomena are that which will proceed in the world; therefore,
conditioned phenomena are the paths of the three periods of time.
Because it is the path of the world,
it is called the "world-path" (*loka-vartman*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
Furthermore, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called "worldly" (*loka*) because they are subject to destruction.
Because it is the basis for impermanence,
it is called a "path.
The world itself is the path.
It is called the "worldly path" (*loka-vartman*);
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. Therefore, the treatise says:
"Or it is impermanent."
"Because it is swallowed and consumed. The commentary explains:
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are transmuted by impermanence (*anitya*);
impermanence is that which swallows and consumes them.
"Speech" refers to verbal expression;
its essence is sound.
This is the basis upon which speech relies.
This is called the "simultaneous meaning. As for the term "simultaneous meaning," it refers to the meaning of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
this is the meaning expressed [by the word].

Because it falls within the three periods of time together with the expressive name, it is called "the meaning of being simultaneous. Although the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is indeed an object, [it does not fall within the three periods].
It does not fall within the three periods of time;
it is not designated as having a simultaneous meaning, nor is it a basis for verbal expression. There is that which is detached.
"Detachment" means eternal detachment;
it is precisely nirvāṇa. All conditioned phenomena [are characterized by this].
Because it possesses that detachment,
it is called "possessing detachment," just as one who possesses wealth is called "wealthy" or "one who has property."
"Thing" (*vastu*) has the meaning of "cause.
Because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) possess a cause, they are called "possessing things" (*savastuka*).
Regarding the phrase "the verse and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes that which possesses a fruit, namely,
conditioned phenomena that possess a fruit.
The unconditioned has no fruit;
therefore, the conditioned is said to have a fruit.
Such categories as these are the various distinct names for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Next, the second [section] clarifies the synonyms for *sāsrava* (that which is with outflows). The verse says:
That which is *sāsrava* is called the "appropriated aggregates" (*upādānaskandha*), And it is also described as "contending" (*saraṇa*).
And suffering, its origin, the world, the bases of views, and the three realms of existence.
Regarding the commentary: "Those with outflows are called the aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha), because afflictions are called 'clinging'."
This is because they are able to grasp at birth and death.
Since the aggregates arise from grasping,
they are called "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha).
It is named after its cause,
just as fire from grass chaff;
the fire arises from the grass chaff.
It is called "grass-chaff fire.
Alternatively, because the aggregates (skandhas) pertain to grasping (upādāna), they are called "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha).
It is named after that to which it belongs,
just as in the case of a king and his ministers;
the ministers belong to the king.
They are called the aggregates of the king's ministers;
alternatively, because they involve the grasping that gives rise to existence, they are called the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).
It is named after its fruit,
just as a tree that bears flowers and fruit is called a "flower-and-fruit tree" because it produces flowers and fruit.
Regarding the term "with contention" (*saraṇa*): afflictions are called "contention" because they disturb the side of virtue and cause harm to oneself and others.
Therefore, they are called "contentious.
These are tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*),
because contention increases in accordance with them.
It is called "with contention" because that contention exists therein,
just as it was previously stated that they possess those outflows (āsrava).
That which is called "with outflows" (sāsrava) refers to the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya),
namely the outflows within the three realms.
Because it contradicts the noble mind,
it is collectively termed "suffering"; it is not,
however, the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).
The suffering of oppression,
because that painful feeling exists only in the desire realm. Accumulation refers to the truth of accumulation (*samudaya-satya*),
which consists of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
Because it gathers and brings about suffering,
it is called "origination" (samudaya). "World" (loka) carries the meaning of that which is subject to destruction.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) have two kinds of disintegration: first, disintegration by way of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
The second is the world of antidotes;
thus it is called the mundane.
This refers to the untainted Truth of the Path.
Although it is destroyed by the four characteristics,
because it lacks the second [characteristic], counteractive destruction, it is not called "mundane."
It is also called a "basis for views.
"Views" refers to the five views, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Extreme views,
false views, and the grasping of views.
The clinging to rules and observances:
these are outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) that serve as the basis for views.

Therefore, they are called "bases of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*). As for what are called the "three realms of existence" (*bhava*), they are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The various contaminated phenomena within the formless realm possess three meanings by which they are designated as the "three existences" (trayaḥ bhavāḥ).
First, the cause of existence,
which is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Second, the basis of existence.
The basis is precisely the Truth of Suffering;
the three [realms] are the three modes of existence (bhava).
These three meanings are fully subsumed herein.
Therefore, it is called the "three realms of existence" (*tribhava*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes those associated with defilement (*sāsrava*) and other such categories.
These are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
This is the second section concerning their various distinct names.
This clearly elucidates the essential nature.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, a general exposition of the essential nature.
Second, the specific explanation of the names and meanings;
third, the analysis through various categories.
Within the general determination of the essence, there are three parts.
First, the correct identification of the essence;
second, the clarification of its comprehensive inclusion; third, the manifestation of its expansion and contraction.
Regarding the first [section], the actual determination of the essence, it is divided into three parts:
first, the explanation of the aggregate of form; second, the explanation of the [remaining] three aggregates.
Third, the aggregate of consciousness.
Regarding the exposition of the aggregate of form, it is divided into two parts:
first, the formal establishment of the aggregates; second, the establishment of the bases and elements.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the opening of the chapter;
second, the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, regarding the opening of the chapter:
the treatise states, "The preceding discussion of the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the aggregate of form?"
The verse says:
Form consists only of the five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest.
The commentary explains: the five faculties.
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five objects—visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and tangible objects—and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
These constitute the eleven types.
This is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
From this point onward, each section will be explained in detail according to its respective chapter.
Regarding this, there are three parts:
first, the explanation of the five faculties;
second, the explanation of the five objects.
Third, the explanation of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
First, regarding the explanation of the five sense-faculties (*indriya*),
the verse says:
That consciousness relies upon pure matter; these are called the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
Commentary: "That" refers to...
Those are the aforementioned five faculties, beginning with the eye.
"Consciousness" refers to the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body— the five consciousnesses,
such as visual consciousness and so forth.
Depending upon the five faculties, such as the eye,
they receive their names based on that dependence;
thus, they are called "eye-consciousness" and so forth.
The verse states that it is called "that consciousness" because it is the consciousness that depends upon it;
that which relies on pure matter (rūpa-prasāda) is the support (āśraya) of that consciousness.
The five kinds of pure matter are called the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
These are the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
Because its essence is pure,
like the radiance of a precious jewel,
it is called "pure form" (viśuddharūpa).
Next follows the second [section], the explanation of the five objects of the senses.
The verse says:
Visible form is of two kinds, or twenty; Sound has only eight varieties.
Taste has six [types], smell four; touch has eleven as its nature.
The commentary states: "Form is of two kinds, or twenty" means that form is of two types.
First, appearance;
second, shape.
Or twenty [factors].
When expanded, they become twenty:
twelve are visible colors and eight are shapes.
Thus, there are twenty [types of form].
Regarding the twelve types of color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*):
blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist. Regarding the eight types of shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*): [the remaining eight].
Long, short, square, round, high, low, regular, and irregular—these are called "light" (*āloka*), referring to the radiance of the sun.
The radiance of the moon, stars, fire, and medicinal herbs is called "luminosity" (*ābhāsa*).
When these are obstructed, light arises.
Among these, other visible forms are called "shadow";
the opposite of this is "darkness."
That is to say, when shape is even, it is called "regular";
when shape is uneven, it is called "irregular.
Other types of form are easy to understand.
Therefore, it is not explained here that sound consists of only eight types:
first, sound that is agreeable to sentient beings, caused by appropriated great elements;
second, sound that is disagreeable to sentient beings, caused by appropriated great elements.
1. Sounds caused by appropriated primary elements that are not designated as sentient beings and are agreeable;
2. Sounds caused by appropriated primary elements that are not designated as sentient beings and are disagreeable.
5. Sounds caused by non-appropriated primary elements that are agreeable to sentient beings.
6. Sounds caused by non-appropriated primary elements that are disagreeable to sentient beings.
1. Sound caused by non-appropriated great elements that is not designated as a sentient being and is agreeable;
2. Sound caused by non-appropriated great elements that is not designated as a sentient being and is disagreeable. [Within the bodies of sentient beings...]
The sounds produced are termed "appropriated," referring to speech, hands, and so forth.
Among these, vocal karma is called "sentient designation" because it is capable of expressing [meaning];
sounds such as clapping hands are called "non-sentient designation" because they are not capable of expressing [meaning].
[This applies to] winds, forests, rivers, and so forth.
The sounds produced are said to have non-appropriated primary elements as their cause.
Regarding those that are non-appropriated yet designated as sentient beings:
This refers to the vocal sounds of a magically conjured person;
although this body of the conjuration lacks sensory appropriation (*upātta*).
Because it is capable of expressing [meaning], it is called "sentient being" (*sattva*);
the remaining meanings are easy to understand. Regarding the six tastes:
Because bitter, sour, salty, pungent, sweet, and bland are distinct; as for the four kinds of fragrance,
they are pleasant fragrance and unpleasant fragrance.
Because there is a distinction between equal fragrance and unequal fragrance.
Sandalwood, aloeswood, and the like are called "excellent fragrances.
Onions, leeks, and the like are called "unpleasant fragrances.
Within these excellent and unpleasant fragrances, those that augment the physical body are termed "equal fragrances."
That which causes the body to diminish is called an unequal odor;
that which neither increases nor diminishes it is called a pleasant or unpleasant odor.
Therefore, within pleasant and unpleasant odors, each is further divided into equal and unequal odors;
thus, four types of odor are established. As for the eleven types of tangibles:
First, earth;
second, water;
third, fire.
Fourth, wind;
fifth, lightness;
sixth, heaviness.
Seventh, slippery;
eighth, coarse;
ninth, hunger.
10. thirst; 11.
cold. That which is solid is called earth.
Moisture is called water;
warmth is called fire;
movement is called wind.
That which can be weighed is called "heavy.
The opposite of this is called "light. That which is smooth and supple is called "slippery" (*snigdha*).
That which is coarse and rigid is called "rough" (*karkaśa*).
The desire for food is called hunger;
the desire for warmth is called cold;
the desire for drink is called thirst.
Cold, hunger, and thirst—
these three are what the mind desires;
they are not direct objects of sensory contact.
There are three types of contact that give rise to these three desires:
cold, hunger, and thirst.
This is the fruit of contact,
but it is not contact itself. What is now called "contact" [is so designated] because...
They are designated by way of their results;
therefore, the treatise says:
"These all [refer] to the causes."
Because it establishes the name of the fruit. As a verse says:
"The appearance of the Buddhas is bliss; the proclamation of the True Dharma is bliss."
The harmony of the Sangha is joy; practicing together with diligence is joy.
(Commentary:
"The appearance of the Buddha," etc.)
In reality, it is not pleasure itself; rather,
because it is capable of producing pleasure,
it is designated by the name of its fruit.
Contact is also like this.
Following this, thirdly,
the unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is explained.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the unmanifest (avijñapti);
second, the explanation of the primary elements (mahābhūta) that produce it.
Now, first of all, to correctly explain the non-informative (avijñapti),
the verse says:

"Whether the mind is distracted or absent, it follows the stream as pure or impure, and is of the nature derived from the primary elements; for this reason, it is called 'unmanifest' (avijñapti). Commentary: Regarding the phrase "whether the mind is distracted or absent": [it refers to the state where] the mind is either distracted (*vikṣipta*) or in a state of non-cognition (*acittaka*). "Follows the stream" means it continues in accordance with the flow [of the primary elements]. "Pure or impure" refers to its being either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*). "Derived from the primary elements" (*bhautika*) indicates that it is produced by the great elements (*mahābhūta*). For these reasons, it is designated as "unmanifest."
Regarding the state of manifesting non-informative matter (*avijñapti*):
"one with a distracted mind" refers to when this wholesome non-informative matter [arises] while other unwholesome or neutral minds are present.
It is called "disturbed mind" because it disturbs virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). A virtuous mind is called "undisturbed mind" because it shares the same virtuous nature.
This refers to unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Any other wholesome or neutral mind is termed a "distracted mind" (*vikṣipta-citta*).
Because it is a non-manifestation (avijñapti) of confusion and evil, an evil mind is called a "non-confused" mind;
this is because they share the same nature of being unwholesome. Therefore, there are wholesome and unwholesome minds.
Regarding the distracted and non-distracted [states], the indeterminate mind is called "distracted" alone,
because there is no indeterminate unmanifest [form].
Therefore, the treatise says:
"A distracted mind refers to other minds besides this [state]; a mindless state refers to the attainment of non-conception."
The term "and so forth" in the phrase "the attainment of cessation, etc.
indicates that there is a non-disordered state of mind; that is to say, it refers to states such as a disordered mind.
The term "and so forth" includes the non-distracted mind;
"without mind" includes the state of having a mind.
The distracted and non-distracted mind;
the pair of the scattered state;
the mindless and the possessing of mind.
This establishes a pair of positions;

therefore, the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the verse applies to both locations. As for "following the flow," this clarifies the characteristics of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
"Following" (anu) means conforming,
because their natures are similar.
"Flowing" (sṛti) means wandering through cyclic existence.
Because it arises in a continuous succession.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"a similar continuity."

It is called "flowing" (srotas) because it accords with the stream; it is called "similarity" (anuvartana) because it accords with the continuity; and it is called "stream" (pravāha) because it flows. Regarding "pure and impure":
this brings forth the essence of the non-informative (avijñapti). Non-informative matter is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
It does not pertain to the indeterminate nature;
it is termed "pure" or "impure. Regarding the phrase "that which is derived from the primary elements," this serves to distinguish the specific phenomena.
To distinguish [this] from various acquisitions (prāpti):
although acquisitions themselves extend across the four stages and share a similar continuity that might be confused with the characteristics of non-informative matter (avijñapti),
acquisition is not derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta).
Because it excludes all other acquisitions,
it is therefore further stated that it is "derived from the great elements," namely,
unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Because they are derived from the great elements (*mahābhūta*); "derived" (*nirmita*) has the sense of "cause" (*hetu*).
There are five causes: first, the producing cause (*janana-hetu*).
Second, the basis; third, the cause;
fourth, the establishment; and fifth, the maintenance.
The five types of nourishment will be explained hereafter; by this, the exposition of the non-informative (avijñapti) is concluded.
"By this" means that by virtue of these three preceding phrases,
the designation "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) is established.
The term "it is said" indicates that this is the statement of the Master’s school.
Although the unmanifest (avijñapti) has the nature of matter and action just like the manifest (vijñapti) action, [it differs in its mode of existence].
However, because it does not indicate [an action] so as to make it known to others,
it is called "non-indication" (avijñapti).
This concludes the second section below.
Regarding the luminous capacity to produce the primary elements (mahābhūta), there are two types:
first, the substantial four primary elements;
second, the nominal four primary elements.
Furthermore, first, regarding the explanation of the actual primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the treatise says:
"It was previously stated that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is derived from the primary elements.
What, then, are the primary elements?"
The verse says:
The great elements refer to the four realms— earth, water, fire, and wind—
which are capable of performing the functions of supporting and so forth, and possess the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
The commentary states: "The primary elements (mahābhūta) refer to the four elements" is the heading.
It explains "great" (mahat) through three meanings.
Because they are of one substance and are pervasive;
that is to say, the four great elements pervade all derived matter.
Its substance is vast and expansive,
because its form and appearance are great within the two types of intensified aggregates.
That is to say: the great earth and great mountains represent the increase of earth; the great rivers and great oceans represent the increase of water;
and the blazing furnace with its fierce flames represents fire.
Fire increases in intensity; black winds and whirlwinds increase in intensity.
Because these three can give rise to various great functional activities, they are like the earth, which is able to support the world.
Fire can destroy the first dhyāna;
water can destroy the second dhyāna;
wind can destroy the third dhyāna. This is the explanation according to the Ekārthika school.
Because it serves as the basis for derived matter (upādāya-rūpa),
it is called a "seed" (bīja).
Because they are great and are seeds,
they are called "great elements" (mahābhūta).
This is because they are able to maintain their own intrinsic nature.
They are called "elements" (*dhātu*).
The phrase "earth, water, fire, and wind" enumerates their number;
the phrase "capable of performing the functions of supporting and so forth" clarifies their activity.
Regarding the statement that "earth can perform the function of supporting," the term "etc.
includes water performing the function of cohesion and fire performing the function of maturation.
Wind has the function of growth.
Its essential nature consists of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion;
this identifies its substance.
Earth is solid;
water is moist;
fire is warm.
The wind moves.
This concludes the first section; hereafter begins the second, which clarifies that [the body] is provisionally designated based on the four great elements.
The treatise asks: "What are the distinctions among the elements such as earth?
The verse says:
"Earth refers to color and shape; names for water and fire are likewise established according to worldly convention.
Wind is also thus, being both an element and [a conventional designation].
Commentary: "Earth refers to color and shape" explains the conventional designation of earth.
"Earth" refers to that which has as its essence the visible objects of color and shape;
that is, blue and so forth.
It is established based upon visible color.
The "long," "short," and so forth are established based on shape and form;
these are not substantial earth.
The solid earth-element is firm;
it is apprehended solely by the tactile faculty (kāyendriya) and not seen by the visual faculty (cakṣurindriya).
The designation "earth" is conventionally established upon visible form and shape;
it is subsumed within the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana).
"It is that which is seen by the eye.
Regarding "establishing names according to worldly conceptualization," this explains the basis for establishing provisional designations.
That is to say, when people in the world point out the ground to one another,
they do so by means of its manifest color and shape.
Thus they point it out to one another.
The Buddha, following worldly conventions,
establishes this provisional name.
"The same applies to water and fire" explains the conventional designations of water and fire;
these are merely conventional designations of water and fire.
It takes manifest color and shape as its substance; in this respect,
it is analogous to the conventional earth.
The same applies to "name" (nāman).
As for the phrase "the wind is likewise also an element" (dhātu),
this explains the provisional designation of "wind."
"Wind is itself the element" is the explanation of one master;
there is no such thing as a conventional wind.
Wind is itself the element (*dhātu*).
An element is the essence (*svabhāva*).
Essence is itself motion.
Because the world establishes the name "wind" based on motion,
it posits motion as wind.
This refers to actual wind;
therefore, there is no provisional wind. As for the statement "it is also thus," this is the explanation of one master.
It is admitted that there is a conventional wind,
just as the previously mentioned conventional earth, water,
and fire depend upon manifest color and shape.
The establishment of wind is also like this;
because it relies upon manifest color and shape,
it is said to be likewise.
As it is said in the world regarding the "black wind" or the "whirling wind":
"black" refers to color,
while "whirling" refers to shape.
This is used to manifest form, because it indicates wind. Question: Beginning with the eye faculty and ending with the unmanifest (avijñapti).
"For what reason, World-Honored One,
do you say it is 'form'?
The answer to this discussion has two interpretations.
The first explanation states:
It is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) because it is subject to transformation and decay; "transformation" refers to...
This reveals momentary impermanence.
"Destruction" (bhaṅga) reveals the impermanence of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class).
"Who is able to transform and destroy? is the question.
That is to say, because it is touched by the hand,
it immediately undergoes transformation and decay;
as explained at length, up to...
The contact of mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like— this "transformation and disintegration" (vipariṇāma) is precisely the sense of being "afflicted and ruined.
This answers the preceding question.
The following passage cites scriptural authority; thus, in the *Arthavargīya*, the Venerable Dharmatrāta says:
"Those who seek after various desires constantly give rise to longing."
"If various desires are not fulfilled, one is afflicted and ruined as if struck by an arrow.
This verse was spoken by the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni for King Bahudhānīya.
This king was by nature greedy and desired to gather treasures from the sea;
Māra transformed himself into a minister [to assist him].
He came and informed the king,
"I am able to gather jewels," and thus he made an appointment with the king.
When the appointed day arrived,
the Māra did not come;
the king was filled with grief and distress.
As if an arrow were lodged in his body,
the Buddha spoke this verse for that king.
Now, the intention [of this passage] is to prove that matter (*rūpa*) can be afflicted and destroyed.
Furthermore, the treatise states: "Some say it is called matter because it undergoes transformation and resistance.
This is the explanation of the meaning of matter by the second master. "Transformation" refers to being subject to decay and destruction; "resistance" refers to physical obstruction.
If that were so, atoms should not be designated as "form" (rūpa), because they lack the quality of being subject to transformation and resistance.
This is the second explanation for the objection:
because a single atom is not an accumulation,
it lacks the quality of transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*).
This objection is not valid;
there is not a single atom that exists in isolation,
for it is a collection of many atoms that constitutes [matter].
This answers the objection regarding the definition of "resistance" (rūpaṇa).
There is not a single atom that exists in isolation at a distinct location in the present;
for the bases and objects of the five consciousnesses must necessarily be accumulated.
The basis refers to the five sense faculties, and the objects refer to the five sense fields.

Since the atoms that serve as these bases and objects must necessarily be accumulated, does it not follow that the definition of "matter" (rūpa) as being subject to transformation and resistance is established?
[This applies to] the past and the future as well.
It should not be difficult to call it "form" (rūpa).
A present collection of atoms can indeed be designated as form.
If the atoms of the past and future were dispersed,
they should not be designated as "form" (rūpa). This [designation] would likewise apply to what has been and what is yet to be.
Because it possesses resistance and because it belongs to that same category;
this is the answer, as in the case of fuel for burning.
That which has previously undergone transformation and resistance in the past,
and that which is a dharma destined to arise in the future, shall undergo transformation and resistance.
Therefore it is called "form" (*rūpa*).
As for those of its kind,
this refers to future dharmas that do not arise.
Although this phenomenon of non-arising is not subject to future transformation and obstruction,
it belongs to the category of that which is subject to transformation and obstruction.
It is also called "form" (*rūpa*),
just like firewood. [This addresses] the objection that various non-informative forms (*avijñapti-rūpa*) should not be designated as "form."
The sense faculties and their objects consist of ultimate atoms;
because they possess the quality of resistance, they can be designated as "form.
Non-informative matter (avijñapti), however, does not consist of ultimate atoms.
Because it lacks resistance and obstruction,
it should not be matter (*rūpa*).
Some say it is manifest matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
Because it possesses resistance and obstruction (*sapratigha*),
the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) also receives the designation "form" (*rūpa*) by following that [manifest form].
"Just as when a tree moves, its shadow necessarily moves accordingly"— this is explained as the resolution of the objection regarding the non-informative (*avijñapti*). In total,
there are three masters who provide this explanation.
This is the first [explanation],
according to the masters of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
The shadow arises from the tree.
When a tree moves, its shadow necessarily moves.
Non-informative matter (avijñapti) arises from informative matter (vijñapti); this refers to the categories of informative form and non-informative form.
This explanation is incorrect,
because it lacks resistance and changeability.
Furthermore, at the time when the manifest [action] ceases...
The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) should cease, just as when a tree ceases, its shadow necessarily follows in cessation. [Commentary: This is the explanation.
This is the Master of the Treatise’s refutation of the explanation by the masters of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
You originally [defined matter] as that which is subject to transformation and resistance.
Explaining form (*rūpa*):
Since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) lacks resistance and obstruction,
how can it be established as form?
Therefore, it is said that this explanation is incorrect because [space] lacks the quality of transformation and resistance.
Furthermore, the analogy is refuted as follows:
A shadow arises from a tree;
when the tree perishes, the shadow also perishes.
So too, the unmanifest arises dependent upon the manifest.

The cessation of informative action (vijñapti) and the cessation of non-informative action (avijñapti) are distinct; however, at the time when informative action ceases, non-informative action does not cease.
Since their cessations are not equivalent, [the two are different].
How could form possibly be the same?
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* refutes this, stating:
"The morality that follows the mind (*cittānuvartin*) does not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*)."
"It ought not to be form (*rūpa*).

There is an explanation that because its basis, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), possess the quality of resistance and transformation (*pratigha*), non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) is also called "form. This is the second explanation from the Sarvāstivāda school resolving the difficulty regarding non-informative action.
If that is so, because their supports possess resistance (*sapratigha*), the five [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness, [are likewise resistant].
It should also be called "matter" (rūpa). The commentary explains:
this is the Master of the Treatise refuting the Sarvāstivāda school.
Unmanifest [matter] (avijñapti) depends upon the primary elements (mahābhūta).
It is called "matter" (rūpa) because it conforms to the primary elements (mahābhūta).
The five sense organs are the bases for visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses].
The name-and-form [of the unmanifest] follows the sense-faculties and consciousness;
this objection is not equivalent,
for the unmanifest depends upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
At the time of transformation,
it is like a shadow depending on a tree or light depending on a jewel;
the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, do not depend on their respective faculties, such as the eye, in that same manner.
"Because it can only act as a contributory condition for its arising"—
this is the explanation offered by the ancient masters of our own school (svayūthya) to defend their position.

Their argument is that the Proponent (vādin) has challenged the existence of non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) by questioning how it could rely upon the five sense organs (pañcendriya) as its support.
This objection is not consistent.
It is said that the unmanifest (avijñapti) depends upon the primary elements (mahābhūta), which are its direct cause.
Just as a shadow relies upon a tree with the tree as its direct cause, and light relies upon a jewel with the jewel as its direct cause,
it is precisely due to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Looking toward non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa),
it possesses the five causes, such as arising and so forth; therefore,
it is called the "direct basis" (pratyaya).
Because it is closely dependent upon them,
the primary elements (mahābhūta) are called "matter" (rūpa),
and the unmanifest (avijñapti) is also called "matter."
Furthermore,
the five faculties, such as the eye, act as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to assist in the arising of the five consciousnesses.
However, because these are only remote bases and not direct bases,
visual consciousness and the others are not designated as "form" (rūpa) based on the five sense organs.
The statement that "this shadow depends on the tree" and "the light depends on the jewel" does not,
for the time being, accord with the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding that school’s position,
it is explained that the atoms of manifest color,
such as shadows and so forth, each individually rely upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
This is the author of the treatise refuting the interpretation of the ancient masters,
stating that their view incurs the fault of contradicting their own tenets.
In your school, it is held that both the shadow and the light each have their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their direct support.
Now, you say that the shadow relies on the tree and the light relies on the jewel;
is this not a violation of your own tenets?
Even if one grants that shadows and light depend upon trees and jewels, the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) does not depend on them in the same way;
for it is maintained that although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its basis may perish, the unmanifest form does not perish along with them. Thus it is explained.
This passage is the Master of the Treatise’s concessive refutation of the ancient masters;
thus he says, "Even if it were granted.
If the tree-jewel perishes, its shadow and light must necessarily perish.
If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) cease, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) does not cease;
therefore, it is said that unmanifest form is not identical to its basis.
Since the bases are not identical, the analogy is invalid.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation regarding that objection:
the five [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness and so forth.
The basis is indeterminate;
some possess resistance,
namely the five faculties beginning with the eye.
Alternatively, there may be that which lacks resistance;
namely, the support for the unmanifest (avijñapti) which is the uninterrupted mind.
It is not so [in the case of the former].
Therefore, the previous objection is certainly inconsistent.
The principle that "matter" (rūpa) is defined by transformation and resistance is thus established. This is the explanation.
This is the third [point],
the correct explanation provided by the Master of the Treatise:
that non-informative matter (avijñapti) depends upon the primary elements (mahābhūta).
However, it is the support for transformation and resistance (*vipariṇāma-vighāta*). Unlike the five consciousnesses, which have two types of supports,
the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) receives the designation "matter" (*rūpa*) because its support consists of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The above has correctly explained the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
From this point, the second major section correctly establishes the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The verse says:
Herein, the faculties and their objects are asserted to be the ten bases and elements.
The commentary says: Within this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The five faculties and the five objects are established as ten bases within the classification of the doors of bases.
Within the classification of the *dhātus*,
these are established as ten *dhātus*.
Thus, the two preceding sections differ from one another.
This concludes the explanation of the aggregate of form.
Next, the second [section] clarifies the three aggregates beginning with feeling.
The verse says:
Feeling has the nature of experiencing; perception has the nature of grasping images;
the four remaining [aggregates] are called the aggregate of formations. Thus are the three beginning with feeling.
"Non-informative [matter] and the unconditioned are called the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the constituent of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The commentary states: "Feeling is the reception that accords with contact.
This explains the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha).
Feeling (vedanā) is so named because it is able to experience that which accords with its cause, contact (sparśa).
This refers to the phrase "in accordance with contact."
To clarify the meaning of "cause," the cause is contact itself,
because it is capable of producing sensation.
Contact is conducive to feeling;
therefore, it is called "conforming.
Feeling is able to experience that which conforms to the cause of contact.
It is called "experience" because it conforms to contact. Question: Why is it that feeling (*vedanā*) is able to experience contact?
Answer: Feeling arises from contact;
it acts in accordance with contact.
Feeling is said to experience because it resembles the aspect of contact;
it is like the worldly expression that "the son experiences [the legacy of] his father."
The charm and excellence of the son are all like those of the father;
therefore, it is named "Neck" (*ling*). The remaining mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are as follows:
That which perceives only the objective field but cannot perceive contact is called "reception of the objective field" (viṣayavedanā).
It experiences only one [object];
because it is uniquely capable of experiencing contact, it is called "reception by its own nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*). Another interpretation states:
This term "conformable-to-contact" (*sparśānvaya*) is used to indicate the preceding object;
because it conforms to the object of contact,
it is called "feeling conformable to contact" (*sparśānvayā vedanā*), which is capable of experiencing other mental factors.
Although they both perceive objects,
only feeling is predominant because its intrinsic nature is that of feeling.
One alone receives the name [of being an outcast].
It is like ten people sitting together in one place,
where one person is a thief.
Suddenly, a person nearby cried out,
calling for help and shouting "Thieves!
Although all ten people heard the sound of the thief, they [did not respond].
Those that are truly thieves lead to partiality and strength;
such is the nature of the mind and mental factors.
Although they share the same objective domain,
it is actually the experiencer who perceives;
moreover, this perception is particularly predominant.
Therefore, it alone is named "feeling" (vedanā).
This has three types:
namely, suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Perception (saṃjñā) takes the grasping of images as its essence.
To clarify the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): perception is able to grasp the images of suffering and pleasure, enemy and friend, male and female, and so forth;
therefore, it is called the aggregate of perception. Fourth, the remainder are named the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
This clarifies the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The four [aggregates] refer to form, sensation, perception, and consciousness.
Apart from these four aggregates, all other mental factors (*caitta*) are included within the aggregate of formations.
There are forty-four [mental factors] and fourteen dissociated [factors].
These constitute fifty-eight dharmas.

These four aggregates and the remainder are collectively termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). It is called "formations" based on two meanings: volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*) and flux (*prasyanda*).
According to this perspective,
the five aggregates, including form and the others,
are collectively designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*), because the category of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) subsumes a vast number of phenomena.

They are designated by the name "formative action" (*saṃskāra*) because they are preeminent in that regard. Likewise, the three beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), as well as the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are designated as the "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) and the "element of phenomena" (*dharmadhātu*). This is established according to the system of bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The three factors, sensation and so forth, include perception and mental formations;
thus they are called "three.
Together with the unmanifest, they constitute four.
Together with the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena, these constitute seven. These seven dharmas,
among the twelve bases (āyatana), [are included as follows].
It is called the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), it is called the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
From this point onward:
Third, the elucidation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
This section contains two parts:
first, the elucidation of the aggregate of consciousness itself.
Second, resolving objections.
First, regarding the explanation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*),
the verse says:

"Consciousness (vijñāna) refers to the individual discernment [of objects]. This should be understood as the sense-sphere of mind (manāyatana) and the seven elements (dhātus). The six consciousnesses, when they have passed away, become the mind. Commentary: Regarding "consciousness refers to the individual discernment": this means that each [consciousness] individually discerns its respective object. The term *vijñāna* is derived from the prefix *vi-* meaning "individual," the root *jñā* meaning "to know," and the suffix *-ana* indicating the agent. Thus, it signifies that which performs the act of discerning. It is called "consciousness" because it discerns by way of distinguishing the specific characteristics of each object. Furthermore, the six consciousnesses—visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental—arise in succession; once they have ceased, they constitute the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the seven elements (*dhātus*). Therefore, it is said that the six consciousnesses, having transformed, become the mind. This establishes that the mind is not a separate entity from the six consciousnesses, but rather their state immediately following their cessation. Thus, the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are comprised within these six consciousnesses and the single element of mind. This concludes the explanation of the aggregate of consciousness. As for the remaining aggregates, they will be explained later. The first aggregate has been fully explained. The second aggregate, form (*rūpa*), is now to be discussed. What is form? It is the four great elements and the form derived from them. What are the four great elements? They are earth, water, fire, and air. What is the earth element? It is solidity. What is the water element? It is cohesion. What is the fire element? It is heat. What is the air element? It is motion. What is form derived from the great elements? It is the five sense-faculties and their five objects. What are the five sense-faculties? They are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. What is the faculty of the eye? It is pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness. What is the faculty of the ear? It is pure matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness. What is the faculty of the nose? It is pure matter that serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness. What is the faculty of the tongue? It is pure matter that serves as the basis for gustatory consciousness. What is the faculty of the body? It is pure matter that serves as the basis for tactile consciousness. What are the five objects? They are visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. What are visible forms? They are color and shape. What are colors? They are blue, yellow, red, white, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, sunlight, brightness, darkness, and space. What are shapes? They are long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, fine, coarse, distant, and near. What are sounds? They are those produced by sentient beings and those not produced by sentient beings. What are sounds produced by sentient beings? They are vocal sounds. What are vocal sounds? They are sounds arising from the four great elements that serve as the basis for vocal expression. What are sounds not produced by sentient beings? They are sounds other than vocal sounds. What are sounds other than vocal sounds? They are sounds arising from the four great elements that do not serve as the basis for vocal expression. What are odors? They are pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. What are pleasant odors? They are those that are agreeable to the nose. What are unpleasant odors? They are those that are disagreeable to the nose. What are neutral odors? They are those that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable to the nose. What are tastes? They are sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. What are tangibles? They are the tangible objects derived from the four great elements, such as smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst. What is smoothness? It is the quality of being soft. What is roughness? It is the quality of being hard. What is heaviness? It is the quality of being difficult to lift. What is lightness? It is the quality of being easy to lift. What is cold? It is that which causes one to desire warmth. What is hunger? It is that which causes one to desire food. What is thirst? It is that which causes one to desire drink. These are the various categories of form. What is the aggregate of feeling? It is the experience of sensation. What is the aggregate of perception? It is the grasping of signs. What is the aggregate of formations? It is the conditioning of volition. What is the aggregate of consciousness? It is the individual discernment of objects. What is the sense-sphere of the eye? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the visible form? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of color and shape that serves as the object of visual consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the ear? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of sound? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of sound that serves as the object of auditory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the nose? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of odor? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of odor that serves as the object of olfactory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the tongue? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for gustatory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of taste? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of taste that serves as the object of gustatory consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the body? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for tactile consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the tangible? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of the tangible that serves as the object of tactile consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the mind? It is the internal sense-sphere consisting of the six consciousnesses and the mind-element that serves as the basis for mental consciousness. What is the sense-sphere of the mental object? It is the external sense-sphere consisting of all phenomena that serve as the object of mental consciousness. What is the element of the eye? It is the internal element consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness. What is the element of visible form?
