It is the external element consisting of color and shape that serves as the object of visual consciousness. What is the element of the ear? It is the internal element consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for auditory consciousness. What is the element of sound? It is the external element consisting of sound that serves as the object of auditory consciousness. What is the element of the nose? It is the internal element consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness. What is the element of odor? It is the external element consisting of odor that serves as the object of olfactory consciousness. What is the element of the tongue? It is the internal element consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for gustatory consciousness. What is the element of taste? It is the external element consisting of taste that serves as the object of gustatory consciousness. What is the element of the body? It is the internal element consisting of pure matter that serves as the basis for tactile consciousness. What is the element of the tangible? It is the external element consisting of the tangible that serves as the object of tactile consciousness. What is the element of the mind? It is the internal element consisting of the six consciousnesses and the mind-element that serves as the basis for mental consciousness. What is the element of the mental object? It is the external element consisting of all phenomena that serve as the object of mental consciousness. What is the element of visual consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the eye and visible forms. What is the element of auditory consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the ear and sounds. What is the element of olfactory consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the nose and odors. What is the element of gustatory consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the tongue and tastes. What is the element of tactile consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the body and tangibles. What is the element of mental consciousness? It is the consciousness that arises based on the mind and mental objects. What is the element of the eye? It is the internal element consisting of the past, future, and present visual faculty. What is the element of visible form? It is the external element consisting of past, future, and present visible forms. What is the element of the ear? It is the internal element consisting of the past, future, and present auditory faculty. What is the element of sound? It is the external element consisting of past, future, and present sounds. What is the element of the nose? It is the internal element consisting of the past, future, and present olfactory faculty. What is the element of odor? It is the external element consisting of past, future, and present odors. What is the element of the tongue? It is the internal element consisting of the past,
This clarifies the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
That which discerns is called consciousness;
this consists of six types.
Because their discernment is distinct,
they are called "separate. This means that,
first of all, visual consciousness discerns visible forms.
"Up to the mental consciousness cognizing phenomena— this is what is called the sense-base of mind and the seven elements. Thus,
in establishing the system of bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), this aggregate of consciousness is included within the twelve bases.
This is precisely what is called the sense base of mind (manāyatana).
Within the framework of the eighteen elements (dhātus),
it is called the seven mental elements (cittadhātu).
Beyond the six consciousnesses,
the mind-element (manodhātu) is added,
making seven mind-elements. It should be understood that the six consciousnesses transform into the mind-element.

It should be understood that when the six consciousnesses have ceased and passed away, they are able to give rise to subsequent consciousnesses; this is what is meant by the existence of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
As the basis for these, it is called the mind-element (manodhātu);
thus one should know the six consciousnesses.
Abiding in the present world, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*);
in the past, it is called mind (*manas*).
Next, the following explains away potential objections.
Within this, there are two [objections]:
first, the objection regarding the separate establishment of the *dharmadhātu*;
second, the objection that the twenty-eight *dhātus* would not be established.
Furthermore, regarding the first point,
which raises an objection concerning the distinct establishment of the *dharmadhātu*,
the treatise states:
If that is so, the six consciousnesses are themselves the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
What else could be said besides this?
Furthermore, it constitutes the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
The verse says:
"By means of the six groups of consciousness themselves, that which has just ceased is the mind."
The commentary states: "Body" (kāya) refers to the aggregate (rāśi).
These six groups of consciousness first pass away into the past.
It is called "immediately preceding extinction" because there is no interval between them.
That is to say, these six consciousnesses,
having ceased without interval,
serve as the support for subsequent consciousnesses.
That which is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is so named because "mind" (*manas*) has the sense of being a basis;
past consciousness is designated as "mind."
Because it serves as the support for the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), this second point—
that the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are not undermined—
arises as a challenge to the preceding question.
The treatise says:
"If that were so, the actual elements (dhātus) would be only twelve."
Alternatively, there should be seventeen [elements],
because the six consciousnesses and the mind are mutually inclusive.
For what reason, then, can eighteen elements be established?
The verse says:
Because it establishes the basis for the sixth [consciousness], one should know that there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The commentary explains: "Because it establishes the basis for the sixth" means:
This establishes the basis for the realm of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth,
each have their own distinct support (*āśraya*).
This refers to the five faculties, such as the eye, and the sixth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since these have no distinct physical bases,
the sphere of mind (*manodhātu*) is established in order to provide a basis for them.
Regarding "the eighteen elements should be known":
this establishes the eighteen elements. Having already established the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), [the others follow].
Because each of these six consciousnesses has its respective basis,
they constitute the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
This is because there are six bases, six supporting [consciousnesses], and six objects.
This constitutes the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).
As for the six bases, they refer to the six faculties, namely the eye and so forth.
The six that can serve as supports refer to the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth.
The six objects of these refer to—
This refers to the six objects, beginning with form.
Following this, the second section clarifies the comprehensive inclusion.
The verse says:

All phenomena are subsumed in total; they are comprised by one aggregate, one sense-field, and one element through their own intrinsic nature and not otherwise, because they are devoid of the nature of others.
The commentary states:
"The summary inclusion of all phenomena by means of one aggregate, base, and element" correctly clarifies the manner of their mutual inclusion.
All phenomena are subsumed by means of a single aggregate of form and a single sense base of mind.
It is due to the single dharma-realm. Why is this so?
Briefly stated, all phenomena do not exceed five categories.
First, matter;
second, mind;
third, mental factors.
The four mental non-concomitants,
the five unconditioned phenomena,
and all material phenomena.
All mental factors are entirely subsumed within the aggregate of form;
all [mental phenomena] are entirely subsumed within the single sense base of mind.
All mental factors (*caitta*), as well as the dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*),
together with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
are entirely subsumed within a single dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*); therefore, these three are mentioned.
"Comprehensively encompassing all phenomena; it encompasses their own intrinsic nature and nothing else, because they are devoid of other-natures," this clarifies the limits of the inclusion.
As for the term "encompassment" mentioned previously:
It encompasses only its own nature and does not encompass the nature of others; therefore,
it is said to be "not other."
Because a phenomenon and its other-nature are always mutually exclusive,
they do not encompass one another.
Regarding inclusion by way of intrinsic nature:
matter includes only matter,
and mind includes only mind.
For example, the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*),
and the truths of suffering and its origin are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) because they share the same nature as form; however,
the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) and the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*) are not so subsumed.
And [it includes] the Truth of Cessation and so forth,
because they are not of the nature of form (*rūpa*).
From this, the third major section [begins].
Explaining the enumeration and its combinations.
This section contains two parts:
first, explaining the combination of the enumeration.
Second, the explanation of the enumeration of openings.
First, regarding the first [point],
the explanation of the enumeration of combinations.
The treatise states:
"The three locations of the eyes, ears,
and nose each have two [openings]."
For what reason is the nature of the elements not twenty-one?
The verse says:
"Because the category, the object, and the consciousness are identical; although there are two, the substance of the realm is one.
The commentary explains:
"Identical in category" means they share the same intrinsic nature as the eye. "Identical in object" means...
Because they both take visible form as their object,
the consciousnesses are the same. Because they both serve as the support for visual consciousness, the supports are the same.
For this reason, although there are two [eyes], they are established as one;
the ears and nose should also be distinguished in this same way.
Next, the second [section],
which clarifies the opening of the enumeration,
the treatise states:
If that is so, for what reason does birth depend upon two bases?
The verse says:
"However, for the sake of beauty, each [sense organ] arises as two.
Regarding the phrase "however, for the sake of beauty," the treatise provides two interpretations.
First is the interpretation of the first master.
Because the physical body that serves as its basis is majestic and handsome,
although the essential nature of the realm is one,
it arises in two locations.
If the sense organs of the eye and ear were each located in only one place, and the nose had no two nostrils; [then there would be no such thing as distinctness].
"The body is not majestic.
This interpretation is incorrect.
The Master of the Treatise refutes it, saying:
If it were so from the beginning,
who would say it was ugly?
Furthermore, this applies to cats, owls, and the like.
What is its dignified excellence? The second correct explanation is that it serves as the basis for the arising of consciousness, which is clear and dignified,
as is observed in the world.
When one eye is closed and so forth,
the discernment of forms and other objects becomes indistinct.
Therefore, each of the three faculties gives rise to two locations.
From this major section:
Second, the detailed explanation of the meanings of the names.
This consists of six parts.
First, the explanation of the names of the three dharmas.
Second, the causes for the arising of the teaching;
third, the establishment and abolition of the aggregates;
fourth, the sequence of the names.
Fifth, the establishment and refutation; sixth, the subsumption of alternative names. First, regarding the explanation of the names of the three dharmas, the treatise states:
"It has already been explained that the aggregates (skandhas) are subsumed within the bases (āyatanas) and elements (dhātus)."
I shall now explain its meaning.
What is the specific significance of these aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)?
The verse says:
"Aggregation, gateway for arising, and lineage—these are the meanings of the aggregates, bases, and elements.
The commentary states: the first phrase explains the meaning.
The next phrase provides the conclusion.
"Aggregation" (rāśi) means accumulation;
it is synonymous with "aggregate" (skandha).
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Whatever form there may be,
whether past..."
Whether future, whether present,
or internal.
Whether external,
whether coarse,
or whether subtle.
Whether inferior, superior,
or proximate.
If they are distant,
all such things are briefly condensed into a single aggregate and designated as the "aggregate of form" (rūpaskandha). This is the intended meaning of this sutra.
The meaning is presented through five gates. First is the gate of the three periods of time:
that which has already ceased due to impermanence is called the past;
that which has not yet arisen is called the future.
That which has already arisen but not yet ceased is called "present. This is the second section on the internal and external doors.
One's own body is called "internal";
all other bodies and non-sentient things are called "external."

Alternatively, according to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five faculties such as the eye are distinguished as "internal form" and so forth, while the five objects are distinguished as "external. Third, regarding the gate of the coarse and the subtle:
form is of three kinds.
First, that which is visible and resistant,
namely the objective sphere of form (*rūpa*).
Second, that which is invisible and resistant.
That is to say, the five faculties beginning with the eye,
as well as sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
Three of these are invisible and non-resistant.
This refers to non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
Among these three types of matter,
that which possesses resistance (sapratigha) is called coarse.
That which is non-obstructive is called subtle;
alternatively, it is established through mutual dependence,
as in the case of invisible obstructive matter.
That which is visible and resistant is called "subtle" in comparison to that which is invisible and non-resistant.
The fourth is the gate of inferiority and superiority regarding coarseness:
that which is defiled is called "inferior," and that which is non-defiled is called "superior. Among the eleven types of form, [this distinction applies].
The five faculties beginning with the eye,
as well as the eight [objects] of odor, taste, and touch,
are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
The two types, visible form and sound,
pertain to all three moral natures;
non-informative matter pertains only to the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*),
the wholesome and the indeterminate are termed "non-defiled," while the unwholesome is termed "defiled. Fifth is the gate of remoteness and proximity.
The past and future are called "distant," while the present is called "near.
Just as these five categories exist within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), so too do they apply to the other aggregates.
Up to the aggregate of consciousness, there are likewise five doors;
it should be understood that the same applies,
with the sole exception of the single door of coarse and subtle.
It is distinct from the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
namely the four aggregates associated with the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and so forth.
Based on the five sense faculties, it is called coarse;
[it refers to] the four aggregates associated with the sixth consciousness.
It is only in relation to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that it is called subtle; alternatively, it may be distinguished according to the stages (*bhūmi*),
namely within the nine stages.
The lower stages are called coarse;
the upper stages are called subtle. "Gate of arising" (jātimukha) means the sense of a place.
That is to say, the six sense faculties and the six objects are the gateways and locations for the arising and growth of the mind and mental factors.
Because the arising of the six consciousnesses necessarily depends upon the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) in order to be produced, the treatise states:
"This has the meaning of being able to produce and grow that activity. This is according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
The essence of the dharma exists prior [to its manifestation];
it cannot be said to be produced, for it merely brings forth its function. As for what is called "lineage" (gotra):
This is the meaning of *dhātu*.
There are two explanations in the treatise.
First, regarding the interpretation of "lineage" (*gotra*):
This refers to the "lineage" (*gotra*);
it carries the sense of being the basis for birth.
It refers to the eighteen constituents (*dhātus*).
They act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because each produces its own corresponding outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*); they are the fundamental source for the arising of these phenomena.
Just as a single mountain containing many families of copper, iron, gold, silver,
and so forth is called a "multiverse" (bahudhātu),
so too is this single body.
Alternatively, within a single continuum, there are eighteen categories of dharma-lineages,
which are called the eighteen *dhātus*. To explain:
The "families" such as gold and silver refer to the ores of gold, silver, and so forth.
As for the term "a single body":
A single sentient being's body;
a single continuum; a single continuum of phenomena.
This single body and single continuum correspond to the previous analogy of being "within a single mountain.
Question: If that is so, what of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
They should not be called "elements" (*dhātu*),
namely the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*),
because they are not homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*).
Because it does not constitute the basis for arising.
Answer: It is because the mind and mental factors are the basis for arising. That is to say, the mind and mental factors arise taking unconditioned phenomena as their object.
Although it does not function as a cause, it can serve as an object,
for it is the basis from which the mind and mental factors arise. Some say that the term "dhātu" (element) expresses the meaning of "category."
This refers to eighteen phenomena,
whose categories and intrinsic natures are each distinct and different.
These are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
According to this master’s interpretation,
"family" (*gotra*) refers to a genus or class.
This refers to the eighteen dharmas,
each being distinct from the others,
just as the surnames Cui, Lu, and so forth are distinct.
Each [school] differs.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
all three categories (triskandha) are substantially real.
According to the Sautrāntika school, the aggregates (skandhas) and bases (āyatanas) are conventional designations,
while only the elements (dhātus) are real.
According to the Master of the Treatise,
only the aggregates (skandhas) are conventional (prajñapti),
while the other two are both real (dravya).
Second, this clarifies the causes for the arising of the teaching.
The treatise states:
For what reason, O Blessed One,
[do you teach] regarding the objects of knowledge by way of the aggregates and so forth?
They are taught as threefold.
The verse says:
Because of the three [types of] delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught as three.
The commentary states:
Because the sentient beings to be converted are of three categories.
The Blessed One taught the three gateways of the aggregates and so forth for those who are deluded;
there are three types of delusion,
or one may be deluded regarding mental factors.
Because they collectively grasp [the aggregates] as a self,
the five aggregates are taught for them; for it is within these five aggregates that [this grasping occurs].
One aggregate is matter;
one aggregate is mind; and the mental factors are divided [into a separate category].
Because there are the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations,
the five aggregates are taught;
this serves to refute that attachment, or [the view] that one is merely deluded about form.
Because they collectively grasp [these] as a self,
the twelve bases (āyatana) are taught;
for within these twelve bases, [the self is not to be found].
Ten bases are material;
only the mind-base and the dharma-base are non-material.
Therefore, the gateway of the bases (āyatana-mukha) is taught to refute that attachment; for some, being deluded regarding form and mind,
grasp them collectively as a self.
For their sake, he taught the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). By means of these eighteen elements, he extensively explained matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*):
ten elements are matter, and the remaining eight are mind.
Therefore, the gateway of the elements (*dhātu*) is taught in order to refute that attachment. "The faculties (*indriya*) are also threefold" refers to superior,
middling, and inferior faculties.
Those of superior faculties are sharp and discerning;
they understand through a brief explanation.
For their sake, the five aggregates are expounded.
Those of medium capacity understand somewhat later,
gaining comprehension only when the teaching is fully explained.
Those of inferior capacity are the most dull-witted.
It must be explained extensively;
therefore, the realms are discussed. Furthermore, there are three types of pleasure:
for the sake of providing brief, intermediate, and extensive expositions of the text.
These three— the aggregates and so forth— are taught in their respective order.
From this, the third [section follows].
This section clarifies the establishment and rejection of the aggregates (*skandha*). Within it, there are two parts:
first, the actual clarification of the establishment and rejection of the aggregates.
Second, explaining that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*).
First, regarding the formal explanation of what is excluded and what is established,
the treatise says:
For what reason did the Blessed One state that all other mental factors are collectively placed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha),
while feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) are treated separately?
Regarding the two aggregates of mental factors (*caitta*),
there are forty-six, excluding only feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
The remaining forty-four bases are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
As for the remaining mental factors, the verse says:
"Because they are the root of contention, the cause of birth and death, and the cause of sequential order."
Regarding the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are separately established as aggregates (*skandha*).
Commentary: The first two lines explicitly set forth the three reasons [for this distinction].
The final two phrases conclude the separate aggregates.
Regarding the "three causes," the first is the cause of the roots of dispute.
There are two such roots of dispute.
That is to say: attachment to various desires and attachment to various views;
these two constitute feeling and perception.
Respectively, they serve as the most excellent causes:
by the power of the taste and the force [of craving], one becomes greedily attached to various sensual desires.
"By the power of inverted perception,
they become greedily attached to various views.
Explanation:
"All desires" refers to the five types of exquisite sensory objects.
"All views" refers to the five [wrong views], beginning with the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The essence of all desire-greed and all views is affliction (*kleśa*).
The afflictions are called "contention," and contention itself is called the "root.
The two dharmas of sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) serve as the causes for this root of contention.
The cause of the root of contention is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Second, regarding the cause of birth and death:
it arises because one gives rise to perverted perceptions due to attachment to sensation (*vedanā*).
Because of the cycle of birth and death,
feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) serve as the causes of birth and death;
they are the causes of saṃsāra.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Third, as for the explanation of the sequential causes, they shall be analyzed immediately following this;
by means of the three aforementioned causes, [the relationship] regarding the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) [is established].
One should know that feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately as aggregates (*skandha*).
Following this, the second point clarifies why the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not an aggregate.
The treatise asks: "For what reason are the unconditioned phenomena said to be included within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), but not subsumed under the aggregates?"
The verse says:
The aggregates do not include the unconditioned, because their meanings are incompatible.
The commentary says: The first phrase is the formal thesis.
The subsequent verse provides an explanation, yet its meaning is inconsistent.
There are three interpretations in the treatise; the first interpretation states:
The three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) do not correspond to the meaning of form (rūpa) and so forth;
that is to say, their essence is not form.
Up to and including: it is not consciousness; its unconditioned essence is not form, as it is incompatible with the meaning of form, up to and including:
its essence is not consciousness.
Because its meaning is not compatible with that of consciousness, it is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*). Question:
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not one of the five aggregates, [how is it categorized?]
"Why is it not established as a sixth aggregate?
Answer: "It also cannot be described as a sixth aggregate, because it does not correspond to the meaning of 'aggregate'."
The meaning of "accumulation" (rāśi) is "aggregate" (skandha);

since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) do not possess the meaning of accumulation, they are inconsistent with that definition and cannot be established as aggregates. A second interpretation states:
Furthermore, the mention of the "aggregates of clinging" (upādānaskandha) is intended to reveal the basis for defilement and the dual basis for both defilement and purification.
The term "aggregate" (skandha) is used to signify these two meanings; since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) lack both of these meanings entirely,
they are not established as aggregates because they do not correspond to the definition.
The appropriated aggregates (upādānaskandha) are with outflows (sāsrava);
thus, they manifest the basis of defilement.
The five aggregates without outflows (anāsrava) [are otherwise].
This is precisely the pure basis (*śuddhāśraya*).
Therefore, by speaking merely of the aggregates (*skandha*), both the defiled and the pure are encompassed. The third interpretation states:
Some say that just as when a jar is broken it is no longer a jar,
so too when the aggregates cease, they should no longer be aggregates. To this,
the explanation is given:
That is to say, when a jar is broken, it is no longer a jar;
it is not subsumed under the category of "jar.
The cessation of the aggregates is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not included within the aggregates (skandha);
this is the third explanation.
The Master of the Treatise refutes it, saying:
In that case, it would follow by analogy that there is an error regarding the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).
The explanation says:
The meaning here is this:
the cessation of the aggregates is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
and that which is unconditioned is not included within the aggregates.
The spheres and bases that are cessation are unconditioned;
however, there may also be that which is unconditioned yet is not a sphere or base.
Therefore, the spheres and bases are cited as the illustrative example.
That third [section] establishes the faults [of the opponent's position].
From this fourth [section],
the sequence of the names is clarified.
This is divided into two parts:
first, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*);
second, the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Regarding the first, the sequence of the aggregates:
The treatise says: "Thus it is.
Having already explained the establishment and exclusion of the aggregates, the sequence shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"According to coarseness, defilement, vessel, contents, and the distinctions of the realms, they are established in this order.
The commentary says: These two lines contain four meanings in total.
First, the sequence according to coarseness;
second, the sequence according to defilement;
third, the sequence according to the analogy of vessels and so forth.
Regarding the sequence according to the distinctions of the realms:
first, following the order of coarseness, because it possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), form (*rūpa*) is the coarsest among the aggregates; that is to say, among the five aggregates.
The aggregate of form possesses resistance,
whereas the other four are without resistance;
therefore, form is the coarsest.
First, form (rūpa) is discussed.
Among the formless [aggregates], sensation (vedanā) alone possesses a coarse aspect of activity.
Therefore, when worldly convention speaks of the pain in one's hand and so forth as being "formless," it refers to the four aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*);
among these, it is specifically the aspect of sensation that is most prominent.
How is this known? Therefore, an analogy is cited, namely "the hand" and so forth.
To say "pain" refers specifically to the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*).
It does not mention the perception of hands and so forth;
it clearly shows that feeling arises dependent upon perception.
Therefore, feeling is mentioned first, as it depends on the two types of perception, which are coarse.
The perceptions of male and female are easily understood. The commentary explains that "in relation to" means "in contrast to.
The second refers to the two aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding these two,
because they are coarse,
it is said that the perception dependent on them is coarse.
Next, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is explained. The formations (saṃskāra) are coarser than consciousness because formations such as greed and hatred are easy to discern;
these [formations] include greed, hatred, and so forth.
Since these are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) and are easy to understand,
it is clear that they are known as the aggregate of formations.
The aggregate of consciousness is coarser than the other aggregates; consciousness is the most subtle,
as it grasps the general characteristics of objects.
"Because it is difficult to differentiate.
The commentary explains:
"The object has two aspects."
First is the general characteristic,
which refers to form, sound, and so forth.
Second is the specific characteristic.

That is to say, while the mental factors (caitta) apprehend specific distinctions— such as the disagreeable or agreeable— the consciousness (vijñāna) apprehends the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
Therefore, it is difficult to distinguish and is the most subtle. Second, regarding the sequence of following defilement:
it may be from beginningless time.
Since the beginning of birth and death,
men and women have mutually cherished and delighted in form.
This is because one is attached to the savor of pleasant feeling;
furthermore, attachment to feeling arises from inverted perception,
and this inverted perception arises [from ignorance].
Because karma and afflictions are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), these afflictions arise based upon consciousness; thus,
one is defiled in accordance with them.
Regarding the third sequence, that of the "vessel and so forth" (*bhājanādi-krama*):
the phrase "vessel and so forth" includes,
by way of the term "and so forth," food, drink, condiments, cooks, and those who eat.
Now, when one wishes to invite guests,
one first seeks out eating vessels;
once those vessels have been obtained, [one proceeds].
Next, he sought rice and flour to serve as food and drink.
Once the rice and flour were prepared, [he proceeded].
Next, he sought salt and vinegar to serve as flavoring agents and entrusted them to the kitchen staff.
He ordered them to prepare the mixture.
Once the food and drink were ready,
they were served to the guests.
It causes one to eat.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is like a vessel;
it is like a vessel in the world.
Just as food and drink are the basis for sustenance, so too is form;
for it is the basis for feeling.
Feelings are like food and drink in the world;
they are either harmful or beneficial.
Feeling is also like this:
pleasant feeling benefits the person,
while painful feeling harms them.
Perception is like an auxiliary flavor;
it is like salt or vinegar in the world,
which assists in producing the flavor of food.
Perception is also like this:
when one gives rise to thoughts of enmity,
one experiences the flavor of painful sensation.
When one conceives the thought of endearment,
one experiences the savoring of pleasant feelings;
such conduct is like that of a cook.
Because within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) there are karma and afflictions capable of producing maturation (vipāka),
just as a worldly cook prepares food and drink.
Consciousness is likened to the eater because it experiences the retribution of the fruit;
thus, the sequence of the aggregates is established according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth. Fourth, regarding the sequence according to the distinction of the realms:
Within the desire realm,
there are various exquisite sensual objects whose forms and characteristics are clearly manifest.
First, the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is explained. Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
there are superior forms of joy and so forth,
by which the characteristics of feeling (vedanā) are clearly manifested.
Next, the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is explained. Among the three formless [aggregates],
perception (saṃjñā) is the clear manifestation of the apprehension of the characteristics of space and so forth.
Next, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is explained: within the realm of existence (bhava),
volition (cetanā) is preeminent,
as its mode of activity (ākāra) is clearly manifest.
The commentary states:
"Within the Realm of Existence (bhavāgra), it refers to the Stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)."
That is to say, volition is karma;
it is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha),
because it is not [mere] perception (saṃjñā).
It is capable of producing the fruit of eighty thousand kalpas in the Peak of Existence;
thus, its volition is most excellent and its mode of activity is clearly manifest.
Next, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is explained.
Since consciousness (vijñāna) dwells within these preceding four aggregates, consciousness is explained last.
That is to say: consciousness abides within form;
consciousness abides within feeling;
consciousness abides within perception.
Within the state of consciousness abiding and proceeding,
four are that which is dwelt upon,
and consciousness is that which dwells.
Therefore, consciousness is explained last,
following the sequence of a field and its seed as found in the world.
First the field, then the seed.
The field is a metaphor for the four aggregates;
consciousness is a metaphor for the seed.
Because the order of the aggregates is established based on these four preceding meanings,
these five aggregates [are arranged as follows].
There is no fault of increase or decrease.
Furthermore, the treatise says:
"Precisely because it is thus."
For various reasons of sequential order,
feeling and perception are established as two separate aggregates apart from formations;
that is to say, feeling and perception.
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
their characteristics (*nimitta*) are coarse and give rise to defilement;
they share the same category as food and provide mutual assistance.
Because it is predominant within two realms,
it is established as a separate aggregate; the reasons for its position at the beginning of the sequence will be explained immediately hereafter.
This is that very text. Regarding "the characteristics of the aggregates":
it refers to the gates of sensation and perception.
The "arising of defilement" refers to the gateway through which feeling and perception give rise to defilement;
the "nutriment of similar kind" is feeling.
This "concomitant assistance" is perception (*saṃjñā*).
This constitutes the gateways of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.
Among the two elements, it is the stronger one.
Feeling is predominant in the realm of form;
perception is predominant in the formless realm.
This is the gateway to the sequential order of the realms of feeling and perception.
Therefore, the sequential cause encompasses these four gates.
Next, the second [section] clarifies the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
The treatise states:
Within the sections on the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*),
one should first explain the sequential order of the six sense faculties (*indriya*).
From this, the sequence of objects and consciousnesses can be understood.
The verse says:
The objects of the first five [consciousnesses] are only present; The objects of four [of these] are only derived matter.
The remaining functions are distant, rapid, and clear; or they follow the sequence of their respective locations.
Regarding the first three phrases, the commentary explains that the sequence is clarified in terms of the objects.
The fourth phrase clarifies the sequence according to their locations.
Regarding the first five objects, they exist only as present.
The objects of the first five faculties refer to the first five among the six faculties, namely,
the eye and so forth.
It apprehends only present objects;
therefore, it is mentioned first.
As for the sixth faculty, the mental organ (manas):
The objects apprehended are not fixed;
there are four types of objects of the mental consciousness:
those of the three time periods and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Among these four, one may at times take one,
or two, three, or all four.
Therefore, it is stated later that "the four objects consist solely of derived matter.
This refers to the first term of the preceding [verse].
When this [term] "flowing" (*srotas*) is applied here,
it should be understood as referring to the objects of the first four [faculties]; that is, among the five faculties.
The objects of the first four faculties are exclusively derived matter; therefore,
they are mentioned first.
The body and its object are not fixed;
therefore, it is mentioned later.
That is to say, the body perceives touch.
There are eleven types of tangibles.
Four are primary elements:
earth, water, fire, and wind.
Seven are derived [matter], such as smoothness,
roughness, and so forth;
they are sometimes associated with the body faculty.
Either it apprehends the primary elements (mahābhūta),
or it apprehends the derived matter (upādāyarūpa), or it apprehends both.
Therefore, it is not fixed.
As for the other functions being explained as far-reaching and swift:
"Others" refers to those external to the aforementioned four—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
thus they are called "others.
Among these four faculties:
The eye and ear are mentioned first because they apprehend distant objects;
the nose and tongue are not like this.
Therefore, it is said later: "Among the eye and the ear,
the eye is mentioned first because its function reaches further than that of the ear."
One sees mountains and rivers from afar because one does not hear their sounds;
furthermore, the function of the eye is rapid.
Because one first sees people striking bells and drums from afar and subsequently hears the sound;
as for the two faculties of the nose and the tongue:
Both [the nose and the tongue] are equally distant [from the object];
yet the nose is mentioned first for two reasons.
First, swiftness;
second, clarity.
Regarding "swiftness":
For example, when facing various fragrant and delicious foods and drinks,
the nose first perceives the odor,
and the tongue subsequently tastes the flavor.

Second, regarding clarity: the nose can perceive the subtle fragrance within flavors, whereas the tongue cannot perceive the subtle flavor within fragrances. Alternatively, it follows the sequential order of their respective locations.
The "bases" (sthāna) refer to the six sense faculties;
they are the bases upon which [the elements] rely.
Because these bases have degrees of superiority and inferiority, [the elements are so designated].
To distinguish the sequence of the faculties:
the eye is the support that is situated highest of all.
Next are the ears, nose, tongue, and body;
the body mostly resides below.
The mind has no fixed location.
There are those that arise depending immediately upon the sense faculties;
therefore, they are mentioned last. The commentary explains:
this refers to the six groups of consciousness.
Collectively, these are termed "mind.
The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth,
arise in dependence upon the five sense faculties.
It is not the sixth consciousness;
therefore, it is said that that which arises depending upon the sense faculties exists from this fifth [consciousness].
Regarding the clarification of the establishment and abolition of names,
the treatise asks:
"For what reason are all ten bases subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)?"
Only in one instance is the name "form-base" (rūpāyatana) established;
furthermore, there are twelve bases (āyatana).
Their substance is entirely dharma;
it is only with respect to one kind that the designation "dharma-base" (dharmāyatana) is established.
The verse says:
Because it differentiates, is most excellent, and subsumes many superior dharmas,
one location is named "form" (rūpa), and one is named the "dharma-location" (dharmāyatana).

The commentary states that the three characters "for the sake of distinction" (viśeṣaṇārtham) apply to the following two phrases. First, regarding the phrase "in one place it is called 'form' for the sake of distinction": *Commentary:* The three characters "for the sake of distinction" apply to the two subsequent phrases. First, as for the phrase "in one place it is called 'form' for the sake of distinction": [the text continues].
The various distinctions between the nature of the object and the nature of the subject are what is called "differentiation."
That is to say, the five objects such as form constitute the nature of the objective field,
because they are the spheres of perception; [likewise] the five faculties such as the eye.
It is called "having an object" because it possesses an objective sphere. Regarding these ten bases,
if they are collectively termed "form" (rūpa):
Thus, there would be no such distinctions between the object and the subject;
it is for the sake of establishing these distinctions that they are established as ten.
There is only one [instance of] name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Furthermore, while the nine [bases], such as the eye and so forth, each have their own distinct names,
this alone is the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana).
It has no separate name of its own,
being distinguished by the nine names such as "eye" and so forth.
Although it is designated by a general name,
it receives its specific name; as for the term "most excellent," it clarifies that the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) obtains this general designation.
Among the ten bases, the base of form is the most prominent; therefore,
it is established as the general name [for the aggregate of form].
Form has three meanings by which it is called "supreme":
first, because it is resistant.
Second, because they are visible;
third, because they are commonly referred to as "form" (rūpa) by the world at large. Among the nine bases, such as the eye, there is only the single characteristic of being resistant (sapratigha).
There are two further meanings for which it is not called "supreme": furthermore, it is designated as the "sphere of phenomena" (dharmāyatana) for the sake of differentiation;
this explains the sphere of phenomena.
If one speaks of "dharmas" in general,
there is no differentiation; it is by means of differentiation that they are so designated.
One dharma-base (dharmāyatana) is established;
it should be understood as being like [the base of] form (rūpa).
As for that which subsumes many predominant dharmas:
This clarifies that the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is established as a general designation because it subsumes many phenomena; specifically,
there are sixty-four phenomena.
These are called the manifold dharmas (bahudharmāḥ):
there are forty-six mental factors (caitasikāḥ) and fourteen dissociated factors (viprayuktāḥ).
There are three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*);
these are the various dharmas.

Question: If a phenomenon is subject to resistance regarding its objective field (*viṣayapratighāta*), is it also subject to resistance regarding its object of cognition (*ālambanapratighāta*)?
Answer: It should be understood according to the subsequent clause.
That which is an obstruction by way of its object (ālambana-pratighāta) is necessarily an obstruction by way of its sphere (viṣaya-pratighāta),
because this applies to the mind and mental factors.
Because when arising in dependence upon an object, it necessarily apprehends that object;
thus, it possesses resistance with respect to its own objective domain (*viṣayapratighāta*), but does not possess resistance as an object of cognition (*ālambanapratighāta*).
This refers to the five faculties, such as the eye; because these faculties, such as the eye,
are able to grasp their respective objects, they are termed "resistant with respect to the objective sphere" (viṣayapratighāta).
Because it does not take an object as its condition,
it is not an obstructive [resistance] with respect to the object of cognition. According to the Sautrāntika school,
the Venerable Kumāralāta [states this].
He spoke thus: "Kumāra—
here translated as 'Noble Youth'— is one in whom the mind desires to arise elsewhere."
That which obstructs and prevents [an object] from arising should be known as "possessing resistance" (sapratigha).
"Lacking resistance" (apratigha) is the opposite of this. The meaning of this verse is as follows:
For example, when the mind intends to arise toward a visible form,
it may be obstructed by a sound.
The mind then does not arise.
When the mind does not arise,
it is called "having an object" (sālaṃbana).
At the very moment the mind is arising,
it is termed "non-obstructive" (apratigha);
this differs from the Sarvāstivāda school, which asserts that the mind is "obstructive" at the stage when it has already arisen.
Since this treatise follows the commentary by the master Kumāralāta, the treatise states:
"This is what is accepted; among these, excluding the eight neutral [factors] of form and sound, the remaining three types [are as follows]."
Regarding the classification by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
among these ten types of matter, the two categories of visible form and sound are excluded.
The remaining eight kinds are of an indeterminate nature;
the two characters "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) have their meaning connected to the preceding phrase.
The remainder refers to visible form and sound;
these pertain to all three natures.
Regarding the "three natures":
First, wholesome;
second, unwholesome;
third, indeterminate.
If a phenomenon is praiseworthy, it is placed within the category of the white and is termed "virtuous" (*kuśala*).
If a phenomenon is censurable, it is placed within the category of the black.
That which is called "unwholesome nature" is neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy;
it is called "indeterminate."
Furthermore, because they cannot be defined as either wholesome or unwholesome with respect to their ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*),
they are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
These are the eight types beginning with the eye.
They cannot be designated as being of a wholesome or unwholesome nature;
they are comprised within the indeterminate. This applies to both form and sound when they arise from a wholesome mental force.
The bodily and vocal intimation that arises from such [a mind] is subsumed under the category of the wholesome nature. If, however,
it proceeds from the power of an unwholesome mind...
The bodily and vocal intimation that arises from an indeterminate mind is designated as unwholesome.
That which is comprised of bodily and vocal intimation arising from such [states] is called neutral (avyākṛta),
as well as that which does not arise from the mind.
Collectively, these are termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). Regarding the two—form and sound:
bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) is form;
vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti) is sound.
Regarding "origination" (samutthāna):
it refers to the fact that the mind-king and its mental factors (citta-caitta) are equally able to originate [the action].
Since visible forms and sounds are neither inherently good nor evil by their own nature,
they are determined as good or evil based on the mind that gives rise to them.
If the mind is wholesome,
the bodily and vocal actions it initiates are also called wholesome.
If the mind is unwholesome,
the bodily and vocal actions it initiates are also called unwholesome.
Therefore, bodily and vocal [actions], as well as names, are called "virtuous by origination.
From this, the fourth section follows: the classification according to the three realms.
The treatise says: Having already explained the wholesome and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*),
how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)? How many are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
The verse says:

Those bound to the desire realm are eighteen; those bound to the form realm are fourteen, excluding the two [objects] of odor and taste and the two [consciousnesses] of smell and taste; those bound to the formless realm are the final three.
The commentary states:
Those bound to the desire realm are complete with eighteen [factors].
Those bound to the form realm...
There are only fourteen types,
excluding the objects of smell and taste, as well as the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses.
Regarding the exclusion of smell and taste:
Because it is of the nature of substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) lacks substantial food; therefore,
there is no odor or taste, and the consciousnesses of nose and tongue are excluded.
Because there is no object of perception:
olfactory consciousness perceives fragrance, and gustatory consciousness perceives flavor; since fragrance and flavor are absent, [those consciousnesses do not arise].
There are no nose-consciousness or tongue-consciousness, nor are they bound by form;
there are only the final three types,
namely the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
The mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), the five faculties such as the eye (*cakṣurādi-pañcendriya*),
and the five objects such as form (*rūpādi-pañcaviṣaya*).
These ten are material;
being immaterial and devoid of matter,
they do not possess these ten.
Because these ten do not exist,
the five consciousnesses also do not exist.
Therefore, the treatise says:
Because their bases and objects do not exist,
the five consciousnesses also lack the five sense organs as their bases and the five sense objects as their conditions;
therefore, only the final three [consciousnesses] are associated with the formless realm.
From this, the fifth [section]:
the gate of the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The treatise states:
The bondage by realm has already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements,
how many are with outflows?
How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
The mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are common to both; the remainder are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).
The commentary states:
"The mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are common" means they are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
That is to say, the mind and mental consciousness;
those subsumed under the Truth of the Path are termed untainted (anāsrava).
The remainder are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).

If the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is the truth of the path (mārgasatya), it is called "without outflows" (anāsrava); the remainder are called "with outflows. Within the dharma-element, there are mental factors (caitta-dharma) that are without outflows, which are termed the truth of the path.
The remaining fifteen elements are exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava), except for the Truth of the Path and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Because it is not included therein.

is the section on "with vitarka and vicāra."

the treatise states:
"Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)," and so forth.
How many have both vitarka and vicāra?
How many have no vitarka and only vicāra?
How many have neither vitarka nor vicāra?
The verse says:
The five consciousnesses possess only vitarka and vicāra; the last three possess all three; the rest possess none.
The commentary says: This refers to the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
There are [states] with vitarka and vicāra,
because they are always associated with vitarka and vicāra;
namely, the five consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
There are two reasons why it is always associated with vitarka and vicāra: first,
its mode of activity (ākāra) is coarse.
Second, they operate through external doors. Due to these two causes,
the visual and other consciousnesses are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
Since its meaning is definitive,
the word "only" (eva) is stated.
Regarding the phrase "the latter three [exist] in three [realms], while the remainder do not exist":
The latter three refer to the mind (*manas*), phenomena (*dharma*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Among the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousnesses (*vijñāna*),
each occupies the final position.
The repetition of the word "three" clarifies that these three realms all encompass the three grades.
The three categories are called "the three.
Regarding these three categories:
first is the category with vitarka and vicāra.
The second is the category of those with no vitarka and only vicāra;
the third is the category of those with neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Therefore, the treatise says:
From this point onward, the three realms all comprise three categories:
the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
And the associated dharma-realm.
Excluding vitarka and vicāra, there are forty-six mental factors within the dharma-realm.
It is called the dharma-element associated with names.
Among the forty-six mental factors,
vitarka and vicāra are excluded.
The remaining forty-four mental factors are taken;
that is to say, the two types, vitarka and vicāra,
do not pertain to all three categories.
Therefore, it is excluded.
The intended meaning of this passage is to clarify that [the practice] applies to all three grades.
If one is in the desire realm or in the first dhyāna,
there is vitarka and vicāra;
if one is in the intermediate dhyāna, [there is neither].
Without vitarka and with only vicāra:
the second dhyāna and all stages above it.
Up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
there are the mental element of clarity (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) devoid of both vitarka and vicāra,
as well as forty-four associated dharma-elements (dharmadhātu).
Within the various stages (bhūmi),
it encompasses all three grades.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
Included within the dharma-realm;
not associated with mental factors;
the intermediate dhyāna.
Vicāra is likewise; within the dharma-element (dharmadhātu),
there are fourteen dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra),
the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), and non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
The name refers to non-associated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*).
These non-associated factors, along with the *vicāra* of the intermediate dhyāna, are the same as the aforementioned third category: that which is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Therefore, speech is also like this;
that is to say, it is not an associated dharma,
because it does not associate with vitarka and vicāra.
It is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Within that intermediate dhyāna, because there is no vitarka among the mental factors of the stage, it is [called] with vicāra.
Because it is not associated with vitarka,
it is called "without vitarka.
Vicāra does not associate with a second vicāra.
Therefore, it is called "without vicāra" (sustained thought).
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"At all times, one investigates..."
It is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra.
Because there is no second vitarka and it is associated only with vicāra, its vitarka is the same as that of the second category mentioned previously.
It is called "without vitarka and with vicāra only" because two instances of vitarka cannot arise simultaneously;
therefore, there is no second vitarka.
Because there is no second vitarka,

since it does not belong to any of these three categories, what should it be called? It should be called "without vicāra and with only vitarka."

for *vicāra* does not associate with a second *vicāra*.

it is said to possess "only vitarka."

"for this reason" means because there is a fourth category consisting of those with vitarka alone and without vicāra.
The stage with vitarka and vicāra refers to the desire realm and the first dhyāna;
it is characterized by both vitarka and vicāra.
This refers to the other associated mental factors, excluding vitarka and vicāra.

Second, those without vitarka and with only vicāra;
this refers specifically to vitarka itself.
Third, those without vitarka and without vicāra.

there are fourteen dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra).

The treatise raises the following question:
If the five groups of consciousness possess vitarka and vicāra,
how can they be said to be without conceptualization?
The verse says:
It is said that there are five types of non-conceptual [cognition],
because they consist of the discursive wisdom on the mental level and the various mental recollections, through the functions of calculation and recollection.
The commentary states:
The first two lines resolve the objection;
the latter two lines establish the essential nature.
The classification of conceptualization is briefly of three types: first,
conceptualization by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
The second is conceptualization through calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), and the third is conceptualization through recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
Although the five groups of sensory consciousness possess the first type of conceptualization by way of their intrinsic nature, they lack the other two.
The treatise says:
"Just as a horse with only one leg is called 'legless,' so it is said in the sutras."
Regarding the statement that "non-conceptualization" refers to the nature of conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*):
its essence is exclusively vitarka (applied thought).
This will be discussed later among the mental factors (*caitta*).
This shall be explained by itself: "By means of the wisdom of the scattered mind-ground" refers to the essence of discursive conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
"Scattered" means not being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It determines the wisdom within the middle [state] and is associated with the mental consciousness;
it distinguishes this from the five sensory consciousnesses.

Therefore, the scattered wisdom associated with the sixth consciousness is called "discriminative conceptualization" (vikalpa-vikalpa). As for its essence being the various mental attentions of the manas:

The essence of recollective discrimination (*anusmṛti-vikalpa*) consists of all mindfulnesses associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction.
It is called "recollection" because it involves conceptualizing through mindfulness, pervading both concentration and distraction;
therefore, it is termed "all.

"Half of the dharma-element" refers to...
Within the dharma-realm, there are four categories of phenomena; here,
we are concerned solely with those phenomena that are mental factors.
Because they do not include everything,

"the rest" refers to the ten material elements (rūpadhātu) and those non-associated factors (viprayuktadharma) subsumed within the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).

"Preceding" refers to the first seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and the entirety of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*);
these eight, together with sound (*śabda*).

That which is collectively grasped and maintained, and taken as a basis,

Because increase and decrease occur in mutual succession and follow one another, those [objects] are subsumed within the mind and mental factors by means of the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
It serves as the basis;
if it includes the four objects that support the sense faculties,
it is because they serve as its bases.
The nine elements, beginning with the eye,

Because they are appropriated,
the eyes and other [senses] follow along with the mind in terms of benefit and harm.
When the mind experiences joy and happiness, the body also benefits;
if the mind is afflicted by suffering, the body also suffers.
This concludes the ninth section on the derived matter from the primary elements.
The tenth is the gate of accumulation and non-accumulation.
The treatise raises the question:
"Among the eighteen elements..."
How many are of the nature of primary elements (mahābhūta)? How many are of the nature of derived matter (upādāyarūpa)?
How many are of a nature that can be accumulated?
How many are not of a nature that can be accumulated?
The verse says:
Within the element of touch there are two; the remaining nine are derived from matter.
"One part of the dharmas is likewise" and "the ten material [dharmas] are accumulative.
The commentary states:
The first three lines answer the ninth question.
The following sentence answers the tenth question.
Regarding "the element of tangibility (spraṣṭavya-dhātu) contains two [types]":
tangibility refers to that which is perceived by the body.
Contact (spraṣṭavya) is of two kinds:
first, the primary elements (mahābhūta),
namely earth, water, fire, and wind.
The two derived [elements] are the seven, such as smoothness and roughness. Regarding "the other nine are derived from matter":
"the others" refers to the remaining five sense faculties, beginning with the eye.
The four objects, beginning with visible form—
excluding tangible objects—
these are the nine material elements (rūpadhātu).
"Only that which is derived [matter],
and likewise a portion of dharmas" refers to a portion of the dharma-dhātu.
The matter of non-informative action (avijñapti-rūpa) is the same as the nine elements mentioned previously;
it is also exclusively derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).
Therefore, it is likewise with what is spoken.
Within the dharma-realm there are four categories of phenomena:
first, associated dharmas.
Second, non-associated dharmas;
third, non-informative matter;
fourth, unconditioned dharmas.
Now, we take only the unmanifest (avijñapti);
therefore, it is said that it is "one part. Regarding the ten material forms that can be accumulated:
the five sense organs and the five sense objects are called the ten material forms.
That which is composed of atoms is called "accumulable"; by extension,
this principle applies to the other eight [bases].
It cannot be accumulated,
because it is not composed of atoms.
From this point downward:
The eleventh is the section on the cutter and the cut;
the twelfth is the section on the burner and the burned;
the thirteenth is the section on the weigher and the weighed.
The treatise raises the question:
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are capable of cutting,
and how many are objects of cutting?
How many can burn?
How many are burned?
How many can weigh?
How many are designated as such?
The verse says:
It is said that only the four external elements are capable of cutting and being cut.
"Also that which is burned and that which can weigh; that which can burn and that which can be weighed. Regarding the dispute [concerning these], the commentary states:
"As for the first two lines..."
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are called the four external elements;
these are what is termed "that which cuts" and "that which is cut."
The four elements (catvāri mahābhūtāni) that constitute an axe are called "that which cuts" (chettṛ); the four elements that constitute firewood and so forth are called "that which is cut" (chedya).
This is what is called "that which is cut.
Question: What kind of phenomena are called "cutting"?
Answer: Aggregates of matter such as firewood.
They are pressed together so as to continue arising;
tools such as axes separate them,
causing each to arise again individually.
This dharma is called that which cuts, as well as that which is burned and that which weighs.
Just as the four external objects are termed that which cuts and that which is cut,
their substance is likewise that which is burned and that which weighs.
Regarding "that which can burn" and "that which is weighed" in the context of dispute: "dispute" refers to contentious argumentation.
There are two different interpretations for "that which can burn" and "that which is weighed."
This is called a contentious argument (*vivāda*). That is to say,
some may claim that the nature of both the burner and the weighed object is also as previously described.
Only the four external elements— or alternatively, some say—
that only the fire element can be called "that which burns."
That which is referred to as "heaviness" is the tangible quality of heaviness among the tangibles produced [by the elements].
This is the fourteenth [topic] from here.
The fifth section, the Gate of Fivefold Classification,
poses the following question in the treatise:
"Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*)?"
How many are nurtured (*aupacayika*),
how many are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*),
and how many possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*)?
How many last for a single moment?
The verse says:
The five internal [bases] consist of the matured and the nurtured; Sound does not arise from maturation.
The eight unimpeded [knowledges] are of the nature of outflow and also of the nature of maturation;
the remaining three are real and consist only of mental factors (*dharma*). The last three alone are momentary. Commentary:
Regarding the five internal [bases] that are both matured and nurtured:
the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth,
belong exclusively to these two categories.
There are those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those nurtured (*aupacayika*).
That which is obtained through the influence of karma is called "born of maturation" in the present life.
By means of food, drink, and so forth,
that which is small is made large,
and that which is emaciated is made fat.
The five faculties, such as the eye, which are nourished by name-and-form,
are not unconditioned in essence; therefore,
they are not called "substantial."
Furthermore, the initial moment of the patience regarding suffering is not designated as a single kṣaṇa.
[This concerns] the five faculties, such as the eye.
Since it is produced by a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) and possesses the nature of outflow (niṣyanda),
why is it not said to be "common" to outflow?
Answer: The meanings elucidated by the five categories are distinct in essence;
they do not subsume one another.
If the five faculties, such as the eye,
are not fully subsumed under that which is born of maturation (vipākaja), only then are they established as being subsumed under that which is nurtured (aupacayika).
If these two categories were not exhaustive, one would then establish "outflow" (niṣyanda) as a separate category; however,
these two categories now encompass all faculties without exception.
Since there is no nature of the eye and other faculties apart from these two categories, the eye and other faculties are not established as being of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Although there are also outflow results within the internal [bases] such as the eye,
they do not constitute a distinct nature apart from the nature of maturation and that which is nurtured.
For this reason, the meaning of "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) is not explicitly stated [in the verse].
The treatise provides four explanations: first, that which is produced by a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is called "born of maturation."
Just as a chariot drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart"—
a term formed by omitting the intermediate word— it is explained in this way [to refer to] maturation (*vipāka*).
It may belong either to the cause or to the fruit.
If it belongs to the cause,
then the maturation itself is the cause.
It is called the "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*); this is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
If it refers to the fruit, [it is a genitive tatpuruṣa].
The cause of maturation is called the "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
If one says it is "born of maturation" (vipākaja),
this is explained solely by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound;
that is, that which is produced by a cause of maturation is called "born of maturation."
The two characters "cause" (yin) and "object" (suo) are omitted,
and it is simply called "born of maturation" (vipākaja),
just as one says "ox-cart" (niuchē) for "cart drawn by an ox," omitting the two characters "drawn by" (suojiā). The second interpretation states:
Alternatively, when the karma that has been created reaches the time of its fruition,
it transforms and becomes capable of ripening.
Therefore, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Because the fruit arises from that,
it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This refers to the karma that has been performed,
which, before reaching the attainment of its fruit,
exerts the function of grasping that fruit.
Upon reaching the time of attaining the fruit,
it gives rise to the function of giving the fruit;
this is the function of giving the fruit.
Because it differs from its previous function of grasping the fruit,
it is termed "change" (*vipariṇāma*).
Change is itself alteration (*anyathātva*).
Because it is that which ripens,
it is called "ripening" (vipāka). Here,
"ripening" (vi) is equivalent to "maturity" (pāka).
Therefore, it is called "ripening" (*vipāka*).
This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The fruit arises from that.
It is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the birth of maturation."
This is the meaning of that interpretation:
maturation resides in the cause, while arising belongs to the fruit. The third interpretation says:
The fruit obtained by that [cause] is of a different category from its cause;
because it is that which has matured, it is called "maturation" (vipāka).
The meaning of this interpretation is that while the fruit is neutral (avyākṛta),
the cause is either wholesome or unwholesome.
Therefore, it is said that because the result is of a different category from its cause, it is termed "distinct.
Furthermore, it is that which is matured.
"Vipāka is itself arising.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. The fourth explanation states:
"Alternatively, it refers to the cause."
The meaning of this interpretation is that the name "result" (phala) is applied metaphorically;
the term "result" refers to maturation (vipāka),
which is identical to the second interpretation.
The cause is not itself the maturation;
however, when this cause is termed "maturation," it is because the name of the effect is applied to the cause.
It is called "ripening" (*vipāka*) because it possesses ripening;
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
A fruit that arises from a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) is called "born of ripening" (vipākaja);
this is a dependent determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) meaning "the birth of ripening. As for that which is "nourished" (aupacayika), it refers first to that which is capable of nourishing.
There are four kinds:
first, food and drink;
second, requisites for support, such as ointments and bathing.
Third, sleep; fourth, meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
These are the four superior conditions.
It provides benefit to the five faculties,
causing the small to grow large and the emaciated to become robust.
That which is called "nourished by designation" (nāman-poṣita) is capable of being nourished by all three natures (trividha-svabhāva),
whereas that which is "nourished" (poṣita) itself is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Now, regarding the five categories, this refers to what is produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*). Sound has no [sound] produced by maturation (*vipākaja*);
sound consists of two types.
First, that which is of uniform outflow (niṣyanda);
second, that which is nurtured (aupacayika).
There is none that is produced by maturation (vipākaja).
Furthermore, while resultant matter arises spontaneously,
sound proceeds according to volition.

Because they are interrupted, there is no birth from maturation (*vipākaja*). Regarding the eight unimpeded [realms] being both outflow-born (*naiṣyandika*) and of the nature of birth from maturation:
these are the seven mental elements and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Because they are not accumulated,
they are called the eight unimpeded [faculties].
These possess the nature of being both outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
If it arises from a homogeneous cause or a pervasive cause,
it is termed "of the nature of outflow" (niṣyanda);
that which is produced by being drawn forth from a retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) is [termed "retribution"].
It is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Because it is not accumulated, there is no "nurturing" (*aupacayika*). As for the other three:

"Others" refers to the remaining four— visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects. These four are termed "others" because they are external to the aforementioned five sense organs (the eye and so forth) as well as the eight unimpeded [bases].
The remaining four of these pertain to all three categories and possess the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
That which is nurtured,
that which has the nature of outflow, and that which is truly only a phenomenon— these are designated as "real" when they are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It does not undergo transition through the four characteristics,
for its essence is firm and solid;
it is subsumed within this dharma-realm.
Therefore, only the dharma-realm alone is said to possess substantial reality;
as for the moments [of consciousness], only the latter three do.
The mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are called the last three;
these alone exist for a single moment within the three realms.
This refers to the first moment of the path of seeing,
the category of the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*); it consists of this single momentary mind alone.
Ultimately, it is not produced from a cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*),
because it is not a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*);
therefore, it is called "a single moment" (*eka-kṣaṇa*).
Other conditioned phenomena are none other than outflows;
[this includes] the mind associated with the patience of suffering.
It is called the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu).
In relation to what follows, it is called "mind" (manas);
in relation to what precedes, it is called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna).
The dharmas that arise together with sensation and so forth are called the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
From here below is the fifteenth [section].
Regarding the attainment of the gate of accomplishment:
according to the Sarvāstivāda school,
if one attains the "characteristic of arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "attainment."
If one attains [a state] up to the present, it is called "accomplishment" (siddhi).
At the time of accomplishment, it is not called "attainment" (prāpti);
at the time of attainment, it is not called "accomplishment. As for what is termed the "characteristic of arising" (jāti-lakṣaṇa):
Regarding the future world as well.
The treatise says:
"Thus, the [minds] born of maturation and so forth have already been explained."
Now this should be examined:
if there is an eye-element that one has not previously possessed, [how is it acquired?]
Is that which is now attained and accomplished also the visual consciousness? If it is the visual-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu), [is it so]?
Previously unaccomplished,
it is now accomplished;
is it also the eye-element?
Regarding such questions as these,
a brief response should now be given.
The verse says:
Regarding the statement, "The eye and the eye-consciousness element are acquired either independently or together, but not simultaneously," the commentary explains:
"The eye and the eye-consciousness..."
Regarding the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning "obtaining either individually, together, both, or neither":
"individually" refers to the two simple (single) propositions.
"Both obtainable" refers to the category of "both.
"Neither" refers to the category of "neither."
The term "and so forth" clarifies the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) regarding attainment and non-attainment.
For now, we shall consider only the first single alternative.

This refers to obtaining the eye-faculty but not yet obtaining consciousness; it refers to those born in the desire realm who gradually obtain the eye-faculty. The phrase "gradually obtaining the eye" indicates birth from a womb, an egg, or moisture.
