If one were of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), [the faculties would be obtained instantaneously].
Because the faculties are acquired all at once.
Now, regarding the eye faculty, it is a result-of-maturation (vipāka) and is ethically neutral (avyākṛta).
Only the factors co-arising with it are acquired;
therefore, in terms of gradual acquisition, one is said merely to "acquire the eye. Eye-consciousness, however, pertains to all three moral natures.

There are cases where both [the sense organ and consciousness] are acquired simultaneously; first, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), when visual consciousness has already arisen, one now gradually acquires the eye faculty.
This is because, after birth has been taken, the consciousness is established prior to the [full] accomplishment of the faculties.
Therefore, it is not called "attainment. Furthermore, when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, one is born into those respective dhyānas;
at the initial arising of the intermediate state (antarābhava), there is only the eye faculty (cakṣur-indriya) but no eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
Because consciousness has not yet arisen, it is not called "attainment. This is the second single phrase:
attainment of consciousness without attainment of the eye; that is, one who has already been born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages.
Regarding the phrase "visual consciousness arises": the word "arises" (現) means "presently" (正), and the word "arises" (起) means "to be produced" (生).
When consciousness is in the state of being produced, it is termed "arising" (現起).
This consciousness that arises exists in the state of arising;
it is currently in the future.
At that time, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*).
When the eye-faculty is in the present, it is called "possession" (*samanvāgama*) but not "attainment. As for the third alternative:
Both the faculties and consciousness are acquired simultaneously;
that is, when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm or the Brahma-world. [The faculties and consciousness of] the desire realm and the Brahma-world [are acquired at once].
Among these, there is the initial stage where both the faculties and consciousnesses are present; at that time, it is called "attainment.
As for the fourth phrase, which is neither [of the preceding cases]:
This means excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Regarding the word "etc. (ādi) in the verse, it includes the accomplishment of the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the first case:
one who possesses the eye faculty but does not possess eye-consciousness.
This refers to those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages,
in whom eye-consciousness does not arise.
As for the second phrase:
One achieves eye-consciousness but does not achieve the eye-faculty;
that is to say, one born in the desire realm.
Those who have not yet obtained the eye-faculty,
or those who have obtained it and subsequently lost it;
that is to say, those born in the desire realm.
The consciousness must necessarily be accomplished because the dharmas of the stage have been established.
This applies to those who have not yet attained the faculties.
This refers to the moment of initial conception in the womb.
As for those who "have attained it and then lost it," this refers to those born blind after birth.
Since the eye-faculty is absent,
it is not established.
As for the third phrase:
That is to say: being born in the desire realm and having obtained the eye faculty without losing it;
and being born in the Brahma-world.
If one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and perceives visible forms,
both the sense faculty and consciousness are present.
The fourth phrase refers to those cases excluding the aforementioned characteristics;
from this point, it is the sixteenth.
Regarding the internal and external gates,
the treatise states:
"Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)."
How many are internal?
How many are external?
The verse says:
The twelve internal [bases], such as the eye, and the six external [objects], such as form—
so it is explained.
There are twelve internal [bases].
The six sense faculties and the six consciousnesses—
these twelve elements (dhātus)—
are so called because they are the bases upon which the mind depends.
That which is based upon and closely associated with [the internal] is called "internal";
these are the six objects, such as form and so forth.
It is the object-condition for the mind;
because the object-condition is remote,
it is designated as "external."
Seventeenth from here is the section on the homogeneous and the partially homogeneous.
The treatise says:
Among the eighteen elements (dhātus),
how many are "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and how many are "counter-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga)?
The verse says:
Dharmas have the same *sabhāgatā*; the others have two; [this refers to] performing or not performing one's own karma.
The commentary says:
Regarding the "homogeneity of dharmas":
"dharma" refers to the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
Within this dharma-element, [there is]...

There is only the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and no "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga). Generally speaking, the six objects are called "homogeneous" because they invariably serve as the objective referents (ālambana) for the cognizing consciousnesses.
"Certainty" has two meanings.
First, as with the five objects such as form,
they are definitely the objects of perception for consciousness.
It is called "concentration" (samādhi).
This means that the five consciousnesses are termed concentration because they take their objects without distraction. Now, these five objects are also given the name "concentration."
This means that because it is definitely the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the five consciousnesses, at the time when the five consciousnesses take it as their object:
It is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
Although it is an object of mental consciousness,
because it is not determinate, [it is not perceived].
Therefore, it is not of the same category [as the sense faculties]. The second dharma-object is called concentration;
its essence is itself concentration, and it is perceived exclusively by the mental consciousness.
Because this is determinate, it is necessarily taken as an object by the mental consciousness; therefore,
in relation to the mental consciousness, it is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
The treatise states: "There is not a single dharma-realm that does not, within it, already, currently, or about to give rise to boundless mental consciousness;
therefore, this dharma-realm is always termed the 'homogeneous portion' (sabhāgatā) of boundless mental consciousness."
This is the contemplation of non-self.
Because the objects of its focus are boundless,
that which has already arisen, is currently arising, and will arise [is all included].
That which has already arisen in the past,
that which is currently arising in the present,
and that which will arise in the future.
Regarding the remaining two:
that is to say, the other seventeen elements all possess both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
When they perform their own specific function, they are called "homogeneous."
That which does not perform its own function is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Regarding "performing its own function," "function" (karman) refers to functional activity.
Just as with the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses,
when considered in terms of their capacity to apprehend objects,
they are called "their own functional activity."
If it cannot apprehend its object,
it is said not to perform its own function; this refers to the five objects, such as visible form and so forth.
To take something as an object is called performing its own function;
not to take it as an object is called not performing its own function. In this context, the eye faculty [performs its function] with respect to visible forms that are present.
Already seen. Being seen. To be seen.
This is called the "homogeneous eye.
Thus it is explained in detail,
up to the faculty of mind.
Regarding each of their respective objective spheres,
one should explain the specific functions of their own karma;
such is the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) eye.
There are only four kinds;
namely, not seeing form,
which has already ceased.
Those that are currently ceasing, those that will cease,
and those dharmas that are not subject to arising.
Just as the eye has four [aspects],
so too does the body element have four kinds.
One should know that the eye [faculty] is its corresponding homogeneous part (*sabhāga*);
it is of only one kind, namely, the non-arising dharma (*anutpattidharman*).
That which is destined to arise must necessarily be of the same class;
therefore, that which does not arise is termed "of the same class as that" (tat-sabhāga). Regarding the realm of form, it is [the eye] that has already seen, is currently seeing, or will see.
These are called "concordant matter" (sabhāga-rūpa) and "non-concordant matter" (tatsabhāga-rūpa);
they are of only four kinds.
That is to say, it is not seen by the eye;
it has already ceased,
or is currently ceasing.
It should be extinguished;
and as for dharmas that do not arise,
just as it is with form, so it is with them.
It should be understood that the same applies up to the object of touch.
The homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) is likewise threefold.

That is the fourth [category], the "homogeneous" (sabhāga). Regarding the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, there are three types of "homogeneous" states: those that have already arisen, and so forth.
Because they are currently arising or about to arise,
their homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) is one.

Because they are exclusively dharmas that do not arise, as explained in the case of the *dhātu* (element). Question: For what reason are they called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
Answer: There are three explanations for this. The first explanation states:
The triad of faculty, object, and consciousness further intersect with one another; therefore,
they are called "parts" (bhāga).
They are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) because they possess a commonality of engagement. Regarding the second interpretation, it says:
"Alternatively, 'part' (bhāga) refers to..."
That which has already performed its activity and has performed its own function is called "already performed action" (kṛtakarma).
They are called "homogeneous" (sabhāga) because they possess the same functional parts. The third explanation states:
"Alternatively, 'parts' (bhāga) refers to..."
This is the contact that arises;
it is the contact born from the conjunction of the three;
it is the contact produced simultaneously.
Therefore, it is called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
Regarding "that which is similar to that" (tat-sabhāga),
the treatise says:
Because it is not of the same class as that [homogeneous] and yet shares a commonality of type with it,
it is called "similar-to-that" (tat-sabhāga).
The commentary says:
For example, when the eye does not see form,
it is called "non-concordant" (asabhāga).
This is not of the same class;
it shares a commonality of category with that eye which sees visible forms.
It is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga); as for the phrase "the same category," it is because they share the same intrinsic nature as the eye and because they mutually induce one another.
Furthermore, because they are mutually connected,
following this is the eighteenth [section]:
the threefold gate of abandonment.
The treatise says:
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
How many are to be abandoned by cultivation?
How many are not to be abandoned?
The verse says:

Fifteen are abandoned solely by cultivation; the latter three realms are common to all three [types of abandonment]; the non-defiled are not born from the six; and those in the form realm are definitely not abandoned by insight. Commentary: The fifteen faculties are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The final three faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—pertain to all three types of abandonment: they may be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), by cultivation, or are not to be abandoned at all. The non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*) faculties are not produced from the six [senses]. Furthermore, those faculties belonging to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are definitely not abandoned by insight.
The fifteen elements are the five sense organs and the five consciousnesses.
And the five objects are abandoned solely by cultivation;
the latter three realms are common to all three [types of abandonment].

The mind-object base (*dharmāyatana*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are common to all three types of abandonment. As for the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element,
they are associated with eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Together with their co-existent dharmas and their concomitant acquisitions,
all are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). Within the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are ten afflictions.
In the truths of origination and cessation, there are seven each,
excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
In the truth of the path, there are eight.
Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
these four truths comprise thirty-two [factors].
In the higher realms, hatred (*dveṣa*) is excluded.
There are twenty-eight;
that is to say, because anger is excluded from each of the four truths respectively.
This makes twenty-eight.
Each of the two upper realms likewise has twenty-eight, totaling fifty-six.
Together with the thirty-two [latent dispositions] of the desire realm,
they constitute eighty-eight.
These are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
These are afflictions of discrimination,
because they arise from delusion regarding the principles [of reality]. As soon as one perceives the Truths, [they are abandoned].
Because they are all abandoned by that [vision],
they are called "abandoned through vision. "Vision" refers to the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Vision is that which cuts off;
delusion is that which is cut off.
[Delusion] is that which is cut off by vision.
It is called "abandoned by vision" (*darśana-prahātavya*);
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
As for the "concomitant factors" (*sahabhū-dharma*):
This refers to the mental factors associated with the delusions of view,
together with the four characteristics [of arising, abiding, change, and cessation]. These are the three [factors] beginning with the manas.
With the exception of those abandoned through seeing,
all other contaminated phenomena are abandoned through cultivation; because they also include the uncontaminated,
they are called "not to be abandoned."
"Non-defiled [dharmas] are not born of the six [consciousnesses];
form is definitely not abandoned by insight.
This addresses an external objection.

That is to say, the Sautrāntika school maintains that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the bodily and vocal actions that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
That is to say, once one has attained the path of seeing,
those ordinary beings and others will never again be reborn [in that state].
Since it is diametrically opposed to the path of seeing,
it should be abandoned by seeing.
To answer this objection,
there is this verse.
Nevertheless, this dharma...
It is certainly not abandoned by insight.
Briefly stated, that which is not abandoned by insight is of three kinds in total.
First, the dharmas that are not associated with the outflows (anāsrava), namely the wholesome (kuśala) and the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Second, those not produced by the six [consciousnesses].
This refers to the five consciousnesses.
Because they do not arise from the sixth mental consciousness,
they are called "not produced by the sixth."
Third, as for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), these three types of phenomena are certainly not abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*);
they are not directly initiated by delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*).
Therefore, it is called "non-defiled.
It is not produced by the six [consciousnesses], nor does it arise from delusion regarding the principles of the truths.
Form-dharmas (*rūpa*) are not directly produced by the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Nevertheless, as for the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*):
This is non-defiled and is comprised within the indeterminate nature;
it refers to bodily and vocal unwholesome karma.
Because these are material phenomena (rūpadharma),
these two types are not to be abandoned by insight (na darśana-prahātavya).
The nineteenth from here is the gate of "seeing and non-seeing.
Within it, there are two parts.
First, the direct exposition;
second, the incidental discussion.
Regarding the first, the direct exposition:
The treatise asks: Among the eighteen elements (dhātus),
how many are vision (dṛṣṭi) and how many are not vision?
The verse says:
The eye and a portion of the dharma-dhātu are said to be the eight kinds of vision;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not vision, because it does not deliberate.

The eye sees visible forms when it is of the same class (*sabhāga*); it is traditionally taught that the consciousness which depends upon it cannot see them because of obstructed visible forms. [Commentary: The eye sees visible forms when it is *sabhāga*. It is traditionally taught (*kila*) that the consciousness which depends upon it (*tad-āśrita-vijñāna*) is not capable of seeing them, because of the presence of obstructed visible forms.
The eye is entirely seeing, because it observes and illuminates forms. A portion of the dharma-realm, consisting of eight types, is called "seeing";
these refer to the five defiled views, such as the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and so forth.
Sixth is mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*),
which refers to wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The seven types of right view of those in training (śaikṣa) refer to all untainted views within the continuum of one in training.
The eighth is the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*),
which refers to all untainted views (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) within the body of one beyond training.
These eight are wisdom;
because they investigate and evaluate their objects,
they are all termed "views."
That which is subsumed within the dharma-realm is called "one part.
Question: For what reason is it called mundane right view?
It is associated exclusively with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The verse in response states: "The wisdom (*prajñā*) arising simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses is not 'view' (*dṛṣṭi*), because it does not judge and because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)."
Because it cannot be definitively determined,
it is not a [true] vision; thus, the latter four lines of the verse refute the school that maintains the existence of a perceiving consciousness (*vijñāna-dṛṣṭi*).
That is to say, the Venerable Dharmatrāta maintains that visual consciousness sees,
while the Venerable Vasumitra asserts that the visual faculty sees.
Therefore,
the treatise says:
"If that is so, as for the eye faculty..."
It cannot be definitively determined.
Why is it called the difficulty of seeing the family of consciousness?
Because one is able to clearly and intelligently contemplate and observe all forms.
Therefore, it is also called the "view that the eye sees," which is the answer given by the Master.
If it were the eye that sees, then [seeing would occur] whenever other consciousnesses are functioning.
This objection should also be understood as applying to the term "view" (*darśana*).
According to this school's tenet,
the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
If it is granted that the eye sees, then why does it not see when other consciousnesses are active and the eye is devoid of consciousness?
"Not all eyes are capable of direct perception," is the answer from the proponent of the eye as the seer.
"Who is it that can directly perceive? is the inquiry.
This refers to the fact that it is the homogeneous eye (*sabhāga-cakṣus*), in its state of conjunction with consciousness,
that is able to see, and not anything else; this explains the fifth line of the verse.

If that were so, then it would follow that it is the consciousness supported by the eye that sees form, rather than the eye-consciousness seeing it; this is the objection raised by the proponents of the "eye-seeing" theory.
The eye is not like that.
It is established that eye-consciousness is certainly not the seer; this explains the sixth point.
What is the evidence for this?
It is traditionally taught that [the visual faculty] cannot perceive obstructed forms; therefore, the eye-faculty is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*).
It is logically impossible to see a form that is obstructed; if it were consciousness that sees,
[it would see such forms].
Because consciousness is non-obstructive, walls and the like do not hinder it; thus, one should see obstructed forms.
This is the response from the school of those who maintain that the eye sees.
This explains the seventh and eighth phrases.
According to the Sautrāntika school,
it is the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) that sees.
It is provisional and not real.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The masters of the Sautrāntika school..."
They spoke thus: "How can we gather together here,
clawing at the empty sky?"
With the eye, visible forms, and other conditions as causes, visual consciousness arises;
these [factors] are involved in the act of seeing.
What constitutes the "agent" and the "object"?
It is merely in accordance with worldly convention that such verbal designations are provisionally established.
The eye is called that which sees;
consciousness is called that which cognizes.
Regarding these, the wise person—
One should not be attached or fixated upon it.
From this second point,
there are seven ancillary discussions within this section.
First, the sequence of seeing with the two eyes;
second, the separation and union of the six faculties and the six objects;
third, the relative magnitude of the faculties and their objects.
The four [types of] consciousness and the sixth consciousness are subsumed under the category of "worldly" (*loka*).
The five eyes and so forth receive their names based on what they attain;
the six consciousnesses are established by name according to their respective faculties (*indriya*).
Seventh, the distinctions regarding the similarities and differences of the supporting stages (*āśraya-bhūmi*).
First, concerning the first [point]:
as for the sequence of seeing with both eyes.
The treatise says:
When seeing a form, is it seen by one eye?
It is seen by both eyes;
there is no fixed rule for this.
The verse says:
"Or because when both eyes see simultaneously, the perception of forms is distinct.
Commentary: The great masters of the Abhidharma [state this].
Everyone said:
"Sometimes both eyes see at once;
by opening both eyes, the perception of forms is distinct."
Because when one eye is closed, [the object] is not clearly perceived;
therefore, we know that at times both eyes see forms.
Furthermore, when one eye is opened...
When one touches a single eye,
one immediately sees two moons and so forth before one's eyes.
If one were closed or one were touched,
this phenomenon would not occur; therefore,
at times both eyes see simultaneously.
It is not that the support is distinct [from the consciousness] such that consciousness becomes twofold; rather,
it abides without a specific location.
Therefore, it is not the same as obstructive matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*).
This concludes the second section:
the separation and conjunction of the six sense organs and their objects.
The treatise says:
"If this school asserts that the eye sees, the ear hears, and so forth up to the mind cognizing,
then those are the objects apprehended by them."
When the sense faculties correctly apprehend their objects,
do they reach them or not?
The verse says:
The eye, ear, and mental faculties do not reach their objects; these three are explained as being contrary [to the others].
Regarding the faculties of the eye, ear, and mind:
Grasping that which does not reach the object-field means that the eye can see various forms at a distance,
such as medicinal substances within the eye itself.
Thus, one cannot perceive that which is close to the auditory faculty, even though the ear is able to hear sounds from a distance.
Then it would be unable to hear,
because the mind is formless;
thus it cannot be said to reach [the object].
Therefore, these three faculties apprehend objects that are not in contact [with them].
Regarding the three contradictions:
The third refers to the nose, tongue, and body.
These three apprehend objects that have reached them;
therefore, they are the opposite of the aforementioned [two].
Third, regarding the relative magnitude of the sense faculties, their objects, and their dimensions,
the verse says:
One should know that the three [faculties] beginning with the nose perceive objects of equal size.
Commentary: "The nose and so forth" refers to...
The tongue and body are included in "and so forth.
These three can only apprehend objects that are equal in size to themselves.
Regarding the term "equal in size":
Just as the atoms of the sense organs are subtle, so too are the atoms of their objects;
for the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth arise from the union of corresponding [atoms]. As for the eyes and ears, they apprehend their objects [at a distance].
The size is indeterminate;
that is to say, the eye sometimes sees what is small,
such as when it perceives the tip of a hair.
Sometimes one perceives the large,
as when seeing mountains and the like;
sometimes one perceives the equal.
Just as one who sees grapes with an unstable ear perceives the distinctions of size and so forth in the sounds of mosquitoes, gadflies, clouds, and lutes.
The sound of clouds is thunder;
because it arises depending upon the clouds,
the people of the West call it thunder.
It is the sound of clouds.
The mind has no substantial obstruction;
its shape, magnitude, and distinctions cannot be discerned.
Regarding the fourth point from here—
the six consciousnesses being subsumed under the worldly basis—
the treatise states:
As previously stated,
there are six kinds of consciousness,
namely the visual consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).
Up to the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
Just as the five consciousnesses take only the present as their object,
does the mental consciousness likewise take all three times and the non-temporal (*atīta-anāgata-pratyutpanna-asamskrta*) as its objects?
Is it the case that the supports for these various consciousnesses are likewise? No;
how so? The verse says:
"The subsequent support is exclusively past; the five consciousnesses have either [the simultaneous] or [the subsequent] as their support.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "The subsequent support is exclusively past."
The latter is the sixth consciousness;
among the six consciousnesses,
it is so called because it occupies the final position.
This sixth consciousness relies solely upon the past mind that has just ceased; as for the five consciousnesses,
their supports may be simultaneous with them.
Alternatively, it indicates indeterminacy:
the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness,
have two types of bases.
The first is the past,
namely the immediate mind;
the second is the present.
The five faculties, such as the eye,
are called "simultaneous" because their consciousnesses exist in the present together with them; alternatively, it is said that this also refers to the past.
Therefore, the supports of the five consciousnesses are either [the sense organs] alone or both [the sense organs and the immediately preceding consciousness]. Question:
Is that which serves as the nature of the support for visual consciousness also its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If this is a visual consciousness,
it is also the immediately preceding condition for another visual consciousness.
Is it the nature of the basis?
One should respond by establishing four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first alternative:
The co-nascent eye-faculty is the nature of the support for visual consciousness;
it is not an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) consists exclusively of mind and mental factors;
the eye faculty, however, is matter (rūpa).
Therefore, it is not this condition.
As for the second phrase,
it refers to that which has ceased immediately prior.
Regarding the mental factors (caitta-dharmas) and the element of mind (manodhātu), the expression "immediately preceding cessation" indicates the past.
A past mental factor does not serve as an equal-and-immediate condition for a present visual consciousness, because it is not a mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
It is not the nature that serves as the support for visual consciousness.
As for the third phrase,
it refers to the past mental faculty (*manas*).
The mind that has ceased without interval serves as the basis for the present visual consciousness,
because it is a mental factor.
Furthermore, it is the visual consciousness as its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
As for the fourth phrase:
This refers to the teachings set forth excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
As it is with the eye,
so it is for everything up to body-consciousness.
It should be understood that the same applies here. Question:
If it is the nature of the support for the mental consciousness, would it then also be the mental consciousness itself?
Is it the equal-and-immediate condition?
If it is the mental consciousness,
then it is the equal-and-immediate condition.
Furthermore, is it also the nature upon which the mental consciousness relies?
Answer: It conforms to the preceding clause.
Answer: It refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for its nature as the basis (*āśraya*), it is definitively the mental consciousness.
The equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) is the support for mental consciousness;
since this is precisely the mind-faculty (manas-indriya),
it falls under the category of the "concurrent" (ubhayathā) proposition.
There exists that which serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mental consciousness, yet does not function as its support (*āśraya*).
This refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that have just ceased; they do not constitute the mental king (*cittarāja*), [and thus are not its support].
It is not the basis. According to the Mahāvibhāṣā,
answers to questions regarding dharmas do not exceed four types.
To ask about the narrow by means of the broad is answered according to the preceding clause; to ask about the broad by means of the narrow is likewise answered accordingly.
This is answered by way of a sequential response (*anuloma-paścātpādaka*);
as they mutually possess both breadth and narrowness,
one should formulate four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
If there is no difference in width, the answer is: "It is so.
Furthermore, if one asks now whether that which is the support of the mental consciousness is also its equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
This is asking about the broad by means of the narrow;
that is to say, because the support of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is exclusively the mind-king (*cittarāja*),
it is the narrow immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
"Comprehending both mind and mental factors" is a broad answer that accords with the preceding statement;
it is an answer that accords with the preceding question.

That is to say, if something is the nature of the support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is necessarily an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This is an answer in the form of a "consequent clause" (*paścātpādaka*) that addresses a broad question with a narrow one;
that is, the previous question is reformulated.
If it is the case that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the mental consciousness is also the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for that mental consciousness?
This is already asking about the broad in terms of the narrow;

that is, the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) of the mental consciousness is "broad" because it extends to both the mind-king (citta) and its mental factors (caitta). As for its nature as a support (āśraya):
Since this refers exclusively to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*),
one should provide an answer by means of a subsequent-phrase formulation (*paścātpādaka*):
that is to say, if it is of the nature of the support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It must be this equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
because it follows the subsequent phrase; if one takes the nature of the support of visual consciousness and [compares] it with the equivalent-immediate condition.
To ask this is to point out that there is mutual disparity in breadth and narrowness:
the basis of visual consciousness,
which extends to both matter and mind, is broad.
To say that it does not apply to mental factors (caitta) is narrow;
if it refers to the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya),
which applies to both mind and mental factors, it is broad.
Not pervading matter is narrowness.
From this fifth [point],
the eye and so forth obtain the designation of "basis" (āśraya).
The treatise asks:
For what reason does consciousness arise by depending upon two conditions simultaneously?
It receives the name "basis" because it resides in the faculties and not in the objects, as the faculties and objects serve as two conditions.
The verse says:
"Consciousness varies according to the transformation of the faculties; therefore, the eye and so forth are called the 'bases' (āśraya).
Regarding the commentary:
"According to the transformation of the faculties."
Consciousness changes in accordance with the sense faculties; for if the faculty undergoes transformation,
consciousness likewise becomes different.
That is to say, if the faculties are benefited,
their consciousness becomes clear; if the faculties are impaired, [the consciousness becomes obscured].
Because consciousness would then become dull;
it is not that a change in the object causes a difference in consciousness,
for consciousness follows the sense faculty.
Because it does not follow after objects,
the designation "name" (nāman) applies only to the eye and so forth, and not to others.
Regarding the phrase "the eye and so forth":
These are the six elements, beginning with the eye. From this sixth [element],
consciousness receives its designation according to its respective sense faculty.
The treatise asks:
For what reason are form and the other [objects] precisely that which are cognized?
And they are called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," but not "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness.
The verse says:
"Because of those and the uncommon cause, consciousness is explained according to the sense faculty.
Commentary: "Those" refers to what was previously stated.
The "bases" (āśraya) refer to the eye and the other [senses].
Furthermore, regarding the "unshared causes" (asādhāraṇa-hetu),
these are the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
It serves as the uncommon cause for the visual consciousness and so forth;
that is to say, the eye is [the cause] only for its own visual consciousness.
Serving as the basis for [visual consciousness],
it is called the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*).
If form were to be common to both one's own and others' visual consciousnesses, [it would not be an uncommon cause].
Furthermore, that which is apprehended by both one's own and others' mental consciousnesses is a common cause.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the others.
It should be understood that the same applies even to bodily contact. Regarding the five faculties, such as the eye, they are superior by virtue of two reasons:
first, the superiority of their basis.
Second, it is named "consciousness" because of its unique cause;
it follows the sense organ rather than the object. However, according to the treatise:
The five sense organs alone clarify the uncommon cause;
the five objects clarify the common cause.
Regarding the statement that the mental faculty (manas) is not the illuminator of dharmas:
this means that while the mind can give rise to the five consciousnesses,
it is not their exclusive cause.
Dharmas are objects of the mental consciousness alone;
thus, they are termed "unshared causes. Although the mind itself is not an unshared cause, it is the mental consciousness [that takes them as its object].
Because it is the nature of the support,
it is called "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna) in accordance with its support.
Although dharmas are the specific cause [of dharma-consciousness],
they are not called "dharma-consciousness" because they are not its support.

Now, as for these five faculties, they receive their designation from the sense organs because of the excellence of their physical bases and because they are their specific causes; this [dual condition] does not apply to their objects.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses are named after their respective organs.
It is, for example, like the sound of a drum or malted barley.
Although the sound of a drum is caused by both the hand and the drum,
it is called "the sound of the drum" and not "the sound of the hand."
The drum has two meanings.
First, it is the preeminent basis,
because sound arises in dependence upon the transformation of the drum.
Second, regarding the uncommon cause:
because it produces only the sound of the drum,
the hand lacks two of these meanings.
It is not called the sound of the hand;
the drum is a metaphor for the sense organ,
and the sound is a metaphor for consciousness.
The hand is a metaphor for the object;
how much more so can the phenomenon (dharma) be known?
It is merely called "barley sprout."
It is not called "water, etc., sprout.
Barley has two meanings;
this is explained by analogy with the drum.
From this seventh [topic],
there is a distinction based on the similarities and differences of the stages (*bhūmi*).
The verse says:
The eye is not lower than the body; visual consciousness is not higher than the eye.
For the eye and visible forms relative to consciousness, all three are of every level; for the body, it is likewise for both.
As it is for the eye, so it is for the ear; for the next three [senses], they are all of their own level.
The body-consciousness [belongs] to its own level or a lower level; it should be known that the mental consciousness is not fixed.
Commentary: To explain this verse:
Furthermore, one must first know that the body,
the eye, and visible forms— these three—
all pertain to all five stages.

This refers to those in the desire realm and the four dhyānas. Eye-consciousness exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna. Regarding the statement "the eye is not below the body," this means that the eye-faculty, in relation to the body, [is either equal to or above it].
It is either equal or superior, never inferior.

Furthermore, when the eye of the desire realm sees the forms of the desire realm, this is called "equal" because the eye and the body belong to the same level (*bhūmi*); thus it is said that the body resides in the desire realm.
One attains the eye of the fourth dhyāna.
This means that while the eye exists on a higher level, there is certainly no body residing on a higher level that gives rise to an eye belonging to a lower level.
Because one who is born in a higher stage possesses a superior eye of their own,
there is no need to produce the inferior eye of a lower stage; therefore,
the eye [is not coextensive] with the body.
It never abides below; the visual consciousness is not superior to the eye.
Regarding the visual consciousness in relation to the eye, it is equal or inferior, but not superior. "Equal" means being of the same level (*bhūmi*).
For example, when the eye of the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm,
the visual consciousness and the eye belong to the same stage.
If one uses the eye of the second dhyāna...
When one sees the forms of the first dhyāna,
the form and the consciousness belong to the first dhyāna,
while the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.
This refers to visible form and consciousness; both are of a lower stage relative to the eye.
Because the visible form of a higher stage is subtle, the eye of a lower stage cannot perceive it. Therefore, visible form is not of a higher stage than the eye.
Because the higher consciousness does not rely on the eyes of a lower level, consciousness is not "above" the eyes.
For this reason, visual consciousness is not above the eyes; as for form being [the object] of all consciousnesses:
Because form, in relation to consciousness, extends equally across the upper and lower realms,
it is said to be "all. This is just as with the consciousness of the desire realm.

The eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna perceives forms of the desire realm; this refers to the relationship between form and consciousness. The eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna perceives forms of the desire realm.

This refers to the case where form is viewed from the perspective of consciousness below. One who has attained the divine eye of the second dhyāna relies upon the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna to perceive forms of the second stage.
This refers to form in relation to consciousness. Regarding "the same applies to the body":
the two refer to form and consciousness;
these two, in relation to the body, may be equal to it, superior to it, or inferior to it.
Just as form relates to consciousness,
so it is said to be likewise.
It is like being born in the desire realm with a body.
When eye-consciousness of the desire realm arises and cognizes a form of the desire or form realms,
this is precisely consciousness of form.
"Expecting the body to be equal to the ground" means that while the body is in the desire realm,
one produces the higher divine eye and initiates the consciousness of the first dhyāna.
Having fully understood the form of the first dhyāna—
this is precisely the consciousness of form with respect to the body.
When one is born in the second dhyāna,
one relies upon the consciousness of the first dhyāna to perceive the forms of the lower stages.
This is precisely the consciousness of form (*rūpavijñāna*).
It refers to that which is below the body.
This is the meaning cited above.
This is a brief mention of one corner;
it is not an exhaustive enumeration.
The wise should understand that as it is with the eye, so it is with the ear.
This explains the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).
To rephrase the preceding verse: "The ear does not descend below the body;
the consciousness of sound does not ascend above the ear."
Sound is [the object] of all consciousnesses;
the same applies to the body.
Regarding the term "consciousness" used here:
This refers to the ear-consciousness. Regarding the statement that "the next three all belong to their own level," the "next three" refers to the nose, tongue, and body.
Because they follow immediately after the eye and ear,
they are called the "three successive [elements].
That is to say, the fourfold set consisting of the nose faculty, nose-consciousness, odor, and the body.
The tongue faculty and tongue-consciousness;
the four types of taste-objects;
the body faculty and body-consciousness.
Contact is of three kinds.
When these are compared with one another,
they all generally belong to their own respective stages.
That is to say, because these three types [of consciousness] grasp their objects by reaching them, the two consciousnesses of the nose and the tongue [function in this manner].
Because it belongs exclusively to the desire realm, the body-consciousness alone—
relative to the body and tangible objects—
pervades both its own level and lower levels.
Because it differs slightly from what preceded, the verse says:
"Body-consciousness [belongs to] its own level and lower levels.
Regarding "its own":
This refers to birth in the desire realm or the first dhyāna; that is, in the desire realm or the first dhyāna,
the body-consciousness (kāya-vijñāna) in relation to the body-tangible (kāya-spraṣṭavya).
Because they all share the same stage (*bhūmi*),
it is called "one's own.
As for "lower":
When one is born into the three higher meditative absorptions,
one borrows the consciousness of the first dhyāna to perceive the tactile sensations of those higher stages.
This refers to the body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna);
in relation to the body and its tangible objects, it belongs to a lower stage. Regarding the statement "it should be known that the mind (manas) is not fixed": it should be understood as follows.
It should be understood that the four factors of the mind-element (manodhātu) are indeterminate.
That is to say, there are times when the mind, body, consciousness, and mental objects all belong to the same level;
and there are times when they belong to different levels, either higher or lower.
During the states of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and at the time of taking birth,
they correspond accordingly,
being either identical or different.
This will be analyzed in detail later in the "Chapter on Concentration" (*Samādhivarga*).
The above seven sections constitute the conclusion of the digression.
Next, the correct treatise is distinguished.
From this point, the twentieth [section]:
among the eighteen elements (dhātus).
Chapter Twenty-one: Within the six consciousnesses,
how many are the objects of which consciousness?
How many are permanent?
How many are impermanent?
This is the twenty-second gate.
How many are faculties (*indriya*)? How many are not faculties or gates (*dvāra*)?
The verse says:

The five external [objects] are cognized by two; the eternal dharmadhātu and a portion of unconditioned phenomena are faculties. Together with the internal [faculties], there are twelve realms. Explanation: The five external objects—visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—are each cognized by two consciousnesses: their respective sensory consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The eternal dharmadhātu refers to the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), specifically *ākāśa*, *apratisaṃkhyānirodha*, and *pratisaṃkhyānirodha*. A portion of these unconditioned phenomena constitutes the faculty of the mind (*manendriya*). When combined with the six internal bases (the five sense organs and the mind), these constitute the twelve internal realms. Thus, it is said that together with the internal realms, there are twelve.
Regarding "the five external [objects] are cognized by two":
the five objective spheres, such as visible form and so forth,
are called the five external [objects].
Furthermore, among the five objects,
two are cognized by two types of consciousness,
while one is cognized by five types of consciousness.
Two are cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Excluding these five elements,
there are the remaining thirteen elements.
The meaning should be understood by analogy:

it is cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is not an object of the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*). As for the eternal *dharmadhātu*, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Only one portion of the dharma-dhātu is eternal, namely the unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
By implication, the remaining dharmas are impermanent. Regarding the phrase "the remainder of dharmas": it refers to those [dharmas] other than the unconditioned.
It refers to the remaining portion of the dharma-dhātu, excluding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Regarding the phrase "the remaining realms," it refers to the entirety of the other seventeen realms. The Treatise states:
Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of twenty-two faculties (indriya),
namely: the eye faculty (cakṣur-indriya) and the ear faculty (śrotra-indriya).
The nose faculty,
the tongue faculty,
and the body faculty.
The faculty of mind,
the female faculty,
and the male faculty.
The life-faculty,
the faculty of pleasure,
and the faculty of pain.
The faculty of joy,
the faculty of grief,
and the faculty of equanimity.
The faculty of faith,
the faculty of diligence,
and the faculty of mindfulness.
The faculty of concentration,
the faculty of wisdom,
and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

Regarding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) and the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the various great masters of Abhidharma, following the sequence of the Sūtras,
all deviate from the order of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) found therein.
The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is explained after the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) because it possesses an object (*sālambana*). The commentary states:
the Sūtra follows the sequence of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Immediately after the five faculties, such as the eye,
the mental faculty (manas) is explained. This treatise follows the sequence of the "faculty with an object" (sālambana) gate, following upon the "faculty without an object" (anālambana) gate.
Only after the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is the mind-faculty (manendriya) mentioned; that is to say,
the first eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty.
The fourteen [bases], beginning with the mind, are the "bases with objects.
As for the statement that "a portion of the phenomena-base (dharmāyatana) is a faculty": [it refers to the following].
Within the dharma-realm,
one portion constitutes the faculties;
namely, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
The five faculties of sensation, beginning with pleasure;
the five faculties beginning with faith;
these eleven faculties.
This is subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). A portion of the latter three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) is likewise subsumed within the dharma-element,
because the three untainted faculties have nine faculties as their essential nature.
These are the five faculties of mental pleasure, joy, equanimity, faith,
and so forth. Among these nine faculties,
there is only the single faculty of the mind.
They are not included within the dharma-element.
The remaining eight faculties are included within the dharma-element.
Therefore, among the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
one portion is taken and designated as being subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
Together with the twelve internal elements (*ādhyātmika-dhātu*), [these constitute the eighteen elements].
The five elements beginning with the eye,
together with the seven mental elements,
are called the twelve.
It is not merely that a single portion of the dharma-dhātu constitutes the faculties; rather, the twelve internal elements collectively constitute the substance of the faculties.
Specifically, the five elements such as the eye-substance subsume the five faculties such as the eye-faculty.
The seven mind-elements (cittadhātu) subsume the faculty of mind (manendriya).
The two— the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu)—
subsume one portion of the final three untainted faculties (anāsravendriya).
As for what is called "one part," it consists of the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) and has nine faculties as its substance.
Among the nine faculties, it includes only the mental faculty (manas-indriya);
therefore, it is said to be "one part."
The female faculty and the male faculty are subsumed within a portion of the body faculty.
This shall be analyzed later; the meaning is to be inferred accordingly.
As for the remaining five elements—form and so forth—and one portion of the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu):
All [of these] have as their essence that which is not a faculty (*indriya*). *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-śloka-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Two;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-śloka-vyākhyā*, Fascicle Three.
Chapter Two: Analysis of the Faculties (Indriya-vibhaṅga), Part One. Regarding the "Analysis of the Faculties":
they are called *indriya* because their function is preeminent and sovereign (*adhipati*). This chapter provides a detailed exposition thereof.
This is called "discrimination by name.
As for why the Chapter on Faculties (*indriya-varga*) is explained immediately after the Chapter on Elements (*dhātu-varga*):
the Chapter on Elements clarifies the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
The Chapter on Faculties (*Indriya-varga*) elucidates the functions of all phenomena.
Since functions arise based upon their essential natures, the faculties are explained next. The commentary on the verses of this chapter is divided into three sections.
First, the explanation of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*);
second, the explanation of the co-arising phenomena;
third, the explanation of the six causes and four conditions. Regarding the first, the explanation of the twenty-two faculties:
This is further divided into five parts:
first, the explanation of the meaning of "faculty" (indriya);
second, the clarification of the establishment and abolition of the faculties.
1. The essence of the three knowledges (*vidyā*).
2. The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). 3. Various classifications.
First, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*), there are two parts:
first, the presentation of the Sarvāstivāda school's position.
Second, the description of the divergent schools.
First, regarding the description of the Sarvāstivāda school, the treatise states:
"Thus, having already enumerated the various faculties according to their elements (*dhātu*)."

Regarding this, what is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)? [This asks about the meaning of faculty. It is called a "faculty" because it is preeminent (*parama*), sovereign (*īśvara*), and illuminating (*prakāśana*).
By this, the general meaning of "faculty" as "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) is established. [This answers the meaning of faculty.]
Because the substance of the faculties (*indriya*) is supreme,
they are called "most excellent" (*parama*); because the function of the faculties is supreme, [they are so called].
It is called "sovereignty.
Because its essence, substance, and function are both preeminent, it is called "radiant manifestation.
It is by virtue of possessing this most excellent sovereignty and radiant manifestation [that it is so named].
It is called "predominant" (*adhipati*).
The meaning of "predominance" is used here to explain the sense of a "faculty" (*indriya*).
This meaning of predominance—
With respect to whom does what have predominance? With respect to which of the twenty-two faculties does what exercise predominance?
The verse says:

It is said that the five [faculties] have predominance over four [things], the four faculties over two kinds, and the five and eight faculties each have predominance individually within the defiled and the purified. Commentary: The five faculties—faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—have predominance over four things: they are the cause for the arising of the five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), they are the basis for the attainment of the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), they are the antidotes to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and they are the causes for the purification of the three realms. The four faculties—the female, male, life, and mind—have predominance over two kinds of things: they govern the distinction between male and female, and they govern the continuity and cessation of the life-stream, as well as the maintenance and transformation of the mental continuum. The five faculties (the five spiritual faculties) and the eight faculties (the five spiritual faculties plus the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known") each have predominance individually within the categories of the defiled and the purified; that is, they govern the process of affliction and the process of purification, respectively.
Regarding the tradition that the five function with respect to four:
each of the five faculties, such as the eye,
functions with respect to four matters.
It can serve as a dominant condition in two ways:
first, by adorning the body;
second, by guiding and nourishing the body.
Third, the production of consciousness and so forth;
fourth, uncommon functions.
For instance, regarding the faculties of the eye and ear:
Adorning the body refers to those who are blind, deaf, or physically deformed.
Guiding and nourishing the body refers to...
"Because one avoids dangers by seeing with the eye and hearing with the ear":

this refers to the arising of the two consciousnesses of the eye and the ear, as well as their associated mental factors (*caitta*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the other mental factors. "Unshared function" (*asādhāraṇa-kārya*) means...
This means that the eye can see forms and the ear can hear sounds because their functions are distinct;
as for the faculties of nose, tongue, and body, they serve to adorn the body.
As with the eye and ear, that which guides and nourishes the body refers to the nose’s smelling of odors and the tongue’s tasting of flavors.
The body perceives tangible objects;
odor, flavor, and tangible objects— these three—
are of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
"Because they are capable of experiencing, they give rise to consciousness and so forth" means that they produce the three consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors.

"Their functions are not shared" means that the three functions of smelling, tasting, and feeling—namely, the apprehension of odor, flavor, and tangibles—are each distinct. "The four faculties [function] in two ways."
The female and male faculties, as well as the life and mind faculties,
are each able to exercise predominance over two matters.
Furthermore, regarding the female and male faculties,
there are two types of predominance:
first, the differentiation of sentient beings.
Second, the distinction of differentiation.
Regarding the differentiation of sentient beings:
it is by means of these two faculties.
It causes all sentient beings to be distinguished into the categories of female and male,
thereby differentiating them.
Due to these two faculties,
there are distinctions such as physical form, speech,
and the breasts; specifically, the male form is large.
The female form is small;
for males it is called "masculine" (xióng),
and for females it is called "fine" (xì).
The male breast is small;
the female breast is large. Regarding the two types of life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*): [the male and the female].
First, it can continue the past *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class);
second, it can sustain the present *nikāyasabhāga*. Regarding the mental faculty (*manas*), there are two functions:
first, it can continue future existence (*punarbhava*).
Second, regarding the "concomitance with mastery": what is called "subsequent existence" (punarbhava) refers to the existence of birth (upapattibhava).
It is from the state of the intermediate existence (antarābhava) that the mind of craving and aversion arises.
Thereupon, the existence of rebirth arises.
A sutra cited in the treatise states:
"At that time, the gandharva..."
Within these two types of mind,
either one manifests; that is to say,
it may be accompanied by craving.
Alternatively, there are *gandharva*s associated with anger and so forth;
this term means "seeking fragrance" (*xunxiang*),
which is a name for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Among those who are male,
they give rise to love for their mother and anger toward their father.
Among women, there are those who give rise to love for their father and give rise to hatred toward their mother.
The *Sūtra on Following the Sovereign* states:
"The mind can lead the world; this is the meaning of sovereignty.
The mind can universally encompass and follow along; this is the meaning of following."
In this way, the mind is the single dharma that acts with sovereign mastery over all;
it functions within the five and eight [categories] of defilement and purity.
The five refer to the five feelings, such as pleasure and so forth.
The eight refer to the five faculties beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). These [operate] within the context of defilement and purification.
They increase respectively.
Regarding the predominance of the five feelings,
such as pleasure, in terms of defilement:
Because the latent tendencies (anuśaya) such as greed increase in accordance with them;
that is to say, feelings of joy and pleasure are conducive to greed.
The feelings of sorrow and suffering are conducive to hatred;
the feeling of equanimity is conducive to delusion;
and so are the eight faculties beginning with faith.
Regarding "the predominance of purification," this refers to the fact that pure phenomena arise and increase accordingly.
Following this, the second section sets forth alternative explanations.
The verse says:
Predominant over the cognition of their own respective objects, The six faculties are established in total.
From among the body, two faculties are established, Based on predominance over the female and male natures.
Because they exercise sovereignty over the co-existent factors of affliction, purification, and increase,

one should know that life, the five feelings, faith and the others, as well as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" are established as faculties.
Regarding the phrase "in the attainment of successive paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth,
it is predominant," the commentary explains: "predominant with respect to its own object" means...
This refers to the six groups of consciousness,
because they are capable of cognizing objects;
[and] the six faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
Because they can produce the six consciousnesses and possess predominant efficacy in cognizing their respective objects,
there are the six [bases], such as the eye.
These are established collectively as faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the establishment of two faculties based on the body,
these are the female and male faculties.
Because it exercises predominance over the female and male sexes, there exist the physical form,
voice, and activities of a female body.
The distinction of aspiration and inclination is what is called "femininity.
As for its function:
[This refers to] sewing clothes and so forth.
As for inclinations and pleasures (*abhiprāya*), they consist of delighting in cosmetics and perfumes.
There are distinctions in the physical forms, voices, activities, and inclinations of males.
It is called "masculinity.
"Action" refers to activities such as writing and so forth.
Those whose inclinations and pleasures lie in archery and horsemanship;
these two types differ by virtue of their male and female faculties.
Regarding the statement that the female and male faculties have predominance over the two genders because they have predominance over coexistence, affliction, and purification:
this refers to the latter two phrases.
To explain these two phrases:
one should know that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) abides within the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga).
Regarding predominant influence, it should be understood that the five feelings have predominant influence with respect to the phenomena of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Greed increases in accordance with pleasant feeling;
hatred increases in accordance with painful feeling;
and delusion increases in accordance with neutral feeling. It should be understood that this applies to faith and the other [faculties] as well.
Regarding pure phenomena,
there is predominant efficacy by means of the five [faculties] beginning with faith.
At the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*,
one subdues the various afflictions (*kleśa*) because they lead to the Noble Path; thus it is said, "one should know."

It is taught that each of these [three] can individually serve as a faculty; the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) function with respect to the attainment of subsequent paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth.
Regarding those that possess predominance,
the phrase "is likewise" indicates that this applies to each one individually by way of analogy.

Each can serve as a faculty: that is, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) has a predominant influence regarding the attainment of the path of the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is the path of seeing (darśanamārga); the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (ājñendriya) is the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
because the path of seeing induces the path of cultivation.

It is predominant with respect to the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*); the faculty of having known is predominant with respect to the path for attaining the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
There is that which possesses predominant influence,
namely the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātendriya); this constitutes the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

The faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), because it leads from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to the path of no-more-learning.
The faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) exercises a predominant influence over the faculty of one who has fully known (ājñātāvīndriya).
The faculty of one who has already attained knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya) possesses predominant efficacy with respect to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Through the faculty of one who has final knowledge,
the mind attains liberation; when the mind is liberated, [it is liberated from the influxes].
Only then does one realize nirvāṇa;
therefore, it possesses predominant efficacy with respect to nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"One whose mind is not yet liberated cannot attain nirvāṇa. The verse states: "The subsequent [moments]."
Since the faculty of "having known" (ājñātendriya) follows after the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya),
and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (ājñātāvīndriya) follows after the faculty of "having known," they are called "successive" (uttarottara).

The word "etc. further indicates that there are other explanations. Some say that the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has a predominant function regarding the cessation of afflictions to be abandoned through seeing, while the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) [has a predominant function regarding the cessation of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation].
The faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñātāvīndriya) possesses predominant efficacy regarding the cessation of those afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life,
it has a predominant function;
by means of this faculty of having fully known, [one attains it].
Because it is able to experience the activities of joy and bliss within the body of liberation,
this concludes the second major section.
The clarification of the establishment and abolition of the faculties (*indriya*) consists of two parts: first,
the exposition of one's own school’s position.
Second, the presentation of divergent views.
First, regarding the exposition of our own school’s position,
this is intended to introduce the arising of the inquiry.
The treatise says:
"If they are established as faculties because of their predominance,"
Ignorance and its like, being fundamental natures,
should be established as faculties;
they are the causes of ignorance and so forth.
Since each [cause] possesses a distinct predominant influence over its respective results,
such as the formations (saṃskāra), this objection is raised from the perspective of one's own school.
The twelve links of dependent origination mutually induce one another,
possessing a predominant influence.
The vocal organ and so forth should also be established as faculties; that is, the vocal organ,
the hands, the feet, and the organs of excretion and reproduction.
Because they possess predominance, respectively, over speech, execution, renunciation,
and the pursuit of pleasure.
The commentary explains:
This is raised as an objection based on the Sāṃkhya school of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
That school establishes five sense organs (indriya).
The vocal organ is the fleshly tongue;
it possesses predominant efficacy with respect to speech.
The hand possesses predominant efficacy with respect to grasping.
The feet have a predominant function in walking;
the anus has a predominant function in the elimination of waste.
Sexual pleasure arising from the urinary organ has a predominant function;
therefore, it should be established as a faculty (*indriya*). Such matters [are to be treated] in this way.
One should not establish [these] as faculties,
because that which is accepted as a faculty possesses such characteristics.
The verse says: The mind’s basis, its differentiation, its abiding, its defilement, its provisions,
and its purification— it is by these measures that the faculties are established.
The commentary states:
"That upon which the mind relies" refers to the six faculties, beginning with the eye.
These six internal bases are the foundation of sentient beings.
As for their distinctions:
The differentiation of the characteristics of these six sense bases is due to the female and male faculties.
This refers to their abiding.
Furthermore, by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
these six faculties persist for the duration of a single lifetime.
This constitutes the defiled state.
These six faculties become defiled by means of the five feeling-faculties.
This is their provision.
These six faculties can serve as the provisions for untainted,
pure dharmas by means of the five [faculties] beginning with faith.
As for this "purity":
These six faculties become untainted and pure by means of the latter three faculties. Because these faculties are established,
all matters are brought to ultimate completion.
Therefore, one should not admit that ignorance and so forth,
nor the vocal organs and so forth,
are also established as faculties.
Because that [entity] lacks predominant influence within this context.
From this point onward,
the second section sets forth alternative explanations.
This is the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins.
The treatise states:
"Furthermore, there are other masters."
To explain the characteristics of the faculties separately,
the verse says:
They are either the basis for the process of transmigration, Or [the basis] for arising, abiding, and experiencing.
The fourteen [factors] prior [to cessation] are established; the subsequent [factors] of cessation are likewise.
*Commentary:* The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that this is the opinion of other masters (*apara-ācārya*).
The twenty-two faculties are established in accordance with the processes of saṃsāra and cessation.
Regarding the term "saṃsāra":
It takes consciousness as its essence,
because it flows and wanders within the cycle of birth and death.
There are four aspects of transmigration:
first, the basis of transmigration, namely the six sense faculties such as the eye;
second, the arising of transmigration.
Because they arise from those [roots],
by means of the female and male faculties,
the three [realms] abide in cyclic existence.
This means that by means of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya),
because one abides in dependence upon it,
there is the experience of the fourfold process of transmigration.
Because they are able to experience [objects] by means of the five faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*). Thus far,
the discussion has been based on four meanings.
The establishment of the preceding fourteen faculties can be understood through reflection. As for what is called "cessation and extinction," it refers to the stilling of birth and death.
It is called "cessation" (nirodha).
The attainment of nirvana constitutes the essence of cessation.
In the stage of cessation (nirodha),
the latter eight faculties are established based on the same four principles as mentioned previously.
First, the basis for cessation and extinction,
which refers to the five faculties beginning with faith and all wholesome dharmas.
Because it is the root of birth;
second, the cessation of birth occurs by means of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
Because this is the first to arise within the group of those fixed in rightness (samyaktva-niyāma),
the three [factors] abide in cessation.
By means of the faculty of "having known," the attainment of nirvāṇa is brought about through its arising in a continuous succession.
Fourth is the attainment of enjoyment through cessation,

by means of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*), because of enjoying the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). Furthermore, the treatise concludes:
By this, the measure of the faculties neither decreases nor increases;
it is precisely due to these conditions.
Regarding the statement "the sequence is established by this," it refers to the process of this cyclic existence (saṃsāra) and its cessation (nivṛtti).
[This is explained] by means of the twenty-two faculties (indriya).
It must not be increased or decreased further.
From this point begins the third major section, which clarifies the essential nature of the faculties (*indriya*).
Among these, the six faculties beginning with the eye,
together with the two faculties of female and male— these eight faculties.
The Chapter on Elements has already explained the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
These six will be analyzed below. There are only the five feelings (*vedanā*), beginning with pleasure (*sukha*).
Regarding the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya), there is no further place for further analysis;
therefore, they shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Displeasure of the body is called suffering; that same [displeasure], when pleasurable, is called happiness, as well as the mental pleasure of the three dhyānas; in other places, this is called joy.

Displeasure of mind is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow). The intermediate state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is not distinguished from the other two [roots].
