That which is called "suffering" (duḥkha) when the body is not at ease refers to bodily sensation; that is,
sensation associated with the five consciousnesses.
"Body" refers to the basis;
since sensation arises depending upon the body,
it is called "bodily sensation."
Because it is the sensation of the body;
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. As for the term "displeasure":
This has the meaning of "affliction.
That which can afflict within bodily sensation is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
That very same [bodily sensation] when it is pleasant is called pleasure (*sukha*).
That which is bodily feeling is what is called "this very pleasure. Among bodily feelings,
that which is capable of providing benefit is [pleasure].
This is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Regarding "the mental joy of the third dhyāna":
"mind" refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is the third dhyāna.
Feeling associated with the mind that is capable of providing benefit is also called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This refers to the third dhyāna.
Because the five consciousnesses are absent,
there is no physical sensation of pleasure.
The term "pleasure" (sukha) refers exclusively to mental satisfaction; elsewhere, this same term is called "joy" (prīti),
except in the third dhyāna,
where it applies to the three lower stages.
What is called "other places" refers to the lower three stages:
the desire realm and the first two dhyānas. As for "this":
This is the sixth consciousness-mind.
It means that this mind finds joy in the three lower stages.
This is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). In the third dhyāna,
the mind is joyful and tranquil.
Because it is free from craving for joy,
it is designated solely as the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) within the three lower stages.
Because the mind is coarse and agitated due to the presence of joy and craving,
it is called only the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). That which is not mental pleasure is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
Associated with mental consciousness,
it is the feeling that causes affliction;
it is a lack of joy in the mind.
This is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). Regarding "the neutral equanimity (*upekṣā*) is not distinct from the two":
"neutral" means neither pleasant nor unpleasant;
that is, it is the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*).
This neutral feeling is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
"The two" refers to both body and mind.
The body consists of the five consciousnesses;
the mind is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
Equanimity (upekṣā) resides in both body and mind.
Since they are equally non-conceptual and arise spontaneously,
although they pertain to both [realms], only one faculty, the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), is established. Furthermore, the treatise states:
Mental suffering and pleasure arise largely from conceptual discrimination;
this is not the case for bodily [suffering and pleasure].
Due to the power of their respective objects,
Arhats and others likewise give rise [to such thoughts].
Therefore, these faculties are established;
body and mind are each distinct.
To explain:
"Those that are mental pleasure and pain" refers to the sensations (vedanā) of the mental level;
pleasure and pain reside in the mind.
Because they arise from conceptual discrimination,
suffering is called sorrow,
and pleasure is called joy.
The sensation of pleasure exists in the third dhyāna,
where it is non-conceptual; it is for the sake of distinguishing this that [the term "pleasure" is specified].
Therefore, it is said that [feeling] arises from much conceptualization.
The two feelings of suffering and pleasure exist within the five bodies of sensory consciousness.
Because they are non-conceptual,
they are said to be "not so," namely,
the five bodies of consciousness.
Because it follows the power of the object,
it is called non-conceptual;
[this applies to] Arhats and others.
Since the noble ones are the same as ordinary beings in this regard, these sensations of suffering and pleasure exist within the five groups of sensory consciousness;
they are termed "suffering" and "pleasure."

In the sixth consciousness, these are termed joy (*saumanasya*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*). Regarding the establishment of the three faculties based on the nine [faculties] during the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning:
the "nine" refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), joy, pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
If one is on the path of seeing,
based upon these nine faculties,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is established.
If one is on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
based on these nine faculties, the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya) is established.
In the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
the faculty of one who has full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is also established based on these same nine.
The treatise says:
On what basis are these three names established?
This refers to being on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
where there is something previously unknown that one must know as the progression of the path proceeds.
Therefore, it is said that they are called "the unknown to be known. The commentary explains:
the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments of mind, namely, the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the seven knowledges (jñāna).
These fifteen moments of mind,
regarding the objects of the Four Noble Truths,
have never been known before.
One should know that the aspect of activity proceeds;
for example, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering arises simultaneously with the acquisition of doubt.
Not yet having known the Truth of Suffering is called "not previously known"; subsequently,
upon reaching the stage of knowledge [it is known].
Because it must be known, it is called "to be known. Just as this is the case for the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), so it is for the others.
The same applies to the other seven patiences; therefore,
patience is collectively termed "that which is yet to be known."
Although the seven intermediate knowledges are capable of correct cognition,
this is because they arise during the interim before the knowledge of the truths has become universal.
It is also called "that which is yet to be known.
Therefore, it is said that those who practice the path of vision (darśanamārga) are called "those for whom there is yet to be known."
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"If one is on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
there is nothing previously unknown."
However, in order to eliminate the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
one repeatedly cognizes that very same object once again.
Therefore, he is said to be "one who has already known.
The commentary explains:
From the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*),
these are collectively termed the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
If one is on the path of cultivation,
the eight truths of the upper and lower realms have been fully known.
There is nothing previously unknown;
it is solely for the purpose of severing the afflictions that delude one regarding phenomena—
namely, greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.
Because of the four latent tendencies (anuśaya),
one repeatedly gives rise to knowledge and cognition regarding the objects of the Four Noble Truths.
It is called "already known.
Therefore, it is said that for one who practices the path of cultivation,
it is called "already known."
Because one knows by means of having already known; furthermore, the Treatise says:
"In the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), one knows that one has already known."
Therefore, it is called "knowledge"; this explains "knowledge.
It refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), which constitute the realization that what was to be known has been known.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge.
One who possesses this knowledge is said to be "endowed with knowledge"; this explains the meaning of "endowment" (samanvāgata).
"To possess this" means to achieve it; alternatively,
it refers to one who has practiced this knowledge until it has become their very nature.
This is called "endowed with full knowledge"; this second [explanation] explains "endowment" in terms of cultivation.

That is to say, because one has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one knows for oneself as it truly is: "I have fully understood suffering."
There is no further universal knowledge;
this is explained at length as the exposition of the essence of knowledge,
namely, the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
This is the essence of full knowledge:
knowing for oneself as it truly is,
"I have fully understood suffering."
The aspect of this knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is that there is no further full comprehension;
it is the aspect of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
"I have abandoned the origin [of suffering]"—this is the knowledge of exhaustion.
That there is no further cutting off is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
That "I have realized cessation" is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).
This knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is not further realized;
"I have cultivated the path"—this is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). This knowledge of non-arising is no longer to be cultivated.
Because this meaning is included therein,
it is said, "and so forth, as extensively explained," which refers to the full exposition of all those faculties (*indriya*).
It is called the faculty of "that which is yet to be known" (ājñātavyendriya), and so forth.
The commentary states:
"This is an explanation of the names."
"That person" refers to one who has not yet known what is to be known, and so forth;
"one who practices" refers to such a practitioner.
Those [faculties] belong to persons;
the faculties belong to phenomena. "That which is yet to be known" and so forth [refer to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"].
Because the practitioner possesses these faculties within their human body,
they are called the "faculties of that which is not yet known and is to be known," and so forth.
The faculty of "that which is to be known by one who has not yet known" (ājñātāvyājñendriya) and so forth are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds.
What has been explained above concludes the third section on the essential nature of the faculties.
From here begins the fourth major section.
The analysis by way of various categories consists of six parts therein.
The first is the category of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Second is the gate of maturation versus non-maturation;
third is the gate of having maturation versus lacking maturation;
fourth is the gate of the three natures.
The section on the fivefold classification of realms.
The sixth is the section on the three types of abandonment. First, regarding the initial gate of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), the treatise states:
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:

Only the last three are untainted (anāsrava); it should be known that the [roots] with form, life, sorrow, and suffering are exclusively tainted (sāsrava). The remaining nine roots pertain to both. Commentary: The "last three" refers to the faculty of knowing what is not yet known (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñendriya), and the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya). These three are exclusively untainted because they are the nature of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the fruit of the path (phalamārga). The five faculties with form—namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) are exclusively tainted, as they are the basis for defilements and are associated with the realm of existence. The two faculties of sorrow (daurmanasya) and suffering (duḥkha) are also exclusively tainted, being associated with the afflictions of the desire realm. The remaining nine—the four faculties of feeling other than sorrow (i.e., pleasure, joy, equanimity, and mental pleasure), the five faculties of faith and so forth (śraddhā, vīrya, smṛti, samādhi, prajñā), and the faculty of mind—are classified as belonging to both categories, as they can be either tainted or untainted depending on their association with worldly or supramundane states.
Only the last three are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*):
namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "having fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Because these three faculties are situated at the very end,
they are called the "last three."
The essence is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); as for those with form, life-force, sorrow, and suffering, one should know that these are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the phrase "those with form": this refers to the seven material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
The five faculties beginning with the eye,
together with the female faculty and the male faculty— these seven faculties.
These are subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and are thus called "possessing form" (rūpin).
There are seven sense faculties that possess form.
As for "life, sorrow,

and suffering are exclusively outflowing (sāsrava), while the remaining nine faculties pertain to both," this means they pertain to both the categories of the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava).
That is to say: the faculties of mind, joy, pleasure, equanimity, and the five beginning with faith.
These nine all pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Following this, the second [section].
Regarding the gate of "resultant" and "non-resultant," the treatise states:
"Thus, having already explained the contaminated and the uncontaminated..."
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are maturation (*vipāka*) and how many are not maturation?
The verse says:
Life is exclusively maturation; Sorrow and the last eight [faculties] are not so;
The mental faculty and the remaining four feelings Each and every one of these are common to both [types].
The commentary states:
"Life is exclusively maturation" means that there is only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Concentration is definitely a result of maturation (*vipāka*),
because it is summoned by karma.
As for why sorrow and the latter eight [mental factors] are not:
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the subsequent eight faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are not maturation (*avipāka*).
This is because the faculty of sorrow pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The eight faculties beginning with faith are exclusively of a wholesome nature,
because they are determinate (vijñapti).

Therefore, they are not maturation (vipāka). Form, mind, and the remaining four types of sensation—each of these twelve faculties (the seven types of form, the mind-faculty, and the four sensations excluding sorrow)—pertain to both [categories]. "Form" refers to the seven types of form.
Together with the mind-faculty and the remaining four sensations (excluding sorrow), these constitute the twelve faculties.
Each and every one of these belongs to the category of both being and not being maturation (*vipāka*). That is to say,
the seven material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
That which is summoned by karma is precisely the ripened result (vipāka);
if it is nurtured (aupacayika), it is not a ripened result.
The mind and the four feelings that are summoned by karma are precisely the maturation (vipāka).
If it is of a wholesome or unwholesome nature,
or among the indeterminate,
it consists of deportment and craftsmanship.
Furthermore, the "attainment-result" (prāpti-phala) is not a maturation (vipāka);
therefore, there are twelve faculties.
This applies to both gates.
From this third [section] begins the gate of "having maturation" and "lacking maturation."
The treatise says:
Thus, the [classification of] the twenty-two faculties, such as the ripening faculty and so forth, has already been explained.
How many have maturation?
How many lack maturation?
The verse says:

Regarding the statement that "sorrow definitely has maturation":
it should be understood that the faculty of sorrow definitely has maturation.
Based on the meaning of "only" (*eva*),
the verse employs the term "certainly" (*niyatam*).
"Only" (*eva*) indicates that it refers specifically to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
It is solely the maturation (vipāka).
It is called "transcending" because it possesses two meanings:
it transcends the sequence of the faculties (indriya-krama).
First, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is discussed.
Regarding the two meanings:
first, sorrow is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because they arise through forceful reflection;
secondly, they are not untainted (anāsrava), because they belong exclusively to the realm of distraction (vyagra-bhūmi).
For this reason, the sequence is bypassed;
it is stated first that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) necessarily possesses maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding the statement that the first eight and the last three lack [maturation]:
the "first eight" refers to the first eight faculties, beginning with the eye.
The latter three are the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
These constitute the eleven faculties.
There are definitely no ripened results for eight [faculties], namely the eye and so forth,
because they are indeterminate in nature.
This also applies to the final three faculties.
Because these are untainted (*anāsrava*), they cannot produce a fruit; therefore, they lack maturation (*vipāka*).
As for the mental faculty (*manas*) and the remaining [faculties]—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth—each of them pertains to both [categories].
Excluding the mental faculty (*manas*), the remaining four feelings (*vedanā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*),
these ten faculties each pertain to both categories: those with maturation (*savipāka*) and those without maturation (*avipāka*).
That is to say: volition, feeling, perception, and formations;
whether they are wholesome or unwholesome in nature, as well as those that are with outflows (sāsrava).
That which is of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) or is untainted (anāsrava) has no ripening fruit (vipāka);
as for the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), it possesses the nature of being either wholesome (kuśala) or unwholesome (akuśala).
That which is of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) has no maturation (vipāka);
however, if the five faculties such as faith (śraddhā) are with outflows (sāsrava), they do have maturation.
Those that are designated as having maturation (*savipāka*) are so called because they possess maturation;
those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) lack maturation. Therefore, these ten [factors] pertain to both categories.
From this, the fourth [section].
Regarding the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the treatise states:
"Thus, having already explained [the categories] such as those with maturation (*savipāka*)," etc.
Among the twenty-two faculties,
how many are wholesome and how many are unwholesome?
How many are indeterminate?
The verse says:
Only the last eight faculties are exclusively wholesome; the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasya) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The mind and the other sensations are of three kinds; the first eight are exclusively indeterminate.
The commentary states:
"Only the last eight faculties are wholesome."
That is to say, the eight faculties beginning with faith are called the "last eight faculties" (antyāṣṭa-indriya),
as they are exclusively of a wholesome nature (kuśala-svabhāva). As for the faculty of mental grief (daurmanasya), it pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because it arises from volitional effort;
it is of both wholesome and unwholesome natures. As for the mind and the other sensations, they are of three kinds.
The mind-faculty and the other four faculties, excluding the faculty of grief—these five are associated with all three natures; the first eight are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The first eight, beginning with the eye-faculty, are exclusively of an indeterminate nature.
The five faculties beginning with the eye,
together with the male, female, and life faculties,
are called the eight faculties.
From this, the fifth [section],
the gate of the realms of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*).
The treatise says:
Having thus explained the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, [one may ask]:
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
How many are bound to the formless realm?
The verse says:
In the desire, form, and formless realms, respectively, the last three are excluded.
"Combined with female, male, sorrow, and suffering, along with the remaining [states of] form, joy, and pleasure. Commentary:
The first phrase indicates the three realms.
"Respectively excluding the latter three.
"Respectively" refers to the meanings set forth below.
This is paired with the first phrase;
hence it is said "in successive order.
The last three [phrases] are excluded.
This clarifies those bound to the desire realm. Within the desire realm,
there are nineteen faculties.
Excluding the last three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), because those three faculties are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*); this also includes the female and male faculties,
as well as the faculties of grief and suffering.
It is explained as being bound to the realm of form. Within the realm of form,
it is as previously excluded.
Excluding the last three faculties and additionally removing the four faculties of female, male, sorrow, and suffering,
the remaining fifteen faculties are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
As for the exclusion of females and males:
it is because they have abandoned sexual desire; furthermore, it is because the female and male organs are physically unattractive.
The Sūtra states that those in the form realm who are called "male" possess the characteristics of a male.
It is not said that they possess the faculty of pleasure but lack the faculty of suffering.
Because their bodies are pure and sublime, it is not a basis for suffering; furthermore, because they lack unwholesome states, it is not an object of suffering. They also lack the faculty of grief.
There is śamatha because it moistens the continuum; as for the continuum, this body is not a basis for sorrow.
Furthermore, because there is no occurrence of affliction or harm therein, it is not an object of sorrow. This applies equally to other forms of joy and bliss.
This clarifies the connection with the formless realm. Within the formless realm,
it is just as it was in the form realm.
Excluding the last three faculties, as well as the female and male faculties, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of suffering;
furthermore, excluding all other material forms (*rūpa*) and the faculties of joy and pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "all other material forms":
The five faculties beginning with the eye,
together with the male and female faculties, are termed "the rest.
Excluding these, the remaining eight faculties are [meant].
Those bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) consist of the five beginning with faith (śraddhā),
as well as vitality (jīvita), mind (manas), and equanimity (upekṣā).
From this, the sixth [section]:
the three gates of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The treatise says:
Having thus explained those factors bound to the desire realm and so forth,
among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
How many are to be abandoned by cultivation?
How many are not to be abandoned?
The verse says:
The mental [faculty] and the three feelings are common to all three [types of abandonment]; the sorrow [faculty] is abandoned by insight and cultivation;
nine are abandoned only by cultivation; five are abandoned by cultivation, and none are abandoned by neither.
This is the explanation.
Regarding "the mind and the three feelings are common to all three":
the mind and the three feelings are common to the three types of abandonment.
Regarding the three feelings,
they are joy, pleasure, and equanimity;
these are the four faculties mentioned above.
If they are with outflows (sāsrava),
they are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation; if they are without outflows (anāsrava), [they are abandoned through seeing].

Only that which is not to be abandoned; as for the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), it is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) when associated with delusions regarding the nature of reality (*tattva-moha*),
and all other remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) states are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
These are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
They do not extend to those that are not subject to abandonment (*aheya*). Regarding the "nine that are abandoned only by cultivation":
the nine refer to the seven material faculties, the life-faculty, and the faculty of suffering.
Only those abandoned through cultivation; the seven material faculties and the life-faculty are of indeterminate nature because they are non-defiled.
The faculty of suffering is associated with the five consciousnesses.
It is not produced by the sixth consciousness.
As previously stated, it is undefiled;
nor is it produced from the six [senses] as form.
Since they are certainly not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), these nine faculties are not abandoned by insight;
for they are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
Those that are not to be abandoned are not included.
Regarding the five that are cultivated but not the three that are neither: the five are as follows.
The five faculties, such as faith and the rest,
are cultivated through both [paths] and are not abandoned by either; however, if they are with outflows (sāsrava), [they are abandoned by the path of cultivation].
These are to be abandoned by cultivation; if they are untainted,
they are not to be abandoned.
Because they are non-defiled, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) do not pertain to what is abandoned through seeing;
they are exclusively not subject to abandonment,
as they are not non-untainted phenomena.
Because these are what are to be abandoned.
The above constitutes the fourth [section].
The analysis by way of various categories is complete.
From this, the fifth [section] clarifies miscellaneous distinctions;
therein are six [parts].
First, the gate of obtaining maturation upon taking birth;
second, the gate of the number of faculties that cease at the stage of death;
third, the gate of the number of faculties used to attain the fruits [of the path].
4. The section on the fixed number of faculties for those who have attained accomplishment;
5. The section on the minimum number of faculties;
6. The section on the maximum number of faculties.
Now, first, regarding the gate of obtaining maturation through taking birth,
the treatise says:
The various categories of meaning for the different gates have already been explained.
Now, in which realm is how many ripening faculties (*vipākendriya*) first acquired?
The verse says:
Those born from desire—womb-born, egg-born, and moisture-born—initially obtain two [faculties] as maturation;
those born by transformation initially obtain six, seven, or eight. In the form realm, six; above that (the formless realm), only life.
Explanation:
Regarding those born from womb, egg, or moisture who initially obtain two types of maturation:
"desire" refers to the desire realm;
"womb, egg, or moisture birth" refers to these modes of birth.
This excludes those born by transformation.
Among these three modes of birth,
this refers to the initial stage of taking birth.
One obtains only the two ripening faculties of body and life, because these three faculties arise gradually; thus, no other faculties are obtained.
Regarding those born by transformation (upapāduka) who obtain six, seven, or eight [faculties]:
In the initial stage of birth by transformation,
one acquires six, seven, or eight faculties.
Regarding the statement that one acquires six faculties:
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and life-faculty;
this refers to the time at the beginning of the kalpa,
when beings were formless and born by transformation.
There are those who possess six faculties and acquire seven faculties,
such as the various devas and others.
The six faculties are as described above.
Adding the male or female faculty makes eight;
those who obtain eight faculties are said to be in the evil realms.
There may be two sexual organs, as is the case with those born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Their six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are as described above,
with the addition of the two sexual organs, male and female.
Regarding "in the form realm, six [are acquired] at first, and only life [is acquired] above":
"form" refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
there, one initially acquires the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
As it was stated regarding those without form within the desire realm,
"above there is only life" refers to the formless realm.
That which is superior to the two lower realms is called "upper.
First, there is the superiority of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
which is the cause for the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Second is the excellence of birth;
this is the fruit of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), wherein one initially acquires only a single faculty (indriya).
This refers solely to life.
From this point downward is the second stage: the state of death.
Regarding the number of faculties that are extinguished,
the *Śāstra* states: "This refers to the explanation of the maturation faculties (*vipākendriya*)."
Having first attained [the faculties], in which realm does one die,
and how many faculties cease last?
The verse says:
At the moment of death, the faculties cease: in the formless realm, three; in the form realm, eight;
in the desire realm, nineteen or eighteen for sudden death, and four for gradual death; for those of good [karma], five are added.
Thus it is explained.
Regarding the phrase "the faculties that are in the process of ceasing at the moment of death," this single line flows into the following three lines.
All of these are explained together.
Regarding the "three colors and eight [factors] of the formless realm": within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are three types of color and eight factors.
At the stage of imminent death,
there are three faculties that cease:
namely, life, mind, and equanimity.
Regarding the eight [faculties] of the form realm: when one passes away from the form realm,
eight faculties cease at the moment of death.
This refers to the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, and the five faculties beginning with the eye.
The treatise states:
"All beings born by transformation."

"One must possess all faculties [at the moment of death] because one undergoes birth and death"—this explains the preceding meaning. Regarding "those who die suddenly in the desire realm [possessing nineteen, eighteen, or eight [faculties]":
this refers to sudden death in the desire realm.
Nineteen, eighteen, or eight faculties [are present] at the final cessation;
as for the cessation of ten faculties:
This refers to a person of dual sexual organs at the moment of sudden death; [at that time],
the five faculties, beginning with the eye, [cease].
The female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, mind faculty,
and equanimity faculty— these nine faculties cease at the final moment of death.
This refers to those with only one sexual organ;
among the ten mentioned previously, they die instantaneously,
excluding the female and male organs.
The extinction of eight faculties refers to a person without sexual organs who dies suddenly of the ten aforementioned faculties.
Excluding the two [faculties] of female and male, because they lack physical form. Regarding "the four wholesome [faculties] gradually increase by five":
"gradually" refers to gradual death.
When one dies gradually in the desire realm,
at the moment of passing away,
only four faculties cease.
These are body, life, mind, and equanimity.
Regarding "the five increase in the wholesome":
"wholesome" refers to a wholesome mind.
When one dies with a virtuous mind,
five additional faculties are increased,
namely, the five beginning with faith.
The aforementioned sudden and gradual deaths,
involving the extinction of the three faculties and so forth,
are explained with reference to those who pass away while in a defiled or neutral state of mind.
If one dies with a wholesome mind,
faith and the other [faculties] are further increased within the preceding stages.
Therefore, the first three faculties increase up to eight faculties;
the first eight faculties cease.
Increasing to thirteen;
when the previous nine faculties have ceased,
adding [one more] increases it to fourteen.
Previously ten faculties ceased;
now they increase to fifteen.
At death, four faculties cease gradually.
Increasing to nine faculties:
this refers to death with a wholesome mind in the three realms,
all of which possess the five [faculties] beginning with faith.
From this point onward,
the third section clarifies the number of faculties required for the attainment of the fruit.
The treatise states:
Within the analysis of the faculties (*indriya*),
all phenomena pertaining to the faculties should be thoroughly examined and discerned.
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
how many are capable of realizing which fruit of the religious life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*)?
The verse says:
Nine attain the two extreme fruits; seven, eight, or nine attain the middle [fruit];
twenty-one become arhats. Regarding the statement that one may rely on a single [fruit], the commentary explains as follows:
Regarding the nine who attain the two extreme fruits:
"extreme" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*).
Because they abide at the beginning and the end,
they are called "extremes.
These two extremes constitute the two fruits.
The first fruit, stream-entry, is realized through nine faculties.
Regarding those obtained by means of nine faculties:
That is to say: the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity,
the five faculties beginning with faith,
and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
It is already known that there are nine;
as for the fruit of stream-entry,
it relies upon the threshold concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
Therefore, it is exclusively the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
The treatise states:
"The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*)."
The faculty of "I-have-known" (ājñātendriya) exists in the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga);
it exists in the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
These two support one another to attain the first fruit,
according to their respective order.
Regarding the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), it can function as both an inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and a supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*).
The commentary explains: "The 'unknown-to-be-known' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) resides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)."
The fifteenth mind is the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti); it is the faculty of having known (ājñendriya).
Regarding those on the path of liberation,
it refers to the sixteenth moment of mind,
which is the knowledge of the subsequent category of the path (mārgānvayajñāna).
That path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) serves as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the acquisition of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti).
This is called the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*).
As for the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it [is associated] with the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyogaprāpti*).
Arising simultaneously,
it maintains the acquisition of disjunction;
this is called the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*).

The acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) is the acquisition [of the fruit] with respect to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The fruit of arhatship is acquired by means of nine faculties (*indriya*).
That is to say: the faculty of mind, the five faculties beginning with faith,
the faculty of one who has already known, and the faculty of one who possesses complete knowledge.
There are eight [factors];
by taking any one from among joy, bliss, and equanimity,
nine are thus established.
The Arhat’s supernormal power is realized through nine stages.
These nine stages are: the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and [the four dhyānas and four formless attainments].
The four fundamental dhyānas and the three formless attainments,
excluding the Peak of Existence.
If one realizes it by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna,
and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
the feeling is exclusively equanimity (*upekṣā*). If one relies on the first and second dhyānas...
The sensation of joy is realized by relying on the third dhyāna; the sensation of pleasure is realized [by relying on the fourth dhyāna].
Thus, regarding the three sensations:
Take whichever one of these you prefer.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñendriya) resides in the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga)."
The faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) resides in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
These two support one another to attain the final fruit.
Respectively, they function as the inducing cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) and the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*) for the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
The commentary explains:
"The faculty of having already known (ājñātāvīndriya) residing in the path of immediate succession" refers to the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi).
The faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) that exists in the path of liberation is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);
it severs the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The ninth uninterrupted path is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The ninth path of liberation—
It is called the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
Its uninterrupted path (ānantaryamārga) serves as its homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).
The acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*); the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
The possession of dissociation (visamyoga-prāpti) is called the supporting cause (niśraya-hetu). Among the seven, eight, and nine [fruits],
"two" refers to the two intermediate fruits.
These are the fruits of the Once-returner and the Non-returner.
Among these two fruits,
there are either seven faculties.
Alternatively, there are eight faculties or nine faculties for the realization [of the fruit].
Specifically, regarding the attainment of the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) by means of seven faculties:

This refers to the mundane path, which is realized through successive stages and attained by means of seven faculties: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The five faculties, such as faith and so forth, rely exclusively on the *anāgamya* stage when realizing the fruit of a Once-returner; therefore,
they are only acquired or abandoned [at that point].
It does not pertain to other feelings; it is attained by means of eight faculties based on the supramundane path.
Seven faculties are as previously described.
Adding the faculty of "having known" makes eight; this applies to one who has attained the fruit of a once-returner and has transcended it by being doubly detached from sensual desire.
Just as the fruit of stream-entry is realized by means of nine faculties: having previously, while in the stage of an ordinary person,
abandoned six grades of craving.
He is called one who has doubled his detachment from desire;
now he enters the path of seeing and proceeds until the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna).
To transcend the stage of stream-entry and directly realize the second fruit is called "transcendent realization."
What has been explained above is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), which is attained through the seventh,
eighth, or ninth [moment of the path].
One should understand this well: those who attain the fruit of non-returning by means of the mundane path do so through realization according to the successive stages.
It is attained by means of seven faculties:

namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Regarding attainment by means of eight faculties, there are two types of such groups of eight.
Furthermore, regarding the first eight:
based on the supramundane path,
the seven faculties are as described above.
Adding the "already known" makes eight.
As for the second set of eight:
it employs the mundane path.
They are realized in successive order;
namely, the five faculties of mind, joy, equanimity, faith, and so forth.
Therefore, the treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the sequential realization of the fruit of non-returner: if,
within the ninth path of liberation, [one attains it].
Upon entering the fundamental stage,
relying on the mundane path,
it is attained by means of eight faculties.
That path of uninterrupted transition is associated with the sensation of equanimity;
within the path of liberation...
Furthermore, there is the feeling of joy;
these two support one another,
enabling the attainment of the third fruit.
Regarding the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*), there are two causes as previously stated.
The commentary explains: "If one realizes [the fruit] by leaping over [stages]..."
It is certain that one does not rely on the preparatory stage (anāgamya);
rather, from within the ninth path of liberation,
one enters the fundamental [dhyāna].
As for "by transcending":
having first attained the fundamental [attainment],
one no longer aspires or seeks further.
Therefore, one does not enter [the fundamental dhyānas]. As for the one who realizes [the fruits] through successive stages,
because they have not yet attained the fundamental [dhyānas], they [realize them] within the preparatory concentration (anāgamya).
Regarding the ninth liberation:
if one wishes to enter it,
one attains entry into the fundamental [state].
The equanimity-feeling within the path of uninterrupted transition refers to the equanimity of the preparatory stage (anāgamya-bhūmi).
The joy-feeling within the path of liberation refers to...
The fundamental joy of the first dhyāna arises from the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) by which the afflictions of the lower stages are abandoned.
Because of rejoicing in the higher stage,
one enters the fundamental [dhyāna] within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Regarding those who attain it by means of nine faculties:
There are two kinds of ninefold [attainments].
First, regarding the ninefold attainment of the initial [stage],
it refers to the "transcendent realization" (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti).
Therefore, the treatise states:
"One who has completely abandoned sensual desire and realized transcendence."
It is attained by means of nine faculties,
as previously described for the leap-over attainment; this refers to the stage of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) when one was formerly at the level of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Having severed the nine grades of afflictions,
one is said to be completely detached from desire;
now one enters the path of seeing.
The subsequent path knowledge of the ultimate path transcends the first two fruits and directly realizes the third.
This is called "transcendent realization.
Although this is the general description,
there are distinctions.
This means that because there are distinctions among the levels (bhūmi) upon which it relies,
one may take any one from among pleasure (sukha), joy (prīti), or equanimity (upekṣā).
Regarding the preceding fruit of transcendence, it is said in the treatise that there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and above. The commentary explains:
"Although this is the general statement..."
That is to say, when stated in general, there are nine;
their number is the same as that of the Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin),
yet there is a distinction between them.
Within the faculties (*indriya*), there is a distinction in the designation "feeling" (*vedanā*);
it is not the same as that of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
"Because this [fruit] has distinctions based on its level (bhūmi)" explains the aforementioned term "distinction. That is to say,
this fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin).
Because they are realized based on six stages,
there is a distinction between the stages.
If one relies on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) or the *dhyānāntara* (intermediate dhyāna)...
The realization of the fourth dhyāna employs only the feeling of equanimity,
based upon the first and second dhyānas.
One realizes it by means of the feeling of joy,
relying on the third dhyāna;
one realizes it by means of the feeling of pleasure.
Therefore, among the three feelings,
one may be selected at will;
this is precisely what is meant by the term "faculty" (indriya).
There is a distinction. Regarding the second ninefold category:
those who realize the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) by following the sequence employ the supramundane path (lokottaramārga).
If, within the ninth path of liberation,
one enters the fundamental stage.
It is attained by means of nine faculties:

namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
That path of immediate succession is associated with equanimity.
Within the path of liberation,
there is furthermore the sensation of joy;
thus, there are two sensations.
Because it is the supramundane path,
the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*) is added; therefore, the treatise says:
Based on the supramundane path,
it is attained by means of nine faculties;
these are the same eight faculties as previously mentioned, with the addition of the faculty of "I-have-known" (ājñendriya).
Regarding the ninth uninterrupted path and its corresponding liberation path,
because they coexist with these [eight faculties], the eight faculties are as previously described;
this is likewise based on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
The number of middle eight faculties plus "already-known" (ājñātāvīndriya) makes nine.
This is because [the faculty of] immediate liberation co-exists with this.
This is the faculty of having known (*ājñātendriya*).

Because it coexists with both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it must be added [to the list]. According to what has been explained above:
Regarding the statement in the verse that there are "seven, eight, and nine," it should be understood that there are two kinds of seven:
namely, one set of seven for each of the once-returner and the non-returner.
There are three kinds of eightfold [attainments].
That is to say, among the fruits of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin),
there is one kind of eightfold attainment.
Within the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), there are two kinds of eight; within the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), there are three kinds of nine.
Within the fruit of once-returning, there is one kind of nine.
"Among the Non-returners, there are two [categories], nine [subdivisions]. Regarding the "eleven Arhats," this is raised as an objection by citing the *Mūla-śāstra*.
Thus, the treatise states:
It is asked:
"Does not the *Mūla-abhidharma* ask, 'By how many faculties [is this attained]?'?"
One attains arhatship by means of eleven faculties (*indriya*). Why,
then, is it said that one attains the eleven faculties by means of nine faculties?
Mental joy, pleasure, and equanimity;
the five faculties beginning with faith;
and "already known" and "fully known."
Regarding the statement "based on what is possible for one":
this addresses the preceding objection by relying on the fact that within a single body, all eleven faculties can potentially exist.
Therefore, the root treatise states: "In reality, there are nine;
thus, nine faculties are taught.
As the treatise says:
In reality, one attains the fourth [fruit] by means of only nine faculties;
as for why the root treatise states that eleven faculties are involved:
It is said based on the possibility within a single body; that is,
it is possible for there to be a single *pudgala*.
From the stage of one beyond training,
after having repeatedly fallen away,
by means of joy, bliss, and equanimity.
One [of these] manifests at present,
and subsequently one further realizes the fruit of arhatship;
for this reason, the fundamental treatise speaks of eleven faculties.
However, there is never a single moment when the three feelings arise simultaneously;
therefore, it is now stated that [the attainment of the fruit] is necessarily by means of nine or more faculties. The commentary explains:
The fruit of arhatship,
because it is realized throughout nine stages,
is realized through the three feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity. Furthermore, according to the Sarvāstivāda school:
It is admitted that Arhats may repeatedly fall away; therefore,
within a single lifetime—
It is admitted that there are three types of feeling for one who realizes arhatship;
however, at the moment of realization,
there is only one type of feeling.
Therefore, it is said that there are nine faculties;
each is established according to a specific meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another. The Treatise says:
Regarding the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala),
why is it not stated in this manner? The intention behind this objection is that [it refers to] the third fruit.
It is permitted that one may repeatedly regress through the realization of all six stages;
it is possible for the realization of the three types of sensation to occur within a single lifetime.
Why does the fundamental treatise state that there are eleven faculties,
using the absence of the faculty of pleasure as proof for the fruit of non-returning?
However, at a later time, there is the possibility of falling away;
yet, even after such falling away, because one subsequently attains [the state] through joy, the previous objection is answered. The commentary explains:
If one realizes [the fruit] through the faculty of pleasure,
one will certainly not fall away; if one were to fall away,
there would necessarily be no subsequent realization through the faculty of pleasure.
Therefore, one should know that for those who realize the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*),
there is necessarily no joy (*prīti*) or equanimity (*upekṣā*); and for those who realize joy or equanimity, [there is necessarily no pleasure].
Because there is necessarily no pleasant feeling [in that state],
it is impossible for three types of feeling to be simultaneously present within a single body; thus, there is no scriptural evidence for such a possibility.
Because it refers to the meaning of attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*),
it cannot be said that eleven faculties [are involved].
Furthermore, the treatise states:
It is not the case that one who has previously attained the third dhyāna by transcending desire through leaping (vyutkrāntaka) can later undergo retrogression from this fruit of freedom from desire.
It is attained through two paths because it is extremely firm and stable.
The commentary explains:
This passage explains why the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) serves as proof of non-retrogression.
Because this faculty of pleasure exists in the third dhyāna, one who realizes it through the successive stages [of attainment]...
Because one has attained only the first dhyāna, the realization of the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) must necessarily be by way of transcendence (vyutkrāntaka);
that is to say, while in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one has severed the afflictions (kleśa) of the second dhyāna.
At a later time, it is possible to rely upon the third dhyāna to give rise to the path of seeing and realize the fruit of non-returning; therefore,
we know that there is "leaping over" (vyutkrāntaka).
He gives rise to the faculty of pleasure;
this transcendent person will ultimately never fall back.
Because it is attained through two paths:
first, that which is attained through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) when one has exhausted the afflictions of the desire realm while still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, one now enters the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
which is attained through the Noble Path; this refers to a person who realizes [the truths] in successive order.
Since it is attained through the single path alone, it may be regressed.
This aforementioned meaning is obscure.
The treatise contains essential points;
therefore, I have recorded them in full.
This is the fourth [section] from here.
Regarding the accomplishment of the faculties,
the *Viniscaya-mukha-śāstra* states:
Now it should be investigated:
among those various faculties, which ones are possessed?
How many are necessarily accomplished?
The verse says:
One necessarily accomplishes life, mind, and equanimity; Each of these three is necessarily accomplished.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four;
if one possesses the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses five faculties.
If one possesses the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven.
If one possesses female or male [faculties] or the faculty of grief, one possesses eight faculties each;
if one possesses the [five] faculties of faith and so forth, one possesses eleven; if one possesses the two untainted (anāsrava) faculties, one possesses thirteen.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Regarding the statement that one necessarily accomplishes three— vitality (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—
this refers to the fact that these three faculties are necessarily accomplished;
that is to say, at the time one possesses vitality.
There must be the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). If one possesses the faculty of equanimity, there must necessarily be the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);
it cannot be absent. If one possesses the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) or bodily sensation (*kāyendriya*), each is necessarily accompanied by four [faculties].
That is to say, when one possesses the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya),

there must necessarily be the faculties of life (jīvitendriya), mind (manas), and equanimity (upekṣā). Likewise, when one possesses the faculty of the body (kāyendriya), there must also necessarily be the faculties of life, mind, and equanimity.
Therefore, it is said that they are distinct.
Regarding "accomplishing the bliss but not the body," this refers to noble beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
one accomplishes the untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya) belonging to the lower three dhyānas; yet,
while accomplishing the body, one does not accomplish the faculty of pleasure.
This refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has been reborn in the fourth dhyāna;
such a person lacks the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
for that faculty has already been abandoned in the three lower dhyānas.
Since they are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana),
they cannot achieve the lower untainted bliss (anāsrava-sukha); therefore,
they do not possess the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
This constitutes the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Regarding the attainment of pleasure (*sukha*) but not joy (*prīti*), this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) being born in the third dhyāna. Regarding the attainment of the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as joy, each necessarily constitutes five faculties.
The eye and so forth include the ear, nose, and tongue.
If one possesses the eye faculty,
one necessarily possesses five.
That is to say, the body, life, mind, equanimity, and the eye faculty.
Just as it is with the eye,
so too do the ear, nose, and tongue each constitute five faculties.
To explain this by analogy with the eye-faculty:

the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) consists of five faculties, namely, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), the mind-faculty (manindriya), the equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya), the pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya), and the joy-faculty itself.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"One born in the stage of the second dhyāna has not yet attained the third dhyāna."
Regarding the question, "Having abandoned the lower [level] but not yet attained the higher, what faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) will one then possess?"—
the intent of this passage is to challenge the previous claim that one must necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure in the second dhyāna.
In its own stage there is no pleasure (sukha),
yet there is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
In the first dhyāna, there is the pleasure of the three consciousnesses.
Now that it has already been abandoned,
and because the mental pleasure of the third dhyāna has not yet been cultivated and attained, [it does not arise].
If one says that having abandoned the lower [levels] but not yet attained the higher,
what faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) will be accomplished? One should say that the defiled faculty of pleasure of the third dhyāna is accomplished.
The answer is given because others have not yet attained it.
As long as one has not severed the defilements of the third dhyāna,
one necessarily possesses [it].
"Others who have not yet attained" means that others have not yet attained the [other] faculties (*indriya*). "If one accomplishes the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
one necessarily accomplishes seven" means that such a person necessarily accomplishes seven faculties, including that faculty of suffering.
These are the faculties of body, life, mind, joy, pleasure, equanimity,
and suffering. Now, that which constitutes the faculty of suffering necessarily belongs to the desire realm.
Therefore, these seven types must not be omitted.
Among the four kinds of feeling (vedanā):

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is excluded because it is abandoned through detachment from desire. If one possesses the female or male faculties, as well as the faculties of sorrow, faith, and so forth, each constitutes eight;
that is to say, when one possesses the female faculty.
There must be eight; seven faculties are as in the case of suffering,
with the addition of the female faculty.
The male faculty is also eightfold:
seven faculties are as [described] for suffering,
with the addition of the male faculty.
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is likewise eightfold;
it is like the seven faculties [of suffering] with the addition of the faculty of grief.
If one accomplishes faith and the others,
each constitutes eight [faculties]:
namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, and the five faculties beginning with faith.
Regarding "the two untainted [roots] and eleven":
this refers to the two untainted faculties— namely, the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya) and the faculty of "already knowing" (ājñendriya)—
each of which consists of eleven faculties.
The eleven faculties of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) are:
the life-faculty, the mental faculty, the faculties of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith,
and the faculty of one who has already known.
Regarding "possessing eleven":
among the aforementioned eleven faculties, the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) is excluded.
Including the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," there are thirteen initial untainted [faculties];
that is to say, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
One who possesses the first untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya) necessarily accomplishes thirteen faculties.
Regarding these thirteen:
This refers to the five faculties of body, life, mind, joy, and equanimity, as well as suffering, faith, and so forth;
to these is added the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), together with the faculty of the body and the faculty of suffering.
If one has established the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," one must necessarily be in the desire realm;
therefore, bodily suffering certainly exists.
From this, fifth, regarding the section on the minimum number of faculties (*indriya*) established:
the treatise says:
Regarding those who possess the absolute minimum,
how many faculties do they accomplish?
The verse says:

At minimum, eight [faculties] are non-virtuous: [the five faculties of sensation,] the faculty of life, the faculty of mind, and the faculty of ignorance. When one is born in the formless realm, [one possesses] the virtuous [faculties of] life, mind, and equanimity. The commentary states: [The minimum number of non-virtuous faculties is eight: the five faculties of sensation, the faculty of life, the faculty of mind, and the faculty of ignorance. When one is born in the formless realm, one possesses the virtuous faculties of life, mind, and equanimity. The commentary states:
The minimum number is eight for those who lack wholesome states;
these refer to icchantikas,
who are said to be devoid of wholesome states.
If they possess the minimum number, they are endowed with eight faculties:

namely, the five feeling-faculties, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, and [the equanimity faculty]. This refers to a fool born in the formless realm who possesses the wholesome, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, and equanimity.
"Fools" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
because they have not yet seen the Truths.
If such individuals are extremely few in number...
One accomplishes eight faculties:
namely, the five beginning with faith,
plus the three consisting of life, mind, and equanimity.
Regarding this sixth section,
"The Maximum Number of Faculties," the treatise states: "As for those who possess the maximum number [of faculties]..."
How many faculties are accomplished?
The verse says:
At most, nineteen are accomplished; for those with both sexual organs, three pure faculties are excluded.
The noble one who has not yet abandoned desire, excluding two purities and one gender—thus it is said that at most nineteen [faculties] are attained. Commentary:
"At most, nineteen are attained" means:
The first is the thesis;
"the two forms, excluding the three purities" is the explanation.
This clarifies that for those born as distinct beings, nineteen faculties serve as the basis for acquisition.
That is to say, a person with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) is necessarily not an *ārya*;
therefore, they do not possess the three purities.
As for the "three purities," they refer to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
Apart from these three, [there is nothing else].
The remaining nineteen faculties may all be possessed [by them].
Regarding "a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire, excluding the two pure [faculties] and one gender":
this clarifies that such noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire can possess the maximum number [of faculties].
This also constitutes nineteen faculties:
namely, those of the first two fruits and the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka).
This refers to noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire.
The phrase "excluding two purities and one gender" clarifies the faculties that are excluded.
If one abides in the path of vision (*darśanamārga*),
with the exception of the two purities of "already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and "fully known" (*ājñendriya*).
If one abides in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Excluding the two purities of "not-yet-known" and "already-known," and excluding one of the two sexual organs from among the female and male faculties.

One type is excluded because no noble being (ārya) possesses both sexual organs; therefore, the noble beings of the desire realm possess these three pure faculties and the remaining nineteen faculties.
All [these] capacities are fully possessed.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-kaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Three;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-kaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Four.
From this major section, the second part clarifies the co-arising of all phenomena. Within it, there are two sections:
first, the explicit clarification of simultaneous arising; second, the detailed differentiation of their distinctions. Regarding the first, the explicit clarification of simultaneous arising:
First, it clarifies that material phenomena arise together;
second, it clarifies that the four categories arise simultaneously.
First, regarding the clarification that material phenomena arise together:
The treatise raises the question:
Now it should be investigated that all conditioned phenomena differ according to their respective characteristics.
Arising is also distinct for each [phenomenon].
"Are there any phenomena that necessarily arise together?"—this is the general question. "There are those that necessarily arise together"—this is the general answer. That is to say: all phenomena.
Briefly, there are five categories:
first, matter;
second, mind.
Third, mental factors;
fourth, formations dissociated from mind;
fifth, unconditioned phenomena.
"Unconditioned and unarisen.
Here, this is not stated as a general designation for all phenomena;
rather, the intention is to refer to those that are co-arisen.
To simplify the discussion on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), we shall first distinguish matter (*rūpa*) and determine its co-arising; this is a specific inquiry into matter.
The verse says:
In the desire realm, a subtle aggregate (*paramāṇu*) without sound And without sense-faculties consists of eight substances.
The body faculty consists of nine things; the other faculties consist of ten things.
The commentary states:
"In the desire realm, a subtle aggregate that is without sound and without faculties consists of eight things."
"Desire" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Subtle" has the meaning of being fine;
it does not refer to an atom (*paramāṇu*).
The aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*) is extremely subtle;
the designation "subtle aggregate" (*aṇu-skandha*) is established for that which is manifest (*prabhāsvara*), as nothing subtler than this exists.
This [aggregate] is found in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is without sound and without the body faculty (*kāyendriya*). These eight factors arise together, and not one is diminished.

Regarding the "eight factors," they refer to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and air—and the [four] derived qualities of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. When the body faculty is present, there are nine factors.
There is a collection of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) in which nine factors arise together;
eight factors are as previously described.
The body constitutes the ninth.
Regarding the ten faculties that possess remaining [faculties],
these are the eye, ear, nose, and tongue.
These are called the remaining faculties.
Each of these— eye, ear, nose, and tongue—
is born simultaneously with ten factors.
Furthermore, for example, wherever there is the eye-faculty,
there must necessarily be the body-faculty;
above these, there must necessarily be earth, water, fire, and wind.
Visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility;
thus, ten [bases] are established.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the others.
The same applies to the three [faculties] of ear, nose,
and tongue, as well as to the ten matters;
thus the treatise says:
The eye, ear, nose, and tongue are necessarily not separate from the body;
yet, when viewed in relation to one another, their locations are distinct. This refers to the aforementioned two lines.
The first phrase reveals that there must necessarily be a body;
the latter two phrases clarify that the four sense organs are each distinct.
One cannot add the ear and so forth upon the eye. If sound should arise within any of the aforementioned aggregates,
[it is perceived by the ear].
The numbers increase accordingly:
nine, ten, and eleven refer to the preceding eight with the addition of sound to form nine.
The first nine, with the addition of the prefix *pra-*, form ten;
the first ten, with the addition of the prefix *pari-*, form eleven.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
Because the locus of sound does not arise apart from the sense faculty;
that is to say, it is appropriated.
The great elements (mahābhūta) arise as causes,
and because the meaning of "root" (indriya) is implicit here,
this text specifically points it out.
Second, regarding the clarification that the four categories arise simultaneously,
the treatise states:
Having thus already established the co-arising of the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
the co-arising of the remaining absorptions shall now be established.
The verse says:
"Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; [so do] the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena or their acquisitions.
The commentary explains: Regarding the phrase "mind and mental factors necessarily arise together":
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together;
if even one of them is absent, the others do not arise.
As for the various characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) or their acquisitions (*prāpti*).

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are precisely all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); these are of four kinds, namely: form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), and [conditioned phenomena dissociated from mind].
Mental non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) refer to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
These various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) necessarily arise together with the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the two characters "must be simultaneous" (必俱) from the preceding sentence extend to this point;
one should say that the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) must be simultaneous. Alternatively, regarding "acquisition" (prāpti):
acquisition refers to the acquisition [of dharmas] upon all conditioned phenomena.
This means that within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
only those factors pertaining to sentient beings arise simultaneously with their acquisition (*prāpti*).
It does not apply to insentient things; therefore, it is said that "it may be.
From this point upward, the two sections differ.
Always first. This concludes the section on the simultaneous arising of the primary [factors].
Next is the second.
The main text provides an extensive analysis of the distinctions [among mental factors].
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the mental concomitants (caitasika-dharma).
Second, the explanation of the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is explained within the context of the mental factors (*caitasika*),
and the text is divided into four sections.
First, clarifying the five stages;
second, clarifying the co-arising with meditative concentration;
third, clarifying the distinctions among similar types.
The fourth section clarifies the distinctions among various names.
Regarding the first part, which explains the five stages (*bhūmi*),
the first subsection provides a general enumeration of their names and numbers.
Second, the detailed explanation of the names and entities.
First, regarding the general indication of the names and numbers,
the treatise says:
Regarding what was previously mentioned as "mental factors" (caitta), what are they?
The verse says:
Regarding the statement, "Mental factors are, for now, fivefold," the commentary on the differences among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and so forth explains:
"Mental factors are, for now, fivefold."
This indicates the positions of the mental factors (*caitta*).
The phrase "the great ground dharmas and so forth differ" enumerates their number.
1. The universal ground-dharmas (mahābhūmika).
2. The great wholesome ground-dharmas (kuśalamahābhūmika).
3. The great afflictive ground-dharmas (kleśamahābhūmika).
The four great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*),
the five minor afflictive mental factors (*parītta-kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*). Regarding a brief explanation of the name "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
the treatise states:
"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to a sphere of activity.
If this is the sphere of activity for that [phenomenon], then this is said to be the ground of that phenomenon; this explains the meaning of the single character "ground."
The "ground" (bhūmi) is the sovereign mind;
it is so called because it is the sphere of activity for the mental factors (caitta).
Thus, it is termed a "ground."
This refers to the sphere of activity.
To say "if it is thus" means this is the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
To say "it is that" refers to those mental factors (*caitasika*).
As for "the sphere of activity," it refers to...
The mind is the sphere of activity for mental factors.
To say that this [mind] is the ground (bhūmi) for those phenomena is because the mind is their sphere of activity.
This very mind is said to be the ground for those mental factors (caitta-dharma). Because it is the ground of great dharmas (mahā-dharma), it is called "Great Ground" (mahā-bhūmi);
this explains the two characters of "Great Ground."
The term "great" here refers to the ten mental factors (caitta), namely sensation (vedanā),
perception (saṃjñā), and so forth.
Because feeling, perception,
and so forth, pertain to all mental states across the three natures.
Therefore it is called "Great.
If one speaks of the "great earth," this likewise refers to the sovereign mind (citta-rāja).
The mind is merely the earth element,
yet it is not the "great" [earth].
What is now called "great earth" is as follows:
The ground of the Great Dharma is called "Great Ground" (*mahābhūmi*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound.
In this context, those factors that belong to the universal ground are called the universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma).
This means that the dharma is always present in all minds; this is the explanation of the three characters "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika).
Regarding the phrase "in this":
it refers to within these mental factors.
Among these mental factors (*caitasika*),
the ten mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) belong to the category of universal factors (*mahābhūmika*).
They are called "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma). Because they are factors that exist on the universal ground,
they are termed "universal mental factors."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound).
Thus, one should know that the term "Great" (*mahat*) refers exclusively to the mental factors (*caitta*).
If one speaks of "great earth," this refers to the sovereign mind; thus,
it is called a "universal mental factor" (mahābhūmika-dharma).
This refers back to the mental factors (caitta).
Above this, there are two layers of *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds;
one should reflect upon this well. This is the second [section] below.
This section provides a detailed explanation of the names and essential natures,
correctly elucidating the five stages (*bhūmi*).
The text is divided into five parts.
Furthermore, regarding the first category, the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
the treatise asks:
"What are those factors?"
The verse says:
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and desire; wisdom, mindfulness, attention, resolve, and concentration—these are present in every state of mind.
The commentary states:
The first three phrases provide the enumeration;
the fourth phrase—
Thus, it receives the name "universal mental factor" (mahābhūmikadharma).
"Feeling" (vedanā) means experiencing;
this is of three kinds.
Suffering,
pleasure, and that which is neither.
Because there is a distinction [between them], neither is it the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), nor is it perception (*saṃjñā*), which is the grasping of an image—
meaning the grasping of specific characteristics within an object. Volition (*cetanā*) is that which performs formative activity (*abhisamskāra*).
This means it enables the mind to engage in activity.
Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the act of touching;
it arises from the conjunction of the three: the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
There is the capacity for contact and engagement.
"Desire" refers to the longing for the tasks to be performed.
"Wisdom" refers to the capacity for discernment regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) refers to clear recollection of an object such that it is not forgotten.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is that which directs the mind toward an object.
It has the nature of being able to arouse the mind’s alertness.
As for resolve (*adhimokṣa*),
it is the ability to confirm or ascertain an object.
This matter is thus; it is not otherwise.
Generate a sublime resolve.
Samādhi is here translated as "equipoise" (samāhita).
It refers to holding the mind in a state of equality.
It functions toward a single object;
furthermore, because it sustains the mental factors, it is conventionally designated as "mind.
It pervades all states of mind.
This explains the name of the stage of "attaining liberation" (vimukti).
These ten mental factors (caitta) pervade all categories of consciousness (cittakalāpa), including those of the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The other mental factors (*caitasika*) cannot be universal; therefore,
these alone are designated as "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmikadharma*).
Second, regarding the explanation of the universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*),
the treatise states:
The "Great Wholesome Ground" (mahākuśalabhūmi) is called the "Great Wholesome Ground" (mahā-kuśala-bhūmi); this explains the three characters of "Great Wholesome Ground.
It refers to the ten mental factors (caitta), such as faith (śraddhā) and so forth.
Because it accompanies all wholesome minds and is designated as "greatly wholesome," the mind-king is called the "Great Wholesome Ground" (*mahābhūmi*),
for it is the sphere of activity for these greatly wholesome dharmas.
