"Great wholesome ground" (mahākuśalabhūmi) is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore,
it is called the "great wholesome ground."
This refers exclusively to the mind-king.
Among these, whatever dharmas belong to the great wholesome ground (mahābhūmika).
It is called the "great wholesome ground-factor" (*mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharma*). This explains the four characters of the term *mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharma*.
Herein, "herein" refers to among these mental factors (*cetasika*).
That is to say, the ten [mental factors] beginning with faith;
because they belong to the category of the great wholesome ground, they are called the "great wholesome ground factors" (mahākuśalabhūmika).
"Great wholesome ground-dharmas" is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
What are those dharmas?
The verse says:
Faith, heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, shame and dread, the two roots,
and non-harming— diligence alone pervades all wholesome minds.
The commentary states:
Faith is clarity and purity.
It is like the water-clearing jewel, which is able to purify turbid water.
The mind possesses the pearl of faith,
which causes the mind to become clear and pure.
Some say it concerns the Four Noble Truths, the Three Jewels, and the karmic results of wholesome and unwholesome actions.
"Acceptance with forbearance is called faith;
furthermore, non-negligence consists in cultivating all wholesome dharmas."
The treatise says:
"Apart from all wholesome dharmas, what else could be called 'cultivation'? This is the meaning of the objection."
Wholesome dharmas are themselves cultivation.
Apart from wholesome dharmas,
what else could be called cultivation?
This is called non-negligence (*apramāda*).
That is to say, its nature consists of focused attention toward what is wholesome; this answers the preceding objection.
Concentration is cultivation;
it is called heedfulness.
In the sūtras of other schools:
There is such an explanation:
that which is able to guard the mind is called "heedfulness and pliancy."
"Lightness" refers to agility;
"tranquility" refers to composure.
These pertain to wholesome states (*kuśala-dharma*).
That which possesses capability is called the mental faculty of capability (*cittakarmaṇyatā*). Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the relinquishing of lethargy and agitation,
causing the mind to become balanced.
The two types of conscientiousness— shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*)—
will be explained later.
As for the verse’s mention of "two faculties":
This refers to non-attachment and non-hatred,
which are the two roots of goodness.
Non-delusion is not mentioned here.
The wholesome root of non-delusion has wisdom as its essence;
it is included among the previously mentioned universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
Since wisdom has already been included [in the preceding categories],
it is not mentioned again among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). As for "non-harming" (*avihiṃsā*):
This means being free from harm and affliction.
"Diligent" refers to vigor,
which has the nature of enabling the mind to be courageous and resolute.
The verse states, "only pervading wholesome minds," which explains the meaning of the term "attaining the stage" (bhūmi-prāpta).
That is to say, it refers exclusively to pervading wholesome minds.
Because the previously mentioned faith and other factors possess these two meanings:
first, they are exclusively of a wholesome nature;
second, they pervade all wholesome minds.
Just as the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma), although they pervade all wholesome minds,
are not exclusively wholesome.
Only faith and the others possess both meanings,
and thus they receive the designation of "great wholesome ground-dharmas" (mahābhūmika-kuśala).
From this, the third [section].
To clarify the universal factors of great affliction (*mahā-kleśa-bhūmika-dharma*),
the treatise states:
"Thus, the universal factors of great wholesomeness have already been explained."

Regarding the term "the ground of great afflictive dharmas" (*mahākleśabhūmi*): explaining these four characters, "the ground of great affliction," they refer exclusively to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
The mind is the ground of the great afflictions;
thus it is called the "great affliction ground" (*mahā-kleśa-bhūmi*), according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis. Regarding the phenomena within this [ground]:

That which belongs to the great ground of affliction is called the "great afflictive mental factors" (*mahākleśabhūmikadharma*); this explains the five characters of the term *mahākleśabhūmikadharma*.
Among these mental factors, they refer to the six beginning with delusion (*moha*).
Because these are factors belonging to the category of the great ground of affliction,
they are called the "great affliction ground factors" (mahākleśabhūmikadharma).
The term "great affliction-ground" (mahā-kleśa-bhūmika) is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Thus, one should understand that the three characters "great affliction" (mahā-kleśa) [refer to the great afflictions].
The four characters "only," "ignorance" (*moha*), and so forth, refer to the great afflictive ground;
the character "mind" (*citta*) refers to the sovereign mind-king (*cittarāja*).
The five characters for the "universal mental factors of great affliction" (mahākleśabhūmikadharma) still refer to ignorance (*moha*) and the others;
one should reflect upon this well. That is to say, these factors always exist within a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*); this explains the aforementioned great meaning. What are those factors?
The verse says:
Delusion, negligence, indolence, lack of faith, lethargy, and restlessness are always exclusively defiled.
The commentary says:
Delusion (*moha*) is ignorance;
it is also called nescience (*avidyā*), because it arises from being deluded regarding objects. It is also called lack of wisdom (*ajñāna*).
Because there is no decisive resolution, it is also called "lack of manifestation" and "lack of clear comprehension. "Laxity" refers to negligence;
it is the failure to cultivate various virtues, whereas [the opposite] is the cultivation of various virtues.
The factor to be countered is laziness (*kausīdya*),
which refers to a lack of mental vigor and fortitude.
This refers to what was previously stated:
lack of faith, which is the direct opposite of diligence.
It causes the mind not to be clear and pure;
this is what was previously described as that which is counteracted by faith.
"Lethargy" (styāna) refers to mental and physical heaviness with respect to wholesome phenomena.
It is incapable of performing its function;
it is also termed the incapacity of body and mind.
*Uddhata* means restlessness (*auddhatya*).
It causes the mind not to be tranquil;
it is always and exclusively defiled.
This explains the meaning of the term "attaining the stages" (*bhūmi*).
"Universal" (vyāpin) means "constant.
Among these six types mentioned above,
one is exclusively defiled.
The second category, however, is universally defiled;
possessing these two characteristics,
it alone receives the name "universal ground of great afflictions" (mahā-kleśa-bhūmika-dharma).
Furthermore, for instance, although sensation and the other [mental factors] are pervasive and defiled,
they are not exclusively defiled.
Although the ten afflictions, such as anger and the rest, are exclusively defiled,
they are not universally defiled.
Therefore, none of these are designated by the name "great afflictive ground.
Following this fourth [section],
that which clarifies the "great unwholesome ground factors" is presented.
The treatise says:
Thus have the universal factors of great affliction and the universal factors of great unwholesomeness been explained.
It is called the "Great Unwholesome Ground" (*mahā-akuśala-bhūmi*). This explains the four characters of "Great Unwholesome Ground.
It refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*);
the mind-king is the ground for great unwholesome dharmas.
It is called the "Great Unwholesome Ground" (*mahā-akuśala-bhūmi*).
This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
In this context, it refers to those factors that belong to the Great Unwholesome Ground.
It is called the "great unwholesome ground-dharma" (*mahā-akuśala-bhūmika*).

This interpretation of the five characters of "great unwholesome ground-dharma" indicates that these dharmas, such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth, are always present within an unwholesome mind.
This refers to shamelessness and so forth,
because they are all factors belonging to the category of the great unwholesome ground.
It is called the "great unwholesome ground-dharmas" (*mahā-akuśala-bhūmika-dharma*).
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the dharmas belonging to the great unwholesome ground. What are those dharmas?
The verse says:

Only in all unwholesome minds are there lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The commentary says: [These two mental factors] exist exclusively within every unwholesome state of mind.
Regarding this "pervasive unwholesome mind," it explains that shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) acquire the designation of "great unwholesomeness."
They are lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya). The former is exclusively unwholesome in nature;
the latter pervades all unwholesome states of mind.
Possessing these two meanings,
it alone receives the designation of "great unwholesome.
This is similar, for instance, to [the case of] feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Although these are universal unwholesome states of mind,
they are not exclusively of an unwholesome nature; this refers to the seven afflictions such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth.
Excluding flattery, deception, and arrogance—
these seven, together with anger,
although they are exclusively of an unwholesome nature.
Because they are not universally unwholesome states of mind,
neither of these two modes of activity receives the designation of "greatly unwholesome."
As will be explained later,
this is the fifth section:
the explanation of the factors of the minor defilement ground (parīttakleśabhūmika).
The treatise says:
Thus has been explained the category of the great unwholesome mental factors (akuśala-mahābhūmika) and the category of the minor afflictive mental factors (parīttakleśabhūmika).
The three characters "minor affliction ground" (kṣudrānuśaya-bhūmi) refer to minor afflictions;
these are anger and the others.
This is the minor affliction ground.
This refers immediately to the mind-king (*cittarāja*).
The mind-king is the ground for the factors of minor affliction;
thus, it is called the "ground of minor afflictions" (*parīttakleśabhūmi*).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).

Herein, whatever dharma belongs to the *parītta-kleśa-bhūmi* (minor defilement stage) is called a *parītta-kleśa-bhūmika-dharma* (dharma of the minor defilement stage); thus, the five characters "this parītta-kleśa-bhūmika-dharma" [are explained].
The ten beginning with anger (*krodha*):
that is to say, anger and the others belong to the category of the minor defilement ground (*parīttakleśabhūmi*);
therefore, they are called the "minor defilement ground factors" (*parīttakleśabhūmikadharma*).
The "dharmas of the minor defilement ground" (parīttakleśabhūmika) are explained by the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
This means that those dharmas which constitute a portion of the defiled mind are designated by the name "minor defilements."
Because it does not pervade all [phenomena], it is said to be "partial. What are those phenomena?
The verse says:
Anger, concealment, avarice, envy, vexation, Harmfulness, resentment, guile, deceit, and arrogance—
Such categories as these are called the "mental factors of the minor defilement ground. Commentary:
These ten, beginning with anger,
are called the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*);
that is to say, they possess three characteristics.
First, it is abandoned solely through cultivation;
second, it arises in the mental consciousness level and is associated with ignorance;
third, it manifests individually.
Because it possesses these three meanings,
it alone is designated as the "ground of minor afflictions" (parīttakleśabhūmi). For example, this is like the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), such as feeling (*vedanā*),
and the six universal afflictive mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika-dharma*), such as delusion (*moha*).
And the two factors of lack of shame and lack of dread;
among the indeterminate factors, greed, hatred, vitarka, vicāra,
and sleep— these various dharmas.
All three meanings apply here.
Although the two types— conceit and doubt—
are associated with mental delusion (*manas-moha*), [they are not included].
When both are absent, it is abandoned only by cultivation; pride is abandoned through both seeing and cultivation;
doubt is abandoned only by seeing;
and although regret is abandoned only by cultivation—
Because they are associated with the ignorance of the "deficient" mind and are of a wholesome nature,
they are all not termed "minor defilement-ground dharmas."
The above five sections, though differing,
collectively conclude the detailed explanation of the essential nature of the fifth stage.
From here begins the second [section].
This clarifies that concentration and birth occur together.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the desire realm.
Second, the explanation of the higher realms.
First, regarding those that arise simultaneously with the desire realm,
the treatise asks:
In this context, it should be explained: in which category of mind (*cittapakṣa*) are how many mental factors (*caitta*) determined to arise simultaneously?
The verse says:
Because desire is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, there are twenty-two mental factors within the category of wholesome states of mind. At times, kaukṛtya (remorse) is added;
in unwholesome states that are not shared [with other afflictions], and when associated with views, there are only twenty.
The four afflictions, anger, and so forth; The twenty-one [mental factors] of regret;
The eighteen obscured [factors]; The twelve are admitted as unobscured;
Sleep is compatible with all; If present, each increases by one.
The commentary states:
To understand this verse,
one must first know [the nature of] the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are five types of mind-moments (*citta-varga*).
Namely: the wholesome is of one kind; the unwholesome is of two kinds.
One is associated with non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī-avidyā*); this refers to this type of mind-moment.
There is only ignorance and no other afflictions.
It is associated with the two [types of] greed, hatred, and so forth. There are two types of neutral (avyākṛta):
first, the obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta).
The two [types of] non-obscured neutral [states]. Now, this verse explains co-arising based on these five categories;
because there are vitarka and vicāra in the realm of desire, there are twenty-two mental factors within the category of wholesome minds.
In the desire realm, there must necessarily be vitarka and vicāra; therefore,
within the category of wholesome states of mind, [these two factors are present].
Twenty-two are co-emergent:
namely, the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) and the ten great wholesome mental factors (kuśalamahābhūmika).
As well as vitarka and vicāra, there are times when kaukṛtya (remorse) increases;
however, this kaukṛtya is common to both virtuous and non-virtuous natures.
Within a virtuous mind...
Because existence and non-existence are not fixed,
it is said that "at times" [this occurs].
If a wholesome mind is present, [it arises].
In the aforementioned category of mind,
with the addition of remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
twenty-three [mental factors] are formed. Regarding what is called "remorse":
The treatise offers three interpretations. It says:
"What is the meaning of 'evil action' (akuśala-karman)? It asks about the essence of that which is evilly performed."
This is called being difficult to answer;
it refers to giving rise to a mind of aversion toward the tasks one has undertaken.
Whether evil or good,
whether performed or not performed,
both reside within its sphere. One should know that herein, it takes unwholesome actions as its object.
It is called "remorse" (kaukṛtya).
That is to say, it is the nature of mental regret that takes remorse as its object.
The commentary states:
Since the matter of the misconduct did not accord with one's wishes,
remorse subsequently arose.
This very remorse, arising with the mental state of regret (*kaukṛtya*) as its object, is termed "regret.
Regret is the objective referent.
It is not remorse;
it is now called "remorse" because one has performed evil deeds.
This is named after its object.
The following is the treatise:
for example, the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
It is called "emptiness" (śūnyatā).
Non-attachment toward the impure is called "the foul" (aśubha).
The commentary states:
This passage provides an illustration to establish the explanation.
It concerns the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
It takes meditative concentration as its essence;
it is now called "emptiness" because it takes emptiness as its object.
The name is derived from its object. The meditation on impurity has non-attachment as its essence;
it is called "impurity" here because it takes the impure as its cognitive object.
It is named according to its object;
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is likewise. Furthermore, it is observed in the world that [names] are designated based on their locus of dependence.
This explains the basis upon which [the mental state] depends. For example, when one says that all the villages, towns, and kingdoms have gathered together,
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is precisely the basis for subsequent regret.
Therefore, it is designated as "remorse" (kaukṛtya) based on its support.
The commentary states:
The intention of this second explanation is as follows.
Since remorse arises only after one has first committed a misdeed,
it is known that misdeed (*kaukṛtya*) is the basis for remorse (*vipratisāra*).
Now, to call remorse "the evil-doer" is to manifest the dependent phenomenon by means of its basis.
Just as when a person relies on a village, that village is the basis of reliance;
if people gather together, one says "the village has come," which refers to the village as the basis of reliance.
This reveals the person who is the basis [of the fruit]. Furthermore, the name of the cause is metaphorically applied to the essence of the fruit,
as when one says, "these six bases of contact."
"One should know this as the result of past karma.
The commentary states:
"This is the third explanation."
The cause is this misconduct;
the fruit is remorse.
Now, it is called "remorse."
Regarding the phrase "one who performs evil deeds":
this is because the name of the cause is applied to the effect,
as in the expression "the speaker."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"These six bases of contact" refers to the six faculties, beginning with the eye.
These six bases of contact are the fruit;
past karma is the cause. When the Sūtra says that the six bases of contact are karma, [it means they are the result of past karma].
This is also a case of applying the name of the cause to the effect.
Question: What kind of regret (*kaukṛtya*) is designated as wholesome?
The answer is: it is the nature of mental regret regarding what was done or not done among wholesome or unwholesome deeds;
that is, with respect to a previous time.
One fails to perform what is wholesome and performs what is unwholesome;
later, one feels regret.
It is called "good regretful action" (*kaukṛtya*). That which is contrary to this is called "unwholesome.
This refers to having previously performed a wholesome act.
To not commit evil and later feel regret for it is called unwholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse).

Therefore, these two types of regret (*kaukṛtya*) arise respectively based on the two bases of the wholesome and the unwholesome. Regarding the statement that "in the unwholesome [mind], when not associated with wrong view,
there are only twenty [factors]," this clarifies the category of the unwholesome mind.
Twenty mental factors arise together.
Regarding "unwholesome and unshared," this refers to the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
"View" refers to unwholesome view. "Concomitant" means being associated with an unwholesome mind;

specifically, it is twofold: first, association with non-specific (unshared) ignorance (*asāmānyāvidyā*), and second, association with unwholesome views. Now, regarding the category of unwholesome minds characterized by non-specific ignorance:
There must necessarily be twenty mental factors arising simultaneously,
namely: the ten universal factors (mahābhūmika) and the six universal defiled factors (kleśamahābhūmika).
The two [factors] of the great unwholesome ground,
as well as vitarka and vicāra; the second unwholesome [factor],
which is associated with the category of mind characterized by views.
That is to say, within this mind,
there may be wrong views,
or there may be the grasping at views.
In some cases, there is the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and likewise twenty mental factors arise together;
their names are exactly as explained previously in the section on the unshared [factors].

Among the five views, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), these two views are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) views. Question: Regarding this category of mind associated with unwholesome views:
There are twenty-one in total.
Twenty are as previously stated;
one additional unwholesome view should be added.
Why are both said to be twenty? The answer is:
it is not because of an increase in views;
there are not twenty-one.
This is because, within the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma),
it is specifically the function of wisdom (prajñā) that is designated as "view" (dṛṣṭi).
Seeing has wisdom as its essence;
within the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),
wisdom is already fully included.
Therefore, they are not repeated. Regarding the twenty-one factors consisting of the four afflictions, anger (*krodha*), and so forth, along with remorse (*kaukṛtya*):
these comprise three categories.
First, the four afflictions.
Greed, hatred, doubt, and pride.
Second, "anger and so forth" refers to the ten minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The three types of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) refer to the remorse found among the unwholesome states.
These are the three categories of mind.
Each is accompanied by twenty-one mental factors arising simultaneously.
First, regarding the category of mind associated with the four afflictions,
there are twenty-one [factors].
That is to say: the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika), the six universal factors of great affliction (kleśamahābhūmika),
and the two universal factors of the unwholesome ground (akuśalamahābhūmika).
Together with vitarka and vicāra,
these twenty, plus any one of the [root afflictions] such as greed, constitute [the twenty-one].
The name is the twenty-first. Regarding the twenty-one factors such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth:
twenty are as previously stated, with the addition of one, namely anger.
Regarding the twenty-one unwholesome factors of remorse (*kaukṛtya*):
twenty are as previously stated,
with the addition of one factor of remorse.
"Being obscured, there are eighteen" refers here to the obscured-unspecified mind of the desire realm; that is to say,
it is associated with the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
These two types of views can obscure the Noble Path; alternatively,
they may be obscured by delusion.
It is called "obscured" (nivṛta).
Because it cannot bring about a fruit,
it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
This obscured mind (nivṛta-citta) must necessarily arise together with eighteen mental factors (caitta),
namely, the ten universal factors (mahābhūmika).
The six universal mental factors of great affliction,
along with vitarka and vicāra;
herein, views do not increase.
It should be understood as explained previously. Regarding the statement "the non-obscured [mind] is admitted to be twelvefold":
this refers to the non-obscured minds of the desire realm, such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth.
This [consciousness] arises together with twelve mental factors (caitta), namely:
the ten universal factors (mahābhūmika) along with vitarka and vicāra. As for the word "admitted" (kila):
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
regret does not extend to the indeterminate;
therefore, with respect to the unobscured-indeterminate mind:
Only twelve [mental factors] are admitted;
this differs from the intention of the Sautrāntikas,
for *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is also associated with neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds.
Because one adds remorse (*kaukṛtya*) to the indeterminate mind,
there would be thirteen [mental factors]; however, this is not what is accepted.
If it is argued that sleep is universally non-contradictory because it increases by one in all cases,
this is because sleep pervades all three moral natures; thus, within the aforementioned categories of mind, [it would apply].
There is no contradiction in their being present everywhere;
whichever category they belong to,
they are all said to increase therein.
That is to say, among the aforementioned wholesome [states],
twenty-two are increased to twenty-three.
If the previous twenty-three increase to twenty-four,
they are unwholesome or indeterminate.
This should be understood by analogy.
Second, this clarifies those born together with the higher realms.
The treatise says:
Having already explained the mental states that arise together with those of the desire realm,
we shall now explain those of the higher realms.
The verse says:
In the first dhyāna, unwholesome states and remorse are excluded;
in the intermediate dhyāna, torpor is further excluded; in the higher [dhyānas], vitarka and so forth are additionally excluded.
The commentary states:
Regarding "the first dhyāna excludes the unwholesome, as well as remorse and torpor," this refers to the first meditative absorption (prathama-dhyāna).
As in the preceding case of the desire realm,
all mental factors (caitta-dharma) are present,
with the sole exception of the unwholesome ones.
There are ten unwholesome [mental factors]:
namely, anger (dveṣa), which is one;
and the seven [factors] beginning with resentment (krodha) among the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
Excluding deceit, guile, and pride,
as well as lack of shame and lack of dread;
these are the ten afflictions.
It is exclusively of an unwholesome nature.
It does not exist in the form realm, with the exception of *kaukṛtya* (remorse).
*Kaukṛtya* is associated with the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
there is no remorse because of the departure from sorrow; with the exception of sleep,
the form realm lacks physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Therefore, there is no sleep.
Furthermore, "the intermediate concentration excludes vitarka" refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
Excluding those previously excluded,
and further excluding applied thought (*vitarka*),
all other factors are present.
Regarding the phrase "furthermore, above [the first dhyāna], vitarka and so forth are eliminated":
"above" refers to the second dhyāna and beyond,
up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
In these two dhyānas and above,
one eliminates what was previously eliminated,
while additionally eliminating vicāra and the rest.
This includes deceit and guile;
all others possess them as well.
The Sūtra speaks of deceit and guile.
Extending up to the Brahma-heaven,
it is therefore only in the first dhyāna that there can be flattery and deception.
Because in the stage of the first dhyāna, the minister and the sovereign depend upon one another,
they necessarily practice flattery and deception,
as stated in the sūtras.
The Great Brahmā King, while dwelling among his own assembly of Brahmās,
was suddenly questioned by the bhikṣu Aśvajit.
At what stage do these four great elements cease entirely without remainder?
The Brahmā King, not knowing the state of cessation without remainder,
gave a deceptive and evasive answer:
"I am among this assembly of Brahmās."
The sovereign creator,
the transformer,
and the progenitor.
"The one who nurtures is the father of all sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, [he continued].
He led the assembly outside,
spoke with flattering words of apology,
and had them return to question the Buddha. The commentary explains:
The Great Brahmā King does not know that he relies upon the "not-yet-arrived" stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the four dhyānas;
among these six stages, [he is unaware].
One arouses the untainted path to sever the defilements of the fourth dhyāna,
as well as those based on the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space.
One gives rise to the path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga) to sever the defilements of the fourth dhyāna;
these are the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Because it pertains to the state of cessation without remainder,
this is an evasive answer;
such is the nature of an evasive response.
This is subsumed under false speech;
the use of sycophantic words and apologetic expressions clearly manifests flattery.
The "creator" is one who thinks, "I am able to construct the world.
The "transformer" is...
I am able to transform the world.
As for "giving birth," I am able to give birth to all sentient beings. As for "nurturing," [I am able to nurture them].
"I am able to nourish all sentient beings.
From this third point,
the distinctions between similar types are clarified.
This consists of two sections:
first, the explanation of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth;
second, the explanation of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*).
Furthermore, regarding the initial clarification of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and so forth,
the treatise states:
"Next, that which was previously analyzed shall now be explained."
Among the various mental factors (*caitasika*),
there is a slight distinction between shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
What is the distinction between affection (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*)?
The verse says:
Lack of shame and lack of dread are not held in high regard; one does not see fear in transgression.
Love and respect are called faith and shame (*hrī*). They exist only in the realms of desire and form. Commentary:
"Lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame" is the heading;
"not respecting" refers to [the lack of shame].
This explains "shamelessness" (āhrīkya).
Not revering the worthy and good is called shamelessness.
That is to say, one lacks respect and reverence toward virtuous qualities and those who possess such qualities.
To have no sense of dread or difficulty,
and to have no sense of dependence or subordination,
is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame).
This refers to the factors that are the opposites of reverence. As for "virtue," it refers to the virtues of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
As for "a person of virtue":
He is a person endowed with precepts, meditative concentration,
and wisdom. "Without hesitation or difficulty" means being free from fear and dread.
"Not being subject" means not performing the etiquette of a disciple. "Not seeing fear in transgressions" explains the absence of shame (*anapatrāpya*).
That which is censured and loathed by all noble beings is called "transgression."
In regard to these transgressions,
not seeing that they can bring about a terrifying result is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of shame).
In this context, the word "fear" indicates that which produces fear because it is an undesirable result. Other masters say that it refers to the transgression committed.
To feel no shame regarding oneself is called *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect); to feel no shame regarding others is [called *anapatrāpya* (lack of decorum)].
This is called lack of shame (*āhrīkya*).
One should understand that the distinction between *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame) is the reverse of this.
This means the opposite of the first explanation:
there is respect and veneration,
as well as a sense of caution and apprehension.
That which has something to which it is subjectively attached is called *hrī* (self-respect).
Seeing fear in transgression is called *apatrāpya* (moral dread).
To reverse the second explanation:
regarding the transgressions one has committed,
one observes oneself with a sense of shame.
That which is called "shame" (hrī) is defined as having a sense of shame regarding oneself;

that which is called "embarrassment" (apatrāpya) is defined as having a sense of shame regarding others. "Veneration" (gaurava) refers to faith (śraddhā), while "shame" (hrī) refers to [the aforementioned].
This explains the distinction between affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*).
Affection is precisely faith (*śraddhā*);
reverence is precisely shame (*hrī*).
"Affection" (preman) means fondness;
its essence is faith (śraddhā). However, there are two kinds of affection: first, that which is defiled (kliṣṭa);
[the second is that which is undefiled].
Second, there is non-defilement.
Defilement refers to craving,
such as that for one's wife or children.
Non-defilement refers to faith,
such as the affection one feels for teachers and elders;
this verse uses the term "affection" (preman) to denote it.
The second [type] is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
There is faith that is not craving;
this refers to faith that arises from the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of and conviction in suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*). Thus, there is faith.
Because it is loathsome, it is not "desirable.
There is that which is "desirable" but not "faith," namely, all defiled forms of desire.
That which arises from greed is craving;
it is defiled and not faith.
There is also a type of faith that is craving.
This refers to faith directed toward cessation and the path.
Because one accepts them with forbearance, faith arises;
because they are objects of delight, there is craving.
There is that which is neither faith nor affection;
this refers to anything other than the characteristics mentioned previously. Respect means reverence.
Its essence is precisely shame (*hrī*).
As previously explained regarding shame— namely, that it consists of respect and so forth—
there are instances of shame that are not respect.
That is to say, when shame arises based on the truths of suffering and its origin, it is "shame" (hrī) because it involves a sense of disgrace;
it is something to be loathed rather than revered. There is also a form of shame that encompasses both disgrace and reverence.
That is to say, shame (*hrī*) has cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as its objects; respect (*gaurava*) is accompanied by shame, and esteem (*bhakti*) is accompanied by respect.
These two exist only within the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*).
The three realms are thus distinguished by such affection and reverence;
they exist within the desire and form realms.
They do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Question: Do you not believe that faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*), which are among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-kuśala-dharma*), also exist in the formless realm?
Answer: There are two kinds of affection and respect:
those directed toward phenomena (*dharma*) and those directed toward persons (*pudgala*).
Affection and respect directed toward phenomena exist throughout the three realms.
The intention here is to state that because these take the *pudgala* as their object,
they exist in the realms of desire and form,
but not in the formless realm.
*Pudgala*. This is translated as "one who repeatedly undergoes rebirth" (*shuququ*).
It refers to one who repeatedly takes up various states of existence (*gati*).
From this second [section] onward, the investigation of vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), and so forth is clarified.
The treatise states:
Thus, the distinction between affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*) has been explained.
What, then, is the distinction between discursive thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), conceit (*māna*), and arrogance (*mada*)?
The verse says:
Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind; Māna is the inflation of the mind in relation to others;
Mada is the loftiness of the mind due to attachment to one's own qualities, Being haughty and having no regard for anything else.
The commentary states:
Regarding the coarseness and subtlety of the mind in vitarka and vicāra,
*vitarka* refers to seeking.
Vicāra refers to investigation;
the coarse nature of the mind is termed vitarka.
The subtle nature of the mind is called *vicāra*.
There is also another explanation.
The two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are the formative activities of all speech;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
Only when there is vitarka and vicāra can there be speech;
it is not the case that this activity of speech occurs without vitarka and vicāra.
The coarse is called vitarka (applied thought),
and the subtle is called vicāra (sustained thought).
These are the factors of speech.
This is the cause of speech. Regarding "pride (*māna*) is the nature of uplifting one's own mind in relation to others":
pride refers to [the state] in relation to others;
it is the nature of the mind uplifting itself.
Weighing the distinctions between the qualities of oneself and others,
one’s mind becomes self-exalting and arrogant,
looking down upon others with contempt.
Therefore, it is called pride (*māna*). Regarding "haughtiness (*mada*) arises from being stained by one's own qualities":
"one's own qualities" refers to one's own person, such as qualities like physical form and strength.
It refers to that which, preceded by an attachment to one's own qualities through arrogance,
causes the mind to be haughty and unrestrained,
characterized by a lack of consideration for others.
The treatise states:
Other masters say that just as the specific state of exhilaration arising from wine is designated as "intoxication," [so too is this case].
Thus, the specific manifestation of joy and elation born of craving is called *mada* (intoxication).
This is the defining characteristic that distinguishes *mada* from *māna* (pride).
The two preceding sections differ;
both together constitute the third [section],
which clarifies the distinctions between the similar.
From this fourth section,
which clarifies the distinctions among various names,
the treatise says:
Nevertheless, regarding the mind and mental factors,
various names and designations are established in the sūtras according to their specific meanings.
Now, the distinctions among the meanings of these terms shall be analyzed.
The verse says:
Mind, thought, and consciousness are one in essence; The mind and mental factors have a basis.
"Having objects and having mental aspects; the meaning of association has five [aspects].
Regarding the explanation that "the substance of mind (citta), mentation (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna) is one":
"Accumulating and giving rise to [phenomena] is called mind (*citta*," which means it is that which can accumulate and give rise to the three types of karma.
"Deliberating is called thought (*manas*)," and "discerning is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, there is another explanation which says:
Because the realms of purity and impurity have various distinctions,
it is called the "purity of mind," which is goodness.
"Impure" means evil; "realm" (dhātu) means essence (svabhāva).
That which is this [essence] becomes that for another.
Because it acts as the basis [for the other faculties], it is called "mind" (manas). "That very same" refers to this very mind;
it takes the sense of being the support [for the others].
This explains the meaning of *manas*.
Because it acts as the basis upon which [consciousness] relies, it is called "mind" (*manas*). Consciousness is that which relies upon the mind.
According to the two preceding interpretations,
although these three— citta, manas, and vijñāna— differ in their names and meanings, [they refer to the same entity].
Their substance is one.
Regarding the five meanings of the mind and mental factors— having a basis, having an object, having an aspect, and being associated—
this explains the dharmas of the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, there are four names;
although their meanings differ,
their essence remains one and the same.
First is that which has a basis (*sāśraya*).
This refers to the mind and mental factors;
all of these are termed "having a basis."
It is so called because it relies upon the sense organs as its support. As for these supporting sense organs,
they are the six organs, beginning with the eye.
Second, it is called "having an object" (*sālambana*), because it grasps an objective referent (*ālambana*).
As for the objective referent, it refers to the six objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Third, it is called "having an aspect" (*sākāra*).
This means they share the same mode of apprehension (*ākāra*).
For example, when the mind and its mental factors take a blue object as their condition,
they all bear the reflection of that blue.
The aspect upon this consciousness is called the "aspect of activity" (*ākāra*).
"Activity" (*ākāra*) refers to the act of cognitive engagement.
This refers to the mind that acts as the perceiver.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the mental image;
that is, the characteristics upon the formations (saṃskāra).
The characteristic of practice and understanding is called "aspect of practice" (*ākāra*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.
The mind and its mental factors both possess the characteristic of blue;
although these characteristics of blue are numerous.
Because it is the same blue, it is called "having the same aspect" (*ekākāra*). Alternatively, it is called "having an aspect" (*sākāra*).
The treatise says:
"Regarding the distinctions among the categories of objects, [it is] by way of their origination and mental aspects. The commentary explains:
"The distinctions among the categories" means:
The objects are not one and the same. Regarding "simultaneous origination" (*samutthāna*):
it refers to the mind and mental factors arising together in equal measure. The fourth is "association" (*samprayoga*).
Because they are equally conjoined.
"Equally conjoined" refers to the mind and mental factors.
They are said to be associated because they are equal in five respects:
first, their basis.
Second, the object of focus;
third, the mental aspect;
fourth, the time.
Because all five matters are equal.
Regarding "equality of time":
This refers to the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta), because they arise, abide, change, and perish simultaneously.
As for "equality of substance" (dravya-samatā):
"Phenomena" refers to their essence.
Within a single corresponding [state],
they are like the single essence of the mind.
The same applies to each of the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*);
there are no two [simultaneous] feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Because they are associated together.
What has preceded is not the same;
this constitutes the first [section].
The explanation of mental factors is concluded.
From here begins the second major section,
which explains the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Within this, there are three parts:
first, a general indication of the names and numbers;
second, a detailed citation and explanation.
Third, the analysis by way of various categories.
First, regarding the general indication of names and numbers,
the treatise states:
The extensive analysis of the meaning of mind and mental factors has already been explained.
As for the formations dissociated from mind, what are they?
The verse says:
Mental formations dissociated from mind: Acquisition, non-acquisition, homogeneity, Non-ideation, the two meditative attainments, vitality, Characteristics, the group of names, and so forth.
The commentary states:
Regarding the verse’s mention of "the two attainments," these are the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and [the attainment of cessation].
It is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
As for its characteristics, they are the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth:
the phrase "and so forth" includes phrase-bodies (*padakāya*) and syllable-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*).
In total, there are fourteen.
1. Acquisition (prāpti).
2. Non-acquisition (aprāpti).
3. Spheres of homogeneity (sabhāgatā).
Fourth, the fruit of non-conception;
fifth, the meditative attainment of non-conception;
sixth, the meditative attainment of cessation.
7. The life-faculty;
8. Arising; 9. Abiding.
10. Differences;
11. Cessation; 12. The set of names (nāmakāya).
The thirteen word-bodies (*padakāya*) and the fourteen phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*);
these are the fourteen kinds.
Its substance is not a mental factor;
because it does not associate with the mind,
it is called "dissociated from the mind."
Within the framework of the five aggregates,
these are subsumed under the aggregate of formations;
therefore, they are called "formations dissociated from mind."
From this second [section] onward,
there is a separate citation and explanation.
Within this, there are seven [parts].
First, the explanation of acquisition and non-acquisition;
second, the explanation of the homogeneous class (sabhāgatā); third, the explanation of the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika).
The fourth explains the two meditative attainments;
the fifth explains the life-faculty;
and the sixth explains the four characteristics.
Seventh, the explanation of the group of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.
Within the first of these, the explanation of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
there are further two sections.
First, the clarification of essential nature;
second, the clarification of differentiation.
Regarding the first, the clarification of essential nature:
The treatise says: Within this context, we shall first examine the characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The verse states:
Acquisition is defined as obtaining and possession; Non-acquisition is the opposite of this.
"Acquisition and non-acquisition exist only within one's own continuum and with respect to the two cessations.
The commentary states:
the first two lines clarify their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The final two phrases clarify the basis.
"Attainment" refers to the accomplishment of the protection;
this explains the essential nature of attainment.
There are two kinds of attainment:
first, acquisition;
second, accomplishment. Within acquisition, there are two types.
First, obtaining what was not previously obtained;
second, obtaining what was previously lost.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Having not yet obtained or having already lost, now one obtains. The commentary explains:
"Having not yet obtained, now obtaining" refers, for example, to not yet having obtained the precepts.
Now that the precepts have been received,
they have newly reached the stage of arising;
because they are about to be perfected.

Regarding the term "now obtained after having already lost": it is like when one who was previously seated in meditative concentration encounters conditions that cause them to abandon that concentration; this is called "already lost. Now obtaining it again is what is meant by "now obtained."
It is later re-cultivated until it reaches the stage of the "characteristic of arising" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*),
as it is about to be accomplished.
Regarding the phrase "now attained" (*idānīm-labdha*):
it means that a dharma which was previously not obtained has now been obtained.
That which was previously attained is not lost now; this attained dharma flows on into the present.
This is called "attainment.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Having attained it, one does not lose it."
It is called "accomplishment" (siddhi) because it is known that [the result] is obtained at that time;
it is not called "accomplishment" at the very moment of accomplishment itself.
"It is not called 'attainment' (prāpti)" means that "non-attainment" (aprāpti) is the opposite of this;
this explains the intrinsic nature of non-attainment.
One should understand that non-attainment is the reverse of this [attainment].
That is to say, if there is a phenomenon that has not been previously lost and which has been acquired again.
However, at this initial moment of loss,
this non-possession (aprāpti) of the dharma first reaches the state of arising (jāti-lakṣaṇa).
That which is called "not obtaining" flows into the present existence;
this is termed "non-accomplishment."
Therefore, one should know that when [the fruit] is not obtained,
it is not called "non-accomplishment"; nor is it non-accomplishment at the time [of its acquisition].
"It is not called 'non-attainment' [in this context].
"Acquisition and non-acquisition exist only with respect to one's own continuum and the two types of cessation" explains the basis upon which acquisition and non-acquisition depend.
Regarding "one's own continuum":
"one's own" excludes others;
"continuum" refers to the body.
This excludes that which is not a continuity.
That which is not a continuity refers to insentient things.
Acquisition and non-acquisition exist only with respect to one's own continuum;
therefore, the treatise says:
It is not another continuum,
because there is no accomplishment of dharmas belonging to another body;
nor is it a non-continuum.
Because there is no accomplishment of non-sentient phenomena,
the "two cessations" refer to cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Among unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*),
acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exist only with respect to the two types of cessation (*nirodha*); that is to say, if one practices the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

At the time of realizing cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), there is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that cessation. At the time of not realizing it, [there is no such acquisition] regarding that cessation.
There is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
Within the state where conditions are lacking, one attains cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, there is the acquisition (prāpti) of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
When conditions converge,
one does not obtain non-analytical cessation.
Thus, non-acquisition exists upon analytical cessation; therefore,
regarding the two types of cessation...
There are acquisitions and non-acquisitions.
The treatise states:
"All sentient beings..."
There are none who do not possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), except for those whose conditions are lacking, excluding the first moment [of the path],
as well as noble beings still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana-ārya*) and all others.
Ordinary beings bound by all fetters and all other sentient beings possess [the cessation through deliberation];
as for the noble ones at the first moment [of the path], they likewise possess it.
This refers to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because the afflictions have not yet been severed, such a person is called a "noble one bound by all fetters" (*sakalabandhana-ārya*).
This noble one has no cessation through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for all other sentient beings...
All noble ones (ārya) are definitively without the accomplishment of space; therefore,
regarding space, it is not said that there is attainment.
Because acquisition (*prāpti*) does not exist, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) also does not exist;
for the thesis clarifies that acquisition and non-acquisition are established as being mutually exclusive. [End of] the treatise. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*:
Section 158 states: There are four kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*).
First, that which is simultaneous with those dharmas; this is "acquisition simultaneous with the dharma" (*sahaja-prāpti*).
It is also called "attainment following like a shadow follows a form.
Second, when it exists prior to that dharma, it is "attainment prior to the dharma," which is also called "attainment led by the bull-king."
Third, that which exists after those dharmas is "subsequently attained" (prsthalabdha);
it is also called "attained following the Vātsīputrīya.
Fourth, that which is neither prior to, nor subsequent to, nor simultaneous with those dharmas refers to the attainment regarding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The dharmas thus attained are of six kinds. First,
there are dharmas that are attained.
Only those that are both [appropriated and non-appropriated] are obtained, such as the retribution-born (*vipākaja*) and other such factors;
these are the two types of dharmas that are objects of apprehension.
There is only prior acquisition, as in the case of the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Some say that these also have simultaneous acquisition; this should be included in the fourth category. The explanation says:
Regarding the fourth category:
this refers to the dharmas obtained in the fourth [dhyāna],
which universally include both those obtained simultaneously and those obtained previously.
Regarding the three types of dharmas that are attained:
they consist solely of both simultaneous attainment (*sahaja-prāpti*) and subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-prāpti*), such as the prātimokṣa vows and so forth.
Regarding the four types of dharmas that involve apprehension (*upalabdhi*), there is only the simultaneous attainment (*sahapratilambha*) and the prior attainment (*pūrvapratilambha*),
such as the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) and so forth.
Regarding the five dharmas that are acquired, they possess acquisition both prior to, subsequent to, and simultaneously with [the dharma itself],
just as is the case with other wholesome, defiled, and so forth, dharmas.
Regarding the six dharmas that are objects of attainment,
it cannot be said that they exist prior to, posterior to, or simultaneously with one another; yet there are those who attain them.
This refers to the dharmas of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The commentary explains:
"The first [category] consists of those produced by maturation (*vipākaja*), and so forth."
This includes, by way of inclusion,
those who have not repeatedly practiced deportment or the arts.
And as for obscured-unspecified matter and so forth—
because these various dharmas possess inferior power.
Only the simultaneous acquisition of dharmas: secondly, the conventional knowledge at the limit of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣya-saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth.
The "and so forth" includes the associated mind and mental factors.
This refers to entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Upon reaching the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation,
one is able to cultivate conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) in the future;
it is acquired through the acquisition that precedes the dharma.
This term "cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to "attainment-cultivation" (pratilambha-bhāvanā); that is to say,
the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) is untainted (anāsrava).
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Therefore, conventional knowledge does not arise during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
because the superior conditions for its arising are lacking.
Regarding the explanation that one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):
"superior conditions" refers to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
It is the body that serves as the basis.
Within the Path of Seeing,
there is only the body that serves as the basis for the Path of Seeing.
Because there is no physical basis for conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the superior conditions are lacking;
thus, conventional knowledge never arises at all.

Therefore, there is no subsequent attainment of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with or subsequent to the [supramundane] dharma. Question: Why is it that conventional knowledge can be cultivated at the conclusion of the three types of inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not at the conclusion of the inferential knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?
Answer: It is cultivated for two reasons:
first, because there is the direct realization (abhisamaya) of entities, namely conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Since beginningless time,
one has already known suffering, abandoned its origin, and realized its cessation; now, through the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), [these are fully realized].
One also knows the suffering, abandons the origin, and realizes the cessation;
this is because it performs the same function as conventional knowledge.
One is able to cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and so forth,
because the two [truths] encompass all objects of the truths;
that is to say, regarding the three truths.
Suffering can be fully understood;
its origin can be fully abandoned;
its cessation can be fully realized.

When the truths have been thoroughly examined, one should also cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), as for those who do not cultivate conventional knowledge:
this is because conventional knowledge does not pertain to the [noble] path.
Because there has never been a full realization of the objects [of knowledge]; and because there is no full realization of all objects,
meaning that it is absolutely impossible to fully know the path in its entirety.
It may be cultivated universally because the lineages (gotra) are manifold. Question:
Why is it that among the three truths, the term "limit" (anta) does not apply to the truth of the path?
The answer is: because it is able to know all suffering,
sever all origins [of suffering],
and realize all cessations [of suffering].
Yet there is no one capable of cultivating all paths;
the Buddha, moreover, has attained the cultivation of cultivation regarding the path.
Because both are inexhaustible,
there is "boundless sound. Third, regarding the prātimokṣa vows and so forth—
the term "and so forth" includes the non-restraint of evil conduct and the like.
The Prātimokṣa vows, being determinate (vijñapti), pertain to both the dharmas and the subsequently attained [wisdom].
That is to say, although the precepts belong to the past,
they are acquired through their arising in the present;
thus they are accomplished and not lost.
This prātimokṣa restraint is not a form that follows the mind,
because its power is weak and inferior.
One cannot previously attain the "patience concordant with the knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) and so forth;
the phrase "and so forth" includes the associated mind and mental factors.
That is to say, the patience concordant with the knowledge of the path.
This is subsumed under the path of approach; up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna),
it is subsumed under the resultant path.
In the path of attaining the fruit,
because one abandons the path of the candidate,
it is therefore called the subsequent patience (anvaya-kṣānti).
There are no states acquired after [meditative attainment]. Fifth, there are the remaining wholesome, defiled, and so forth;
"and so forth" includes the neutral states such as those resulting from supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-phala*).
Aside from these four preceding categories, [there are no others].
The remaining [attainments] are so named because their power is strong;
they encompass the three types of acquisition (prāpti). The sixth is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The dharma of non-analytical cessation is not subsumed within the three time periods; therefore,
it cannot be said to exist prior to, posterior to, or simultaneously with [other dharmas].
As for the existence of various acquisitions (*prāpti*),
this means that at the time one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), there is an acquisition with respect to that cessation through deliberation.
Regarding the state where conditions are absent, there is acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). Question:
How can there be "acquisition prior to the dharma" (*pūrvapratilambha*) in the case of the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*?
Answer: Although the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* possesses only simultaneous acquisition (*sahabhū-prāpti*),
the future *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*—
That is to say, there is an acquisition prior to the dharma that exists in the present; thus,
it is said here that the present patience has an acquisition prior to the dharma.
This is explained in terms of the categories of patience (*kṣānti*),
because the dharmas attained are stated according to their categories. Furthermore,
it is interpreted as this present patience.
Although it exists only as co-existent with the dharma, if it does not manifest,
then there is that which precedes the dharma.
There is a statement that can be made regarding its possible inclusion:
it is said that for present patience (*kṣānti*), there is the prior acquisition of dharmas. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that this refers to present patience.
Although it is exclusively co-existent with the dharma and does not precede it,
for this reason, present receptivity (kṣānti) possesses acquisition prior to the dharma when it exists in the future.
This is an acquisition in the future;
viewed horizontally across the time periods,
it actually exists subsequent to the present forbearance.
As for why it is called "prior to the dharma" and not "subsequent to the dharma," it means that by this [attainment],
one simply does not give rise [to those afflictions] immediately.
Its arising must necessarily occur prior to that present receptivity (*kṣānti*);
it is said that there is a "prior acquisition" (*pūrvaprāpti*) in terms of its potential capacity for arising. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 158, states:
All non-acquisitions (aprāpti) are,
in total, of three kinds.
The first occurs prior to that dharma.
Second, those that follow after those dharmas;
third, those that are neither before nor after them—
the dharmas that are not obtained.
There are likewise only three types.
First, regarding dharmas that have not yet been attained,
there is only non-acquisition prior to the dharma itself.
This refers to those dharmas belonging to the category of sentient beings that will never arise in the future,
as well as the mental factors associated with the final moment of mind at the point of entering nirvana without remainder.
And there is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Second, regarding the dharmas that cannot be acquired:
these are the non-acquisitions (*aprāpti*) of those dharmas both prior to and subsequent to them; that is to say, all other sentient-dharmas as appropriate.
There are three types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) regarding phenomena that do not exist: there is no non-acquisition of a phenomenon that is either prior to or subsequent to it;
rather, it refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the dharma of non-analytical cessation, there can never be a non-acquisition (aprāpti) that coexists with that dharma;
for when the dharma is present before one,
it is precisely what has been acquired.
Because there must be that which is attained, it is not something that can be attained; there is neither attainment nor non-attainment,
nor is there merely the non-attainment of dharmas that subsequently exist.
It is not because those [dharmas] have been constantly accomplished since beginningless time, nor because they will necessarily arise until that category is exhausted.
The commentary explains:
"First, regarding future dharmas of sentient beings that will never arise."
This refers to the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) cultivated at the conclusion of the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).
This is conventional knowledge.
Because it does not pass through the present,
it is called "future";
yet it is not insentient.
That which is categorized as a sentient being attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
which is termed "ultimate non-arising" prior to the path of vision (darśana-mārga).
This conventional knowledge is always accompanied by non-possession;
this is called "non-possession prior to the dharma."
After the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), there is always the arising of possession (*prāpti*);
furthermore, there is no non-possession (*aprāpti*). This also applies to the final moment of consciousness when entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This refers to a certain class of beings in the future who,
with a mind of maturation or deportment,
form the intention to enter nirvana.
Before this mind has arisen,
there is always a non-possession (aprāpti) that does not possess this mind;
this is called "non-possession prior to the dharma" (pūrvāprāpti).
Once this mind has arisen,
it must enter nirvana;
for then it would be identical to that which is insentient.
There is no non-acquisition subsequent to the knowledge of exhaustion,
because there is nothing further upon which to rely;
furthermore, there is no knowledge of non-arising.
Prior to its arising,
there is always a non-possession;
this is called "non-possession prior to the dharma."
Once this wisdom has arisen, it is necessarily non-retrogressive;

therefore, there is no subsequent non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of that [wisdom]. It is not the case that one has always possessed it since beginningless time, nor is it something that must arise again once it has been abandoned, because the entire class of such [states] has already been exhausted.
These sixteen characters are intended to refute the objection regarding the afflictions of view within the sphere of non-perception; that is to say,
according to the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty.
The translation of the *Vibhāṣā* is completed.
Someone raised an objection regarding the delusions of view within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
challenging the Tripiṭaka Master as follows:
The combined [non-acquisition] exists only for dharmas that are subsequently non-acquired;
the intent of this objection is that the afflictions of wrong views have been established since beginningless time.
There is no non-acquisition of what has not yet been attained;
once abandoned through the Path of Seeing, there is never again a falling back from it regarding past afflictions of seeing.
Logically, there ought to be a "non-acquisition" (aprāpti) that follows only from a dharma;
why is this not the case? Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master added sixteen characters to the *Vibhāṣā*.
To resolve this objection,
the meaning of those sixteen characters is as follows: it refers to the delusions of view within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Prior to its being severed,
it is termed "not yet relinquished.
Within this state of not yet having been relinquished,
There is certainly no one who gives rise to future non-perception or views-afflictions that enter the past and reach exhaustion.
This is because the afflictions of the future are of infinite varieties and arise without end.
Furthermore, when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and severing the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*),
regarding the future afflictions of view within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Since there is non-acquisition (aprāpti) prior to the existence of a phenomenon, past afflictions of view and ignorance cannot be described solely in terms of their category;
it is impossible for there to be only non-acquisition subsequent to the existence of a phenomenon.
From this second [section],
the distinctions are clarified.
Within it, there are two parts.
First, the distinction of acquisition (prāpti) is clarified;
second, the distinction of non-acquisition (aprāpti) is clarified.
Within the first [section], the distinction of acquisition is clarified.
The text is further divided into two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the distinctions;
second, the detailed explanation in response to specific inquiries.
Furthermore, first, regarding the clear exposition of the specific distinctions:
the treatise states,
"The intrinsic nature has already been analyzed."
What are the distinctions? This is asked in general;
first, one should distinguish them by asking specifically.
The verse says:
The dharmas of the three time periods each have three [types of acquisition]. Those that are wholesome and so forth have only wholesome and so forth [acquisitions];
those with a specific realm have acquisitions belonging to their own realm. Unconditioned acquisitions pertain to all four [realms];
those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have three [types of acquisition]; and those not to be abandoned have two kinds.
The commentary states:
"The three categories for each of the three periods of time" refers to the gateway of the three periods of time.
The dharmas of the three periods of time each have three kinds of attainment,
namely: past dharmas.
There is acquisition of the past;
there is acquisition of the future;
there is acquisition of the present.
In this way, future and present dharmas each have three kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*). First, regarding past dharmas:
There are acquisitions of the past;
these are either prior to the dharma or simultaneous with the dharma.
Alternatively, it may be that the dharma [of attainment] is posterior. This refers to the relationship between the attainer and the attained dharma;
at this moment, both are situated together in the past.
However, past dharmas possess only a single acquisition (*prāpti*),
such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth belonging to the past.
Or there may be two acquisitions,
as in the case of the past,
such as the prātimokṣa vows and so forth.
There are those that are acquired through all three [ways],
such as the precepts associated with the Path (mārga-samvara) in past lives.
There are also those acquired through only one.
Whether two are acquired or three are acquired,
all are termed "past acquisitions within past dharmas."
Therefore, the acquisition of past [dharmas] is of three kinds;
one should reflect upon this well.
Regarding past dharmas that are acquired in the present,
such as the prātimokṣa precepts,
they fall away into the past.
It is not lost in the present;
it is acquired through the arising of acquisition (*prāpti*).
This is precisely what it means for a dharma to exist in the past.
Because they abide in the present and abide after the dharma;
those who obtain [the fruit] in the present within the category of past dharmas.
"Only dharmas are subsequently attained. Regarding "past dharmas are attained in the future":
this means that while the dharma is past, its attainment (prāpti) exists in the future.
This is the subsequent attainment (pṛṣṭhalabdha) of the future;
it is called "subsequent to the dharma" when viewed horizontally across the [three] time periods.
Although all [these acquisitions] follow the dharma,
if one considers the sequence of their arising and functioning,
there are also cases in the future where there is an "antecedent acquisition" (pūrvapratilambha) belonging to a past dharma.
For example, there are dharmas such as the precepts concomitant with the Path (mārga-sahabhū-śīla) in past lives that were previously acquired and have already passed away into the past.
That dharma was previously attained;
its varieties are numerous,
and those that have arisen have not yet ceased.
It is still to be obtained in the future.
As for this future obtainment,
it is already non-arising.
Since its arising must necessarily occur prior to that past dharma,
the past dharma is acquired by means of a future acquisition.
There are also cases where [the attainment] occurs prior to the dharma;
one should reflect upon this well.
Regarding the case where the attainment of a present dharma occurs in the past:
Regarding the acquisition of a present dharma: that which is acquired prior to the dharma is called "acquisition before the dharma" (*pūrvaprāpti*);

that which is acquired simultaneously with the dharma is called "acquisition together with the dharma" (*sahaprāpti*); and that which is acquired subsequent to the dharma is called "acquisition after the dharma" (*paścātprāpti*). These are designated according to a horizontal perspective across the time periods (*adhvan*).
Although all [dharmas] follow after [the present],
if one discusses the sequence of their arising and functioning,
there are also dharmas of the present within the future.
It is obtained prior to the dharma.
This should be understood according to the explanation regarding the past; one should reflect upon this well.
Regarding future dharmas, those whose acquisition (prāpti) occurs in the past or present are exclusively acquisitions that precede the dharma.
Regarding future dharmas, those whose acquisition occurs in the future are either acquisitions that precede the dharma [or simultaneous with it].
Either simultaneous with the dharma,
or subsequent to the dharma;
although in the future there is no sequential order of before and after.

The distinction between "prior" and "subsequent" is stated in terms of their respective categories and in terms of their capacity to give rise to activity. Regarding the statement that "wholesome [factors] and so forth are only wholesome [factors] and so forth": it means that they are exclusively wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, and do not belong to other categories.
This is the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Regarding "wholesome and so forth," it refers to the wholesome dharmas that are attained.
The phrase "and so forth" includes unwholesome and neutral dharmas. The term "only wholesome, etc.
refers to the acquisition that is capable of obtaining [the dharma].
The term "and so forth" includes unwholesome and indeterminate [states] as well;
that is to say, wholesome, unwholesome,
and indeterminate phenomena.

In their respective order, there are three types of acquisition (*prāpti*): wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. Regarding the acquisition of those bound to a specific realm and the acquisition of those not so bound, these pertain to the fourfold classification;
this refers to the gate of the bound (*baddha*) and the unbound (*abaddha*).
That which is bound refers to the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three realms.
As for these bound phenomena:
Acquisition belongs only to its own realm: that is to say, the acquisition of dharmas of the desire realm belongs only to the desire realm;
if it is the acquisition of dharmas of the form realm, [it belongs only to the form realm].
Furthermore, if a dharma belongs to the form realm or the formless realm, its acquisition (prāpti) likewise belongs to the formless realm when it is an outflowing (sāsrava) acquisition;
this is determined according to what is acquired. Therefore, there are dharmas that are bound [to a realm].
In whichever realm one may reside,
the acquisition (prāpti) that is capable of acquiring [a dharma] is of the same nature as that which is acquired; it is unconditioned by the realm.
These are the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). There are two kinds of untainted dharmas:
first, conditioned untainted dharmas, which refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
The two unconditioned [phenomena] are untainted: cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation.
That which "attains all four" refers to those phenomena that are unbound.
The acquisition [of cessation] can obtain four kinds. That is to say, the acquisitions of the three realms and the untainted acquisition (anāsrava-prāpti) are called the four kinds.
Now, regarding the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha):
It pervades the three realms of existence;
that is, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is categorized according to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) are bound to all three realms,
they are therefore obtained as being bound to all three realms. This is like the case where,
in the desire realm, the conditions [for rebirth] are lacking.

The acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is itself bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta). If it is acquired through the absence of conditions for the form realm (rūpadhātu), its acquisition is itself bound to the form realm.
If it pertains to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)...
The acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) occurs due to the deficiency of conditions;
since it is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the treatise states:
"The acquisition of non-analytical cessation."
It pervades the three realms of existence;
if it is the acquisition of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), it belongs to the realm of form and the formless realm.
"And with the untainted" (*anāsrava*): the commentary explains that this refers to the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is categorized according to the path by which it is realized; if it is by means of a tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*), [it is so classified].
That which is attained by one who realizes cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is that which is bound to the realms of form and formlessness (rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu).
Because the contaminated path belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is capable of realizing it,
one thereby attains the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It penetrates both of those realms;
however, within the desire realm,
there is no path capable of severing [the afflictions].

Therefore, the acquisition of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) does not extend to the desire realm; this refers to the analytical cessation realized through the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
The acquisition of that cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is likewise exclusively untainted (anāsrava),
corresponding to the path by which it is realized.
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
If it is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), it is exclusively untainted.
It is attained through the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya). It is determined according to what has been attained;
the Truth of the Path is untainted (anāsrava).
That which is attained is also untainted (anāsrava).
Therefore, the dharmas that are unconditioned (asaṃyukta) are, in summary, [untainted].
These consist of four types: those pertaining to the three realms and the untainted (anāsrava).
