The three categories of "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" constitute the gateway of the three trainings (triśikṣā).
The verse says "not a letter" (a-akṣara),
which extends to the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa); that is to say, it refers to that which is neither of learning (naivaśaikṣa) nor of no-more-learning (naivāśaikṣa).
Third is "that which can obtain obtaining.
This refers to dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
their acquisition (prāpti) pertains to all three types.
First, those in training;
second, those beyond training;
third, those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
Furthermore, because the verse text is concise,
it only indicates that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner; however, according to the prose commentary,
the three types of learners are fully explained.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"If there are dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), their acquisition (prāpti) is exclusively of those in training. The commentary states:
The dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) refer to the conditioned and untainted (anāsrava) factors within the continuum of one who is in training.
Because the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) are conditioned (saṃskṛta),
and because acquisitions (prāpti) are determined according to what they acquire,
their acquisition is also [of] one in training. As for the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)...
It is attained only by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary states:
"The dharmas of one beyond training" refers to...
Within the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
there is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); for the dharmas of one beyond training are conditioned.
Since it is determined according to what has been attained,
the possession (*prāpti*) is likewise without training (*aśaikṣa*). There is a distinction in the possession of that which is neither with nor without training (*naiva-śaikṣa-na-aśaikṣa*).
That is to say, the acquisition of these dharmas is generally said to be threefold. [Commentary:
This passage correctly explains the verse.
The dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
although they are one,
are obtained through the attainment of those dharmas.
This refers to the distinction in attainment because it penetrates all three trainings.
As for "dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner":
This refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as well as the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. (The above is from the treatise.
The commentary states: Because contaminated phenomena cannot be cultivated.
Therefore, those dharmas within the bodies of those who are neither in training nor beyond training are called "neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training.
As for unconditioned dharmas, they cannot be cultivated so as to cause them to increase; hence [they are also classified as such].

It is also neither-learner-nor-non-learner dharma. Furthermore, regarding contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*), there is only acquisition (*prāpti*) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, because contaminated dharmas are determined according to their respective acquisitions.
The acquisition of that [acquisition] is also neither-learner-nor-non-learner;
this includes the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as well as that which is not induced by the Noble Path (āryamārga).

The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also like this. The commentary states: [the same applies to] the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The acquisition of these two is determined by the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), and is not obtained through the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). This is because their acquisition is determined by the path capable of realizing them;
thus, this acquisition is also neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The phrase "it is also like this" means that its intent is clear and identical to what preceded;
it refers to that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
If there is one who is still in training (śaikṣa),
the acquisition (prāpti) of the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) realized by them is also [of the state of] training.
Because that which follows the path capable of realization consists of those in training (śaikṣa);
as for the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that is realized is also of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because it follows the path that realizes it,
which is itself of the state beyond training; therefore, it is known to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
And as for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*),
although they are neither-learner-nor-non-learner phenomena (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma*),
their respective acquisitions (*prāpti*) are capable of obtaining them.
This encompasses the three trainings;
one should reflect upon this well. "Not among the two kinds to be abandoned" refers to the three gates of abandonment.

As for the "two kinds":
Regarding dharmas that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*),

second, those not to be abandoned.
This is because the verse is concise.
Only the acquisition (*prāpti*) that is not to be abandoned (*aheya*) is indicated;

Therefore, the treatise says:

There is a distinction regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
This refers to the attainment of these dharmas.
To state it in brief, there are two types; this is the correct explanation of the verse.
As for "there are two":
Cultivation is the abandonment of the non-dual.
To distinguish them specifically:
they are all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.

This explains that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas not to be abandoned (*aheya*) can also be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
it is determined according to its basis (*āśraya*).
It is abandoned solely through cultivation;
it is that which is acquired by means other than the Noble Path.
Judged according to their capacity for realization,
they are also abandoned solely through cultivation;
therefore, it is said that "it is also thus."
The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) realized by the noble path,
as well as the acquisition of the truth of the path (mārga-satya).
"Only that which is not to be abandoned" (a-prahātavya) in this passage explains the acquisition (*prāpti*) of dharmas that are not to be abandoned;
it applies universally to those not to be abandoned.

That is to say, the acquisition obtained by means of the Noble Path is determined according to what it realizes: if it is the acquisition of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it follows the nature of what is acquired.
Therefore, in all cases, they are not [the view of] annihilationism.
Second, following the specific objections,

The treatise states:

These two supernormal powers (abhijñā) involve emanation (nirmāṇa); they are the result of supernormal power (abhijñā-phala) and are morally neutral (avyākṛta).

Because its power is strong,

that which it gives rise to consists of bodily and vocal actions.

Explanation: [End]

because when a dharma is present, it is necessarily possessed by one who has acquired it.

there are cases where a non-possession (aprāpti) of that phenomenon exists prior to it.

this refers to the case where the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the dharma that is not acquired both currently exist in the past.

there is only the subsequent non-attainment of that dharma.

this is based on a horizontal perspective across the time periods.

if one discusses the sequence of their arising and functioning,
there are also non-acquisitions of past dharmas belonging to the category of future dharmas that arise prior to those dharmas.
It may be said accordingly: regarding future dharmas,
non-acquisition (aprāpti) of a future dharma occurs either prior to that dharma.
Alternatively, regarding phenomena that occur later,
although there is no sequential order of before and after in the future, they are distinguished according to their distinct categories of intrinsic nature.
The sequence of before and after is spoken of in terms of the arising of function based on capacity.
This concerns the category of future phenomena.
Regarding non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the past and present,
it refers exclusively to the non-acquisition prior to the arising of the dharma.
Among present dharmas, [this is not the case].
Regarding non-acquisition (aprāpti) of the past,
it refers exclusively to the non-acquisition that precedes the dharma.
Among present dharmas...
Regarding future non-acquisition (*aprāpti*),
although from a trans-temporal perspective all [dharmas] follow after [the mind], [it is still distinguished by its temporal status].
If categorized according to the sequence of the arising of their functions,
there are also non-possessions (*aprāpti*) prior to present dharmas within the category of future dharmas. Regarding the three types—
those bound to the three realms and those unbound— the "three realms" refers to the classification by way of realm-bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*).
That which is not bound to the three realms is the dharma that is not acquired; the third is the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of that which can be acquired,
namely, the dharmas belonging to the three realms and those that are unbound.
Each has its own non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) pertaining to the three realms.
For instance, regarding the phenomena (*dharma*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
there exists a non-acquisition pertaining to all three realms.
This refers to sentient beings of the desire realm who do not acquire dharmas of the desire realm,
nor the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of those bound to the desire realm; as well as sentient beings of the form realm.

Sentient beings of the desire realm do not acquire dharmas of the desire realm; this is not an acquisition belonging to the form realm. Sentient beings of the formless realm do not acquire dharmas of the desire realm;
this is not an acquisition belonging to the formless realm. This is because non-acquisition is determined according to its basis.
Therefore, according to their respective bases,
they pervade all three realms;
just as the non-acquisition (aprāpti) of dharmas belonging to the desire realm exists across the three realms.
Regarding the dharmas of the form and formless realms,
there are non-possessions (aprāpti) belonging to the three realms;
these are explained by analogy with those of the desire realm.
Regarding non-tied dharmas,
if one has not attained them within the three realms,
one has not attained the non-tied dharmas of the desire realm.
Non-acquisition is not bound to the desire realm;
it does not acquire dharmas that are unbound;
and non-acquisition is not bound to the form realm.
The formless [attainments] cannot be non-bound dharmas.
If it were granted that the non-acquisition of the formless realm is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*),
this would explain that non-acquisition does not extend to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This refers to the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Since it is accepted that the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the Noble Path is designated as "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*),
the treatise cites the root text as follows:
What is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is the non-acquisition of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
"Non-acquisition" is merely another name for "non-possession" (*aprāpti*).
It is not reasonable to say that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is untainted (*anāsrava*). [Commentary:
The above is the treatise (*śāstra*).
"Non-attainment is another name for non-possession" and below are the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] explanations of the two preceding lines.
This is also the case in this treatise.
Since it is known that not having attained the Noble Path is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (pṛthagjanatva).
It is clearly known that this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is necessarily not untainted (*anāsrava*).
This state of being an ordinary person...
This is precisely what is meant by "non-acquisition.
Therefore, we know that non-acquisition does not apply to the untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 45,
states: "The Venerable Vasumitra spoke as follows."
It enables sentient beings to give rise to diverse views, diverse afflictions,
to perform diverse karmas,
and to undergo diverse births.
Therefore, they are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "attaining [the state of] Dharma and changing levels, one abandons [it]":
this refers to the gate of abandoning non-possession (*aprāpti*).
This refers to the relinquishment of non-acquisition.
It does not exceed two categories:
first, the relinquishment through the acquisition of a dharma.
Second, abandonment through changing the stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding abandonment through the acquisition of a dharma:
for example, the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the noble path is designated as "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
When one attains the Noble Path,
one abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);
this constitutes the substitution of "attainment" (*prāpti*) for the place formerly occupied by "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*).
Abandonment by changing the stage refers to when one is born from a lower stage into a higher stage.
When one descends from a higher stage to a lower stage,

For example, when one is born from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) into a higher realm, one abandons the non-acquisition of the desire realm;
this is because the non-acquisition of the desire realm follows its respective basis (*āśraya*).
Because the basis is abandoned,
non-possession (*aprāpti*) is also abandoned.
As it is with the desire realm, so it is elsewhere.
The same applies to the other realms;
therefore, one abandons them by changing planes,
solely through the change of plane.
One abandons non-possession (*aprāpti*);
it is not necessarily the case that there is a "possession" (*prāpti*) that takes the place of non-possession.
However, such is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Including the two previous types of abandonment,
this refers to the abandonment upon changing levels;
therein, although one does not universally abandon the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) entirely.
There is also a partial relinquishing of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*),
such as when one is born from a lower stage into a higher stage; at that time,

"Homogeneity" marks the heading; "of sentient beings" refers to...

Realms, stages, destinies, and births;

one subsequently abandons desire.
Whether arising from birth, or through hearing, or through reflection—
such wholesome states as these are the causes for rebirth in the happy realms.
Because good and evil arise in combination,
birth in the five destinies is indeterminate.
This concludes the fourth major section from here.
Explaining the two attainments.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, explaining the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Second, the explanation of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Third, the explanation of the body upon which it relies.
First, regarding the explanation of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*):
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished the state of non-conception,
what is the general question regarding the two meditative attainments?
This refers to the summary answer concerning the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation;
first, the attainment of non-perception.
What are its characteristics? To ask specifically, the verse says:
"Thus, the attainment of non-conception / Is in the final dhyāna; it seeks liberation."
Wholesome, it is experienced only in the next life; it is not attained by noble ones and belongs to one lifetime.
The commentary states:
Such is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
It was previously explained that the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the cessation absorption (*nirodha-samāpatti*) possess substantial reality;
likewise, there exists another distinct entity.
The cessation of mind and mental factors, which is dissociated from the mind,
is called the attainment of non-conception.
Approximately equal to the cessation of the mind,
it is called "thus. It is the meditative absorption of non-perception.
It is called the "attainment of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti); alternatively, it is the "attainment in which perception is absent," hence it is named the attainment of non-perception.
As for those who speak of "non-conceptualization" (asaṃjñin), they are merely conventional designations;
they are people who cultivate non-conceptualization.
Because those who cultivate the state of non-conception accomplish this meditative absorption,
it is called the "attainment of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
"Absorption of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is an *tatpuruṣa* compound.
As for the expression "or absorption that is without perception":
"Non-conception is itself concentration" is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
As for "the subsequent dhyāna":
To clarify the basis for its cultivation:
the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
Because it is the very last among the meditative absorptions (dhyāna),
those seeking liberation [seek it therein].
This clarifies the mental attention [of those who hold such views].
That is to say, the various non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) reckon that the fruit of non-conception (asaṃjñi-phala) [is liberation].
Regarding it as true liberation,
they cultivate the attainment of non-conception for the sake of seeking that state.
"Wholesome and experienced only in the next life" refers to the wholesome [state] from the perspective of its three moral natures.
This is the state of non-ideation (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
It is exclusively of a wholesome nature. Because it is wholesome,
it can bring about rebirth in the Heaven of Non-conception.
The five aggregates as maturation (*vipāka*) that are exclusively to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) clarify the time of retribution;
this refers to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
In the second birth, one will necessarily experience its fruit.
The word "only" (唯) is used to exclude [karma] that is to be experienced in the present life (順現報) or in subsequent lives (順後報).
And because it is of indeterminate experience,
the treatise says:
"If one gives rise to this meditative absorption..."
It is traditionally taught that even if one subsequently falls away from it,
one will certainly regain it within the present life.
This means that one who is able to give rise to [this concentration] will be reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in the heavens;
therefore, having attained this meditative absorption, one can certainly never enter the state of right determination and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*). This is the intent of the text.
This clarifies that [the karma] is exclusively to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), and not something obtained in a single lifetime by an *ārya*.
"Non-*ārya*" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has practiced [the path].
This refers exclusively to non-Buddhists who cultivate the attainment of non-conception;
they are certainly not noble ones (ārya).
The treatise states:
Because the various noble ones [do not enter] into the attainment of non-conception.
Just as one who sees a deep pit does not wish to enter it,
one must likewise maintain the state of non-conceptualization.
One cultivates this concentration with the thought of renunciation, regarding it as true liberation.
All noble ones do not grasp at outflows as being true liberation.
And because it is true renunciation,
one must certainly not practice this meditative absorption; so it is explained.
They reckon that the Heaven of No-Thought constitutes true liberation;
this is the attainment of non-conceptualization.
This is true renunciation;
there is no renunciation of birth and death.
To "attain a single lifetime" means:
This clarifies its accomplishment;
that is, at the moment the first thought-moment of the attainment of non-perception arises.
Only that which is obtained in the present life is called "one lifetime," such as when one first receives the prātimokṣa precepts.
This state of non-ideation,
from the second moment onward until it is relinquished.
Because it is determinate (*vijñapti*),
it also becomes past;
there is a phenomenon that is subsequently attained.
Therefore, one should know that the first moment of thought constitutes only a single lifetime,
whereas the second moment and those following it do not.
If one has not yet emerged from meditative absorption,
[the attainment] generally constitutes both the past and the present, because it is devoid of mind.
There is no cultivation of the future,
nor is there any acquisition prior to the dharma;
this is the case once one has emerged from meditative absorption.
It is established as being only past.
The treatise says:
"If [it concerns] the noble ones..."
When one cultivates and attains the stage of the fourth dhyāna,
if it is as in the case of the dhyānas themselves,
can one also attain the past and future states of the attainment of non-conception?
The commentary states:
The intent of this question is as follows:
suppose a noble one first cultivates and attains the fourth dhyāna.
Past dhyānas have already been lost,
and future dhyānas have not yet arisen; however, because they were previously practiced,
[the practitioner can still access them].
At present, they are obtained collectively;
for the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) involving mind are accomplished throughout the three periods of time.
This noble person is thus like one who possesses the meditative absorptions.
Is it also possible to have previously practiced the past non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti),
as well as the future non-conceptual absorption that has not yet arisen?
Since the attainment of non-perception belongs to the fourth dhyāna,
when a noble one cultivates and attains the fourth dhyāna,
they have already attained the meditative concentration of the past and future mental states.
Since there is no perception of the past and future, there must also be acquisition (*prāpti*) of them;
therefore, this question is asked. [The opponent] replies that others also do not acquire them.
Other ordinary persons who attain the fourth dhyāna likewise cannot attain the meditative absorption of non-conception regarding going and coming.
How much more so for a sage? Why is this so?
Although he has practiced it in the past, [he does not need to learn it anew].
Because it is without intrinsic mind,
it must depend upon preparatory effort and be attained through the cultivation of skillful means.
Therefore, when first attained,
it is attained as belonging to only one lifetime; this answers the previous objection regarding that state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Although one may have practiced it in past lives, because of the absence of mind [at that time], [it is not retained].
At this time, one must further cultivate preparatory application (*prayoga*) before it can be attained;
thus it is known.
Ordinary persons may cultivate and attain the fourth dhyāna,
yet because they have not cultivated the attainment of non-conception,
it cannot be obtained by them.
From this, secondly, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is explained.
The treatise states:
Next is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). What are its characteristics?
The verse says:

The attainment of cessation is likewise; it is for the sake of peaceful dwelling, belongs to the Peak of Existence, is wholesome, and its two feelings are indeterminate. It is acquired by noble ones through application;
it is not attained prior to Buddhahood because of the thirty-four moments [of thought].
The commentary states:
The first phrase establishes the essential nature;
the subsequent three phrases distinguish its specific characteristics.
The fifth and sixth phrases clarify that this is attained by a Buddha.
The same applies to the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
This attainment of cessation possesses substantial reality;
it extinguishes both mind and mental factors.
It is the same as the aforementioned state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*); because it extinguishes both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
it is likewise described in that way.
"For one who dwells in tranquility" clarifies the mental application (*manasikāra*); this refers to the aforementioned attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Seeking liberation,

one takes the mental attention (*manasikāra*) characterized by the perception of renunciation as a precursor; this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is for the sake of seeking peaceful abiding.
Preceded by the mental attention to the perception of cessation,
"the Peak of Existence" indicates the basis for clarity.
The aforementioned non-ideation attainment relies upon the fourth dhyāna;
this cessation attainment [relies upon the same].
It relies solely on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This is because all lower stages are termed "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*), as their mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are coarse and agitated.
It is difficult to bring to rest.
This stage of the Peak of Existence is called "Non-perception."
Because its modes of activity are subtle and easy to cease,
there is only the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Regarding the statement, "There is the attainment of cessation; it is wholesome, associated with two feelings, and indeterminate":
"wholesome" refers to the gate of the three natures.
This refers to the attainment of cessation.
Its nature is exclusively wholesome;
it is neither indeterminate nor defiled.
That is to say, it is a wholesome mind.
"Because they are what give rise to [the result]" refers to the two types of indeterminate feeling (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
This clarifies the timing of the retribution; the "two feelings" refer to those that are to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*).
It is conducive to the latter two types of feeling.
This attainment of cessation is conducive to both birth and the subsequent life.
And there is that which is of indefinite timing.
This refers to the maturation (vipāka):
there is karma to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya) or in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya).
The verse states "indeterminate," which encompasses two types of indeterminacy:
first, those whose retribution is fixed but the timing is indeterminate.
Because the timing of both [types of] retribution is indeterminate, the Treatise says:
"There may be some that are indeterminate in their experience; this refers to cases where the retribution is fixed but the timing is indeterminate."
Or they may not receive any at all;
that is to say, if one attains parinirvāṇa in a lower realm.
At this time, both [the body] and the report [of its state] are indeterminate,
as when an Arhat attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and enters parinirvāṇa.
It does not receive a fruit; this attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) only brings about the maturation (vipāka) of the four aggregates within the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
The noble ones who attain it through application are those who clearly cultivate [the path].
This is the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Only noble ones attain it.
The treatise states:
"It cannot be produced by ordinary beings."
Because it fears annihilation,
it can only be produced through the power of the Noble Path.
Nirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa*).
Because it is entered through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-praveśa*). Explanation: This refers to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It arises based on the Peak of Existence;
since that [state] is already formless,
if the mind were further ceased, [what would remain]?
It would then result in annihilation;
therefore, it is feared. When a noble one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), [they do not fall into such a state].
One forms a mind of resolute conviction as if entering nirvana; thus,
it does not arise in ordinary beings.
Regarding that which is attained through application:
this attainment of cessation is attained solely through application.
It is not acquired through the abandonment of defilements,
because the mind [of that state] does not exist;
it requires great preparatory effort.
Only then can it be attained. Furthermore,
at the time of its initial attainment,
one attains only that which belongs to the present life.
From the second moment until it is relinquished,
they collectively constitute the past and present.
If, after emerging from meditative absorption,
one only achieves the past [attainment], this clarifies that the Buddha’s attainment of the attainment of cessation is not prior [to his enlightenment].
"Attaining it upon becoming a Buddha" clarifies that at the time of attaining Buddhahood,
one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
It is not the former;
it is not obtained through prior preparatory practice (*prayoga*).
It is said to be obtained upon attaining Buddhahood.
This reveals attainment through separation from defilement;
that is to say, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he attains the state of Buddhahood.
At this time, having become free from passion,
one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) without relying on further preparatory effort.
Rather, they are attained through cultivation.
Thus, the Treatise says:
"The Buddha does not possess a single virtue that is acquired through preparatory application (*prayoga*)."
When the temporary arising of sensual pleasure manifests before one,
all perfect virtues [are lost].
They arise according to one's inclination;
therefore, all the Buddha’s manifold virtues are attained through the removal of defilement (*vairāgya*). The commentary explains:
"It is simply at the time of removing defilement."
One attains all merits; therefore,
these merits are called "attained through detachment from defilement" (vairāgya-prāpta) and arise in accordance with one's inclination.
It is not a preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The World-Honored One had never previously arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)."
When one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
how does one become one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
The explanation says:
Regarding the stage of training for a bodhisattva:
before having yet arisen from the meditative absorption of cessation,
at the time of attaining buddhahood,
There must be an obstruction to concentration.
How, then, can one achieve liberation through both parts?
As for "liberation through both parts":
This means being free from the obstacles to meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
Because one has attained mastery over the arising and cessation of meditative absorption,
it is as if one has already arisen [from it].
It is called "liberation through both" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*). "Jie" (解) means "to answer.
This refers to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
At the time of attaining Buddhahood,
although it has not yet arisen,
because one has attained mastery over it.
As for those who have already attained it, they are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
because they possess the minds that enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It is called "liberation through both parts.
It is precisely by this principle that it is termed "attained through the removal of defilements."
Because it arises subsequently without depending on preparatory effort (*prayoga*),

non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) does not constitute the essential nature of the meditative attainment; for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) cannot be acquired prior to its actual occurrence.
Therefore, it is not obtained. The Western masters state that a bodhisattva in the stage of training first gives rise to this meditative absorption.
"One attains bodhi later.
Why, then, is that statement not accepted here?
The explanation is as follows:
This is the position of the Sautrāntika school:
they maintain that upon emerging from the path of seeing, a bodhisattva immediately enters the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Only after emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation does one sever the Peak of Existence; therefore,
the knowledge of exhaustion arises.
[They] become those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration].
The master of the treatise asks the Sarvāstivāda school:
"How is it in this regard?"
I do not permit that assertion. If one were to permit it,
it would accord with the Venerable Upagupta.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"As that treatise explains,
one should say that the Tathāgata first enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)."
"Subsequently, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises.
The commentary explains:
"The Master [Vasubandhu] aligns himself with the masters of the Western [Sarvāstivāda] school."
Therefore, this explanation is provided.
Regarding the phrase "because of thirty-four moments of thought," it is intended to refute the assertions of the masters of the Western [Dharmaguptaka] school.
This refers to the land of Kaśmīra.
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the attainment of cessation does not arise prior [to the attainment of non-conceptualization].
Subsequently, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises.
Why is this so? It is traditionally taught that a Bodhisattva possesses thirty-four moments of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*).
Because one attains enlightenment;
within the clear realization of the truths,
there are sixteen moments of mindfulness.
In the detachment from craving for the Peak of Existence,
there are eighteen moments of thought;
that is to say, the abandonment of the Peak of Existence.
The nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation;
thus, there are eighteen.
Adding the preceding sixteen,
they total thirty-four. All Bodhisattvas [possess these].
One definitely first becomes free from attachment to the sphere of nothingness before entering the path of seeing.
There is no longer any need to abandon the afflictions of the lower stages;
within this interval,
there is no possibility for a mind of a different category to arise.
The commentary states:
The Bodhisattva first severs craving for the sphere of nothingness,
and subsequently relies upon the fourth dhyāna.
Thirty-four moments of thought arise;
since these thirty-four moments consist exclusively of uncontaminated (anāsrava) mind,
it cannot be said that one emerges from the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
One arises from the attainment of cessation because the mind that enters the attainment of cessation is tainted (*sāsrava*).
This contaminated mind, when compared to the thirty-four moments of thought,
is called "dissimilar";
therefore, it cannot arise.
From this, thirdly, the basis for the two meditative absorptions is clarified.
The treatise says:
It has already been explained that the two meditative attainments have many points of similarity and difference;
yet, within those, there are further similarities and differences.
The verse says:
"The two meditative attainments depend on the desire and form realms; the attainment of cessation first occurs among humans.
Regarding this, the commentary states:
"The two meditative attainments depend on the desire and form realms."
This explains the basis of the body.
As for the two meditative attainments,
they refer to the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.
Both of these arise based on bodies of the desire and form realms.
Question: Why does the previously mentioned attainment of non-conception not depend on the formless realm?
The principle is beyond doubt.
Why does the attainment of cessation not rely on the formless realms?
Answer: The life-faculty proceeds in dependence upon two factors.
One form and two minds:
if one arises in the desire realm or the form realm and enters the attainment of cessation.
Although at that time there is no mind,
the life-faculty continues to function in dependence upon form when one is born in the formless realm.
Since there is already no material body,
if one enters the meditative attainment of cessation,
then there is neither form nor mind.
If one asks upon what the life-force depends for its continuation,
it would then be subject to annihilation;
this is not what is meant by entering meditative concentration.
Therefore, one does not arise from the meditative attainment of cessation in the formless realm.
The treatise states:
"If there is someone who does not permit this, they must also rely on the form realm."
To claim that one gives rise to the attainment of non-conception would contradict this passage from the treatise, which states: [as follows].
There may be those who possess form and possess this existence, yet do not possess the five aggregates;
namely, sentient beings bound by attachment to the realm of form,
or those born in the heavens of those possessing perception.
One dwells in a mind of a different class,
or enters the attainment of non-conception,
or enters the attainment of cessation.
Or one is born in the Heaven of Non-conception and has already entered the state of non-conception;
this is called "this existence in the realm of form where this existence does not consist of the five aggregates."
The commentary states:
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, some say that it is not permitted for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to give rise to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*).
Therefore, the root treatise is cited to demonstrate that [those views] are incorrect:
"There are some who possess form" refers to sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). "This existence does not consist of the five aggregates" means...
Although they are sentient beings possessing form,
they do not possess the five aggregates (skandhas).
In the past, Kāśyapa Buddha taught that the five aggregates are the five elements (dhātus).
There are four such types: first,
those born in the heavens of perception who abide in a mind of a different category.
Those born in the heavens of perception refer to the gods within the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
excluding the Heaven of No Perception (asaṃjñisattva).
The remaining devas are called "possessing perception.
Within the realm of those possessing perception,
they give rise to the mind of the formless realm.
Furthermore, because the untainted mind and the mind of the form realm differ in their nature,
they are not of the same class.
The name refers to a different category.
This [state] consists only of the two aggregates of form and formations;
it lacks the other three aggregates.
1. Because they are not bound by form; 2.
those born in the heaven of perception who have already entered the attainment of non-perception;
3. those born in the heaven of perception who have [already attained it].
They enter the meditative attainment of cessation;
they are born four times in the Heaven of No-Thought,
having already attained entry into the maturation of non-perception.
In these latter three categories,
feeling, perception, and consciousness have ceased;
there is only the two aggregates of form and formations.
Therefore, these four categories do not possess the five elements;
this is the original text of the treatise.
Since it has already been stated that one is born in the heaven of those with perception (saṃjñā-deva),
or enters the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), or enters the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Thus, it is known that the two meditative attainments arise in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding "the attainment of cessation first arises among humans":
this clarifies that the attainment of cessation first arises among human beings; that is to say, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Because it has been practiced since beginningless time, it arises easily;
thus, it can first arise within both realms.
This attainment of cessation has never been practiced; therefore,
it is difficult to emerge from it when the time comes.
Therefore, it is only among human beings that one can enter the meditative attainment of cessation,
because among humans there exists the power of verbal expression.
Because of the benefit of the sharpness of wisdom.
The treatise says:
"This occurs among human beings."
Once initial cultivation has begun,
one is first subject to regression before being reborn in the form realm.
"Based on a body belonging to the realm of form,
it is subsequently cultivated and brought forth again.
The commentary explains:
There is falling back from the attainment of cessation; therefore, one is born in the form realm,
just like those who do not fall back.
They are born directly into the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Having been born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), by the power of prior habituation,
they are able to attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

However, regarding these two meditative attainments which extinguish both mind and mental factors, the fact that only "the non-percipient" and "the extinction of feeling and perception" are mentioned refers to their preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Because there is a partial aversion toward this,
it is specifically designated.
For example, as the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon:
There is suffering and pleasure which constitute birth and death.
Desiring to cultivate the state of non-perception,
one first forms this thought:
The desire realm possesses suffering;
the first, second, and third dhyānas possess the sensations of joy and pleasure.
Not understanding the fourth [point],
there are those who maintain that there is equanimity as well as other mental states and mental factors,
and they speak as follows:
In the fourth dhyāna, although suffering and pleasure have been transcended,
there still remains conceptualization and perception.
"Since I have not yet attained nirvāṇa,
I must now bring about my cessation.
Thus, during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga),...
This refers to a partial aversion toward perception. If the noble ones perceive that there is the experience of fatigue within the realms of desire and form, [they cultivate this].
In the fourth dhyāna, there are coarse and moving perceptions belonging to the formless realm;
[one practices] in order to seek a state of tranquil abiding.
Desiring for a time to rest the mind,
one therefore focuses specifically on the loathing of sensation and perception during the stage of preparatory application.
Therefore, these two concentrations are designated by names based on their preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Therefore, the treatise states:
"Within the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of these two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
there exists that which is characterized by aversion toward this [existence]."
If one knows feeling and so forth in this manner,
it is termed only "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
The commentary explains:
Although the knowledge of others' minds cognizes mental factors,
it nevertheless requires preparatory cultivation.
However, because one merely desires to know the mind,
it is called "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna) by virtue of its preparatory application (prayoga).
However, these two meditative attainments have twenty-two factors as their substance.
Prior to the cultivation of these attainments, there are twenty-one mental factors and one mind-king. As for the twenty-one mental factors:
That is to say: the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*),
and either interest (*prāmodya*) or aversion (*daurmanasya*).
In order to eliminate these,
there are twenty-two entities known as non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
The term "substitute" refers to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and so forth;
therefore, the cessation of as many mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as are involved constitutes the essential nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
From here begins the fifth major section,
which elucidates the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The treatise states:
The two meditative attainments have already been explained.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
The verse says:
The essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is longevity (*āyus*); it is able to sustain warmth and consciousness.
Commentary: The first line reconciles the terminology.
The subsequent phrase serves as a proof.
The treatise states:
"The essence of life is itself longevity."
Therefore, the Abhidharma states:
What is the life-faculty?
It is the lifespan of the three realms.
The commentary states:
Since "life" (*āyus*) is used here to explain "destiny" (*jīvitendriya*),
it is known that destiny is identical to life.
This remains further unclarified:
what dharma is called "life" (āyus)?
It is said that there is a distinct dharma.
That which is able to sustain warmth and consciousness is called life-force (*āyus*).
This is the sixth [topic] following this.
Explaining the four characteristics.
This section contains two parts:
first, the formal explanation of the four characteristics.
Second, the resolution of difficulties.
Regarding the first [section], the elucidation of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the first part elucidates the primary characteristic (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*).
Second, the explanation of the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). First, regarding the explanation of the primary characteristics (*mūlalakṣaṇa*),
the treatise states:
The life-faculty has already been explained.
What are the four characteristics?
The verse says:
"Characteristics" refers to the nature of arising, abiding, change, and cessation of all conditioned phenomena.
[Commentary: The first line provides the topical outline.
The latter phrase establishes the essence.
"Characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) refers to the defining attributes;
that is to say, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
These are the phenomena that possess characteristics.
"All conditioned things" refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which are produced through causes and conditions.
Therefore, they are called "dharmas such as form and mind," which arise from causes and conditions.
Because they possess those [characteristics],
they are called "conditioned.
A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is a defining mark.
This refers to the essential nature of the characteristic-dharmas, which renders them conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the treatise says:
Because these four are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*),
if a phenomenon possesses them,
it must be conditioned.
That which is contrary to this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. To explain:
The explanation of the meaning of the characteristics: "The nature of arising, abiding, change, and cessation" identifies their essential substance (*svabhāva*).
Within this context, regarding phenomena (*dharma*):
That which can cause arising is called "birth";
that which can provide stability is called "abiding";
that which can cause decay is called "change."
That which can be destroyed is called "cessation.
"Nature" (svabhāva) has the meaning of "essence" (tattva).
This refers to the Sarvāstivāda school.
This is because the four characteristics possess substantial reality.
The treatise states:
"Is it not said in the Sūtra that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned?"
The commentary states:
This citation of a sutra serves as a challenge.
The sutra speaks of the three characteristics.
The treatise now speaks of four;
does this not contradict [the claim that] there are three, which are the defining characteristics?
"Conditioned" refers to the phenomena that possess characteristics; the particle "of" (之) indicates a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
The repetition of the term "conditioned" is intended to make known these characteristics.
This indicates the nature of the entity,
because it constitutes the conditioned;
these three characteristics are as follows.
Regarding the characteristics of the conditioned,
it should be stated that there are four within this sutra.
The commentary states:

Within this sūtra, it would logically have to speak of four [characteristics]. Why, then, is it not so stated? It refers to the characteristic of abiding; yet the sūtra speaks of "abiding and change" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
This is another specific name for it;
just as arising is called "origination" and ceasing is called "exhaustion."
It should be understood in this way:
"change of state" (sthity-anyathātva) is another name for "aging" (jarā). To explain:
There are three masters who explain the sūtra;
this is the explanation of one master.
The sūtra does not speak of "abiding," but speaks of the three characteristics.
First, arising;
second, duration and change;
third, cessation.

However, what the Sūtra refers to as the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) is here [in this treatise] stated to be another name for the characteristic of difference (*anyathābhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
This refers to the differentiation based on abiding;
because it is that by which [the state] differs,
it is called "differentiation of abiding" (sthity-anyathātva).
"Arising" (*utpāda*) is a synonym for birth (*jāti*);
"cessation" (*nirodha*) is a synonym for the characteristic of exhaustion (*kṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, one should know that "distinct characteristic" (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) is another name for "subsistence-alteration" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
If a dharma causes conditioned phenomena to flow through the three time periods,
this sūtra describes it as the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
It is to cause all sentient beings to give rise to revulsion and fear;
that is to say, those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are driven by the power of arising.
Causing [the conditioned entity] to flow from the future into the present,
it is driven and constrained by the power of the characteristics of change and cessation.
It causes [them] to flow from the present into the past,
causing them to decay and change.
And because they are subject to decay and destruction, one dwells within those formations,
grasping at them for the sake of happiness,
always delighting in never being separated from them.
Therefore, it is not established among the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
"This is the interpretation of the sūtra’s intent by the first master."
Because the three characteristics undergo transition and movement, the Sūtra speaks of them;
because abiding is peaceful and stable, the Sūtra does not speak of it.
Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) abide by their own characteristics; thus,
the characteristic of abiding would be conflated with them.
Therefore, the Sūtra does not mention it. The Commentary states:
This is the explanation of the Sūtra by the second master.
That the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is profoundly still is its abiding in its own characteristic (svalakṣaṇasthiti).

Some say that this sutra explains that "staying" (sthiti) and "alteration" (anyathātva) are combined as one, and thus termed the characteristic of "staying-and-alteration" (sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa).
The commentary states:
This is the teaching of the third master. The Sūtra speaks of "abiding and change" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
When these two views are combined,
they differ from the first master’s position,
which holds that it is exclusively a distinct characteristic (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the purpose of asking such a comprehensive question?
It is for the sake of causing [beings] to cultivate revulsion toward and relinquish that which sentient beings are attached to— namely, existence (*bhava*).
They are spoken of in conjunction with distinct entities, just as when one points out that Kālī is together with Śrī.
Therefore, it is certain that there are four conditioned characteristics. This is the answer.
The two sisters, Śrīkālī and Kālakarnī,
were constantly following one another.
The elder sister’s name was Śrī; wherever she went,
auspicious things occurred.
The younger sister was named Kṛṣṇakarṇī; she was so named because her ears were black.
Wherever one goes,
it can cause decline and loss;
yet the foolish crave auspiciousness.
To cause those with wisdom to cultivate revulsion and relinquish [attachment],
one first demonstrates the "Black Ear" (Kṛṣṇakarṇī) and then abides in the metaphor of "Auspiciousness" (Śrīvatsa).
The negative example is "Black-Ear," which is stated in conjunction with the dissimilar [case] in order to induce weariness toward [sensual] abiding.
From this second [section] onward, the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are explained.
The treatise says:
Since these characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) are themselves conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
one must further inquire whether they possess another set of four characteristics, namely arising and so forth. If there were yet another set, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, it is difficult [to maintain] because there are other characteristics such as "arising" (jāti) and so forth; these characteristics are conditioned (saṃskṛta).
There are four distinct characteristics, and upon these characteristics, there are further characteristics.
This would result in the fallacy of infinite regress.
One should say that there is yet more;
however, this is not an answer to the double [query] by means of infinite regress. Why is this so? What is the evidence? The verse says:
Regarding the statement, "This has the 'arising of arising' and so forth, which have the capacity for one and eight," the commentary explains:
the first line answers the question.
The second phrase answers the objection.
"This" refers to the four primary characteristics mentioned previously. "Arising-of-arising" and so forth [refer to the secondary characteristics].
The four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). This means that for each of the aforementioned four primary characteristics,
there are four types of secondary characteristics— namely, arising-of-arising and so forth—
by which they become conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The treatise states:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are conditioned by way of four primary characteristics."
The primary characteristics of the conditioned exist by means of the four secondary characteristics. To explain:
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) constitute the conditioned by virtue of the four primary characteristics; these primary characteristics,
in turn, constitute the conditioned.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the four secondary characteristics, arising arises," and so forth:
the term "and so forth" includes abiding-abiding, change-change, and cessation-cessation; these constitute three names.
The first is called "the production of production" (*jāti-jāti*), and so forth. In this term, the upper character "production" (*jan*) refers to the minor production,
while the lower character "production" (*jan*) refers to the major production.
Because the "birth of birth" (jāti-jāti) gives rise to the "great birth" (mahā-jāti),
it is said to abide within the minor characteristic of birth;
it abides in its own primary characteristic (mūla-lakṣaṇa).
It is called "abiding-abiding.
It differs from the minor characteristics;
it differs from the primary characteristics.
It is called "distinct.
It ceases within the minor characteristic;
it ceases by the cessation of the primary characteristic.
The first is called "the extinction of extinction," which is explained in the same manner as "the arising of arising.
The second is called the "subsidiary characteristic" (anulakṣaṇa).
Because they follow their own primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa), these three are called "minor characteristics" (anulakṣaṇa);
this is because they characterize a single phenomenon (dharma).
The primary characteristic (mūla-lakṣaṇa) also has three names.
The first is called the "primary characteristic," because it is the characteristic that gives rise to the fundamental [nature].
The second is called "great characteristic" (*mahālakṣaṇa*),
because it characterizes the eight factors.
The third is called "arising and so forth" (*jātyādi*).
Because it gives rise to eight dharmas,
it differs from "minor birth" (*upapattibhava*), which gives rise only to birth itself;
therefore, it is simply called "birth."

The same applies to the characteristics such as duration (*sthiti*) and so forth. Regarding the capacity [of a characteristic] to function upon one or eight [factors], this universally resolves infinite difficulties.
Is it not the case that the primary characteristics are like the phenomena they characterize?
Each [primary characteristic] should have four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas),
and these in turn would each have four, resulting in an infinite regress.
To resolve this difficulty:
Therefore, there is this verse:
"The four primary characteristics have efficacy with respect to the eight [dharmas], while the four secondary characteristics [have efficacy] with respect to the four [primary characteristics]."
Because there is a distinction in their functional capacities regarding a single entity,
there is no fault of infinite regress.
For example, when the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) brings about a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*).
Nine factors arise together.
The first is the primary dharma,
namely the intrinsic nature of matter (*rūpa*).
Above this, there must necessarily be four primary and four secondary [factors],
thus constituting nine dharmas.
Within these nine dharmas:
Arising cannot arise by itself;
excluding its own self-nature,
arising can give rise to the other eight [dharmas].
Abiding within its own characteristics,
it cannot abide by itself;
it abides through the other eight dharmas.
Within the primary characteristics, "aging" (jarā) cannot age itself;
it ages the other eight dharmas.
Within the primary characteristics, "cessation" (nirodha) cannot cease itself.
Because they cause the extinction of the other eight factors,
the four primary characteristics possess functional efficacy with respect to those eight factors.
Among these nine dharmas,
arising does not arise by itself;
it is the "arising of arising" that causes it to arise.
Abiding does not abide by itself;
abiding comes from abiding.
Difference does not differ by itself.
Because it is distinct from what is distinct,
cessation does not cease by itself;
it is through the cessation of cessation that it ceases.
Therefore, the four secondary characteristics possess functional efficacy within a single dharma.
By this principle, there is no fault of infinite regress;
therefore, the treatise says:
Therefore, for [the characteristics] such as birth (jāti) and so forth, there are further secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa);
these secondary characteristics are only four.
There is no fault of infinite regress.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned."
The treatise states:
"However, the reason the Sūtra repeats the term 'conditioned' (saṃskṛta) is to make it known that these characteristics indicate something is conditioned."
Do not say that these signs indicate the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*),
just as white egrets do not indicate the absence of water;
nor should you say that they indicate the goodness or evil of conditioned phenomena.
"Just as the appearance of a young girl indicates whether she is auspicious or inauspicious.
The commentary explains:
"It is like seeing a white heron from afar."
The manifestation indicates the presence of water;
it is like a young girl possessing auspicious marks,
which indicates she will give birth to a virtuous son.
Just as there are ill-omened signs that portend the birth of an evil child,
so too these four characteristics now signify only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
It does not signify that the conditioned exists in the same way that a white heron signifies the presence [of fish].
Furthermore, these four characteristics do not manifest the nature of being conditioned, wholesome, or unwholesome;
thus they differ from a young girl, who manifests what is wholesome and what is not.
From this second point onward,
the difficulties are explained according to the Sautrāntika school.
The four characteristics are conventional designations.
We do not accept the tenet that the future has substantial existence,
nor that there is a real characteristic of arising.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"If arising exists in the future, it would give rise to the dharmas that are to be produced."
Why do all future phenomena not arise simultaneously?
The verse says:
"Arising can give rise to that which arises, / Not apart from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Explanation: These two lines [state as follows].
This answers the objection from the Sautrāntika school.
"Causes" (hetu) refers to the six causes;
"conditions" (pratyaya) refers to the four conditions.
The treatise states:
"It is not that the power of the characteristic of arising alone produces [the dharma], independent of the conjunction of other causes and conditions."
Because that which produces and that which is produced [must exist], all future phenomena do not arise simultaneously.
From this point, the seventh major section explains the "name-aggregates" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.
The treatise states:
Having thus explained the various characteristics of conditioned phenomena,
what is the meaning of the categories such as "name-groups" (nāmakāya) and so forth?
The verse says:
"Name-bodies and so forth are what are called the collective designations of concepts, phrases, and syllables.
The commentary explains:
"Name-bodies and so forth" is the heading;
"that which is called" below is the formal explanation.

The term "and so forth" includes the phrase-body (*pada-kāya*) and the phoneme-body (*vyañjana-kāya*). Regarding the statement that "conception (*saṃjñā*) is a general designation for chapters and syllables," this explains the preceding point;
it explains the name by means of conception.
Explain the phrases by means of the chapters;
explain the text by means of the characters;
explain the body [of the teaching] by means of the general exposition. The *Śāstra* states: "Name" refers to the formation of conceptual designations (*saṃjñā*).
The commentary explains:
"Perception" (saṃjñā) means grasping an image,
or it has the sense of a convention.
If one apprehends the name as a mental image, then this "apperception" (saṃjñā) is a mental factor (caitta),
just as when one speaks of the "name of form" (rūpa-nāman).
It can produce the perception of form;
because it is the cause, it is called the "producing perception," and it is termed the "constructing perception."
If it is in the sense of a convention,
then perception itself is the name;
this refers to the noble ones.
Together they establish a convention,
instituting names such as "form" and so forth;
this name is itself perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because it is able to express meaning through these names and concepts, it is called "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*). In Sanskrit,
this is *nāma* (with the first syllable in the rising tone).
In the Tang dynasty, it was translated as "name" (míng). This follows the meaning [of the original term] and accords with its significance.
"Proceeding toward the object" means that, following the sound,
it proceeds toward its objective sphere.
The invocation of form and so forth is called that which expresses meaning. The treatise states:
"A phrase (pada) refers to a sentence (vākya)."
It is the ultimate determination of meaning,
such as the chapters explaining that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and so forth;
or it is that which can discern the distinctions in the correspondence between function, quality, time, and their specific characteristics.
This chapter is titled "Phrases.
The commentary explains:
take, for instance, a single form (*rūpa*).
There is the activity of seeing which can give rise to the function of consciousness;
[it perceives] qualities such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
In the past, future, and other such times,
being conjoined with the four characteristics is called "associated.
As for "non-associated":
It is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*),
meaning that it is able to distinguish that "form" is that which is seen and so forth;
this chapter is termed a "phrase" (*pada*).
In Sanskrit it is called *pada*;
its meaning is translated as "phrase," and its precise translation is "trace."
This means that just as an elephant's body has four footprints,
so too does a single verse consist of four lines in total.
Therefore, we now translate it as "sentence" (jù) based on its meaning.
In Sanskrit it is called *vākya*,
which is translated here as "chapter" (zhāng).
A "chapter" (*pariccheda*) is so called because it brings the exposition of meaning to completion;
thus, a chapter explains a section (*varga*). A "text" (*grantha*) is...
This refers to syllables (*akṣara*).

For example, as when one speaks of syllables such as *a*, *ā*, *i*, and *ī*; these are syllables among the formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and are not like the characters of written script found here in this land.
In Sanskrit it is called *vyañjana*;
in the Tang language it is called "text" (*wen*), which carries the meaning of that which manifests.
It closely manifests names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*).
This serves to clarify the meaning far more clearly.
It is the custom in the Western Regions to refer to fans, salt, and vinegar by these names.
It is also called *vyajana*;
it is that which manifests meaning,
just as a fan manifests wind.
Salt and vinegar can manifest the flavors within food;
therefore, the old translation of "taste" (rasa) as [the object] is erroneous. "Body" (kāya) has the meaning of an aggregation.
This is a general explanation.
The Meaning of Collection (*saṃgraha-artha*): This refers to the collective designation of two, three, or more names for the purpose of aggregation;
therefore, "collective designation" explains the meaning of *kāya* (body/aggregate).
The treatise states:
"To speak of 'general exposition' (saṃgraha) means the sense of a collective compilation."
Regarding the meaning of "aggregation," it is said that this refers to the *ucchā* element (*dhātu*).
The explanation states:
In the grammatical science (*śabda-vidyā*) of the West,
the creation of words consists of the verbal root (*dhātu*), the affix (*pratyaya*),
and the suffix (*upapada*). The root is the fundamental meaning.
The phonemes assist in forming various meanings.
Now, *ut-cha* is a verbal root (*dhātu*).
This was originally established by the founders of the script.
Within the sense of aggregation,
the verbal root *uc* is established;
subsequently, by means of a suffix (*pratyaya*).
The *uddeśa* section is transformed into the three *muktipatis*; in the language of Tang,
this is called "General Exposition" (*zongshe*).
Having understood the meaning of the general exposition,
it begins with *uḍḍāna*;
*uḍḍāna* has the sense of a collective summary.
It is clearly understood that a collective statement is also a composite;
this text uses the verbal root *ud-√ci* in the sense of a composite.
This is explained by way of a general statement as a collective sense; thus,
the term "body" (kāya) has been explained through this general statement.
Thus, we know that a collection of many names constitutes a "name-body" (nāmakāya) and so forth.
However, a single name is a "name" (nāman), not a "name-body";
two names constitute a "name-body."
As it is said regarding "form" and "sound":
when three names have passed, they are called a "word-group" (padakāya).
As it is said regarding "form," "sound," "odor," and so forth.
There are three names.
One is a phrase; it is not a phrase-body (*padakāya*).
Two phrases constitute a phrase;
they also constitute a phrase-body (*padakāya*). From three phrases onward, [they constitute a sentence].
This is called a "phrase-body" (padakāya).
For example: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
all dharmas are without self."
"Nirvāṇa" and "quiescence"—these all consist of three phrases;
they are called a "group of many phrases" (padakāya).
A single character is a "syllable" (vyañjana).
It is not a word-body (*vyañjana-kāya*). Both two syllables are also words,
and they are also a word-body.
That which consists of three or more syllables is called a "multisyllabic phoneme-group" (anekākṣara-kāya),
such as ka, kha, ga, and so forth.
There are three syllables;
they are called a "multitude of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*).
The treatise states:
Furthermore, for example, in ancient times,
among nine different meanings,
a single sound "go" was established in common usage.
Because it serves as the definitive authority for that which expresses [the meaning],
there is a verse that says:
Direction, beast, earth, light, word, Vajra, eye, water, heaven.
Regarding these nine meanings, the wise establish the sound "go" as referring to one direction,
two animals, and so forth.
The third stage,
the fourth light,
and the fifth word.
Six vajras, seven eyes,
and eight deities.
The nine waters all share the single sound "gou," which signifies these nine meanings.
To point at a direction is called *gou*;
*gou* then refers to a cardinal point.
To point at a beast is called *gou*.
"Gou" (瞿) refers to a beast;
the rest may be understood by analogy.
This concludes the third [section].
The analysis by way of various categories consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the names and so forth.
Second, the explanation of the *sabhāgatā* and so forth.
First, regarding the explanation of "names" (*nāman*) and so on,
the treatise states:
To what realm are these name-bodies and so forth bound?
Are they included within the category of sentient beings?
Is it not included among the category of sentient beings?
Is it produced by karmic maturation (*vipākaja*)?
Or is it nurtured growth (*aupacayika*)?
It should be analyzed whether these are of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda), whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The verse says:
They are comprised within the sentient beings of the desire and form realms; they are of the nature of outflow and are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary says:
The mention of "desire and form" refers to the perspective of the realms of existence (*dhātu-bandhana*).

That is to say, these aggregates of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are bound to the desire and form realms; specifically, they refer to the aggregates of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjanakāya*).
They exist in dependence upon sound;
because there is no form and no sound, names and so forth do not exist.
As for those included among sentient beings:
The treatise states:
Furthermore, name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are subsumed under the category of sentient beings;
thus, they constitute the speaker and do not constitute the meaning that is manifested.
The commentary states:
"The 'one who can speak' and the 'one who accomplishes' manifest that there are only sentient beings."
This is not the meaning revealed [by the term];
it clarifies that [the term] does not apply to non-sentient things.
As for "outflow" (niṣyanda):
This is the section on the five categories. These,
such as the name-body (nāmakāya) and so forth,
arise from homogeneous causes (sabhāgahetu).
Among the five categories,
these are exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*); because they are not produced by karma,
they do not pertain to maturation (*vipāka*).
Because they are not material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), they do not pertain to growth (*aupacayika*). As for the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): [they are likewise].
This is the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
It is comprised exclusively of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature; that is to say, the group of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, which arise based on sound.
It is not that the mind-force can directly initiate it;
therefore, it is exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Sound, however, is the mind-force.
Because the roots of goodness can initiate it,
it pervades all three natures.
This is the second [point].
Explaining the *sabhāgatā* and so forth,
the treatise states:
"The other non-associated [formations] are as described above."
The meaning not yet explained shall now be briefly analyzed.
The verse says:

The same applies to *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). Together with the formless [attainments], maturation, and acquisition (*prāpti*), these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to all three categories. Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is definitely of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The commentary states:
The phrase "the same applies to the homogeneous character" (sabhāgatā) indicates that,
like the aforementioned names and so forth, the homogeneous character pervades both the desire realm and the form realm.
Sentient beings;
outflowing; non-obscured and indeterminate.
"And including those without form" means that it is shown that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is not restricted solely to the desire and form realms,
but also extends to the formless realm.

Regarding "and [it is] also of the nature of maturation": this means that the manifesting [mental states] (vijñapti) share the same homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) and are not merely of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda);
they also pertain to the nature of maturation (vipāka).
Because of this, the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) pertains to all three realms (*dhātu*) and encompasses two types of meaning.
Regarding the three realms:
The three realms.
Regarding the two types:
these are the outflowing and the maturation.
Regarding the statement that "attainment (prāpti) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa) apply to all three categories":
"attainment" refers to the act of acquiring; "characteristics" refers to the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena].
This acquisition and its characteristic apply exclusively to three categories:
first, those that are momentary.
Second, the nature of outflow;
third, the nature of maturation.
Above the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).
Acquisition and the four characteristics are momentary;
the remainder is of two types. Non-acquisition is definitely an outflow.
Non-acquisition refers to non-possession (*aprāpti*).
"Absorption" refers to the two absorptions: the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Non-acquisition and meditative absorption produce their effects as similar-cause factors within the five categories.
It is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), because it is not produced by karma; therefore,
it does not pertain to maturation (*vipāka*).
Because they are not material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*),

The path proceeds through the nine stages; only those that are equal or superior serve as its fruit. The same applies to those produced by preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Regarding the phrase "those consisting of hearing, reflection, and so forth," the commentary explains: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 7, Verse 52: "The path proceeds through the nine stages; only those that are equal or superior serve as its fruit. The same applies to those produced by preparatory effort. Regarding "those consisting of hearing, reflection, and so forth": 1. **Hearing** (*śruta-maya*) consists of wisdom born from hearing the Dharma. 2. **Reflection** (*cintā-maya*) consists of wisdom born from reflecting upon the meaning of what has been heard. 3. **Cultivation** (*bhāvanā-maya*) consists of wisdom born from meditative cultivation. These are explained as follows: Wisdom consisting of hearing is the cause for wisdom consisting of reflection; wisdom consisting of reflection is the cause for wisdom consisting of cultivation. Furthermore, within each stage, wisdom consisting of hearing is the cause for subsequent wisdom consisting of hearing, and likewise for the others. Thus, these are established as causes for their own kind and for those that follow. As for the statement "only those that are equal or superior serve as its fruit": this means that a path belonging to a lower stage can only have a path of an equal or higher stage as its fruit, but never one of a lower stage. Similarly, regarding those produced by preparatory effort, the same principle applies: they are fruits of paths that are equal or superior, but not of inferior ones. This establishes the relationship between the paths of the various stages.
