Regarding what is called "the nine stages":
That is to say: the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the four dhyānas.
The three formless [attainments].
Based on these nine stages,
one gives rise to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Each one serves as a cause for the ninth stage;
relying on the stage of "not yet arrived" (anāgamya),
one gives rise to the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
It can serve as the cause for the path-truths of the nine stages,
up to the sphere of nothingness,
giving rise to the untainted path.
It also serves as a homogeneous cause for the ninth stage.
The treatise says:
In all these stages,
it dwells like a guest and is not included within the realms.
They are not grasped as "mine" by craving for the various stages;
therefore, although the paths of the nine stages differ from one another, they serve as causes for one another in succession.
"Because they are of the same category.
The explanation says:
"The untainted (anāsrava) is not bound to any realm (dhātu)."
Although it arises in the various stages,
it is like a guest’s stay;
it is comprised within tainted craving.
Therefore, they are subsumed within the realms of existence (*dhātu*). If, however, they are untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*),
they are not grasped as "mine" by the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) of the nine stages.

Therefore, the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) does not fall within the inclusion of the realms (dhātu-saṃgraha). "Only that which is equal or superior constitutes the fruit" excludes those that are distinct [in quality].
However, it can only serve as a cause for that which is equal or superior,
and not as a cause for that which is inferior;
this is because it is considered part of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) produced through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
How could diligent effort result in an inferior dharma? Therefore,
it serves as a homogeneous cause for that which is equal or superior.
For example, the already-arisen *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the future *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*.
These are the equal causes: if it is the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti),
it is a homogeneous cause for the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) up to the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
This is called "superior": because it is a superior patience (*kṣānti*).
To speak at length, up to the various types of knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), these act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) only for their own kind.
Furthermore, there is no dharma superior to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Moreover, all paths that have already arisen— the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*)— [are subsumed therein].
According to their respective order,
they serve as similar causes for three, two, and one [of the subsequent categories].
The commentary explains:
The path of seeing serves as the cause for the three— namely,
the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
The path of cultivation is the cause for two [paths],
excluding the path of vision.
The path of no-more-learning is the cause for one [path].
This excludes the paths of seeing and cultivation.
Furthermore, among these,
there are the paths of those with dull faculties.
The dull and the sharp serve as similar causes for one another. Furthermore,
all paths of sharp faculties serve as causes for the path of sharp faculties.
As with those who follow by faith,
those resolved through faith,
and the path of occasional liberation.
In their respective order,
they serve as homogeneous causes for the sixth, the fourth, and the second [stages].
The commentary states:
Among the two types of noble ones who have realized the Path,
one is of dull faculty.

There are two types of those who benefit themselves and others: the dull-witted refers to those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin), and the sharp-witted refers to those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin). There are two noble ones in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
First, the dull;
second, the sharp.
"Dull" refers to those whose liberation is through faith (śraddhādhimukta).
"Sharp" refers to those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
There are two types of noble ones on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*):
first, the dull-witted (*mṛdu*).
The two types of benefit:
"dull" refers to those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*);
"sharp" refers to those liberated irrespective of occasion (*asamayavimukta*).
This refers to the three paths,
wherein there are six noble ones in total;
now, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) serves as the cause for these six.
Those with faith and those resolved through conviction serve as causes for four [types of persons],
excluding the two noble ones on the path of seeing.
The path of liberation at that time serves as the cause for two [types of paths],
excluding the four noble paths of seeing and cultivation.
If one follows the path of practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin), the path of attainment through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), or the path of untimely liberation (asamayavimukta),
they proceed according to their respective order.
It acts as a similar cause for three, two, or one [of the subsequent stages].
The commentary explains: this refers to those who follow the Dharma through understanding (dharmānusārin).
It serves as the cause for three [types of individuals]:
namely, those who follow the Dharma (dharmānusārin), those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and [the rest].
It is not at the improper time.
It is "seen-to" (dṛṣṭa-prāpta).
It serves as the cause for two [types of attainment].
Excluding those that follow the Dharma (anudharmaja).
[A state] does not serve as a cause for one [subsequent state] at an improper time.
Excluding those that follow the Dharma and those attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
The treatise states:
"The paths of the higher stages serve as causes for the lower stages."
What is meant by "equal or superior"?
The explanation states:
this refers to the difficulty [of establishing] that the paths of the nine stages serve as mutual causes for one another.
The higher stages are superior;
the lower stages are inferior.
[The higher] serve as causes for the lower.
This then serves as a cause for that which is inferior,
not for that which is equal or superior.
The treatise says:
It is due to the increase of causes and due to the faculties,
namely, the path of seeing and so forth.
In the successive stages, beginning with the lowest of the low grade and so forth,
the causes continue to increase.
The commentary says:
This answers the preceding objection.
It is not because the earth has upper and lower levels [that the Buddha’s body appears differently].
This causes the paths and so forth to have distinctions of superiority and inferiority;
even though they rely upon a lower stage,
when compared to the path of a higher stage, [they are inferior].
There are two causes by which it is designated as "superior":
first, through the increase of its cause.
The second [type] is also due to the faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding growth by way of cause: this refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and those that follow.
This explains "increase" (*vṛddhi*).
By the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) are included.
In each successive stage,
the cause becomes increasingly superior;
that is to say, one cultivates the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
After the path of seeing,
the path of no-more-learning follows the path of cultivation;
these are called "successive stages."
Furthermore, the path of seeing and so forth each consist of nine grades, from the lowest-of-the-low to the highest-of-the-high.
These constitute the nine grades of stages.
In each successive stage,
the cause also becomes increasingly superior,
just as when the path of seeing arises in a higher realm.
It serves as the cause for the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) of the lower stages and so forth,
as well as for the superior and inferior-inferior grades [of the higher stages]. Furthermore,
the path of a higher stage serves as the cause for the lower, middle, and superior grades of the path of a lower stage.
It serves as the cause because the causes increase through successive stages.
Second, by way of the faculties (*indriya*):
The path of those with dull faculties in a higher stage serves as the cause for the path of those with sharp faculties in a lower stage;
the treatise does not explain this regarding the faculties.
This is because it is easy to understand.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Although within a single continuum, there is no possibility for the two paths—those of following faith and those of following dharma—to manifest simultaneously."
"And that which has already arisen serves as the cause for the future.
The commentary explains:
This passage resolves a latent objection.
The intent of the objection is as follows:
it is objected that [the self] is preceded by and dependent upon the sense faculties,
just as within a single body.
Once the path of practice through faith (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*) by means of dull faculties has already arisen,

it is impossible for the path of practice through Dharma (*dharmānusāri-mārga*) by means of sharp faculties to arise again; how, then, can it be said that the path of dull faculties in a higher stage serves as the cause for the path of sharp faculties in a lower stage?
Therefore, it is said that although there is a single continuum, two paths cannot arise within one body;
yet, in the higher realms, the path of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) has already arisen.

There is no logical contradiction in [the dharmas] of a lower stage being the cause for those of the future that follow the practice of the dharma (*dharmacarita*). The same applies to those produced through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
This clarifies that the dharmas produced by contaminated preparatory effort are the same as those previously mentioned regarding the uncontaminated;
they only correspond to those that are equal or superior.
Because it acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it is said to be likewise. Regarding "that which is produced by hearing and reflection" (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) and so forth,
this precisely clarifies the essential nature of the wholesome states of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
Regarding the phrase "consisting of what is produced by hearing and reflection," etc., the word "etc.
includes what is produced by cultivation.
It is based on hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The meritorious qualities accomplished are called "that which is accomplished.
These are the three types of wisdom.
Only by applying effort and practice can it be brought forth;
this is called "virtue of application" (prayoga-kuśala).
Dharmas acquired through hearing serve as homogeneous causes for the wisdom acquired through hearing.
These are called the "equalities":
the dharmas accomplished through hearing,
together with the wisdoms of reflection and cultivation.
To serve as a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is what is called "superior.
Volition (cetanā) serves as a homogeneous cause for both volition and cultivation (bhāvanā).
Excluding those produced by hearing, because they are inferior due to being based on hearing,
those produced by cultivation serve as homogeneous causes only for [dharmas] produced by cultivation.
Excluding the two [types of wisdom] consisting of hearing and reflection, because these two are inferior; there is no wisdom of cultivation in the desire realm,
because it is a distracted stage.
In the two upper realms there is no volition;
for when one raises the mind with the intention [to act],
one immediately enters meditative absorption.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is neither seeing nor hearing, because the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*) is absent.
The treatise explains the causes by way of the three realms;
this can be understood through reading. These [wholesome states] of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*) are grouped into nine grades (*navavidha*).
If it is of the lowest-low grade,
it serves as the cause for nine grades;
if it is of the lower-middle grade...
It acts as a cause for the eight [levels],
up to the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra),
which acts as a cause only for the highest-of-the-high.
Because the previously mentioned inferior states are excluded,
the innate wholesome dharmas are considered in relation to one another across nine grades.
They serve as causes for one another;
the same applies to defiled states,
namely those acquired at birth that are wholesome.
Or from the inferior grade,
one may give rise to the middling or superior grades;
or from the superior grade, one may give rise to the middling or inferior grades.
Because each [of the nine grades] subsequently manifests one after another,
the nine grades can thus serve as causes for one another in succession.
The same applies to defiled states.
This may be explained by analogy with "attainment through conformity.
There are four types of non-obscured neutral [states] in total.
That is to say: those born of maturation,
those of the modes of deportment,
and those of the spheres of craftsmanship.
The transformative minds,
in their respective order,
serve as causes for four, three, two, and one [subsequent mind].
The commentary states:
This is because what follows is superior to what precedes it.
From this, the fourth [section].
Explaining the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).
The treatise says:
"Thus, the characteristics of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) have already been explained."
What is the characteristic of the fourth, the associated cause?
The verse says:
The associated cause is determined by mind and mental factors sharing the same basis.
The commentary states:
As for the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
It must necessarily share the same basis to be called "associated"; therefore,
it is said to be "definite."
This refers to the expression "having a common basis," which indicates that they necessarily share the same support (*āśraya*) and the same object (*ālambana*).
Sharing the same conduct,
being simultaneous,
and sharing the same purpose.
The possession of five meanings is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).
As the treatise says:
In this context, the word "same" indicates that the basis is one;
that is to say, if a visual consciousness takes this particular momentary eye-faculty as its basis.
The associated sensations and so forth likewise take this very eye-faculty as their basis,
extending up to the mental consciousness.
It should be understood that the associated dharmas,
which likewise rely upon the mental faculty (manas), are also the same.
The commentary states:
The mind and its mental factors do not differ in their basis.
This is called "the first.
From this fifth [section] onward,
the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu) is explained.
The treatise says:
Having thus explained the characteristics of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*),
what are the characteristics of the fifth, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
The verse says:

"Universal [factors] refer to those previously mentioned as universal; they are the cause of defilement within their own stage. The commentary says: [They are so called because] they serve as the cause for the defilements of the same level.
The pervasive factors refer to the eleven pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*) along with their associated and co-existent dharmas.
Eleventh, the pervasive messengers:
this refers to the seven [factors] within the truth of suffering,
namely, the five views.
Doubt is ignorance. There are four truths of origination.
Wrong view, adherence to views,
and doubt.
It is ignorance (*avidyā*).
These various factors serve as causes for all defiled phenomena across the five categories;
therefore, they are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*).
"Universal" (sarvatraga) is itself the cause;
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
That is to say, that which was previously described as "universal."
It takes only those previously arisen universal dharmas as its cause;
this refers to that which arose previously.
Excluding the future,
it passes through the present alone;
this applies to those belonging to the same stage (*bhūmi*).
It does not serve as a cause for defiled dharmas of a different stage (*bhūmi*).
The treatise states:
"Because this serves as a universal cause (*sāmānyahetu*) for defiled dharmas."
It is established separately from the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) because it also serves as the cause for the defiled dharmas of other categories;
by its power, [it produces those results].
The defiled dharmas of other schools,
as well as their attendants,
also arise and grow.
The commentary explains:
It acts as a universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu) and takes the fruits of the five categories (pañca-nikāya).
This is called the cause of penetration (*abhisamaya-hetu*). As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it produces only fruits of its own category (*sva-nikāya*).
It is not a pervasive cause.
As for what is called "retinue," it refers to the afflictions.
These are the associated and co-existent dharmas.
Following this, the sixth [section] clarifies the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The treatise says:
Having thus explained the characteristics of the omnipresent cause (sarvatraga-hetu),
what are the characteristics of the sixth, the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu)?
The verse says:
The ripening cause consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome that is exclusively with outflows.
The commentary says:
Only unwholesome states and wholesome states with outflows are causes of maturation,
because they are dharmas that mature.
Question: For what reason does the indeterminate (avyākṛta) not bring about maturation (vipāka)? Answer: Because its power is weak, like a rotten seed.
Question: For what reason is the untainted (anāsrava) [not subject to maturation]?
It does not produce a ripened result (*vipāka*).
The answer is: because it lacks the moisture of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is like a genuine seed that lacks the nourishment of water.
Furthermore, it is not bound to a specific realm;
how then could it induce a retribution that is bound to such a realm?
Other dharmas possess both [of these characteristics].
Therefore, it is able to bring about [the result],
just as a genuine seed is moistened and nourished by water.
Regarding the term "vipāka" (maturation):
according to the Sarvāstivāda school,
its cause is either wholesome or unwholesome.
The fruit is indeterminate; because it matures as something of a different category [from its cause],
it is called "maturation" (vipāka).
The four [causes], such as the co-existent cause,
ripen only as similar types; that is to say, the cause and its fruit are of the same kind.
Because their nature is identical, they can function as a single efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Furthermore, this includes both similar and dissimilar maturation; that is to say, there are results that are of the same nature and results that are of a different nature.
Therefore, since the present ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) matures only as something of a different category,
it alone is designated by the single name "ripening cause."
From this major section,
the third explains temporal inclusion (*adhvan-saṃgraha*).
The verse says:
"Universal [causes] and similar-type [causes] belong to two time periods; the other three belong to all three time periods.
Regarding the phrase "two time periods":
The universal and homogeneous [causes] function only across two time periods, namely the past and the present.
As for the three [types of causes] belonging to all three time periods:
This means that the three causes associated with maturation (vipāka-hetu) exist simultaneously and pertain to all three time periods.
Since the verse does not specify the temporal locus of the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu), [it is understood to apply to all three times].
The meaning should be understood by analogy:
they pertain to the three periods of time and to that which is not of time.
That which is not of time is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
From here begins the second major section,
which clarifies the attainment of the fruit through its causes.
Within this, there are four parts.
First, a general indication of the essence of the fruit;
second, the assignment of fruits according to their causes;
third, the specific manifestation of the characteristics of the fruit.
Regarding the four causes for taking and giving at that time, first,
as for the general indication of the essence of the fruit,
the treatise says:
The characteristics and temporal determinations of the six causes have already been explained.
What are their effects? They are established in relation to those causes.
The verse says:
"Fruits are conditioned and disjunction; the unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit.
The commentary explains:
The first phrase establishes the essence;
the second phrase resolves an objection. "If the fruit is conditioned disjunction" explains the essence.
There are two kinds of results:
first, the conditioned, which refers to the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Adhipati, niṣyanda, and vipāka.
These constitute the six causes;
because they are that which is produced and brought forth, they are termed "fruits."
The second is disjunction (visamyoga),
which has analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) as its essence and is realized by means of the Path.
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is called a fruit; the Path is its cause of realization, not its cause of production.
Therefore, this cause of realization is not subsumed within the six causes. As for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it possesses neither cause nor fruit.
This explains away the doubt.
The treatise says:
"If that is so, then the unconditioned..."
Since it is admitted that this is a fruit,
there must be a cause; it necessarily stands in relation to that cause.
For it can then be said that this is a fruit;
furthermore, this unconditioned is admitted to be a cause.
There must then be a fruit;
for it is only in relation to that fruit that one can designate this as the cause.
The commentary states:
Since the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala),
it ought to be called "having a cause" (sahetu).
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can be a productive cause (*kāraṇahetu*),
it should be said to possess a fruit.
To dispel this doubt:
Therefore, there is this verse:
"That which is unconditioned has no cause," because it lacks the six causes.
This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Although their essence is a fruit,
they are fruits that are to be realized.
Because it is not a fruit produced by being drawn forth by the six causes, it is called "causeless.
As for the unconditioned being without fruit: [it is because]...
Because it lacks the five fruits;
that is to say, unconditioned phenomena do not obstruct arising.
The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is established [as a separate category] because it cannot serve as a proof; furthermore,
there is no fruit of disjunction (visamyoga-phala).
It is without appropriation or utilization,
and it possesses no conditioned fruit; therefore,
it is analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
This cause has no fruit;
this fruit has no cause.
The remaining two are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
These are causes, not effects;
therefore, the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are all devoid of both cause and effect.
The old translation stating that "the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is neither cause nor effect" is erroneous;
the unconditioned is indeed an efficient cause (kāraṇahetu).
It cannot be said that it is not a cause;
the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is the fruit of disjunction (visamyoga-phala).
It cannot be said that it is not a fruit.
It is neither identical to nor its own self-nature;
being non-identical means it is not "other.
Therefore, one can say it is non-existent.
It cannot be said that this is incorrect.
The treatise asks:
"For what reason do you not allow that all paths of uninterrupted transition [are moments of the path of seeing]?"
The fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala) is difficult to reconcile with [the function of] the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu),
because [the latter] merely does not obstruct arising.
The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is established;
since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is unarisen, what could the Path (*mārga*) possibly do? This answers the previous objection.
If that is so, what is the fruit?
How is the meaning of "fruit" to be understood?
To this it is said: there are two questions here.
First, since a single path is not a cause,
it is unknown what its fruit might be.
Second, that which is without a cause cannot be a fruit.
What is the meaning of "fruit" (phala)?
It refers to the fruit of the Path.
Because it is obtained through the power of the Path, it is called the "fruit of the Path."
The answer is: "Whose fruit?
Regarding "attained through the power of the Path," the answer concerns the meaning of "fruit."
If that were so, the fruit of the path would be nothing but its acquisition (*prāpti*),
for it is the path that possesses the capacity to bring about acquisition.
Regarding the phrase "because of non-analytical cessation," the commentary explains:
"attainment" refers to the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
Because it is induced by the Path, it ought to possess functional efficacy;
yet this is not so,
with respect to its acquisition and its analytical cessation.
The answer is given because there are distinctions in the functional capacities of the Path.
How so? It is because the Path possesses the capacity for attainment; this is the evidence.
The answer is: because it can produce [them].
Attainment (*prāpti*) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), for the Path (*mārga*) is able to produce it. Question: How does the Path have efficacy with respect to cessation (*nirodha*)?
This means that because it is capable of realization, [the path] realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For this reason, although the path is not the cause of cessation, [it is still called the cause].
And it can be said that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) constitutes the fruit of the Path;
this is the second [point].
This clarifies the correspondence between causes and fruits.
The treatise states:
"The general exposition is now complete."
Among the various fruits,
it should be explained which fruit is obtained by which cause.
The verse says:

The subsequent cause is the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*); the preceding cause is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), the similar fruit (*sabhāgaphala*), the pervasive fruit (*sarvatragaphala*), and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*); the simultaneous and associated causes are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
The commentary states:
The subsequent cause refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) among the six causes.
Because it is taught last,
the first is the maturation fruit (vipākaphala),
which is obtained through this cause. As for the phrase "the preceding cause":
This refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),
because it is mentioned first among the six causes.
The subsequent dominant fruit is that which is obtained through this cause;
it is the fruit acquired by virtue of the dominant power of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
It is called "predominant" (*adhipati*).
It is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the fruit of the predominant."
That is to say, the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) receives the designation "predominant" (adhipati) because it does not obstruct [the arising] of phenomena.
Alternatively, there may also be a productive cause (kāraṇa-hetu) that possesses superior power,
such as the ten bases and elements [acting] upon the five groups of consciousness.
Regarding the karma of sentient beings within the receptacle world,
it is said that there are ten locations.
The five faculties and the five objects directly produce the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, as for the ear and other faculties...
Regarding the arising of visual consciousness and so forth,
there is likewise a successive power of predominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
because upon hearing [the teaching], one immediately gives rise to the desire to see.
That is to say, because one hears with the ear,
one then delights in seeing forms,
whereby visual consciousness subsequently arises; this is the faculty of the ear.
There is a dominant force capable of producing visual consciousness. Regarding those that are similar, pervasive, and of uniform outflow:
these two types of causes [are as follows].

Regarding "attaining the fruit of outflow and the fruit of human effort associated with coexistence": "associated with coexistence" means that [factors] which coexist attain the fruit of human effort.
As for the term "fruit of human effort": [it refers to the result produced by the activity of a person].
Because there is functional activity,
as in the case of a worldly person engaged in activities such as farming.
Because it is the activity of a person, it is called "human effort" (puruṣakāra). Since the fruit arises from that cause,
it is called the "fruit of human effort" (puruṣakāraphala).
The "fruit of human effort" (puruṣakāra-phala) is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound,
just as worldly usage speaks of the "crow-foot medicinal herb" (*kākapada-auṣadhi*).
The General Drunken Elephant.
A medicinal herb resembling a crow's foot is named "Crow's Foot" (Kāyastha).

Minds and mental factors arise from four conditions; the two meditative attainments arise from three; the rest arise from two. This is because they are not produced by a creator god, nor by succession, and so forth. [Commentary: The various minds and mental factors arise from four conditions. The two meditative attainments—the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—arise from three conditions. The first three phrases distinguish dependently arisen phenomena;
the fourth phrase alone—
This refutes the tenets of the non-Buddhists.
Regarding the statement that "mind and mental factors arise from four [conditions]": it means that mind and mental factors arise by way of the four conditions.
In this context, "causal condition" refers to the nature of the five causes.
As for the "equal-and-immediate condition":
This refers to the mind and mental factors,
which must be induced and produced by the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) of the prior moment.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is so called because it arises by taking an object as its condition.
The dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) is...
Except for its own nature, all other phenomena do not constitute obstructions.
Regarding the two meditative attainments, they arise solely from three [conditions]:
namely, the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation.
It arises from three conditions;
because it is not a cognitive object, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is excluded.
Regarding "by way of causes and conditions," this refers to two types of causes:
first, the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
This refers to the four characteristics—arising and so forth—of those born in the two meditative attainments;
the two similar-cause factors (sabhāga-hetu), namely previously arisen wholesome dharmas of the same stage; and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
In the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva),
all wholesome dharmas belong to the same level (bhūmi).
If it is the attainment of cessation,
all wholesome dharmas exist within the Peak of Existence.
This refers to the same stage. As for the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),

It acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the production of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*),

The treatise says:
"These two meditative attainments are produced by the mind and obstruct the arising of the mind."
Therefore, it is equal to the mind;
however, it serves only as an equal-and-immediate [condition], not as an equal-and-immediate object-condition (*samanantarālambana-pratyaya*). This is the explanation.
"Mind and so forth":
the "and so forth" includes mental factors (*caitta*).
The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding those that arise from two conditions:
The remainder refers to material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) and non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra);
these two categories of phenomena.
It is produced by the two conditions of cause and predominance;
because it is not a cognizing subject,
the object-condition is excluded.
"It is not produced by mind and so forth;
it lacks an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); it is not due to the sequence of [rebirth from] heaven," etc., which directly refutes the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This has two aspects:

The next category is similar;
for example, the ash-smearing heretics who cling to Maheśvara.

It is able to give rise to all phenomena.
Within my Buddha-dharma,
there is only dependent origination.
Because it can produce all phenomena, it is said to be "not a god" (*anīśvara*), and so forth; this includes [the notions of] the Self (*ātman*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and so on.
Next, as for "and so forth":
"Successive" refers to the sequence.
"And so forth" includes that which is meaningless and that which contradicts worldly conventions;
these three types of reasoning are thus established.
This refutes the non-Buddhists.
Regarding the sequential principle,
the treatise states:
That is to say, [the view] that all things in the world arise from a single cause, such as Īśvara or others.
Then all things should arise simultaneously,
rather than arising sequentially;
yet we observe that all phenomena arise in succession.
Therefore, one knows that it certainly does not arise from a single cause.
Regarding that which is without benefit,
the treatise says:
Furthermore, [proponents claim that] Īśvara and others, exerting great effort,
produce all worlds.
What benefit or profit is obtained?

"Alas! What use is this sovereignty?
This statement from that verse is truly well said.
Rugged and sharp, they are capable of incinerating;

The commentary explains:
[this refers to] the ash-smearing non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthika).

He has three eyes and eight arms;

This verse describes the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body). There were three asuras who,

He proceeded toward the Heaven of the Vaśavartin Devas.

They are all extinguished at once;

which burns the three kingdoms.

Being smeared with blood in return is truly fearsome;
they constantly oppress and harm sentient beings. These are those who delight in eating flesh, blood, and marrow.
This reveals what is consumed.
Rudra means "the Violent and Wicked."
The Lord Maheśvara has one thousand names;

The treatise says:
Furthermore, if one believes and accepts that all that exists in the world is solely Maheśvara.
To claim that [an effect] arises from a single cause is to deny the visible world and all other causal conditions, such as human effort and so forth.

Therefore, there is no phenomenon that arises from a single cause alone.
Following this second point,

The treatise states:

the first phrase, written in large characters,

That is to say, with respect to derived matter, the four great elements can serve as five types of causes.
First, the life;
second, the basis;
third, the establishment.
The four supports and the five nurtures;
these are the five causes.

these four great elements are subsumed under the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu).

once the derived matter has been produced, [it persists].
It follows along with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),

it is described as a supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*).
Because the primary elements sustain derived matter,
they are described as the "establishing cause" (*pratisthā-hetu*), just as a wall supports a painting.
That which causes the continuity of derived matter (upādāyarūpa) to remain uninterrupted is called the sustaining cause (dhṛtihetu),
because it is a cause of growth (puṣṭihetu).
This is explained as the cause of nourishment.
In this way, it is revealed that the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (bhautika) function respectively as the causes of arising, transformation, maintenance, support, and growth.

"This is the cause of reliance.

when one derived matter is considered in relation to another derived matter, it functions as only three causes.
That is to say: coexistent,
homogeneous, and maturation [causes].
The co-existent cause refers to the two types of action— bodily and vocal— that follow the mind.
The sevenfold non-informative [karma] acts as a cause through mutual succession. Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it consists of all that has arisen previously.
Subsequently, those of the same class are all capable of acting as causes.
As for the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu):
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions that can bring about the eyes and so forth;
this is precisely cause and effect.
"Both are derived. Regarding the phrase "the Great [element] has only one cause," the word "derived" (造) from the preceding sentence flows over into this context.

namely, the derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
With respect to the four great elements,
it serves as only a single cause,

Because the two types of karma— bodily and vocal—

Second, clarifying the extent of the attainment of minds.

First, the explanation of the twelve minds;

First, the enumeration of the twelve types of consciousness;

First, regarding the enumeration of the twelve types of consciousness:
The treatise first asks:
Previously, it was stated in general that all minds and mental factors serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those that follow.
It has not yet been definitively stated which mind arises immediately after which mind,
how many types of minds arise,
or from how many types of minds which specific mind arises.
Now, to provide a definitive explanation, I shall establish the preceding inquiry. To state it briefly:
there are twelve minds that serve as the answer.
What are the twelve minds? The verse says:
In the desire realm there are four minds: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
In the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded; the untainted has two types of mind.
The commentary states:
First, within the desire realm, there are four kinds of mind.
That is to say: wholesome,
unwholesome, obscured-unspecified,

In both the form and formless realms, there are three types of consciousness each;
that is, excluding the unwholesome,
the rest are as described above.
These ten types are said to be with outflows (sāsrava); as for the mind without outflows (anāsrava), it is as follows.
There are only two kinds,

From this, secondly, the actual exposition of the mutual arising [of the dharmas] is presented.

Regarding how these twelve minds arise from one another,

The wholesome [minds] of the desire realm arise from nine; these, in turn, arise from eight.

The obscured-unspecified arises from seven; the unobscured-unspecified is as explained for the form realm. there, within the defiled mind at the moment of rebirth-linking, [the latent dispositions] continue.
Because it would necessarily be defiled.

Second, remoteness of aspect;

The mind of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) contemplates the fourth dhyāna solely through the aspects of suffering, coarseness, and obstruction.

Regarding the two untainted minds:

"I would rather give rise to a wholesome mind of a lower stage than give rise to a defiled mind of a higher stage.

Excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm,

That is to say, a mind of one in training.

Regarding "arising from five":

this refers to the wholesome minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) within the three realms. Regarding "able to produce four": [this refers to the aforementioned wholesome minds].
Regarding the five preceding [minds],
only the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) is excluded.
From this second [category].

The twelve become twenty: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms are divided into those acquired through application and those acquired by birth; the non-obscured-neutral minds of the desire realm are divided into four:
