Each is divided into two types,
namely, those acquired through application and those acquired by birth, as they are distinct from one another.
The non-obscured [neutral] states of the desire realm are divided into four types of mind:
first, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
2. The paths of deportment;
3. the spheres of craftsmanship;
4. the minds of fruition—these are the unobscured-neutral [minds] of the form realm.
It is divided into three types,
excluding the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
because in the higher realms there is no performance of various types of crafts at all.
In the formless realm, there is only one type of unobscured [neutral mind],
namely that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Therefore, including the previously mentioned non-obscured [neutral states], they constitute eight types;
thus, there are twelve in total.
There are twenty minds,
namely eight from the desire realm:
two wholesome [minds],...
Two are defiled;
four are neutral minds.
There are six types in the form realm.
The first eight [mental states] exist in the higher realms,
excluding the two— unwholesome and craft-related minds.
The four [minds] of the formless realm also exist there.
Beyond the aforementioned six,
one further excludes the two minds of deportment and supernormal fruition;
this includes both those in training and those beyond training.
Thus, there are twenty [types of consciousness]. Regarding the "consciousnesses of the modes of deportment" (*airyāpathika-citta*):
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are called the modes of deportment.
This has visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility as its substance.
Because these modes of deportment take them as their objects of cognition,
they are called "paths."
The deportment itself is the path;
it is called the "path of deportment.
It takes the path of deportment as its object.
The mind is called the "mind of deportment" (*airyāpathika-citta*);
this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. This mind of deportment is, in total, of three kinds.
The first type of deportment-mind is exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The second type of deportment-mind has two objects of cognition.
It encompasses the four consciousnesses beginning with the eye-consciousness—
excluding the ear-consciousness—
and includes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Third, those resembling the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*) pervade all six consciousnesses; they are,
for example, minds that casually perceive external forms, sounds, and so forth.
This is called "resembling the path of deportment.
Second, regarding the mind of the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*),
there are two types of the sphere of craftsmanship.
First, manual craftsmanship,
such as carving and engraving;
second, verbal craftsmanship.
This refers to things such as singing and so forth;
if it is bodily craftsmanship,
its essence consists of the four objects.
When bodily skill arises,
it does not depart from the four objects;
this is also the case for verbal skill.
These two types of craftsmanship have the five sense objects as their essence, because when speech arises, it is not separate from those five sense objects.
Because the mind takes it as its object,
it is called a "base" (āyatana);
craftsmanship itself is the base.
The sphere of craftsmanship is called *śailpasthāna*;
the mind of the sphere of craftsmanship is called the "craftsmanship-mind" (*śailpasthāna-citta*).
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
This mind of craftsmanship is,
in brief, of three kinds.
The first is the mind of craftsmanship,
which occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The second is the mind that takes craftsmanship as its object.
The [mind] associated with the five sensory consciousnesses as well as the mental consciousness—
these three types of mind resembling craftsmanship—
likewise pertain to all six consciousnesses.
The "result-of-attainment minds" (abhiññā-phala-citta) refer to the mind capable of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta),
as well as the result-of-attainment minds of the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
This mind capable of transformation takes the four objects— form and so forth— as its objective conditions;
that is to say, it transforms these four objects.
It also takes sound as its object,
because there is a mind of the result of communication that initiates speech.
The treatise says:
The three types of non-obscured minds, such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*),
take visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as their objective referents (*ālambana*).
The arts and crafts, and so forth,
also take sound as their object;
these three types of mind are exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The modes of deportment,
the spheres of craftsmanship,
and the preparatory application.
It is also said to be associated with both the four consciousnesses and the five consciousnesses.
Regarding the explanation that "this refers to applied thought (*vitarka*)," it means the mind that takes postures (*iryāpatha*) and so forth as its object. Other masters say:
There is the mental consciousness induced by the modes of deportment as well as by the spheres of craftsmanship.
"It is able to fully possess the objects of the twelve bases (āyatana).
The commentary explains:
"This master speaks based on the mind that resembles the path of deportment (airyāpathika-citta)."
From this point begins the second major section,
which clarifies the extent to which the mind is attained.
The treatise states:
Among the twelve minds previously described,
which mind manifests,
and how many minds can be obtained?
The verse says:
Within the defiled minds of the three realms, one acquires six, six, and two kinds [of non-restraint];
for the wholesome, there are three types of form; for the trainings, four; and for all others, they are acquired by themselves.
The commentary states:
"In the defiled minds of the three realms, one attains six, six,
and two types" clarifies the defiled mind.
Regarding the number of minds acquired:
from a defiled mind of the desire realm, six minds are acquired;
from a defiled mind of the form realm, six minds are likewise acquired.
The defiled mind of the formless realm obtains only two minds. Furthermore, regarding the fact that the defiled mind of the desire realm obtains six minds:
this refers to the defiled mind of the desire realm.
In the state of being currently manifest,
six types of mind can occur;
namely, the three belonging to the desire realm.
Wholesome and unwholesome [minds] are obscured;
in the realms of form and formlessness, there is one mind each that is obscured-unspecified.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the mind constitutes the sixth [perfection].
Now, regarding the first attainment of the wholesome mind of desire,
the treatise states:
The wholesome mind of the desire realm arises through the reconnection of the roots of goodness via doubt, as well as through falling back from a higher realm.
"At that time, it is called 'attainment' (prāpti).
The commentary explains:
"This is because the roots of goodness are reconnected through doubt."
That is to say, it is through doubt that right view arises and one is able to reconnect with the roots of goodness.
"Doubt" refers to a defiled mind;
this is the arising of a wholesome mind of the desire realm from a defiled mind.
As for "retrogression of the realm":
This refers to the defiled mind by which one falls away from the upper realms and is reborn in the desire realm.
Rebirth in the desire realm necessarily occurs through a defiled mind.

At the very moment when defilement arises, a wholesome mind of the desire realm also acquires the "acquisition of prior acquisition" (prāptiprāpti) regarding those dharmas. As for the acquisition of unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and obscured-neutral minds of the form realm: [it occurs in the same manner].
The treatise says:
"Due to falling away through the arousal of afflictions,
and due to falling back to a lower realm."
One acquires two minds of the desire realm—
those that are unwholesome and those that are obscured—
and [one acquires] those of the form realm.
First, the obscured mind. The commentary explains:
"By arising from afflictions through falling back" refers to the case of one who has already become detached from the afflictions of the form realm.
At a later time, one falls away due to the arising of desire-taints.
At the very moment when the affliction of desire arises and the mind becomes defiled,
there are unwholesome states and obscured states belonging to the desire realm.
This also includes the obscured mind of the form realm;
at this time, one attains them collectively.
As for "receding from a realm":
Descending from the formless realm to be reborn in the desire realm,
one acquires two types of defilement belonging to the desire realm within the mind at the moment of conception.
This also includes the defiled minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding the acquisition of the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
the treatise states:
Due to falling away through the arousal of afflictions,
one acquires one obscured mind of the formless realm as well as a mind of a learner (śaikṣa).
Therefore, it is said that one attains the six [knowledges].
Regarding those who fall away due to the arising of afflictions,
this refers to the fruit of arhatship.
When one gives rise to afflictions of the desire realm and,
upon regressing, gives rise to desire-tainted states,
one acquires the obscured-unspecified [states] of the formless realm.
And regarding the mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*): when a defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is manifesting, one acquires six minds.
These are the three of its own realm and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The obscured-unspecified states of the formless realm and the acquisition of the mind of one in training; thus, there are six.
Furthermore, regarding the initial acquisition of the three [types of] desire-realm non-obscured [neutral states] within one's own realm,
the treatise states:
"By way of retrogression from the realm."
One attains one unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm,
as well as three minds of the form realm,
including the defiled mind of the form realm.
"Also by falling away and attaining [a lower state]"— the commentary explains:
"By falling away from the realm" refers to the case of one who has passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When one is reborn in the form realm (rūpadhātu),
at the very moment the defiled state of linking rebirth (pratisaṃdhivijñāna) in the form realm arises,
there are three minds belonging to its own realm.
In the desire realm, there is one type of fruition-mind (*phala-citta*);
at this time, it is acquired in its entirety.
Regarding the defiled mind of the form realm, it is also acquired through falling away (*parihāṇi*).

This clarifies that the acquisition of defiled form is obtained not only through falling back from a higher realm, but also through falling back due to the arising of afflictions belonging to the form realm. As for the acquisition of the obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa):
The treatise states:
"Due to falling away through the arising of afflictions,
one acquires a single obscured mind of the formless realm."
And upon attaining the mind of one in training (śaikṣa),
it is said that "six [faculties] are acquired.
As for those who fall away due to the arising of afflictions:
This refers to an arhat; because they fall away due to the arising of afflictions pertaining to the form realm,
they acquire the obscured-unspecified [states] of the formless realm.
And as for the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*).
Regarding the defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) attaining two minds, the treatise says: "The defiled mind of the formless realm."
In the state of being currently manifest,
among the twelve minds,
one attains only two minds.
Due to falling away through the arousal of afflictions,
one acquires that defiled mind as well as the mind of a learner (śaikṣa).
Thus it is said that one "attains two [types of regression].
Regarding the phrase "regression due to the arising of afflictions," this refers to an Arhat.
When one falls away due to the arising of afflictions of the formless realm, at the very moment the defilement arises,
one acquires the defilement of its own realm.
And there is the mind of training (*śaikṣa*). Regarding "the wholesome [mind] of the form realm has three [types], and the [minds] of training have four":
this refers to the wholesome mind of the form realm.
In the stage of being present before one,
among the twelve types of mind,
three types of mind may be attained.
The first refers to the acquisition of the wholesome [states] of one's own realm,
as well as the neutral states of the desire and form realms that are the result of supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala).
This constitutes the three minds.
The reason for this is that they arise through progressive advancement.
One attains those three minds,
namely, by entering the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) from the desire realm.
One attains a wholesome mind of the form realm;
this is called ascending from the desire realm into the form realm.
It is termed "progression."
Having severed the afflictions of desire until they are exhausted,
one enters the fundamental stage via the ninth path of liberation,
attaining the realms of desire and form.
Second is the mind of the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*). This is precisely the entry from the stage of application (*prayoga*) into the fundamental stage (*maula-bhūmi*).
This is called "progression. Regarding the four types of those in training (*śaikṣa*):
it refers to the state when the mind of one in training is actually present.

It can accommodate four minds: the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as the two supernormal fruit-minds of the desire and form realms, together with the wholesome mind of the formless realm; thus, there are four.
Regarding "attaining the mind of one in training":
By virtue of first entering the state of correct determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
one attains the mind of a learner (*śaikṣa-citta*) at the stage of the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
Second, regarding the attainment of the two types of fruition-minds of the supernormal powers belonging to the desire and form realms:
this refers to the mind that, by means of the noble path, becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm and enters the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
One attains the supernormal powers (abhijñā-phala) of the two realms.
As for the attainment of the wholesome states of the formless realm,
this also occurs by means of the Noble Path.
One who is free from the defilements of the form realm attains the wholesome states of the formless realm;
therefore, the treatise says:

This can be understood from the preceding text concerning both the initial entry into the state of rightness and departure from corruption (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and the abandonment of desire for the realms of form through the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
"Others are all obtainable by oneself" means that "others" refers to those previously mentioned, namely,
the minds other than the defiled ones and so forth.
Namely, the wholesome [states] of the desire realm,
the indeterminate [states] of the three realms,
and the wholesome [states] of the formless realm.
Since these are all minds of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
the remaining characters of the verse include these six types of mind.
However, when these six minds are actually manifesting,
they can only be attained by oneself and do not constitute another. The *Śāstra* says:
Others provide a general summary of this point,
stating in verse:
"The wise say that when a defiled mind arises, nine [factors] are acquired."
Six [types of acquisition] are obtained from within a wholesome mind; those that are indeterminate are only indeterminate.
Commentary: This is a verse cited by the Master of the Treatise from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*.
This clarifies the extent of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of minds.
That treatise states that nine minds are acquired when a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) arises;
this treatise, however, states that fourteen defiled minds are acquired.
That is to say, there are six in the desire realm,
six obtained in the form realm,
and two obtained in the formless realm.
This treatise, based on the re-acquisition of defiled minds,
speaks of fourteen minds;
that treatise, however, refers to single acquisitions.
Only nine minds are mentioned; however,
within these fourteen minds discussed in this treatise,
there are five minds that are acquired repeatedly.
This refers to the defiled mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
It is acquired on two occasions:
first, it is acquired at the time of being defiled by the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The second is acquired at the time of defilement in the form realm;
according to the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, this excludes one type of mind.
It is also the defiled mind of the formless realm.
And with the mind of training,
each is obtained three times;
that is to say, at the time of being defiled by the three realms.
All [of these] are attained. In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, two [factors] are excluded from each;
together with the aforementioned single mind, five are excluded in total.
Therefore, it is said that nine [attainments] are obtained;
each is based on a single meaning and they do not contradict one another. Regarding the six obtained within a wholesome mind:
That is to say: the non-obscured [neutral] of the desire realm; the wholesome and non-obscured [neutral] of the form realm;
and the wholesome of the formless realm, as well as the learner’s and the non-learner’s minds. Thus, six minds are established.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* (Zaxin) bases its calculation on single acquisitions.
Only these six minds are spoken of;
however, this treatise states that seven minds are attained based on the principle of "repeated attainment" (punar-lābha).
This refers to the three wholesome [minds] of the form realm;
the four [minds] of the learner (*śaikṣa*) make seven minds in total. Among these seven:
Excluding two types of heavy [karma]. Regarding the "two types of mind," this refers to the non-obscured [neutral] states of the desire and form realms.
Each is obtained twice:
first, at the time of wholesome form;
second, at the time of the mind of training (śaikṣa).
Excluding one mind from each [category],
take the remaining five minds,
together with the one mind of the adept (aśaikṣa).
Thus, they constitute six. The Treatise says:
To encompass the preceding meanings, it further states a verse:
Regarding "by means of rebirth and by means of entering meditative absorption":
the first, "by means of rebirth," refers to falling back from a higher realm; the second, "by means of entering absorption," refers to [attaining birth in a higher realm].
This refers to the previously mentioned wholesome form-sphere states and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding the third [category], it refers to those who have fallen away from detachment and those who have attained detachment;
these are the minds that were previously free from the defilements of the desire realm.
Regarding the fourth case, "the time of falling back," this refers to falling back due to the arising of afflictions as mentioned previously.
Regarding the fifth case, "attaining the state of continuity with the roots of goodness": it refers to the stage of continuity with the roots of goodness.
This refers to the continuity of the roots of goodness through the previously mentioned state of doubt;
it does not refer to what was previously accomplished, and thus clarifies the meaning of "attainment.
As for this term "attainment":
To achieve it at this present time is called "attainment.
This is the Master of the Treatise.
To summarize the preceding meanings,
they are collectively organized into five sections,
condensed into a single verse for clarity.
Please examine this closely.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa), Fascicle Seven; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Eight.
From this, the third section clarifies the Worldly Realm (*loka-dhātu*). Within it, there are two parts: first, the clarification of the sentient world (*sattva-loka*);
second, the clarification of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). Regarding the clarification of the sentient world, there are two further divisions.
First, a general exposition of sentient beings;
second, a classification of their groupings. Regarding the general exposition of sentient beings, it is further divided into three sections.
First, the birth of sentient beings is clarified;
second, the abiding of sentient beings is clarified;
third, the passing away of sentient beings is clarified. Regarding the first, the clarification of the birth of sentient beings:
It is further divided into nine types:
first, an exposition of the three realms;
second, an exposition of the five destinies.
The third [treatise] clarifies the seven stations of consciousness;
the fourth clarifies the nine abodes of sentient beings;
and the fifth clarifies the four stations of consciousness.
Sixth, the elucidation of the four modes of birth;
seventh, the elucidation of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); eighth, the elucidation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The ninth section clarifies the four modes of existence (*bhava*). Below this,
the first part clarifies the three realms (*dhātu*).
The treatise states:
"Having already relied upon the three realms,
[the author] has distinguished the mind and so forth."
Now it should be explained:
what are these three realms?
Within each of them, [what is the case]?
How many distinct locations are there?
The verse says:
Hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, Humans, and the six classes of desire-realm devas.
The Desire Realm is said to have twenty [locations], distinguished by the hells and the continents.
Above this, seventeen locations constitute the Form Realm;
therein, each of the first three dhyānas has three [levels], while the fourth dhyāna has eight.

In the formless realm there is no location; due to birth, there are four kinds [of existence] based on the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-force (*jīvita*), which cause the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession.
Commentary:
The first line clarifies the desire realm;
the next line clarifies the form realm;
and the final line clarifies the formless realm.
The first two phrases list the names of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
In Sanskrit they are called *naraka*; here [in Chinese] they are translated as "place of suffering" (*kujù*).
The term "yi" (義) is translated as "hell" because there are prisons beneath the earth; however, this is not the primary translation.
As for the term "animal" (pāśu), it refers to those who move horizontally.
Because they move horizontally, those called "ghosts" (preta) refer to those in other births who delight in stealing the property of others;
furthermore, they are numerous.
The ancestors they worship are many,
and they frequently harbor expectations for their own survival and livelihood; moreover,
they are mostly timid and inferior by nature, with bodies and minds that are fickle and restless.
Therefore, they are called ghosts (*preta*).
As for those called humans (*manuṣya*), because they possess much deliberation and reflection, they are named humans. As for those called devas (*deva*),...
Because there is radiance;
or again, because they are honored and exalted,
their spiritual power is sovereign and free.
Because they are prayed to by the multitude,
they are called "devas. As for the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*),
the first is the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Second and third, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
third, the Yāma Heaven, which in this language is translated as "Time-Portion."
That is to say, in that celestial realm,
from time to time and for the most part,
they cry out, "How joyful!"
Fourth is Tuṣita Heaven, which is translated here as "Contentment with Joy.
Regarding the pleasures of the five sensory desires:
They give rise to a mind of contentment.
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations [experience] the five objects of sensual desire.
Because they transform themselves.
Sixth are the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods;
among those who transform others' creations, [they exercise mastery].
Because of attaining mastery, the third phrase is called "the desire realm," which concludes the above [discussion].
Above this are the five destinies (*gati*).
The receptacles and sentient beings together are collectively termed the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the statement "twenty," it clarifies that there are twenty locations within the desire realm.

"By way of the differences among the hells and continents" clarifies the twenty bases [of the intermediate state]. Among the five destinies mentioned above, it is by way of the differences among the hells [that these are distinguished].
Furthermore, due to the differences among the continents,
there are twenty [types of beings].
There are eight hells.
The names of the hells differ.
First is the Reviving Hell (*saṃjīva*),
which refers to those sentient beings therein.
Although they undergo various forms of cutting, stabbing, grinding,
and crushing, as soon as they encounter a cool breeze,
they immediately revive and return to their original state.
Because they are revived as before,
it is established as the name Saṃjīva (Reviving).
Second is the Black Rope Hell (Kālasūtra).
First, their limbs are measured with black ropes;
only afterward are they cut and sawn.
Therefore it is named Kālasūtra (Black Rope).
Third is the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell,
where there are numerous instruments of suffering.
Because [the denizens] all come together to press against one's body and join forces to slaughter each other,
it is named Saṃghāta (Crushing).
The fourth is the Hell of Wailing (Raurava),
where beings are oppressed by manifold sufferings and utter piteous cries in various tones.
They utter cries of resentment,
which is called "Wailing.
These are the five great hells of Wailing.
Driven by intense suffering,
they let out great cries of lamentation,
wailing and calling out their grievances.
The sixth is the Great Screaming Heat Hell,
where fire swirls around one's body.
It blazes intensely all around;
because its heat and suffering are unbearable, it is named "Blazing Heat" (Tapana).
This is the seventh, the Hell of Intense Heat (Pratāpana).
Whether internally or externally,
within one's own body or another's body,
fierce flames burst forth from both.
Because they mutually burn and harm one another,
and because the heat within them is extreme,
it is called "Extreme Heat" (Pratāpana).
As for the eight hells of uninterrupted suffering (*avīci*),
the experience of suffering is continuous;
that is, there is no interval of pleasure between sufferings.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. As for the distinction of the continents, there are four great continents:
first, Jambudvīpa in the south.
On the southern edge of this continent,
there is a Jambū tree; it is from this that the name of this continent is derived.
Some are named after the trees that stand upon them;
some are named after their fruit.
Thus it is called Jambudvīpa.
Second is Pūrvavideha Island;
it is so called because the physical forms there are superior, or because the bodies there are superior to those of Jambudvīpa.
The first is named Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body Continent).
The third is Aparagodānīya (Western Cow-Trade Continent),
so called because they use cattle as their currency for trade.
Therefore, it is named Goḍānīya Island.
Fourth is Uttarakuru Island,
which is translated here as "Superior Place."
Some say it is called "Superior Birth" because it occupies the most excellent position among the four continents.
It is called a "place of victory" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because it gives rise to that which is most excellent;
it is called a "victorious birth" (*jaya-janman*). [These are] the hells and the continents.
These together constitute twelve [realms],
including the six heavens of the desire realm,
as well as animals and hungry ghosts.
There are twenty abodes.
As for the realm of sentient beings,
it extends from the Heaven of Great Brahmā (Īśvara).
From the Avīci Hell up to the receptacle world,
and even down to the wind-circle,
all are subsumed within the desire realm.
These seventeen abodes above are designated as the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
They are situated above this Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
There are seventeen places called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*):
three for each of the first three dhyānas, and eight for the fourth dhyāna.
This constitutes the seventeen names.
It refers to the three dhyānas,
each of which has three locations.
The fourth dhyāna has eight locations where it exists exclusively; together,
these constitute seventeen locations.
The receptacles and sentient beings together are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
This is the first dhyāna.
There are three abodes:
the first is named the Brahmakāyika Heaven,
[inhabited by] Mahābrahmā.
Second, they are called the Brahmā-purohita (Ministers of Brahmā),
because they serve as attendants to the Brahmā King.
Because he acts as a minister and assistant,
he is called the third, Mahābrahmā;
he is born from extensive goodness.
Therefore, he is named Brahmā. This Brahmā is great;
thus, he is named Mahābrahmā.
Because they have attained the intermediate dhyāna,
because it is their first birth,
and because it is their final passing away.
Because his majestic power and other qualities are superior,
he is named Mahābrahmā.
This is the second dhyāna.
There are three heavens.
The first is the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttābha),
which is within the second dhyāna.
The light is minimal; therefore, it is named the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābhā).
Second is the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābhā).
The radiance increases further,
its measure being difficult to limit;
therefore, it is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.
Third are the Ābhāsvara devas;
their radiance surpasses that of the former,
illuminating their own realm everywhere.
Therefore, it is called the "Extreme Radiance" (Ābhāsvara) Third Dhyāna.
There are three heavens therein:
first, the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttābha).
Because it is a pleasant sensation on the mental level,
it is called "pure" within the third dhyāna.
This [heaven] has the least amount of purity;
thus it is called "Limited Purity.
Second are the Immeasurable Purity Gods.
This purity is increasingly superior;
because its measure is difficult to limit,
it is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha).
Third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
Because this purity is all-pervasive, it is named "Universal Purity. This is the fourth dhyāna.
There are eight heavens.
First is the Cloudless Heaven (Anabhraka),
located in the space below this [heaven].
Having no fixed place of abode,
they are like clouds gathered in dense masses;
therefore, they are called "clouds."
Above these heavens,
there is no further Cloud-ground;
they reside at the head of the Cloudless [Heaven].
Therefore, it is named "Cloudless.
As for the second, the Heaven of Merit-Born,
there are further ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess superior merit.
Because one can only attain rebirth there [by means of this],
it is called "Birth of Merit" (Puṇyaprasava).
Third is the Vast Fruit Heaven (Bṛhatphala).
Within the realm of form,
among the class of ordinary beings,
this is the most excellent.
Therefore, they are called the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*).
Fourth is the Heaven Without Affliction (*Avṛha*);
"affliction" (*vraṇa*) refers to mental agitation and confusion.
Because this is the very first among the "Untroubled" (Avṛha),
it receives the name "Untroubled."
Fifth, the gods of the Heatless Heaven (Atapa).
Having already attained the mixed cultivation of superior and medium grades of meditative concentration,
they are able to effectively suppress and eliminate superior and medium grades of hindrances.
Because one's intention is harmonious and supple,
and is free from all feverish afflictions,
it is called "Without Fever" (Atapa).
Sixth, the Śuddhāvāsa devas;
having already attained the superior grade of the meditative absorption of mixed cultivation,
their state as a fruition is easily manifested.
Therefore, they are called "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa). Seventh are the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana),
who have already attained the superior mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
Being free from the hindrances to meditative concentration,
the remaining categories have become extremely subtle;
because vision is utterly clear and penetrating.
These are named the Sudarśana Heaven and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; among the heavens that possess form, these are the highest.
Because there is no other place that can surpass this, it is called Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate).
These five heavens are named the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Heavens;
they are inhabited exclusively by noble beings (ārya).
Because they are free from the intermixture of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are called the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), [these are the highest].
The establishment of seventeen heavens is according to the Sautrāntika school.
As for the Sarvāstivāda school:
Only sixteen heavens are established,
excluding the Mahābrahmā Heaven;
that is to say, the Brahmā-purohita Heaven.
Within it is a lofty terrace named Mahābrahmā,
the dwelling place of the sole sovereign.
There is no other ground;
it is just as when the World-Honored One sits with the fourfold assembly surrounding him.
Therefore, a separate Great Brahmā Heaven is not established.
As for the exclusion of the Heaven of Non-conception,
this refers to [its inclusion within] the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala).
There is a sublime and superior realm called the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva-deva),
which is not a separate level of existence.
Therefore, it is not established [as a separate realm]. As for the Sautrāntika masters who establish Mahābrahmā,
they refer to the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmarāja).
Although their abodes are not distinct from those of the Brahmapurohitas and others,
their physical forms and lifespans differ.
Because they are all unequal,
it is necessary to establish them separately;
such is the position of this Sautrāntika school.
Excluding the Heaven of Non-conception;
for the Heaven of Non-conception is [included] with the Heaven of Vast Fruit.
Regarding the body and lifespan, etc.,
the Asaṃjñisattvas are subsumed within the Bṛhatphala heaven and are not established as a separate realm. This is according to the Sthavira school.
The Great Brahma Heaven is also established because of differences in body and lifespan;
the Heaven of Non-conception is likewise established.
This refers to the Bṛhatphala [heaven],
because cause and fruit are distinct; by virtue of this,
it belongs to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
There are thus eighteen heavens.
Regarding the statement that the formless realm has no location:
this clarifies that the formless realm has no spatial location whatsoever.
Because non-material phenomena have no spatial location.
Regarding the statement that "arising is of four kinds," this clarifies that although formless phenomena lack a physical location, [their arising is still categorized].
Arising from maturation,
there are four distinctions:
first, the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space.
Prior to cultivating this meditative absorption,
during the stage of preparatory application,
one feels revulsion toward the material body.
Contemplating infinite space and forming the perception of the infinity of space is called the sphere of infinite space.
Second is the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana). Having become weary of the previously [contemplated] external emptiness,
one further contemplates internal consciousness.
Forming the perception of infinite consciousness is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana).
Third is the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Next, one becomes weary of infinite consciousness,
contemplates nothingness,
and forms the realization of nothingness.
It is named the Sphere of Nothingness.
Fourth is the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception;
this refers to the essential nature of that meditative absorption.
It is not that the coarse perceptions of the preceding seven stages are called "non-perception"; rather,
it would be so if perception were entirely absent.
It is then identical to the darkness of ignorance;
because there is still subtle perception,
it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
The first three formless attainments are named after their preparatory practices;
the fourth formless attainment is not.
One should accept this according to its actual meaning.
Furthermore, the treatise says:
"How else can it be known that they have no spatial location? This refers to the question regarding their specific location.
Because those who have attained that meditative concentration are reborn in that very place immediately upon the end of their lives; furthermore,
when they pass away from there and are born into the desire or form realms, [they do so by means of that same attainment].
This is because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises in that very place.
The commentary explains that this answers the preceding question;
that is to say, it refers to those who attain that meditative absorption in that very place.
This refers to whichever continent one follows;
it is the very place where one cultivates and attains the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). That is, at the very place where one cultivates meditative concentration.
At the end of his life, he undergoes birth in the formless realm;
later, passing away from the formless realm,
he is born in the desire or form realms.
Furthermore, because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises within the very sphere of meditative concentration attained through cultivation in the past.
It is clearly known that form does not exist and has no location;
it is that which continues as a stream based on the homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) and the mind of command, and so forth.
This clarifies the basis for the formless realm.
In the realms of desire and form, there is a body;
the mind functions in dependence upon that body.
In the formless realm, there is no body;
the mind proceeds in dependence upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Question: Why are they called the "desire realm" and so forth?
Answer: "Realm" (*dhātu*) is a general term.
Desire and so forth are the particulars;
because the particulars depend upon the general,
they are termed the "desire realm" and so on.
It should be stated that the realm to which desire belongs is called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
likewise, the realm to which form belongs is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
That which belongs to the realm of form is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); that which belongs to the realm of the formless is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The qualifying terms are omitted,
and it is simply called the "desire realm" and so forth,
just as one says "pepper drink."
And the *vajra-kaṭaka*.
"Drinking" (*pāna*) and "ring" (*kaṭaka*) together constitute the general name.
This refers to *marica-vajra* (pepper-vajra).
These are also alternative names;
based on their specific characteristics, they are collectively termed "pepper drink" (*maricā-pāna*) and "vajra-ring" (*vajravalaya*).
To be complete, one should say "the drink belonging to pepper" and "the ring belonging to the vajra"; here,
the word "belonging to" has been omitted.
It is merely called "pepper drink" and so forth;
how much more so can the Dharma be known?
Now, regarding the word "desire" used here:
"What dharma does he teach?
Answer: "Briefly stated, it is the craving induced by edible food and sexual intercourse. The explanation says:
"Sexual craving and craving for food are what is termed 'desire' (*kāma*)."
As a verse in the Sūtra says:
"The various exquisite objects of the world are not true desire;
true desire refers to the greed of human conceptualization."
"Sublime objects remain as they were in the world;
the wise have already removed desire for them. This verse was spoken by the Buddha.
Śāriputra was a human being.
To recite with the intention of seizing upon a greedy mind is called desire, not its object.
This refers to the heterodox practitioners of wrong livelihood.
He then rebuked Śāriputra, saying:
"If the sublime objects of the world are not true desire,
then true desire refers to the greed of human conceptualization."
"A bhikṣu should be called a person who indulges in sensual desires," because he gives rise to evil conceptualizations and discursive thoughts.
This is the intended meaning of that non-Buddhist.
To take external objects as the true essence of desire is not far from the position of Śāriputra, who held that it is difficult to abandon them.
If the sublime objects of the world were true desire,
and if true desire were not the greed of human conceptualization,
then your teacher should be called a person who experiences desire.
"Because they constantly contemplate pleasing and wonderful forms," the commentary explains:
"This refers to non-Buddhist teachers who actually contemplate pleasing forms."
Śāriputra replied, "Your teacher truly contemplates pleasing forms,
yet he is not called one who indulges in sensual desire."
Knowing clearly that true desire is greed and has nothing to do with external objects or non-Buddhist paths,
he departed in silence.
From this point, the second section clarifies the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
The treatise states:
"The three realms have already been explained."
What are the five destinies?
The verse says:
Among these, the hells and so forth are called the five destinies by their own names.
"Only non-obscured neutral; sentient beings, not the intermediate state. Commentary:
The first two lines list the names of the five destinies.
The final two lines provide a detailed classification of various categories.
Among these, regarding the statement that the five destinies (*gati*) are designated by their own names, such as "hell" and so forth,
within the three realms (*tridhātu*):
There are the hells and so forth,
which are designated as the five destinies;
that is to say, those previously mentioned.
The hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods—
these are called the five destinies (gati).
They are exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Regarding the differentiation of the three natures:
the substance of these five destinies does not extend to the wholesome or the defiled.
It is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate;
it is summoned by past karma and is thus an indeterminate state born of maturation (vipākaja).
If they were common to both the wholesome and the defiled,
the five destinies would become intermingled;
that is to say, within a single destiny...
Because it possesses the karma and afflictions of the five destinies; furthermore,
it does not extend to the external receptacle world,
for within the external receptacle world, all five destinies are present.
Because they are experienced in common.
As for sentient beings not being intermediate state beings:
the five destinies are comprised exclusively within the category of sentient beings.
The essence [of the intermediate state] is not a "destination" (gati). A destination is that which is gone toward;
since the intermediate state is that which goes, the intermediate state is not a destination.
The *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra* states:
"The four modes of birth encompass the five destinies."
They are not included within the five destinies or the four modes of birth.
What is it that is not included?
It refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Thus it is explained.
Because among these there is birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), they are subsumed under the four modes of birth (*yoni*);
because they are capable of going [to those realms], they are not subsumed under the destinies (*gati*). This concludes what has been explained above.
The five destinies do not include the wholesome, the defiled, the external vessel-world, or the intermediate state;
this clearly shows that while the realms (*dhātu*) are broad, the destinies (*gati*) are narrow, because those [realms] include the wholesome and the defiled.
Because the external vessel-world is subsumed within the three realms;
by this principle, if it were the essence of a destiny (gati), [it would follow that the vessel-world is also a destiny].
It must be comprised within the realms (*dhātu*).
There are cases that belong to a realm but are not part of a destiny (*gati*),
namely those that are wholesome, defiled, and so forth.
Third, this section clarifies the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The treatise states:
Within the three realms and the five destinies,
there are seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) according to their respective order.
What are these seven?
The verse says:
Diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; Diverse bodies and a single perception.

Reversing this notion of the body as one, and because there are no [realms] below the formless [realm], there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). The remainder are not [stations] because they are subject to destruction.
Thus it is explained.
Those with different bodies and different perceptions constitute the first station of consciousness;
this refers to the entirety of the human realm.
A portion of the heavenly realm.
Therefore, the treatise says: "The Sūtra states:"
There are sentient beings with form who have diverse bodies and diverse perceptions,
such as humans and some classes of devas.
This is the first station of consciousness.
"A portion of the devas" refers to the devas of the desire realm.
And regarding the first dhyāna,
excluding its arising at the beginning of a kalpa, the commentary explains:
"It is as it arose at the beginning of a kalpa."
This is the second station of consciousness;
therefore, it is excluded here.
It will be explained next.
Regarding the term "difference of body":
it refers to the difference in physical appearance;
they are distinguished by this difference of body.
There are some who possess different bodies; therefore, they are called "those with different bodies.
As for the phrase "due to different bodies":
To clarify this by way of its essential nature:
when it is said that there are distinct bodies,
this is stated in reference to their actual accomplishment.
Regarding the difference in perception (*saṃjñā*):
it is because there is a distinction between the perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.
Because they differ in perception,
or possess differing perceptions,
it is called "difference in perception."

Regarding the statement "due to differences in perception," this is explained in terms of the essential nature [of the object]. Regarding the statement "there are differing perceptions," this refers to the subject.
According to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the second phrase refers to the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) within the first dhyāna.
It takes up [the period] beginning at the start of the kalpa.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"There are sentient beings with form."
Diverse bodies with a single perception;
this is the second station of consciousness,
such as the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude.
Regarding this, the commentary on the *Kalpa-ārambha* states:
"In reality, this also includes the Brahmā-pāriṣadya and the Brahmā-purohita;
it mentions only the Brahmakāyika devas for brevity."
The first instance is cited to include the subsequent ones. Why is this?
Because at the beginning of the kalpa, when those various Brahmā assemblies arose, they gave rise to such a conception.
"We are all born from the Great Brahmā King.
At that time, O Great Brahmā..."
They also give rise to this thought:
"All these Brahmā assemblies have been born from me."
Because they share the same perception and the same cause,
they are called "unified in perception";
this refers to the body of the Great Brahma King.
Its dimensions are lofty and vast;
its appearance is majestic and virtuous;
its speech is luminous.
Each and every one of them is distinct from the other Brahmā hosts;
therefore, they are called "distinct bodies. [End of] the Treatise. Question: For what reason do the Brahmā King and the Brahmā hosts give rise to the notion of a single cause?
Answer: It refers to the Great Brahmā King,
who at the beginning of the kalpa dwelt alone.
Having no attendants at all,
he then made this vow:
"How might I cause all other sentient beings [to be likewise]?"
When I was born into this same class of beings,
the Ābhāsvara devas saw me and felt compassion.
Passing away from that place,
he was reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas.
As soon as the Brahma King had made his vow, [he was reborn].
Because he saw that beings were born from him,
the Great Brahmā King gave rise to this thought:
"I am the manifest creator."
Those Brahmā hosts,
upon first seeing that Mahābrahmā was preeminent in majesty and virtue,
further recollected and understood it to be due to the vow previously made by the Brahma King.
"I have come to be born here.
For this reason, the Brahmā assembly gives rise to such a thought:
"We were all born from the Great Brahmā King. This is the first instance of reversing the perception of the body.
Within this single phrase,
there are two layers of consciousness-abiding (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
To say "the opposite of this" means:
That is to say, reversing the previous case where the body was one and perception varied,
one should state that the body is one and perception varies;
this is the third station of consciousness.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"There are sentient beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions."
Regarding the statement that the Ābhāsvara Heaven constitutes the third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
it is explained that in reality, this also includes the Parīttābha Heaven.
Regarding the Heaven of Immeasurable Light,
the mention of "Only the Heaven of Utmost Purity" (Ābhāsvara) is an instance of citing the last to include the first.
Those devas manifest their forms;
as their physical appearances do not differ,
they are said to have "one body."
Because the two perceptions of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure alternate and intermingle,
it is called "differentiation of perception.
It is traditionally taught that those gods have become weary of the faculty of joy belonging to the fundamental stage.
The faculty of equanimity belonging to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) arises and becomes manifest;
having become weary of the faculty of equanimity of the preparatory stage,
the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*) belonging to the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) arises and becomes manifest.
Just as a wealthy and noble person, having grown weary of sensual pleasures,
then experiences the joy of the Dharma;
and having grown weary of the joy of the Dharma...
Furthermore, experiencing sensual pleasures with a single perception of the body is the fourth station of consciousness.
The treatise says:
"There are sentient beings with form who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) heaven."
Regarding this fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the commentary states:
"In reality, it also includes the Heaven of Limited Purity (*parīttaśubha*) and the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*apramāṇaśubha*)."
The mention of "only the Śubhakṛtsna devas" is a case of citing the last to include the first.
As for the phrase "a single body":
Those whose physical appearance is no different and whose speech and thoughts are identical experience only pleasant feelings and perceptions.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"In the first dhyāna,
due to defiled perception (saṃjñā)..."
Therefore, it is said that in the second dhyāna, there is a single perception by virtue of two wholesome perceptions.
Therefore, it is said that in the third dhyāna, perception is different by virtue of the perception of ripening.
Therefore, it says, "The conceptualization is one," which is explained as follows:
this passage concludes the preceding section and distinguishes the differences.
Regarding "due to defiled perception," this refers to the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
which has the notion of sameness as its single cause.
By way of the perception of maturation (*vipāka-saṃjñā*),
that is, the perception of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā-saṃjñā*), because it is summoned by karma.
There are no three lower [levels] within the formless realm;
excluding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
it refers to the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The fifth station of consciousness;
the sphere of infinite consciousness is the sixth station of consciousness;
and the sphere of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Thus, "there are seven stations of consciousness" is the summary.
Regarding the term "abodes of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti): it refers to that in which consciousness delights to abide.
If [the abodes] consist of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu), they constitute their essence.
If the four aggregates of the formless realm constitute its essence,
then those others which do not possess the quality of being subject to destruction are excluded.
The remainder refers to the three evil destinies,
the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
In all these locations, there is no abiding of consciousness;
as for what is said regarding "having impairment":
This excludes the three miserable destinies.
That is to say, the three miserable destinies involve the experience of intense suffering.
It can impair consciousness;
the mention of "possessing destruction" serves to distinguish it from the fourth dhyāna.
And there is the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This refers to the fourth dhyāna,
wherein there is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).
In the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there is the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti),
which is capable of destroying consciousness.
Because it causes the continuity [of existence] to be severed, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Furthermore, the treatise says:
It is further said that sentient beings from other places,
whose minds delight in coming to dwell there, arrive at this place.
Because they do not seek further rebirth,
they are called "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*) within the various evil realms.
Both meanings apply;
there is no fourth dhyāna,
for the mind constantly seeks liberation.
This refers to ordinary beings who seek to enter the state of non-perception,
as well as to noble ones.
They delight in entering the Pure Abodes or the formless realms;
if they are gods of the Pure Abodes,
they delight in realizing cessation.
It is explained that because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dull and inferior, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
this refers to the fourth dhyāna.
The Cloudless Heaven, the Heaven of Merit-Born,
and the Three Heavens of Vast Fruit are abodes accessible to both ordinary beings and sages.
If they are ordinary persons,
they seek to enter the state of non-conception;
if they are noble ones, [they do not].
Those who delight in wisdom seek to enter the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; those who delight in meditative concentration [seek the same].
Seeking entry into the formless [realms]—
the rest may be understood accordingly.
From this fourth [dhyāna].
Explaining the nine abodes of sentient beings,
the treatise states:
"In this manner, the seven stations of consciousness are distinguished."
Based on this, the nine abodes of sentient beings are further explained.
What are these nine?
The verse says:

It should be understood that these, together with the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings (*navasattvāvāsāḥ*); the others are not so, because they are not places where one dwells with pleasure.
Thus says the commentary.
The first seven stations of consciousness,
together with the Peak of Existence and the station of non-perception.
These are called the nine;
all classes of sentient beings exist only within these nine.
Because they dwell with joy and delight,
these are established as abodes for sentient beings;
all other places are not.
Because one does not delight in dwelling there.
"Other places" refers to the various evil realms.
It is not that the classes of non-sentient beings take pleasure in dwelling there;
rather, it is because the rākṣasas of evil karma force them to reside there.
That fourth dhyāna is like a prison;
it does not provide an abode for sentient beings.
Excluding the Heaven of Non-conception,
the remaining eight heavens are not abodes of sentient beings.
As explained in the commentary on the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), from this point the fifth section clarifies the four stations of consciousness.
The treatise states:
The sūtras cited previously speak of the seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti),
while other sūtras further speak of the four stations of consciousness.
What are these four?
The verse says:
One should know that the four stations of consciousness consist of the four aggregates, exclusively of their own level.
It is said that consciousness alone does not abide. Regarding the explanation of the inclusion within the four categories of the contaminated (*sāsrava*):
as for the term "four stations of consciousness" (*catasraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*).
This indicates the name.
One should know that the two characters "flowing into" (liú rù) connect to the following phrase.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Consciousness dwells in dependence on form;
consciousness dwells in dependence on feeling."
Consciousness abides following perception;
consciousness abides following formations.
These four are that which is abided in.
Consciousness is that which abides;
because it is that upon which consciousness abides, they are called the four stations of consciousness.
It should be understood that "the four aggregates" identifies their essential nature: form,
sensation, perception, and formations.
They are called the four aggregates;
the four contaminated aggregates constitute the substance of the stations of consciousness.
Regarding "belonging to its own level":
it takes only the four aggregates of its own level as its substance;
for consciousness, being appropriated by craving for the aggregates of its own level, follows the power of that craving.
Depending upon and adhering to that,
it is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
If [it occurs] in another stage (*bhūmi*), [the same applies].
Because it is not embraced by craving,
it is not a station of consciousness.
Therefore, the treatise says:
It is not that consciousness, through the power of craving,
clings to and depends upon the aggregates of form and so forth belonging to a different level.
Regarding the statement that consciousness alone does not abide:
this clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness is not itself a station of consciousness;
that is to say, this aggregate of consciousness.
This is consciousness that abides;
it cannot itself be established as the locus in which it abides.
Therefore, consciousness is not a station for consciousness.
The treatise states:
That which is the consciousness capable of abiding cannot itself be called that which is abided in.

Yet, since one sees the luminous image of the mirror within the shadow, that image is not real. This is the fourth [point].
Some say that where there is one place, two cannot coexist;
yet the surface of a mirror and the reflection of the moon are spoken of as being two.
Near and far are seen differently,
like looking at water in a well;
if they were to arise simultaneously, [this would not occur].
How can they be seen separately?
Therefore, one knows that all images are, in principle, actually non-existent. Thus it is explained.
Within a single mirror, there are two images:
that of the face and that of the moon;
when one looks at the image of the face, it appears near.
If one observes the image of the moon, it appears distant.
If these two images were real, how could they possibly exist in the same location?
They are seen as distinct in terms of near and far.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"However, through the power of the conjunction of all causes and conditions..."
To cause such a vision to arise through the functional distinctions inherent in the nature of all phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "difficult to conceive," the commentary explains:
"causing such a vision to arise" refers to the power of the mirror's substance and so forth.
"Returning to see that the original face is actually without image;
it is not something produced by two successive moments.
This explains that because the aforementioned [comparison] is unequal, it is not a valid analogy.
Regarding "non-continuity":
the image you have established does not constitute a single continuum.
It is not identical to the dharma.
As for what is called "continuity," this ceases and that arises.
Since the reflection appears solely from within the mirror,
it is clearly known that the substance of the object and the substance of the image are each distinct.
It is not a single continuum;
furthermore, the image and its original object exist simultaneously.
Therefore, one knows that the substantial entity and its image are not a continuous series.
If the phenomena of death and birth were a single continuous series, [this would be the case].
If one must die here and be born there,
you are taking a reflected image— which is not a single continuous stream—
and using it as an analogy for death and birth, which are indeed a single continuous stream.
It is unreal and so forth.
As for the phrase "arising from two," it refers to the image you have established.
It arises dependent on two conditions,
which are not equal to the phenomenon [itself],
namely: the original object and the mirror.
These are the two conditions.
Existence at birth arises solely with existence at death as its condition;
thus, existence at birth comes into being.
The dharma of dependent origination is singular;
you, however, use the dharma of dual-dependent origination as an analogy for the dharma of singular-dependent origination.
This, therefore, cannot be equated with the Dharma;
thus, it is not a valid analogy. This has already been established according to correct reasoning.
To refute that school's position,
it is known that there must necessarily be an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) between death and birth;
for this is established by the mention of the *gandharva* and by five or seven sūtras.
This cites scriptural evidence.
As a sutra states:
"One who enters the mother's womb..."
It depends on three factors:

Since this sutra specifically mentions the *gandharva*, [it follows that...].

The *gandharva*— which here means "seeking fragrance"— is this [intermediate being].

known as "seekers of fragrance" (gandharva).
This is because it is stated in the *Pañcavastuka* and the *Saptavāstuka* sūtras.
As stated in the Sūtra:

Because one attains parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava), one is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin). As for the seven sūtras: [text follows].

Due to the proximity, mediocrity, or distance of place and time—

Regarding the third noble person: they have reached the intermediate state between the two realms and simultaneously attain parinirvāṇa at that very moment.
When approaching the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), but before yet having taken birth there, one attains parinirvāṇa;
in this case, both the place and the time are distant. Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika school [holds this view].
Furthermore, another commentary states:
"During the intermediate period of his lifespan,

Therefore, it is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin), not because of an intermediate existence (antarābhava).
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:

Because they attain parinirvāṇa;

In the *Uddāna* verses, it is stated that the assembly of noble sages is collectively comprised [of forty], with ten for each of the four dhyānas. (Commentary): In the first dhyāna, there are ten persons.

Furthermore, having attained the first dhyāna, [one proceeds].

Furthermore, having attained the first dhyāna, [he becomes the third person].
The one currently attaining parinirvāṇa constitutes the third person;
together with the seven noble persons mentioned previously,
they form ten individuals.

The second, third, and fourth dhyānas are explained by analogy with this enumeration. Each of the three formless attainments has seven [types], as three of the ten—namely those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state—are excluded.
There are only six for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as it is excluded from the aforementioned seven.

This is according to the wording of this verse.
