All [of these] are false and illusory.
Furthermore, the Mahāsāṃghika school cites a verse from a sutra to prove that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
The verse says:
"O Dvija, you have now passed the prime of life. The commentary says: There was a non-Buddhist Brahmin named Dvija.
Having come to see the World-Honored One when he was old,
the World-Honored One rebuked him,
saying, "You are now old."
Having passed the stage of full growth,
there are five stages outside the womb:
first, the infant.
1. Infancy; 2. Childhood; 3. Youth; 4. Maturity.

Fifth is old age. Having reached extreme decline and being on the verge of approaching King Yama, when one stands at the stage of senility and wishes to proceed along the path ahead, yet lacks provisions—meaning one lacks the provisions of morality, concentration, and wisdom—one seeks to remain in the interim.
The Mahāsāṃghika school of the Aśokadatta lineage states:
This verse says, "There is no abiding in the intermediate state.
This clearly shows that there is no intermediate existence (antarābhava); if there were an intermediate existence, it would be evident.
Regarding the phrase "there is that which ceases," the Master of the Treatise explains and clarifies it as follows:
The meaning of this verse is to demonstrate that among those people,
there is no sense of even a moment's pause, as they swiftly return to destruction.
It is called "having no place of rest.
Alternatively, within this there is that which is called "having no place of rest," which serves as the point of arrival for what is produced.
Nor does it pause for even a moment,
because its movement is unimpeded.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Eight.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa, Treatise Volume Nine.
This is the third section: the analysis by way of various categories (*dvāra*). There are eleven categories in total; among them, there are three:
first, explaining the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); second, explaining the nine categories beginning with the eye; third, explaining entry [into the womb].
Regarding the gate of the womb:
first, to clarify the shape within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
the treatise states:
To which realm of rebirth shall one go?
What is the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that arises?
The verse says:

Because this is projected by a single karma, it is like the *mūlaprakṛti* (fundamental form) of the future existence; "fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*) refers to that which precedes death. It abides after the moment of birth. [Commentary: The term "fundamental existence" (*mūlabhava*) refers to the state prior to death. It is said to "abide after the moment of birth" because it persists from the very instant of conception until the point immediately preceding death. This existence is projected by a single karma, and thus its nature is uniform throughout, much like the fundamental form of a future existence. It is so called because it constitutes the primary basis for the continuity of the individual. It is distinguished from the "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*), which connects death and rebirth, and from the "arisen existence" (*upapattibhava*), which consists of the specific states following birth. It is the underlying substratum that maintains the continuity of the aggregates until the final moment of life.
The first two lines clarify the form;
the latter two lines explain its inherent existence.
This is because it is projected by a single karma, and thus its form is like that which will exist in its future state.
This refers to the intermediate state (antarābhava),
which is projected by the same karma as the future state of existence (mūlabhava).
Because their karma is identical,
the form of the intermediate state (antarābhava) corresponds to that of the future existence (mūlabhava).
This means that the being in its prior existence has a human form,
and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) likewise has a human form;
the same applies to other realms of rebirth.
Question: Within the belly of a single dog or similar creature, the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of all five destinies (*gati*) can arise simultaneously.
Since the intermediate state of hell is already present there, [how is this possible]?
How is it that [the fire] cannot burn the mother’s womb?
Answer: Because he resides in the state of *pūrvakālabhava* (existence prior to birth), he is not constantly burned either.
If this is so even for those who merely visit the *ūrdhva-kṛtsna* (upper realms), how much more so for those who dwell in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
As for the term "visiting the upper realms":
They roam through the Sixteen Increasing Heavens (*ṣoḍaśotsada*). There is no fire there.
Furthermore, it is explained as follows:
The intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) of the various destinies,
though dwelling within a single womb,
do not touch one another nor are they burned.
Because it is obstructed by karma.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The dimensions of the intermediate state of the desire realm [are as follows]."
Although he was like a child of five or six years of age,
his faculties were clear and sharp;
he was among the bodhisattvas.
Just as in the prime of youth,
his physical form was perfectly proportioned and complete with all the primary and secondary marks of excellence.

Therefore, while dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), when about to enter the womb, he illuminates a hundred *koṭis* of the four great continents; this light refers to the intermediate state of a Bodhisattva. If that is so, why is it [said otherwise]?
In the dream of the Bodhisattva’s mother,
she saw a white elephant calf enter her right side; this was an auspicious omen of his birth and was not related to the intermediate state (antarābhava).
The Bodhisattva answered because he had long since abandoned rebirth in the animal realm, as in the case of King Kṛkin’s dream.
Regarding the ten things seen by King Kṛkin—King Kṛkin is also called King Kāryakara (the Doer of Deeds)—they were: a great elephant, a well, and parched grain.
A sandalwood grove,
a young elephant,
and two monkeys.
The vast and firm robe;
strife and contention;
the white elephant of exquisite and majestic appearance.
Possessing six tusks and four legs,
he enters the mother’s womb with full awareness,
reclining like a sage hidden in a forest.
Such dreams as these merely indicate omens of other future events;
they are not like what has been seen above—this is the meaning of the treatise. The commentary explains:
King Kṛkin, the father of Kāśyapa Buddha,
had these ten dreams.
They came and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said, "This is a portent of the future disciples of the Śākyamuni Tathāgata during the period of his bequeathed Dharma.
The King had dreamed of a great elephant.
He was confined within a room that had no other doors or entrances,
save for a small window.
The elephant’s expedient means was to cast itself out;
yet its tail remained obstructed by the window.
Those who are unable to leave behind represent the disciples of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma,
who are able to renounce their parents, wives, and children.
Having left the household life, he still harbored thoughts of fame and profit within it,
like a tail obstructing a window; furthermore, he dreamed of a thirsty man.
Seeking water to drink,
he came upon a well endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.
The well follows after the thirsty person,
yet the person does not wish to drink;
this symbolizes the various monastics and lay followers of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma.
They are unwilling to study the Dharma.
Even those who know the Dharma do so for the sake of fame and profit.
He taught him accordingly,
yet he still did not learn. Furthermore, he saw another person in a dream who was carrying one *śīrṣa* of pearls.
He bought one sheng of flour.
This indicates that a disciple of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma,
for the sake of seeking profit, [acted thus].
He preached the Buddha’s true Dharma for others,
and again he saw someone in a dream.
To exchange sandalwood for common wood represents the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma.
He extensively studied external scriptures through the internal True Dharma; furthermore, he dreamed of a wondrous garden where flowers and fruits flourished in abundance.
"The mad bandits have utterly destroyed it.
This signifies that the disciples of the Final Dharma will extensively extinguish the garden of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma. Furthermore, he saw in a dream various small elephants.
Driving away a single great elephant and causing it to leave the herd symbolizes the various evil factions among the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma.
The monastic community that has broken the precepts expelled those of virtuous character. Furthermore, he dreamed of a monkey whose body was smeared with filth and excrement.
Tangtu encountered his own followers,
and they all avoided him;
this symbolizes the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma.
Using various evil deeds, he slandered the virtuous and good;
seeing him, everyone avoided him from afar. Furthermore, he dreamed of a monkey.
In truth, he possesses no merit;
yet the multitude together support and lift him up,
and the waters of the ocean are poured over his head for consecration.
He was established as king.
This illustrates how the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma, along with various evil factions, elevated monks who had violated the precepts to the headship of the community.
Furthermore, in a dream he saw a garment that was both firm and wide;
eighteen people each held a small portion of it.
Though they pulled from all four sides,
his robe remained unbroken;
this symbolizes the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma.
The Buddha’s True Dharma was divided into eighteen schools;
although they held slight differences in their tenets, [they remained consistent].
Yet the True Dharma still remains;
by practicing in reliance upon it,
all shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, he dreamed that a great multitude gathered together and waged war against one another,
until almost all had perished.
This indicates that among the disciples of the bequeathed Dharma,
each of the eighteen schools has its own followers.
The various schools hold differing tenets and thus engage in mutual strife and contention.
These are the ten dreams.
It merely indicates a portent;
it is not as it appears.
As for the Bodhisattva’s mother dreaming of a white elephant:
This auspicious omen must have been preceded by something other than a white elephant.
Its intermediate state (antarābhava) possesses a physical size equal to its future birth-state;
it is born together with its clothing.
Because shame and modesty are increased [in the higher realms],
the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not accompanied by clothing;
this is because they all lack shame and modesty due to their habitual tendencies from previous lives.
Only the Bhikṣuṇī Śvetā, by the power of her original vow,
possessed clothing that appeared spontaneously in every lifetime.
It never leaves the body,
changing according to the times,
until the final moment of parinirvāṇa.
One also uses these same garments to wrap the corpse for cremation and burial.
"Prior existence" (pūrvakālabhava) refers to that which exists before death, immediately following the moment of birth.
The existence (bhava) induced by past karma is called "prior existence" (pūrvakālabhava).
This prior existence—
The intermediate aggregates that exist after the end of the previous life and before the beginning of the subsequent life.
The existence as a fundamental entity is what is called "birth-existence" (upapattibhava),
which refers to the aggregates at the very first moment of taking birth.
What is called "death-existence" (cyuty-bhava) refers to the death-aggregate (marana-skandha) at the very last moment of life in both the desire realm and the form realm.
They are complete with four types of existence;
however, in the formless realm,
they lack only the intermediate state.
There are further three existences.
Following this second [section],
the nine gates beginning with the eye are explained.
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished the shapes,
the remaining meanings shall now be distinguished.
The verse says:
Those of equal purity see with the divine eye; They possess supernormal power, speed, and complete faculties;
they are unimpeded and irreversible; They feed on fragrance and do not remain for long.
With inverted minds they seek the realm of desire; those born from moisture or by transformation are stained by odors or locations;
among the heavens, the first three have their heads upward while the others are horizontal; in hell, the head is turned downward.
Thus it is explained.
This consists of nine sections.
Regarding those who see with the pure divine eye,
the first is the section on the objective sphere of vision.
This refers to the intermediate state body (antarābhava),
which is perceived solely by the eyes;
it is seen by eyes of the same class.
The intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) of the five destinies each see those of their own kind;
secondly, they are seen by those with the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Regarding the "pure divine eye," it refers to the divine eye attained through cultivation,
because it is utterly pure.
One who can see the intermediate state (antarābhava) by virtue of having attained the divine eye (divyacakṣus) cannot, however,
observe it [in this manner].
Because the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is extremely subtle,
other masters say that the eye of the celestial intermediate state (*deva-antarābhava*) possesses vision.
One can see the five destinies;
among humans, those with eyes can see four destinies.
With the exception of those in the intermediate state of the gods,
the eyes of those in the intermediate state of hungry ghosts (preta) are able to see the three realms of existence.
Excluding humans and devas,
the intermediate state beings of the animal realm possess eyes that can see two destinies.
This excludes humans, devas, and ghosts.
Those in the intermediate state of the hells possess eyes that see only their own kind. Regarding the swiftness of karmic power: it is as follows.
The second is the gate of swift movement:
soaring freely through the air;
this is the meaning of "supernormal power" (abhijñā).
It is attained through karma and is thus called "karmic supernormal power" (karma-abhijñā).
Because the force and function of this supernormal power are swift, it is termed "rapid."
Among them, there was one who had attained the most rapid supernormal power of action (*karmarddhi*),
such that even the World-Honored One himself could not obstruct or suppress it.
Because the power of their karma is most intense, they possess the sense faculties.
Regarding the third gate of possessing faculties: all intermediate state beings (antarābhava) possess the five faculties. They are "without resistance" (apratigha).
The fourth is the gate of non-obstruction.
"Obstruction" (pratigha) refers to being impeded;
intermediate existence (antarābhava) soars through the air.
It cannot be obstructed by things such as Mount Vajra; therefore,
it is called "non-obstructive" (apratigha).
It has been heard that when a glowing red iron ball is broken apart,
living insects are seen within it; this is the fifth door of the irreversible.
This refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the five destinies (*gati*), which cannot be diverted.
Among these, the intermediate state of humans arises.
One merely proceeds toward the human realm;
it is absolutely impossible for one to pass away from within a human intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and arise in another intermediate state.
The same applies to the devas and others. Regarding those who consume fragrance:
this is the sixth category of food.
Those in the intermediate state (antarābhava) take fragrance as their food.
Because they subsist on odors,
they are called *gandharva*.
If they possess little merit, [they are born as such].
They consume only foul odors;
those with great merit take exquisite fragrances as their food, while those who do not dwell long [in this state] do not.
Regarding the seventh stage, the gate of abiding:
the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* say that this abiding lasts for only a short time.
All intermediate state beings,
because they delight in seeking birth,
proceed swiftly to receive rebirth.
It will certainly not remain for long.
Furthermore, other masters say that at most it lasts for seven times seven days.
The Venerable Vasumitra says it lasts for at most seven days;
the Mahābhikṣu Dharmatrāta says:
There is no fixed limit to its duration;
as long as the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged,
the intermediate state (antarābhava) persists.
Therefore, among the wheel-turning kings,
the fruit is only bestowed all at once when human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years.

Because the Blessed One has taught that the power of karma is inconceivable, those who, with perverted minds, incline toward sensual objects— whether moisture-born, transformation-born, or those defiled by odors—
this is the eighth gateway for rebirth.
Regarding "perverted mind":
This clarifies that in the intermediate state (antarābhava), one first gives rise to a perverted mind and rushes toward the objects of desire;
this is by means of the visual faculty produced through the power of karma.
Although dwelling in a distant place,
one is able to see the parents at their union in the place of birth and gives rise to perverted thoughts.
If one is in the intermediate state as a male,
one gives rise to craving for the mother and conceives a mind of desire.
If she is among women,
she conceives love for her father and gives rise to sensual desire.
Reversing these two conditions,
one simultaneously gives rise to a mind of anger;
thus, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:
At that time, among the two types of mind,
one or the other manifests in the gandharva.
That is to say, it is either craving or aversion.
Due to giving rise to these two kinds of inverted minds,
one then claims that one's own self is united with what is loved.
When the impurities that have been discharged flow toward the womb,
[the intermediate being] perceives them as its own.
He then gives rise to joy;
once this mind has arisen,
the intermediate state (antarābhava) ceases.
Taking birth in an embodied existence,
if one is male, one dwells in the womb leaning against the mother's right flank.
Facing away and crouching;
if it is a female in the womb,
she rests against the mother's left side.
It remains facing the abdomen;
being neither male nor female,
it dwells within the mother's womb.
One abides according to the manner in which desire arises;
there is certainly no intermediate state being (antarābhava) that is neither female nor male.
Because the intermediate state body necessarily possesses the sense faculties;
furthermore, this intermediate state body is either male or female.
Subsequently, as the fetus develops,
it finally becomes neither male nor female,
as explained above.
These are born from wombs and eggs;
the others are born from moisture and by transformation.
This shall now be explained in sequence.
Regarding the "place of moist, transformative, and perfumed defilement":
in discussing the process of taking birth,
it is necessary in all cases for defilement to arise.
Since moisture-born beings do not have a womb,
upon what basis does defilement arise?
Therefore, it is said that moisture-born beings are born because they are defiled by odors.
That is to say, by smelling a fragrance from afar and knowing its place of origin,
one immediately gives rise to attachment and craving,
and goes there to undergo rebirth.
Karma has degrees of superiority and inferiority;
fragrance has purity and impurity.
As for those born by transformation:
It arises because of the place of defilement;
that is to say, observing from afar and knowing the place where one is destined to be born,
one then gives rise to craving and attachment.
One goes there to undergo rebirth;
according to whether one's karma is good or evil,
the place will be pure or defiled.
Because they give rise to perverted thoughts regarding the realm of hell,
they also produce craving and attachment.
That is to say, that intermediate state being may see itself beset by cold rain and freezing winds,
and see the extremely hot hells.
Delighting in the sensation of warmth,
they throw themselves into it;
or else they see themselves being tormented by hot winds and fierce fires.
Seeing the cold hells,
their hearts desired coolness,
and they threw themselves into them.
The former masters have stated as follows:
"Because one previously saw oneself and one's own companions at the time they were performing evil deeds."
Rushing toward that place— where those with heads facing upward in the Heaven-Headed (Tian-shou-shang) hell have their heads turned downward—
is the ninth section on the characteristics of the intermediate state (antarābhava), namely, the intermediate state of the gods.
The head rises upright,
as if arising from a seat; this applies to humans,
ghosts, animals, and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The mode of movement is like that of humans and others; however,
for those in the intermediate state of hell,
it is with head downward and feet upward.
Thus, there is a verse that says:
"Falling headlong into hell,
with feet above and head below."
This aforementioned discussion concerning the disparagement of the sages who delight in tranquility and practice asceticism refers to those who,
after dying among humans, are reborn again within the human realm.
If it extends to other realms of existence,
its mode of activity is not fixed;
thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
If one dies in hell and is reborn again in hell,
it is not necessarily with head downward and feet upward.
If one dies among the devas and is reborn among the devas,
it is not necessarily with the head downward and the feet upward.
If one dies in hell and is reborn in the human realm,
the head should rise upward.
If one dies among the gods and is reborn in the human realm,
the head should be directed downward.
From here begins the third section, clarifying the gateway of entering the womb.
The treatise states:
"The inverted mind was previously explained."
Do all intermediate states (*antarābhava*) necessarily enter the mother's womb in this manner? No, they do not.
The Sūtra states that there are four ways of entering the womb. What are these four?
The verse says:
First, one is fully conscious upon entering; the second and third [are so] both while staying and exiting.
In all stages, as well as in the egg, there is always ignorance;
the first three types of entry into the womb— namely, those of the Wheel-turning King and the two Buddhas—
are due to the superiority of both their karma and their wisdom, corresponding respectively to the four [types of birth] and the remaining births.
The commentary states:
These two verses constitute the eleventh gate, that of entering the womb.
All who enter the womb do so through no more than four stages.
The first is entering with full awareness.
First is the stage of entering the womb;
one only knows the entry into the womb,
but does not know the dwelling or the exit.
Regarding "those who emerge while abiding in two or three [stages]":
"abiding in two" refers to the two stages of entering the womb.
This means knowing the dwelling in the womb,
as well as the entering of the womb;
the third [case] includes both entering and exiting.
This is the third stage, the position of entering the womb.
This means knowing the exit from the womb while simultaneously knowing the abiding and the entry.
The word "simultaneously" (兼) is used to indicate that the subsequent stages include the preceding ones.
"Regarding 'in all stages': this refers to the fourth stage of entering the womb—
the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging."
Those who are entirely without knowledge,
as well as those in the egg stage who are perpetually without knowledge—
these constitute the first four stages.
It speaks only of birth from a womb;
as for those born from eggs, their stages such as entering the womb and so forth [are not mentioned].
Not knowing during the three periods [of conception] is called "constant ignorance.
This constant ignorance is identical to the fourth stage of the preceding womb-birth.
The verse says "and" (ca). Question:
How can it be said that those born from eggs enter the womb? Answer: It refers to entering the embryonic matrix (garbha).
Answer: It refers to those born from eggs;
they must first enter the womb. This is stated according to the designation used at the very beginning.
Alternatively, the term "egg" may be stated according to its future designation;
that is, one first enters the womb and is subsequently born from an egg.
To speak of the embryo as an "egg" is to describe it according to its future state,
just as one speaks of rice while it is being boiled.
He immediately said, "Cook the rice," according to its proper name.
As for the first three types of entry into the womb— namely, those of a Wheel-turning King and the two kinds of Buddhas:
These are categorized by way of analogy.
The first is entry into the womb,
which refers to a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).
At the time of entering the womb,
he possesses unerring perception and understanding,
and enters the womb with full awareness.
The second entry into the womb is that of the Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer), who is unaware of the stages of staying and emerging.
Regarding the process of entering the womb,
one is fully conscious of the entry and the abiding, but not of the emergence.
The third entry into the womb refers to the Unsurpassed Awakening (anuttara-bodhi), [occurring] during the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging.
They are all able to have correct knowledge.
As for the "two Buddhas," they refer to the Pratyekabuddha and the Mahābuddha.
"Because both karma and wisdom are preeminent" explains the reason for what preceded.
First, karma is preeminent.
One enters the womb with full awareness,
namely a wheel-turning monarch,
because he has cultivated vast merit in previous lives.
Second is the excellence of wisdom: being fully aware when entering and remaining [in meditative absorption],
which refers to the uniquely supreme awakening.
Because of long-standing practice, extensive learning, and superior analytical discernment,
the third [type] excels in both merit and wisdom;
that is, unsurpassed enlightenment.
Because of the superior merit and wisdom cultivated through kalpas of austerity;
"the four remaining births" and "the two characters" correspond respectively to the preceding terms.
Those whose karma, wisdom, and both are superior are Universal Monarchs and the two types of Buddhas.
Fourth, as for those born in other ways:
The fourth refers to the fourth type of entry into the womb,
in which one is entirely lacking correct awareness during all stages: entering, abiding, and emerging.
Excluding the first three types,
those born from the womb and from eggs are inferior in both merit and wisdom.
All of these are subsumed under the fourth stage of entering the womb.
From this point, the second major section refutes the objections of non-Buddhists;
specifically, these are the objections raised by the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists.
The treatise states:
Among these, the non-Buddhists who cling to a self say:
"If it is granted that sentient beings transition to other worlds,"
Thus, the thesis that "I" exists as grasped by me would be established.
Now, in order to refute that,
the verse says:
There is no self, only the aggregates, produced by afflictions and karma;
through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one enters the womb like the flame of a lamp.
Like a drawn-out succession that increases, this continuity proceeds by means of delusion and karma.
"Furthermore, one proceeds to other worlds; therefore, the wheel of existence has no beginning.
Commentary: The first line [of the verse].
This clarifies non-self:
there is only the continuity [of consciousness] entering the womb due to afflictions and karma.
The final line clarifies that the cycle of birth and death is devoid of a self and consists of nothing but the aggregates (*skandhas*).
"Non-self" correctly negates the non-Buddhists; that is to say,
it negates the non-Buddhists' attachment to a self.
At the time of death,
one is able to relinquish these aggregates;
at the time of taking birth, [one assumes new ones].
It is that which can continue the remaining aggregates. If there were no self,
who would be able to continue the aggregates?
Therefore, there is a self.
To refute this attachment,
it is said that there is no self.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The internal agent (puruṣa) certainly does not exist."
"Because [entities] such as form and the eye cannot be apprehended," the commentary notes:
"The heterodox schools (tīrthikas) cling to a self,
which they designate as the 'person' (puruṣa)."
It is like the functioning of a person.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
"This [consciousness] certainly does not exist in the same way as the five objects, such as form and so forth."
This is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The five faculties, such as the eye and so forth,
are known through inference (*anumāna*).
Your current apprehension of me is not like the perception of form by the eye and so forth, which is known through direct and inferential cognition;
therefore, it is unattainable.
The Blessed One has also said:
"There is karma and there is its maturation,
but an agent cannot be found."

This refers to that which is able to relinquish these aggregates and is able to continue other aggregates, with the sole exception of the conventional designation of dharmas (dharma-prajñapti). [Commentary: The note explains: "It means..."
The "agent" is merely another name for the self.
The birth and death of sentient beings result from the maturation of karma.
It is not by virtue of a creator that there is a real self.
What is meant by the designation "dharmas"? It is asked: because this exists, that exists.

"Because this arises, that arises. This is the full exposition of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The commentary states: "The above is the treatise. The explanation says: [followed by the commentary].
Because these [factors] such as ignorance exist,
those [factors] such as volitional formations come to be;
because those [factors] such as ignorance arise, [the subsequent factors arise].
Those formations and so forth arise;

the twelve links of dependent origination are conventionally designated as "self," which is called a "conventional designation of phenomena" (*dharma-prajñapti*). "Merely the aggregates" refers to this.
This is the correct establishment of the tenet:
there are only the five aggregates;
there is no real self whatsoever.
To conventionally designate a "self" upon these aggregates is the correct principle.

"It is not that which is negated" refers to the explanation of the objection: that the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is brought about by the actions of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since there is no real self,
one must admit that the aggregates themselves are able to pass from this life to another world,
entering the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the womb.
To refute this objection,
there is this verse: "The aggregates perish moment by moment."
It is not possible to transition from this life to another world;
rather, it is solely through the power of the habitual cultivation of afflictions and karma that the aggregates of the intermediate state (antarābhava) continue in succession and enter the womb.
"Entering the womb like a lamp-flame, increasing sequentially as it is drawn forth" correctly clarifies the continuity [of consciousness].
For example, although a lamp-flame perishes moment by moment, [it appears to continue].
Yet, it is able to continue in succession and transition to another world;
the aggregates (skandhas) are likewise,
and thus their transition is without loss.
Therefore, although there is no self,
it is established that the aggregates continue in succession and enter the womb, solely by virtue of afflictions and karma acting as causes.
Just as it is drawn forth by karma,
the aggregates within the womb are caused to increase sequentially;
as for this sequential increase:
This refers to the process of gradual development, beginning from the *kalala* stage up to the *praśākhā* stage.
That the continuity [of existence] proceeds to another world by means of afflictions and karma clarifies the revolving of the three realms of existence;
that is to say, it increases in succession.
Until the end of life, the continuity of the manifest aggregates persists;
within this present existence,
one further gives rise to afflictions and karma.
With this as the cause,
one proceeds further toward another world; thus,
the wheel of existence has no beginning.
This clarifies that [existence] is beginningless.
Thus, through the causes of afflictions and karma, birth occurs.
Birth, in turn, acts as a cause,
giving rise to afflictions and karma;
from these afflictions and karma [proceeds further existence].
There is further rebirth;
thus, one knows that the wheel of existence revolves without beginning. Furthermore, the treatise clarifies the meaning of sequential increase, citing a verse from a sutra as follows:

At the beginning is the *kalala*, here translated as "congealed mucilage" or "conjunction"; next arises the *arbuda*, here translated as "bubble"; from this arises the *peśī*, here translated as "flesh-and-blood"; from the *peśī* arises the *ghanā*, here translated as "solid flesh"; next is the *praśākhā*, here translated as "limbs and joints"; and finally, the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the sensory faculties (*indriya*) and physical forms, gradually develop and increase, including the hair and other features.
It is always the fifth stage.
The above constitutes the five stages within the womb.
From here begins the eighth major section.
This explains the twelve links of dependent origination.
First, the twelve links of dependent origination are explained in detail;
second, they are briefly summarized through analogies to reveal their meaning.
Regarding the first [section], which extensively explains the twelve links of dependent origination, there are two parts:
first, a general exposition;
second, a detailed explanation.
Within the general analysis,
it is further divided into six sections.
First, the general determination of the stages of the members.
First, the specific manifestation of the essential nature;
second, the clarification of the original intent of the teaching;
third, the subsumption of the extensive by means of the concise.
Fifth, resolving doubts and difficulties through refutation;
sixth, reconciling and explaining the scriptural text.
First, regarding the general determination of the stages of the factors:
The treatise says:
"In this way, the continuity of the aggregates is described as having three births as its stages.
The verse states:
Thus, regarding these dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the twelve links consist of two for each of the three time periods—
the past and future— while eight belong to the middle period; this is according to the explanation based on the complete [set].
The first two lines indicate the headings and enumerate the items;
the latter two lines establish the members according to worldly convention.
As for the twelve members:
First, ignorance; second, volitional formations;
third, consciousness.
Fourth, name-and-form;
fifth, the six sense bases;
sixth, contact.
7. Feeling (vedanā);
8. Craving (tṛṣṇā);
9. Grasping (upādāna).
10. Existence;
11. Birth; 12. Old Age and Death.
Regarding the "three time periods":
the first is the prior limit, which is the past.
The second is the posterior limit, which is the future.
The third is the middle limit.
This refers to the present life.
Regarding "two for each of the prior and posterior limits," this means that two factors are established for each of the prior and posterior limits.
Ignorance and formations belong to the prior limit;
birth, old age, and death belong to the posterior limit;
the eight intermediate factors are based on a complete [lifespan].
This clarifies the establishment of the eight factors within the middle limit (*madhyānta*).
Excluding those belonging to the prior and subsequent limits, the remaining eight factors exist in the present life,
according to the complete [set].
The eight factors of the middle period are not possessed by all sentient beings;
the present mention of "eight" is stated according to the case of those who are complete.
Passing through the eight stages is called "perfection.
As for those who die prematurely:
They do not possess all eight factors;
there are cases where they possess only two factors and so forth,
such as those who die within the womb.
Furthermore, these eight branches are taught with reference to the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
not the form or formless realms.
This means that within the form realm (rūpadhātu),
there is no branch of name-and-form (nāmarūpa),
because those beings are born by transformation (upapāduka).
Because the faculties are all present at once;
and because if there were no name-and-form and the member of the six sense bases in the formless realm,
it would contradict the fact that they are said to be fully present in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, as that realm is not devoid of form.
He says: The Buddha told Ānanda,
"If consciousness were not to enter the womb..."
"Does name-and-form attain vast increase? "No,
World-Honored One," and so on, as extensively explained.
The commentary states:
Since this sutra says that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth only increase once one has entered the womb.
It is clearly known that the eight limbs are taught with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
because beings in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) do not enter a womb.
At times, only two divisions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are taught.
First, inclusion in the prior limit;
second, inclusion in the posterior limit,
namely the factors from ignorance through feeling.
These seven links are subsumed under the past limit.
As for the five links from craving up to old age and death,
these are subsumed under the future limit.
Because cause and effect are subsumed within the two divisions of the preceding and the succeeding.
As for the cause and effect of the preceding:
This means that ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the causes,
while consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five members are the results.
As for the subsequent cause and result:
That is to say, craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes,
while birth, old age, and death are the effects;
this is explained in terms of cause and effect.
It is divided into two sections.
From this second [section],
the essential nature is specifically revealed.
The treatise says:
What dharmas constitute the essence of the members such as ignorance?
The verse says:
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; the various past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*);
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is at the moment of actual conception; and that which precedes the six sense bases is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
From the arising of the sense organs such as the eyes, the six bases exist prior to the three [aggregates];
they differ in being the causes for the three types of feeling. That which is not yet understood is called contact (*sparśa*);
it occurs before sensual craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving consists of the desire for the necessities of life and for sexual pleasure.
Seeking everywhere for the sake of obtaining various objects is called "grasping" (*upādāna*);
it refers to that which truly creates [the conditions for existence]. The karma that draws forth the fruit of future existence is called "becoming" (*bhava*);
it binds one to future existence. Upon reaching that state, one undergoes old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
The commentary states:
"Ignorance at the stage of past afflictions" refers to the previous birth.
When afflictions arise,
it is called the stage of latent defilements;
the five aggregates at this stage [constitute the basis].
Up to this point, when the fruit has ripened,
it is collectively termed ignorance (*avidyā*). Since these constitute the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), [they are so designated].
Regarding the singular designation of "ignorance" (avidyā),
the treatise states:
"That [craving] and ignorance..."
Because they function simultaneously;
because they manifest through the power of ignorance.
As it is said that when a king travels,
he is not without his retinue,
because the king is preeminent among them.
In summary, Master Xingjie says:
"That" refers to the five aggregates at the stage of those past afflictions.
One who has accumulated various karmas in past lives is called a "practitioner" (yogācāra);
that is to say, one at the stage of having initiated various karmas during previous births.
The five aggregates in this stage are collectively termed "karma";
karma is termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Because they have the sense of being "constructed," these twelve links all possess the term "position" (*avasthā*).
Therefore, the first phrase extends its application through to birth and old age and death. Regarding "consciousness as the very moment of linking to rebirth in the aggregates":
when one is in the mother's womb or similar locations, at the precise moment of linking to rebirth, the five aggregates existing in that single kṣaṇa are termed "consciousness."
Because the consciousness that takes rebirth is predominant,
"consciousness" is designated separately; as for "name-and-form," it is so called from the point after conception until before the six sense bases.
The five aggregates that exist during all the intermediate stages prior to the arising of the six sense bases.
Collectively, these are termed name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
The intermediate stages refer specifically to the period within the womb.
From kalala to praśākhā constitutes the five stages.
The treatise states:
"In this context, one should have spoken of the four bases arising first;
yet it speaks of six."
Because it is established based on completion, the four bases exclude the body and mind. Regarding the "six bases prior to the three [factors] preceding the arising of the eye and other faculties":
this refers to the *praśākhā* stage, which encompasses many moments.
After name-and-form and prior to the arising of the eye and other faculties through the threefold conjunction,
the five aggregates at this stage are called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are first fully established,
as the characteristics of the faculties become manifest;
therefore, only the six sense bases are designated.
Regarding "contact" (*sparśa*), it is that which has not yet been fully understood as the cause of the three types of feeling.
The "causes of the three feelings" refers to the objects of the three feelings.
The objective sphere is called the cause;
it is that which can produce sensation.
This refers to the period after birth from the womb.
From the age of three or two years onward,
the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness can produce impingement-contact;
at this stage, the five aggregates [are present].
They are collectively termed "contact" (*sparśa*).
Because the characteristic of contact is manifest,
the name "contact" is designated.
Because one has not yet fully understood the objects of the three types of feeling,
it is not yet called "feeling."
Regarding those who receive [the act] prior to sexual passion:
this refers to those from five or six years of age up to fourteen or fifteen years of age.
Having already understood the characteristics of the distinctions among the causes of the three types of sensation,
but not yet having given rise to sensual desire,
the five aggregates in this stage are collectively termed "sensation" (vedanā).
Because its enjoyment is superior,
it is designated separately by the name "grasping.
Those who crave sensual pleasures and sexual desire for the requisites of life [are included herein].
From fifteen years of age onwards,
they crave exquisite requisites,
and sensual desire manifests in their conduct.
Before extensively seeking [objects of desire],
the five aggregates at this stage are collectively termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*),
because the function of craving is predominant.
The name "craving" (tṛṣṇā) is designated separately.
That which, for the sake of obtaining various objects, universally rushes about and seeks them out is called "grasping" (upādāna).
Grasping refers to greed (rāga).
As he grew older, he craved the objects of the five desires and roamed in all directions in search of them.
Without fearing toil or weariness,
the five aggregates of this stage are collectively termed "grasping" (upādāna),
because grasping is predominant therein.
Names are established based on designations. As for the distinction between craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*):
that which first arises is called craving.
When the continuity becomes increasingly intense,
it is established separately as "grasping" (*upādāna*).
This grasping takes the object within that continuity.
Because it becomes firm and intense, some say that it is precisely the karma capable of producing the result of future existence;
because of its frantic pursuit,
one accumulates the karma capable of drawing forth the result of future existence.
In this stage, the five aggregates are collectively termed "existence" (*bhava*).
Karma is also termed "existence," because it brings about future results.
Because of the superiority of karma,
it is designated by the name "to be born"; as for the phrase "one who is to be born," this refers to one who,
from this point, relinquishes their life.
The actual linking of existence is "birth" (jāti).
At this stage, the five aggregates are collectively designated by the name "birth.
This refers to the future link of birth.
Just as consciousness in the present gives rise to manifestation in the future,
it is established by the name "birth."
At present, consciousness is predominant;
it is designated according to its actual experience.
This continues until one experiences old age and death.
In a future life, after having taken birth,
there is the constituent of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Next, the branch of the six sense bases arises;
next, the branch of contact arises;
next, the branch of sensation arises.
The five aggregates belonging to these four stages are collectively termed "old age and death.
Such is old age and death.

That is to say, in this present world, the four factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling follow after the factor of birth, wherein the characteristics of aging and death become manifest;
thus, the designation "aging and death" is applied. The treatise states:
Furthermore, there are four distinctions among the members of dependent origination:
first, the momentary;
second, the continuous.
Third is the state of being;
fourth is the distant continuity.
What is a moment (*kṣaṇa*)?
That is to say, in a single moment,
one who kills out of greed fulfills all twelve links [of dependent origination].
Delusion refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Volition (*cetanā*) is precisely the mental factor of formation (*saṃskāra*), which is universal (*mahābhūmika*); since greed necessarily exists, volition must also be present.
The discernment of various objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); when greed arises, consciousness is present.
It is that which cognizes the object.
The three aggregates co-arising with consciousness are collectively termed "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa). The annotation states: "Regarding the 'three aggregates'..."
The three aggregates of form, perception,
and formations arise together with consciousness. Of these, the aggregate of perception takes the entirety [of its constituents], while the aggregate of form takes only a small portion—
excluding the five sense faculties and both informative and non-informative matter.
Because the members [of dependent origination] are established separately, the remaining aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is taken up;
this refers to the four objects of the sense faculties along with their physical bases (*āśraya*). A small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is also taken up.

Excluding ignorance, volition, contact, feeling, craving, as well as lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness— since these arise and cease simultaneously and are established as separate factors—
one takes the remaining factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
These are precisely the mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth.

They are called the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*) because they abide in name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Since the five faculties, such as the eye, abide in name-and-form, these five faculties are designated as the six sense bases.
Although there are five [factors],
they are called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) because they are subsumed within the six bases. As for the six bases in relation to the others...
The coming together of the conditioned—the contact of the six sense bases—is itself the faculty.

When consciousness encounters other objects, there is contact through the conjunction of the three. That which experiences contact is called feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling associated with greed is greed itself; that is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is precisely what constitutes the act of killing.

This is the mind of greed (*lobha*). The various entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) associated with it are called "grasping" (*upādāna*), namely: lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*);

these are termed the entanglements and are associated with greed. The two types of action—bodily and vocal—arising therefrom are called "existence" (*bhava*; specifically *bhavaṅga*); for example, when one commits killing.
The two karmas of body and speech are called the "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*). Thus, the stage at which these phenomena arise is called "birth" (*jāti*);
their maturation and transformation is called "aging" (*jarā*); and their dissolution and destruction is called "death" (*maraṇa*). These are the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Transformation through maturation is the characteristic of change. Furthermore,
some say that it is momentary and continuous,
as described in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
All five aggregates existing within the twelve links of conditioned existence are subsumed under the category of "states" (avasthā);
these constitute a remote, continuous succession that is beginningless.
This concludes the preceding section of the treatise titled "Explaining the Name 'Distant Continuity'.
The commentary states: as for the term "moment" (*kṣaṇa*), it refers to a single moment.
"Continuous binding" (saṃyojana) refers to the arising of cause and effect in uninterrupted succession.
This applies whether the entities involved are sentient or non-sentient.
All possess arising and ceasing;
because they continue in succession from moment to moment, they are bound together in an unbroken chain of kṣaṇas.
This applies to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
While the previous interpretation held that "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers exclusively to sentient beings,
this master’s interpretation holds that "moment" also extends to non-sentient things.

The dependent origination of states (*avasthika-pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the twelve links of the five aggregates across the three time periods, categorized according to karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*) and karma of indefinite timing (*aniyata-vedanīya-karma*).
Regarding "distant continuation":
this refers to the preceding state in relation to karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
And as for karma of indefinite timing,
it spans many lifetimes;
it is the cause and effect of a long continuity from time without beginning.
From here, thirdly, the intention of the original teaching is clarified.
This section contains two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the intention of the teaching.
Second, dispelling the delusions of others.
First, regarding the intended meaning of the initial statement,
the treatise says:
What is the intention behind the Blessed One’s statement regarding this?
The verse says:
It is traditionally held that this is taught in terms of stages; the names of the members are established according to their predominance.
The commentary states:
"As for 'the tradition permits [this] as being taught in terms of stages,' it means that the tradition permits it."
The World-Honored One spoke of the twelve links solely in terms of their sequential stages;
he did not base it upon a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or the like.

Was there something that existed?

Regarding the phrase "because it is said to be [the cause of] fetters and so forth":
"Teaching" refers to what is taught in the Sūtras.
"Fetters" (saṃyojana) refers to the nine fetters;
the term "etc. includes the three bonds (bandhana), the ten proclivities (anuśaya), the three outflows (āsrava), and the four floods (ogha), as taught in the Sūtras.
Since all [of these] possess ignorance,
how could they lack a real substance such that they are described as "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth?
Regarding the phrase "not because of a view of non-wisdom," this refutes the assertion of certain other masters.
Those other masters assert as follows:
Ignorance has unwholesome wisdom as its essence;
therefore, it is said that just as one with bad wives and children is called "one without wives and children."
If such corrupted wisdom were to be called ignorance (*avidyā*),
the Master of the Treatise refutes this.
Therefore, it is said that [ignorance] is not [simply] a view of wrong wisdom.
That is to say, defiled wisdom is termed "wrong wisdom" (*kuprajñā*);
since a view exists therein, it is not ignorance (*avidyā*).
Just as with the view of a self-identity and so forth,
these are views that are wisdom; since wisdom possesses the quality of viewing, it is called "view."
"Rather, it is ignorance,
because it is associated with views"—
this refutes their attempted rebuttal.
That is to say, other masters state:
"If that were so, then it would follow that wrong wisdom (*kuprajñā*) must be admitted to be ignorance (*avidyā*), for it is not [proper] vision."
For example, the wisdom associated with craving and so forth is non-insight (dṛṣṭi) and is unwholesome wisdom (kuprajñā). Since it is not insight,

To refute this defense, it is stated that [it] is associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-samprayukta*).
This means that because this ignorance is associated with views,
one knows that ignorance cannot be wisdom.
If ignorance were wisdom,
how could two wisdoms exist in mutual association?
Since it has already been admitted that ignorance (avidyā) is associated with views (dṛṣṭi),
it is known that ignorance is not wisdom (prajñā).
