Explaining the hells.
The treatise asks:
"Furthermore, in what location?"
Setting aside the *naraka*s and the great *naraka*s,
what are their dimensions and how many are there?
The verse says:
Below this, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas], is the Avīci Hell; its depth and breadth are as described above.
There are seven other hells, and eight secondary hells (utsada), each numbering sixteen.
That is to say, the Hot Ashes, Excrement, and Feces;
the Sword-Blade Forest, and the River—each of these [five] hells resides at one of the four cardinal directions. As for the remaining eight cold hells, the commentary explains:
Twenty thousand yojanas below this Jambudvīpa lies the great hell of Avīci.
Its depth and breadth are as before,
namely two myriads each; thus,
the distance from here to its bottom is...
It is forty thousand yojanas in extent; therein,
one undergoes uninterrupted suffering.
It is not like the other seven hells, where the experience of suffering is not constant;
therefore, it is called "Uninterrupted" (Avīci). For instance, in the Saṃjīva hell:
Although the bodies of sentient beings have been subjected to various forms of cutting, piercing, grinding, and crushing, they may,
upon briefly encountering a cool breeze blowing upon them, [recover].
They return to life as they were before;
for this reason, it is established with the name Saṃjīva (Reviving).
In the Avīci hell,
such things do not exist;
so say other masters.
Within Avīci, there is no interval of pleasure amidst the suffering; therefore,
it is named "Uninterrupted" (Avīci).
In the other hells,
although there is no [karmic] maturation (*vipāka*), there is a flow-on result (*niṣyanda*).
These are the seven *naraka*s.
They are situated one above the other,
stacked in succession. What are these seven?
1. The Extremely Hot Hell;
2. The Intensely Hot Hell;
3. The Great Wailing Hell.
Fourth, the Screaming Hell;
fifth, the Hell of Massed Aggregates;
sixth, the Black Rope Hell.
Regarding the Seven Saṃjīva hells:
some say that these seven are situated alongside the Avīci hell.
Because there are sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*) for each of the eight great hells (*naraka*), the Blessed One spoke this verse:

"These eight hells, I say, are exceedingly difficult to cross. Their ground is made of glowing iron, and they are surrounded by iron walls. On all four sides there are four gates, opened and closed with iron doors. Skillfully arranged in their dimensions, each has sixteen secondary hells. Extending for many hundreds of *yojanas*, they are filled with those who have committed evil deeds. Heat pervades them everywhere, and fierce fires burn constantly and intensely."
The commentary states: Regarding the sixteen increases,
they are located outside the gates on the four sides of the eight hells.
Each has four locations.
The first is the *Kukūla* (Hot Ashes) *Utsada*;
that is to say, within this *utsada*.
In the Hell of Hot Ashes, the ash reaches up to the knees;
when sentient beings wander there,
as soon as they set foot down, it sinks in.
The skin, flesh, and blood are all scorched and sloughed off;
yet as soon as they lift their feet, it grows back again.
They are restored to their original state.
Second is the Excrement Heap (Gūthakṛtsna).
This refers to within this heap.
Its interior is filled with corpses, excrement, and mud,
and it teems with *narkuṭa* worms whose beaks are as sharp as needles.
Its body is white and its head is black;
all sentient beings who wander there become this very insect.
They bore through skin and break through bone,
devouring the very marrow;
this is the hell of the three blades.
That is to say, within this increase,
there are further three kinds:
first, the Path of Razor Blades.
That is to say, within this place,
blades are laid face-up to form a great road.
When sentient beings wander there,
as soon as they set foot down,
their skin, flesh, and blood [are consumed].
They were all cut to pieces and fell down;
yet as soon as he lifted his foot, they grew back again,
restored to their original state.
Second is the Forest of Sword Leaves.
This means that the leaves of this forest consist entirely of sharp, keen sword blades.
Sentient beings wander there;
when the wind blows, leaves fall and strike their limbs, cutting and piercing them.
Their flesh and bones were scattered about,
and spotted dogs tore at and devoured them.
Third is the Forest of Iron Thorns;
this means that upon this forest there are sharp iron thorns.
It is sixteen finger-widths long.
When sentient beings are driven by distress,
they climb up and down this tree.
The thorns have sharp points;
as one pierces upward and downward,
there are iron-beaked birds.
They peck and probe at the eyes, hearts, and livers of sentient beings,
vying with one another to devour them on such paths as the Road of Razor Blades.
Although the three types differ,
the iron staff is the same; therefore,
they are subsumed within a single increase.
Fourth is the Cāṇdīra-nadī-vardhana (The Increase of the Fierce River). This means that within this increase,
it is filled with hot, brackish water.
Sentient beings move within it,
sometimes floating and sometimes sinking;
sometimes going against the current and sometimes with the current.
Being steamed and boiled,
their flesh and bones are reduced to a pulp;
even if they wish to flee, [they cannot].
On both banks, there were various hell-wardens holding swords and spears in their hands.
They were warded off and forced to turn back;
there was no way for them to escape.
This river is like a moat.
The first three [heavens] resemble gardens, each having four *cūḍikās* on its four sides;
therefore, it is said that they all have sixteen.
This refers to the superior [arrangement].
Because they are places of being subjected to punishments and harms,
they are said to be "increased" [in suffering] within the primary hells.
Having just been harmed,
because they undergo further suffering, some say:
Sentient beings emerging from hell undergo intense suffering;
therefore, it is called "increased" (*utsada*). [The Buddha] asked about the various hells.
Are the hell-wardens sentient beings?
Answer: Some say they are non-sentient. Question: Since they are non-sentient, how do they perform actions?
Answer: It is due to the karmic power of sentient beings, just as with the winds at the beginning of a kalpa; although the winds themselves are not sentient, they arise through such power.

Question: If that is so, how does this accord with the explanations of the venerable Dharmatrāta and Subhūti?

As that verse says: "One who constantly harbors the poison of anger in the mind, delights in accumulating various evil karmas, and rejoices at seeing the suffering of others, shall become a henchman of Yama upon death. Based on this verse:
Is it not the case that these are insentient objects? Answer:
They are the messengers of King Yama and the various rākṣasas who hurl sentient beings [into the hells].
Those who cast beings into the hells are called the minions of Yama;
they are actual sentient beings.
Since those who inflict harm upon sentient beings do not exist within the hells,
the hell-wardens are not actual sentient beings; though some say they are sentient beings.
Question: If that is so, for what reason is fire unable to burn them?
Answer: This is because they are obstructed by the power of karma, or because they have brought about a different primary element (*mahābhūta*).
Therefore, they are not burned. Furthermore, there are eight other cold *naraka*s.
The first is Arbuda (translated as "Blister"), where the body is afflicted by a freezing wind, causing blisters to form.

third is Aṭaṭa; fourth is Hahava.
"Five tigers, tiger-mother"— these three are the sounds of cold.

the first two hells are named according to the transformations of the body.

As discussed above regarding the sixteen hells,
all sentient beings [fall therein].

To a greater or lesser extent;
whether two or one— such are the distinctions among the stations.

From this seventh [level] upward,

Regarding the dimensions of the abodes of the sun and moon,

[This section] explains the increase and decrease of day and night.
The *Śāstra* says:
"The sun, the moon, and the various stars..."

that is to say, all sentient beings.
Through the predominant power of karma,

The place where he dwells is forty thousand yojanas from here,

Question: It may be so with the wind blowing in the same direction;

Answer: Other masters say:
Fragrance has no principle of "upward incense," because it does not exceed the boundaries of its tree; thus,
the explanation that it "incenses against the wind" is stated.
The phrase "not exceeding the tree boundary" refers to the area outside the trunk of the tree,
extending fifty yojanas in each of the four directions along its branches and twigs.
It was as if he were standing beneath a tree;

this person, by virtue of being within the realm of the tree, [experiences it].

Because one obtains the fragrance of the branches and twigs upon its head, it is said that [the fragrance] does not exceed the boundaries of the tree. The Master of the Treatise provides the correct explanation, saying:

Possessing such virtues,

One thousand sets of four great continents,

Seven barley grains make one finger-joint. Seven finger-joints make one finger-breadth. Seven finger-breadths make one span. Two spans make one cubit. Four cubits make one fathom. Five hundred fathoms make one *krośa*. Eight *krośas* make one *yojana*. A *yojana* is the distance traveled by the sun in one day. There are four types of *yojanas*: the small *yojana*, the medium *yojana*, the great *yojana*, and the *yojana* of the Buddha’s power. The small *yojana* is the distance from the eastern sea to the western sea; this is called the small *yojana*. The medium *yojana* is the distance from Mount Sumeru to the Iron Ring Mountains; this is called the medium *yojana*. The great *yojana* is the distance from Mount Sumeru to the edge of the world; this is called the great *yojana*. The *yojana* of the Buddha’s power is the distance that the Buddha’s light can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the Buddha’s power. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the small vehicle, the *yojana* of the great vehicle, the *yojana* of the Bodhisattva’s vow, and the *yojana* of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. The *yojana* of the small vehicle is as previously described. The *yojana* of the great vehicle is the distance that the light of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the great vehicle. The *yojana* of the Bodhisattva’s vow is the distance that the Bodhisattva’s vows can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the Bodhisattva’s vow. The *yojana* of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is the distance that the Tathāgata’s wisdom can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the world, the *yojana* of the Dharma, the *yojana* of the mind, and the *yojana* of emptiness. The *yojana* of the world is as previously described. The *yojana* of the Dharma is the distance that the Dharma-realm pervades; this is called the *yojana* of the Dharma. The *yojana* of the mind is the distance that the mind can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the mind. The *yojana* of emptiness is the distance that the nature of emptiness pervades; this is called the *yojana* of emptiness. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the past, the *yojana* of the future, the *yojana* of the present, and the *yojana* of the three times. The *yojana* of the past is the distance that the traces of the past reach; this is called the *yojana* of the past. The *yojana* of the future is the distance that the projections of the future reach; this is called the *yojana* of the future. The *yojana* of the present is the distance that the manifestations of the present reach; this is called the *yojana* of the present. The *yojana* of the three times is the distance that the three times interpenetrate; this is called the *yojana* of the three times. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the body, the *yojana* of the land, the *yojana* of the Dharma, and the *yojana* of the mind. The *yojana* of the body is the distance that the bodies of all sentient beings can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the body. The *yojana* of the land is the distance that the lands of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the land. The *yojana* of the Dharma is the distance that the Dharma-realm pervades; this is called the *yojana* of the Dharma. The *yojana* of the mind is the distance that the minds of all sentient beings can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the mind. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the small, the *yojana* of the medium, the *yojana* of the great, and the *yojana* of the immeasurable. The *yojana* of the small is as previously described. The *yojana* of the medium is ten times the small *yojana*. The *yojana* of the great is ten times the medium *yojana*. The *yojana* of the immeasurable is beyond calculation and cannot be measured; this is called the *yojana* of the immeasurable. Furthermore, there are four types of *yojanas*: the *yojana* of the provisional, the *yojana* of the real, the *yojana* of the conventional, and the *yojana* of the ultimate. The *yojana* of the provisional is the distance that provisional teachings reach; this is called the *yojana* of the provisional. The *yojana* of the real is the distance that the true reality reaches; this is called the *yojana* of the real. The *yojana* of the Buddha is the distance that the wisdom and power of the Buddhas can reach; this is called the *yojana* of the Buddha. The verse says:
One should know that there are four kalpas: namely, the kalpa of destruction, formation, intermediate destruction, and great destruction.
The kalpa of destruction begins when beings are no longer born in the hells and continues until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted.
The kalpa of formation begins from the arising of the wind and continues until the first being is born in the hells.
An intermediate kalpa begins from an immeasurable lifespan and decreases until life lasts only ten years;
it then increases and decreases eighteen times more, finally increasing again to eighty thousand years.
This period, from the completion of formation until the end of the abiding, is called twenty intermediate kalpas.

The periods of formation, destruction, and the emptiness following destruction each last for eighty intermediate kalpas; these constitute one great kalpa. There are three incalculable [great] kalpas. The commentary states: Formation lasts twenty intermediate kalpas, Destruction lasts twenty intermediate kalpas, And the period of emptiness lasts twenty intermediate kalpas. Thus, these three periods together constitute one great kalpa. Three such incalculable great kalpas constitute the time required for a Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood. The term "incalculable" (asaṃkhyeya) means that it cannot be calculated by ordinary numbers. It is not that there is no way to calculate it at all; rather, it refers to a number so vast that it exceeds the capacity of ordinary calculation. It is not that there is no method of calculation; rather, it is because the number is too great to be expressed in ordinary terms. For example, when one says "one hundred," it is understood as a specific quantity; yet, if one were to count from one up to one hundred, the process would take a long time. Similarly, when one speaks of an "incalculable" kalpa, although it is a vast duration, it is not impossible to reach its end through counting. However, because the number is so immense, it is termed "incalculable. This is like saying "a hundred" or "a thousand"—it is not that there is no way to count them, but rather that the number is so large it is called "incalculable. There are four kinds of kalpas:
first, the kalpa of destruction;
second, the kalpa of formation.
Among the three [types of destruction], regarding the four great elements,
what is called the "kalpa of destruction" (saṃvartakalpa) is as follows:
This refers to the point when sentient beings no longer arise in the hells,
continuing until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted.
There are two types of destruction.
First, the destruction of a single world-system; second, the destruction of a realm.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of destruction.
First, the destruction of sentient beings;
second, the destruction of the external vessel-world,
which refers to this world-system.
After remaining for twenty intermediate kalpas,
there follow another twenty intermediate kalpas of equal duration;
then the kalpa of destruction arrives.
When, at that time, sentient beings in the hells pass away and no new births occur, [the hell realms become empty].
This marks the beginning of the kalpa of destruction,
continuing until not a single sentient being remains in the hells.
At that time, it is said that the hells have already been destroyed.
Those beings who possess karma fixed for the hells are drawn by the power of their karma and placed into the hells of other directions.
By this, one may infer the same for the animal and hungry ghost realms;
however, in each case, those who previously resided in their own abodes are destroyed first,
followed by those who dwell interspersed among humans and devas.
They perish together with the gods and humans.
At that time, among the human realm,
there is one person on this continent.
Without a teacher, by the nature of reality,
he attained the first dhyāna;
arising from that dhyāna, he emerged.
He uttered these words:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion are exceedingly pleasant and exceedingly tranquil."
Upon hearing this, the others all entered meditative absorption;
at the end of their lives, they were all reborn in the Brahma world.
This continues until all sentient beings on this continent have perished;
this is called the destruction of the people of Jambudvīpa.
[The same applies to] the two continents to the east and west.
This should be explained by way of example:
when their lives end in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), they are reborn among the devas of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Because they lack the capacity for meditative absorption and are free from desire, those in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) are shown not to enter absorption;
nor are they born in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
This applies even down to the human realm, where there is not a single sentient being [who possesses such qualities].
At that time, it is said that the human realm has already been destroyed.
When, among the gods of the Four Great Kings, even a single one spontaneously attains the first dhyāna, [the destruction of the human realm is complete].
Eventually, all beings were reborn in the Brahma-world,
and at that time, the realm of the Four Great Kings was entirely devoid of sentient beings.
This is called the destruction of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The other five heavens of the desire realm should be explained by analogy with this.
Even down to the desire realm,
there is not a single sentient being who can be called a sentient being of the desire realm whose intermediate existence has already perished.
At a time when, in the Brahma-world,
a certain sentient being [attains realization] through the natural dharma without a teacher.
Having attained the second dhyāna and emerged from that meditative absorption,
he uttered these words:
The joy and bliss born of concentration are exceedingly pleasant and exceedingly tranquil;
having heard this, the other devas [were moved].
They all enter that meditative absorption;
at the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
and even as far as the Brahma-world.
When sentient beings have all perished,
this is called the destruction of the world of sentient beings;
only the receptacle world remains.
Dwelling in empty space,
all sentient beings throughout the other worlds of the ten directions [are likewise].
In this trichiliocosm, as karma is exhausted, seven suns gradually appear;
all the oceans dry up and parch.
The mountain caves were ablaze;
the three wheels of the state and its islands were all consumed by the flames.
The wind blows fierce flames that burn upward through the celestial palaces,
even unto the Brahma palaces.
Leaving not even a trace of ash or ember,
the flames from their own respective levels burn the palaces of those same levels.
A disaster of one stage cannot destroy another stage; however,
because they are produced through their mutual characteristics, this statement is made.
The fire from below, driven by the wind,
burns the upper realms;
this refers to the fire of the desire realm.
The fierce flames ascend;
conditioned by this, they draw forth the fire-flames of the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The same applies to the other calamities.
Thus, beginning from the gradual destruction of the hells up until the exhaustion of the receptacle world, this is collectively termed the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).
The above explains the first verse-line. As for what is called the kalpa of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*):
It means arising from wind,
until the first sentient beings are born in hell;
that is to say, this world-system.
Once destroyed by the calamities,
for twenty intermediate kalpas there is only empty space.
After this long period has passed,
there must next be twenty intermediate kalpas of equal duration; thus,
the kalpa of formation (vivartakalpa) arrives.
Through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings,
a subtle wind gradually arises within space.
This receptacle world is about to be formed; as a preceding sign,
the winds gradually increase in intensity.
The establishment [of the world system] is as previously described,
including the wind-circle, the water-circle, the gold-circle,
and so forth; however, first the palaces of Mahābrahmā up to those of the Yāma Heaven are established.
Subsequently, the wind-circle and so forth arise;
this is called the establishment of the external vessel-world.
First, a single sentient being [appears].
Passing away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven,
he was reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā as the Great Brahmā King.
Thereafter, other sentient beings also passed away from that realm and were born among the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).
Some are born among the Brahma hosts;
some are born in the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
and gradually descending, they are born even into the human realm.
Uttarakuru, Aparagodānīya, and Pūrvavideha.
Those born in Jambudvīpa are subsequently reborn among the hungry ghosts, animals, or in the hells;
it is the natural law that they perish last.
It will necessarily be the first to be completed.
If, for instance, a single sentient being is born in the Avīci Hell, it is the first such occurrence.

The twenty intermediate kalpas of formation have now been completed; this explains the fifth and sixth phrases above. Following this, there are another twenty intermediate kalpas called "abiding after formation."
They arise in succession;
that is to say, from wind arises the formation of the receptacle world,
continuing until the final period.
Sentient beings gradually came to dwell there;
the lifespan of the people on this continent lasted for immeasurable eons.
Upon reaching the beginning of the kalpa of abiding,
the lifespan then gradually decreases,
diminishing from an immeasurable number of kalpas.

Reaching the ultimate limit of ten thousand years is designated as the first intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) within the [great] kalpa; this concludes the explanation of the seventh and eighth phrases. Thereafter, for eighteen [intermediate kalpas], there are both increases and decreases.
That is to say, from a lifespan of ten years it increases up to eighty thousand years, and from eighty thousand years it decreases down to ten years;
during the twentieth kalpa, there is only increase and no decrease,
beginning from a lifespan of ten years.
When it increases to eighty thousand [years],
it is called the twentieth kalpa of increase.
This pattern applies to all kalpas of increase.
It does not exceed eighty thousand years;
during all kalpas of decrease,
it lasts only until ten years at its minimum.
Within eighteen kalpas, one increase and one decrease constitute a full cycle;
the duration of time is equal to that of the initial decrease and the subsequent increase.
Therefore, the duration of these twenty kalpas is equal.
This is collectively termed the "kalpa of abiding after completion. The above explains the ninth through the twelfth phrases. As for the remaining periods of formation and destruction:
And when it has been destroyed, it is empty;
although there is no increase or decrease,
there are twenty distinctions.

However, because the duration of time is equivalent to that of the *sthiti-kalpa*, each period of formation likewise constitutes twenty intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*); this explains the thirteenth and fourteenth phrases. Regarding the first intermediate kalpa of the formation period:
The receptacle world arises;
thereafter, during the nineteen intermediate kalpas,
sentient beings gradually come to dwell therein.
During the latter of the twenty intermediate kalpas of destruction, the receptacle world is destroyed;
this occurs during the first nineteen intermediate kalpas.
Sentient beings gradually depart.
Thus it is said that there is formation,
abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
Each consists of twenty intermediate kalpas;
accumulated, they form eighty.
These eighty together constitute the measure of a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
Question: What is the nature of an eon (*kalpa*)?
Answer: It consists solely of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*);
time has no separate substantial entity.
It is established according to the Dharma.
Question: The sutras speak of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; what kind of kalpas are these that, when accumulated, constitute the "three incalculable kalpas"?
Answer: Multiplying the preceding great kalpas by ten, a hundred, and a thousand, they accumulate until they form three incalculable kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Question: Since they are called "incalculable," [how can they be defined?]
Why, then, is it said that there are three *kalpas*?
Answer: It is not by saying "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) that one expresses what cannot be counted;
rather, the *Vimokṣa-sūtra* explains this among sixty numerical categories.
*Asaṃkhyeya*. This is the fifty-second unit of enumeration. Question: What are the sixty?
Answer: As it is said in that sutra:
There is a sequence of numbers without remainder:
one is the beginning;
ten ones make ten.
Ten tens make one hundred;
ten hundreds make one thousand;
ten thousands make ten thousand.
One hundred thousand is a lakṣa;
ten lakṣas is a prayuta; ten prayutas is a koṭi.
Ten koṭis make one madhya;
ten madhyas make one ayuta; ten ayutas make one mahāyuta.
Ten *ayuta* make one *nayuta*. Ten *nayuta* make one *mahā-nayuta*.
Ten *mahā-nayuta* make one *pranayuta*.
Ten *pranayuta* make one great *pranayuta*. Ten great *pranayuta* make one *kankara*.
Ten *kankara* make one great *kankara*.
Ten *kaṅkara* make one *bimbara*; ten *bimbara* make one *mahābimbara*;
ten *mahābimbara* make one *akṣobhya*.
Ten acyutas make one mahācyuta; ten mahācyutas make one vibhava;
ten vibhavas make one mahāvibhava.
Ten *vibhava* make one *udvaṃsaka*;
ten *udvaṃsaka* make one *mahodvaṃsaka*;
ten *mahodvaṃsaka* make one *vibhūta*.
Ten *bhaṅga* is a *mahābhaṅga*. Ten *mahābhaṅga* is a *diśti*. Ten *diśti* is a *mahādiśti*.
Ten mahātitibas are one hetu; ten hetus are one mahāhetu;
ten mahāhetus are one karabha.
Ten *kalāpas* make one great *kalāpa*.
Ten great *kalāpas* make one *indrā*.
Ten *indrās* make one great *indrā*.
Ten *indra*s constitute one *samāpta*;
thirteen *samāpta*s constitute one *mahāsamāpta*;
ten *mahāsamāpta*s constitute one *gati*.
Ten *koṭi* make one *mahā-koṭi*.
Ten *mahā-koṭi* make one *nayuta*. Ten *nayuta* make one *mahā-nayuta*.
Ten *niyuta* (拈筏羅闍) make one *muda* (姥達羅);
ten *muda* make one *mahāmuda* (大姥達羅);
ten *mahāmuda* make one *balam* (跋藍).
Ten *balas* make one great *bala*;
ten great *balas* make one *sanya*;
ten *sanyas* make one great *sanya*.
Ten *saṃjñā* make one *vibhūta*;
ten *vibhūta* make one *mahāvibhūta*;
ten *mahāvibhūta* make one *balākṣa*.
Ten *vāraṇa* make one *mahāvāraṇa*;
ten *mahāvāraṇa* make one *asaṃkhyeya*.
Within this numerical system:
The other eight [types of calculation] are forgotten.
If one were to count great kalpas,
they would reach the number of an asaṃkhyeya within this system of calculation.
This is called an "incalculable kalpa.
When these incalculable kalpas are further accumulated to three, it is [called a great incalculable kalpa].
The sūtras state that they are "three incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This does not mean that they cannot be calculated or known;
rather, it is for this reason that they are described as "three incalculable eons."
Question: For what reason do bodhisattvas make vows and practice with diligence for a long period of time before finally aspiring to the fruit of Buddhahood?
Answer: Unsurpassed Bodhi is extremely difficult to attain;
it is not achieved through mere vows and practices alone.
It is impossible for them to attain enlightenment;
a bodhisattva must pass through three incalculable eons,
cultivating the great provisions of merit and wisdom.
Only after practicing the six pāramitās and hundreds of thousands of ascetic austerities will one realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, one must certainly resolve to make vows for a long duration.
Question: If other skillful means can also lead to nirvāṇa, [why is this necessary?]
What is the purpose of a bodhisattva’s long cultivation of ascetic practices?
The answer is: for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, they seek awakening and make aspirations for a long duration.
How may I become fully capable of rescuing all sentient beings from the torrential flood of the ocean of suffering,
and for that purpose, renounce the path to nirvana?
One seeks unsurpassed enlightenment and asks how it benefits oneself when its purpose is to rescue other sentient beings.
Answer: The Bodhisattva saves sentient beings because he fulfills his own compassionate heart;
therefore, he uses it to save others.
This is immediately for one's own benefit.
Question: Who believes that such a thing as this exists regarding a bodhisattva?
Answer: There are those who harbor the intent to benefit themselves, yet lack great compassion;
toward such sentient beings [one should act accordingly].
This matter is indeed difficult to believe: that one who lacks the intention to benefit oneself possesses great compassion toward such sentient beings.
This matter is not difficult to believe for those who have long practiced a lack of pity.
Although it brings no benefit to oneself,
one delights in harming others;
this is something universally known in the world.
In this way, although such a bodhisattva has long practiced compassion and lacks any personal benefit, [they still act].
Yet he delights in benefiting others;
how could one not believe this?
Furthermore, as for this bodhisattva:
Due to the differences in their spiritual lineages (gotra), this aspiration arises:
to regard the suffering of others as one's own suffering,
and to take the happiness of others as one's own happiness.
One does not regard one's own suffering or happiness as matters of personal concern;
nor does one perceive any benefit for oneself as being distinct from the benefit of others.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:

The person of inferior capacity exerts effort and skillful means, constantly seeking their own happiness. The person of middling capacity seeks the cessation of suffering, for happiness is not the basis of suffering. The person of superior capacity constantly and diligently seeks their own suffering and the peace and happiness of others, as well as the eternal cessation of the suffering of others, because they regard others as themselves.
This refers to the "superior person," namely the bodhisattva.
The intended meaning is that the bodhisattva regards others as he regards himself.
Therefore, seeing the happiness of others is itself one's own happiness.
This is the second [point].
Regarding people during the *kalpa* of illumination:
within that period, first there is the appearance of a Buddha or a solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*),
and second, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Regarding the first of the three types of sages who appeared at the beginning of the eon— the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas—
the treatise states:
Thus has the differentiation of the measure of kalpas been explained.
As for the appearance of Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas in the world:
Is it during the period of increase (*vivarta-kalpa*)?
Or is it during the period of decrease (*saṃvarta-kalpa*)?
The verse says:

From eighty thousand years down to one hundred, when the Buddhas appear in the world, it is during the periods of increase and decrease of the Pratyekabuddhas. Regarding the "Rhinoceros-like" [Pratyekabuddha], it is said: "after one hundred kalpas. *Commentary:* When the lifespan of human beings decreases from eighty thousand years down to one hundred years, Buddhas appear in the world. During these periods of both increase and decrease, Pratyekabuddhas appear. Among them, those who are like the rhinoceros (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa) attain enlightenment after cultivating the path for one hundred great kalpas.
From this point, the lifespan of the people of this continent was eighty thousand years;
it gradually decreased until their lifespan reached a minimum of one hundred years.
During this interval, various Buddhas appeared in the world.
Question: For what reason does no Buddha appear during the period of increasing [fortune]?
Answer: Because the pleasure of sentient beings increases.
Because it is difficult to teach them to cultivate revulsion [for cyclic existence]. Question: For what reason does the lifespan decrease to one hundred years when no Buddha appears?
Answer: Because the five corruptions have increased to such an extreme that they are difficult to transform.
As for what are called the "five corruptions":
First, the turbidity of lifespan;
second, the turbidity of the eon;
third, the turbidity of afflictions.
Fourth is the turbidity of views;
fifth is the turbidity of sentient beings.
This occurs when the kalpa is in its final stage of decline.
Because life and so forth are base and inferior,
like dregs and filth,
they are called "turbidities" (kaṣāya).
That is to say, the turbidity of lifespan (āyuṣka-kaṣāya) impairs life;
the turbidity of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya) impairs the necessities of existence; and [the turbidities of] afflictions (kleśa) and views (dṛṣṭi) [impair the spiritual faculties].
It causes the decline of wholesome qualities because,
due to the defilement of afflictions,
one becomes addicted to sensual pleasures.
Due to the turbidity of views,
because of his own ascetic practices;
or due to the turbidity of afflictions.
It impairs the virtues of householders;
or, due to the defilement of views,
it impairs the virtues of those who have gone forth.
If there is turbidity of sentient beings,
it causes the decline and loss of one's own physical stature, complexion, strength,
mindfulness, wisdom, diligence, and valor.
Furthermore, because they are free from illness,
whereas those with many ailments are impaired by their lack of health. Pratyekabuddhas appear throughout both the increasing and decreasing phases of a kalpa.
However, there are two distinct types of pratyekabuddhas:
the first is the group-dweller (vargacārin).
That is to say, there are those who belong to a group;
secondly, there are the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas],
who appear in the world alone.
Like the single horn of a rhinoceros,
the pratyekabuddhas who wander in groups were formerly śrāvakas.
Those who have attained the first three fruits subsequently attain the state of no-more-learning;
they do not awaken through another.
It is renamed "Solitary Victor" (Pratyekabuddha).
Other masters say that he was previously an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Having previously cultivated the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) as a śrāvaka,
he now realized the path for himself and attained the name of a Pratyekabuddha.
It is told in the Itivṛttaka:
On a certain mountain there were five hundred non-Buddhist ascetics practicing austerities,
and there was a monkey.
In the past, he lived in close proximity to a pratyekabuddha and observed his majestic deportment.
Later, the monkey went to the place where the external ascetics were and displayed the majestic demeanor of the pratyekabuddha he had previously seen.
When the various sages beheld this,
they all conceived a sense of reverence and admiration;
in an instant, they all realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
If he were already a sage from the beginning,
he would not need to practice asceticism.
As for the one who is like a rhinoceros horn:
One must cultivate the provisions for enlightenment for one hundred great eons before finally attaining the fruit of the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].
Second, from this point on,
the appearance of the Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is explained.
The treatise states:
When does a Wheel-Turning King appear?

(1) First question: how many kinds? (2) Second question: how many appear together? (3) Third question: what is his majesty? (4) Fourth question: what are his marks? (5) Fifth question. The verse says:
The Wheel-Turning Kings appear when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years or more;
those with wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron rule over one, two, three, or four continents respectively. In reverse order, they are solitary like the Buddha;
others welcome them, they go to them themselves, or they subdue them. They conquer through strife or battle, yet without causing harm.

Does it employ those same great elements that produced the first moment of the unmanifest (avijñapti) to produce subsequent moments,
or does it arise from a separate set of great elements to produce the subsequent moments of the unmanifest?
Answer: According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are three explanations for this.
The first interpretation states:
That is to say, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that produce the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the first moment are used to produce the non-informative matter of subsequent moments.
The second interpretation states:
A separate set of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arises,
which suspends the creation of numerous future non-informative forms (*avijñapti*).
A third explanation states:
At the moment of the first thought,
one gives rise to a multitude of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and projects forward a multitude of future non-informative forms (*avijñapti*).
In each and every moment, the four great elements are produced separately. From this, thirdly,

It is bound exclusively to the desire realm and is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

This untainted precept arises in accordance with the place where the body is born.

that is to say, when one is born in the desire realm and the untainted (anāsrava) state manifests before them.

Regarding this manifest and unmanifest [karma], what is their nature?
Furthermore, to what category do they belong?
The primary elements and their derivatives.
The verse says:
Non-informative matter is non-appropriated, and it is also of the nature of outflow and belongs to the category of sentient beings.

The non-informative [matter] based on the dispersed [atoms] is of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*); it arises from different primary elements and is accompanied by sensation (*sāvedana*). The informative [matter] based on the fixed [atoms] is nurtured (*aupacayika*); it arises from different primary elements and is not accompanied by sensation (*anavedana*).
Non-informative matter belongs solely to the nature of outflow; when it pertains to the body, it is possessed of appropriation (*upātta*).
The commentary states:
The first six phrases clarify the categories of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which they depend.
The latter two phrases clarify the informative [matter] and its categories, as well as the primary elements upon which it relies. Regarding "unmanifest [matter] is non-appropriated":
this means that unmanifest matter is not grasped by consciousness.
Whether in a state of meditative concentration or in a distracted state,
all non-informative matter (avijñapti) lacks the quality of resistance or obstruction (apratigha).
That which is called "unappropriated" and is also a "homogeneous outflow of sentient beings" refers to non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
It arises from a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) and is of the nature of outflow (niṣyanda).
The word "also" indicates that this [homogeneous cause] exists momentarily (kṣaṇika).
This refers to the non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) that is concomitant with the path and co-arises with the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti),
because it is not a result of outflow (naiṣyandika).
Regarding the statement that "names have moments" and "sentient things are enumerated":
furthermore, this unmanifest [form] arises based on the internal body and is included within the category of sentient beings;
as for the scattered [unmanifest], it arises from the nature of outflow (niṣyanda) and is produced by distinct primary elements (mahābhūta) associated with sensation.
This clarifies the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) depends.
"Dissociated" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
specifically the non-informative matter of the Prātimokṣa vows.
The "basis" refers to the unmanifest [form] and its supporting primary elements;
these are the primary elements of the distracted state.
It arises from a homogeneous cause and is exclusively of the nature of an outflow.
Furthermore, these primary elements—
Because it is the fruit of a distracted mind,
it is called "appropriated" (upātta);
it must necessarily possess the mind of attachment.
Because it is grasped as its own substance,
there is the statement that it arises from the "appropriated" (upātta) great elements;
this indicates the sevenfold non-informative matter (avijñapti), namely the three bodily and four vocal [paths of action].
Each is distinct and individually composed of the four great elements;
when the seven branches are dispersed and mutually related to one another.
Because they do not share a single fruit,
these seven factors each have their own distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
"Those great elements born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja*), which are nourished (*aupacayika*), without sensation (*anupātta*),

and undifferentiated (*aviśiṣṭa*)," clarifies the great elements upon which the unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) born of meditative concentration depends. This refers to the unmanifest karma born of meditative concentration.
There are two kinds in total:
namely, the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts. These two are non-informative (avijñapti).
The primary elements that serve as its basis are exclusively of the nature of nurturance (*aupacayika*),
because while in meditative concentration, one is necessarily able to nurture the four great elements.

The primary elements (mahābhūta) born of meditative concentration are exclusively of a nourishing nature (*aupacayika*). Furthermore, these primary elements of concentration are non-appropriated (*anupātta*),
because during the state of meditative equipoise, they are not grasped by consciousness.
It is certainly not the case that a mind possessing affection grasps these primary elements as its internal self;
for there are no unappropriated primary elements that are distinct [from those that are].
This demonstrates that the seven branches of the non-manifest (avijñapti) of meditative concentration are produced by the same four primary elements (mahābhūta),
because these primary elements coexist with the mind of concentration.
Because the concentrated mind is unitary,
these primary elements (mahābhūta) likewise possess only one [characteristic].
Furthermore, these seven branches,
when viewed in relation to one another,
share a single fruit.
There is no difference in their being derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). As for the statement that informative matter (*vijñapti*) is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*),
this refers to the bodily and vocal informative matter.
Arising from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
it is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*);
it belongs to the body and is appropriated (*upātta*).
Among these, bodily intimation is termed "appropriated" because it belongs to the body.
Because vocal intimation does not belong to the body,
it is without appropriation (anupātta).
Nevertheless, there are newly arisen derivative primary elements (bhūta) that pervade the parts of the body.
One performs manifest karma,
yet does not destroy the original body,
nor does the body become larger.
The maturation [result] is porous;
because it has interstices,
they are able to accommodate one another.
From this second [section] onward,
the nature, realm, and stage are elucidated.

The treatise states:
"The distinctions between the two, three, and five categories within the section on karma have already been analyzed."
Regarding the distinctions of these natures, realms, and stages,
the verse says:
There are no informative [karmas] in the other three realms; the unwholesome exists only in the desire realm.
Non-informative [karma] is present throughout the desire and form realms. Informative [karma] exists only in the two levels that possess sustained thought (*vicāra*).
In the desire realm, there is no obscured-unwholesome informative [karma], because it lacks a motivating cause (*samutthāna*).
The commentary states:
Regarding "the absence of designation and the other three," these are the distinctions of the three natures.
That is to say, non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) does not extend to the indeterminate;
it possesses only the nature of the wholesome or the unwholesome.
Therefore, it is called "informative speech" (*vijñapti-vāk*).
The remainder refers to manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) and mental volition (*cetanā*).
All [three types of action] pertain to the three natures.
Question: For what reason does non-informative action (avijñapti) not pertain to the indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
The answer is that because the power of an indeterminate mind is weak and inferior,
it cannot induce a strong non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*).
Since the fruit may continue to arise even when [the cause] is undergoing cessation,
non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Unwholesome [karma] exists only in the desire realm;
it consists of non-informative action (avijñapti), informative action (vijñapti), and volition (cetanā). Among these, it is unwholesome.
It exists only in the desire realm;
it is both wholesome and indeterminate,
and is present in all stages.
"Non-manifest [form] (avijñapti) pervades the desire and form realms" means that this clarifies non-manifest form does not extend to the formless realm,
because the great elements (mahābhūta) do not exist in the formless realm.
Since the primary elements (mahābhūta) do not exist,
how could there be non-informative matter (avijñapti)?
Furthermore, there are [only] body and speech.
Only then does restraint exist;
within the formless realm,
there is no activity of body or speech.
Therefore, there is no restraint.
Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika masters speak as follows:
Śīla arises in order to counteract immoral conduct;
it exists only within the realm of desire.
There are various forms of unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*). Formless states are distant from the desire realm in four ways:
first, by way of their basis (*āśraya-viprakarṣa*).
Second, remoteness of aspect;
third, remoteness of object;
fourth, remoteness of antidote.
Therefore, within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there is no non-informative matter (avijñaptirūpa); as for informative matter (vijñapti), it exists only in the two [lower realms] where there is sustained thought (vicāra).
The desire realm and the first dhyāna are called "possessing vitarka and vicāra.
Informative matter exists only within the stages possessing vitarka and vicāra.
Only when there is vitarka and vicāra can [speech] be manifested.
From the second dhyāna upward, [this is no longer the case].
Because there is an absence of vitarka and vicāra,
there is no non-informative karma (avijñapti-karma).
As for the claim that in the desire realm there is no obscured-neutral informative karma (nivṛtāvyākṛta-vijñapti), it is because such karma lacks a motivating cause (samutthāna).
This clarifies that obscured manifest karma exists only in the first dhyāna. Now,
when discussing manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*), it is analyzed in terms of the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*).
By this, good and evil are distinguished.
As for "co-arising" (samutthāna),
it refers to that which can give rise to the mind.
Because within the desire realm there is no obscured mind capable of manifesting informative action (*vijñapti-karman*),
there is no obscured informative [action].
It does not exist in the desire realm.
Although the two views of self-identity and extremes do exist in the desire realm,
they are associated with an obscured mind.
This is abandoned by insight and cannot initiate karma.
Now, that which initiates karma—
It is abandoned solely through cultivation.
Question: What is meant by "obscured manifest karma" (āvṛta-vijñapti-karman) of the first dhyāna?
Answer: It is as when the Great Brahmā King [spoke] to Aśvajit.
When one gives rise to a mind of flattery and deception and initiates bodily or vocal karma,
it is called "obscured manifest action."
The treatise says:
Furthermore, for what reason [do these states] exist from the second dhyāna upward?
There is no non-informative action (avijñapti-karman) whatsoever; in the desire realm, there is no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) informative action,
because there is no motivating mind that initiates such action.
Only a mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra is capable of initiating karma;
this is not the case from the two higher meditative attainments upward.
There is absolutely no such mind.
Furthermore, the manifest mind is severed only by cultivation.
Because the afflictions to be abandoned by insight operate within the internal [mental] door,
this is so within the desire realm.
It is certain that there are no obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) afflictions abandoned through cultivation; therefore,
[this applies to] manifest karma (vijñapti-karman).
The three higher realms are entirely devoid of them.
Regarding the fact that there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) in the desire realm, one may understand this by reflecting upon the preceding treatise.

The verse says:
Ultimate goodness is liberation; its intrinsic nature consists of shame, dread, and the faculties.

Associated with that, associated therewith, and co-arising—such as material action (rūpa-karma) and so forth—are the opposites of these [wholesome factors] and are thus termed unwholesome (akuśala). The two [types of] superior indeterminate (avyākṛta) and the two constants [space and cessation] are explained as follows:
[the commentary states:]...
Regarding "supreme, ultimate liberation":
nirvāṇa is called liberation because within nirvāṇa...
It is the ultimate peace and security;
all sufferings are utterly stilled,
just like being free from illness.
This is wholesome and eternal;
therefore, it is called "supreme.
This is because it possesses substantial reality.
Furthermore, it is called "meaning" (artha);
therefore, this nirvana is termed "ultimate goodness" (paramārtha-kuśala).
Regarding the faculties of natural shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*):
"faculties" refers to the three wholesome roots, namely non-attachment and so forth,
as well as the two, shame and dread of blame.
These five dharmas are wholesome by nature,
just like excellent medicine.
Regarding "that which is associated with what is wholesome by nature":
the former "association" is the heading,
while the latter "association" is the explanation.
That is to say, those preceding [states], such as non-attachment and so forth,
along with the other minds and mental factors,
are by their very nature not wholesome.
Being associated with that,
one obtains the designation "wholesome";
this is called "wholesome by association."
Regarding the phrase "like water mixed with various medicines" and so forth:
"formative action of form" refers to the manifest and unmanifest actions of body and speech, and so on.
This includes the four characteristics and acquisition within the category of dissociated factors,
as well as the two mindless attainments;
these are the various dharmas [referred to].
It is called "virtuous by designation" because it is virtuous by intrinsic nature and by association.
It receives the designation "wholesome" because it is originated by that [wholesome state],
just as milk produced by the infusion of a potent medicinal decoction [is so named].
To reverse these, they are called unwholesome;
reversing these four wholesome states,
one establishes the four unwholesome ones.
Ultimate unwholesomeness refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra; it is by virtue of these saṃsāric phenomena [that they are so designated].
Suffering is its intrinsic nature;
it is utterly unstable,
like a chronic illness.
Inherently unwholesome refers to shamelessness, lack of remorse,
greed, hatred, and so forth.
The three unwholesome roots are by nature unwholesome,
just like poisonous medicine.
Associated unwholesome [factors]:
with the exception of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and so forth,
they are the remaining mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Only when associated with such factors as shamelessness and lack of dread does it receive the designation "unwholesome," like water mixed with poison.
Unwholesome by way of origination refers to bodily and vocal actions among the dissociated [factors].
The four characteristics and acquisition are unwholesome by virtue of being associated with that intrinsic nature and being originated by it;
they are like milk produced from a poisonous decoction.
Regarding "the two eternalities that are superior and indeterminate":
these are the ultimate indeterminate,
namely space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The second is the eternal dharma. Because it is eternal,
it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Because it is not realized through the Path,
it is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
In reality, however, it is a conditioned indeterminate.
This is called "indeterminate by nature" (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*).
This treatise does not discuss it in detail;
it is fully explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
It should be understood that among the indeterminate (avyākṛta) states, there is no indeterminate arising through association (samprayoga-samutthāna).
Question: If it is by the power of arising...
It causes bodily and vocal actions to become wholesome or unwholesome;
furthermore, the great elements capable of producing these very actions also arise as their co-emergent motivation.
Why are the great elements (mahābhūta) exclusively of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta)?
Answer: Because the agent’s mind originally intended to initiate action.
Since they are not the four great elements,
the analogy does not hold.

To clarify the meaning of "origination" (*samutthāna*),

As stated above, the afflictions abandoned through seeing cannot manifest bodily expression.
If that is so, for what reason does the Sūtra state that one gives rise to wrong intention by means of wrong view?
Regarding "wrong speech," "wrong action," and "wrong livelihood," the commentary explains as follows:
It is wrong view.
Since this is an affliction abandoned through seeing,
it arises from wrong view.
If one asks, "How can the delusions of view give rise to wrong speech and so forth?"—
this is the general answer that shows there is no contradiction.
For what reason is this investigated?
The verse says:

This should be understood according to the sequence: The term "active" (*pravartaka*) and the term "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*) apply as follows:
Consciousness abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is exclusively active; The five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are exclusively concomitant;
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertains to both; That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and that which is maturation (*vipāka*) are neither.
Regarding the transformation into virtuous and other natures, each corresponding transformation may admit three types of *muni*;
the virtuous must be identical. The indeterminate may correspond to either [virtue] or virtue itself. Commentary:
The first stanza explains the two types of origination;
the second stanza [explains the same].
The subsequent single verse explains the distinctions with respect to the six consciousnesses.
The distinction between similarities and differences is made by way of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). "There are two kinds of origination" is the heading.
The origination of informative and non-informative matter is of two kinds:
that which is caused and that which occurs at that very moment.
This is the enumeration of names:
first, simultaneous motivation (*sahaja-samutthāna*);
second, momentary motivation (*kṣaṇika-samutthāna*).
The thought prior to the initiation of karma is called the "causative motivation" (*hetu-samutthāna*),
because it exists beforehand as the cause; [then there is] the thought concurrent with the karma.
It is called "simultaneous origination" because it occurs at the same moment.
Just as it should be understood that [the mind] is termed "arising" and "concomitant," the cause—
the originating mind— is likewise so designated.

meaning that it is able to transform karma;

Because it can induce [the action] at the time of performing it, momentary origination (kṣaṇasamutthāna) is called "concomitant" (anuvartaka).
This means that it evolves in accordance with karma;
because it is not dissociated from the consciousness at the very moment of performing an action, the consciousness to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-vijñāna) evolves alone.
The following four lines provide an analysis;
this is the first line. It refers to consciousness abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya-vijñāna*).
They can only function as a turning force;
they serve merely as remote causes that assist the mind of vitarka and vicāra.
It can initiate informative action (*vijñapti*),
but it does not function as a concomitant (*anuvartaka*) with respect to a mind directed toward external objects.
At the moment of the actual arising of the action,
because that which is abandoned by seeing does not exist, "those directed toward the external" refers to those abandoned by cultivation, namely the five consciousnesses that merely follow along;
this is the second phrase.
This refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness;
because they are devoid of conceptual discrimination,
they are incapable of acting as a turning agent.
Because it arises from the external doors,
it can function as a concomitant transformation;
the mental consciousness that is abandoned through cultivation applies to both.
This clarifies the "concordant" category.
Because consciousness abandoned through cultivation involves conceptual discrimination.
And it is able to act as the primary mover;
because it arises through the external gateway,
it also acts as the secondary mover.
The phrase "neither outflow-free nor resultant" refers to that which is neither;

because they exist only within meditative concentration.
It cannot initiate karma;

If it is a ripening mind (*vipākacitta*), [it is likewise].
Because it arises spontaneously,

Regarding the statement that "in the case of the transformation [of the mind] into the wholesome and so forth, the corresponding transformation (anuvartaka) may each be of three types," this clarifies that the natures of the transforming and the corresponding transformations differ. As for "the wholesome and so forth":
[this refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral natures].
This includes both the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
Third is the three natures,
which refers to the transforming mind.
If it is wholesome,
the subsequent mind may be of any of the three natures; this refers to the evolving mind.
If it does not follow along with what is unwholesome,
it may also be of the three natures;
if the turning mind is neutral (avyākṛta), [the same applies].
The statement that "the subsequent transformation may also admit the three natures,
while the Sage’s wholesome [states] must be identical" clarifies the Buddha-mind.
That is to say, when the Buddha’s mind undergoes a transformation, if it is of a virtuous nature,
the subsequent conforming mind [is likewise].
It must also necessarily be wholesome;
therefore, it is said that they are necessarily the same.
As for the indeterminate, it follows whichever [state] is wholesome.
The Buddha’s mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If it were a primary motivating mind (*maulacitta*), then its corresponding derivative mind (*anuvartakacitta*)—
It is either of a wholesome nature or it also extends to the indeterminate;
therefore, the word "or" is used.
This is because when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, teaches the Dharma,
his mind either increases or remains without withering or ceasing.
Therefore, the indeterminate evolving mind can be accompanied by a wholesome concomitant mind;
this is what is meant when it is said that the Buddha possesses an indeterminate mind.
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
it is accepted that the Buddha possesses both resultant and supernormal (abhijñā) consciousnesses.
Regarding deportment,
there are three types of neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
This is according to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
