At what time are the precepts generated? This is the inquiry of the Sautrāntika school, following the preceding treatise.
The verse says:
"Declaring oneself a lay follower (upāsaka) brings forth the precepts"—this is explained as being "like that of a bhikṣu and others.
Regarding the phrase "declaring oneself a lay follower brings forth the precepts": [it means that by making this declaration, the precepts are generated].
The answer is: at the time of generating the precepts.
In the Mahānāma-sūtra, the term "upāsaka" (lay follower) is used.
At this time, the precepts are generated.
As the Sūtra says:
"I declare myself to be an upāsaka; may the Venerable One remember me as such."
Out of compassion and protective mindfulness,
he then took the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
uttering the words "lay follower" and so forth.
Because one has given rise to the vow of restraint,
the original mind seeking the precepts intended to receive the five precepts.
Therefore, having received the three refuges, one immediately undertakes the five precepts;
as the Sūtra further states: "From this day forward, I..."
This is the intended meaning of this sutra, because it speaks of "casting off birth" until the end of life.
It speaks of abandoning killing and so forth;
it omits "killing" and the like,
and speaks only of abandoning [taking] life.
Therefore, as previously stated,
one has already undertaken the five precepts;
regarding the phrase "as in the case of a bhikṣu," etc.:
This provides an illustration to explain and establish the point.
"Teaching" refers to the scriptural teachings on abandoning killing and so forth,
such as those concerning a bhikṣu.
When the one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) are completed, the bhikṣu precepts are generated.
The subsequent explanation of the four grave rules of training (*catur-guru-dharma-śikṣāpada*) is intended to cause them to recognize their characteristics and maintain them firmly.
The same applies to the lay follower's precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*):
having first received the three refuges,
one generates the lay follower's precepts.
The subsequent explanations regarding the relinquishing of life and so forth are intended to cause the characteristics of consciousness to be firmly maintained; therefore,
they are called "near-attendants" (*upāsaka*).
One must certainly possess the restraint.
From this second assembly, the sutra text continues;
the verse says:
If all [vows] are fully endowed with the restraint (*saṃvara*), why speak of "one part" and so forth?

This refers to the explanation based on the capacity to maintain [the vows]. Regarding this, the first two lines [of the verse state]: [The commentary explains: "Regarding this, the first two lines..."
The citation of the sutra presents a challenge;
the final phrase provides a comprehensive explanation.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"Only if one possesses the restraint (saṃvara) is one called an upāsaka."
For what reason did the Blessed One say there are four types? First,
one who can train in a single portion, namely, a single precept.
Second, those capable of training in a small portion, namely the two precepts;
third, those capable of training in a large portion, namely the three or four precepts;
fourth, those capable of training in the complete portion, namely the five precepts.
This refers to the explanation based on the capacity to uphold [the precepts],
which is the interpretation according to the established tenets (siddhānta). In reality, however, it is a lay follower (upāsaka).
One must possess the five precepts;
that is to say, regarding the ability to uphold them,
one speaks of "a single portion" and so forth.
Because it is able to maintain what was previously received,
the term "able to train" is used;
otherwise, [it would not].
One should say that it is "one part of feeling" and so forth.
Since the sutra does not state "one part of feeling" and so forth,
it is clear that this refers to the capacity for training.
Speaking in terms of what can be maintained,
this third section clarifies the three grades of precepts.
The treatise states:
"All these vows of restraint, such as those of the upāsaka and so forth."
By what cause are the inferior, middling, and superior grades attained?
The verse says:
"Inferior, middling, and superior follow the mind. The commentary says:
If one receives the precepts with a superior-grade mind,
one obtains superior-grade precepts;
this continues down to receiving them with an inferior-grade mind.
One attains the lower grade of precepts;
thus, the precepts follow the mind and are distinguished into three grades.
For this reason,
there may be some arhats who possess only the lower grade of precepts.
Ordinary beings produce the superior grade of precepts.
Following this, the fourth section clarifies the essence of the Three Refuges.
The treatise says:
"Regarding all those who take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—
what is it that they take refuge in?"
The verse says:
Taking refuge in the Buddha, the Sangha, and the two kinds of dharmas of the Aśaikṣa,
as well as nirvāṇa which is analytical cessation— this is called being fully endowed with the three refuges.
The commentary states:
"One who takes refuge in the Buddha does not take refuge in the Buddha's physical body."
One takes refuge only in the dharmas of no-more-learning that constitute Buddhahood,
because it is by means of these dharmas of no-more-learning that one becomes a Buddha.
Furthermore, the Buddha has attained the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*), because these are preeminent.
Moreover, the Buddha has attained the dharmas of one beyond training.
Because it is able to awaken all [beings], by virtue of these three meanings,
it is the refuge. As for the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*),
they are said to be within the body of the Buddha.
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising have the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) as their essence. As for taking refuge in the Saṃgha,
it means taking refuge in the two kinds of dharmas that constitute the Saṃgha.
These are the so-called dharmas of training and the dharmas beyond training;
these two kinds of dharmas.
Because it is that which can bring about the Sangha of the four paths and four fruits,
one takes refuge in it.
As for taking refuge in the Dharma:
One takes refuge solely in nirvana;
nirvana is precisely cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Within the bodies of all sentient beings...
The analytical cessation that is realized is wholesome and eternal,
because it has the single characteristic of quiescent extinction.
Regarding the general refuge: according to the author of the treatise,
one who takes refuge in the Buddha does not merely take refuge in the Buddha’s dharmas of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣadharma*).
They also take refuge in the Buddha-body;
for by harming the birth-body,
they commit the offense of immediate retribution.
Therefore, one should know that the Buddha’s body is also the true essence of the Buddha;
thus, one must take refuge.
As for taking refuge in the Sangha:
It is also included within the refuge in the Saṃgha, because the body upon which it relies is that of a bhikṣu; therefore,
it is universally subsumed under the refuge.
This act of taking refuge has vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) as its essence.
Question: What is one who takes refuge?
What is its meaning?
The answer is: it has the meaning of providing relief, because one takes refuge in the Three Jewels.
Because it liberates one from suffering.
As the Blessed One said:
"All people are oppressed by fear."

"Many refuges" refers to the names of various mountain deities; "gardens and groves" likewise refers to the names of their deities; and "solitary trees and *caityas*" refers to the deities of solitary trees—where *caitya* denotes a non-Buddhist shrine.
This refuge is not supreme;
this refuge is not noble. By means of this refuge, one does not [attain liberation].
Those who take refuge in the Buddha, as well as those who take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha, will be able to liberate themselves from all suffering.
Within the Four Noble Truths, one constantly observes with wisdom:
knowing the truth of suffering as suffering; knowing the truth of the origin of suffering as the origin; knowing the permanent transcendence of all suffering;
and knowing the Eightfold Noble Path as the truth of the path.
The Truth of Cessation, which is the secure Nirvana—
this refuge is supreme; this refuge is most venerable.
One must take refuge through this;
it can liberate one from all sufferings.
Therefore, one takes refuge.
This serves as a gateway of skillful means for all places where one undertakes the vows of restraint;
following this is the fifth [chapter].
This clarifies the departure from misconduct.
The treatise asks:
For what reason did the World-Honored One, in other instances of restraint, [not mention it]?
Regarding the establishment of the abstention from unchaste conduct,
within the single code of discipline for a lay follower (*upāsaka*),
it is prescribed that one must abstain from sexual misconduct; that is, one who abstains from sexual misconduct.
One does not engage with one's own wife at an improper time. The verse says:
"Sexual misconduct is most censurable; it is easy to abandon and to attain non-doing.
The commentary says:
There are three reasons for this:
first, sexual misconduct is the most censurable of all desires.
Because it involves violating another's wife and because it leads to rebirth in the evil destinies,
it is not non-celibacy.
Second, because it is easy to distance oneself from;
that is to say, it is easy to distance oneself from misconduct,
whereas those living at home are addicted to sensual desires.
Regarding the abstention from unchaste conduct:
because it is difficult [to maintain], the abstention from unchaste conduct is not prescribed [as a formal precept].
This is because one attains the three types of non-doing.
This refers to the fact that all noble ones are determined never to engage in sexual misconduct.
They attain the restraint of non-action;
as noble ones who have undergone rebirth,
they are perfected in natural morality (*śīla*).
Even though many lifetimes may pass,
because one does not commit an offense,
one remains free from unchaste conduct.
This is not the case;
for it refers to the first two types of noble ones,
who possess their own wives.
There is non-celibate conduct;
because of the three aforementioned causes,
one is therefore a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
One must restrain from sexual misconduct.
Otherwise, a noble one (ārya) would have to undergo rebirth and would violate the lay follower’s precepts (upāsaka-śīla).
Because one has one's own wife,
this sixth section clarifies that taking a wife does not constitute an offense.
The treatise says:
"There are those who first receive the upāsaka vows and subsequently take a wife or concubines."
Regarding those wives and concubines,
it need not be asked whether they obtained the restraint at the time they first received the precepts.
In reality, it should be so;
do not answer that one obtains the prātimokṣa restraint with respect to only a portion [of beings].
If that is so, how is it? It is not difficult for the latter to violate the precepts.
The verse says:
"One acquires the restraint according to one's vow; it is not [acquired] universally throughout the continuum.
Regarding this, the commentary states:
"One acquires the restraint according to one's vow."
One obtains the restraint (saṃvara) according to the original vow one undertook.
The original vow states:
I vow to abandon the transgression of sexual misconduct toward all sentient beings;
this does not apply to my own mental continuum as a whole.
This means that by vowing not to speak of oneself as having abandoned unchaste conduct throughout the entire continuum of all sentient beings,
one obtains the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct toward those beings.
One must not abandon the precept against unchaste conduct;
therefore, taking a wife or concubine later does not constitute a transgression of that prior precept.
From this, the seventh [topic] clarifies the avoidance of false speech.
The treatise states:
For what reason is it that only the abstention from false speech is prescribed as the lay follower's precept, rather than the abstention from divisive speech and the others?
This is also due to the three causes previously mentioned;
namely, that false speech is the most censurable of all.
Because it is easy for householders to distance themselves from [worldly attachments],
all noble ones [attain this].
Because it is attained through non-action.
Furthermore, there is another reason.
The verse says:
"By opening the way for false speech, one thereby transgresses all rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
The commentary explains:
"Rules of training" is a name for ethical discipline (*śīla*). It is called a "rule of training" because it is that which is to be trained in.
Because it is that which one ought to train in.
To "transgress" means to violate; if one utters deceptive speech, one then transgresses the training rule.
When being interrogated,
regarding the precept they have transgressed,
they immediately say, "I did not do it."
Consequently, they frequently transgress the precepts; therefore, the Buddha,
wishing to cause them to uphold them firmly, [established this rule].
In all codes of discipline,
false speech is prohibited;
this is the eighth [precept] from here.
This clarifies the abstention from drinking alcohol.
The treatise asks:
For what reason, among those various prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*), [is this specifically addressed]?
There is no prohibition against abstaining from other [vices];
only the drinking of alcohol is forbidden.
The verse says:
Among the prohibitions, one abstains only from alcohol; this is for the sake of protecting the other vows.
[The commentary] states: although the prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*) are many, [one abstains only from alcohol].
Excessive drinking: this refers to those who drink alcohol,
whose minds become largely dissolute and negligent.
One will inevitably violate the code of discipline;
therefore, to protect that discipline,
the drinking of alcohol is prohibited.
There is no fixed measure for alcohol;
even a small amount can cause intoxication.
Therefore, the Buddha strictly prohibited it.
Even drinking as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of grass is not permitted;
although drinking alcohol is not an intrinsic transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), the Buddha prohibited it and forbade its consumption.
Because one incurs an offense by transgressing a prohibition,
it is called a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*),
such as killing living beings and so forth.
Before the precepts were established,
the Noble Ones certainly did not transgress them;
therefore, it is called a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Because its nature is that of a transgression;
furthermore, the characteristic of a natural transgression consists solely in action performed with a defiled mind.
Drinking alcohol for the purpose of treating illness is permitted provided one has no defiled mind, so long as it is not done for the sake of intoxication or disorder.
Therefore, it is not an intrinsic transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Main Text, Volume 14 (13);
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Main Text, Volume 15.

This is the fifth major section, which clarifies the distinctions regarding the attainment of the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*). Within this, first, it clarifies the similarities and differences regarding the place and time of attainment;
second, it clarifies the sentient beings, the factors (*aṅga*), and the causes; third, it clarifies the attainment of the restraints for evil places and intermediate states.
Below this, first is the clarification of the similarities and differences regarding the place and time of attainment.
The treatise says:
"This distinct prātimokṣa..."
From the dhyāna and untainted [samādhis],
one obtains one of the three types of restraint.
Can one also obtain the other two? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
From all [three] and from two [types of action], one obtains the restraint of the desire realm;
from the fundamental [action] at all times, one obtains the meditative and the outflow-free [restraints]. Commentary:
The first two lines clarify the attainment of the Prātimokṣa vows;
the latter two lines...
This explains the morality of the path of attaining clarity (*ālokalabdha-mārga-śīla*).
Regarding those who obtain the restraint of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-saṃvara*) from all [aspects] and both [types of] manifestation:
first, it is obtained from all [aspects].
One obtains the restraint of desire (kāmadhātu-saṃvara) in two ways; second, one obtains the restraint of the desire realm from two [sources];
third, one obtains the restraint of desire from the present.
"From all" refers to the fundamental courses of action,
as well as the preliminary and concluding phases.
This source from which offenses arise is called "all," namely, the Prātimokṣa.
Because one is free from the root offenses as well as the preliminary and subsequent offenses,
one obtains the Prātimokṣa vows regarding all bases for the arousal of evil.
Regarding "obtaining from two":
"two" refers to two categories.
The first is the category of sentient beings.
There are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). "Natural" refers to such acts as taking life;
"prohibited" refers to such acts as staying overnight with women.
The second category consists of non-sentient things; these include both natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
"Natural" refers, for example, to stealing external property.
Prohibited actions refer to such things as digging the earth and so forth.
Now, by undertaking the virtuous precepts,
one is able to abstain from both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Therefore, one obtains the Prātimokṣa vows from two types of occasions for the arising of offenses.
Third, those obtained from the present.
The treatise states:
"It is acquired from the present aggregates, bases, and elements,
not from those of the past or future."
This means that this restraint operates with respect to sentient beings;
since the past and future are not states of sentient beings, [the restraint does not apply to them]. Thus it is explained.
Regarding "the locus of sentient beings":
first, the sentient being;
second, the locus of the sentient being.
There are two kinds of locations:
first, the locus of support;
second, the locus of abiding.
By abstaining from sexual misconduct,
one generates the precept with respect to the protection of sentient beings;
likewise, if one abstains from taking life.
Precepts are generated with respect to the physical bases of sentient beings;

if one does not dig the earth, precepts are generated with respect to the dwellings of sentient beings. One obtains meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) states at all times from their very roots.
First, the meditative and untainted precepts are obtained from the fundamental [attainment];
second, the meditative and untainted precepts are obtained from constant time.
Regarding "from the fundamental":
That is to say, from the point of the fundamental paths of action,
one attains the restraint of the meditative path;
these two restraints [are as follows].
Within the state of meditative concentration,
there is only the fundamental [concentration]; before and after the concentration, it does not exist.
Because these types of restraint do not exist,
there are no stages of preliminary application (*prayoga*) or subsequent completion (*pṛṣṭha*).
This is because the restraints of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the path (*mārga-saṃvara*) consist solely of the fundamental [action].
Therefore, when receiving the precepts,
they are obtained only with respect to the fundamental points of misconduct.
Because it is possible for the Prātimokṣa vows to exist both during the preparatory stage and the subsequent stage.
Therefore, the precepts are obtained in all three instances.
The Treatise says:
If one attains the meditative absorption (dhyāna) or the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara),
it should be understood that this arises only from the fundamental courses of action (mūla-karmapatha),
and not even from their preliminary (prayoga) or subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages.

Furthermore, regarding the treatise on [the precepts] from the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*) upward: second, "obtained at all times" means that "all times" refers to the three periods of time. That is to say, the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the restraint of the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*) are obtained from the three periods of time.
Because the morality of the path of meditative concentration functions together with the mind;
that is to say, the mind conjoined with morality can take the three periods of time as its object.
Therefore, the morality concomitant with the mind also prevents [unwholesome actions] of the three periods of time.
Based on the distinctions mentioned above, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). As for the first proposition:
This means that one obtains the prātimokṣa vows from the present preparatory acts, the subsequent acts, and all prohibited offenses,
because they belong to the present and because they constitute the preparatory acts and so forth.
One does not obtain the precepts of the fixed path. As for the second phrase,
it means that because one follows the fundamental paths of action of the past and future through their very foundation,
one obtains the precepts of the fixed path.

Because they belong to the past and the future, one cannot obtain the Prātimokṣa precepts [from them]. As for the third phrase, it refers to obtaining them from the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) of the present, because they belong to the present.
One obtains the prātimokṣa precepts because they are the foundation;
one also obtains the dhyāna and the path precepts. As for the fourth phrase:
This means that because the preparatory and subsequent stages belong to the past or the future,
there is no separate prātimokṣa-śīla [in those states], since they are merely the preparatory and subsequent stages of that [present] discipline.
There is no fixed path-restraint (*niyama-śīla*). Furthermore, the treatise states:

"It is not the case that at the very moment one correctly attains the wholesome restraint (*kuśala-saṃvara*), there can be definitively present unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*) and so forth."
Therefore, one should say that it is obtained from the present basis.
In reality, however, one should say that it protects the future.
It certainly should not be said that it protects the past or the present. The explanation is as follows:
This passage is the Master of the Treatise refuting the first phrase of the third preceding [position].
This refers to having correctly attained virtuous discipline;
how could there be unwholesome courses of action and so forth in the present life?
This includes the first phrase,
as well as the preparatory and subsequent stages, and the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Having refuted [the objection], he speaks correctly:
"Therefore, it should be said that [the fruit] is obtained from the present state.
The meaning of this is as follows:
In the first and third phrases,
the character "place" (處) should be added;
in this sense, there is no contradiction.
This means that although the substantial entities of the paths of action and so forth do not exist in the present,
there are still bases for the initiation of such karma;
therefore, with respect to the paths of action and their bases:
There is no contradiction in the meaning of "arousing the precepts. If one discusses the arousal of the precepts, it may pertain to all three periods of time;
however, in terms of the principle of preventing transgressions, they should logically pertain to the future.
Because it prevents [the future] from arising;
the past has already ceased,
and the present has already arisen.
It cannot be prevented.
From this second point onward,
the causes of the factors constituting sentient beings are clarified.
The treatise says:
"All those who obtain discipline (*saṃvara*) or non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) do so with respect to all sentient beings,
all factors (*aṅga*), and all causes (*hetu*)."
Is there a difference?
There is certainly a difference in this case.
What is the nature of this difference?
The verse says:
Discipline arises from sentient beings; It is said to be indefinite regarding its factors and causes.
Non-discipline arises from all sentient beings; It is not indefinite regarding its factors or causes.
The commentary states:
"The Vinaya originates from all sentient beings" means it originates from every single sentient being.
Because it is through the arousal of the vow of restraint (*saṃvara*). One arouses the vow of restraint only by abiding in a state of benevolent intention toward all sentient beings.
If they were different, this would not be the case,
because the underlying disposition toward evil would not have been entirely extinguished.
As for the statement that the causal factors are indeterminate:
"Limbs" refers to the seven limbs.
"Cause" refers to the mind that receives the precepts. Regarding the "indefinite limbs":
there are those who obtain [the precepts] from all the limbs, namely the bhikṣu-precepts; and there are those who obtain them from four limbs.
Regarding the statement that the morality of those such as the *pravrajita* (renunciants) has indeterminate causes:
this means that because the inferior, middling, and superior minds do not arise simultaneously, there may be cases where one abides in morality that is not caused by all [three grades of mind].
That is to say, whether with an inferior,
middling, or superior mind,
one receives the vows of an upavāsastha, an upāsaka, or a śrāmaṇera.
Or there may be one who abides in the precepts by means of all causes;
that is to say, having received the lay devotee’s precepts with an inferior mind, they subsequently give rise to a medium mind and receive the śrāmaṇera precepts.
Thereafter, he gave rise to the superior mind and received the bhikṣu precepts;
thus he was endowed with these three minds.
It is called "the cause of all.
The treatise says:
"If a person does not establish five kinds of fixed limitations..."
Only then can one receive the Prātimokṣa vows.
This refers to the determination regarding sentient beings, the factors, the locations, the time, and the conditions; specifically, the determination regarding sentient beings means thinking:
"I [shall refrain] only with respect to certain types of sentient beings."
One should abstain from killing and so forth.
Regarding the determination of the factors (*aṅga*), one reflects: "I shall observe only this particular factor of the vow."
One is able to maintain [the precepts] without transgression.
Regarding "certainty of place," it means thinking:
"I shall [abstain] only within that particular category and region."
One should abstain from killing and so forth.
Regarding the "fixed time," it means one thinks:
"I shall [abstain] only at a specific time, such as on a certain day or month."
One is able to abstain from killing and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "conditioned by specific circumstances," it means: "I shall abstain except in the case of circumstances such as combat."
One is able to abstain from killing and so forth;
however, if one undertakes these as five fixed limitations,
one does not obtain the restraint (saṃvara).
One merely attains a semblance of the sublime conduct (*sucarita*) that corresponds to restraint;
as for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), it arises from all sentient beings and all factors, but not from causes.
This refers to non-restraint.
It is acquired with respect to all sentient beings,
because the mind intends to kill all sentient beings;
it is acquired with respect to all constituent parts.
This refers to non-restraint,
which possesses all its constituent parts:
the three of body and the four of speech.
Because all have committed evil.
"Not the cause" means it is not the cause of everything.
Because minds of inferior grade and so forth do not arise simultaneously. Question:
What about those such as sheep-slaughterers?
A person of non-restraint does not take what is not given throughout their entire life.
Regarding his own wife and concubines,
he dwells with a mind of contentment;
he is mute and unable to speak.
Regarding the four faults of speech:
how can they possess all the constituent factors?
Answer: Because they universally impair the virtuous *āśaya* (intentional disposition). It is the *āśaya* [that is impaired].
This refers to the "intention" (āśaya). Although one may be mute and unable to speak, by gesturing with the hands, the body expresses the meaning one wishes to convey;
thus, the factor [of speech] is complete.
If one does not undertake it for the duration of one's life,
nor possesses all the constituent branches,
and furthermore does not extend it to all sentient beings.
However, if one merely commits an evil act while remaining in the middle [state],
it is not termed "non-restraint" (asamvara). According to the Sautrāntika school,
this depends on the duration for which the commitment was made.
Whether the auxiliary means are complete or incomplete,
and whether they are applied universally or not to all sentient beings.
All obtain non-restraint;
the same applies to the lay devotee's precepts,
according to however many are received.
All obtain the precepts,
with the sole exception of the eight precepts,
because their duration is brief.
One must necessarily possess the constituent factors and extend [the vow] to all sentient beings before the precepts can arise.

Those who lack restraint (asamvara) refer to such individuals as sheep-butchers, poultry-butchers, pig-butchers, bird-catchers, fishers, hunters, robbers, executioners, prison wardens, dragon-binders, dog-cookers, those who set snares and traps, wicked kings, judges, those who inflict punishments, and those who preside over hearings and adjudicate legal cases.
As for "binding dragons," it refers to binding dragons and snakes by means of incantations and esoteric arts.

however, within the desire realm (kāmadhātu),
there exists karma such as that of the gods.
Because they undergo [experiences] as humans and so forth due to the power of other conditions,
they are not immovable.
Third, this clarifies the karma of the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
The treatise states:
Furthermore, it is said in the sūtras that there are three types of karma,
such as that which leads to pleasant experience and so forth. What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Wholesome [actions] up to the third dhyāna are conducive to pleasure;
All unwholesome [actions] are conducive to suffering; Wholesome [actions] of the higher realms are conducive to neither.

Others say that [the experience] also exists in the lower realms; because it draws forth maturation from the intermediate state, and because these three types of karma are admitted not to mature sequentially, there are five types of karma to be experienced accordingly.
These are: by way of intrinsic nature, by way of association, and so forth.
"And due to the differences in their objects, maturation, and manifestation.
The commentary states:
The first verse correctly clarifies the three types of sensation.
The next verse cites scriptural evidence;
the final verse clarifies the experience of the favorable:
that which is conducive to pleasure, pain, and neither.
This is the summary:
first, karma conducive to pleasant feeling;
second, karma conducive to painful feeling.
The three types of karma that accord with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling and so forth are not the other two.
As for "wholesome [karma] up to the third [level] accords with pleasant [feeling]," it refers to the following.
This explains the experience of pleasant sensation,
which begins from the desire realm and extends up to the third dhyāna.
All wholesome karmas are termed "conducive to pleasant feeling," while all unwholesome [karmas] are conducive to painful [feeling].
This explains karma that accords with painful feeling.
Unwholesome karma of the desire realm is called karma that accords with painful feeling.
"Supreme goodness accords with neither [of the two]" explains the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant,
which exists above the third dhyāna.
All wholesome karma from the fourth dhyāna up to the peak of existence.
This is called "supreme goodness" (śubha) and is termed "karma that accords with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The treatise states:
It should be understood that these various karmas do not result only in the experience of feeling;
they also result in the requisites for those feelings. Thus, there are both the feelings and their requisites.
Regarding this, it is said that "receiving and understanding" (*prativedha*) is what is meant.
This [term] "provision" (*sambhāra*) applies equally to both [the lower and middle stages]. Others say that there are also cases where maturation is produced from the middle stage.
Still other masters say:
Below the third dhyāna,
there is also a third type of karma that is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome],
which is conducive to rebirth; "middle" refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
Because karma of the intermediate dhyāna brings about an intermediate maturation,
it is clearly known that [the result] belongs to a lower stage.
There is karma of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling,
which means being born in the intermediate state where there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Therefore, those karmas induce fruits that are neither concordant nor discordant.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that these three types of karma do not ripen sequentially,
the intent of the citation is to clarify that there is the relinquishing of maturation (*vipāka*) in the lower realms.
This is the statement from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. It asks:
"Is it possible for the three types of karma to experience their maturation (vipāka) neither before nor after one another? The commentary explains:
"It is experienced at the same time," meaning it is neither before nor after; that treatise answers:
"There is what is called 'matter (rūpa) that is karma conducive to pleasant experience (sukha-vedanīya-karman').'"
Karma conducive to painful feeling;
the mind and mental factors [conducive to such];
and karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Regarding "factors dissociated from mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and so forth, as explained at length:
"favorable to pleasant form" (*sukha-rūpa-anukūla*) means...
Among humans and devas, there are the five faculties— eye and so forth— and their objects:
visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Karma conducive to painful mental states refers to that which brings about painful feelings in the realms of humans and devas, as well as the associated phenomena;
it is karma conducive to feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Regarding those factors dissociated from mind:
among humans and devas, they consist of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character of the group (nikāyasabhāga).
"Attaining the four characteristics" constitutes the first section of the text. Within the extensive exposition, there is yet another section;
a brief citation from the *Abhidharmakośa* follows.
It simply says "and so forth," up to the detailed exposition in the second section of the text:
"karma conducive to pleasant feeling."
The formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) that can induce the human destiny, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and so forth— four [factors]—
are the matter (rūpa) of karma conducive to painful feeling (duḥkhavedanīya-karma).
This refers to karma that produces feelings of neither-pain-nor-pleasure within the realms of humans and devas— namely, the karma pertaining to visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles—
and the primary minds and mental factors associated with them.
This karma can induce neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*),
as well as its associated and resultant maturation (*vipāka*).
Now, I shall cite that passage.
Taking the second section of the text as evidence to explain the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant,
it is clearly understood that the ripening of karma resulting in a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant occurs within the desire realm.
There is the abandonment of the maturation (vipāka).
This is because the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the three types of karma receive their maturational fruits simultaneously;
from this, it is proven.
The lower stages also possess karma that is neither conducive to [rebirth] nor conducive to extinction.
This is because these three types of karma do not ripen simultaneously outside of the Desire Realm,
and because there is no suffering in the higher realms.
The term "three karmas" refers exclusively to the desire realm. Question: Is it not the case that karma is either wholesome or unwholesome, while the experience of its fruit is neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
This karma bestows pleasure.
Since their essential natures are distinct, how can they be said to be "conducive to pleasant feeling" and so forth?
Answer: It is because karma is capable of acting as the cause.
Because it brings about beneficial and pleasant sensation,
it is designated as "conducive to sensation" (anulomavedanīya) with respect to its benefit.
Alternatively, this karma is that which is experienced as pleasure;
that is to say, pleasure is this karma.
Because it is a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*),
the fruit experiences the cause;
this is precisely what is meant by "that which is experienced" (*vedanīya*) as being concordant with "the experience" (*vedanā*).
Alternatively, that pleasure is what is experienced as the result of karma,
because by means of it one is able to experience the maturation (vipāka) of pleasure.
Receiving the fruit because of the cause—
this is precisely that which is capable of receiving,
in accordance with what is received.
"There are five types of experience in accordance with its nature" is the heading;
this is a general statement regarding experience in accordance with its nature.
Briefly, there are five kinds.

Regarding "that which is concordant with its own nature," the following provides the specific explanation: first, that which is concordant with its own nature (*svabhāva-vedanīya*) has the three feelings as its essence, because its own nature is feeling itself.
That which does not contradict its own nature is called "concordant with feeling" (*anuloma-vedanīya*).
Second is that which is concordant with feeling through association (*samprayoga*).
It has contact as its essence;
that is, contact associated with feeling is called "associated with agreeable feeling."
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Contact conducive to pleasant feeling," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the maturation of the object:
the third [category], the object conducive to feeling,
has as its essence the six objects, such as visible form and so forth.
That is to say, the objective referent that accords with the feeling which takes it as its object is called "the object conducive to feeling."
Fourth is the experience that accords with maturation (*vipāka-anubhava*).
This refers to karma that brings about maturation and which accords with the fruit of maturation.
Therefore, it is called "maturation-feeling-conducive.
As stated in the Sūtra: "Karma conducive to feeling in the present life..."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Regarding "due to the distinction of being present," this refers to the fifth [type],
feeling that is experienced when present (*pratyutpanna-anubhava*).
"Manifest" refers to the present;
"feeling" (vedanā) is its actual occurrence,
which constitutes the essence of feeling itself.
That which is not contradicted in the present is called "to be experienced in the present.
As for the distinctions [in this category]:
The five feelings mentioned above constitute their differentiation;
this is what was previously explained.
Regarding "conducive to pleasant feeling" and so forth:
among these five, this fourth is the maturation conducive to feeling (*vedanīya-vipāka*),
because karma is capable of bringing about the maturation of feeling.
Although karma and feeling differ in their essential natures,
they are nevertheless designated as "conducive to pleasant feeling" and so forth.
From this fourth [point]...
This explains the karma of the three times.
Within this, the first section clarifies the four types of karma,
and the second clarifies their distinctions.
The third clarifies karma that has its fruition in the intermediate state; the fourth clarifies determinate karma;
the fifth clarifies karma that bears fruit in the present life.
Sixth, it clarifies that karma immediately yields its fruit.
This first section below clarifies the four types of karma.
The treatise says: "Regarding these three types of karma, there are those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate.
What are their characteristics?"
The verse says:
This [karma] is either determinate or indeterminate; the determinate is of three types, such as that which ripens in the present life and so forth.
Alternatively, it is said that there are five types of karma; other masters state there are four categories.
The commentary states:
"Regarding this [distinction] between the determinate and the indeterminate," this is the heading.
Regarding these three preceding types of karma,
there are those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate. As for the determinate three, such as those conducive to the present life and so forth:
This is a separate explanation. There are three types of karma in the realm of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The first is that to be experienced in the present life (*drstadharmavedanīya*), which refers to what is performed in this very birth.
First, experience to be felt in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Second, experience to be felt in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*),
which refers to that which is produced in this life.
The second is karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*). The third is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*),
which means it is created in this life.
Regarding the third [type of karma], which is experienced after rebirth:
according to the Sautrāntika school, this refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*).
Its power is strongest; it must necessarily be experienced either in the present life or in a subsequent life,
or as karma to be experienced in the very next birth.
Its power is somewhat inferior;
it must necessarily experience its retribution in a future life,
and does not experience it in the present life.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is the weakest in force;
it is not experienced in the present life.
Experiencing only a subsequent experience,
according to the stage of its initial ripening, it is designated as "conducive to the present life" and so forth; together with indeterminate karma,
these constitute four types.
Regarding the term "indeterminate" (aniyata): it refers to being indeterminate in terms of experience,
meaning that the maturation (vipāka) is experienced indeterminately.
Alternatively, because the time [of their maturation] is not fixed across the three periods,
they are designated as "indeterminate."
Alternatively, it is said that there are five types of karma;
some maintain that there are two further types of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-vedanīya-karma*).
That is to say, regarding maturation (vipāka),
there are those that are determinate and those that are indeterminate; these are divided into two kinds.
First, maturation is determinate in nature but indeterminate in timing; that is,
the fruit must necessarily be experienced,
though its timing within the three periods of time is not fixed.
This refers to the indeterminate [karma].
Second, regarding the indeterminacy of both the maturation (*vipāka*) and the time: this means that both the fruit and the timing of its experience are indeterminate.
There exists only karma that is determinate in its fruit but indeterminate in its timing.
There is no case where the time is fixed but the result is not;
rather, when the time is fixed,
the result is necessarily fixed as well.
Because there is no distinct nature apart from the maturation [of karma] at that time.

Regarding the four types of karma and five types of karma, the difference lies only in their expansion or contraction; the underlying principle is not different. As for the fourfold formulation mentioned by other masters:
This refers to what other Dārṣṭāntikas say:
since karma is divided into eight types,
they establish four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
That [cause] is admitted to be determinate with respect to time but indeterminate with respect to its fruit.
Within that indeterminacy,
time is further divided into three [periods].
Because these are combined with the five previous karmas, eight types are established. Regarding the first category:
it is determinate in terms of timing, but indeterminate in terms of maturation (*vipāka*).
This refers to the three types of karma— those to be experienced in the present life and so forth—
which are determinate regarding the time [of their maturation] but indeterminate regarding their results.
If its fruit is experienced in the present life,
it is experienced as present;
if it is not experienced, it will never again be experienced.
In this case, the timing is certain,
but the fruition is uncertain; as it is with those [karmas] that ripen in the present life, so it is with others.
The same applies after birth.
This is divided into three types:
the first is that which is certain to ripen in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya).
The fruit is not fixed.
Second, that which is fixed for rebirth;
its fruit is not fixed.
Third, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives has an indeterminate fruition. Regarding the second phrase:
there is karma for which the maturation is determinate.
Its timing is indefinite;
that is to say, it is an indefinite karma,
yet it will certainly yield its maturation.
This refers to only one case:
namely, karma whose fruit is fixed but whose timing is not fixed.
As for the third alternative, there is karma that is fixed in both respects.
This refers to those [karmas] that accord with the present life and so forth,
which definitely obtain maturation (vipāka).
There are three such types.
First, those that are determinate regarding both the fruit and the present time;
second, those that are determinate regarding both the fruit and the next life;
third, those that are determinate regarding both the fruit and a subsequent life; as for the fourth category:
There is karma that is indeterminate with respect to both;
namely, karma whose timing is indeterminate.
It does not necessarily obtain maturation;
this is simply one case,
namely that the fruit is indeterminate.
The timing is indefinite.
The treatise says:
"That [text] explains various karmas."
In total, there are eight types;
namely, those to be experienced in the present life,
which are both determinate and indeterminate.
Up to the indeterminate [karma],
there are also two types of interpretations. Regarding the three determinate [karmas],
such as those to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), and so forth:
The third phrase is this. Regarding the three types of indeterminate karma, such as that which ripens in the present life,
the first phrase is this.
Regarding the fourth indeterminate [category],
that which is determinate therein is the second phrase;
that which is indeterminate within the indeterminate is as follows.
The fourth phrase is this. From here,
secondly, the distinctions are clarified.
The treatise says:
Regarding these explained distinctions of karma,
what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Four wholesome [karmas] can be performed simultaneously; Only three lead to the acquisition of the homogeneous type (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
In all realms, four types are created; In the hells, wholesome [karma] excludes the present.

Regarding those firm in the stage of detachment from passion: an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) does not produce [karma] that leads to rebirth as a noble one (ārya), nor does a noble one produce [karma] that leads to rebirth in subsequent states. Furthermore, there is no falling away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra). Commentary: [The verse says: "Firm in the stage of detachment from passion; an ordinary person does not produce [karma] leading to rebirth as a noble one, nor does a noble one produce [karma] leading to rebirth in subsequent states; and there is no falling away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence. Explanation: [as follows].
Regarding the "four virtuous [positions]," the author of the treatise evaluates and adopts them,
stating that among the various systems explaining the four types of karma, these are superior from the perspective of principle.
However, within this context,
the determinate and indeterminate are explained in order to clarify the characteristics of the four types of karma taught in the sūtras.
Regarding those that can be performed simultaneously:
these four types of karma can be performed at one time;
that is to say, at a single moment.
One commits sexual misconduct oneself,
dispatches another to commit killing,
or engages in theft or deception.
The paths of action are completed simultaneously;
either one brings about the present life,
or one brings about birth in the future.
Either one [karma] may be determinate after being experienced once, or one may be indeterminate;
or one may create four [types of karma] at once— it is not necessarily the case that all [of these] occur in this manner.
Therefore, it is said with allowance: Question: How many types of karma can project a common destiny (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
Answer: The verse states: "Only three [types] project the common destiny."
Among the four types of karma,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life, it is the homogeneous state of the present body.
Because they are projected by prior karma.
Question: In which realm and in which destiny can one create how many types of karma?
The verse replies, "In all bases, four kinds are created.
The following lines together answer this question; in brief:
In the various realms and destinies,
whether wholesome or unwholesome,
according to what is appropriate for each.
It may be established that there are four types;
excluding the wholesome [karma] of hell-beings from those manifesting in the present—
this below is discussed according to specific distinctions.
Within the hells, there are four kinds of wholesome karma,
excluding that which is to be experienced in the present life.
Because there is no fruit of craving, one may commit four types of evil deeds.
Regarding those who are firm in a stage free from defilement: ordinary beings do not create [new karma] there, and noble ones do not create [karma] that will arise in future lives.
The nature of non-retrogression is called "firmness.
This applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones;
it pertains to their state of being free from defilement.
If one does not fall back to the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and does not create karma for rebirth,
one abandons the defilements of this stage by virtue of that non-retrogressive nature.
Because one will certainly not be reborn in a second life,
there is no karma that produces birth; however,
it is possible to create the other three types of karma.
A non-retrogressive noble one does not create karma for rebirth in a state free from defilement.
Because those of non-retrogressive nature will certainly never again be reborn in the lower stages,
they do not produce [new] karma after being born there; however,
it is possible for them to create the other two types of karma.

Furthermore, regarding those who fall away from the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), this includes noble ones (ārya) who have attained detachment as well as noble ones residing at the Peak of Existence; although they may undergo such retrogression,
[they do not lose their roots of goodness].
Furthermore, they do not create the two types of karma— those to be experienced in the desire realm and those to be experienced in the Peak of Existence—
in subsequent lives, because, as before, they are noble ones who do not regress.
Thus, the verse uses the word "and" (*ca*).
Now, for one who falls away from the state of detachment up to the Peak of Existence,
that fall must necessarily be a falling away from the fruit.
As for all those who fall away from the fruit:
They will certainly not meet their end,
because they shall return to cultivate and attain the fruits [of the path] within the stage of freedom from passion.
Since they will never again be born,
there are no karmic actions subsequent to birth.
This concludes the third section.
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is the performance of karma.
The treatise says:
"Abiding in the state of the intermediate state."
Does one also create karma? And how so?
The verse says:
In the intermediate state of the desire realm, one can create twenty-two kinds of karma.
All are subsumed under those to be experienced in the present life, because their category and homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga) are one.
The commentary states:
"Within the desire realm..."
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
one may perform up to twenty-two types of karma;
that is to say, during the intermediate state.
The five stages within the womb and the five stages outside the womb—
because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) can create the determinate and indeterminate karma for these eleven stages.

The twenty-two names are all subsumed under karma to be experienced in the present life (*drstadharmavedanīya*), because their category and homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) are one. This refers to that which is performed within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The eleven types of determinate karma are all subsumed under those to be experienced in the present life,
because the intermediate state (antarābhava) and the ten stages of the birth-existence (upapattibhava) [constitute the present life].
A single homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga),
because it is without distinction;
this is one homogeneous class.
Since they are projected by the same karma,
there is no distinction between their types; because there is no distinction between their types, [there is no difference].
These determinate karmas are all subsumed under those that ripen in the present life.
Furthermore, regarding this intermediate state (antarābhava):
Because it is projected by the same karma that projects birth-existence (upapattibhava),
it is not said that there is karma to be experienced in the intermediate existence (antarābhava);
this [karma] is precisely what is to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya) or in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya).
Because it is produced by what is drawn forth from indeterminate karma that follows [the previous],
from this fourth [section] there is an explanation of the characteristics of determinate karma.
The treatise says:
What are the characteristics of those karmas that are definitely to be experienced?
The verse says:
Karma committed through intense afflictions or a pure mind, that which is performed habitually,
and that arising toward a field of merit, as well as the karma of harming one's parents— these are fixed.
The commentary states:
The characteristics of various determinate karmas are briefly established by four causes.
First, by means of intense affliction and intense pure mind;
that is, either an intense defilement or an intense wholesome mind.
These are the karmas that are performed.
The second and this [third] are those performed constantly;
although they are not performed with a heavy mind, they are nonetheless performed constantly.
Third, regarding the field of merit:
it refers to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
or those who have attained superior fruits.

This refers to those who have attained the stage of stream-entry or the stage of no-more-learning, or those who have attained superior meditative concentration, namely, the concentration of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi).
Regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): although there is neither heavy affliction nor a heavy pure mind within this field,
nor is it a constant practice,
because the field itself is preeminent.
This is definitely an action that must be experienced [in this life].
Fourth, regarding one's parents, it is the performance of harmful acts according to whether the mind [toward them] is slight or grave.
The results of karma are certain.
These four aforementioned causes are all subsumed under determinate karma.
From this, the fifth [section] clarifies karma that yields results in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*).
The verse says:

Due to the excellence of the field and the intention, as well as karma that is certain to produce a ripened result (*vipāka*) or karma from which one has attained permanent detachment, it is certain to produce a fruit in the present life.
Commentary:
Regarding the excellence of the field and the intention:
first, by way of the excellence of the field;
second, by way of the excellence of the intention.
Regarding the excellence of the field:
it is heard that there was a bhikṣu among the saṃgha.
He spoke with a woman's voice and immediately transformed into a woman,
because his intention was superior.
I have heard that there was a eunuch who,
through the act of saving another eunuch from distress,
was transformed into a man.
There are many such accounts of this kind;
those who have attained the stage of perpetual separation from the karma that would otherwise necessarily produce results in the present life.
This reveals that for an Arhat, there is karma whose fruition is fixed but whose timing is indefinite; likewise,
for a Non-returner (Anāgāmin), wherever they may be situated, the karma associated with detachment from the defilements of that stage is called "karma of the stage of permanent detachment."
Regarding the karma of this stage that is eternally abandoned: it consists of the wholesome and unwholesome karma created within this stage while one has not yet abandoned the defilements,
as well as the wholesome karma cultivated at the stage of abandoning the defilements.
Regarding these various karmas,
those that are determinate in their maturation but indeterminate in timing will necessarily bring about results in the present life.
This means that because one will not be reborn in this stage again,
it brings about results in the present life.
If, in this stage, there exists karma that is to be experienced in a subsequent birth,
it is certain that there is no possibility of permanent freedom from defilement; one will necessarily experience [the results] in a subsequent birth.
One experiences the fruit of maturation.
If both the maturation and the time are indeterminate, [the timing of the experience is likewise indeterminate].
Because they have permanently abandoned defilement,
they no longer undergo further maturation;
this is the sixth [point] from here.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "What kind of field gives rise to karma? Regarding this, it says: "Karma arises from a field. This means that when one performs an action toward a particular field, the resulting fruit is experienced immediately. Thus, it is said: "What kind of field gives rise to karma? It refers to the field of sentient beings (*sattvākṣetra*). Furthermore, there are two types of fields: the field of sentient beings and the field of non-sentient things (*asattvākṣetra*). Among these, the field of sentient beings is superior. Within the field of sentient beings, there are three categories: those who are worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*), those who are not worthy of offerings, and those who are neither worthy nor unworthy of offerings. Among these, the field of those worthy of offerings is superior. Within the field of those worthy of offerings, there are two types: those who have entered the path (*mārgapratipanna*) and those who have attained the fruit (*phalastha*). Among these, the field of those who have attained the fruit is superior. Within the field of those who have attained the fruit, there are two types: those who have attained the fruit of the Śrāvaka and those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha. Among these, the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha is superior. Within the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha, there are two types: those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha through their own power and those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha through the power of another. Among these, the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha through their own power is superior. Within the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha through their own power, there are two types: those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha while still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training (*aśaikṣa*). Among these, the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training is superior. Within the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training, there are two types: those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training by relying on a teacher and those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training without relying on a teacher. Among these, the field of those who have attained the fruit of the Pratyekabuddha having completed their training without relying on a teacher is superior. The verse says:
It is held that wholesome karma devoid of vitarka produces only mental sensation, while unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation;

The commentary states:
"Wholesome actions without vitarka" refers to those from the intermediate dhyāna upwards.
Up to the wholesome karma of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
this is called karma without vitarka;
it produces only mental sensation.
Bodily sensation necessarily arises together with vitarka and vicāra;
therefore, karma devoid of vitarka does not induce bodily sensation.
As for the statement that "evil results only in bodily sensation," evil only brings about suffering,
and this suffering resides in the five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, the bodily sensation and the mental sensation of suffering that arise together are definitively termed *daurmanasya* (dejection).
Sorrow is not a karmic maturation;
therefore, evil does not induce the maturation of mental feeling.
This is the second [point].

"It occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

the following clarifies that there are five causes for insanity in general.
First, through the ripening of karma:
that is, by using drugs or incantations,

Some set fires to burn mountains;

Regarding those who suffer from fear, harm, or opposition:
the second [type] arises from fear;

because the non-humans become angry.

The fear of the great assembly,

As for how they become wholesome or unwholesome accordingly:
"Belonging to" means that which corresponds;

These are called the paths of wholesome action;
those that subsume the aforementioned unwholesome conduct are the paths of unwholesome action.
Regarding the term "coarse category," this excludes those that are not coarse or manifest among the bodily misdeeds.
The offenses of preliminary and subsequent action,

Among the verbal misdeeds, there are the offenses of the preliminary application and the subsequent conclusion,

Regarding what is called a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*):

The preparatory and subsequent stages of wholesome action,

That is to say, [virtuous actions] such as kind speech and so forth are all neither coarse nor manifest,
and are not subsumed under the paths of action.
Among the excellent mental actions,
namely all wholesome volitions (*cetanā*),
these are karma but not the path.
Therefore, it is also not subsumed under the paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Following this, the second [topic] clarifies stealing.

The commentary says:

Engaging in what should not be engaged in:
first, with regard to improper objects.
That is to say, engaging in sexual intercourse with another's wife,
or with one's father,
or with one's mother.
Either toward parents and relatives,
or even toward territories protected by a king;
second, [approaching] by an improper path.
That is to say: engaging with one's own wife in the mouth or other orifices;
and third, engaging in non-appropriate places.
That is to say, within a monastery, at a stūpa, or in a secluded place;
fourth, at an improper time,
namely during pregnancy.
When drinking an infant's milk,
when observing the precepts of fasting,
and even with one's own wife or concubines.
Furthermore, one commits misconduct by engaging in unchaste conduct with a bhikṣuṇī;
this is one interpretation.
The second interpretation is that one incurs an offense against the king because he does not tolerate it.
Even with one's own wife or concubines,
one should not commit transgression when observing the precepts of the fast.
How much more so for those who have left the household life?
To use the weighty case to illustrate the light:
there is nothing but encroachment and insult.
The offense of misconduct is incurred if one violates a maiden.
Regarding the location where the offense is committed: if she has not been promised to another, it is an offense against her guardian.
This and all that remains are obtained from the king.

first, false speech is explained.
Second, the clarification of seeing, hearing,
and so forth. First, regarding the clarification of deceptive speech (*mṛṣāvāda*),

The verse says:

The commentary states:
it must possess four conditions.
The path of action of deception is accomplished when one speaks with a contrary intention regarding the object being deceived.
That is to say, claiming not to have seen what was actually seen, and so forth.
As for the two types of those who are deceived,
they understand the meaning of what has been said.
This is to be understood as follows:
third, the arousal of a defiled mind;

If one does not understand the meaning of the words,

The treatise states:
The sūtras state that there are,
in brief, sixteen types of such expressions;
namely, those regarding what has not been seen.
Not hearing.
Not perceiving. Not knowing.
Regarding the terms "truth," "seeing," and so forth;
or, with respect to what is seen and what is heard.
Regarding that which is awakened to and that which is known,

Regarding that which has not been seen:
Up to not knowing, one says "not seen," and so forth;
or regarding what has been seen.
Up to the objects of knowledge,
they speak of "seeing reality" and so forth;
such are these eight types.
This is called "the words of the noble ones. What are the characteristics of "what has been seen" and so forth?
The verse says:

That which is apprehended by the eye, the ear, the mental consciousness, and the other three [consciousnesses] is designated, respectively, as "seen," "heard," "cognized," and "sensed. Commentary: This refers to the objects perceived through the visual faculty, the auditory faculty, the mental consciousness, and the remaining three consciousnesses (olfactory, gustatory, and tactile), which are termed "the seen," "the heard," "the cognized," and "the sensed" in that order.
If an object is realized by visual consciousness, it is called "seen";
this refers to visible form (*rūpa*).
If an object is realized by the auditory consciousness,
it is termed "that which is heard";
this refers to sound.
If an object is realized by the mental consciousness,
it is called "the knowable," namely,
the objective sphere of phenomena (dharmas).
If an object is realized by the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body,
it is termed "the perceived," namely:
odor, flavor, and tangibility.
The verse mentions "the remaining three," which refers to the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body, as well as their objects:
visible forms, sounds, and mental phenomena.
All [of these] pertain to the three natures;
however, only odor, flavor, and tangibility are of the indeterminate nature.
That is to say, it is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*);
like death, it is devoid of cognition.
Therefore, it can serve as a means of realization.
The name "awakening" (bodhi) is established exclusively [for this] according to the Sautrāntika school;
if it were the five faculties, [it would not be so].
The five objects, such as form and so forth, which are realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), are termed "the seen."
If it is from another,
the six objects as they are heard by report are called "that which is heard."
If one employs one's own mind,
using various forms of reasoning,
to infer what is accepted.
The six objects are termed "that which is to be cognized.
If the mental consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
it realizes these six objects.
It is termed "the knowable.
Among the five objects,
each one may give rise to seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Regarding the four types of verbal expression,
concerning the sixth object,
it is said that there are three interpretations, excluding [the interpretation involving] seeing.
The sixth object is the mental object (dharmāyatana). It is characterized by being invisible,
yet possessing the qualities of being audible, cognizable, and knowable— these three.
Regarding the designation of mental consciousness as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
following the five sensory consciousnesses,
mental consciousness arises immediately and directly.
The five objects realized are directly realized by the mental consciousness within meditative concentration; thus,
six objects are directly realized.
This refers to the mental consciousness of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The treatise states:
"The former masters..."
It is said thus:
that which is currently seen by the eye is called "the seen."
That which is heard from others is called "what is heard"; that which is personally brought forth by one's own mind is [called "what is reflected upon"].
All that is conceptually constructed is called the "cognized," while that which is personally experienced within is [the "felt"].

And that which is personally realized is called the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*). Regarding the phrase "that which is internally experienced": *Note: The term *jñeya* (Sanskrit) refers to the objects of knowledge; the phrase "internally experienced" (*pratyātmavedya*) indicates that this realization is not derived from external sources but is directly apprehended within one's own continuum.*
That is to say, the four objects apprehended by the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue,
and body are called "internal objects of experience" because they are what is personally experienced by oneself.
This refers to the six objects realized by the consciousness of direct perception (pratyakṣa-vijñāna).

This clarifies the three types of speech, such as divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
The treatise states:

The verse says:
Speech with a defiled mind intended to cause division among others is called divisive speech (*paiśunya*).

Others say it is distinct from the three [other paths of action]. This refers to flattery, song, false doctrines, and so forth.
The commentary says:
The completion of divisive speech requires four conditions:
a defiled mind and words intended to cause dissension among others.
There are four conditions for this:
first, a defiled mind;
second, the utterance of speech intended to cause harm to others.
Whether the other party is divided or not,
it all constitutes divisive speech.
Third, regarding those who have heard [the words].
To understand the meaning of what has been explained refers to mutual comprehension.
Fourth is being without error.
Regarding the latter two conditions,
which flow from the preceding ones: unwholesome harsh speech also possesses four conditions.
First, a defiled mind;
second, uttering unpleasant speech to revile others.
Third, understanding the meaning;
fourth, being unerring—
these are termed harsh speech.
The three characters "defiled mind" (染心) flow from the first phrase;
one should say that speech arising from a defiled mind which is unlovely is termed harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
Understanding the meaning without error,
they also follow what has come before;
these are those who engage in various defiled and impure speech.
All speech arising from defiled minds is called frivolous speech;
it refers to words uttered under the influence of defilement.
Because all [of these] are mixed with impurities,
there are various defiled verses that add one extra syllable.
Therefore, when speaking even a single word,
if it originates from the first category [of unwholesome speech], this constitutes frivolous chatter.
It is established by two conditions:
first, a defiled mind;
second, the speech uttered [thereby].
Regarding the statement that "others say [it refers to] things other than the three, such as flattery, song,
and false treatises," there are other masters who say that these are distinct from falsehood and the rest.
The first three types of speech and all other speech arising from an afflicted mind are termed frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
This refers to things such as flattering songs.
"Flattery" (naitṛka) means sycophancy;
for example, when a bhikṣu, through a wrong livelihood, utters sycophantic speech.
"Singing" refers to chanting;
it includes the intonation of recitation as well as the performances of professional entertainers.
"Erroneous discourse" refers to the words and expressions adhered to by incorrect views.
The term "and so forth" includes lamentations arising from an afflicted mind,

All of these constitute frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
Although there are songs and chants when a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) appears in the world, [they do not constitute frivolous speech].
From a mind of renunciation, there arises a non-real defiled mind.
Other masters say that at this time,
the transgressions of marriage and singing are minor.
The path of action is not established.

The treatise states:

Hatred toward sentient beings refers to the desire to inflict harm upon others;

as stated in the Sūtra,

The wrong view that slanders the noble ones.
