This is the second major section, which explains the names and meanings of the paths of action (*karmapatha*). The treatise says:
"Having thus distinguished the characteristics of the ten paths of action, by what meaning are they called 'paths of action'? The verse states:
"Among these, three are exclusively the path; seven are both karma and the path.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "Among these, three are exclusively the path" means:
Among these ten paths of action,
the three beginning with greed are paths alone,
because they are the paths of karma.
The designation "path of action" is established as follows:
volition associated with greed and so forth is called "action," because volition proceeds by means of the operation of that greed and so forth.
Because that [volition] proceeds from the tendencies of greed and so forth;
for volition exerts its formative activity according to the force of those very tendencies such as greed.
Therefore, the three beginning with greed serve as the path for volition;
likewise, the seven [unwholesome] actions are also the path.
The first seven are karma,
because they are bodily and vocal karma;
they are also the paths of karma.
Because it is that wherein volition moves;
because the volition that constitutes the motivation (samutthāna) proceeds by relying upon body and speech;
thus, the seven [paths of action] of body and speech are the domains traversed by volition.
Furthermore, because it is the path of karma;
the preceding seven are karma,
because they are the path of karma.
The designation "course of action" (karmapatha) is established because the superior actions are bodily and vocal karma,
while the inferior actions are the volition (cetanā) that originates them.
It is called "action-action" (*karmakarma*).
Thus, the term "path of action" (*karmapatha*) fully reveals the meaning of both "action" and "path of action."
Although they do not belong to the same category,
they share the common designation of "paths of action";
yet one such action constitutes a distinct path of action from another.
One path is [designated as] another path,
just as in the world, although the names for carts and oxen are the same,
one cart or ox is called "another" cart or ox; thus it is stated in the scriptures.
As for the expression "abodes of consciousness," although there are four such abodes,
their natures and categories differ.

The stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) are designated by the same names, yet one station of consciousness is named after the others. Regarding the seven [paths of action] beginning with abstaining from killing and the three beginning with non-attachment,
they are established under the name of "paths of action" (karmapatha).
This should be explained in the same manner as the preceding section. This concludes the third [point],
which clarifies the abandonment of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) by way of its meaning.
The treatise says:
"Regarding what has been thus explained,
the ten paths of unwholesome karma..."
All of these are contrary to the manifestation of wholesome dharmas.
By which path of action (*karmapatha*) are the roots of goodness severed?
Regarding the severing of the roots of goodness and the reconnecting of the roots of goodness, what is the distinction?
The verse says:
Only wrong view severs the roots of goodness; that which is severed consists of all innate [roots] of the desire realm that deny cause and effect.
They are severed gradually; both [roots and non-attainment] are abandoned by humans of the three continents, whether male or female.
Severance occurs through the functioning of views and is characterized by non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The continuity of roots of goodness occurs through doubt or views; they manifest instantaneously, except for those who have committed the immediate transgressions.
The commentary states:
"Only those who have severed the roots of goodness by means of false view [are excluded]."
Only the highest degree of perfect wrong view can sever the roots of goodness;
however, in this treatise:
The three unwholesome roots— greed, hatred, and delusion—
are said to be able to sever the wholesome because these unwholesome roots can induce wrong view.
The severance of wrong views depends upon those faculties,
just as a fire that burns a village originates from bandits; therefore,
it is said in the world that "the village was burned by bandits."
Regarding those roots of goodness abandoned through birth-attainment,
they are abandoned only within the desire realm.
It refers to innate wholesome states.
That is to say, at the time when wholesome roots are severed, the wholesome states of the form and formless realms [are also severed].
Because they were not previously established, it cannot be said that they are severed.
Question: For what reason is it only the innate wholesome roots (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśalamūla*) that are severed?
Answer: Because the roots of goodness of preparatory application have already been lost;
that is to say, the roots of goodness have been severed.
First, in the stage of preparatory application,
one abandons the wholesome roots of application until the moment of severing the wholesome roots is reached.
"Only the denial of that which is acquired through birth,
as well as the denial of cause and effect,
constitutes the characteristic of false view."
The false view that denies causes is the denial of sublime and evil conduct;
the false view that denies results is the denial of [the fruits of] karma.
There is no fruit of good or evil.
"All" refers to all false views.
All are capable of severing the roots of goodness,
whether they have their own realm as their object or another realm as their object.
Whether it has outflowing objects as its condition or no-outflow objects as its condition, such is wrong view.
All [of these] are able to sever the roots of goodness.
Other masters say that they take only their own realm as an object.
Only those [defilements] that have outflow as their object are able to sever the roots of goodness;
others cannot sever them.
To address that [objection],
it says "all are gradually severed. This clarifies that the severance of the roots of goodness occurs gradually rather than instantaneously.
This refers to the nine grades of wrong view,
which sever the nine grades of roots of goodness through a process of mutual opposition between the counteractive and the concordant factors.
The lowest-of-the-low grade of wrong view can sever the highest-of-the-high grade of wholesome roots,
continuing in this manner up to the highest-of-the-high grade of wrong view.
It is able to sever the lowest-of-the-low grade of wholesome roots.
The progression from the highest grade down to the lowest grade is termed "reversal."
The progression of wrong views from the lower to the upper stages is called "conformity.
Regarding "abandoning both":
"both" refers to the roots of goodness.
As well as the restraint (*saṃvara*).
At the time when the roots of goodness are severed,
both are simultaneously relinquished.
The treatise says:
"If that restraint belongs to this category of mind..."
Regarding the fruit of origination:
when this category of mind is severed,
one relinquishes that restraint.
Because the categories of the fruit and the cause are identical, it is explained that there are nine grades of wholesome mind.
Each is capable of giving rise to the precepts;
the precepts are their fruit. If one were to sever even the inferior grade of goodness, [the precepts would not arise].
One merely abandons the inferior grade of precepts, and so on, until one severs the superior grade of wholesome states;
at that point, one merely abandons the superior grade of precepts. [This applies to] all fruits of the vows.

Some arise from the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*), while others arise from the wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala-citta*). If it arises from a wholesome mind of application,
the restraint (*saṃvara*) is first relinquished.
Regarding the subsequent severance of the roots of goodness, the commentary explains:
through the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for severing the roots of goodness, one abandons the wholesome states of preparatory effort.
At the time of abandoning the preparatory application,
the restraint produced by the roots of goodness of that preparatory application [is also abandoned].
They are abandoned at the same time.
The statement that they are "abandoned first" refers to their abandonment during the stage of prior preparation (*prayoga*). Regarding the persons of the three continents who are male or female:
It is clear that [ignorance] can sever the roots of goodness;
as for its location and the person, it occurs among humans in the three continents of the human realm.
It does not exist in the miserable realms,
because the wisdom that is either defiled or undefiled is not firm therein.
Nor is there a heavenly realm [among them],
because we clearly perceive the fruits of various wholesome and unwholesome karmas;
with the exception of Uttarakuru.
Because they possess an extremely evil *āśaya*, this is referred to as "intention" (*āśaya*);
it pertains exclusively to male and female bodies,
for their mental disposition is fixed.
Regarding "the abandonment of those who act through views" (*dṛṣṭicarita-prahāṇa-aprāpti*):
here, the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) applies both above and below;
it refers exclusively to those who act through views.
They are able to sever the roots of goodness;
they are those who practice what is unlovely,
while others practice what is lovely.
Because those who act according to views possess an evil *āśaya* (disposition) that is extremely restless.
Because the *āśaya* (intent) is extremely firm and deep;
by this principle.
Those such as the *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others are not capable of severing the roots of goodness,
because they belong to the category of those whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*). Furthermore, as for this class of persons:
Because it is like an evil destiny, it is called "the practice of one who sees":
this means that through one's own wisdom, one perceives the principle and then acts accordingly.
One who acts out of attachment merely follows the words of others and practices out of a fondness for them.
Regarding "the abandonment of non-acquisition," it should be understood that its essence is the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of what is to be abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to the stage of severing the roots of goodness,
wherein wholesome acquisitions do not arise and non-acquisitions continue to arise.
It is at the stage when non-possession arises that one is said to have severed the roots of goodness; therefore, this is called the severing of the roots of goodness.
Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is its essence.
Regarding those who have severed the roots of goodness and harbor doubt about existence:
"doubt" refers to doubting existence.
"Seeing" refers to right view.
This means that within the arising of cause and effect, there is a mind characterized by doubt;
this [doubt] may indeed exist.
From a mind characterized by doubt,
one may give rise to right view;
one becomes certain that [the self] exists and is not non-existent.
At that time, the roots of goodness are able to resume their arising;
therefore, it is called "reconnecting the roots of goodness. There is doubt as to whether there is such a reconnecting of the roots of goodness.
Doubt does not sever the roots of goodness;
in order to distinguish it from that which lacks [the capacity to sever them], it is said that doubt exists [as a root].
Regarding "suddenly manifesting for those who have committed the immediate transgressions":
"suddenly" refers to the roots of goodness; it means that the nine grades [of roots] are restored all at once.
Thereafter, at a later time,
it gradually manifests,
just as when an illness is cured all at once.
His strength gradually increases.
"The present" refers to the present life;
it means that one continues the roots of goodness in this present body, with the exception of those who have committed a heinous offense.
The Sūtra states that those who commit the heinous crimes and sever the roots of goodness will certainly manifest [the results] in their present bodies.
Unable to continue their roots of goodness,
they will certainly emerge from hell;
they are on the verge of passing away and being reborn.
Only then can they reconnect with the roots of goodness;
when they have finished experiencing the retribution of the hells,
it is called "about to pass away."
Abiding in the intermediate state and not yet having been born into hell is called "about to be born."
If, by the power of causes consisting of past habitual tendencies toward false views, [one acts].
Those who have severed their roots of goodness will reconnect them at the time of death,
provided that the power of present conditions for false teachings is absent.
When those who have severed the roots of virtue are about to be reborn, they reconnect them through their own power or the power of others;
it should be understood that this is likewise the case for those who "themselves" refer to themselves as seeking [the truth].
He says this refers to encountering evil friends.
Furthermore, it is the destruction of delight,
not the destruction of application.
Such a person is able to reconnect their roots of goodness in the present life; however,
if both are destroyed, [it cannot be so].
It continues only upon death.
One sees that although the precepts have been broken,
the continuity of virtue still persists even in the present life.
When both precepts and views are destroyed,
one must maintain the continuity of the auspicious signs and rituals after death;
this is called "the non-destruction of precepts."
There are those who sever the roots of goodness but do not fall into wrong views; regarding this,
one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding the first phrase:
*pūrṇa* (布賴那) and so forth; here it means "full.
To give rise to wrong views is called "severing the roots of goodness."
Not having committed an act of immediate retribution does not mean one is not fixed in the wrong.
As for the second phrase, it refers to those such as Ajātaśatru.
One who commits a heinous crime falls into wrong determination;
yet, by having faith in the Buddha, they do not sever their roots of goodness.
As for the third phrase:
This refers to Devadatta and others: one who gives rise to false views is said to sever the roots of goodness;
by committing the three immediate transgressions, one falls into the state of fixed wrongness.
The fourth phrase refers to that which excludes the aforementioned characteristics;
it follows from this as the fourth.

"Having taken advantage of this contextual opportunity..."
Having distinguished and determined the roots of goodness,
we shall now further clarify the meaning of the fundamental paths of action regarding the good and evil that have been explained.
Among the two types of courses of action,
how many arise simultaneously and function concurrently with volition?
The verse says:
Karma-paths and volition (cetanā) arise together; In the unwholesome, from one up to eight;
In the wholesome, generally opening up to ten, While specifically excluding one, eight, and five.
The commentary states:
"The paths of action that proceed together with volition" is the heading.
"Volition" refers to the volition that arises simultaneously with the moment [of action].
This clarifies that the path of action and the volition that initiates it function concurrently within the same moment.
"From one up to eight unwholesome [factors]" clarifies that the unwholesome courses of action (karmapatha) may number from one to eight.
It functions together with volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding "functioning as one," there are two types.
Furthermore, regarding the first [type],
it refers to being free from the remaining seven unwholesome material karmas among the three [types of action] beginning with greed.
Whichever one arises—
greed, hatred, or wrong view—
they necessarily do not coexist.
Therefore, they arise one by one and proceed together with volition (cetanā).
Regarding the second "one":
That is to say, through preliminary effort,
such as dispatching an agent to kill and so forth,
one commits the six types of unwholesome karma.
At the time of the non-defiled mind,
one of the preceding six reaches completion.
A wholesome or indeterminate mind is called "unstained"; it is when the defiled mind reaches its culmination [that the state changes].
It is established that both [minds] operate simultaneously;
therefore, it is said to be "uncontaminated.
This means that by excluding contaminated minds, it is established that both [the uncontaminated and the contaminated] operate simultaneously. As for "both operating simultaneously":
That is to say, one brings the karmic action of killing to completion with a mind of hatred; or,
if it occurs in the state of having given rise to greed.
One completes the act of taking what is not given;
or else, one gives rise to greed and completes the act of sexual misconduct.
Sometimes, when greed arises, it constitutes frivolous speech.
These four aforementioned categories are called the two courses of action (karmapatha).
Regarding those that arise together with volition (*cetanā*), as for those that arise with three [mental factors]:
this refers to when one, with a mind of hatred (*dveṣa*),
[directs it] toward a being belonging to another.
The theft consists in moving the object from its original location; the taking of life consists in severing the life-faculty;
both killing and stealing occur simultaneously.
The three [karmas] of killing, stealing,
and sexual misconduct proceed together with volition (cetanā),
as does their prior preparatory action (prayoga).
Sending assassins and so forth;
performing unwholesome physical karma;
greed, hatred, and wrong views.
First, at the moment of its actual arising,
it corresponds to two of the preceding [factors], such as killing, for their completion.
Since greed and the like constitute one [path],
while killing and the like correspond to two,
three [paths] may arise simultaneously.
Regarding the fourfold simultaneous occurrence,
there are three categories. The first fourfold set refers to the desire to destroy others.
Regarding false speech:
there is one path of action of the mental faculty and three paths of action of the vocal faculty.
Because it causes division among others, it is divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
Because it speaks what is false and deceptive, it further constitutes deceitful speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). This is a defiled utterance.
It must necessarily be mixed with impurity.
Thus, there are three types of verbal karma; the second set of four is:
furthermore, wishing to destroy another.
Harsh speech constitutes one path of mental action and three paths of vocal action.
Because it causes division among others, it is divisive speech;
because it speaks what is coarse and harsh, it further constitutes harsh speech; this is defiled utterance.
It must necessarily be mixed with impurity.
Therefore, regarding the three types of verbal karma, the third and fourth [cases] involve a prior preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
By such acts as sending assassins to kill and so forth,
one creates unwholesome karma of form; at that time,
greed and other afflictions manifest before one.
Regarding the previously mentioned [karmas] such as killing,
they are completed according to three [factors]; since greed and the others are each one [factor], [the completion is determined by them].
Because killing and the others each correspond to three [mental factors], four [factors] may arise together.
As for five arising together:
That is to say, having previously engaged in preparatory effort,
one performs a physical action of evil,
and greed and so forth become manifest.
Regarding the six [mental factors] that arise simultaneously with the four ultimate [wholesome states]: when greed and so forth manifest, [these six arise together].
Regarding the seven [mental factors] that operate together with the five ultimate [afflictions]: when greed and so forth are manifest, they function in conjunction with those five.
The six [mental factors] follow the ultimate [states]; this should be understood according to what was stated above.
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of eight:
In the stage of application,
one eliminates the instigators who commit the six types of evil karma, such as killing.
One commits sexual misconduct oneself;
these seven courses of action are completed simultaneously.
Because one practices sexual misconduct, there is necessarily a covetous mind;
thus, eight [mental factors] arise together: covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.
Since self-power manifests itself and necessarily does not coexist [with other powers],
there are no nine or ten [powers].
Arising individually and sequentially together with volition (*cetanā*), these are called "wholesome [actions] by their own power.
Generally opening them up, they extend to ten: namely, the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).
Taking both the manifest and the hidden as the basis,
this is called a general opening;
"hidden" refers to neutral wholesomeness (*avyākṛta-kuśala*).
"Manifest" refers to the restraint (*saṃvara*).
When discussing both the manifest and the unmanifest together,
there are ten that can arise simultaneously.
Based on their manifest characteristics,
there is neither one nor eight [mental factors],
nor is there the simultaneous occurrence of five.
This refers exclusively to the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*) and does not concern those who abide in the intermediate state;
thus it is called "manifest."
Furthermore, regarding the two that function together within the manifest [consciousness], there are two types.
First, as for the initial pair:
This means that when the five wholesome consciousnesses manifest, the seven types of non-distracted wholesome [mental states] are absent.
Because the five wholesome consciousnesses are non-conceptual, they possess non-attachment and non-hatred.
There is one [type] lacking right view;
the second consists of two,
namely those based on the formless realm.
When the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising manifest,
the seven types of non-dispersed wholesome [dharmas] do not exist.
Based on the formless realm,
there are seven types of fixed precepts; based on the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising, there are [the remaining] two.
There is non-greed and non-hatred because seeking has ceased; however,
there is no right view and no non-distracted wholesome states.
This refers to not receiving the non-restraint of the desire realm;
"three [factors] operate together" means they coexist with right view.
When the corresponding mental consciousness is present,
there are no seven types of material wholesome states.
Because of this right view,
there must necessarily be the three paths of action consisting of non-greed, non-hatred, and right view.
As for the absence of the seven material [paths]:
This refers to not receiving the precepts and not entering meditative concentration; thus,
the seven types of wholesome form do not exist.
Regarding the fourfold simultaneous occurrence:
this refers to when an unwholesome or neutral mind is present,
one obtains the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a one-day practitioner (*upavāsa*), or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).
Because they are unwholesome or neutral,
the three [roots] beginning with non-attachment do not exist;
one receives the vows of the Upavāsa and so forth.
Thus, there are four types of virtuous discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
namely the three of body and one of speech;
this refers to the precepts of the four branches.
Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of six [mental factors]:
this refers to when the five wholesome consciousnesses manifest.
One attains the first three types of precepts—
namely, those of the lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth— because they are associated with the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
There are non-attachment and non-hatred;
in addition to the previous four,
non-attachment and non-hatred are added.
Thus, six [mental factors] are established.
Regarding those that operate in conjunction with seven, there are two types.
Furthermore, regarding the first seven [consciousnesses], they are the wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
which lacks accompanying derived matter (*anuvartaka-rūpa*).
When right view is present and associated with it,
one attains the three higher precepts.
This refers to lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) and others;
because they are associated with right view, they necessarily possess the three [wholesome roots]: non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view.
Because one obtains the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth,
there are further four branches;
thus, they constitute seven.
In the second seven-day period,
when an unwholesome or neutral mind manifests in the present moment.
Upon receiving the bhikṣu precepts,
one accomplishes seven types of virtuous non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Regarding the ninefold simultaneous occurrence:
This consists of three types.
The first set of nine refers to the five wholesome consciousnesses.
When it manifests before one,
the bhikṣu-precepts are obtained,
because the five consciousnesses are wholesome.
There are non-greed and non-hatred through which one obtains the bhikṣu precepts;
together with the seven types of material wholesome [karma], they constitute nine.
The second ninth [type of knowledge] is that which,
based on the formless realm, consists of the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
When it manifests before them,
they obtain the bhikṣu precepts by virtue of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
There is one [factor], right view;
there are two, non-attachment and non-hatred;
and one obtains the bhikṣu precepts.
There are seven wholesome [states] of form;
thus, nine are established.
As for the third set of nine:
That is to say, when the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, which are subsumed under meditative concentration, manifest before one.
Because of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
there are seven types of concentration-precepts (*samādhi-śīla*); because of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Because there are non-attachment and non-hatred,
nine [mental factors] are established.
As for the ten that operate together:
This is of two kinds.
The first ten refers to the wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
There is no concomitant matter when right view is present and associated with it.
One obtains the bhikṣu precepts by means of right view;
there are the three factors, such as non-greed,
through which one obtains the bhikṣu precepts.
There are seven wholesome [karmas] of form;
thus, they constitute ten. The twentieth is:
That is to say, all other [factors] have concomitant matter that is associated with right view.
At the stage when the mind is currently arising,
there are seven types of meditative precepts (dhyāna-śīla) corresponding to the derivative matter (anuvartaka-rūpa).
Because it is associated with right view,
there are three factors beginning with right view;
this is called the "tenfold simultaneous occurrence."
The treatise says:
Based on the distinct manifest characteristics,
that which is negated is as follows.
If one considers both the manifest and the hidden states,
there is nothing that is excluded;
this refers to being apart from the vows of restraint (saṃvara).
One commentary (No. 185) explains:
"Virtue that abides in the middle is called 'abstention from the code of discipline' (*virati-saṃvara*)."
This is because they are not vows of restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Regarding "arising together with one":
this refers to an unwholesome or neutral mind.
When it is present before one,
one attains the precept of abstaining from one limb while experiencing another limb.
Regarding the fivefold simultaneous occurrence:
It refers to wholesome mental consciousness that lacks accompanying form and is associated with right view.
Regarding the statement "attaining two factors," etc.,
the commentary explains that there are three [factors], such as right view, which are associated with right view.
Furthermore, by attaining the two branches of seclusion,
they become five. As for the term "etcetera":
In the case of an unwholesome or neutral mind that includes [other factors],
one attains the fivefold abstention.
Regarding the eightfold simultaneous occurrence:
This means that when this mental consciousness manifests,
one attains the understanding of the five factors and so forth.
Prior to this, the mental consciousness possesses the three factors beginning with right view;
it further acquires five branches.
This constitutes the eight [factors]. "Etc. refers to the inclusion of the wholesome five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
When these are present, one attains the sixfold distancing (*ṣaḍ-vidha-viveka*).
From this, it is the fifth.
Virtue and non-virtue are established in relation to their bases.
The *Śāstra* states:
"The paths of virtuous and non-virtuous karma..."
In which realms, destinies, and locations are how many [factors] established as mere possession (*samanvāgama*),
and how many also function as manifest activity (*samudācāra*)?
The verse says:
In the unwholesome hells, [the unwholesome roots] are present; Coarse speech, malicious speech, and anger are common to both [present and possessed];
Greed and wrong view are possessed [but not necessarily present]. In the northern continent (Uttarakuru), the latter three are possessed;
Frivolous speech is common to both present and possessed; The remaining ten [unwholesome courses of action] in the desire realm are common to both.
Skilled in all locations: the latter three [attainments] are both actualized and possessed;
in the formless realms and the realm of non-perception, they are only possessed. The former seven are only possessed;
in other locations, they are both actualized and possessed—excluding the hells and the northern continent.
The commentary states:
In the unwholesome hells, coarse speech, frivolous chatter, and malice pertain to both;
these are the ten unwholesome courses of action.
In the hells, there are only harsh speech and frivolous speech.
Hatred. These three [factors] each pertain to two types:
namely, the two kinds of possession (samanvāgama) and active manifestation (samudācāra).
From mutual abuse, harsh speech arises;
from lamentation, [harsh speech arises].
There is frivolous speech;
because of mutual hatred, there is ill will.
For one who has accomplished greed and wrong view,
these two are accomplished within this hell.
Yet they do not manifest;
because there are no desirable objects,
craving does not manifest, as they directly perceive the fruits of karma.
Wrong views do not arise;
furthermore, because one dies in the hells when karma is exhausted.
There is no path of action consisting of killing;
there is no taking of property;
there is no path of action consisting of theft.
There are no women to be possessed;
there is no sin of sexual misconduct.
The mirror of karma appears before one.
One must not refuse or conceal [the truth],
because it would be useless; thus,
there is no false speech.
Precisely because of this lack of purpose and because they are always separated,
there is no divisive speech.
Regarding the three [faculties] accomplished after the formation of the Northern Continent: in Uttarakuru,
the final three are accomplished.
Greed, hatred, and wrong views do not manifest;
he does not amass wealth or possessions.
Because they regard [others] as themselves,
greed does not manifest; their bodies and minds are supple,
and they are free from affliction and harm.
Hatred does not manifest because there is no malicious intention;
false view does not manifest; and frivolous speech manifests both as active and as latent.
[This refers to] the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
Frivolous speech pertains to both manifestation and accomplishment,
because it occurs at times.
Because a defiled mind used for singing lacks the intention of malice, it does not involve those six [unwholesome courses of action], such as killing and so forth.
Furthermore, because their lifespan is fixed,
there is no killing; and because they possess no property, there is no taking of wealth.
Therefore, there is no stealing.
There is no taking of women.
Therefore, there is no sexual misconduct.
Because the body and mind are supple,
there is no harsh or evil speech,
nor is there anything useless.
They refrain from divisive speech and false speech;
they do not engage in unchaste conduct in that place.
That is to say, those men and women,
holding hands and leading one another,
went beneath the tree.
If tree branches hang down and cover [the path],
one should know that it is a place where one ought to travel;
if the trees do not hang down their branches, one should not go.
Feeling ashamed, they took their leave. Regarding the phrase "the remaining [beings] who desire both [liberation and worldly success]":
this refers to those within the remainder of the desire realm—namely, devas, pretas, and animals.
As for the inhabitants of the three continents,
they possess both the possession (*samanvāgama*) and the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the ten paths of unwholesome action.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction between devas and ghosts.
Regarding animals:
among the seven preceding courses of action,
there are only those that are intermediate.
There is no non-restraint (asaṃvara).
Among humans in the three continents, both types exist.
Regarding the wholesome [faculties], they exist in all places; as for the latter three, they are both acquired through actualization and by birth.
This clarifies the ten paths of wholesome action.
Throughout all places within the three realms and five destinies.
The three [wholesome roots], beginning with non-attachment,

are all present both as actualized factors (*samudācāra*) and as possessed factors (*samanvāgama*). In the formless realm and the heaven of non-perception, the first seven [wholesome roots] exist solely as possessed factors.
This refers to noble beings born in the formless realm who possess the sevenfold untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) of the past and future; because they lack form,
[they do not possess the physical restraint].
They certainly do not manifest in the Heaven of Non-conception,
because there is no mind present there.
Nor does it manifest;

rather, one merely possesses the past and future dhyāna-restraints (*dhyāna-saṃvara*). However, for an Arhat in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), [the restraint] exists within the bodies of the five stages of the past desire and form realms.
Depending on whichever level—
whether two, three, four, or five levels—
one has previously generated and subsequently ceased the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).
When one is born into the formless realm,
one establishes that past [state] which once arose in a single stage; thus,
one establishes the past morality of that single stage.
Up to the point where one has previously arisen in the five stages,
this constitutes the past precepts of the five stages. If, in a future life,
one relies upon a body belonging to the five stages...
Regarding the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*):
it is invariably accomplished in five stages—the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
In other locations, both the possession and manifestation [of this restraint] are generally established, with the exception of those in the hells and the northern continent (Uttarakuru).
The remaining realms of desire and form,
comprising humans, devas, and four of the five destinies,
excluding those in the hells and the northern continent.
These are termed "other instances.
Regarding the seven branches of body and speech,
each applies both to manifest activity (*samudācāra*) and to possession (*samanvāgama*).
However, there is a distinction:
among ghosts and animals,
there is intermediate wholesome [karma].
If it pertains to the form realm (rūpadhātu),
there is only restraint (saṃvara); [it exists] in the three continents and among the gods of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
All are fully present within the middle [category].
Regarding the two types of restraint,
this is the sixth [point] from here.
This clarifies the three fruits of the paths of action.
The treatise states:
"The paths of unwholesome and wholesome action..."
What are the fruits obtained?
The verse says:
All are able to bring about the ripened fruit (vipākaphala), the fruit of equal outflow (niṣyandaphala), and the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala).
"This causes others to suffer, severs life, and destroys majesty.
The commentary states:
"The first two lines generally clarify the three realms."
The final two lines separately explain the reasons for this.
Regarding the fact that the ten paths of unwholesome action all bring about the three results— retributive (vipāka), outflowing (niṣyanda), and dominant (adhipati)—
it is because one dies from here and is reborn in the hells (*naraka*).
This is the ripened fruit (vipākaphala).
When one is reborn among humans,
one experiences the concordant fruit (niṣyandaphala).
That is to say, one who kills has a short lifespan;
one who takes what is not given...
One who lacks wealth and resources will have an unchaste wife if they engage in sexual misconduct.
Because of speaking falsehoods,
one frequently encounters slander.
As for divisive speech:
When one's close friends and kin are discordant,
those who speak harsh and evil words will constantly hear unpleasant sounds.
Because of idle chatter,
one's speech lacks majesty and gravity;
because of greed, one's craving becomes excessive.
For one who is prone to anger, anger increases;
for one with wrong views, delusion increases.
As for the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala):
All their requisites, due to killing,
lack luster and are meager;
due to taking what is not given...
It frequently suffers from frost and hail due to sexual misconduct;
it is filled with much dust and grime.
Because of false speech,
there is much foulness and impurity;
because of divisive speech...
The dwelling place is rugged and crooked due to coarse and evil speech;
the fields abound with thorns and are parched, stony, and saline.
Because of idle chatter,
the seasons change irregularly;
because of greed, the fruit is meager.
Because of anger, the fruit is bitter;
because of wrong views, the fruit is meager or non-existent.
Question: For what reason do these ten each bring about three fruits?
Answer: Because they cause others to experience suffering.
It severs life and destroys majesty;
therefore, first among them, killing causes others to suffer.
One experiences the fruit of maturation because of taking the life of another;
one experiences the fruit of outflow.
It causes others to lose their majesty and results in the experience of increased karmic retribution;
this applies to the remaining paths of unwholesome action as well.
One should reflect upon this according to reason.
By means of this, one should infer accordingly that there are three fruits of wholesome karma.
By abstaining from killing and so forth,
one is born among the gods and experiences the fruit of maturation.
When reborn among humans, one experiences the result concordant with the cause (niṣyanda-phala),
namely, being free from killing.
One attains a long life span;
the other results in the opposite,
as should be explained according to principle.
From here begins the eleventh major section,
which specifically elucidates wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The treatise states:
Furthermore, a sutra states that among the eight factors of the wrong path (*mithyāmārga*),
bodily action (*kāyakarma*) is divided into three.
This refers to wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
Having abandoned wrong speech and wrong action,
what is wrong livelihood?
Although it does not exist apart from them,
they are explained separately.
The verse says:
Bodily and vocal actions born of greed are [included here] because wrong livelihood is difficult to eliminate;
thus, one clings to the requisites for life as being born of greed. This is irrational because it contradicts the sūtras. Commentary:
Vocal karma arising from hatred and delusion is called wrong speech;
bodily karma arising from hatred and delusion is called wrong action.
That which arises from greed—
Because the two types of action— bodily and vocal—
are difficult to eliminate,
wrong livelihood is established separately.
That is to say, greed can seize the minds of all sentient beings;
the karma they initiate through it is difficult to rescue or protect against.
In order to encourage diligent cultivation regarding the True Dharma,
the Buddha sets this apart from the preceding [categories] and explains it as a single [separate] item. As a verse says:
The wrong views of the laity are difficult to eliminate because worldly people constantly cling to divergent opinions;
the wrong livelihoods of those on the Path are difficult to guard because monastics have departed from the world.

Regarding the statement, "Because the requisites belong to others, attachment to the means of livelihood arises," other masters maintain that this refers to the means of livelihood as the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Bodily and verbal actions arising from greed are called wrong livelihood; however,
not all instances of greed are termed wrong livelihood.
Although entertainment, song, and chanting arise from greed, they do not support one’s life;
therefore, they are not wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). As for the claim that [this view] is irrational because it contradicts the Sūtras, this refutes the explanation of other masters.
This explanation contradicts the sūtras;
for in the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*,
it mentions watching elephant fights and the like.
The World-Honored One likewise stands upon wrong livelihood;
he improperly receives external objects and falsely prolongs his life.
Therefore, based on this scriptural passage,
whatever arises from greed is termed wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
This concludes the third major section.
This section provides a comprehensive explanation of various karmas,
divided therein into ten parts.
The first explains how karma attains its fruit.
Second, the exposition of the karma of the root treatise;
third, the exposition of the causes of projection and fulfillment;
fourth, the exposition of the threefold obstructions.
The fifth clarifies the three temporal obstacles;
the sixth clarifies the characteristics of a bodhisattva;
the seventh clarifies generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Eight, clarifying the three categories of karma in accordance with the [Abhidharma] divisions;
nine, clarifying the essential natures of writing and so forth;
ten, clarifying the various alternative names for dharmas.
Regarding the first [section], the clarification of how karma obtains its fruit, it is divided into six parts:
(1) a general clarification of the fruits of all karmas;
(2) the fruits corresponding to the three natures;...
Third, the fruit of the relative correspondence of the three time periods;
fourth, the fruit of the relative correspondence of the various stages;
fifth, the fruit of the relative correspondence of the three trainings.
Sixth, the mutual relationship between causes and effects.
First, to provide a general explanation of the fruits of various karmas,
the treatise states:
As previously stated, there are five kinds of fruits.
Among these, which karma possesses how many fruits?
The verse says:
The path of abandonment consists of outflowing karma, which possesses all five fruits;
non-outflowing karma has four, namely, excluding only the ripening fruit.
Furthermore, other outflowing wholesome and unwholesome karma also have four, excluding the fruit of disjunction.
The remaining untainted (*anāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) [dharmas], excluding the three previously excluded.
Commentary: Regarding the "path of abandonment" (*prahāṇamārga*).
Regarding the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*): by means of the path of uninterrupted transition, one can realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through abandonment,
as well as sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It receives the name "path of abandonment.
As for the statement that "this path is of two kinds," this refers to its encompassing both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the statement that "outflowing karma possesses all five fruits":
this refers to any outflowing karma within the aforementioned path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
It is endowed with five fruits;
being contaminated (*sāsrava*),
it can produce its own level's desirable matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) and outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
This refers to those similar dharmas within one's own stage that are either equal to or superior to it.
The fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) is the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized through the abandonment of afflictions.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) refers to the coexistent human effort (*sahabhū-puruṣakāra*) induced by the Path.
That is to say, it is that which is drawn forth by the Path;
next, it is the immediate human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*);
and finally, it is that which is cultivated by the Path.
Future merit is separated by human effort (*puruṣakāra*),
namely that which is realized through the Path.
Regarding the fact that all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) do not produce the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) or the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala):
this means they are devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
As for other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
excluding those that have already arisen;
and as for uncontaminated karma (*anāsravakarma*), there are four [results], namely, excluding only the ripened result (*vipākaphala*).
Regarding the path previously abandoned,
if it is untainted karma (anāsrava-karma),
it possesses all four fruits.
Because the untainted (anāsrava) does not produce a fruit,
it excludes the ripening [fruit]. Likewise,
among the remaining tainted (sāsrava) wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas], there are also four [fruits], excluding the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga).
Because it differs from the preceding path of abandonment,
it is described as "the remainder"; that is,
the remaining contaminated [phenomena].
Whether wholesome or unwholesome,
they likewise have four fruits,
because they are not the path of abandonment.
Excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*),

the remaining untainted (*anāsrava*) and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) [dharmas] are threefold; excluding those previously excluded, and excluding the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) mentioned before.
The remaining untainted (anāsrava) and indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas have only three fruits.
Excluding the previously excluded [karmas of] maturation and dissociation, because those that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) do not bring about results;
and excluding the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*), because it is not a path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*).
Excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*),
next is the second [category]:
the fruits in relation to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The treatise states:
Having already provided a general analysis of how all karmas possess fruits,
we shall next distinguish them according to various categories.
There are characteristics of the fruits of karma.
Among these, the fruits of the three types of karma—wholesome and so forth—are first distinguished.
The verse says:

Regarding wholesome [actions] and so forth, there are four, two, and three results for the first; two, three, and four for the middle; and two, three, and three for the last. The commentary says: *kuśalādyāḥ kuśalādīnāṃ caturdvitryekam adhyamāḥ / phalaṃ dvitricatustridhā // VAkK_4.89 //* [The results of] wholesome [actions] and so forth, with respect to wholesome [dharmas] and so forth, are four, two, three, and one [respectively]; the intermediate [results] are two, three, and four; and the last are two, three, and three. The commentary states: Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate actions are each divided into three types according to their nature: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. Among these, the results of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate actions, when considered in relation to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas, are respectively four, two, and three; two, three, and four; and two, three, and three. First, regarding wholesome actions: they have four results when related to wholesome dharmas—namely, the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the result of dominance (*adhipatiphala*), the result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and the result of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*). They have two results when related to unwholesome dharmas—the result of human effort and the result of dominance. They have three results when related to indeterminate dharmas—the result of maturation, the result of human effort, and the result of dominance. Second, regarding unwholesome actions: they have two results when related to wholesome dharmas—the result of human effort and the result of dominance. They have three results when related to unwholesome dharmas—the result of maturation, the result of human effort, and the result of dominance. They have four results when related to indeterminate dharmas—the result of maturation, the result of human effort, the result of dominance, and the result of disconnection. Third, regarding indeterminate actions: they have two results when related to wholesome dharmas—the result of human effort and the result of dominance. They have three results when related to unwholesome dharmas—the result of human effort, the result of dominance, and the result of maturation. They have three results when related to indeterminate dharmas—the result of human effort, the result of dominance, and the result of maturation. This concludes the explanation.
Regarding "wholesome and so forth with respect to wholesome and so forth":
the superior wholesome and so forth are karma;
the inferior wholesome and so forth are dharmas.
This includes both unwholesome and neutral [actions]. Taking wholesome and other types of karma as the referent,
they are related to wholesome and other types of phenomena.
This clarifies the number of fruits: namely,
the three types of karma— wholesome and so forth—
and the two aggregates of form and formations.
A small portion constitutes its essence;
the three dharmas, such as the wholesome and so forth,
have the five aggregates as their essence.
Regarding the statement "at first there are four, two, and three":
"first" refers to wholesome karma;
it takes wholesome phenomena as its four fruits.
Excluding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*),
wholesome karma takes unwholesome phenomena as two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
The superior [cause] is that which is produced by being well-guided;
this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
That wholesome dharmas do not obstruct [it] is its dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Wholesome karma [produces] indeterminate dharmas.
They constitute three fruits,
excluding the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*),
because their natures are dissimilar.
Excluding the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), because [non-analytical cessation] is not [a result of maturation];
excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Regarding the phrase "among which there are two, three, or four":
"middle" refers to the unwholesome (akuśala),
as it lies between the wholesome (kuśala) and the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Therefore it is called "middling.
Unwholesome karma takes wholesome dharmas as its two fruits.
Unwholesome dharmas constitute three fruits;
indeterminate dharmas constitute four fruits.
As for what are called the two fruits:
This refers to the predominance of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhipati*).
Regarding the statement "three fruits," this excludes the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
Regarding the statement "the four fruits," this refers exclusively to the state of being free from fetters (*visamyoga*).
Question: [What is the relationship between] the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
What constitutes the outflow (niṣyanda)?
The answer is: the universal unwholesome [karmas], as well as the remaining unwholesome karmas to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya).
It acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Since the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*),
it is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the latter two [fetters], and the fruit of the third [fetter].
"Subsequent" refers to the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Because it follows after the wholesome and unwholesome,
this indeterminate karma takes wholesome dharmas as its two fruits.
Unwholesome dharmas serve as three fruits;
indeterminate dharmas [serve as two].
It also constitutes three fruits. Regarding the taking of wholesome dharmas as two fruits: these are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Regarding the taking of unwholesome dharmas as three fruits: [these are the same two, plus the ripened fruit].
Excluding the ripening [result] and the disjunction [from defilements]. Question:
What are the unwholesome and the indeterminate?
They are outflows (*niṣyanda*).
Answer: The [two views of] self and extremes (*satkāya-antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), being neutral (*avyākṛta*), act as similar-type causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Unwholesome dharmas serve as the outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala) for [unwholesome dharmas],
while neutral dharmas [serve as such] for [neutral dharmas].
Regarding those that serve as the three fruits:
excluding the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) and the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyoga-phala),
these follow from the third [cause].
This clarifies the results of the three periods of time.
The treatise states:
"The three natures have already been analyzed."
In distinguishing the three time periods, the verse says:
Past [karma] has four fruits in each of the three times; the present likewise has four in the future.
The present has two fruits in the present; the future has three fruits in the future.
The commentary states:
This [passage] correlates the karma of the three time periods with the phenomena of the three time periods.
It constitutes the differentiation of results.
These three periods of karma consist of the two aggregates of form and formations.
A small portion constitutes its essence;
as for dharmas of the three periods of time,
the five aggregates constitute their essence.
Regarding "exceeding three by four each," this refers to past karma in relation to the phenomena of the three time periods.
Each constitutes four fruits,
with the exception of disjunction;
as it is for the present, so it is for the future as well.
Karma of the present life,
with respect to future dharmas,
likewise has only four fruits.
It is the same as the number [of fruits] mentioned previously; therefore, it is said that "it is likewise.
Regarding the two fruits manifested in the present:
This refers to karma in the present life,
which, by means of present phenomena,
constitutes two fruits.
That is to say: the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) and the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala);
as for the three [fruits] that have not yet arisen, they are not yet fruits.
This refers to future karma;
with respect to future dharmas,
there are only three fruits.
Excluding the outflowing (niṣyanda) and the dissociated (visamyoga) fruits,
it is not stated that a subsequent action has a preceding fruit,
because a preceding dharma is certainly not the fruit of a subsequent action.
From this fourth [section] onward,
the fruits of the various stages (*bhūmi*) are clarified.
The treatise states:
The three time periods have already been explained;
now the various stages (bhūmi) shall be explained.
The verse says:
"Of the same stage there are four fruits; of different stages, two or three.
The commentary states:
This refers to karma according to the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the method for observing the various stages:
one should know that the activities of the stages serve to differentiate their respective fruits.
Only a small portion of the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
As for the dharmas of the various stages, they pertain to all five aggregates.
Regarding those belonging to the same stage, there are four types of results.
Among the nine stages,
whichever stage's karma it may be,
it is [perfumed] by the dharmas of that same stage.
They constitute four fruits,
excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) and either two or three fruits depending on whether they belong to a different stage;
this applies if they are contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karma*).
Dharmas of a different stage constitute two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
This applies to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) karma.
Taking dharmas of a different stage as three fruits:
to the two previously mentioned fruits,
one further adds the outflow fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
Because it does not fall within the realms [of existence],
there is a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
This is the fifth [topic] following from this.
Regarding the three fruits beginning with "clear knowledge" (vidyā),
the treatise states:
"The various stages have already been distinguished."
Now, to distinguish those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, the verse says:
Those in training [possess] three [kinds of knowledge] for each of the three [paths]; Those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) [possess] one, three, and two.
Regarding "neither-learner-nor-non-learner," there are two, three, or five fruits.
The commentary states:
this is based on the three types of karma, namely, that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.
The three dharmas, beginning with that of the learner (*śaikṣa*),
serve as the distinctions of the fruit; [likewise] the three types of action, beginning with that of the learner.
It consists solely of a small portion of the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*):
namely, the untainted (*anāsrava*) morality within the aggregate of form belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of volition (*cetanā*) associated with the Path; the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*);
a portion of contaminated form (*sāsrava-rūpa*); and the three categories of phenomena beginning with the learner (*śaikṣa*).
This encompasses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
It includes phenomena that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-dharma*), as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (*trividha-asamskṛta*).
"Training in each of the three, threefold" refers to the training of those in training (śaikṣa) with respect to the three dharmas beginning with training itself.
Each constitutes three fruits.
Furthermore, regarding the training in the learner's stage (*śaikṣa*),
the dharmas of the learner constitute the three fruits.
Excluding the ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) and the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala),
unlearned dharmas (aśaikṣa-dharma) function as three fruits.
Furthermore, excluding the ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) and the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala),
non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas serve as three fruits.
Excluding the results of maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*),
there are one, three, and two [results] for the karma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That is to say, regarding the karma of one beyond training:
Taking the dharmas of training as a single fruit,
they are exclusively superior (adhipati).
As for the karma of those beyond training (aśaikṣa):
The dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) constitute three fruits,
excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) and the fruit of disconnection (visamyogaphala).

The karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) has two fruits when taking dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training as its objects: namely, the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala). Regarding the statement that the karma of neither-training-nor-beyond-training has two, two, and five fruits: [it has] two fruits when taking dharmas of training as its objects; two fruits when taking dharmas beyond training as its objects; and five fruits when taking dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training as its objects.
That is to say, non-learner and non-non-learner karma takes learner dharmas as two fruits— namely,
the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*)— and takes non-learner dharmas as two fruits.
This refers to the predominance of human effort (*puruṣakāra-adhipati*); non-learner and non-non-learner dharmas (*naśaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-dharma*) constitute five fruits.
Following this, the sixth [section] clarifies the three fruits, such as those abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*).
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished those [factors] to be abandoned through cultivation and so forth, one should now distinguish those to be abandoned through vision. The verse states:
Regarding karma to be abandoned by seeing and so forth, each one respectively has three, four, and one fruits in the first [category]; two, four, and three fruits in the middle;
and one, two, and four fruits in the last. All should be understood according to this sequence.
The commentary states:
This refers to the three types of karma of abandonment in relation to the three types of dharmas of abandonment.
Regarding the phrase "karma to be abandoned by seeing, etc.": the term "etc.
includes karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Furthermore, non-abandonable karma and karma abandonable by insight have as their substance only a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Karma abandonable by cultivation is neither of these two.
Both take a small portion of the two aggregates of form and formations as their essence. The phenomena abandoned by vision have the four aggregates as their essence;
the phenomena abandoned by cultivation [have the five aggregates as their essence].
Its substance consists of the five aggregates;
it is comprised of non-abandonable dharmas,
namely the five untainted (anāsrava) aggregates.
And as for those having the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their essence:
"each one [acts] with respect to each of the three" means that the karma of the three abandonments (*prahāṇa*) each functions as a fruit with respect to the dharmas of the three abandonments.
This sentence provides the general heading.
Regarding the phrase "the first consists of three, four, and one":
"the first" refers to karma to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Taking the dharmas abandoned by seeing as three fruits;
taking the dharmas abandoned by cultivation [as three fruits].
There are four fruits.
Taking non-abandonable dharmas as one fruit, there are three fruits [of the path].
Regarding these three fruits:
Excluding the results of maturation (vipāka) and those dissociated from bondage (visamyoga),
dharmas abandoned by vision (darśana-prahātavya) are exclusively defiled (kliṣṭa).
It is not a maturation result.
Regarding the statement "four results," this excludes the result of disjunction.
Regarding the statement "one fruit":
this refers exclusively to the increase [of wholesome roots].
Regarding the "middle two, four, and three fruits": [this refers to the intermediate stages].
"Middle" refers to karma to be abandoned through cultivation;
because it lies between the two types of abandonment,
it is called "middle."
If karma to be abandoned by cultivation takes dharmas to be abandoned by seeing as its two fruits.
Those dharmas abandoned by cultivation constitute four fruits;
those dharmas not to be abandoned [constitute]...

There are three fruits. Regarding the two fruits: they are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Regarding the four fruits: [they are the same as above, plus] the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of separation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Excluding dissociation (*visamyoga*).
Regarding the statement "three fruits," this excludes the ripened (*vipāka*) and the outflowing (*niṣyanda*) fruits.
Regarding the phrase "later, one, two, or four":
"later" refers to karma that is not to be abandoned,
because it is [the result of] dharmas abandoned through seeing.
It has one fruit;
with dharmas abandoned through cultivation,
it has two fruits.
Taking the dharmas not to be abandoned as four fruits,
that which is called the "one fruit" is as follows:
This refers to predominance (*adhipati*).
Regarding the statement "two fruits," these are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

Regarding the statement "as for the four fruits, excluding the maturation [fruit], they should all be understood in their respective order": this means that, with the exception of the maturation fruit, the remaining three fruits should be understood according to their sequence.
These apply universally across the six preceding gates as appropriate;
the assigned causes and effects all follow their respective order. As for why [the term] "only" (*eva*) is placed at the end: it is to indicate that the preceding terms are not exhaustive.
The abbreviated method should be thus.
From this, the second major section explains the karma of the root treatise.
The treatise says:
Having distinguished the various types of karma,
one should further ask:
As stated in the root treatise, there are three types of karma:
namely, karma that should be performed,
and karma that should not be performed.
It is neither karma that should be performed nor karma that should not be performed.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Defiled karma is not to be performed; some say that which violates proper decorum is also so.
Karma that is to be performed is the opposite of this; the third category is that which is contrary to both.
The commentary states:
"Defiled karma should not be performed.
Some say that the three types of defiled karma [are what should not be performed].
It is called "that which should not be done" because it arises from improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
Some say that it also refers to that which violates the rules of decorum.

Other masters say that not only is defiled karma called "that which should not be done," but conduct that violates the rules of decorum is also called "that which should not be done. Regarding this violation of decorum:
This is an indeterminate action (*avyākṛta-karman*).
One should act and abide in this manner;
one should wear clothing and consume food in this manner.
If it were not thus, it would be called "that which should not be done," for it would contravene the rules of propriety.
Regarding "actions that ought to be performed," those which are the opposite of what ought not to be performed are called actions that ought to be performed.
Some say that wholesome karma is called "what should be done" (*kārya*); other masters say:
Action that accords with the rules is also called "that which should be done.
The third category is that which is contrary to both.
Contradicting both of the preceding two, it is called the third: that which is neither to be done nor not to be done.
If one relies on the first explanation:
It is exclusively indeterminate karma.
This is according to the explanation of the second master,
excluding the case of formal rules (*ācāra*).
The others are neutral (avyākṛta).
This concludes the third section,
which clarifies the causes of projection and fulfillment.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the extent of karmic retribution;
second, clarifying the nature of the causes that project and fulfill [rebirth].
Furthermore, first regarding the clarification of the quantity of karmic inducement,
the treatise states:
"Does a single karma induce only a single birth?"
Is it for the purpose of projecting many births?
Furthermore, regarding a single birth, is it projected by a single karma or by multiple karmas?
The verse says:
One karma projects one birth; multiple karmas can bring it to completion.
The commentary says:
"One karma draws forth one birth" explains the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*);
it was formerly called "the karma of collective retribution."
According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
a single karma alone can only project a single birth.
If it were admitted that a single karma can project multiple births,
then karmas with fixed timing would become confused;
for if this [single] birth...
Drawn forth by manifold karma,
it should be differentiated according to the various divisions of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
for it is through the differentiation of the fruits of karma that these divisions are distinguished.
This refers to dying repeatedly and being born repeatedly; therefore, we know that a single karma only projects one birth,
whereas multiple karmas are capable of bringing it to completion.
This explains the karma of fulfillment (pūrṇakarma); formerly it was called the karma of distinct retribution (viśeṣavipākakarma).
It refers to the physical body of a single lifetime being complete and adorned.
Xu You’s manifold karmas are like a painter who first sketches the outlines with a single color and subsequently fills them in with various hues.
A single-colored figure represents a single projecting karma;
subsequently, various colors are filled in.
This is a metaphor for the abundance of tainted karma;
therefore, although there are those who equally receive a human body,
among them some possess complete limbs and physical strength, as well as majestic adornment.
There may be some omissions.
From this second [section] onward,
the nature of the causes that project and complete [existence] is clarified.
The treatise states:
"It is not only the power of karma that can project and fulfill all wholesome and unwholesome [actions]."
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are capable of both projecting and completing [rebirth],
because karma is predominant; thus,
although only the name "karma" is designated, it is within this context that [the distinction is made].
Regarding those factors coexistent with karma:
if they can both project and fulfill [rebirth], yet do not act as coexistent factors with karma,
they can fulfill [rebirth] but cannot project it.
Because their power is inferior.
What is the nature of such a category?
The verse says:
The acquisitions of the two mindless attainments cannot induce other [attainments].
The commentary explains:
"The acquisitions of the two mindless attainments" refers to...
The two mindless attainments refer to the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation. These,
together with various karmas—
Because they do not coexist,
they do not act as projecting causes;
they can only act as completing causes for that which has already been acquired.
Good and evil are obtained. They are obtained together with their respective karmas,
because they do not share a single fruit.
Only [karma] that fulfills is not projecting;
apart from these two categories,
all other wholesome and unwholesome [karma] are both.
All [of these] pertain to both the projecting and the completing [causes]. From this fourth [section],
the three obstacles are explained.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the three obstacles;
second, the specific exposition of the obstacle of karma.
This clarifies two points among the three obstacles:
first, the clarification of the essential nature of the obstacles;
second, their differentiation according to location.
Furthermore, first regarding the elucidation of the nature of the hindrances,
the treatise states:
"The Bhagavat said:"
There are three heavy obstructions:
namely, the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and [the obstruction of maturations].
The obstacle of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these three obstacles?
The verse says:
The three obstructions— uninterrupted karma (*ānantarya-karman*), as well as frequently practiced afflictions (*kleśa*) and all evil destinies (*durgati*),
and the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) and the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).
The commentary says:
The "three obstructions" is the heading;
"uninterrupted karma" specifies the essence of the obstruction of karma.
That is to say, the five deeds of immediate retribution are called karmic obstructions:
first, killing one's mother.
Second, killing one's father;
third, harming an arhat;
fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
The fifth is shedding the blood of a Buddha;
furthermore, those who frequently practice afflictions shed the substance of the afflictive hindrance.
There are two types of afflictions.
The first is habitual activity,
which refers to afflictions that arise constantly.
It pervades both the upper and lower grades.
Second is "fierce and sharp," which refers to the upper-grade afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is only with respect to frequent practice that it constitutes an afflictive hindrance;
[this refers to] afflictions of the highest degree.
As for those not characterized by habitual practice,
although they may be intense, because they do not arise constantly,
they are easily subdued and eliminated.
It is not said to be an obstruction;
although the lower-grade afflictions are not intense, they nonetheless exist.
If they are frequent occurrences,
it is because they are difficult to eliminate through counting;
therefore, they are described as hindrances.
Regardless of whether they are superior or inferior among the afflictions,
those that are frequently practiced are called the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As well as all evil destinies,
the northern continent, and the heaven of non-conception—
these constitute the essence of the obstruction of retribution.

The three evil destinies in their entirety, the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and the heaven of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva)—these are the obstructions to maturation (vipākāvaraṇa). Question: What phenomena constitute this obstruction?
Answer: It refers to that which obstructs the noble path and the preparatory application for the noble path;
it is the seven stages of expedient practice (*sapta-prayoga*).
As the treatise says:
Among these three obstructions,
both the afflictions and karma are the most serious.
Because those who possess this [defilement] cannot be cured even within their second birth;
the commentary explains: "Even in the second birth, one does not attain the Way."
It is called "incurable.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The Vaibhāṣika masters provide this explanation."
Because the former induces the latter,
the latter is lighter than the former; the commentary explains that afflictions induce karma.
Karma induces maturation; with respect to the fruit of maturation,
it is determined that no other karma or other birth can intervene.
Therefore it is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya);
or, by committing this karma,
one will inevitably fall into hell.
Because there is no interval within it,
it is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
This is the second [category] from here.
Regarding the analysis by way of categories,
the treatise states:
"One should know that there are three obstructions."
In which destinies does the intermediate state (antarābhava) exist? The verse says:
The immediate [retributions] exist in the three continents; they do not exist elsewhere, such as among the *śaṇḍha* and others.
"Little kindness and little shame; the remaining obstructions pertain to all five destinies.
The commentary states:
"The immediate [retributions] exist in the three continents, but not elsewhere, such as among the *śaṇḍha* and others."
Excluding Uttarakuru,
among the three continents,
there are only females and males.
One who commits an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karman) is not one of the others, such as the *śaṇḍha* and so forth,
because they possess little gratitude and little shame.
Regarding the explanation of *śaṇḍha* and others:
although they may kill their parents, they do not incur the karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).
This is because those parents bestow little kindness upon them.
Because they have little affection,
their sense of shame and dread of blame toward their parents is slight.
Because there is no grave debt of gratitude,
there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
By this principle, [it is established].
Even if ghosts or animals harm their parents,
they likewise do not commit an immediate transgression (ānantarya).
Furthermore, the Venerable One said:
"Among the various classes of animals,
there are those whose cognitive awareness is clear and distinct."
It also constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), just as with a wise horse;
it is as one has heard regarding certain horses.
A man, greedy for his seed,
causes him to unite with his mother;
he then realizes that she is his mother.
He was immediately overcome with shame and died.
Furthermore, if a person harms the parents of a non-human being,
it does not constitute a heinous crime (ānantarya).

they are able to bear all burdens.
Second, from this point on, the cultivation of the characteristics of action is clarified.
The treatise states:
One cultivates the karma of the marks of excellence. What are these marks?
The verse says:
A male of Jambudvīpa faces the Buddha; [the marks] are produced by reflection, cultivated over a hundred other kalpas, and each is adorned with a hundred merits.
(Commentary)
Regarding the Jambudvīpa man who [encounters] the Buddha:
he is one who cultivates the karma for the marks of excellence;
such a person exists only among the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa.
Because their wisdom and insight are sharp,
they must have male bodies,
as they have already transcended the female state. As for the phrase "in the presence of a Buddha":
It was manifested only in the presence of the Buddha.
As for the Buddha’s thought regarding that which is accomplished through reflection:
this refers to the karma of these sublime marks.
The contemplation of the Buddha gives rise to reflection;
it is comprised within that which is accomplished through reflection.
As for the remaining [stages], one must practice them over a hundred kalpas.
Beyond the three incalculable eons,
for an additional one hundred great eons,
he cultivated the karma that produces the marks of excellence.
In the causal stage, this is the natural law for all Buddhas; it is only for Śākyamuni Buddha that [this specific case] applies.
With blazing diligence,
he was able to transcend ninety-one kalpas— specifically nine kalpas.
