This refers to the accomplishment through the cultivation of the excellent marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding "each adorned with a hundred merits," this refers to the thirty-two marks.
Each of these karmas is adorned with a hundred merits.
One hundred instances of wholesome volition are termed "a hundred merits."
For example, when cultivating the mark of the soles of the feet being level and full,
fifty volitions (cetanā) first arise.
Cultivate and refine the vessel of the body until it is made pure;
next, give rise to a single thought.
It correctly draws that [action] forth;
subsequently, fifty volitions arise to bring it to completion.
It is like a farmer who first prepares the furrows and ridges,
next sows the seeds,
and afterwards applies manure and water.
And he irrigates it.
As it is with the feet,
so it is with the remaining marks.
The fifty volitions refer to the ten paths of wholesome action,
each of which consists of five volitions.
Furthermore, regarding the initial karma of non-killing,
there are five types of volition:
first, the volition of abstaining from killing.
Second, the thought of exhorting others to the path;
third, the thought of praising [others' virtues];
fourth, the thought of sympathetic joy.
It should be understood that the same applies from the five types of dedication and intention up to right view.
These are called the fifty thoughts (*cetanā*).
Question: What is defined as a single measure of merit (*puṇya-pramāṇa*)? Answer: Some say:
Except for the karma that results in the wealth and prosperity of bodhisattvas who are close to Buddhahood, all other karma of sentient beings that produces such fruits is called "one unit of merit."
Some say that the karma which brings about a great trichiliocosm constitutes a single unit of merit;
others say its measure is boundless.
Only the Buddha can know this.
From here, the third section clarifies the making of offerings to the Buddha.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, an explanation of the number of Buddhas;
second, an explanation of the Buddhas encountered.
First, regarding the enumeration of the Buddhas,
the treatise states:
"Now, our Great Teacher..."
In the past, when he was a bodhisattva,
how many Buddhas did he make offerings to throughout the three incalculable eons?
The verse says:
Throughout three incalculable eons, He made offerings to seventy thousand Buddhas each;
Furthermore, he successively made offerings To five thousand, six thousand, and seven thousand Buddhas.
The commentary states:
During the first incalculable eon,
he made offerings to seventy-five thousand Buddhas.
During the second incalculable eon,
he made offerings to seventy-six thousand Buddhas.
During the third incalculable eon...
He made offerings to seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
This is the second [section],
clarifying the Buddhas he encountered.
The treatise says:
At the completion of each of the three incalculable eons.
And as for the Buddhas whom they each encountered upon their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment,
the verse says:
Having completed three incalculable eons, he met, in reverse order, the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin. Regarding the first, Śākyamuni:
[the commentary] says:
Regarding the "reversed order," this refers to proceeding from later to earlier; specifically,
it denotes the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
He encountered the Buddha Vipashyin at the completion of the second kalpa, and he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara [at the completion of the third].
When the first kalpa was completed,
he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin and first resolved his mind toward enlightenment.
Encountering Śākyamuni,
he made a grand vow, saying:
"May I become a Buddha."
Just as it is now with the World-Honored One,
so too did that Buddha, the World-Honored One,
appear in the world during the final age.
The True Dharma shall remain for one thousand years;
therefore, the Tathāgata now is in every respect identical to him.
This is the fourth [point] from hereon.
Regarding the clarification of the perfection of the six pāramitās, the treatise states: "I, Śākyamuni..."
In which stage is which perfection (pāramitā) brought to completion through cultivation?
The verse says:
Merely out of compassion, he gave universally; Though his body was mangled, he felt no anger.
He praised the Buddha Tiṣya, And subsequently attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
Regarding the six pāramitās, they are cultivated and perfected in these four stages, respectively, as one, two, one,
and two. [Commentary:]
"One who gives universally out of compassion" clarifies the nature of giving.
This refers to when a bodhisattva gives everything, even down to their eyes and marrow.
Yet he is without stinginess;
it is solely out of compassion,
not seeking a superior rebirth as a human or a deva.
Thus completing the cultivation of this perfection of generosity,
he remains free from anger even when his body is struck.
This clarifies the two: precepts and patience.
If at any time a bodhisattva has their limbs severed, [they should practice these].
With not even the slightest resentment in the mind,
one's cultivation of ethical discipline and patience reaches perfection up to this point.
Though his body was broken, he did not retaliate;
his pure precepts were perfected because his mind was free from anger.
The perfection of patience.
Praising Buddha Tiṣya— here translated as "Perfected One"—
clarifies diligence.
At that time, while the Bodhisattva was practicing with courageous diligence,
he encountered the Tathāgata Tiṣya.
Seated within a jeweled niche,
he entered the fire-element meditative concentration;
his majestic radiance blazed forth brilliantly.
Extraordinary compared to the ordinary,
he gazed upon it with single-minded sincerity,
forgetting to lift his foot from where he stood.
For seven days and nights,
with unwearied and pure mind,
[he recited] with sublime verses.
Praising that Buddha, he said: "In this world,
within the realm of heaven and earth and the abode of the learned, In the celestial palaces and throughout the ten directions,
there is no man, No Bull-King, no Great Śramaṇa, Who, when searching the earth, mountains, and forests, can be found equal to you."
The commentary states:
"Heaven and Earth" refers to that which is above heaven and below earth.
"This realm" refers to this trichiliocosm.
It is the palace of Vaiśravaṇa.
This is called the Hall of Much Learning (*bahuśruta-śālā*),
because his faith, reverence, and fame fill the ten directions.
As for the "Palace of the Departed" (*gata-vimāna*):
This is the palace of Mahābrahmādeva.
Non-Buddhists cling to it as being eternal;
the Buddha, in order to refute this, calls it the "Palace of the Departed" (gati-pada).
"Abodes of the gods" refers to all other celestial abodes,
not merely the Palace of Departure and so forth.
There is no one who resembles the Buddha;
even throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
there is likewise no one who resembles the Buddha.
He searched the ground;
he searched the mountains;
he searched the forests.
There is none who is equal to the Buddha.
Having praised him in this way,
he then transcended nine kalpas.
Having thus brought this perfection of diligence to full completion through cultivation,
one next [attains] unsurpassed enlightenment.
This clarifies meditative concentration and wisdom.
The diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi) is immediately followed by the attainment of Buddhahood.
This is ranked as unsurpassed;
herein the perfections of meditative concentration and wisdom are fully cultivated and perfected.
Regarding these four stages: the first is the stage of giving;
the second is the stage of being free from anger.
The third is the stage of diligence;
the fourth is the stage of the supreme.
"One and two, again one and two" refers to these.
First is the stage of initial giving,
which is one pāramitā; second is the stage of freedom from anger.
These are the two perfections.
Furthermore, the "one" refers to the stage of diligence.
It is also one pāramitā. Furthermore, there are two:
next, the stage of the supreme mundane dharma.
These are the two *pāramitās*. From this point,
the seventh major section clarifies generosity (*dāna*),
ethical discipline (*śīla*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This section is divided into two parts:
first, a brief explanation of generosity, ethical discipline, and meditation;
second, an extensive explanation of generosity, ethical discipline, and meditation.
The first section below provides a brief explanation.
As the treatise states:
The Sūtra states: "There are three types of meritorious actions (puṇyakriyāvastu).
The first is the meritorious action consisting of giving (dāna)."
Second, the meritorious action consisting of the category of ethical discipline;
third, the meritorious action consisting of the category of cultivation.
How are these established as "meritorious actions" (puṇyakriyāvastu)?
The verse says:
The three categories of giving, morality, and cultivation each receive the designation of "bases of meritorious action" (puṇyakriyāvastu) according to their respective natures;
their distinctions are like those of the paths of action (karmapatha).
The commentary states:
Regarding the three categories of giving, morality, and cultivation,
"cultivation" (bhāvanā) is specifically designated as such.
"Category" (jāti) refers to the category of intrinsic nature (svabhāva). That is to say, giving, ethical discipline,
and cultivation each constitute their own distinct categories of intrinsic nature.
Regarding those things called "meritorious actions" that each receives according to what is appropriate:
this refers to the three, such as giving and so forth,
all of which are termed "merit."
Among these, there may be that which is both a meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*) and an action (*karma*); or that which is an action but not a basis;
or that which is a basis but not an action.
The names are each applied according to what is appropriate. Now, within the first category of giving,
there are two types of action— bodily and vocal—
which are termed "bases of meritorious action."
It is called "merit" (puṇya) because it is wholesome;
it is called "karma" because it is an action;
it is called "matter" (vastu) because it is that which is entrusted to volition (cetanā).
"Action" (karma) has the sense of being that upon which something depends. In relation to those [physical and vocal acts],
the volition (cetanā) that is capable of originating them is called "meritorious action" (puṇya-karman) alone.
It is called "merit" (puṇya) because it is wholesome;
it is called "karma" because it is an action.
Volition (cetanā) does not depend on itself.
Therefore, it is not called a "matter" (vastu); rather, it is a dharma coexistent with volition (cetanā) that receives the name "merit" (puṇya) alone,
for its essence is not something produced through action.
Therefore, it is not called "karma";
because volition does not rely upon it correctly,
it is not called "the basis."
Regarding "rightly entrusting intention," this refers to body and speech. Since the categories of ethical discipline (śīla) are exclusively of the nature of bodily and vocal karma,
they all fully possess the designation of "meritorious action" (puṇyakriyāvastu).
This should be explained according to the preceding [analysis]. Among the types of cultivation, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is designated solely as a meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*).
It is called "merit" because it is wholesome;
it consists of volition (*cetanā*) associated with loving-kindness.
Because one relies on loving-kindness as a gateway and thereby engages in formative activity,
loving-kindness is termed a "phenomenon" (vastu).
This refers to the fact that it is the activity of karma. Volition concurrent with loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
as well as the precepts concurrent with it,
are designated solely as "meritorious karma" (*puṇyakarman*).
It is called "merit" (puṇya) because it is wholesome;
it is called "action" (karma) because it is performed.
Apart from volition and morality, it refers to all other co-existent factors.
They receive only the name "merit.
Regarding their distinctions being like those of the paths of action: as it was in the case of the paths of action.
This refers to the first seven types,
which are both karma and paths;
as for the three beginning with greed and hatred, they are only paths.
This path is not karma. The term "path" applies to all ten [paths of action],
whereas "karma" applies only to the first seven.
Now, the same applies to the universality or restriction of meritorious deeds (puṇya-karman):
the name "merit" is universal,
whereas the specific deeds (karman) are not fixed.
These distinctions are the same as those in the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Some say that it consists solely of volition (*cetanā*).
This is true meritorious action.
The nature of meritorious action consists of giving,
ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Taking these three as the gateway,
because meritorious karma proceeds from them;
this is the second [section].
This provides a detailed explanation of giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation. Within this, there are three parts.
First, the explanation of giving.
Second, the cultivation of ethical discipline;
third, the gift of Dharma.
Within the first [category], giving:
It is further divided into nine parts:
first, the explanation of giving;
second, the explanation of the distinctions in the benefits of giving.
First, it clarifies the distinct causes for the fruits of giving;
second, it clarifies that the merit of giving is most supreme;
third, it clarifies that the fruits of giving are immeasurable.
Sixth, clarifying the characteristics of the lightness and heaviness of karma;
seventh, clarifying the performance and accumulation [of karma];
eighth, clarifying the merit of making offerings to a cetiya.
9. Clarifying the fruit through the internal mind.
Herein, first is the clarification of the donor.
The treatise says:
What is the phenomenon called giving?
What fruit does giving bring about?
The verse says:
From this, renunciation is called "giving" (dāna);
that is, for the sake of making offerings or for the benefit of body and speech, as well as that which can produce them. This brings about the fruit of great wealth. Commentary:
On account of this relinquishment, one is called a "giver";
on account of this mind free from greed,
as well as that which can initiate bodily and vocal actions.
Because one is only able to relinquish material wealth [through them],
non-greed and the others constitute the true essence of giving;
that is to say, they are for the purpose of making offerings and for the benefit [of others].
That is to say, one practices giving for the sake of making offerings to and benefiting sentient beings;
this includes the body, speech, and that which gives rise to them.
This clarifies the basis for relinquishment,
namely: bodily and vocal actions,
as well as that which gives rise to them.
It is called the "basis of relinquishment.
That which is said to "initiate" it refers to the mind free from greed.
And because it consists of a single aggregate of mind and mental factors.
As a verse says:
"If a person, with a pure mind—that is, a mind free from greed—"
Having ceased [the thought], one practices giving.
This momentary aggregate of merit consists of five aggregates;
that which initiates it consists of four aggregates.
The bodily and vocal actions that are thus initiated constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
based on this verse, they are collectively designated by the name "giving" (*dāna*).
Therefore, one should know that the five aggregates constitute the essence of giving.
Regarding the phrase "merit belonging to the category of giving" (*dāna-mayī puṇya-kriyā*), the term "category" (*maya*) refers to its "essence."
This clarifies that this merit has giving as its essence,
just as a vessel made of leaves has those leaves as its essence.
The merit consisting of the cultivation of the precepts should be explained accordingly based on this.
This concludes the second [section].
This clarifies the distinctions regarding the benefits of giving.
The treatise asks:
"For what purpose is it beneficial?"
And why does one practice giving?
The verse says:
For the benefit of oneself, others, and both; not for either of these two [alone] does one practice giving.
The commentary states:
"For the benefit of oneself" means for the benefit of one's own person.
And they practice giving.
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned desire,
whether they be ordinary persons or noble ones.
And when ordinary worldlings who are free from sensual desire make offerings to a shrine.
This is called "benefiting oneself," because it brings about karmic maturation;
it is not beneficial for a *caitya*.
Because it is not for one's own enjoyment.
"For the benefit of others" means for the benefit of the bodies of others.
And they practice giving.
This refers to noble ones who have abandoned desire,
bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings.
It is not beneficial for oneself,
because one does not experience the fruit in a second birth.
It is beneficial for others because they enjoy it; thus,
it serves as a benefit for both.
"Both" refers to oneself and others;
one practices giving for the benefit of both oneself and others.
This refers to those who have not yet abandoned sensual desire—
whether they be noble ones or ordinary persons—
as well as those who have abandoned it.
One gives to all sentient beings for the benefit of one's own self in a future birth.
In the second birth, [one gives]...
Because one receives the fruit of giving, it is beneficial to others;
because others enjoy it, one who gives does not act for the sake of these two [self-interest and other-interest].
One practices giving not for the sake of oneself or others;
this refers to noble ones who are free from desire.
An offering made to a caitya does not produce fruit for oneself,
nor is it enjoyed by others.
In both cases, there is no benefit;
it is solely for the sake of showing respect and repaying kindness.
This concludes the third [section].
This clarifies the distinctions among the results of giving;
it is divided into two parts.
First, the differences between the primary [recipient] and others are explained.
Second, the explanation of the lords, wealth, and fields.
Below this, first is the explanation of the differences among the lords and so forth.
The treatise says:
Previously, it was explained in general that giving brings about great wealth.
Now, we shall distinguish the specific causes for the various fruits of giving.
The verse says:
The fruit of giving differs due to the distinctions among the donor, the object, and the field.
Commentary: This refers to the differentiation of the fruits of giving.
It is due to three causes:
namely, the person, the object, and the action.
Because of the distinctions in field, gift, and recipient.
There is a distinction regarding the fruit.
From this second [section], the master,
the wealth, and the field are explained.
This is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the master;
second, clarifying the wealth.
The field of the three knowledges (*trividyā*).
Below this, first is the elucidation of the master.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions based on the donor,
the verse says:

The distinction of the dominant influence arises from faith and so forth; by practicing giving with reverence and the like, one obtains respect and extensive affection, as well as timely and unassailable fruits. [Commentary: The verse states: "By means of faith and the rest, One practices giving with reverence and so forth; One obtains respect and extensive affection, As well as timely and unassailable fruits. [The commentary explains: The "distinction of the dominant influence" (*adhipatiphala*) refers to the specific results produced by the respective causes. "Faith and the rest" refers to the five faculties: faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. By cultivating these, one gives gifts characterized by reverence, respect, and other such qualities. Through this practice, one attains the fruit of being held in high esteem and receiving vast affection from others. Furthermore, one obtains fruits that are appropriate to the time and cannot be taken away. This indicates that the results correspond to the nature of the cause and are not subject to loss.
"Distinctions among donors arise from faith and so forth" means that the differences between donors are due to the possession of the seven kinds of noble wealth, such as faith.
These are the distinguished virtues:
first, profound faith;
second, observance of the precepts.
Third, extensive learning;
fourth, wisdom; fifth, renunciation and generosity.
Sixth is shame (hrī);
seventh is dread of blame (apatrāpya). Some possess all seven; others do not.
Therefore, it is called a difference in the agent;
because of this difference in the agent,
there is a distinction between the gift and its fruit.
Regarding giving with distinctions such as respect and reverence:
"and so forth" includes giving with one's own hands and at the appropriate time.
It is without loss;
this is the third kind of giving.
If there is a donor who possesses the seven noble riches, [their gift is likewise without loss].
By practicing the four types of giving, such as that characterized by respect,
one can bring about the four corresponding fruits, such as being held in high esteem;
that is to say, if a donor...
By practicing the gift of reverence,
one causes others to show respect;
by giving with one's own hands, one attains this result.
One feels a sense of vast wealth and delights in its enjoyment if one gives at the appropriate time.
It is "timely wealth" because it is required at the appropriate time;
provided that there is no harm in giving it.
One will experience wealth that is difficult to deprive,
which cannot be stolen or plundered,
nor destroyed by fire and other such calamities.
From this, the second [section] clarifies the distinctions among wealth.
The treatise states:
Regarding the distinctions based on the material objects given,
the verse says:
The excellence of wealth arises from [the perfection of] form and so forth;
one obtains a beautiful appearance, a good reputation, the love of the multitude, and a body of soft texture, as well as pleasant tactile sensations appropriate to the time. Commentary:
"Material wealth differs by way of color and so forth" means that the material goods offered as a gift may either lack or possess color, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
Therefore, it is called "difference in material wealth," meaning that the material object offered is endowed with excellence of form.
One thus experiences exquisite physical form because of being endowed with fragrance;
one thus experiences a good reputation.
Just as fragrance pervades all directions,
because it is endowed with flavor,
one naturally inspires the love of the multitude.
Because of the perfection of the sense-base of touch (*spraṣṭavya*),
one experiences a supple body and encounters tactile sensations that give rise to pleasant feelings at appropriate times,
such as those of the "jewel-woman" (*strī-ratna*) and others.
If there is a decrease in the fruit,
it is due to the deficiency of the cause.
From this, the third [point follows].
Explaining the differences regarding the field (*kṣetra*). The treatise states:
"It is due to the field to which the gift is given."
What is the distinction?
The verse says:
The fields differ by way of realm, suffering, And kindness and virtue; there are distinctions.
The commentary states:
The fields of those who go toward suffering, those who bestow grace, and those who possess virtue are each distinct.
This is called the difference in the field.
Regarding the distinction by way of the realm of rebirth:
if one gives to an animal...
Giving to one who has committed an offense against the precepts results in a thousandfold reward.
This is called "converging toward difference.
Regarding "due to the distinction of suffering," this refers to the seven types of merit based on existence.
Because one relieves the suffering of others,
the merit is immeasurable; it is as if one had performed a meritorious act for a traveler on the road.
Second, giving to travelers and guests;
third, giving to the sick;
fourth, giving to those who care for the sick.
Fifth, they donate monasteries and groves;
sixth, they provide constant food.
Such are the lay devotees of the Western Regions.
In a remote and secluded place,
fearing that his traveling companions might suffer from hunger,
he built a hut and deposited his wealth therein.
One should store abundant food and drink and offer them universally to all; alternatively,
one may designate offerings specifically for those who have left the household life.
Because one constantly gives food,
it is called "giving constant food.
Seventh is giving at the appropriate time.
Regarding cold, heat, and wind,
because one bestows [relief] upon others according to the season,
there is a distinction based on the nature of the kindness.
It is like [the merit of serving] one's parents and so forth;
it is increased ten thousand billionfold due to the distinction of its virtue.
Giving to one who maintains the precepts yields a hundred millionfold fruit;
this continues up to giving to a Buddha.
One attains immeasurable fruit.
Following this, the fourth [section] clarifies that the merit of giving is most supreme.
The treatise says:
Among all forms of giving,
which is the most excellent?
The verse says:
"For one liberated, giving to one who is liberated; for a Bodhisattva, the eighth gift is most supreme.
The commentary says:
There are three most excellent [recipients]:
first, a person who has attained liberation;
giving to a person who has attained liberation.
That merit is most supreme.
Second, as for the acts of giving performed by bodhisattvas.
This is the cause for bringing extensive benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, and it is also the most supreme among the eight kinds of giving.
38. Among the eight types of gifts:
The eighth is the most excellent:
first, giving to those who have arrived,
that is, giving to those who have come near.
Only then can one give.
Second is giving out of fear:
seeing that one's wealth is about to be destroyed.
First, giving without fail;
second, giving in return for a favor received;
third, giving in expectation of a reward.
Fifth is the practice of ancestral giving,
which means practicing the acts of generosity performed by one's fathers and grandfathers.
Sixth is the giving with the hope for rebirth in heaven.
That is to say, it is for the purpose of being born in heaven.
The seventh is called giving for the sake of renown.
The eighth is for the adornment of the mind.
It is for the purpose of eliminating stinginess,
for the purpose of attaining yogic concentration,
and for the purpose of attaining the bliss of ultimate meaning, which is nirvāṇa.
To practice giving is called the adornment of the mind;
this is the fifth [topic] following that.
This clarifies that the fruits of giving are immeasurable.
The treatise states:
"As it is said in the sūtras."
Giving to one who has entered the stream of the path has immeasurable fruit; giving to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry [has immeasurable fruit].
The measure of the fruit increases further,
and so forth, as extensively explained.
Is there any giving that is not noble?
Is the fruit also immeasurable?
The verse says:
Parents, the sick, a Dharma teacher, and a Bodhisattva in their final birth.
Even if one is not a realized noble being, the fruit of giving is likewise immeasurable.
Commentary: A father.
Second, one's mother;
third, a sick person;
fourth, a Dharma teacher.
Fifth, the bodhisattva in their final existence,
namely one born in a royal palace who dwells in their last birth.
Regarding these five kinds [of recipients],
even if they are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana),
one is still able to gain merit by merely giving to them.
It summons immeasurable merit.
Following this, the sixth section clarifies the characteristics of the lightness and heaviness of karma.
The Treatise says:
"If one wishes to know the characteristics of the lightness and heaviness of various karmas,
one should understand what constitutes lightness and what constitutes heaviness."
The thesis is briefly established by means of six reasons.
What are these six? The inquiry arises as follows;
the verse says:
The subsequent, the field, the fundamental, the preparatory effort, volition, and the intention—
by virtue of these being inferior or superior, karma becomes inferior or superior. Commentary:
This has six causes.
The subsequent arising is the first cause.
This means that after having committed a transgression, one proceeds to commit it again.
"Field" refers to the second cause.
Regarding the performance of acts of harm or benefit toward the four aforementioned fields,
the "root" refers to the third cause.
This refers to the fundamental paths of action;
the preparatory effort is the fourth cause.
That which leads to the fundamental [state] is called the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As for "volition" (*cetanā*):
This is the fifth cause. It refers to the fact that through that volition,
the path of action reaches its completion.
The intention is the sixth cause;
it refers to all underlying purposes.
"I shall perform such deeds as these"—
first, from this intention,
one initiates the preparatory application.
Next, from the preparatory application,
volition is induced;
next, again from volition.
This induces the fundamental [karma].
This fundamental [karma] necessarily arises with respect to a field.
Only after [the preceding] does the subsequent arising manifest;
now, following the sequence of meaning,
we proceed from the end back toward the beginning.
Regarding how karma becomes inferior or superior due to these inferior and superior [factors]:
because each of the preceding six [factors] possesses both inferior and superior degrees,
karma consequently attains the status of being inferior or superior.
Furthermore, among the aforementioned six types of karma,
there are certain actions that become grave solely by virtue of their subsequent performance (*pṛṣṭha*).
It is established that the maturation fruit arises subsequently. Alternatively,
there are certain karmas that become grave due to the field [of the recipient].
Just as an action committed toward a field of gratitude and virtue is grave,
so it is with respect to others.
If one commits the action, it will be light.
Or, in some cases, due to the power of the basis (the field),
the action becomes a heavy category.
It is not due to the other four;
as with one's parents,
the offense of killing is grave.
Stealing from one's parents is minor;
the remaining preparatory actions [are more serious].
When the three factors of intention, motivation,
and action are all of a heavy grade, the karmic result is established as heavy; this should be explained according to the previous analysis.
If there are six causes,
all of which are of the highest degree,
this karma is the most grave.
The opposite of this is the lightest [karma].
Apart from these two extremes,
there is karma that is neither light nor heavy.
From this, the seventh [section] clarifies the performance and accumulation [of karma].
The treatise states:
As stated in the sūtra, there are two kinds of karma: first, karma that is performed;
[second, karma that is accumulated].
Second, the increase of karma.
For what reason is karma called "increased" (*upacita*)? This is the question.
The answer is given by means of five kinds of causes. What are these five questions?
The verse says:
Because it is performed with full deliberation, is free from regret,
possesses an antidote, has companions, and has maturation, this karma is called "accumulated. Commentary:
There are five causes for this.
"By means of deliberate reflection" is the first cause; the word "this" (此) extends to the following two phrases.
Reflective volition that produces karma is called "accumulation";
impulsive volition that acts is [also accumulation].
It refers simply to the act of performing.
"By way of fulfillment" is the second cause.
Regarding the ten courses of action,
one may fall into the evil destinies by means of even a single course of action.
Sometimes one does not fall due to a single karma,
but falls only due to two karmas,
and so on, up to nine.
One does not fall [into the evil realms] by means of these alone; it is only through ten courses of action that one falls into the evil realms,
and thus falls as far as the evil realms extend.
This is called fulfillment.
This fulfilled karma is called growth.
When it is not yet complete, it is merely termed "formative activity" (*abhisamskāra*). The third cause is the absence of remorse as an antidote;
failing to feel regret for having committed evil is what is meant by "absence of remorse" (*kaukṛtya*).
To commit evil and fail to repent or purify it is called "lack of counteractive measures.
This is termed "increase."
If one is able to feel remorse and is able to purify oneself through repentance,
it is merely termed "karmic formation."
Regarding "having a companion," this is the fourth cause;
that is to say, performing unwholesome deeds.
To have unwholesome states as its companions is called "increase";
it has no unwholesome companions.
"Merely being designated as 'formative action' (saṃskāra) due to the presence of maturation (vipāka)" refers to the fifth cause.
This refers to the performance of unwholesome karma that is certain to produce maturation;
this is called "increase."
It does not bring about maturation;
it is merely termed "formative.
One should understand that the wholesome is the opposite of the above.
From this, the eighth [section] clarifies the merit of making offerings to a caitya.
The treatise states:
As previously explained,
those who have not yet abandoned desire and so forth maintain what they themselves possess.
Offering to a caitya is called a gift that benefits only oneself,
as there is no recipient.
How is merit accomplished?
The verse says:
Merit from relinquishing to a *caitya* is like [the merit of] loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth; it does not depend on being received.
The commentary states:
Regarding "merit consisting of the relinquishment of a caitya," there are two categories of merit.
First, relinquishment;
second, receiving.
Relinquishment refers to the relinquishing of wealth.
The merit of giving arises when there is a recipient; that is to say,
the merit of giving arises only when the recipient actually enjoys the gift.
Although there is no recipient for the merit when making offerings to a caitya,
there is still merit consisting of the act of relinquishment.
Just as in the case of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, there is no experiencer;
this is established by citing an example.
It is like the cultivation of loving-kindness and the like.
Regarding equanimity, compassion, joy, and equanimity: when cultivating loving-kindness and the others,
although there is no recipient and no actual benefit conferred upon others, [the practice still occurs].
However, because immeasurable merit arises from a virtuous mind,
one gives to the caitya.
Although there is no actual enjoyment [of these offerings], I respectfully present them as an act of veneration;
for merit arises from the mind.
From this ninth [section],
it clarifies that the fruit arises from the internal mind.
The treatise states:
If one plants the seed of the act of giving in a virtuous field,
it may bring forth desirable fruits.
If it were the case that giving to an "unwholesome field" (akṣetra) could only result in undesirable fruits,
this objection would be irrational. Why is this so?
The verse says:
"In a bad field there is a desirable fruit, because the seed and the fruit do not contradict one another.
The commentary says:
As for "unwholesome fields," these are animals and the like. Although one may give to such unwholesome fields, [the result is still beneficial].
Because one plants seeds of merit through giving,
one in turn invites desirable fruits;
this is truly because there is no inversion between the seed and its fruit.
"Seed" refers to the cause of giving;
"fruit" refers to the result of giving.
This is clearly observed in the field.
The correspondence between seed and fruit is non-erroneous; for example,
from a mṛdvīkā seed, a mṛdvīkā fruit is produced.
Its shape is like that of a jujube fruit;
its flavor is exceedingly delicious;
it is grown from the *jambū* seed.
The *lembu* fruit grows;
its size is like that of a bitter gourd seed.
Its taste is extremely bitter.
From this point begins the second major section,
which clarifies the cultivation of the precepts.
This is divided into three parts:
first, an explanation of ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, an explanation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The three knowledges (*trividyā*) are the fruits of the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*). This is the first [point].
The treatise states:
Now, the category of meritorious action consisting of morality (*śīla*) should be analyzed.
The verse says:
"Abstinence from transgressions and from that which is prohibited Is called morality; each has two types."
"Not a cause for violating the precepts, nor destroyed by them; based on their antidotes, they are extinguished and purified," etc.
The commentary states:
"The three [actions] of the body and the four [actions] of speech."
All unwholesome forms are called natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Because they are natural offenses,
[they are to be avoided].
This is called "transgressing the precepts.
Regarding "prohibitory offenses" (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya), these include such acts as eating at improper times.
Abstinence from transgressing the precepts and from that which is prohibited is both termed "precept" (śīla).
Each of these has two aspects.
Each of these precepts consists of two aspects: the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
The following two lines clarify the four virtues of the precepts.
First, it is not ruined by the violation of precepts;
this means being free from the aforementioned violation of precepts.
Second, it is not ruined by the causes for violating precepts.
The cause refers to afflictions such as greed.
Regarding the third, reliance on the antidotes:
"antidote" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
This is for the purpose of curing previous transgressions of the precepts and their causes.
Regarding the fourth, reliance on cessation:
"cessation" refers to nirvana.
It is dedicated toward nirvāṇa,
not toward superior rebirths as humans or devas. As for the term "pure" mentioned in the verse,
it means being endowed with the four virtues described above.
"Precepts that are pure;
those contrary to this are called impure," and so forth.
There is another explanation:
the purity of ethical discipline arises from five causes.
First, purity of the root.
The first is the purification of the root, which is the abandonment of evil roots.
The second is the purification of the retinue,
which is the abandonment of the means of evil.
Third, one is not harmed by vitarka,
which means being free from evil thoughts.
Fourth, one is sustained by mindfulness.
To be mindful of the Three Jewels is the fifth dedication toward tranquility;
it is the seeking of nirvana.
Second, this clarifies the cultivation of merit through imitation.
The treatise states:
The categories of morality have already been explained.
The category of cultivation shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"Wholesome states in meditative equipoise are called cultivation, because they are extremely capable of perfuming the mind.
The commentary explains:
"Meditative equipoise" refers to *samādhi*.
That is to say, being free from lethargy and excitement is called "equanimity" (samatā),
which induces the arising of meritorious qualities.
It is called "leading" (*āvedha*).
This is a wholesome state of the meditative stage (*samāhitabhūmi*) that is extremely capable of perfuming the mind.
Because it causes the categories of virtue to be perfected,
it alone is termed "cultivation" (bhāvanā).
This is the third [section].
This clarifies the fruits of the cultivation of the precepts. Within this, first the fruits of the cultivation of the precepts are clarified,
and second, the measure of Brahma-merit is clarified.
Furthermore, regarding the fruit of cultivating the first precept,
the treatise states:
"It was previously established that the merit of giving can summon great wealth."
What are the results produced by the two categories of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
The verse says:
Ethical discipline and cultivation, being superior, respectively produce rebirth in the heavens and liberation.
The commentary states:
Morality brings rebirth in the heavens;
this is stated in terms of its predominant result.
In reality, although practicing generosity also brings rebirth in the heavens,
it does not compare to the merit of observing the precepts.
Cultivating this brings about liberation;
this is stated in terms of its preeminent quality.
In reality, however, it is the observance of the precepts.
One may also experience liberation through this,
yet it is not equal to cultivation.
This is the second [point].
This clarifies the measure of Brahma-merit.
The treatise states:
"The Sūtra speaks of four types of persons."
It can produce the merit of Brahmā.
First, to make offerings to the *dhātu*— here translated as "nature," referring to the Buddha’s physical body—
one constructs a *stūpa* in a place where none has previously existed.
Second, for the sake of making offerings to the Saṃgha of the four quarters,
they construct monasteries, donate gardens,
and provide the four requisites of support.
Third, as a disciple of the Buddha,
one who has been divided can bring about reconciliation;
fourth, regarding sentient beings.
One universally cultivates loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables]. What is the measure of such Brahma-merit?
The verse says:
The measure of a single Brahma-merit is defined as that which causes one to be reborn in heaven for an eon (*kalpa*), and so forth.
The Commentary states:
"The former masters, or the Sautrāntikas..."
Alternatively, the master of the Mahāsāṃghika school speaks as follows.
The experience of celestial bliss for one kalpa constitutes the measure of a single Brahma-merit (brahmapuṇya),
which lasts for forty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa).
This is called one kalpa,
because their lifespan is equal to that of the Brahmā-purohita devas.
Thus, there is a verse which says:
When a person possessing faith and right view practices the ten superior deeds,
they generate Brahma-merit.
Because they evoke celestial music for an eon,
these ten superior practices are superior to the aforementioned four merits of Brahmā.
Furthermore, there are six types:
first, sacrificing one's own life to save the life of one's mother;
second, sacrificing one's own life to save the life of one's father.
Third, saving the Tathāgata’s life by sacrificing one’s own life;
fourth, leaving the household life within the True Dharma;
fifth, teaching others to leave the household life.
Sixth, when the Wheel of Dharma has not yet been turned,
they are able to request that the Wheel of Dharma be turned;
this is the intended meaning of the verse cited here.
This establishes that the four merits of the Brahmā realm result in celestial bliss for an eon.
Regarding the word "etc. in the verse, it includes what is stated in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding this expression "the measure of Brahma-merit," it is identical to the measure of merit for a single auspicious mark mentioned previously in the section on the karma of the excellent marks.
This concludes the third major section.
This clarifies the gift of Dharma.
The treatise states:
"The gift of material wealth has already been explained."
What is the gift of Dharma?
The verse says:
The gift of Dharma consists of explaining the sūtras and so forth, according to reality and without attachment.
The commentary states:
Teaching the Dharma without error is called "according to reality."
Not seeking fame or profit is a mind free from defilement;
if one can act in accordance with reality, [this is it].
With an undefiled mind,
one compiles the sūtras and other scriptures so as to give rise to correct understanding.
This is called the gift of Dharma.
From this point, the eighth major section clarifies the goodness that accords with the three divisions.
The treatise states:
Previously, the three types of meritorious actions were explained individually;
now, the wholesome factors corresponding to the three divisions within the Sūtra are being explained.
The verse says:
The factors conducive to merit, to liberation, and to penetration—these three respectively result in desirable fruits, nirvāṇa, and the noble path. They are wholesome.
The commentary states:
"Wholesome actions conducive to merit" refers to wholesome actions that bring about desirable worldly fruits.
The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) refer to the wholesome merits performed that are certain to result in the fruit of nirvāṇa.
This refers to those who turn toward and seek nirvana.
Once this goodness has arisen,
it is said that "nirvana-dharma exists within the body."
If a person, upon hearing it said that there are faults in birth-and-death and virtues in nirvāṇa,
has their hair stand on end and weeps with grief.
One should know that this person has already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Just as seeing sprouts emerge in a place where rain has fallen allows one to know that seeds were previously present within the soil, so too should it be understood here.
The wholesome factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) refer to the four roots of goodness, such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth;
these are capable of inducing the Noble Path.
The Noble Path is called "definitive discernment" (nirṇaya).
Because it brings about the Noble Path,
it is termed "conducive" (anuloma).
From this ninth [section] onward,
the writing of mantras, mudrās, and so forth is clarified.
The treatise states:
As it is said in the world that there are writing, seals, calculation, grammar, and numbers,
what are the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these five?
The verse says:
The three types of action arising from correct reasoning can all produce, in their respective order, the natures of writing, seals, and calculation. Commentary:
[As stated above.]
Those that arise from correct reasoning refer to the actual application of activities such as writing and so forth.
As for the three types of action:
That is to say, the actions of body, speech, and mind;
and that which can initiate them,
namely, the four aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā).
It is capable of producing the three preceding types of karma.
"In sequence" means, for instance,
the three preceding types of karma and so forth.
Respectively, these constitute the essence of those [actions] such as writing and sealing.
Regarding "writing" and "sealing," this refers to prior bodily karma.
And that which produces it has the five aggregates as its essence.
"Writing" refers to writing by hand.
Seals refer to engraved seals;
these are all bodily actions (*kāyakarman*).
Bodily action is form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, because it can give rise to those [other] four aggregates— feeling and so forth—
it encompasses all five aggregates.
These five aggregates can constitute the script-seal; therefore,
they are called the "script-seal."
Regarding the intrinsic nature of calculation (*gaṇanā*) and syllables (*vyañjana*):
"calculation" refers to verbal calculation,
and "syllables" refers to verbal characters.
Therefore, calculation and writing have as their essence the aforementioned verbal karma and the five aggregates that give rise to them.
"Number" refers to volition (*cetanā*).
Volition is capable of counting numbers such as one, ten, and so forth.
Therefore, it is reckoned as having the preceding mental karma and that which can produce the four aggregates as its substance;
from this, it is the tenth.
This clarifies the various synonyms for all phenomena (*dharma*).
The treatise states:
"Now, one should briefly distinguish the various synonyms for all phenomena."
The verse says:
Wholesome and untainted are called "sublime. Defiled, faulty, obscured, and inferior;
Wholesome conditioned phenomena are to be cultivated; Liberation is called "unsurpassed."
The commentary states:
"Wholesome and untainted" refers to the Truth of the Path and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "The wise" refers to those who possess knowledge.
It is called "sublime" because it is praised.
"Defiled" refers to defiled phenomena (*dharma*).
This is called "with fault" because it is censured and loathed;
it is also called "obscured."
Because it obscures the Noble Path,
it is also called "inferior";
because it is extremely base and lowly, it is [the opposite of] wholesome conditioned phenomena.
It is called "that which should be practiced" because it ought to be cultivated and increased. Question: Why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) not called "that which should be practiced"?
Answer: The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is immutable;
it cannot be cultivated so as to cause increase.
Furthermore, cultivation is for the sake of a fruit.
Because it is unconditioned and without fruit,
liberation is not something to be cultivated;
that is to say, it is nirvana.
It is wholesome and eternal;
because it transcends all phenomena,
it is called "unsurpassed."
17. Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa, Treatise Volume Nineteen. The commentary states:
Afflictions such as greed are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies). Because they follow along with sentient beings and increase their delusion and stagnation, they are named *anuśaya*.
This chapter explains them extensively; therefore, it is titled "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*). Regarding this:
This chapter is divided into two parts:
first, the elucidation of the nature of the afflictions;
second, the elucidation of the cessation of the afflictions.
Within the clarification of the essence of delusion, three parts are distinguished:
first, the clarification of the fundamental delusions;
second, the analysis through various categories.
Third, a general explanation of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Within this, the explanation of the fundamental delusions (*mūlakleśa*) is divided into five parts.
First, the explanation of the increased number.
Second, the explanation of what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation;
third, the explanation of the five views;
fourth, the explanation of the four inversions.
Regarding the five categories of knowledge, the seven, and the nine types of pride:
within the first category, the increase in enumeration is divided into four parts.
First, the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are explained.
First, the seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are explained;
second, the ten underlying tendencies are explained;
third, the ninety-eight underlying tendencies are explained.
Furthermore, regarding the first section which clarifies the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
the treatise states:
"The preceding discussion concerned the distinctions among worldly realms."
All arise from karma; karma,
in turn, grows and develops through the presence of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The thesis is that karma free from latent tendencies (anuśaya) lacks the capacity to project existence (bhava).
Why is this so? This is the inquiry.
How many questions are there regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions are the root of all existence; Their distinctions are sixfold.
That is to say: greed, hatred, and also pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
The commentary states:
"The latent dispositions are the root of all existence."
Because these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are the root of all existence (*bhava*),
karma lacks the power to produce existence apart from them.
As for "all existences":
The three realms of existence (*tribhava*). This brief summary should be understood.
There are six distinctions:
first, craving (*rāga*).
Second, greed and hatred;
third, pride;
fourth, ignorance.
The five views and the six doubts;
the verse also says "likewise."
It is not that only hatred is called "greed-hatred";
rather, this indicates that pride and the other [defilements] also increase as latent tendencies toward their objects through the power of greed.
Because all afflictions arise solely through the power of attachment (*rāga*), one should therefore say:
"attachment, aversion, attachment-pride, and so forth, up to attachment-doubt.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the six entities are each distinct.
Secondly, from this point on,
the seven latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are explained.
The treatise states:
If the essential nature of the latent dispositions (anuśaya) consists of only six,
for what reason does the Sūtra speak of seven latent dispositions?
The verse says:

There are seven types of attachment due to the differentiation of craving; because attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) operates within the internal door of the two upper realms, it is established separately to prevent the notion that they constitute liberation.
The commentary states:

"The seventh, 'possessing greed' (*sarāga*), is distinguished from the six by way of greed; it refers to those [defilements] belonging to the two upper realms. This means that the aforementioned six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)— [...]* (Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly here.)
Due to the differences in craving,
it is divided into seven types.
The first is sensual craving (*kāmarāga*).
Second is "possessing greed," which is called the distinction of greed;
this refers to the greed of the desire realm.
That which is called "craving for sensual desire" refers to craving for the objects of the [desire] realm. That which is called "craving for existence" refers to craving for the two higher realms.
"Because it functions within the internal door" explains the term "possessing greed" (*sāsrava*);
it refers to the greed of the two upper realms.
Because it mostly functions by relying on the internal door and only rarely functions by taking external objects as its conditions,
it is established with the name "with-greed" (sārāga); "internal door" refers to its certainty.
Greed arises necessarily conditioned by [an object];
because it takes the internal as its gateway,
it is called "turning toward the internal."
This refers to the two upper realms (*dhātu*),
because there, craving for meditative absorption (*samādhi-rāga*) arises predominantly.
As for that which "partially functions by taking external objects as its objective support":
This means that they also take as their objects external spheres of form, sound, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
This is to preclude the notion of liberation [regarding those states].
Furthermore, it is because non-Buddhists [erroneously] regard the two higher realms as such.
They give rise to the notion that it is liberation;
the Buddha, in order to preclude this,
established the designation "possessing greed."
This reveals that the object of focus is not true liberation.
Herein, "self-entity" (svabhāva) is established by the name "existence.
As for "self-entity":
This refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and its supporting body.
That is to say, those sentient beings [possess] much greed for the meditative absorption of attainment (*samāpatti*) and its supporting body.
Concentration and the body are designated as "existence," because they arise conditioned by existence.
It is called "greed for existence" (*bhavarāga*);
it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound), meaning "greed for existence."
By definition, it is analogous to the greed of the desire realm;
it is called "desire-greed" because one is greedily attached to the external objects of the five desires.
Because it is a craving for desire,
it is also an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound).
This is the third [section].
This clarifies the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The treatise states:
"These are precisely the six kinds of underlying tendencies explained above."
In this treatise, it is further divided into ten sections.
How are these ten established?
The verse says:

The six become ten through the distinction of views; the distinctions are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), false view (mithyādṛṣṭi), the esteeming of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
The commentary states:
The aforementioned six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are distinguished by way of their views.
It is divided into ten types.
Five are views by nature.
The first is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
2. The view of grasping at extremes; 3. False view;
4. Adherence to views.
The five— namely, adherence to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the remaining four such as greed (*rāga*) and so forth—
are not of the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Following this, the fourth [category].
[This] clarifies the ninety-eight [defilements].
The Treatise states:
"Furthermore, these are precisely the six types of underlying tendencies (anuśaya) previously mentioned."
In this treatise, ninety-eight [defilements] are taught.
Based on what meaning are these ninety-eight taught?
The verse says:
Due to differences in aspect, category, and realm, there are ninety-eight [afflictions].
Those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and so forth in the desire realm consist of seventeen, seven, eight, and four [respectively].
That is to say, they are respectively possessed of [the abandonments of] three, two, views, views-and-doubt;
with the exception of hatred in the form and formless realms, the others are as explained for the desire realm.
The commentary says:
The first six phrases clarify the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the final two phrases clarify the two higher realms.
Regarding the differences in the six aspects of practice, the classes, and the realms:
This is the definition.
"Conduct" refers to active conduct,
namely the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Based on the differences in views and practices— namely, the practices of resolve—
they are distinguished as ten types.
These ten categories differ according to their respective realms and divisions.
They total ninety-eight.
As for the categories, there are five categories, namely:
those associated with the vision of suffering.
The vision of origination,
the vision of cessation,
and the vision of the path.

The category of what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for the realms (*dhātu*), they are the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Regarding the three realms:
"To sever seventeen, seven, eight, and four [afflictions] by seeing suffering and so forth in the desire realm" clarifies that there are thirty-six [afflictions] in the desire realm.
"Regarding 'suffering and so forth,' this refers to the inclusion of the other four categories.
'Ten' refers to the ten latent tendencies (anuśaya) that exist within the category of suffering."
"Seven times seven" refers to the seven latent dispositions (anuśaya) each associated with the view of origination and the view of cessation.
The eighth refers to the Truth of the Path.
There are eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
The fourth refers to the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
There are four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This explains the aforementioned number: they consist of those who possess all three [views], those who are free from two [views], and those who possess both views and doubt, respectively.
Those who possess [the views] see suffering; there are ten such views.
Those who are free from three views refer to seven each for the truths of origin and cessation.
It is free from the three [views]: the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
Regarding "being free from the two views":
this refers to the eight factors of the Truth of the Path,
excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
"Those free from views and doubt" refers to the four [factors] cultivated on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
excluding the five views and doubt.
Therefore, the character "view" (dṛṣṭi) mentioned above is stated twice:
once to exclude the three [wrong] views.
The second [section] is the departure from the two views.
Thus, they combine to form thirty-six types of suffering; below this, there are ten [factors], with seven each for origination and cessation.
Two times seven is fourteen;
adding this to the previous total makes twenty-four.
Together with the eight factors of the Path, they total thirty-two.
By adding the four [factors] of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they total thirty-six.
The first thirty-two are as follows.
They are called "abandoned by seeing" because they are abandoned at the very moment the truths are seen.
Subsequently, there are four [types] abandoned by cultivation.
It is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" because,
after having seen the four truths, one repeatedly practices the path at subsequent times.
Because they are severed at that time; the treatise asks:

"In this context, what characteristics are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and so forth, up to: what characteristics are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?"
Regarding the phrase "among these," Master Guang explains it as meaning "among these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)."
Master Bao says that in the preceding text of this treatise,
the five views and doubt are [discussed].
The assignment to the Four Noble Truths is complete.
Regarding the subsequent statement that "the remaining [afflictions],
such as greed and so forth, each pertain to all five categories," this question arises.
Therefore, it should be understood that among these four— greed and the others—
it is the jewel-like understanding that is considered wholesome.
If that which takes what is abandoned by seeing as its object is called "abandoned by seeing," then the remainder is called "abandoned by cultivation. This is the explanation;
this is the answer.
Master Guang said:
"There are two meanings here.
First, perceiving this as an object."
"Taking as an object" means taking these Four Noble Truths as objects.
"These" refers to these Four Noble Truths.
This refers to the five views and doubt;
because they are directly deluded regarding the Four Truths,
they are said to have these as their objects.
The second [category] consists of those abandoned by seeing this [truth], which take as their objects that which is abandoned by seeing; these are the five views and doubt.
That is to say, they are the four beginning with attachment (*rāga*).

It is not that those who are not [yet] kinsmen are deluded regarding the Truths; rather, because [the afflictions] arise based upon the five views and doubt, they are said to be "abandoned by seeing" (darśana-heya) as they take those views as their object. This is the intended meaning here.
If the five views and doubt arise taking the truth of suffering as their object,
they are termed "to be abandoned by seeing suffering."
Up to those that arise with the Truth of the Path as their object,
these are called abandoned by the Path of Seeing.
As for the four [afflictions] such as attachment and so forth:
Those [afflictions] that take as their objects the five views and doubt to be abandoned through the vision of suffering are called "to be abandoned through the vision of suffering," and so on,
up to those to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of the path.
Those [afflictions] that take the three views and doubt as their objects are called "abandoned by the path of seeing the truths.
They do not take the perception of these [truths] itself as their object.
Furthermore, that which is seen as having what is abandoned by cultivation as its object is called "abandoned by cultivation.
According to Master Bao, however:
The commentary states:
These four, beginning with greed,
if they take as their object that which is abandoned by seeing, [are abandoned by seeing].

Those [defilements] that take as their object what is abandoned by seeing are called "abandoned by seeing"; those that do not take what is abandoned by seeing as their object are called "abandoned by cultivation."
Thus, among these thirty-six [factors],
twelve belong to the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*),
namely the five views belonging to the level of suffering (*duḥkha*).
There are two views each regarding the truths of origination and cessation, and three views regarding the truth of the path;
thus, they constitute twelve.
Doubt is divided into four.
The four truths each have one [type];
the remaining four each have five; and the remaining four, such as greed and so forth, [are likewise].
Each penetrates five categories;
four times five makes twenty.
This is because they include the twelve views mentioned previously as well as the four doubts.
In the desire realm there are thirty-six;
in the form and formless realms,
with the exception of hatred, the rest are as described for the desire realm.
In the realms of form and formlessness,
from among the five categories [of fetters],
anger is excluded in each case.
The remainder is the same as for the desire realm;
thus, there are thirty-one each for the form and formless realms.
When the two realms are combined, they total sixty-two.
Including the previous categories, there are thirty-six;
totaling these, they constitute ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
To these, ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are further added.
These are called the one hundred and eight afflictions.
Following this second [section], there is the clarification of what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
The treatise states:
"Among these ninety-eight [defilements] to be abandoned,
the first eighty-eight..."
They are called abandoned by seeing because they are destroyed by the patiences (kṣānti). The latter ten latent dispositions (anuśaya) are called abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Because they are destroyed by wisdom (*jñāna*), these aforementioned [defilements] to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*) are indicated collectively;
this is not a definitive statement, nor is it a response to a question.
It is not so. It is a response.
What is the proof?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) destroyed by patience In the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are abandoned only through vision (darśana-prahātavya).
The others are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation; those destroyed by knowledge are abandoned only through cultivation.
Commentary: The first three lines clarify the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are destroyed by patience (*kṣānti*).
The fourth category consists of those latent dispositions (anuśaya) eliminated by clear wisdom (*prajñā*).

Regarding the latent dispositions eliminated by receptivity (*kṣānti*), those belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are exclusively abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*). "Receptivity" here refers to that which exists within the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

These are the receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma and the subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna-anvayajñānakṣānti*). The previous eighty-eight [defilements] are called the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) destroyed by receptivity.
Among these, those comprised within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*),

because the afflictions of the Peak of Existence can only be abandoned by the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*). As for the others, they are abandoned through both insight and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
In the remaining eight stages,
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) eliminated by patience (kṣānti) are subject to abandonment through both seeing (darśana) and cultivation (bhāvanā).

This refers to the abandonment by the noble ones through the forbearances of the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna-kṣānti*), which is exclusively through vision (*darśana*) and not through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Because they are to be abandoned accordingly, the seven higher stages are abandoned by means of subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*), while the single stage of the desire realm is abandoned [by means of dharma-patience].
The dharma-patience is an abandonment.
If it is an abandonment by an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), it is exclusively through cultivation (bhāvanā) and not through vision (darśana).
Because they are abandoned by mundane knowledge through repeated practice, and because they are destroyed by knowledge only for those who have cultivated [the path],
these refer to the final ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is called "that which is destroyed by wisdom" and is abandoned solely through cultivation;
for all noble ones [do not abandon it through insight].
Because both the universal [knowledge] and the two types of untainted and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) abandon them;
as for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
they possess only conventional knowledge.
Only then can they be severed.
Following this, thirdly,
the five views are explained.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation of the five views;
second, the specific explanation of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, to clarify the five views,
the treatise states:
"Due to differences in their modes of activity."
The fivefold classification has already been listed previously. What,
then, is their essential nature?
The verse says:
Clinging to "I" and "mine," to annihilation and permanence, to denying existence, to regarding the inferior as superior,
and to mistaking what is not the cause or path for such— these are the essential natures of the five views.
The commentary states:
The first three phrases establish the essential nature;
the fourth phrase provides the conclusion.
Regarding "self and what belongs to self":
the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self is called the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); "body" (*kāya*) here refers to existence (*bhava*).
Therefore it is called "the body of existence" (satkāya);
it has the five aggregates of clinging as its essence,
and takes this body of existence as its object.
One clings to "self" and "what belongs to self.
This clinging is itself a view.
Through this view, one takes up a body as its object.
It is called "view of a self-identity" (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
This is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, meaning "the view regarding a self-identity."
In the Western lands [India], it is called *satkāyadṛṣṭi*;
here [in China], it is translated as "view of a disintegrating body" (*huàshēnjiàn*) or "view of an existing body" (*yǒushēnjiàn*).
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Destruction" is *sat*,
and "aggregate" is *kāya*.
This is precisely impermanence.
The meaning of the "aggregation of aggregates" (skandha-samudāya) is impermanence, which is the meaning of disintegration.
"Aggregation" (samudāya) means accumulation.
*Kāya* is *sat*; thus it is called *satkāya*.
It refers to the body (*kāya*) consisting of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
This name is established in order to exclude the notion of permanence;
it is necessary that this notion precede [the arising of the afflictions].
Regarding the statement "because one clings to a self," this is explained as the Sautrāntika interpretation intended to refute the eternalistic views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The name "sat" is established to preclude the conception of a single [unitary] self; the name "kāya" is established [to indicate the collection of aggregates].
This is the view that destroys the body;
it is called the view of destroying the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
[Thus say] the Vaibhāṣika masters.
It is explained as follows:
it is called "sa" because it exists;
the meaning of "kāya" (body) is as previously stated.
Do not, without an object of perception, conceive of a self or what belongs to a self.
Therefore, it is said that this view takes one's own person as its object; it takes the *satkāya* (the transitory collection) as its object.
Because one gives rise to this view, the treatise designates this view as *satkāya* (the view of a real body);
the above is the explanation of the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Regarding "annihilationism and eternalism":
To cling to "I" and "mine," and to grasp at annihilation or permanence,
is called the view of extremes.
Annihilationism and eternalism are called "extremes.
Clinging to them constitutes a "view.
One gives rise to clinging based upon these extremes.
Because it is an adherence to extremes;
it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Adherence to extremes is itself a view (*dṛṣṭi*).
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. To "negate" means to negate cause and effect;
this is termed "wrong view."
The perverse itself is the view;
this is called "perverse view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), following the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. "Inferior" refers to that which is surpassed.
To regard what is inferior as superior is called "adherence to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa). "Views" here refers specifically to the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
The view of extremes,
false views, and the adherence to these three views.
Because one regards it as superior,
it is called "adherence to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa); it is so named because of the grasping of views.
This is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound;
it refers to the grasping at other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) apart from the three views.
To regard these as superior is also called "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
in truth, it should properly be designated as "clinging to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭyādiparāmarśa*).
Omitting the word "and so forth," it is simply called the "clinging to views. Regarding "falsely claiming what is not a cause or path to be such":
this means claiming as a cause that which is not a cause.
To regard what is not the Path as the Path is called the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
"Rules" refers here to [the practices] within the Buddha-dharma.
The "five precepts" and so forth are examples of this.
"Prohibitions" refers to the prohibitions of non-Buddhists,
such as those concerning dogs, cattle, and the like.
To grasp at these prohibitions and precepts as the cause and path [to liberation] is called the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
This is the grasping of rules and observances.
This is an *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. The treatise states:
"For example, those who grasp at Īśvara, Prajāpati, or others as being the cause of the world, or grasp at a self (*ātman*) and so forth."
Born into this world, they give rise to delusion through attachment,
casting themselves into water, fire, and the like.
Various forms of wrong conduct are not causes for rebirth in the heavens;
having falsely given rise to attachment to these causes— this refers to the attachment to what is not a cause as being a cause— one observes and upholds ascetic vows and prohibitions.

The knowledge associated with numerical calculation is not the path of liberation; it is the false arising of a grasping for the path found in the numerical calculations of non-Buddhists, through which they believe they attain nirvāṇa.
In reality, one should establish the categories of "observances and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as the basis for their terminology.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) has been omitted;

it refers only to the term "clinging to precepts and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the grasping at other dharmas that are not [merely] precepts and observances. This concludes the treatise.
From this, the second section specifically clarifies the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The treatise states:
If one gives rise to the view that what is not a cause is a cause,
for what reason does this view arise?
Regarding the statement that it is not abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*): since it arises from delusion regarding the cause,
it should indeed be abandoned by the vision of the origin.
The verse says:
Regarding Maheśvara and others, the false attachment to what is not a cause as being a cause arises from the views of permanence and self; therefore, it is abandoned solely by seeing suffering.
The commentary states:
Those who maintain that the world is produced by Īśvara and other such causes must first conceive of their essence as being eternal.
To give rise to [the notion of] permanence is the inversion of permanence; to grasp [it] as a single self is the inversion of self.
Since the grasping at a self must first exist before the arising of causal grasping,
it is not the case that [the self] is the cause of grasping.
The two perversions of permanence and self arise from [the view of] permanence and self;
they are abandoned only through the vision of suffering.
Therefore, that [view] is not the grasping of what is not a cause as a cause;

it is also abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), because it is subsumed under the view of a self and what belongs to a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) due to its delusion regarding coarse results through the inversion of permanence and self.
Therefore, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering; however, the clinging to rules and observances consists of two general types:
first, that which clings to what is not a cause as being a cause.
Second, regarding what is not the path, one regards it as the path; regarding what is not the cause, one clings to it as the cause.
Furthermore, there are two types [of this].
First, there arises the deluded attachment to a self and permanent phenomena;
second, there arises the deluded calculation that asceticism and the like—performed as the result of past actions—are the causes for rebirth among dogs and other beings in heaven.
These two are delusions regarding the fruit of suffering.
Therefore, all [these views] are abandoned through the vision of suffering. Regarding the misapprehension of what is not the path as the path, there are also two categories:
first, the misapprehension of tainted precepts and so forth [as the path].
It serves as the path to liberation;
because this delusion has coarse results,
it is also abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Second, the false view of clinging to and slandering the path,
as well as doubt,
[regarding] the path to purification.
This clinging to rules and observances strongly opposes the Truth of the Path;
it is abandoned through the vision of the Truth of the Path.
From this fourth [section],
the four inversions are clarified.
The treatise says:
As previously stated, the view of permanence and the view of self arise from inversion.
One should understand that these are not merely these two types of inversion; rather, all inversions are to be understood in this way.
