In total there are four kinds;
namely, first, the perversion of grasping at the impermanent as permanent.
Second, the perversion of perceiving pleasure in what is suffering;
third, [the perversion of perceiving purity] in what is impure.
The inversion of perceiving purity;
fourth, the inversion of perceiving a self where there is no self— this is the answer.
Regarding these four inversions,
what is their essential nature?
The verse says:
The intrinsic nature of the four perversions consists of three views, because they are merely perverted through the addition of exaggeration; perception and mind follow the power of the views.
Thus it is explained.
The first two phrases establish the essence;
the third phrase establishes the criteria for inclusion or exclusion;
the fourth phrase harmonizes with the scriptures.
Regarding the intrinsic nature of the four perversions, it is said that they arise from three views; specifically,
among the views regarding extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*),
only the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) is taken.
One regards it as the inversion of permanence;
among the views of grasping at [wrong] views,
one grasps at and conceives of it as pleasure and purity.
Regarding the inversions of pleasure and purity,
within the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
one takes up only the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi).
"It is because I am mistaken.
Regarding the phrase "only because the inversion is further increased," this cites three reasons.
The four inversions are established on this basis.
As for the three causes, they are:
first, because each is exclusively inverted.
Second, because it is of the nature of speculative reasoning;
third, because it involves false superimposition— namely, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It is not an absolute perversion to hold that the contaminated path attains pure nirvana,
even though it does not constitute the ultimate severance of afflictions or the realization of cessation.
Yet, one is able to temporarily leave defilement behind and realize cessation by taking limited purity as an object; thus,
it is not an absolute perversion.
The view of nihilism and false views do not involve the superimposition of what is unreal,
because they operate without a gateway.
Other factors such as greed and hatred cannot perform such investigation,
because they do not have the nature of insight (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, other afflictions are not of the nature of inversion;
rather, perception and mind follow the power of view.
This is a thorough understanding of the sūtras.
If seeing this were merely an inversion,
why would the sūtra say, "Regarding that which is impermanent"?
In the perception of permanence, there are three inversions regarding thought, mind, and view:
[the inversion of] suffering, impurity, and non-self.
There are likewise three inversions regarding thought, mind, and view concerning [the perception of] pleasure and purity.
Answer: In truth, it should be understood that only view (*dṛṣṭi*) is the inversion;
perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) follow along with the view.
It is also established as a "perversion" (viparyāsa),
because its mode of activity (ākāra) is identical to that of [wrong] views (dṛṣṭi).
According to the masters of the *Vibhāṣā*, these twelve inversions are permanently severed by the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
The Vibhajyavādins state that [the afflictions] associated with views are abandoned through the abandonment of views.
Eight are abandoned by insight alone;
four are abandoned by both insight and cultivation,
namely those regarding pleasure and purity.
Each possesses perception and mind.
These four types of perception and mind have not yet been abandoned by those who have entered the stream (srotāpanna).
Therefore, a verse is cited:
the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Vibhajyavādin, "A person who has attained the first fruit [of the path] is so called because they still possess the inversion of perception."
"Your mind is scorched with fever;
once you have distanced yourself from that perception, greed will subside and the mind will become pure. Based on this verse.
The noble ones possess inversions of perception regarding the mind.
Because of this verse,
the Sautrāntikas maintain that the eight inversions of perception are not yet entirely abandoned by those in training (śaikṣa).
From this, the fifth section clarifies the seven and nine types of pride (*māna*).
Within this, it is divided into two parts.
First, the explicit explanation of the seven and nine types of pride;
second, the explanation that they do not arise when not yet abandoned.
Regarding the first, the explicit explanation of the seven and nine types of pride:
The treatise says:
Is it only the view-propensities (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) that have many distinctions, or do others also have them?
The verse says:
The seven types of pride and nine [afflictions] arise from the three [roots]; All are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation;
Like the "bondage of killing" and others, there are those abandoned by cultivation that do not manifest in the noble ones.
The commentary states:
The first phrase provides the direct answer;
the second phrase clarifies what is abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
The final two lines clarify that one does not practice the cultivation of the path.
Furthermore, regarding the seven types of pride,
the first is pride (*māna*).
2. Pride (māna); 3. Pride beyond pride (adhimāna);
4. Self-pride (asmimāna).
Fifth, overweening pride;
sixth, inferiority pride;
seventh, false pride—these cause the mind to become haughty and uplifted.
The general designation "pride" is established;
however, because its modes of activity differ,
it is divided into seven types.
Regarding others who are inferior, one considers oneself superior;
regarding others who are equal, one considers oneself equal.
Although this accords with the object, [it is not so in reality].
Elevation of the mind is termed conceit (*māna*).
It consists in considering oneself superior to those who are one's equals.
Regarding others who are equal to oneself or superior,
to think of oneself as such is called *atimāna* (overweening pride), because it exceeds the aforementioned types of pride.
To consider oneself already superior to those who are actually superior is called "conceit beyond conceit" (*mānātimāna*),
because it exceeds the conceit [directed toward] others.
Grasping at a self and what belongs to a self,
causing the mind to become uplifted and haughty,
is called "pride of self" (asmimāna).

Relying on the arising of the notion of "I," to claim what has not been attained as already attained is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride); to consider oneself only slightly inferior when one is actually far superior is likewise [a form of] pride.
That which is called "inferior pride" (ūnamāna) consists of considering oneself to possess qualities when one lacks them;
this is termed "false pride" (mithyāmāna).
To accomplish evil conduct is called "lack of virtue.
To rely on evil and be haughty is called "perverse pride" (mithyāmāna). As for the nine types of pride:
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that there are nine types of conceit (*māna*).
The first is the conceit of "I am superior" (*atimāna*).
2. The class of pride of self-equality;
3. The class of pride of self-inferiority;
4. The class of pride of superiority over those who are superior.
5. The class of conceit thinking "I am equal";
6. The class of conceit thinking "I am inferior";
7. The class of conceit thinking "I am not superior."
The eight types of the conceit "I am equal," and the nine types of the conceit "I am not inferior.
These arise from three [types of conceit].
These nine types of conceit flow forth from three of the seven previously mentioned types of conceit.
As for the three types of conceit,
they are: conceit (*māna*), excessive conceit (*atimāna*), and inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*).
First, the class of pride regarding superiority (*abhimāna*) arises from excessive pride (*atimāna*).
Second, the class of pride regarding equality (*asmimāna*).
The third type, the conceit of inferiority (*hīnāsmimāna*), arises from the conceit of superiority (*māna*).
It arises from the conceit of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
The fourth type of conceit, "I am superior," also arises from the conceit of inferiority.
The fifth type of conceit is "I am equal."
The sixth type, the inferiority-conceit (*ūnamāna*), arises from conceit (*māna*).
It arises from over-conceit (*atimāna*).
The seventh type of conceit, "I am unsurpassed," arises from the preceding conceit.
The eighth type of conceit is "I am equal to those who are not equal to me."
It emerges from overweening pride (*atimāna*).
The ninth, the class of pride that thinks "I am not inferior" (*anavamanyanā-māna*),
emerges from base pride (*ūnamāna*).
Question: Regarding the "inferiority-free" form of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am"), what is its high point?
Answer: It refers to when one regards one's own person in comparison with a group of sentient beings whom one holds dear and considers superior.
Although one knows oneself to be extremely inferior,
one regards oneself with respect;
thus, one achieves the "I-am-not-inferior" conceit (*anūnamāna*).
Those that are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation are the seven types of pride and the nine types of pride.
All are seen as abandoned through cultivation.
As for those that arise having the abandonable through seeing as their object:
Those that arise by taking names as their object are called abandoned through seeing; those that arise by taking phenomena as their object are called abandoned through cultivation.
As for the conceit to be abandoned through cultivation,
although it is still possessed by noble ones as long as they have not yet abandoned it, [it does not arise].
Some are manifest, while others are not manifest.
As for those that are not manifest:
The pride of self (asmimāna) is one;
as for the remaining six types of pride,
they may manifest even in noble ones (ārya).
The nine types of pride mentioned previously do not manifest even in the Noble Ones; therefore,
the verse states that there are those abandoned by cultivation which do not manifest.
This refers to the nine types of pride as well as the pride of "I am" (asmimāna).
Regarding the phrase "the noble ones, such as those bound by the fetter of killing," and so forth:
This is an explanation by way of example.
For instance, the fetter of killing is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Although the Noble Ones have not yet severed them,
these fetters certainly do not manifest; as it is with the fetter of killing, so it is with the others.
The same applies to the types of pride.

the afflictions of the Truth of Origination remain bound;
this is called "severance that is not dissociation."
Furthermore, regarding those already abandoned in the preceding chapter,
among the nine grades of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
[the practitioner abandons] the first eight grades.
Whichever category [of afflictions] is abandoned,
it is called "the preceding category already abandoned. Once that preceding category has been abandoned...
If one has not yet abandoned a subsequent category [of defilement],
but is able to take a preceding category as its object,
one remains bound to that preceding category.
Therefore, although a category [of fetters] has been severed in the preceding stage, one may still be bound by it in the subsequent stage;
this is called "severance that is not dissociation."
From this point, the seventh major section clarifies the manner in which delusions increase.
Within it, there are two divisions.
First, the actual explanation of how the afflictions increase;
second, the explanation of the mind accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the first, the actual explanation of their increase:
The treatise says:
"What objects have how many [defilements]?
This is a question concerning the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)."
If one were to answer by distinguishing each individual case, the discourse would become excessively prolix;
therefore, a concise *Vibhāṣā* should be composed.
By means of this, although one exerts only a small amount of effort,
one is able to cross over the great torrent of questions;
that is to say, although phenomena are numerous, they are briefly categorized into sixteen kinds.
That is to say, there are fifteen [factors] consisting of the three realms, five categories, and three [aspects] for each category;
when the untainted factors (*anāsrava-dharma*) are added to these, they total sixteen. These are the objects that the consciousness capable of perceiving them takes as its objective support.
The same applies to their names and numbers; consciousnesses are also sixteen.
One should know which dharma is the object of which consciousness.
It is easy to understand that "what" refers to the object and "which" refers to the latent disposition (anuśaya) that increases; since the consciousness [takes] the object,
the object is the "thing" (vastu),
and the afflictions increase upon that thing.
This shall naturally become clear.
For now, one should understand herein:
which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses?
The verse says: The above is the treatise.

Those [factors] abandoned through seeing suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, when bound to the desire realm, are the objects of three types of consciousness belonging to their own realm and one type belonging to the form realm; they are also the objects of untainted consciousness.
The [objects] of form (*rūpa*) each have three [aspects] from below; the one above is the object of pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*).
In the Formless Realm (*ārūpya*), they pervade all three realms. Each has three [aspects] as the objects of pure consciousness;
those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) all increase the activity of their own respective consciousnesses.

Regarding the statement, "The uncontaminated [dharmas] are the objects of the last three pure consciousnesses within the three realms," the commentary explains that this refers to the first two lines of the verse.
The third line clarifies the three objects cultivated regarding suffering and its origin;
the latter one-line verse consists of the first two lines [of the following].
The first two lines clarify the objects of the path of cessation; the latter two lines clarify the untainted (anāsrava) objects.
"Those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and through cultivation" refers to...
This generally indicates the three categories of the three realms.
As for those bound to the desire realm,
this specifically distinguishes them from the preceding three categories.
Regarding the objects of the three consciousnesses of one's own realm and the single untainted (anāsrava) consciousness:
these are the factors bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) above;
they are each the objects of five consciousnesses that abandon [afflictions] through the cultivation of the truths of suffering and origin.
That is to say, the three [types] of one's own realm, one from the form realm,
and untainted consciousness.
These are called the five consciousnesses.
Regarding the three [factors] of their own realm,
they are as previously explained.
The suffering and its origin are [the objects] of cultivation.
As for "one in the form realm," this refers to that which is abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to the cultivation of the path that takes the suffering and origin of the desire realm as its object, which is attained through the cultivation of the form realm.
As for "untainted consciousness," this refers to untainted consciousness.

It is also cultivated by taking the suffering and origin of the desire realm as its object. Regarding "the three [stages] from each of the lower levels of the form realm, and the one pure consciousness above, are the objects of the form realm":
this refers to that which is bound to the form realm and is abandoned through cultivation regarding suffering and origin.
Each is the object-condition for eight consciousnesses;
namely, the three of its own realm and the three of the lower realms.
"Below" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Three" refers to what was previously stated:
those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), as well as one [type] from the higher realms.
This refers to the consciousnesses of the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
which are able to take the suffering and origin of the form realm as their objects; it also includes untainted pure consciousness (*anāsrava-viśuddha-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, because they also take as their objects the suffering and origin of the form realm that are abandoned through cultivation,
each of these eight consciousnesses is individually capable of taking as its object the suffering and origin of the form realm that are abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the fact that the formless [realms] are the objects of the three types of pure consciousness within each of the three realms:
they are bound to the formless realm and are abandoned through the cultivation of the truths of suffering and its origin.
Each has ten consciousnesses as its objects;
that is, those pertaining to the three realms,
three for each, making nine.
The third refers to the cultivation of the truths of suffering and its origin. There are ten untainted pure consciousnesses (*anāsrava-viśuddha-vijñāna*).
Each of these ten consciousnesses is capable of taking the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) as its object.

Regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*darśana-nirodha-mārga-heya*), all increase as objects of their own respective consciousnesses.
This is explained with reference to the three realms.
First, concerning those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path:
They serve as the objects for the six consciousnesses.
The five consciousnesses are as previously described;
furthermore, the sixth consciousness—specifically that which is abandoned through the vision of cessation—is added.
Those abandoned by the path of seeing are also objects of the six consciousnesses;
the five consciousnesses are as previously described.
Furthermore, adding the sixth consciousness abandoned through the path of seeing and the consciousnesses belonging to its own respective truths is termed "one's own consciousness."
The objects to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path within the form realm each serve as the objects of nine consciousnesses.
The eight consciousnesses are as previously described,
each increased by its own respective one; in the Formless Realm, there are eleven consciousnesses for both the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
It has ten objects;
as before, each increases by its own one.

This is explained according to the previous discussion on the desire realm. Regarding the uncontaminated [objects] and the objects of the three pure consciousnesses within the last three realms: [the details follow the same principle].
This refers to untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma),
which serve as objects for all ten consciousnesses;
that is to say, within the three realms.
Each of the latter three groups refers to those who have seen the cessation [of suffering] and those who have seen the path.
The consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation,
together with the untainted consciousness,
constitute the tenth.
These ten consciousnesses are each capable of taking the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. To summarize the preceding meaning,
a verse is further spoken:
It should be known that those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, are bound to the realms of desire,
form, and formlessness respectively. Regarding the five, eight, and ten objects of consciousness, the commentary explains:
The three categories of the desire realm are the objects of the five consciousnesses;
the three categories of the form realm [are likewise].
The eight consciousnesses take the three categories of the formless realm as their objects; the ten consciousnesses take [all categories] as their objects.
It should be understood that those [factors] abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path each increase their own consciousness as an object;
the six consciousnesses, etc., take pure (anāsrava) dharmas as their objects, serving as the spheres for ten consciousnesses.
As the Treatise says:
Having thus understood these sixteen types of phenomena as the objective spheres of the sixteen consciousnesses,
one should now extensively analyze which underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in relation to which objects.
If I were to comment on each point individually,
I fear the text would become overly prolix;
therefore, I shall [address them] here.
A brief indication of the general direction is provided.
Now, suppose there is a question:
"Among the objects to which one is bound..."
How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)? One should observe that, in total, there are seven types of the faculty of pleasure.
That is to say, there is one in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), namely, the pleasure abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) which exists within the five sensory consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna).
Therefore, it is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the five categories of form in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because they possess mental aspiration (*āśaya*),
they pertain to all five categories.
The seventh untainted [feeling] refers to the third dhyāna;
it is untainted pleasure. It is the untainted faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
They are not subject to the increase of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
as has already been stated previously.
Among the seven, the first six refer to one [category] of the desire realm.
The five [fetters] of the form realm are,
as appropriate, abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
And all the universal [defilements], as well as all those of the form realm,
increase in accordance with the latent dispositions (anuśaya) abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm that take their own category of pleasure as an object.

And the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) toward suffering and its origin can take as their objects the pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Since it permeates all five categories,
all consciousnesses take the faculty of pleasure as their object.
"Everything" refers to the afflictions of the five categories. If someone were to ask:
"What is the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object?"
Furthermore, how many types of latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with the aforementioned pleasant faculty (*sukhendriya*)?
This refers to consciousness upon the pleasant faculty;
one should observe that this consciousness comprises twelve types in total.
This refers to the four [factors] of the desire realm, excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation; that is to say,
the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin within the desire realm.
And those abandoned through cultivation which take the faculty of pleasure as their object, namely,
the Path Truth of the desire realm.
Wrong view, doubt, and ignorance can take the untainted bliss of the truth of cessation as their object.
Because its essence is not the faculty of pleasure,
it is abandoned by the Truth of Cessation and does not take pleasure as its object.
The five categories of the form realm and two of the formless realm; that is,
[the afflictions] abandoned through the vision of the Truth of the Path.
And the path-truth of the formless realm abandoned through cultivation,
as well as wrong view, doubt,
and ignorance.
Because it takes the third dhyāna as its object and consists of untainted bliss,
it is abandoned by the path of truth pertaining to the formless realm.
There is the consciousness associated with the object of pleasure (*sukha-saṃprayukta-vijñāna*).
It is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), and is both innate (*upapatti-labdha*) and acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*).
Because it universally takes as its object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) across nine stages,
it is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
When one attains the third dhyāna with an object of perception,
it is the untainted (anāsrava) faculty of pleasure and consciousness.
This is the twelfth untainted [moment].
All of these are able to take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object; this section above clarifies the consciousnesses that take pleasure as their object, totaling twelve in all.
Specifically, there are four in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
There are five [levels] in the realm of form;
together with the previous, these constitute nine.
There are two in the formless realm.
With the preceding [eleven] added together, there are eleven;
further adding the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), they become twelve. These, as appropriate, consist of four categories within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The conditioned factors of the form realm,
the two categories of the formless realm,
and all universal [factors].
Regarding the phrase "the latent dispositions increase accordingly," the commentary explains:
this passage precisely clarifies that the latent dispositions increase accordingly upon the consciousness that takes pleasure as its object.
In the desire realm, there are four categories;
excluding those abandoned through the vision of cessation. In the form realm, those conditioned by objects include five categories.
They take conditioned phenomena as their object;
excluding, however, wrong view, doubt, and ignorance pertaining to the level of the Truth of Cessation.
That takes the unconditioned as its object.
It is a wrong view and so forth that takes the truth of cessation as its object;
it is not a consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object.
Therefore, they must be eliminated. Regarding the two categories of the formless realm,
these refer to those abandoned through the Truth of the Path and those abandoned through cultivation.
This refers to wrong view, doubt, and ignorance within the category of the Truth of the Path.
These are the conditions for the consciousness that takes pleasure;
below this are greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth.
Because they arise conditioned by false views and so forth,
greed and other afflictions belonging to the level of the Truth of the Path are termed "consciousnesses associated with the faculty of pleasure."

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase accordingly. Since the consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the formless realm takes the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) as its object,
the afflictions (kleśa) to be abandoned by cultivation [increase].
The latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in accordance with [the object] upon a consciousness that takes pleasure as its condition,
as well as those that are universal (sarvatraga).
That is to say, below the suffering and origin of the formless realm,
the universal latent dispositions (sarvatraga-anuśaya) take as their objects those factors to be abandoned by the truth of the path and those to be abandoned by cultivation.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is consciousness. Furthermore, if it should be asked:

"In relation to the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), how many kinds of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase? The explanation is as follows:
This question concerns the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase in accordance with consciousness based on the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
One should examine this consciousness.
In total there are fourteen;
these consist of the previous twelve,
with two additional types added.
That is, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
there are the universal grasping (*parigraha*) factors abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
Thus, there are fourteen consciousnesses.
The consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object, and the consciousness that takes what is superior to the faculty of pleasure as its object—
these follow as appropriate;
for the realms of desire and form, it is as described above.
Regarding the four categories of the formless realm,
with the exception of those abandoned through the vision of cessation:
this passage precisely clarifies how the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in accordance [with their objects].
The preceding commentary on the treatise has been fully annotated so that those who seek out the treatise may easily understand its meaning;
for this reason, it has been set forth.
Secondly, this clarifies the mind accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The treatise states:
If a mind is called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because of them,
then those [dispositions] must necessarily increase (anuśerate) within that mind; this is the question.
This is not fixed; some [afflictions] increase accordingly,
namely those that are associated with the mind.
Furthermore, when the object-condition (*ālambana*) has not been severed but the associated [factors] have already been severed,
then [the defilement] does not increase accordingly. It is based on this methodological principle.
Therefore, this statement was made.
The verse says:
There are two types of minds with latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), namely, those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
The defiled mind pertains to both; the non-defiled is restricted to that which increases [the latencies].
The commentary states:
"The mind with latent dispositions (anuśaya) is of two kinds."
This is the heading.
"Those with defilement and those without defilement" is the enumeration.
There are two general types of mind accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*):
defiled and non-defiled minds.
Due to this distinction,
being associated with afflictions is termed "defiled."
Among those with outflows (*sāsrava*),
wholesome and neutral states of mind are termed "unstained" (*asaṃkliṣṭa*).
Regarding "the defiled mind pervades both":
a defiled mind is termed "possessing latent tendencies" (sānuśaya).
These possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
They are categorized as either having the quality of "increasing" (*anuśayana*) or not increasing;
hence, it is said that there are two types.
There are those that increase through association.
The first refers to defiled minds,
which are associated with afflictions.
The underlying tendencies (anuśaya) have not yet been abandoned.
Second, it refers to the fact that the underlying tendencies associated with this defiled mind have not yet been abandoned.
Therefore, they are said to "increase along with" [the mind]. Those that do not increase along with it refer to the defiled mind;
[in this case], the associated [factors] have already been abandoned.
They do not increase accordingly;
yet they are still said to possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), because they are constantly associated [with the mind]. Their nature as fetters (*bandhana*) has already been severed.
Therefore, they do not increase [in association];
because they do not abandon their nature as companions, they are always associated.
The state of being accompanied must necessarily be uninterrupted, because it possesses the quality of having a companion. This is what is called "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*);
as for "being non-defiled," this refers specifically to those [factors] that increase in accordance with the dispositions.
Because it does not increase [the defilements] in a general manner, it is termed "restricted.
This is because an undefiled mind is not associated with the afflictions.

It is not by virtue of being accompanied [by latent dispositions] that they are called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya); rather, this designation applies exclusively to those [dharmas] in which the latent dispositions increase.
It is called "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya),
meaning that because the latent dispositions take an undefiled mind as their object,
those latent dispositions have not yet been abandoned.
They are called "possessing latent dispositions" (anuśaya).
The term "not yet abandoned" is used because [the dispositions] increase in accordance with them.
Therefore, it is only that which is strictly subject to increase (anuśayana) that is termed "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya).
From this eighth [point]...
This clarifies their sequential arising.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, the explicit clarification of the sequence.
Second, explaining the causes for the arising of delusion.
First, regarding the explanation of the sequence,
the treatise states:
Regarding the sequence in which the ten types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise as described above,
which one precedes and which follows?
The verse says:

Ignorance, doubt, false view of self, extreme views, adherence to precepts and rituals, adherence to views, greed, pride, and hatred arise in this order; the commentary explains: "The preceding induces the subsequent."
First, ignorance;
second, doubt;
third, false view.
4. The view of a self-identity;
5. The view of extremes;
6. The clinging to precepts and observances.
7. Clinging to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
8. Greed (rāga).
9. Pride (māna).
Tenth, regarding anger:
when afflictions arise,
they first stem from ignorance.
One does not understand the truths;
because of this lack of understanding,
doubt subsequently arises.
Because doubt arises regarding the Four Noble Truths,
from this state of uncertainty...
It gives rise to wrong view,
which means definitely repudiating suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
this occurs by way of repudiating the Truths.
It induces the arising of the view of a self-identity;
that is, within the aggregates of suffering,
it negates the principle of suffering.
Because one then resolutely clings to this as a self,
from this view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is induced to arise.
This means that because one relies on the extremes of self-grasping— namely,
the views of annihilationism and eternalism— this view of extremes subsequently gives rise to the grasping of precepts and observances.
One then calculates that prior adherence serves as a means of purification; thus, it arises from the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
It leads to grasping at rebirth;
that is to say, having reckoned [the object] as capable of purification,
one necessarily clings to it as being supreme.
From this adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
greed is subsequently induced;
that is to say, within one's own view.
Because of the depth of this affectionate love,
following this craving,
pride is subsequently induced to arise.
Because one gives rise to arrogance by relying on one's own views and understanding,
following this pride, there is...
Next, it gives rise to aversion;
for one necessarily feels hatred and resentment toward that which contradicts what has been seen.
Thus, for now, the explanation has been given according to the sequential order.
As for those that transcend the sequence,
there would be no standard for their prior or posterior relations.
From this, secondly, the causes for the arising of delusion are clarified.
The treatise states:
By how many causes and conditions do the various afflictions arise?
The verse says:
"Because the latent dispositions have not been abandoned, and because an object corresponding [to those dispositions] appears along with improper mental attention,
it is said that the afflictions possess their causes and conditions. Commentary:
Defilements arise due to three causes and conditions:
first, because the underlying tendencies have not been abandoned.
This is precisely the cause of delusion.
Second, objects appear in accordance with [the individual's] capacity.
Regarding "in accordance with [capacity]":
This is according to what is appropriate;
for example, greed arises toward favorable objects,
while hatred arises toward unfavorable objects, and so forth.
This refers to the objective sphere of the afflictions.
Third, through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*),
one initiates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the arising of the afflictions.
Due to these three aforementioned causes,
the afflictions manifest;
thus it is said that the delusions possess both cause and condition.
Regarding these three causes mentioned above:
this has been explained provisionally based on the presence of both causes and conditions;
however, there may also be cases where [a phenomenon] arises solely by relying on the power of the object.
This concerns those such as Arhats of the "regressive" (parihāṇa-dharman) faculty type.
From this, the third major section follows:
a miscellaneous explanation of the arising of various afflictions (kleśa).
This is divided into three parts:
first, an explanation of the four categories beginning with the outflows (*āsrava*);
second, an explanation of the six categories beginning with the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The distinction between the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). This is divided into two parts based on four gates, such as "knowledge" (*vidyā*) and "outflows" (*āsrava*):
first, the definition of their essential nature.
Second, the explanation of the names.
Below this follows the exposition of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The Treatise states:
That is to say, as previously explained:
the latent dispositions (anuśaya) together with the outbursts (paryavasthāna).
The Sūtra explains [them] as the outflows (āsrava), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), and graspings (upādāna).
The outflows refer to the three outflows:
first, the outflow of desire (kāmāsrava).
The second is the outflow of existence (bhava-āsava), and the third is the outflow of ignorance (avijjā-āsava).
As for what is called a "flood" (ogha):
There are four floods (*ogha*):
first, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*);
second, the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*).
The three floods of views (dṛṣṭi-ogha) and the flood of ignorance (avidyā-ogha).
As for the yokes (yoga), there are four yokes.
As explained in the context of the "floods" (ogha),
"clinging" (upādāna) refers to the four types of clinging:
first, clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmopādāna).
2. Clinging to views; 3.
clinging to precepts and observances;
4. clinging to the doctrine of self.
What is the nature of these outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth?
The verse says:
The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, along with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding ignorance (*moha*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The outflows of the two upper realms are exclusively afflictions;
with the exception of delusion, they are neutral, inwardly directed, and belong to the stages of meditative concentration (samāpatti-bhūmi).
Therefore, ignorance is combined [with them] as a single outflow, because it is the root of all forms of existence; thus, it is established separately as one distinct outflow.
The floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) are likewise; they are established separately because views are particularly sharp and because views do not conform to [the other afflictions].
The yokes of desire and existence are not established independently among the outflows (*āsrava*);
furthermore, views are divided into two and named "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Ignorance is not established separately because it is not a grasper.
The commentary states:
the first two lines clarify the three outflows (*āsrava*).
The next line clarifies the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*);
the subsequent line clarifies the four graspings (*upādāna*).
Those afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), together with their envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding delusion (*moha*), are termed the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsava*).
These forty-one entities are called the essence of the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava); that is to say,
they are bound to the realm of desire (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta).
The root afflictions number thirty-one;

together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), they constitute forty-one. In the two upper realms, which are characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*), there are only afflictions, excluding ignorance (*moha*).
These consist of fifty-two entities which constitute the nature of the outflows (sāsrava),
namely those belonging to the two higher realms.
The root afflictions each number twenty-six among the delusions of the five categories.
Each excludes both hatred and delusion.
When the two realms are discussed together,
they thus constitute fifty-two.
Although those two upper realms possess the two envelopments of torpor and restlessness,
they are not established as the substance of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Because these envelopments are few,
and furthermore, these two envelopments arise in dependence upon others.
Because they lack autonomy,
they are alike in being neutral (avyākṛta) and internal;
because they belong to the stages of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi), they are combined as one.
This clarifies that the two upper realms are collectively categorized as outflow-tainted (sāsrava). First,
they are identical in being of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
Second, they both function through the internal door, taking meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the body as their objects;
this is called "functioning through the internal door. Third, they both belong to the stage of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bhūmi*). By virtue of these three meanings, [they are similar].
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the two realms are combined into a single outflow (*āsrava*).
As for why ignorance (*avidyā*) is treated as a separate outflow: it is because ignorance is the root of all forms of existence (*bhava*).
Ignorance within the three realms each has five kinds; thus,
there are fifteen entities herein.
It constitutes the outflow of ignorance;
that is to say, by means of ignorance,
one takes the three realms of existence as one's root.
It is established as a separate outflow (*āsrava*).
The same applies to the floods (*ogha*) and the yokes (*yoga*); that is, the floods and the yokes are likewise [established as distinct].
Because its substance is identical to the outflows (*āsrava*),
the designation is likewise so; that is to say, it refers to the aforementioned outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The analysis of various views is termed the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāma-yoga*).
In this way, when the various views are extracted from among the outflows,
they are called the flood of existence.
That which is called the yoke of existence (bhavayoga),
when analyzed by extracting the various views,
is termed the flood of views (dṛṣṭyogha).
And that which is called the yoke of views— thus twenty-nine entities have been revealed as the flood of desire,
namely: greed.
Hatred and pride each have five kinds, making fifteen in total.
The four types of doubt refer to the doubts underlying the Four Noble Truths;
added to the previous total, they form nineteen.
The nine fetters (paryavasthāna), added to the previous total, form twenty-nine.
Twenty-eight entities are called the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*); that is,
greed and pride each [numbering] ten, pertaining to the two higher realms.
Each has five, totaling twenty. Regarding doubt, there are eight;
in the two upper realms, there are four each.
Including doubt, there are eight;
added to the previous, they total twenty-eight.
There are thirty-six items.
The flood of views refers to the twelve views within each of the three realms— specifically,
the five views associated with the suffering of the lower realm.
There are two each for origination and cessation;
with the four views added, they total nine.
There are three views under the Truth of the Path;
thus, they total twelve.
There are fifteen entities.
It constitutes the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*),
referring to the fivefold ignorance pertaining to each of the three realms.
One should know that there are four yokes (*yoga*),
as explained in the case of the floods (*ogha*).
They are established separately because views (*dṛṣṭi*) are particularly sharp.

The reason that various views are extracted separately and designated as the "flood of views" (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) and the "yoke of views" (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*) is that the nature of views is characterized by intense and sharp investigation.
Because they are seen not to abide in accordance [with reality], they do not exist independently of the outflows (*āsrava*).
To cause one to abide in birth and death is the meaning of "outflow."
The vision of the nature is sharp and intense;
it does not abide in accordance with conventional meanings. By means of this, regarding the outflows (āsrava):
They do not exist as independent names;

they can only be spoken of as "outflows" (*āsrava*) when combined with others. As for the fact that desire and existence are each divided into two—namely, the yokes (*yoga*) and the graspings (*upādāna*) along with delusion and views—this clarifies the essential nature of the four graspings.
The same four yokes:
the yoke of sensual desire together with delusion is called the grasping of sensual desire.
The yoke of existence together with delusion is called the grasping of the doctrine of self.
The yoke of views is divided into two.
The first is called the clinging to precepts and observances;
the second is called the clinging to views.
One should know that these consist of thirty-four entities.
That which desires to grasp the essence is called greed and hatred.
Pride and ignorance each have four and five [factors] respectively, totaling twenty.
Including the four types of doubt, there are twenty-four;
together with the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), there are thirty-four,
totaling thirty-eight factors.
Tell me the essence of grasping (*upādāna*);
it is craving (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*).
Ignorance has ten [instances] for each;
doubt has eight when the upper realms are combined.

The six entities constitute the essence of the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Since there are two types of such grasping in each of the three realms, there are six in total.
If one [grasping] is eliminated, the corresponding path is eliminated.
The thirty entities constitute the essence of the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Within the twelve views, there are ten types of views in each of the three realms.
Excluding the two types of clinging to precepts and observances,
the afflictions of the higher realms are called clinging to the doctrine of self (ātmavādopādāna).
The expression "discourse on self" refers to the internal body;
it is based upon this that one speaks of a "self.
Therefore, the afflictions of the higher realms—
That which has many internal bodies as its object is called "clinging to the discourse of self" (*ātmavādopādāna*);
it is the clinging to the discourse of self.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound). Among all [types of] views,
the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established separately.
Because it alone acts as the enemy of the noble path and because it deceives both the lay and monastic communities—
namely, the lay community.
Practicing self-starvation and other such austerities for the sake of the heavenly realms— such are the various practices of those who have left the household life.
The calculation [of the factors] excludes the desirable objects because they serve as the path to purification; furthermore,
ignorance is not established as a separate [hindrance] because it is not a grasper.
Ignorance is not established as a separate factor for grasping; rather,
it is that which is able to grasp at all forms of existence (*bhava*).
Therefore, it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
That which does not clearly comprehend characteristics is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Because it is not a grasper,
it is not established as a grasping;
it can only be associated with others.
Taken together, these are called "grasping" (upādāna).
These four types of grasping above are explained according to the Sarvāstivāda school. If one follows the Sautrāntika school:
The four types of clinging have greed as their essential nature.
Greed that arises conditioned by the objects of the five desires is called the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmopādāna*).
Craving conditions the arising of the sixty-two views;
this is called the "clinging to views.
Craving conditions the arising of [clinging to] precepts and observances.

This is called the grasping of rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Greed that arises conditioned by the three realms and by the discourse on self (*ātman*) is called the grasping of the discourse on self (*ātmavādopādāna*).
Therefore, those four types of grasping have craving as their essence.
From this second [point].
Explanation of the Names:
The treatise states that these are the *anuśaya*s (latent dispositions), and so forth.
What is the meaning of the term "name" (nāman)?
The verse says:
Subtlety, the two types of increase, pursuance, and binding.
"Abiding, flowing, drifting, conjoining, and grasping—these are the meanings of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), etc.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "Subtle" means...
This explains the meaning of *anuśaya*.
The fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are difficult to discern in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Therefore, it is called "subtle," just like sleep. From the phrase "increasing in accordance" (*anuśerate*) onwards,
the three meanings explain the term "in accordance" (*anu*).
Furthermore, regarding the first two types of increase (*anuśaya*),
they increase through both the object (*ālambana*) and through association (*samprayoga*);
these are the afflictions that are capable of increasing.
Because it increases the dullness and stagnation regarding the object of focus and that which is associated with it, it is called "pursuing."
The second explanation follows the meaning:
it is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the arising of afflictions; this is the acquisition of those afflictions.
They follow sentient beings and constantly act as afflictions. Regarding "following and binding":
this is the third explanation of the meaning of "following" (anvaya).
The active manifestation of afflictions binds sentient beings according to their conditions; they dwell in the flow, drift, and conjoin with grasping.
This explains the names "outflows" (*āsrava*) and so forth mentioned above.
"Abiding" refers to that which causes sentient beings to dwell long within the stream of birth and death,
and causes them to transmigrate through the three realms via the gates of the six sense faculties.
Because they leak out exhaustively,
they are called "outflows" (āsrava).
As for "drifting":
Because they carry away the wholesome factors to the extreme,
they are called "floods" (ogha).
As for "conjunction" (yoga):
They yoke sentient beings together so that they undergo various kinds of suffering; therefore,
they are called "yokes" (yoga).
Grasping serves as the basis for the outflows (āsrava);
because it seizes upon birth and death,
it is called "clinging" (upādāna).
This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the *anuśaya*s and so forth.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa), Fascicle Twenty-one. 19. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Twenty-one.
From this second section, the six gates beginning with "bondage" (*bandhana*) are clarified. This is divided into two parts: first, the actual clarification of bondage and the others;

second, the analytical classification of these gates. Regarding the actual clarification of bondage and the others, there are two further divisions: first, the clarification of the five gates beginning with bondage.
Second, the explanation of the six impurities (*ṣaḍ-mala*).
This is divided into two parts within the fivefold classification beginning with the fetters (*saṃyojana*):
first, the presentation of the headings.
Second, the detailed explanation.
First, regarding the presentation of the headings,
the treatise states:
Thus, having already distinguished the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) together with the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), [one may ask:
are they only as many as the Blessed One has described as the outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), and so forth? Or is it otherwise?
Furthermore, there are others.
The verse says:
Through the distinctions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, five further types are taught.
The commentary states:
Apart from the outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth,
there are distinctions based on the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and other categories.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, fetters;
second, bonds.
1. The three underlying tendencies (anuśaya);
2. The four secondary afflictions (upakleśa); 3.
The five envelopments (paryavasthāna).
From this second section,
there is a separate explanation divided into five parts.
The first is the explanation of the summary verse.
Second, the explanation of fetters (*bandhana*);
third, the explanation of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
fourth, the explanation of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Fifth, the explanation of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*). Within the exposition on the knots (*grantha*), this is divided into three parts.
First, the explanation of the nine knots.
Second, the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) are explained; third, the five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) are explained.
Now, first, what are the nine fetters?
The verse says:
There are nine fetters; "clinging" (parāmarśa) refers to their objects being equal.
The two fetters of views and clinging are established as such because they are both exclusively unwholesome and arise independently.
Among the *paryavasthānas*, only envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are established as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*),
because they function as two distinct types of conduct, because they are the causes of low birth and poverty,
because they manifest as pervasive secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and because they cause distress to both groups [of practitioners].
The commentary states:
Regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first is the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*).
2. The fetter of ill will;
3. The fetter of conceit;
4. The fetter of ignorance.
The fifth is the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), which refers to three types of views. The sixth is the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
These refer to the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*).
Seventh is the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*); eighth is the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
The nine fetters of stinginess;
among these, resentment and envy.
Avarice (mātsarya) is bound only to the desire realm;
the others pervade all three realms. Question: For what reason are the [first] three views so named?
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) are called the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
The verse answers by stating "the object and the grasping," etc.
That is to say, there are three views and two graspings.
The first refers to equality of objects;
the second refers to equality of grasping.
Regarding the phrase "objects and so forth":
"object" (vastu) refers to the essential nature (svabhāva).
There are eighteen objects within the three views.

The two types of grasping also consist of eighteen entities; therefore, they are called "equal in number. As for the view of eighteen: [it refers to] the five aggregates of clinging as the basis, with each being viewed through four aspects. Thus, there are twenty views; however, because the view of self and the view of what belongs to self are subsumed within the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*), they are excluded, leaving eighteen. Furthermore, since the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and the view of eternity (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) are both included within the view of non-existence (*vibhavadṛṣṭi*), they are likewise excluded, resulting in eighteen. Alternatively, the view of self and the view of what belongs to self are combined into one, and the view of annihilation and the view of eternity are combined into one, thus making eighteen. This is why it is said that the view consists of eighteen.
That is to say, beneath the [truth of] suffering there are the two views of self-existence (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi);
beneath each of the four truths,
there is also false view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
These combine to form six views.
Since there are six for each of the three realms,
they constitute eighteen.
Regarding the eighteen [factors]:
under suffering (duḥkha) there are two grasping-factors (upādāna);
under origination (samudaya) and cessation (nirodha), there is one grasping-factor each.
That is to say, there is only the grasping at views;
since there are also two types of grasping regarding the lower paths,
they constitute six types of grasping.
There are six for each of the three realms;
thus they are called the eighteen.
As for the phrase "and so forth," it refers to grasping and the rest.
The three views and so forth are the objects of grasping; the two graspings and so forth are the subjects of grasping.
This is the grasping subject;
therefore, it is called "grasping" and so forth. That is to say, by means of the grasping of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Because they hold [wrong views] such as the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) to be capable of purification,
they may give rise to the grasping of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Because one grasps the view of a self-identity and so forth as being supreme,
the view of a self-identity and other such views [arise].

That which is called the "object of grasping" refers to the two types of grasping: grasping at precepts and views. That which is called the "subject of grasping" refers to the [grasping at self and what belongs to self].
Regarding the phrase "because the two are exclusively unwholesome and arise spontaneously":
this refers to envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*),
which are exclusively of an unwholesome nature.
Furthermore, envy and stinginess arise only through the power of volition.
It does not follow after others;
because it arises solely through its own power,
it is called "arising through mastery."
The explanation that they are established separately among the *paryavasthānas* as *saṃyojanas* because of their superiority in two respects is irrational.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
"If there were only eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
this explanation would be acceptable."
The claim that there are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) is unreasonable; for this explanation fails to account for the two types:
anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Because they also possess both meanings,
they should be established as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For this reason, it should be said that the faults of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are particularly grave.
First, because they frequently manifest;
that is to say, envy and stinginess frequently manifest.
Second, because they are the causes of low status and poverty.
Envy is the cause of low birth;
stinginess is the cause of poverty.
This is because these three universally manifest as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This means it universally manifests the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of joy and sorrow;
specifically, envy (*īrṣyā*) is associated with sorrow and universally manifests the secondary afflictions of grief.
Avarice is associated with joy;
this fully reveals the secondary affliction of complacency.
It is so called because it disturbs both the monastic and lay communities.
That is to say, those who have left the household life are afflicted by envy and stinginess regarding the teachings,
while those who remain at home are so regarding material wealth.
They are disturbed by the afflictions of envy and stinginess; fifth, they may disturb the devas and asuras,
namely Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
There is the taste of ambrosia;
there are asuras;
there are the forms of women.
The gods are covetous of flavors and jealous of forms;
the asuras are covetous of forms and jealous of flavors;
thus they give rise to strife and contention.
Sixth, because they disturb or cause affliction to the two superior destinies of humans and devas;
seventh, because they disturb or cause affliction to others and their own faction—
“faction” (部) meaning a group or assembly.
That is to say, stinginess afflicts one's own assembly,
while envy afflicts the friends of others;
this is due to the seven aforementioned meanings.
Therefore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*),
only two are established as fetters (*saṃyojana*).
As for the verse stating "because they afflict and disturb the two groups," it means:
One should know that this includes the latter four types of the two categories.
Following this second [section],
there is the explanation of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
The treatise states:
"In other places, the Buddha,
relying on the gate of differentiation..."
Regarding the sound of binding,
it is said that there are five kinds.
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are five fetters that bind one to the lower realms (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*): by two, one does not transcend the desire realm;

by three, one returns to the lower realms. Because they encompass the gates and the faculties, three [of these] cause one not to set out [for liberation], while [the remaining two] consist of being deluded regarding the path and doubting the path.
Because they are able to obstruct the approach to liberation, only the abandonment of three is taught.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, there are five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni*).
1. The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
2. Adherence to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
3. Doubt (vicikitsā).
Four are sensual desire;
the fifth is ill will.
Question: For what reason are these five [factors] established?
They are called "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*). Answer: "Lower" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
these five factors are conducive to and benefit the lower realm.
They are called "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*).
The phrase "by two [factors] one does not transcend the desire realm, and by three one returns to the lower" is the formal explanation of what it means to be "conducive to the lower."
Due to greed and hatred,
one does not transcend the desire realm;
even if one were able to transcend it and be reborn in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), [one would still fall].
Because one returns to birth in the desire realm due to the three [defilements] beginning with the view of a self-identity,
greed and hatred are said to be like prison wardens.
The three beginning with the view of a self-entity are like watchmen; therefore,
these five are called "factors conducive to the lower realm."
Some say that "lower parts" refers to lower sentient beings, namely,
ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
And "taking down to the lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The first three [fetters] are able to obstruct sentient beings from transcending the lower realm.
Because the latter two prevent one from transcending the desire realm, all five are given the name "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*). Question:
Just as with the various stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), [how is this so]?
One abandons six afflictions.
Why, then, does the Sūtra speak of abandoning the three fetters?
To this, there are two teachers who respond.
Regarding the first explanation, the verse states:
"Because they encompass the gates and the faculties, there are three.
As for the phrase "encompassing the gates":
That is to say, the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) resides in one gate,
namely the gate of suffering (duḥkha).
The clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) resides in two gates.
This refers to the gateway of suffering.
Doubt pertains to all four gateways;
that is, the gateways of the Four Noble Truths.
It speaks of abandoning three types because they encompass those three gates.
Having spoken of abandoning the three, it then speaks of abandoning the six.
Regarding the subsumption of the faculties:
this means that the view of extremes arises dependent upon the view of a self-entity,
and the grasping at views arises dependent upon the grasping at precepts and observances.
Since wrong view arises based on doubt,
it is said that the abandonment of these three [factors] subsumes those three roots.
Therefore, it is said that three [fetters] are abandoned;
it has already been stated that six are abandoned.
Alternatively, there is no desire to set out [on the path].
The following is the second explanation.
Alternatively, it is said that this indicates the interpretation of other masters.
In general, there are three types of obstacles for those traveling to a different region:
first, the lack of desire to set out.
Second, being deluded regarding the right path by relying on a false path;
third, doubting the right path that leads to liberation.
There are also three obstacles:
first, the lack of desire to set out,
which arises from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Grasping at a self and what belongs to a self,
they fear liberation and have no desire to set out toward it.
Second is delusion regarding the right path; that is,
due to the adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one clings to what is not the path as being the path.
First, they are deluded regarding the right path.
Third, they have doubts regarding the path;
that is to say, it is because of doubt.
Regarding doubt concerning the path,
the Buddha revealed that the stream-enterer has forever severed such obstacles to the attainment of liberation.
Therefore, it is said that three [fetters] are abandoned.
Following this third [section],
the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are explained.
The treatise says:
In other sūtras, the Buddha [taught] as in the case of the "factors conducive to the lower realm" (avarabhāgīya).
The fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are also of five kinds.
The verse says:
The fetters conducive to the higher realms are also five: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, pride, and ignorance.
They are so called because they prevent one from transcending the higher realms.
The commentary states:
There are five fetters conducive to the higher realms:
first, attachment to the realm of form;
second, attachment to the formless realm.
Three fetters are restlessness in the form and formless realms;
four are conceit in the form and formless realms;
five are ignorance in the form and formless realms.
By means of these five types,
sentient beings are unable to transcend the higher realms; therefore,
they are called the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Because the fault of greed is so grave,
it is discussed separately for the two realms.
This is the second [section].
Explaining the three bonds (*bandhana*).
The treatise says:
"The fetters (*saṃyojana*) have already been explained; what are the bonds?"
The verse says:
"The bonds are threefold by reason of the three feelings. The commentary explains:
There are three kinds of bonds.
First is the bond of greed;
second is the bond of hatred;
third is the bond of delusion.
For what reason are these three said to be bonds?
It is because they depend upon the three types of feeling.
Therefore, three bonds are established;
that is to say, regarding pleasant feeling,
the bond of attachment increases accordingly.
That is to say, regarding painful feeling,
the fetter of aversion increases; regarding neutral feeling, [the fetter of ignorance increases].
Delusion increases through both its object and its association,
because it increases concomitantly with both.
Although greed and hatred also exist within neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
they are not like delusion (*moha*).
Third, this section clarifies the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The treatise states:
The bonds have already been analyzed.
What, then, are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it was previously stated in the commentary that there are six,
up to ninety-eight categories.
The first has already been explained.
From here, the fourth section clarifies the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The verse says:
"Secondary afflictions are these others; they are defiled mental factors belonging to the aggregate of formations.
The commentary says:
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are those others besides these;
that is, those remaining outside of these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The outbursts (paryavasthāna), stains (mala), and so forth, are called secondary afflictions (upakleśa),
because they arise in accordance with the root afflictions (mūlakleśa).
These are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These secondary afflictions are defiled mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
It is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Following this, the fifth [section] clarifies the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
The verse says:

The eight envelopments (paryavasthāna) are shamelessness (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), envy (īrṣyā), avarice (mātsarya), as well as regret (kaukṛtya), torpor (middha), restlessness (auddhatya), and lethargy (styāna); or ten, with the addition of anger (krodha) and concealment (mrakṣa).
Lack of shame, stinginess, and restlessness all arise from greed;
lack of dread, sleep, and lethargy arise from ignorance;
envy and anger arise from hatred; regret arises from doubt; and concealment and contention arise from delusion.
The commentary states:
The first verse indicates the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*);
the subsequent one and a half verses clarify the root [afflictions] and their outflows (*niṣyanda*).
Regarding the eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that there are either ten.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say that there are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):
first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*).
2. Lack of shame; 3. Envy; 4. Avarice.
5. Regret; 6. Drowsiness; 7. Restlessness.
8. Dullness (styāna).
9. Anger (pradāśa).
10. Concealment (mrakṣa).
Lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya) have already been explained in the Chapter on the Faculties (Indriyavarga).
Envy (*īrṣyā*) refers to a state of mental displeasure regarding the various flourishing successes of others.
Avarice (*mātsarya*) refers to that which is contrary to the skillful giving of wealth and the Dharma.
Regret is the same as *kaukṛtya* (remorse),
which has already been explained in the section on the roots (*mūla*).
Sleep (*middha*) is defined as having the nature of causing the mind to become dull and withdrawn.
Although the two types— remorse and torpor—
pertain to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, within the present context of the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), they are [treated as such].
Only those that are defiled are taken;
restlessness and lethargy have also already been explained in the chapter on the faculties (indriya).
To cause the mind to flare up with indignation is termed anger (*krodha*).
To conceal one's own transgressions is... [shamelessness].
These are called concealment (*mrakṣa*),
lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Restlessness is the outflow-result of greed and so forth.
Lack of shame.
Drowsiness and lethargy are the outflows of ignorance. Envy is [the outflow of jealousy].
Anger is an outflow of hatred;
regret is an outflow of doubt.
Regarding concealment (*mrakṣa*), some say it is a derivative of greed (*lobha*);
some say it is a derivative of delusion (*moha*);
and some say it is a derivative of both greed and delusion.
Some say that concealment by the wise is a derivative of greed,
while concealment by the ignorant is not.
This is an outflow of delusion (*moha*).
Regarding the verse’s phrase "concealment and dispute" (*mrakṣa-vivāda*),
there are three different explanations.
Therefore, it is called "contention.
This concludes the second major section,
which clarifies the six stains of affliction.
The verse says:
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are six: malice, resentment, guile, deceit, and pride;
guile and deceit arise from greed, while malice and resentment arise from hatred.
"Malice arises from the grasping at views; Flattery arises from all [wrong] views.
Commentary: The first two lines clarify the six stains (*mala*).

3. Resentment;
4. Flattery; 5. Deception.
The six types of conceit arise from the afflictions;

It is called the "stain of affliction" (*kleśamala*).
"Affliction" refers to the stubborn adherence to various blameworthy matters;

*Vyāpāda* (harm) refers to oppression,
such as engaging in beating or verbal abuse;

Flattery (*śāṭhya*) refers to the crookedness of the mind.
Deceit (*māyā*) refers to deluding others.
Arrogance (*mada*) has already been explained in the section on the roots.
Deceit, pride, and greed are the outflows of delusion;
malice, resentment, and hatred are the outflows of anger;
and vexation and the grasping at views are the outflows of wrong view.
Flattery is the outflow of the five views.
When the verse says "all views," it refers specifically to these five views.
From here begins the second major section:
the analysis through various categories.
This is divided into five parts.
First, the classification by the three types of abandonment;
second, the classification by the three natures;
third, the classification by the three realms.
Four are associated with the six consciousnesses;
five are associated with the five feelings.
Now, regarding the first three categories of abandonment:
The treatise says:

The verse says:

The outbursts (*paryavasthāna*)—shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and dullness (*styāna*)—are abandoned through both insight (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The remaining [outbursts] and the afflictive stains (*kleśamala*) are abandoned only through cultivation, because they function independently.
The commentary states:
Among the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), there are lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Sleep, lethargy, and restlessness.
These five are associated with the delusions of view;
they are abandoned through seeing.
They are also associated with the delusions of cultivation.
These are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The remainder refers to envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*),
regret (*kaukṛtya*), and the six defilements (*kleśamala*).
These eleven [factors],
because they arise spontaneously,
are abandoned solely through cultivation.
It does not follow from other afflictions;
it arises through its own power,
being associated only with ignorance.
Because it is associated with [the mind],
it is called "sovereign.
From this second [point]...
Explaining the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The treatise states:
"These secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)."
Which [paths of action] are associated with which natures?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, three are of two natures; the rest are unwholesome. In the higher realms, all are neutral.
The commentary states:
"The two belonging to desire" refers to the sleep of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Dullness,
agitation, and the third [hindrance].
It pervades both the unwholesome and the indeterminate natures;
when associated with the view of self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) or the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), it is of an indeterminate nature.
As for "other evils," the remaining secondary afflictions are all of an unwholesome nature.

within the two higher realms,
all secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are indeterminate.
All are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
From this, the third [section]:
the classification of the three realms (*dhātu-vibhāga*).
The treatise says:
Regarding these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
which ones are bound to which realms (*dhātu*)?

The verse says: Deceit and guile exist in the Desire Realm and the first dhyāna; the three [other afflictions] exist in all three realms; the rest exist only in the Desire Realm. The commentary explains: [Deceit and guile exist in the Desire Realm and the first dhyāna. The three [other afflictions] exist in all three realms; the rest exist only in the Desire Realm.
Flattery and deceit exist only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "the three realms exist because the multitudes of mental factors depend upon one another":
"three" refers to dullness (*styāna*), agitation (*auddhatya*), and [negligence].
Pride (māna) and the other three [afflictions] all pervade the three realms.
"Other desires": "other" refers to those apart from the five previously mentioned.
The remaining secondary afflictions are bound exclusively to the desire realm.
From this, the fourth [section].
This clarifies the association with the six consciousnesses.
Below this, the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are explained in general.
Among these six consciousnesses:
From which consciousness and in which stage do they arise?
The verse says:
The pride and latent tendencies abandoned through seeing, along with the autonomous secondary afflictions.
All arise solely on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*); the others are explained as being accessible to all six consciousnesses.
[Commentary: This refers to the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, there are the conceit and torpor abandoned through cultivation,
along with the autonomous secondary afflictions,
namely the five previously mentioned envelopments of envy and so forth.
And these are the six stains. These,
such as the views to be abandoned by insight and so forth,
arise solely in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*).
Because it is impossible for [such a state] to arise based on the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*),
the others are generally based on all six consciousnesses.
The remainder refers to the greed, hatred, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, it is associated with the afflictions of the realm of cultivation,
as well as with lack of shame and lack of dread.
Dullness and restlessness are both among the great afflictions.
Lack of faith,
indolence, and negligence.
These are called "the remaining [afflictions].
