Each of these remaining afflictions and so forth arises throughout all six consciousnesses and all stages.
From this, the fifth [section] clarifies the association with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*).
Within it, there are two parts.
First, the association with the root afflictions is explained;
second, the association with the secondary afflictions is explained.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the association with the root afflictions:
The verse says:
The afflictions of the desire realm: Greed is associated with joy and pleasure;
Hatred with sorrow and pain; Ignorance is universal; False view is associated with sorrow and joy.
Doubt and sorrow are associated with the remaining five [mental factors]; joy is associated with all [of them]. All are associated with equanimity.
In the higher stages, they are all associated according to their respective correspondences. They pervade all feelings within their own consciousness.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Among the various afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
craving is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) and the feeling of pleasure (*sukha*),
because it functions through a mode of elation and pervades all six consciousnesses.
Hatred is associated with sorrow and suffering because it functions through a mode of dejection throughout the six consciousnesses.
As for the statement that delusion is pervasive:
That is to say, delusion (*moha*) is universally associated with the preceding four feelings,
because it functions through modes of both joy and sorrow across all six consciousnesses.
As for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it is associated with both sorrow and joy.
This means that because wrong view operates through modes of both joy and grief and belongs exclusively to the mental level,
it is associated with both sorrow and gladness;
one first creates sinful karma.
Subsequently, wrong view arises,
associated with the feeling of joy,
because one does not fear the retribution [of one's actions].
Having previously performed wholesome karma,
one subsequently gives rise to wrong views;
this is associated with the feeling of sorrow.
Because merit is abandoned and wasted;
as for "doubt and sorrow, and the remaining five joys," doubt is associated with the feeling of sorrow.
Because those proceeding with aversion (daurmanasya) operate solely on the mental level (manobhūmi).
As for the remaining five [afflictions] associated with joy (saumanasya), they refer to the other four, beginning with the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
And with pride, there are five.
The remaining five among these are associated with joy.
Because the practice of joy proceeds solely on the level of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*).
As for "all [feelings] associated with equanimity," this is stated in terms of universal association.
All of the above are associated with relinquishment (*prahāṇa-samprayukta*),
because at the time when the continuity of the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is severed.
"They necessarily abide in the sensation of equanimity.
Regarding the phrase "in all higher stages, they pervade all sensations within their respective consciousnesses as appropriate":
this clarifies that all afflictions belonging to the higher realms pervade the various sensations of their own respective consciousnesses according to what is applicable.
It arises simultaneously with all consciousnesses of its own level and is associated with all feelings,
as is the case within the first dhyāna.
There are four consciousnesses.
As for the afflictions arising from the three consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth:
It is associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
If a defilement arises on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*), it is associated with joy (*prīti*) and equanimity. This is the case from the second dhyāna upward.
Up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If one gives rise to afflictions in the Second Dhyāna...
It is associated with joy and equanimity.
If defilements arise in the third dhyāna,
it is associated with pleasure and equanimity.
The fourth [category] consists of the afflictions that arise from the realm beyond [the desire realm], up to and including the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
It is associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*). Following this, secondly,
the association of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) with the five feelings (*vedanā*) is explained.
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished the afflictions (*kleśa*) in their association with the various feelings (*vedanā*),
we shall now further distinguish the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The verse says:

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envy, regret, anger, vexation, harmfulness, resentment, and hatred arise together with mental suffering; stinginess is associated with the sensation of joy.
Deceit, guile, torpor, and concealment are associated with both sorrow and joy;
pride arises with joy, pleasure, and equanimity; the remaining four are universally associated.
Commentary:
Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
envy (*īrṣyā*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*).
Anger, vexation,
and malice.
Regret (kaukṛtya).
These six are associated exclusively with the feeling of mental distress (daurmanasya),
because they function through a mode of dejection and belong solely to the mental level (manobhūmi).
Avarice is associated with the feeling of pleasure;
that is to say, it functions through a mode of joy and belongs exclusively to the mental level. Deceit—
Deceit, torpor, and concealment.
These four [pride-derivatives] are associated with both sorrow and joy, as they proceed through modes of both elation and dejection;
this is because they belong exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). Conceit (*mada*) is associated with joy and pleasure.
From the second dhyāna downwards,
it is associated with the feeling of joy (prīti);
in the third dhyāna, it is conceit (māna).
It is associated with pleasant feeling and proceeds by way of joy;
because it belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), the verse says "all are equanimity."
The aforementioned secondary afflictions are explained here in terms of their general association;
all of them are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Because at the time of the cessation of the continuum,
one necessarily abides in equanimity (upekṣā).
As for the remaining four [mental factors], they are universally associated.
The remaining factors are said to be lack of shame (āhrīkya),
lack of dread (anapatrāpya),
and mental torpor (styāna).
Restlessness.
These four are universally associated with the five feelings,
as they proceed through both joyful and sorrowful modes of activity.
Because they pervade the six consciousnesses,
following this third [section],
the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are clarified.
The treatise says:
Now, next, one should examine what the characteristics of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are.
The verse states:

The five [hindrances] exist only in the desire realm; because their objects, antidotes, and functions are the same, although there are two [categories], only one hindrance is established. They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they obstruct the aggregates (*skandha*).
Thus it is explained.
The first two lines clarify the "covering" (āvaraṇa);
the latter two lines concern abrogation and establishment.
Regarding the statement that the five [hindrances] exist only in the desire realm:
The Buddha taught that there are five hindrances:
first, sensual desire.
Second, ill-will;
third, torpor and drowsiness;
fourth, restlessness and remorse.
Fifth, doubt. However,
these five hindrances exist only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
as stated in the Sūtra regarding these five types.
It is purely perfect,
because it is a collection of unwholesome states;
there are no unwholesome states in the higher realms.
Thus, we know that these exist only in the desire realm.
Question: For what reason are the two factors of torpor and sleep, as well as the two factors of restlessness and regret, [restricted to the desire realm]?
They are combined into a single "cover" (āvaraṇa).
The verse replies that they are established as one cover because their function—namely, being an antidote to nutriment—is the same.
Although there are two, they are posited as a single cover.
"Food" refers to that which is consumed; "antidote" refers to that which counteracts, and is thus not food.
As for the statement that they are the same in being "food": [it means they both function as sustenance].
Furthermore, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness likewise possesses five kinds of nutriment:
first, lethargy.
Second, lack of delight;
third, yawning;
fourth, irregularity of diet.
This refers to being excessively satiated.
The state of the five consciousnesses being dull and inferior arises from fatigue.
Regarding the statement that they are "identical in cultivation," these two are not [ordinary] food;
namely, the perception of light.
Regarding their similarity in function:
both of these are capable of causing the mind to become sunken and dull, as well as [giving rise to] the two hindrances of restlessness-remorse.
Regarding the statement "the food is the same," it refers to four types of mental applications (*vitarka*). The first is the application of thought toward one's relatives (*jñātivitarka*).
2. Discursive thought regarding the country;
3. Discursive thought regarding immortality;
4. Discursive thought regarding recollecting the past.
It refers to recollecting and seeking out according to the events that have passed.
As for the phrase "the same as the remedy":
These two are not sustenance;
that is to say, śamatha. As for the statement that their functions are the same:
These two cause the mind to be non-quiescent.
Question: All afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth possess the nature of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For what reason did the World-Honored One teach only these five?
The verse replies: "Because they are hindrances and aggregates, there are only five," namely, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Drowsiness and torpor can obstruct the aggregate of ethical discipline;
restlessness and remorse can obstruct the aggregate of meditative concentration.
Because concentration and wisdom are absent,
there is doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths;
because of this doubt, one is able to obstruct the aggregate of liberation.
And because the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation cannot arise [without them],
there are only these five.
It is established as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
According to the Sautrāntika interpretation,
torpor and drowsiness obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Restlessness and regret are obstacles to wisdom;
since concentration is logically an obstacle that must precede wisdom,
this concludes the second major section.
Explaining the cessation of delusions.
This is divided into six sections.
First, explaining the four causes for severing delusions.
Second, the explanation of the four kinds of remedies;
third, the explanation of the locus for severing afflictions;
fourth, the explanation of the four types of remoteness.
The fifth clarifies that by severing delusions, cessation is attained;
the sixth clarifies the nine kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). Below this, the first section clarifies the four causes for severing delusions.
The treatise says:
One should now reflect upon and investigate the universal [factors] pertaining to other realms.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions that take contaminated phenomena as their objects and are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path: at the stage of their abandonment,
[the corresponding non-possession arises].
One does not know its object;
when one knows its object,
it is not yet severed.
"Regarding these various afflictions,
by what cause are they abandoned? This explains that the preceding is a question.
Those that function as universal [defilements] with respect to other realms are the nine defilements that take the higher [realms] as their object.
These are the objects of those universal [defilements].
This refers to the suffering and origin [of suffering] belonging to the upper realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding those who abandon the various afflictions (*kleśa*) that take out-flowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) as their conditions by means of seeing cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*): this refers to [the abandonment of] those [afflictions] below cessation and the path.
These are greed, hatred, and pride;
that is to say, greed and hatred.
Pride. Taking wrong view, doubt, and ignorance as its objects, it arises;
thus it is called "having outflows as its object."
The objects of these [afflictions] such as greed are namely wrong view, doubt, and ignorance.
Regarding their state of abandonment:
Regarding the stage of abandoning the universal [defilements] of other realms:

this refers to the time when the receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin arise. As for those [defilements] that take the cessation and the path as their objects and have outflow (*sāsrava*), [the same applies].
The stage of abandonment refers to the time when the patiences (kṣānti) arise within the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path.
Regarding those who do not know their objects of focus:
when they sever the pervasive afflictions of other realms,
they do not know the suffering and its origin of the higher realms.
When the path that leads to cessation takes the outflow-tainted as its object,
one does not know that wrong view, doubt, and ignorance [which are to be abandoned];
this is because of the patience and knowledge regarding the path to cessation.
It is because one knows only the truths of cessation and the path.
As for "knowing that their objects of focus are not abandoned at that time," this refers to knowing the objects of focus of the universal [defilements] pertaining to other realms.
This refers to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of origin regarding the higher realms.
As for those universal [defilements] of other realms that are not abandoned:

This means that because they have already been abandoned, they are not [further] abandoned. Regarding the afflictions with outflow (sāsrava) that take cessation and the path as their objects: below this [point], there are afflictions having outflow as their object.
Regarding the "time of the object-condition" (ālambana-kāla):
this refers to the knowledges and patiences regarding suffering and its origin.
This is because the knowledges and patiences regarding suffering and its origin cognize suffering and its origin.
In the lower stage of the path of cessation,
there are false views and doubt.
Ignorance has suffering and its origin as its essence; therefore,
the knowledge and acceptance regarding suffering and its origin arise.
One is able to know them; yet,
as for those [afflictions] such as greed, hatred, and wrong views,
they are not severed.
This means that because the receptivity to the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna-kṣānti) has not yet arisen and ceased.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"It is not necessary to fully comprehend the object of cognition (*ālambana*) in order to abandon [the afflictions]"; this answers the preceding question.
If that is so, by how many causes in total is the abandonment of afflictions brought about? This is the counter-question.
It is answered in general by four kinds of causes.
What are the four questions?
The verse says:
Because of fully knowing the object of cognition, and because of abandoning that which cognizes it.
"Because one abandons that object of focus, and because the antidote arises, there is abandonment.
Regarding the explanation:
the first three phrases [refer to this].
The first phrase clarifies the cause for severing the afflictions of view;
the fourth phrase clarifies the cause for severing the afflictions of cultivation.
Furthermore, the abandonment of the delusions of view is generally due to three causes.
Regarding "thoroughly knowing the objects of perception":
This is the first cause.

It is called "abandonment through the thorough knowledge of the object" (*ālambana-parijñāna-prahāṇa*), meaning that the afflictions (*kleśa*) which take their own realm as an object are abandoned by the abandonment of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
By means of its own realm as an object—
because it takes the truths of suffering and origination within its own desire realm as its object—
the patience regarding suffering and origination arises.
Since one has already known suffering and its origin,
one knows that the afflictions which take one's own realm as their object are abandoned;
they are abandoned by means of the thorough knowledge of their objects.
As for the objects of perception,
they are suffering and its origin,
as well as the cessation and the path which are abandoned through vision.
The afflictions that take the untainted as their object consist of wrong view and doubt.
Ignorance conditions the untainted [states] regarding cessation and the path;
it arises through the forbearances regarding cessation and the path.
Because they know the truths of cessation and the path,
those wrong views and doubts [are abandoned].
Ignorance is immediately severed;
it is called "severed" because its object has been fully known.
That which is called the "object-condition" (ālambana) refers to the truths of cessation and the path. "Because one abandons that which takes it as its object" is the second reason.
This is called "abandonment by way of abandoning its object," meaning that through the vision of suffering and its origin,
one abandons [afflictions] that take other realms as their objects.
The afflictions that take one's own realm as their object and the afflictions that take another realm as their object—
these afflictions taking another realm as their object are the objective conditions (*ālambana*).
The afflictions that take their own realm as an object are the minds capable of such apprehension.
When these afflictions taking their own realm as an object are severed, [the mind becomes liberated].
Those afflictions that have other realms as their objects are abandoned accordingly;
this is called "abandoning by abandoning those which take them as objects. As for what is meant by "those which take them as objects":
This refers precisely to having one's own realm as an object-condition (*ālambana*). "Because one abandons that object-condition" is the third reason;
this is called "abandoning by means of abandoning that object-condition."
This refers to seeing cessation and the path,

which abandons the afflictions conditioned by outflows; for the afflictions conditioned by outflows, such as craving and so forth directed toward cessation and the path, are inferior [to those directed toward the truths of suffering and origin].
The taintless objects of the afflictions that take wrong views and so forth as their conditions—
namely, the afflictions that have the taintless as their object— are called "objects of perception."
If the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is severed,
the defilements (*kleśa*) that take it as their object and are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are also severed accordingly;
therefore, this is called "severing [defilements] by severing their objects."
Regarding the term "object-condition" (ālambana),

this refers to the afflictions that take uncontaminated phenomena as their object. Regarding "abandonment through the arising of the antidote," this clarifies the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
Due to the fourth cause,
these are abandoned through the arising of their antidote; that is to say,
the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation.
By means of the nine grades of the counteractive path,
even the highest-of-the-high grade of afflictions is abandoned by the lowest-of-the-low grade of the path.
As an antidote, even for the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions,
there is the highest-of-the-high path.
This serves as an antidote.
This gateway of antidotes shall be explained in detail later.
Secondly, from this point on,
the four kinds of remedies are clarified.
The treatise states:
Regarding what is called "antidote," how many types are there in total?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of remedies: namely, abandoning, maintaining, distancing, and aversion.
The commentary states:
there are four remedies.
First is the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
because it abandons the afflictions.
Second is the antidote of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*),
which refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is because this path is able to maintain the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That which follows the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) is called the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga).
Third is the antidote of distant separation (dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa).
This refers to the path of advancement (*viśeṣamārga*),
because it causes the abandoned afflictions to become even more distant.
This occurs after the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
This is called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).
Fourth is the counteractive of aversion (*vidūṣaṇapratipakṣa*),
which refers to the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
Because one generates profound weariness and aversion toward the truth of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayasatya*),
prior to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*).
This is called the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
The Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu] explains this passage as follows:
"The first preparation."
Second, the uninterrupted [path];
third, the path of liberation;
fourth, the path of superior progress.
Third, this section clarifies the stage of severing delusions.
The treatise states:
From what is it definitively established that the various afflictions are eternally severed?
The verse says:
"One should know that from the object of perception, the various afflictions can be brought to cessation.
Commentary: One should know that the various afflictions...
At the time of their permanent abandonment,
it is impossible to cause them to be separated from the associated dharmas because they are closely conjoined; rather, one can only cause the afflictions to be distanced from their objects.
Because that object of focus is no longer produced,
following this fourth [stage].
This clarifies the nature of the four types of distance.
The treatise states:
"As for what is called 'the portion that is distant'..."
How many kinds of remoteness are there?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of remoteness, Namely: nature, opposition, location, and time.
Regarding the verse: "As with the primary elements and ethical discipline / In different directions and the two times," etc., the commentary states:
the first two lines provide the heading.
The following two lines provide the explanation.
There are four types of remoteness (*dūratā*): first, remoteness by way of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dūratā*).
Second, remoteness of remedy;
third, remoteness of location;
fourth, remoteness of time.
"Like the great elements" means that although the four great elements coexist, they are [considered distinct] because their characteristics are remote from one another.
It is also called "distant," as in the case of *śīla* (ethical discipline),
such as the observance or violation of precepts.
This is called "remedying the distant.
Although within a single body there may be both the observance and the violation of precepts, [the former can remedy the latter].
Because they are countered by their respective characteristics,
they are also called "distant.
As for "different locations":
It is like the eastern and western oceans;
these places are far apart,
even though they belong to the same world-system.
Because their locations are separated,
they are also called "distant.
Regarding the two periods of time:
Regarding "the past and future worlds," this is called remoteness in time (*kāladūra*).
Although these two periods are established upon a single dharma, [they are distinct].
Looking toward the present world,
it is also called "distant" because of the separation by time.
The word "etc.
is used to clarify that the examples cited are not exhaustive;
for instance, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and so forth are also termed "distant by nature" (*lakṣaṇadūra*).
For example, the natures of good and evil are called "distant" in terms of their remedy;
likewise, the southern and northern oceans are called "distant" in terms of their location.
Therefore, the term "equality" is employed.
From this, the fifth section clarifies the attainment of cessation through the severance of delusions.
The treatise states:

It was previously said that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the arising of the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*). When this path attains further progress, [the afflictions are abandoned].
Regarding the first question: Are the various afflictions that have been abandoned abandoned again? And regarding the second question:
Is the disjunction [from those afflictions] obtained again?
Regarding the second question: "Is there a repeated attainment?
The verse says:
"No defilements are severed again; disconnection may be repeatedly attained."
"Namely, during the six occasions of counteracting, attaining the fruit, and refining the faculties.
The commentary states:
The first phrase answers the first question.
The last three phrases answer the second question:
that no afflictions are severed twice means that all afflictions are severed instantaneously.
If one does not regress further,
there will certainly never again be the possibility of severing afflictions at a later time.
Regarding "there is a re-acquisition of disjunction":
"disjunction" refers to the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
When one advances on the Path,
one again gives rise to superior acquisitions (viśeṣa-prāpti) and attains the previously unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Therefore, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, it is admitted that there is "re-acquisition" (*punar-lābha*); as for what is called re-acquisition:
In total there are six periods:
namely, one for the cultivation of livelihood and four for the attainment of fruition.
The sixth moment is the time for refining the faculties (*indriya*).
"The time when the antidote arises" refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Regarding the time of attaining the fruits:
this refers to attaining the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning.
The non-returner and the arhat fruit at the time of refining the faculties.
This refers to refining dull faculties so that they are transformed into sharp ones.
Within these six periods:
Regarding the dissociation from various afflictions,
as one progresses through the superior stages of the Path,
one repeatedly gives rise to superior acquisitions.
As with those bound to the desire realm,
[those bound to] the form and formless realms are abandoned through the vision of the four truths.
It is abandoned by the vision of the three truths,
excluding the truth of the path;
it comprises all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
It is acquired at six times;
it belongs to the form and formless realms;
and it is abandoned by the vision of the Truth of the Path.
All unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are attained at only five times; this is because they are attained at the time when their antidote arises.
Since the fruit is attained immediately,
one should not divide this into two distinct periods.
The commentary states:
When the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) arises, it is called the time when the antidote is produced.
One immediately attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). Therefore,
among the six periods [of cultivation],
with the exception of the one [category] of abandoning through cultivation in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-bhāvanā-heya*), [the remaining five are abandoned].
The five types of unconditioned [attainments] are also acquired during five periods,
excluding the fruit of stream-entry and the abandonment through cultivation in the desire realm.
The sixth category, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
is acquired at only four times;
that is to say, within the aforementioned five [times].
Furthermore, one moment is excluded;
for when one attains the fruit or engages in livelihood,
there is no difference in time.
The commentary states:
When the sixth path of liberation arises,
it is called the time of the arising of the antidote.
One immediately attains the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

This excludes the case of simultaneous abandonment and cultivation. It refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states resulting from the seventh and eighth stages of the cultivation-abandonment (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is also attained during the four seasons;
among the four types of attainment of the fruits,
the first two are excluded.
Regarding the cultivation-elimination of the desire realm,
the unconditioned [attainment] of the ninth grade is acquired at only three times.
That is to say, among the four previously mentioned,
one further excludes "at one time," because the fruit is attained at the very moment the antidote arises.
The commentary states:
When the ninth path of liberation arises,
it is called the time of the arising of the remedy.
One immediately attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*),

with the exception of the simultaneous cultivation and abandonment [of afflictions] in the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*). This is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the cultivation of abandonment.
Excluding the Peak of Existence and the ninth category of unconditioned phenomena,
all remaining unconditioned phenomena [are included].
It is also attained during three periods;
among the four types of attainment of the fruits,
the first three are excluded.
The ninth [dhyāna], the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
is attained at only two times;
namely, within the first three [periods].
Furthermore, with one exception:
because the fruit is attained at the very moment of cultivation.
The commentary explains:
The ninth path of liberation arises;
this is called the time when the remedy is produced,
at which point one attains the fruit of arhatship.
This excludes those who attain realization simultaneously.
This explanation is given in reference to those of dull faculties and those who realize the stages sequentially.
As for those of sharp faculties:
In that case, there is no refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*). However, for one who transcends the fruits, it is not fixed.
From this sixth [section],
nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are clarified;
this is divided into six parts.
First, the nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are identified.
Second, the six pairs of fruits are clarified.
Third, the conditions for establishing thorough knowledge are established.
The fourth clarifies the accomplishment of universal knowledge;
the fifth clarifies the accumulation of the locus of universal knowledge;
the sixth clarifies the attainment and relinquishment of universal knowledge.
Below this, first, is the enumeration of the names of the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Briefly, there are two types of thorough knowledge.
First, the thorough knowledge of wisdom;
second, the thorough knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of wisdom:
It refers to untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) that knows the objects of the four noble truths (catur-āryasatya) in their entirety.
This is called the thorough knowledge of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*). As for the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*),
it refers to the various abandonments themselves.
Cessation is precisely analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
because it is manifested through abandonment,
analytical cessation is termed "abandonment."
Regarding the "full knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): this is because the name of the cause is applied here to its fruit.
Thorough knowledge is the cause;
abandonment is called the fruit.
Therefore, abandonment is termed "thorough knowledge."
This is the designation of the cause established upon the fruit.
The treatise says:
This is a question regarding the establishment of a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) for the sake of severing all [defilements].
It is answered that this is not so.
How is this questioned?
The verse says:
There are nine thorough knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
In the desire realm, for the first two categories of abandonment, there is one and two respectively, totaling three. For the upper realms, it is likewise.
The remaining five are the fetters conducive to the lower realm; the three are those that are completely severed in the form realm.
Explanation: The first phrase indicates the number.
The next three phrases clarify the six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) of seeing the truths;
the final two phrases clarify the three thorough knowledges of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding "the first abandonment of the desire realm has one":
That is to say, regarding those bound to the desire realm,
one complete knowledge (*parijñā*) is established for the abandonment of the first two truths, suffering and its origin.
"Two [factors] each one, making three combined":
"two" refers to the desire realm and the two truths of cessation and the path.
Each establishes a single complete knowledge (*parijñā*).
Regarding the statement that these three are combined:
this refers to the four truths of the desire realm.
These constitute three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):

first, the thorough knowledge of the abandonment [of defilements] through the vision of suffering and its origin; second, the thorough knowledge of the abandonment [of defilements] through the vision of cessation.
Regarding "the three thorough knowledges (parijñā) abandoned by the path of seeing; the same applies to the three of the higher realms":
the four truths of the two higher realms together constitute three thorough knowledges.
As with the enumerations of the desire realm,
it is said that "it is likewise" for the one [realm] of form and the formless.
The full comprehension of what is abandoned through seeing suffering and its origin;
and the two full comprehensions of what is abandoned through seeing cessation, pertaining to the form and formless realms.
The three types of the formless realm are the full knowledges (*parijñā*) abandoned through the path of seeing;
these are the six types of full knowledge above this.
The abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of the truths within the three realms constitutes the six types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

"Severance of dharmas" (dharmaprahāṇa) is a name for analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Regarding "the remaining five [fetters] leading to the lower realms, the form realm, and all [fetters] leading to the higher realms":
"the remaining" refers to the three realms.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation, three types of thorough knowledge (parijñā) are established for their abandonment,
because they are external to those abandoned by seeing.
It is termed "the remainder.
When the afflictions of the desire realm are exhausted,
one complete parijñā (perfect knowledge) is established.
This is called the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The essence of this thorough knowledge, together with the preceding [thorough knowledge] of the truths (*satyadarśana*), constitutes [the category].
The six kinds of thorough knowledge,
their cultivation and abandonment,
and the nine grades of the unconditioned.
Taken collectively, these are termed the "thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the five fetters that bind one to the lower realms.
Thus, the treatise says:
"The five fetters that bind one to the lower realms."
"Because it exhaustively and universally knows [them] along with those previously established. The commentary says:
"Along with those previously [mentioned], namely, the vision of the truths (satyadarśana). Regarding "the three types of complete abandonment of form":
"form" refers to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
When the afflictions of the path of cultivation are exhausted,
one complete knowledge is established,
termed the "complete knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for form and name."

Regarding "the abandonment of all": this refers to the establishment of one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) upon the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is termed the "thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters.
The essence of this thorough knowledge is the collective synthesis of the paths of vision and cultivation within the three realms, as well as the unconditioned.
This is designated as the essence of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana*).
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The exhaustion of all fetters."
This includes the aforementioned thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), as it is established together with the preceding [categories]. The commentary explains:
"Together with the preceding" refers to the [afflictions] abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The verse says "three," which establishes the three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) based on the cultivation of the path within the three realms.
Question: For what reason are the abandonments through cultivation in the form and formless realms [treated as such]?
The thorough knowledge is established separately;
it is not abandoned by insight.
The answer is: by means of the form and formless realms.
The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are established as distinct types of thorough knowledge because their antidotes differ.
The abandonment through vision and its antidote are treated together in the summary of thorough knowledge.
This is the second [section].
Explaining the six pairs of fruits,
the treatise says:
"That which has been established in this manner."
Regarding the nine kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
one should distinguish therein how many constitute the fruits of the path.
The verse says:
Among these, six are the fruits of patience; the remaining three are the fruits of knowledge.
All are the fruits of the *anāgamya* stage; five or eight are the fruits of the fundamental [dhyānas].
One fruit of the Peak of Formlessness; the three roots are likewise.
Two are worldly fruits; nine are noble. Three are the fruits of Dharma-knowledge; two are of subsequent knowledge.
Six are the fruits of the category of Dharma-knowledge; five are the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge.
The commentary states:
There are six pairs of fruits here.
The first two lines clarify the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The next two lines clarify the fruits of the preparatory stages (*anāgamya*) prior to the fundamental [dhyānas].
The following two lines clarify the fruits of the preparatory stages and the fundamental stages of the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
The final line clarifies the fruits of the mundane and noble paths.

The next single phrase clarifies the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). The following two phrases clarify the fruits belonging to the categories of the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge.
Within this, there are six fruits of patience (*kṣānti*).
Within the category of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*),
there are six fruits of receptivity (*kṣānti*, specifically *dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*), namely the six [moments] of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*).
It is also thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the eight patiences and the six kinds of thorough knowledge.
That which is obtained through this patience is called the fruit of patience.
As for the remaining three being the fruits of wisdom:
The remainder refers to the three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) pertaining to what is abandoned through cultivation;
these three are the fruits of such knowledge.
Because it is attained through wisdom alone.
"All those not yet reached" refers to the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi).
Because it is able to sever the afflictions of both the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms,
it possesses all nine fruits of thorough knowledge;
therefore, it is said to be "all."
Regarding the "five or eight fundamental [dhyānas]," the Vaibhāṣika masters state that these refer to the fundamental dhyānas.

There are only five fruits because the fundamental stage (maulabhūmi) can only permanently sever the afflictions of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) that are abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). Therefore,
there are three fruits for those who have seen the truths (*satyadarśana*) in the higher realms.
Because they cannot abandon the afflictions of the desire realm, they do not attain the two fruits of cultivation and abandonment; therefore,
there are four thorough knowledges (parijñā) pertaining to the desire realm.
"It is not the fundamental fruit. Regarding "or eight":
the word "or" indicates the explanation of the master Sunaksatra (Miaoyin).
That [text] states that there are eight fundamental results of full knowledge (*parijñā*);
to the aforementioned five,
it adds three further results of full knowledge pertaining to the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That is to say, having first been in the stage of an ordinary person and become detached from the defilements of the desire realm,
one subsequently relies upon the fundamental dhyāna stages.

At the time of entering the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), regarding those [defilements] bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the four truths, it is accepted that a distinct path (*mārga*) induces the acquisition of the outflow-free state (*anāsrava-prāpti*). As for what is meant by "a distinct path inducing": [It refers to] the fact that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) induces the acquisition of the outflow-free state for those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), whereas the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) induces the acquisition of the outflow-free state for those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*). This is because the acquisition of the outflow-free state for those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision is induced by the path of vision itself, while the acquisition of the outflow-free state for those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation is induced by the path of cultivation. Thus, the paths of vision and cultivation are distinct in their capacity to induce the acquisition of the outflow-free state for their respective objects of abandonment.
This refers to the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and the dharma-patience (*dharmanirvedhabhāgīya*).
This is the stage of the distinct path (*viśeṣamārga*),
wherein the attainment that can acquire [the fruit] arises.
One attains the three kinds of thorough knowledge (parijñā) regarding the truths of the desire realm; therefore,
this is the vision of the truths (satyadarśana).

The three types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are also the fruits of the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), with the exception of the [thorough knowledge] concordant with the lower portion (*avarabhāgīya*).
Because the lower fetters are exclusively the fruit of the *anāgamya* stage; that is to say,
they belong to the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
The path of seeing that has arisen cannot possibly involve the cultivation of those afflictions of the desire realm,
because it serves as their antidote for abandonment.
Because the paths of seeing and cultivation differ,
one does not cultivate [them]. Therefore,
there are five thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) of the factors conducive to the lower realm.
It is not the fruit of the fundamental stage; it is the fruit of the limit of the formless realm (*ārūpya-anta-phala*).
Regarding "one limit": this refers to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), because it is proximate to the sphere of infinite space.
It is called the "limit of the formless" because,
by means of the contaminated path arising from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space,
one is able to exhaustively abandon the afflictions of the form realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
"Only the exhaustion of craving for form is the fruit of full comprehension. "The same applies to the three roots" refers to the first three [formless attainments].
Excluding the Peak of Existence from the fundamental [realm],
one attains only the fruit of full comprehension (*parijñā-phala*), which is the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana-kṣaya*).
The first enumeration is the same as before;
therefore it is said, "likewise, there are two conventional fruits," meaning there are two fruits of the conventional path.
This refers to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*),

which is called "conducive to the lower realms" (*avarabhāgīya*) because it can sever the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
And the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*); these are the two fruits of full knowledge (*parijñā*).
Regarding the nine noble [knowledges]:

This refers to the power of the Noble Path, which is able to exhaustively sever the afflictions of the three realms pertaining to both seeing and cultivation, thereby attaining the nine fruits of complete knowledge (*parijñā*). Regarding the three types of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*): [text continues].
The fruit of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) consists of three [knowledges].
This is because the power of the knowledge of phenomena is able to exhaustively sever the afflictions of the three realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Three universal knowledges (*parijñā*) are the fruits of what is to be abandoned by cultivation; two are the fruits of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
That is to say, the power of subsequent knowledge can only permanently abandon [the afflictions of] the form and formless realms.
Because they are abandoned through cultivation, one attains the exhaustion of craving for form and the exhaustion of all fetters;
these are the two fruits of complete knowledge (*parijñā*). Regarding the six fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*):
"Category" (*pakṣa*) means "class.
This is because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmanirvedhabhāgīya*) belong to the same class.
This is called the category of Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna).
It was previously stated that through the acceptance of dharmas (dharmanirvedhabhāgīya), one attains three fruits; likewise, through dharma-knowledge, one attains three fruits.
Now, regarding the category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), since both patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are explained together,
one attains six fruits. As for the five fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*):
The analysis of this category is the same as explained previously. It was stated above that *anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent patience) attains three fruits,
while *anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge) attains two fruits.
Now, regarding the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), both patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are explained together;
therefore, five fruits are obtained.
Third, this clarifies the object of universal knowledge (*parijñeya*).
The treatise states:
For what reason are they not established as distinct thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) for each individual abandonment,
but are instead established solely according to the nine stages mentioned previously?
The verse says: Because one attains the acquisition of the untainted, the abandonment [of defilements], the deficiency of the Peak of Existence,
the cessation of the two causes, and the transcendence of the fruits, nine thorough knowledges are established.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, the fruits of the six patiences are established based on three conditions.
First, the attainment of the untainted abandonment (*anāsrava-prahāṇa-prāpti*),
which means attaining the untainted analytical cessation (*anāsrava-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Second, the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra-vikalatā*).
This refers to the stage of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Among the five categories of afflictions,
it is because one has not yet accomplished [the abandonment of] even one category of affliction.
The term "incomplete" refers to the deficiency [of causes].
Third, the cessation of both causes means the cessation of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of its own category.
And because it is a universal cause for other categories,
it is called the "extinction of both causes.
This means that each of the five categories serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for its own respective category.
If suffering and its origin are mutual pervasive causes,
they belong to the remaining three categories.
Using suffering and its origin as pervasive causes: just as ordinary beings are able to sever suffering and its origin,
there is the cessation of both causes,
lacking the remaining two conditions.
Although they have attained the unconditioned,
they do not establish it as "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) when it comes to the noble ones.
Upon entering the stage of the path of seeing,
until prior to the manifestation of the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*),
although one has attained untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*).
The remaining two conditions being absent,
"thorough knowledge" (parijñā) is not established; that is to say, in the case of the subsequent patience regarding suffering (duḥkhe ’nvaya-kṣānti).
Although the afflictions of the Peak of Existence have been severed, they still manifest;
yet this is not called a deficiency.
Upon reaching the stage of the Dharma-patience regarding the origin [of suffering] within the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*),
although the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is deficient,
the dual causes have not yet been extinguished.

Because the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) of the lower realm has not yet been extinguished; that is to say, although the patience regarding the origin of suffering (*samudaye-dharmajñānakṣānti*) severs the category of the origin,
it has not yet ceased to be present.
Therefore, it is not called "cessation. At the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*),
the three conditions are fully present.
One then establishes universal knowledge;
therefore, this occurs during the stages of subsequent dharma-knowledge and subsequent type-knowledge.
The unconditioned states attained are all established as "thorough knowledges" (parijñā) because they possess three conditions;
those who have transcended a realm [are likewise so established].
This explains how the three fruits of knowledge are established based on the four conditions;
that is to say, by adding "transcending a realm" to the previous three— namely, transcending the desire realm.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* master establishes the "full knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters" because one transcends the realm of form; he establishes the "exhaustion of craving for the realm of form" because one transcends the formless realm;
and he establishes the "full knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters."
In total, five conditions are established;
to the aforementioned four,
the dissociation from both fetters is added.
That is to say, being free from the fetters of one's own category as well as the fetters of other categories is called "freedom from both types of fetters."
The distinction between [the category of] "associated with" (*saṃprayukta*) and "caused by" (*hetu*) is that the latter is broader while the former is narrower; that is to say,
"being bound" (*bandhana*) refers exclusively to latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This is because it refers to the factors that are associated with and co-existent with [the path].
Following this, the fourth section clarifies the accomplishment of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The treatise asks:
Who accomplishes how many thorough knowledges (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:

For one abiding in the stage of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), there is none; for one in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), from one up to five may be attained, and six, one, or two are attained through cultivation. For one beyond training (aśaikṣa), only one is attained. The commentary states: [The commentary continues: "In the stage of seeing the truths, there is none" means that while one is still in the process of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing, no faculty of the path of cultivation has yet been acquired. "From one up to five may be attained" means that in the path of cultivation, depending on the level of abandonment, one may attain from one up to five faculties. "Six, one, or two are attained through cultivation" means that when one attains the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) or non-returner (anāgāmin), six faculties are attained; when one attains the fruit of stream-enterer (srotāpanna), one faculty is attained; and when one attains the fruit of arhat (arhat), two faculties are attained. "For one beyond training, only one is attained" means that when one has reached the state of an arhat, only the faculty of one who has completed what was to be done (kṛtāvīndriya) is attained. This concludes the explanation.
Regarding those who do not abide in the stage of seeing the truths:
the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments of mind;
five of these moments have already passed.
There is no complete knowledge [of all aspects].
Alternatively, one may possess from one to five [knowledges] during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Upon reaching the sixth stage— the dharma-knowledge of origination (samudaya-dharmajñāna) and the subsequent patience regarding origination (samudaya-anvayakṣānti)—
one accomplishes only a single thorough knowledge (parijñā).
Upon reaching the eighth moment, the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the dharma-patience regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*),
two full knowledges (*parijñā*) are accomplished.
Upon reaching the tenth [moment], the dharma-knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharmajñāna), and the subsequent patience regarding cessation (nirodhānvayakṣānti),
three thorough knowledges (parijñā) are accomplished.
Upon reaching the twelfth [moment], the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), as well as the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*),
one accomplishes four universal knowledges (*parijñā*).
Upon reaching the fourteenth [moment], the Dharma-knowledge of the Path (mārga-dharmajñāna),
and the fifteenth, the Subsequent Patience regarding the Path (mārgānvayakṣānti),
one accomplishes five universal knowledges (parijñā).
Therefore, it is said that [the stages] range from one to five.
Regarding "cultivating and accomplishing six and two":
"cultivation" refers to abiding in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
From the knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) up until one has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire,
one possesses six universal knowledges (parijñā).
Furthermore, for one who has abandoned desire,

there are also six types of full knowledge (parijñā) when regressing. This refers to one who has completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm but has not yet exhausted craving for the form realm.
One achieves a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
namely, the [thorough knowledge] of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), or for one who has previously abandoned desire,
the entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the ultimate path,
it has not yet arisen at the time of the superior fruit-path when the craving for the form realm has been exhausted.
Furthermore, one also achieves one [defilement],
namely that which is conducive to the lower realm (avarabhāgīya). Moreover, from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm, there is falling away through the arising of a fetter of the form realm.
Furthermore, for one in the stage of no-more-learning who falls away due to the arising of the fetters of the form realm,
there is likewise the possession of one [fetter] conducive to the lower realms. This is the case when craving for the form realm has been eternally exhausted.
Two types of full knowledge are accomplished:
namely, that regarding the lower fetters and that regarding the exhaustion of craving for the form realm— or, alternatively, for one who has previously abandoned craving for the form realm.
Entering the path of seeing,
one subsequently gives rise to the path of superior fruit that exhausts craving for the form realm, following the knowledge of the subsequent category (mārgānvaya-jñāna).
Until one has completely abandoned craving for the formless realm, one possesses two [fetters]:

those conducive to the lower realms and that which consists in the exhaustion of craving for the form realm. From the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one may give rise to the entanglements of the formless realm.

Regarding those who have regressed, they also accomplish one [of the two]—namely, the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūparāga*) among the factors conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*). As for the two types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), they accomplish only one, namely, the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanakṣaya*).
This is the fifth from here.
This clarifies the comprehensive knowledge of the collection.
The treatise asks:
For what reason is one a non-returner?
The fruit of arhatship consists of the total collection of all abandonments,
which constitutes a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The verse says:
Because of transcending realms and attaining fruits, there are two locations for the full comprehension of the aggregates (*kṣayajñāna*).
The commentary explains:
Because two conditions are present,
there is a comprehensive and universal knowledge:
first, the transcendence of realms.
Second is the attainment of the fruit;
at the time of becoming free from the defilement of desire,
one transcends the desire realm.
Because one has attained the fruit of non-returning; because, at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the formless realm, one transcends the formless realm;
and because one has attained the fruit of no-more-learning.
Therefore, regarding these two fruits,
one attains comprehensive thorough knowledge;
from this, the sixth [fruit] follows.
Regarding the thorough knowledge of the attainment of clarity and equanimity,
the treatise asks:
"Who abandons?"
Who attains them?
How many kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are there?
The verse says:
One, two, five, or six are abandoned; the same applies to what is acquired, with the exception of five.
The commentary states:
"Abandoning one" means:
That is to say, through falling away from the path of no-more-learning,
one relinquishes the exhaustion of all fetters;
this is the first thorough knowledge.
Furthermore, when one falls away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm, one relinquishes the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm;
this also applies when one falls away from the state of being entirely free from desire.
The abandonment of the five lower fetters constitutes one full comprehension (*parijñā*).
The abandonment of two [fetters] refers to those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
From the exhaustion of craving for the form realm,
one falls away due to the arising of fetters of desire; thus, one relinquishes the exhaustion of craving for the form realm.
And the two types of full knowledge regarding the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*). Furthermore, at the time of attaining arhatship,
one also abandons the former two types of full knowledge.
"Abandoning five" refers to one who has previously abandoned desire and then enters the path of seeing.
Upon attaining the path of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the ultimate path when realizing the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin),
one acquires one factor conducive to the lower [fetters].
One abandons the previous [five] path-of-seeing thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
As for the statement that one abandons six:
This refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire;
when such a noble one attains the abandonment of desire,
they obtain the single full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*).
One abandons the six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) that were the fruits of the preceding patience (*kṣānti*).
The same applies to their acquisition; "excluding five" refers to the acquisition of the thorough knowledges.
There are those who attain one,
those who attain two,
and those who attain six.
As in the previous case regarding the abandonment of numbers,
it is likewise stated here; however,
this excludes the attainment of the five [supernormal powers].
Regarding the statement "attaining one," this refers to attaining what has not yet been attained among the nine thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).
Each is attained gradually;
all are called "attaining one. This refers to the preceding stage of the Path of Vision (darśana-mārga).
Regarding the statement "accomplishing two, three, four, five,
etc.," this is spoken in terms of accomplishment;
for accomplishment encompasses both the prior and the subsequent stages.
Attainment refers only to the initial moment;
therefore, within gradual attainment,
there is no such thing as attaining two, three, four, five, or more [factors] at the very first moment.

This is also [the case for] thorough knowledge (*parijñā*). Regarding the statement below that "two and six are obtained," this refers exclusively to what is attained from the perspective of falling back (*parihāṇi*).

This is not attained gradually; rather, it occurs when one who has reached the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) falls away due to the arising of defilements pertaining to the realm of form (rūpāvacara-kleśa).
It is also called "attaining one," namely the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*).
As for the statement "attaining two":
That is to say, when one falls away from the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) due to the arising of the fetters of the formless realm (ārūpya),
it is called "attaining two."
This refers to the exhaustion of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) and the [attainment of] the factors conducive to the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya*).
Regarding the statement that "six are attained":
That is to say, from the regression of a non-returner (anāgāmin),
one attains the fruit of patience (kṣānti-phala) within a single moment; this is the sixth.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā, Main Text, Fascicle Twenty-one and Twenty-two.
"Worthy" (*bhadra*) refers to being harmonious and virtuous;
"noble" (*ārya*) refers to being holy and correct. This chapter extensively elucidates these matters, and is therefore titled "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*).
Within this chapter, there are three major sections: first, a general clarification of the essence and nature of the Path;
second, an elucidation of the Truths realized by the Path;
and third, a differentiation of persons based on the Path.
Furthermore, first, regarding the elucidation of the essential nature of the Path,
the treatise states:
"Thus, the abandonment of afflictions and so forth has already been explained."
Regarding the nine superior stages,
one attains the designation "thoroughly knowing";
however, this attainment necessarily occurs through the power of the Path.
What are the characteristics of this path by which [the afflictions] are abandoned?
The verse says:
It has already been stated that the abandonment of the afflictions occurs through the vision of the truths and through cultivation.
The path of seeing is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertains to both types.
Commentary: The various afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been explained in detail above regarding their abandonment.
This is due to the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Among these, the path of seeing consists exclusively of the untainted (*anāsrava*),
whereas the path of cultivation comprises both types— namely, the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted.
Regarding the fifteen moments of mind:
because the path of seeing can swiftly counteract the three realms, within a single moment for each of the four truths—
Because it suddenly severs the nine grades of what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*),
the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) lacks this capacity; therefore,
it is exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
From this second [section] onward,
the truths realized by the path are clarified;
herein, it is divided into two parts.
First, the elucidation of the four truths;
second, the elucidation of the two truths.
Within the elucidation of the four truths, there are two parts.
First, the correct elucidation of the Four Noble Truths;
second, the specific revelation of the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the first, the elucidation of the Four Noble Truths:
The Treatise says:
As was stated above,
it is by means of seeing the truths that this truth which is seen [is realized].
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The four truths have already been named: namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Their own nature is likewise; this is explained according to the sequence of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).
Regarding the phrase "the four names of the truths have already been explained": [this refers to what was stated previously].
This refers to the *Dhātuvarga*.
At the beginning it states, "The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path.
This explains the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Cessation through deliberation is called disjunction;
this refers to the Truth of Cessation,
as well as suffering, its origin, and the world.
This explains the truths of suffering and its origin.
As for their sequential listing:
first is suffering.
Second, accumulation;
third, cessation;
fourth, the path.
Question: Regarding this present chapter,
which enumerates the Four Noble Truths,
what difference is there in their essential nature from that which was explained in the Chapter on the Elements (Dhātuvarga)?
The verse replies: "Their own essence is likewise.
This means that because their essence is identical to that [of the primary consciousness], the word "likewise" (tathā) is employed.
Question: Regarding the sequence of the Four Noble Truths, for what reason is it thus?
Answer: The verse states that the sequence follows the order of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). "Clear realization" refers to...
This refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). That which was previously observed during the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is explained first.
Question: For what reason is the sequence of the clear realizations (abhisamaya) necessarily fixed?
Answer: It is because of the [stages] beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata).
The stage of application (*prayoga*). Because one observes in this manner, [it is called] the stage of application.
Question: For what reason is it the stage of application?
Is it viewed in this way?
The answer is: if there is any phenomenon that is an object of craving and attachment.
It is capable of causing affliction and serves as the cause of suffering; thus,
one first contemplates it as suffering.
Next, one further contemplates suffering as to what its cause is,
thereby contemplating the Truth of Origination.
Next, one further contemplates suffering as to by what it is extinguished.
He then contemplates the truth of cessation.
Next, he further contemplates what constitutes the path for the cessation of suffering,
and thus he contemplates the truth of the path.
Just as one first perceives an illness, then seeks its cause,
subsequently contemplates recovery,
and finally seeks an efficacious medicine.
Therefore, the Sutra of the Excellent Physician states:
"Now, one who is a king among physicians is said to possess four virtues."
One who is able to extract the poisonous arrow:
first, being skilled in knowing the symptoms of the disease;
second, being skilled in knowing the cause of the disease.
Third, he is skilled in knowing when a disease has been cured;
fourth, he is skilled in knowing excellent medicines.
The Tathāgata is likewise.
He acts as a great king of physicians because he understands, in accordance with reality, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The sequence of contemplation in the stage of preparatory application is thus, and the sequence in the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is likewise.
Just as one who has already observed the tracks of a horse galloping across the ground [knows its path],
"clear observation" (abhisamaya) should be understood as signifying the meaning of manifest perfect awakening (abhisambodha).
This refers to the objects of the truths as perceived through present mental application and investigation.
Question: Why are these called "Noble Truths" (āryasatya) in the sūtras?
Answer: Because the Noble Ones perceive the four truths.
Because it is free from inversion, it is called a Noble Truth (*āryasatya*).

Thus, there is a verse that says: The Noble Ones declare the cessation of suffering, Nirvana, to be bliss; The non-Noble ones declare it to be suffering, for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) call Nirvana suffering. The Noble Ones declare the outflowing (*sāsrava*) to be suffering; The non-Noble ones declare it to be bliss, speaking of the bliss of the outflowing.
From this second section,
the Truth of Suffering is explained in detail.
The treatise states:
It is only one portion of feeling— namely, the painful feeling among the five types of feeling—
that constitutes the intrinsic nature of suffering; all else is not.
How can it be said that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are the truth of suffering?
The verse says:
Suffering arises from conjunction with the three types of suffering; All things are so according to their respective natures.
"Agreeable, disagreeable, and the remaining impure conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Regarding the commentary:
"Suffering arises from the conjunction with the three types of suffering."
This is the definition.
The Truth of Suffering is designated as such because it is comprised of the three types of suffering.
First is the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
That is to say, painful feeling is suffering when it arises and suffering while it persists.
This is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Second is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), which refers to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
it is pleasant when it arises.
The suffering at the time of change is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*);
the third is the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation;
it constitutes suffering by way of its conditioned nature,
because it is produced by a multitude of causal conditions.
Because it is characterized by impermanence,
it is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). As for "all that is appropriate":
All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava) are, as appropriate,
conjoined with the three types of suffering.
All are termed the Truth of Suffering.
First, agreeable contaminated phenomena are conjoined with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
This is called suffering.
Second, there are the disagreeable tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
That which is conjoined with the suffering of suffering is called "suffering.
Third are the remaining contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
That which is conjoined with the suffering of conditioned existence is called "suffering. It should be understood that, apart from the agreeable and the disagreeable,
all other contaminated phenomena are likewise [to be known as] suffering.
In this context, that which is agreeable is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*); that which is disagreeable is called... [the suffering of suffering].
Regarding what is called "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): this is discussed for the time being from a specific perspective;
in reality, it is actually agreeable (*manāpa*).
And those things that are disagreeable are all called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),
because they are impermanent by nature.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering because they are suffering by their very nature as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*); this suffering of conditioned phenomena is subtle.
Only the Noble Ones perceive it.
Thus, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta said in verse:

"Just as when a single eyelash is placed upon the palm of the hand, a person does not notice it, yet if that same lash is placed upon the eye, it causes pain and distress; the fool is like the palm of the hand."
The suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) is like an eyelash that one does not perceive; for the wise, it is like an eye.
Because this very conditioned existence gives rise to extreme revulsion and fear, all foolish worldlings [fail to see it].
The mind that experiences suffering and fear in the Avīci Hell is not as [intense] as that of the noble ones toward the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Because the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are suffering by way of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
Question: If it is also admitted that there is pleasure among all phenomena...
For what reason is it said that only suffering is the Noble Truth?
Answer: Within the Sarvāstivāda school, there is one class of commentators who explain it as follows.
Because pleasure is so slight,
it is like placing a mung bean into a heap of black beans;
the small is overwhelmed by the many.
It is called a "heap of black beans.
What wise person would drain water from it to wash away an abscess?
A slight pleasure arises;
one reckons an abscess to be pleasure. The Sautrāntika patriarch explains this in verse:
Because it can serve as the cause of suffering;
because it can accumulate manifold sufferings; and because there is a longing for that [existence] despite its being suffering.
It is said that pleasure is also called suffering; the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains the correct meaning as follows:
"In reality, one should say that all conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*) and pleasure [are suffering]."
Their essence is entirely suffering,
because they share the same single flavor as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
for this reason, they are called "suffering."
It is a truth that there is no pleasure; furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika school, the Mahāsāṃghikas, and others, there is certainly no real pleasure.
Feeling is exclusively suffering, yet fools, through their perversions, falsely claim it to be pleasure.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"You should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering. The Sarvāstivāda school asserts that pleasure truly exists.
The Buddha’s statement that one should contemplate pleasant feelings as suffering reveals that pleasant feelings possess two natures.
First, there is the nature of pleasure;
this is by way of its own characteristic,
because its intrinsic nature is pleasure.
Second is the nature of suffering (*duḥkhatā*), which refers to the perspective of distinct characteristics;
it is because [pleasure] is also a phenomenon subject to impermanence and decay. Therefore, it is said that one contemplates pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) as suffering.

This is explained in terms of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and not in terms of the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Thus, there is a verse that says:

The Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, because they know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and involve the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), and that conditioned things are subject to change and involve the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), have taught that "all feelings are suffering. Regarding these two preceding explanations:
The author of the treatise critiques,
saying: "The masters of the Abhidharma maintain that pleasure exists as a real entity."
This statement is logical. Furthermore, in the Sarvāstivāda school, suffering and its origin are a single entity divided into two aspects as cause and effect;
that is, the essence of the truth of suffering is considered from the perspective of its being a cause.
It is also called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). According to the Sautrāntika school,
craving alone is taught to be the essence of the Truth of Origination.
Because the Sūtra speaks only of craving as the origin [of suffering], the Sarvāstivādins say:
"The Sūtra speaks of craving as the origin because it refers to what is predominant."
In reality, all [conditioned phenomena] are the truth of origination (samudaya-satya).
Therefore, the Blessed One [said]:
It is stated in a verse:
"Karma, craving, and ignorance act as causes,
summoning future formations and causing the continuity of all existences."

Regarding the term *pudgala*: since this verse states that karma and ignorance act as causes to summon results, we know that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone is not the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Following this, secondly, the two truths are explained.
The treatise states:
There are two kinds of truths:
first, conventional truth; second, ultimate truth.
Second is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). What are the characteristics of these two truths?
The verse says:

When that [object] is broken, it is no longer perceived; likewise, when analyzed by wisdom, the remainder is also thus. Like a jar or water, these are conventional; other than this, they are called ultimate. Commentary: When a jar is broken into shards, the cognition of "jar" no longer arises. Likewise, when water is analyzed into its constituent parts by wisdom, the cognition of "water" no longer arises. These two—like the jar and the water—are conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
