That which is different from these is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding "that which ceases when the cognition of it is destroyed":
if there is a cognition of a certain object,
that object ceases to exist once the cognition is destroyed.
This is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
For example, when a jar is broken, the cognition of a "jar" no longer exists;
likewise, when a garment is torn, the cognition of a "garment" also ceases to exist.
Therefore, things such as jars and garments are called conventional truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Regarding the phrase "if one analyzes them with wisdom and [finds] the rest is likewise":
this means that if there is an object which, when analyzed by wisdom, [yields] the rest...
When that perception is absent, it too is merely conventional;
just as when water is analyzed by wisdom into its constituent elements of color, odor, taste, and tangibility,
the perception of "water" ceases to exist.
It is the same as when fire is analyzed:
the perception of fire then ceases.
Therefore, these [elements] are water and fire.
This is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the phrase "conventional [truth] such as a jar or water":
the conventional jar belongs to the first category.
The water as it appears in the conventional world belongs to the second category;
however, this water in the jar—
When it has not yet been analyzed,
this designation is provisionally established and is called "conventional."
According to conventional reasoning,
it is said that jars and so forth exist;
this is real and not false.
That which is designated as conventional truth;
that which is different from this is called ultimate truth—
different from this [designation of] "jar" or "water."
This is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), such as blue and so forth,
when reduced to its most subtle particles (*paramāṇu*).
The perception of form is ever-present;
yet when analyzed by wisdom down to its constituent atoms, such as taste and so forth, it vanishes.
The faculty of taste is ever-present;
yet when wisdom analyzes the four aggregates, such as feeling,
it reaches down to a single moment.
Since that cognition is ever-present,
those [objects] such as form and so forth are called ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
This exists as ultimate reality;
therefore, it is called the "ultimate" (paramārtha).
It is based on the principle of the ultimate.
To say that form and so forth exist is true and not false;
this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). This is according to the Sautrāntika explanation.
The phenomena apprehended by untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the subsequent worldly right wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika-samyagjñāna*) are called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Apart from this, any other cognition that apprehends phenomena is termed conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
From here begins the third major section,
which distinguishes individuals based on the noble path;
it is divided into three parts.
First, the preparatory application for the noble path;
second, the classification of persons according to the three paths;
third, the distinctions among the various paths.
Within the explanation of the preparatory application (*prayoga*),
it is further divided into two parts:
first, the general heading.
Second, the detailed explanation.
Herein, the first section provides a general indication of the practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*).
The treatise states:
Having already distinguished the various truths,
one should now explain how to diligently practice through skillful means.
Proceeding toward the path of seeing the truths.
The verse says:
One who is about to proceed toward the path of seeing the truths Should abide in ethical discipline and diligently practice.
Those produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation—namely, the objects consisting of names, both [names and meanings], and meanings.
Commentary: This refers to those who are about to enter the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*).
One should first abide in ethical discipline,
and thereafter diligently cultivate the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation; for it is through the wisdom accomplished by hearing, reflection, and meditation that [liberation is attained].
Wisdom is called that which is accomplished;
based on the wisdom accomplished through hearing,
one gives rise to the wisdom accomplished through reflection.
Based on the wisdom arisen from reflection, one gives rise to the wisdom arisen from cultivation.
Question: What is the distinction between these three types of wisdom?
Answer: Wisdom derived from hearing takes only names as its object,
because it is not yet able to set aside the words to contemplate the meaning.
The wisdom resulting from reflection takes both names and meanings as its objects,
because one has not yet completely set aside the words to contemplate the meaning.
The verse says "both," which refers to name and meaning.
This is the wisdom produced by cultivation.
It takes only the meaning as its object,
for one has already been able to set aside the words and contemplate the meaning;
this is the second [stage] following that.
This provides a detailed explanation of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*). It is divided into four parts,
the first of which explains the purification of the physical vessel.
Second, the stage of the five cessations of the mind;
third, the four foundations of mindfulness;
fourth, the four roots of goodness.
Below this, first is the clarification of the purification of the body and the vessel-world.
The treatise states:
"All those who wish to apply themselves with diligence to cultivation..."
How does one purify the vessel of the body so that cultivation may be swiftly accomplished?
The verse says:
Possessing physical and mental seclusion, it is free from the great desire of insufficiency—namely, seeking much for what has been obtained or not yet obtained;
it is the antidote to its opposite and pertains to the three realms; it is untainted and has non-attachment as its nature.
The four noble lineages are likewise: the first three consist solely of contentment, while the fourth consists of the requisites for life and one's work.
They serve to counteract the arising of the four types of craving—the desire for "mine," for the self, and for objects—by providing temporary relief and ultimate eradication.
The commentary states:
The purification of the body-vessel is briefly due to three causes.
First, physical and mental seclusion.
Second, contentment and fewness of desires;
third, abiding in the four noble lineages;
and possessing physical and mental seclusion.
Physical seclusion means dwelling apart from social entanglement;
mental seclusion means...
To be free from unwholesome thoughts and to be without insufficiency or great desire—
this is the second cause.
As for "being without insufficiency":
Contentment is the absence of great desire;
it is having few desires.
The first two are easily accomplished through contentment and fewness of desires.
Question: How is it that there is neither insufficiency nor great desire?
What is the distinction between these two kinds of non-existence?
The verse replies: "That which has already been attained and that which has not yet been attained; the state of seeking much is called 'non-existent'."
It refers to the further longing for robes and other requisites after they have already been obtained;
this is called lack of contentment.
This is what contentment lacks:
if one has not yet obtained robes and so forth,
one further harbors excessive longing for them.
This is called "great desire," which is something that those with few desires do not possess.
It is the opposite of [the quality] being treated.
This clarifies contentment and fewness of desires, which are the opposites of discontent and great desire. Regarding the three elements:
[they are] contentment and fewness of desires.
If they are with outflows (sāsrava),
they pertain to all three realms;
if they are without outflows (anāsrava), [they do not].
These pertain to the nine stages (*bhūmi*).

The two types of objects to be countered exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). That which has the nature of untainted non-attachment (*anāsrava-alobha*) consists of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*).
It also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Its essence is non-attachment (*alobha*).
There are two kinds of that which it counteracts.
"That which has greed as its nature—
the four noble lineages are also thus" explains the third reason.
Because they can give rise to the various noble ones,
they are called "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa).
As for the essential nature of these four noble lineages:
This is also non-attachment,
similar to the previous [contentment] such as joy (*prīti*) and so forth; therefore, it is said that "the former three are merely contentment."
1. The noble lineage of contentment with clothing;
2. The noble lineage of contentment with food and drink;
3. The noble lineage of contentment with bedding and seating.
The four noble lineages consist of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation;
that is, delighting in the abandonment of afflictions and delighting in the cultivation of the noble path.
Question: Since the fourth noble lineage is not contentment,
how can it also have non-attachment as its essential nature?
The answer is: because they are able to relinquish sensual desire and craving for existence, this fourth [noble lineage] also has non-attachment as its nature.
Question: Why must these four noble lineages be established?
The verse replies: "The three requisites for life follow from karma.
The first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are the requisites for life that assist the path.
The last noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) assists in the work of the path by having the disciples relinquish their worldly requisites and worldly occupations.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One established these requisites for the practice of those who cultivate the path, which serve as aids for the arising of the Noble Path.
Liberation is not long in coming. Question:
For what reason are these two matters established in this way?
Answer: The verse says it is for the purpose of counteracting the arising of the four types of craving.
First, attachment to clothing;
second, attachment to food and drink;
third, attachment to bedding and furniture.
There are four types of craving for existence and non-existence;
because they counteract these four cravings,
the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are established.
"Regarding 'mine' and 'my affairs,' because one desires to temporarily rest and permanently eliminate them"—
this is another alternative explanation.
Regarding the objects of desire that belong to oneself,
these are the three beginning with clothing;
it is toward these that one gives rise to a mind of greed.
That which is called "the object of my possession" is desire.
That which is "the object of the self" refers to the body.
The arising of craving within one's own body is called the desire for the self-entity (*ātmabhāva*).
This is because the Buddha intends for his disciples to...
The first three noble lineages are established for the sake of temporarily ceasing the desire for "mine" and the desire for the self;
[the last one] is for the sake of permanently eliminating both "mine" and the desire for the self.
Therefore, the fourth noble lineage is established.
Following this second [section], there is the clarification of the stage of the five methods for settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta-sthāpana*).
These are the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*).
Within them, there are two parts:
first, a general heading.
Second, the detailed explanation.
First, as for the general indication,
the treatise says:
Thus, having already explained the vessel that serves as the basis for cultivation,
by means of which gateways can one correctly enter into cultivation?
The verse says:
There are two essential gateways for entering cultivation: the meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing;
those with predominant craving and discursive thought should practice them respectively.
The commentary states:
There are two essential points for correctly entering the gateway of cultivation.
First, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) can counteract sensual desire (*rāga*).
The second [type], mindfulness of breathing, can eliminate distracted discursive thoughts.
Following this, there is a separate explanation divided into two parts.
First, an explanation of the contemplation of impurity;
second, an explanation of mindfulness of breathing.
Regarding the contemplation of impurity:
It is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the characteristics;
second, the analysis by way of various categories.
Furthermore, first regarding the clarification of the characteristics [of the meditative objects],
the treatise states:
"In this context, one should first analyze the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*)."
What is the method for observing these signs?
The verse says:
To universally counteract the four types of craving, one first analyzes the contemplation of the skeleton.
Expanding to the oceans and then contracting again is called the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*).
Excluding the feet and extending up to the midpoint of the head is called the stage of mature cultivation (*kṛtaparicaya*).
Binding the mind between the eyebrows is called the stage of transcending mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).
The commentary states:
The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity is specifically for the purpose of counteracting attachment.
There are four kinds of greed:
first, greed for color;
second, greed for shape.
Third, craving for exquisite tactile sensations;
fourth, craving for service and offerings.
These take the bloated corpse and so forth as their objects.
One cultivates the contemplation of impurity to remedy attachment to visible color,
taking as its object such things as being eaten by insects.
It counteracts craving for color and form by taking worms,
maggots, and the like as its object;
it counteracts craving for exquisite touch [by taking the same].
Contemplating a corpse without movement cures the craving for offerings; if one contemplates a skeleton,
one cultivates the meditation on impurity.
This universally counteracts the four types of craving,
because within the skeleton there is no object for those four cravings.
Now, one should first explain the cultivation of the contemplation of the skeleton.
This is associated exclusively with attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
"Resolute conviction" refers to conceptual visualization;
that is to say, within form.
One forms the sublime perception of impurity.
This meditation on impurity is so called because it takes only a limited portion as its object.
One does not sever the afflictions.
For one who severs delusions must necessarily take [all objects] as their universal cognitive object.
One can merely suppress greed so that it does not manifest; however, the yoga practitioner cultivates the meditation on the skeleton.
In total, there are three stages:
first, the stage of initial practice;
second, the stage of mature cultivation.
Regarding the third stage, the stage of transcendent mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*), when practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*),
one should first fix the mind upon the parts of one's own body.
One should settle the mind upon whichever place one prefers, whether it be the toes,
the forehead, or elsewhere.
Once the mind has attained stability,
one engages in conceptual reflection based on the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
The skin and flesh rot and fall away,
gradually purifying the bones until one fully contemplates the entire body as a skeleton.
Having seen one set, he further contemplates a second;
gradually, from one room and one monastery, he extends his observation until the entire earth,
bounded by the ocean, is encompassed.
To cause one's resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) to increase,
one gradually condenses the visualization until one contemplates only a single set of white bones.
When this gradual condensation is complete and the contemplation of impurity is accomplished,
it is called the stage of initial practice.
In order to increase the power of conviction through brief contemplation,
one first removes the foot bones from within a single set [of skeletal remains].
One contemplates the remaining bones,
gradually proceeding until only the half-bone of the head remains.
Contemplating half a bone;
when the practice is abbreviated to this extent,
it is called the stage of "already matured cultivation."
In order to achieve mastery over concise visualization and resolute conviction,
one removes the skull and half of the bones of the head and fixes the mind between the eyebrows.
Focusing on a single object,
one abides in profound stillness;
this constitutes the ultimate degree of brevity.
Regarding the stage of "surpassing mental application" (*atikrāntamanasikāra*), the treatise states:
"There is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) which has a limited object (*parīttālambana*), but it is not limited in its mastery (*vaśitā*)."
One should formulate four propositions: when mental attention has become mature and the object of focus is one's own body,
this is called the first proposition.
Because mental attention (*manasikāra*) has matured,
there is no lack of mastery;
because the object of focus (*ālambana*) is a single body, it is called "limited in its object," for mental attention has not yet matured.
The object of focus extends as far as the ocean;
this is called the second stage,
wherein mental attention is not yet matured.
The mastery here is slight,
but because the objects of focus extend as far as the ocean,
it is not that the objects are few; rather, the mental attention has already reached maturity.
The object of focus extending as far as the ocean constitutes the third phrase;
it is the object of mastery.
In neither case is it slight; the mental application (*manasikāra*) is not yet mature.
Taking one's own body as the object constitutes the fourth alternative.
Regarding mastery over the object of focus, both are limited.
From this, the second section follows: the analysis by way of various categories.
The treatise asks:
First, what is the nature of this contemplation of impurity?
Second, upon how many stages (bhūmi) does it rely?
Three questions concerning the objects of focus;
four questions concerning the place of arising;
five questions concerning the modes of activity.
For what reason are there six questions regarding the world?
Are they with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava)? There are seven questions.
Are they acquired through the departure from defilement (vairāgya-lābhika)?
Regarding the eight questions on attainment through application (*prayoga*), the verse says:
Its nature is non-attachment; it exists in ten stages; It takes the desire and form realms as its object; it arises in humans.

The commentary states: "That which has non-attachment as its nature is conditioned by the impure, belongs to one's own world, is associated with outflows, and is acquired through both [types of attainment]."
This answers the first question.
That is to say, the meditation on impurity has non-attachment as its essential nature.
Regarding the "ten stages" (daśabhūmi):
this answers the second question,
as it generally relies upon the ten stages.
This refers to the four fundamental dhyānas, as well as the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) of the desire realm.
Regarding the phrase "the four preparatory stages," this means that each of the four dhyānas has its own preparatory stage. These take the desire and form realms as their objects.
Answering the third question:

[It refers to] those born as humans who perceive only the visible form and shape of the desire realm. Answering the fourth question: [It refers to] those born as humans who perceive both the visible form and shape and the invisible intangible form of the desire realm.
It arises only among human beings,
excluding those of Uttarakuru;
this is because [it does not arise] within the heavenly realms.
Since there is no livid discoloration and so forth,
this contemplation does not exist. This concludes the answer to the fifth question regarding the impure.
"Taking the impure as its mode of activity, it has the world itself as its object.
This answers the sixth question.
If [it] exists in the past...
Conditioned by the past; or if in the present,
conditioned by the present.
If it is in the future and takes the future world as its object,
it is called "conditioning its own time."
If it is a non-arising dharma,
it universally takes the three periods of time as its object;
this applies to those that are with outflows.
Answering the seventh question:
Since this is a conceptual visualization,
it is exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Regarding "attainment through both":
this answers the eighth question.
It refers to attainment through both the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-lābha*) and through preparatory effort (*prayoga-lābha*).
If it has been previously cultivated and attained,
there is attainment through the removal of defilements; if it has never been attained before, [there is attainment through effort].
There is that which is attained through preparatory effort.
From this second point, there follows a separate explanation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
This section is divided into two parts:
first, an explanation of the distinctions in mindfulness;
second, an explanation of the distinctions in the breath.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among types of mindfulness,
the treatise states:
"The characteristics and distinctions of the contemplation on impurity are explained."
Next, the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) should be explained.
What are its specific characteristics?
The verse says:
Mindfulness of breathing has wisdom as its nature and belongs to five stages; it takes wind as its object, relies on the body of the desire realm, and is attained in two ways.
It is real and does not exist externally. There are six [aspects], namely counting and so forth.
The commentary says:
This consists of eight sections. Regarding the wisdom of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*),
the first is the section on the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
This mindfulness of breathing has wisdom as its essence;
"breathing" itself is wind.
Because one recollects and maintains the breath, it is called "mindfulness of breathing.
Although its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*),
it is termed "mindfulness" (*smṛti*).
Because it is sustained by the power of mindfulness,
wisdom attains clarity regarding its object.
The Sūtra speaks of *ānāpānasmṛti*.
*Āna* means "sending forth" (or "bringing in").
"Drawing in the breath" means drawing in external wind and causing it to enter the body.
*Āpana* means "sending away";
it refers to exhaling the breath.
This refers to the meaning of drawing in the internal winds and causing them to exit the body.
Regarding the five stages:
The second is the gate of reliance on stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to relying on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna,
as well as the preparatory stages of the second and third dhyānas.
And it is associated with the intermediate state and the desire realm,
because this mindfulness is associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Thus,
it exists in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate state, and the desire realm.
It is not in other stages.
That is to say, the feelings of suffering and pleasure are capable of inducing vitarka in accordance with them.
This mindfulness counteracts discursive thought;
therefore, it is associated exclusively with equanimity. That which takes wind as its object belongs to the third gateway of the objective sphere.
This concentration takes wind as its object and relies upon a body in the desire realm.
Regarding the fourth point, the door of the basis:
it relies exclusively upon the bodies of those in the human and celestial realms within the desire realm.
Excluding Uttarakuru; "attained by two" refers to the fifth section, the gate of attaining [the faculties].
This includes both attainment through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-lābha*) and attainment through application (*prayoga-lābha*). As for the actual entities:
The sixth is the door of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
This is associated with true mental attention (*bhūtamanasikāra*), not with conceptual construction (*parikalpa*). Regarding "that which does not exist externally":
The seventh section distinguishes the gate of the heterodox;
this is practiced according to the Buddha's teaching,
whereas it does not exist among the non-Buddhists.
Because among the various non-Buddhists there is no one who can teach [it], and because they themselves cannot realize the subtle dharmas. Regarding "calculation" (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth:
this is the eighth section, the Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics.
The distinctions among these characteristics arise from the possession of six causes.
First, number.
Second, following;
third, tranquility;
fourth, insight.
The five turnings and the six purifications.
"Counting" refers to binding the mind.
Taking the inhalation and exhalation as the object,
one counts from one to ten;
herein there are three faults.
First, the error of diminishing the number: taking one to be two.
Second, the error of increasing the number:
taking two to be one.
Third is the fault of confusion:
taking what is entering to be exiting,
and taking what is exiting to be entering.
To be free from these three faults is called correct counting;
any confusion in between constitutes an error.
Furthermore, one should count them sequentially from one,
beginning again from the start once the end is reached,
until meditative concentration is attained. "Following" means binding the mind [to the object].
Taking the inhalation and exhalation as the object,
one does not apply effort,
but follows the breath as it moves.
"Stopping" (śamatha) refers to binding the mindfulness so that it dwells solely at the tip of the nose or upon the toes.
In whatever place one finds pleasure,
one settles the mind there;
"contemplation" refers to observing this wind of the breath.
Having already observed both the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) that coexist with the breath,
as well as the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) that abide in dependence upon that matter.
It takes the observation of the five aggregates as its object;
"transformation" refers to the shifting and turning [of consciousness].
The awareness of the winds of the breath shifts,
continuing up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
"Purity" refers to progressive advancement.
From entering the stage of the path of seeing up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*),
these are included in order to encompass the six aspects.
A verse says: One should know that mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) has six distinct characteristics: namely, counting, following, stopping, contemplating, turning away, and purification.
From this, secondly, the distinctions of the breath are explained.
The treatise says:
How should the distinctions among the characteristics of the breaths be understood?
The verse states:
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body; they proceed according to two distinctions:
they are mental factors (caitta), not appropriated (anupātta), are outflowing (naiṣyandika), and do not have a lower [level] as their object. Commentary:
This consists of six sections.
Regarding the entry and exit of breath following the body:
this is the first section, based on the door of the body.
This means that the breath follows the body,
because the breath is comprised as a part of the body. Regarding "proceeding according to the two distinctions," this refers next to the second basis,
which is the gateway of the breath.
Body and mind are called the "two.
Breath functions in dependence upon body and mind.
It requires the presence of four conditions.
The breath can only turn when it has been exhaled.
The levels upon which a single breath depends are the desire realm and the first, second, and third dhyānas.
It is called the "ground of cessation.
The two pathways for wind are the mouth and the nose.
Third, the opening of the pores.
Fourth, the stage of inhalation and exhalation, wherein coarse mental activity manifests. The first three are termed distinctions of the body.
The last one is called "differentiation of mind.
When born in the formless realm,
all four conditions are absent.
Whether it be the kalala, the arbuda,
or the peśī.
In the fourth dhyāna,
there are only the coarse mind and the stage of breath;
it lacks the other two conditions.
Furthermore, when one is in the desire realm or in the first, second, or third dhyānas,
or when entering the two mindless absorptions,
there are only three conditions.
First, the absence of coarse mind; second, if one enters the fourth dhyāna while remaining in the desire realm or similar states,
there are only two conditions.
The coarse mind is absent and the pores open because the fourth dhyāna is extremely pure and thick;
it draws forth those primary elements (mahābhūta).
It pervades the entire body,
yet the pores do not open. However, if the body is born in the fourth dhyāna,
there is a passage for wind.
This refers to the mouth and nose.
It also includes the possibility of coarse mental states,
namely the arising of the deportment of lower stages.
This refers to the fruition-mind (*abhiṣamaya-citta*).
In the stages above this, two of the remaining conditions are lacking.
Because the breath does not circulate if even one of these conditions is lacking,
the treatise states:
This refers to that upon which the breath within the body depends.
There are various pores and cavities; "pores" (kō) are the channels through which wind passes, while "cavities" (kei) are the openings of the hair follicles.
The stage of inhalation and exhalation:
the coarse mind manifests; this is the fourth object of focus.
At that time, the breath—
Because it is only then that [the mind] can be turned;
this occurs upon emerging from the fourth dhyāna and so forth,
as well as at the time of initial birth.
"Breathing enters first" means that previously there was no breath.
This occurs when entering the fourth dhyāna and so forth,
as well as at the time of death.
Regarding the phrase "the last exhalation of the breath has newly ceased, thus it belongs to the category of sentient beings":
this refers to the third basis, the gate of sentient beings;
the breath is subsumed within the category of sentient beings.
Because it is a portion of the body,
it is not appropriated;
this is the fourth gate concerning non-appropriation.
Breath is not appropriated because it does not combine with the sense faculties. As for "outflow" (niṣyanda): [it refers to that which arises from a similar cause].
The fifth section on the five categories:
Respiration is of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*),
because it is produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Regarding that which does not take a lower stage as its object:
the sixth gate of mindfulness of breathing has as its object only the mind of one's own or a higher stage.
A mind of a lower stage does not take the breath of a higher stage as its object;
for example, when one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a mind of the desire realm.
This refers to the mind of its own stage.
When the minds of the first, second, or third dhyānas arise and take the breaths of the desire realm as their object:
This is the mind of the higher stages.
If it is the breath of the first dhyāna,
it takes only three stages as its object.
The breath of the second dhyāna pervades two stages as its object.
The breath of the third dhyāna...
It takes only its own level as an object;
for if one is born into a lower level,
there is no higher cessation [to be realized].
Furthermore, when one is born in a higher plane and gives rise to a mind belonging to a lower plane,
this is not a mind that takes the breath as its object.
Therefore, the mind of a lower stage does not take the breath of a higher stage as its object;
this is like being born in the first dhyāna.
When a mind of the desire realm arises,
it is exclusively a supernormal fruit (abhijñā-phala). Now, regarding this supernormal fruit:
It takes as its object only the transformed things of the desire realm; if one is born in the two higher dhyānas and so forth,
it gives rise to minds of the first dhyāna and so forth,
including those of deportment and those of fruition.
The *airyāpathika* [mind] takes only the bodily karma of the first dhyāna as its object;
the *nairmāṇika* (result-of-fruit) mind likewise takes only the transformations of the first dhyāna as its object.
Therefore, one gives rise to a mind belonging to a lower stage.
Yet it is unable to take the breath of a higher stage as its object.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 22; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 23.

Third, this section clarifies the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). It is divided into two parts: first, the foundation of mindfulness with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*);
second, the foundation of mindfulness with general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the first, the clarification of specific characteristics, the treatise states:
Thus have been explained the two gateways for entering cultivation.
By means of these two gateways,
the mind attains concentration.
Having attained concentration of mind,
what further practice remains?
The verse says:
Having relied upon the already accomplished serenity (śamatha), one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) for the sake of insight (vipaśyanā).
One contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena according to their specific and general characteristics.
This consists of the wisdom derived from hearing and so forth; the remaining [foundations] involve mixed objects of focus.
It is said that they follow the order of their arising; there are only four because they remedy the [four] inversions.
The commentary states:
Based on having already cultivated and perfected *śamatha*, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as the cultivation of *vipaśyanā*.
Based on the two preceding gates,
one has already cultivated and accomplished *śamatha*,
which in Sanskrit is called *śamatha*.
This is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). Next, one should practice the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) through *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Regarding *vipaśyanā*, in the Sanskrit language it is called *vipaśyanā*.
This is precisely wisdom (*prajñā*).
To observe the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the explanation.
Or, [one observes] by way of specific characteristics.
Alternatively, one contemplates the body,
feelings, mind, and phenomena individually by way of their common characteristics; that is, the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena each have their own distinct intrinsic nature.
This is termed "specific characteristic.
The primary elements and the derived matter constitute the intrinsic nature of the body.
Feeling is the nature of feeling;
mind is the nature of mind.
Apart from these three, there is nothing else.
All remaining phenomena are termed the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). All conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are characterized by impermanence;
this is the path to the truth of suffering.
All that is with outflows (sāsrava) is of the nature of suffering; it is exclusively the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Origin [of Suffering].
And so too are all phenomena (dharmas).
Emptiness (śūnyatā) is not-self by nature; it pervades the four noble truths as well as space (ākāśa) and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
It is not impermanent and so forth;
rather, it is common to all phenomena.
This is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the distinct contemplation of the common characteristic:
it refers, for instance, to contemplating that one's own body and other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) share the same characteristic of impermanence.
Together with other contaminated phenomena,
it shares the same characteristic of suffering;
[it is] with respect to all phenomena.
They share the same characteristics of emptiness and non-self;
the same applies to feeling and the other aggregates. Question: How is it known that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have been perfected?
Answer: When one contemplates the body down to a single atom and a single moment.
This is called the fulfillment of the application of mindfulness to the body;
one then contemplates feelings, the mind,
and phenomena until reaching a single moment.
They are called "fulfilled" by way of sensation and so forth; because they are non-material,
there is not even a single atom whose intrinsic nature consists of hearing and so forth, or which has wisdom as its object, or which is mixed with other [factors].
This explains their essential nature.
There are three types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): first, the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*).
It has wisdom as its essence;
this [wisdom] encompasses the three types of wisdom. As for the term "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) being applied to wisdom:
That is to say, by the power of mindfulness,
one causes wisdom to abide upon its object;
or else, by the power of wisdom.
Because it causes mindfulness to abide upon its object,
it is called "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna). Second is the mixed application of mindfulness,
which refers to wisdom together with its associated mental factors.
Furthermore, all four possess the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as their essence;
because they are mutually intermingled, they are called "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). Third, the foundations of mindfulness with respect to objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).
That is to say: body,
sensation,
mind, and phenomena.
This is the essence,
for it is the objective referent of the foundations of mindfulness; among these three,
they are intermingled and capable of severing the afflictions.
Because it is comprised within wisdom,
its intrinsic nature cannot sever the afflictions;
this is because it is excessively diminished.
Now, the severing of afflictions must necessarily involve wisdom, its concomitant factors, and its intrinsic nature,
which is exclusively wisdom itself.
Therefore, it is excessively deficient;
the application of mindfulness as its object of focus cannot sever the afflictions.
Because it increases excessively;
because it is not co-existent;
it is excessive. This is the foundation of mindfulness with respect to objects.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
first, those that take one's own continuum as their object;
second, those that take another's continuum as their object.
Third, regarding the bodies of one's own continuum, another's continuum,
and both together: for each of these, there are three types of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Because the continuities of self and others differ, there are three each for body,
sensation, mind, and phenomena;
these together constitute twelve.
Regarding the statement "the sequence follows their arising," this refers to the sequence in which the four foundations of mindfulness arise one after another.
That is to say, the body is the coarsest;
next, sensation is coarse;
and next, the mind is coarse.
Dharma is the most subtle,
because it encompasses nirvāṇa; as for those objects that are coarse,
they should be contemplated first.
Therefore, the mindfulness of the body arises first.
Furthermore, the treatise says:
Alternatively, because various forms of sensual desire operate with respect to the body,
there are four foundations of mindfulness.
Contemplation of the body comes first;
yet one becomes attached to the body because of delighting in feelings.
One takes delight in sensation because the mind is not disciplined;
the mind is not disciplined.
Because the afflictions have not been abandoned,
and because the factors include the afflictions,
this is the fourth category of factors.
Therefore, one contemplates sensation and the others in this sequential order;
because they counteract the perversions, there are only four.
Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness:
one contemplates the body as impure and contemplates feelings as suffering.
One contemplates the mind as impermanent and contemplates phenomena as selfless,
in order to remedy those four inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, only four are established. The treatise states:
"Among these four, three are called 'non-mixed objects' (*amiśrālambana*)."
The fourth object of focus encompasses both the mixed and the unmixed;
it is when one contemplates only phenomena (dharma).
This is called "non-mixed object.
It refers to [the mind] being directed toward two, three, or four [of the bases], such as the body and so forth.
To observe them collectively is called "contemplating the manifold" (sambhinna-ālambana).
The commentary explains:
Regarding the four [objects] beginning with the body,
they may be taken as objects either by combining them two by two or three by three.
Alternatively, there are four [types] that take the aggregate as their object; because they involve a mixture of the body and so forth,
they are called "mixed objects."
Secondly, from this point, the general characteristics of objects of cognition are clarified.
The treatise states:
Having thus thoroughly cultivated the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that takes as its object a mixture of the body and so forth,
what is to be cultivated next?
The verse says:
Abiding in that, one dwells in the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas;
contemplating all four objects collectively, one cultivates the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The commentary states:
"Those who dwell there" refers to those practitioners of contemplation.
This is the application of mindfulness through the synthesis of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
One contemplates the four objects of focus— the body and so forth— collectively,
cultivating the four aspects of practice.
That is to say, regarding impermanence and so forth— the previously mentioned distinct characteristics of the states—
there are those with mixed objects of focus,
which may involve two, three, or four; this present [section] concerns those with mixed objects of focus.
The mindfulness foundations of general characteristics take four objects collectively;
because they differ from the preceding ones, they are called the mindfulness foundations of general characteristics.
This is exclusively the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) as a composite and general category.
Following this, the fourth [section] clarifies the four roots of goodness, beginning with "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
Within this, there are five sections:
first, the explanation of the contemplative practice of the roots of goodness;
second, the analysis by way of various categories.
1. The excellence of the roots of goodness of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
2. The transformation of the faculties (*indriya*) among the three vehicles.
3. The distance and proximity of the fruits of cultivation.
Furthermore, regarding the first point, clarifying the practitioner of contemplation,
the treatise states:
"Having cultivated this contemplation..."
What roots of goodness arise from this?
The verse says:
From this, the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) arises, fully contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
Cultivating the sixteen aspects, the subsequent arising of the Summit is likewise.
These two roots of goodness both begin with the Dharma [hearing] and end with the four [applications of mindfulness];
the Patience stage consists solely of mindfulness of dharmas. The lower and middle grades are the same as the Summit.
The highest [level] contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm;
a single moment of one type is likewise the Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgradharma). All are wisdom, excluding acquisition (prāpti). Commentary:
Regarding "from this, the dharma of heat arises":
once the general mindfulness-establishment has been accomplished from this,
the dharma of heat subsequently arises.
This dharma is designated as the "dharma of warmth" (uṣmagata) because it is like warmth;
the noble path is like fire,
for it is able to burn away the fuel of the afflictions.
Because it is a precursor to the Noble Fire,
it is called "Heat" (ūṣmagata). This clarifies the stage of Heat for one who possesses the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths through the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Because this root of goodness of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) persists for a long duration,
it is able to fully contemplate the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, one is able to fully cultivate the sixteen aspects and contemplate the Noble Truth of Suffering by cultivating its four aspects:
impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; and contemplate the Noble Truth of Origination.
One cultivates the four aspects of the noble truth of suffering: cause, origin, arising, and condition. One contemplates the noble truth of cessation through the four aspects:
cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation. One contemplates the noble truth of the path [through the four aspects].
One cultivates the four aspects:
the path, as it is, and emergence.
The meaning of these aspects will be explained later. Next, "the arising of the summit is likewise" means that one cultivates the wholesome root of *ūṣmagata* (heat).
There are inferior, middling, and superior [roots];
at the time of reaching fulfillment,
roots of goodness arise.
It is called the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*);
it likewise contemplates the four truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
As in the preceding case of the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), it is likewise stated here.
These are the two roots of goodness: Heat and Peak (*mūrdhan*).
These are all termed "shakable wholesome" (*cala-kuśala*), because they are subject to regression and instability.
Among the shakable wholesome roots:
The "Summit" (mūrdhan) is the most excellent, like the crown of a person's head;
therefore, it is called the "Dharma of the Summit. Furthermore, this refers to the stage of Patience (kṣānti).
This refers to advancing through the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and retreating from this "Summit" (mūrdhan);
it exists at the juncture between these two states of progress and retreat.
It is like a mountain peak;
therefore, it is called a "peak" (*mūrdhan*). Thus, regarding these two roots of goodness—both of which have four factors as their subsequent [result] and one factor as their initial [cause]:
these are the two roots of goodness known as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "peak."

At the initial stage of establishing the foundation, all are applications of mindfulness through the Dharma; at the subsequent stage of further progress, [they become applications of mindfulness through the body].
These pertain to the four foundations of mindfulness;
those who first establish themselves therein are said to be at the stages of "Heat" and "Summits."
By means of the sixteen aspects,
one first traverses the path of the Four Noble Truths;
this is called the initial placement of the feet.
This refers to its initial arising.
That is to say, within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), there is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Because the stages of Heat and Peak are conducive to the Path of Seeing,
they are established first.
It is only the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), because at the time of subsequent advancement,
there is a slight degree of leisure.
Therefore, one attains the universal cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness. Next, regarding "patience being exclusively the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena":
from the roots of goodness of the "summit" stage, further roots of goodness arise.
It is called the stage of patience (*kṣānti-dharma*),
because it is the most excellent for its ability to accept and affirm the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, because there is no regression,
it is called the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Patience is the initial firm establishment [of the mind].
And as for the subsequent advancement,
it consists solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), because it is proximate to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Therefore, both the beginning and the end consist of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). As for the verse stating that the lower and middle grades are the same as the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*):
this refers to the roots of goodness of this "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
There are inferior, middling, and superior grades.
The two lower grades are the same as the preceding stage of the crown (mūrdhan).
One fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths by cultivating the sixteen aspects.
As for the aforementioned [attainment] which contemplates only the single aspect of suffering within the desire realm for a single moment:
At the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm;
it is designated as "superior patience" because it consists of a single aspect and a single moment of mind.
Now, the inferior, middling, and superior levels of the stage of patience will be briefly explained.
If it is the inferior grade of patience,
one contemplates the four truths in their entirety and cultivates the sixteen aspects.
In the stage of medium-grade patience,
there is a reduction of objects and a reduction of modes of activity. The eight truths of the upper and lower realms are designated as "objects."
By way of the objects of focus, there are sixteen aspects for the Four Truths of the higher realms,
and [the same] for the Four Truths of the desire realm.
There are sixteen aspects;
when taken together, they constitute thirty-two aspects,
which are termed "aspects" (*ākāra*).
Because they are able to take formations as objects,
one should know that there are seven cycles of reducing the object and twenty-four cycles of reducing the formation.
That is to say, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm by means of four aspects;
and so on, up to contemplating it by means of four aspects.
One contemplates the path of the desire realm;
subsequently, one contemplates the paths of the higher realms by means of three modes of practice.
Reducing by one row is called one cycle.
Furthermore, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm using four rows.
In this manner, proceeding until later, one contemplates the paths of the higher realms with two aspects,
thereby reducing the remaining two aspects.
This is the second cycle. Furthermore, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm by means of four aspects;
in this manner, continuing up until contemplating it by means of a single aspect.
Contemplating the paths of the higher realms, one diminishes the remaining three modes of conduct;
this is the third cycle. Furthermore, by means of the four modes of conduct...
One contemplates the suffering of the desire realm;
in this manner, one proceeds until contemplating the path of the desire realm by means of its four aspects.
Not observing the paths of the higher realms is called "diminishing the object.
At the time of diminishing the object:
Although it also involves the reduction of application,
because it is subsumed under the reduction of objects,
it is not called "reduction of application."
This is the fourth cycle.
This fourth cycle is precisely one cycle that reduces the objects of focus (*ālambana*). For example, it is like reducing the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) of the higher realms.
The same applies to the remaining seven aspects of the truths;
they function likewise,
but only with respect to their objects.
The suffering of desire is not reduced;
the remaining seven truths are reduced.
This is called the "sevenfold reduction of objects. To summarize:
In the eight truths of the upper and lower realms,
three aspects are each reduced;
that is to say, at the bottom of the suffering of the desire realm.
Because one aspect remains,
it does not decrease;
as for the remaining seven truths, they are likewise.
Because the remaining one mode of activity (ākāra) is reduced along with its object (ālambana),
it is stated as only three.
Three times eight is twenty-four;
this is called the "twenty-four cycles of diminished practice.
To speak according to the actual principle:
The thirty-first is the reduction of practice (*hāna-prayoga*),
which refers to the remaining seven practices because they involve the reduction of objects (*ālambana*).
Therefore, it is said there are only twenty-four.
Within the reduction of practices,
one practice is reduced first.
This is called the beginning of medium patience.
In this manner, it continues until the time when one eliminates the two lower aspects of the suffering of the desire realm.
There are only two modes of practice and two moments of mind.
Contemplating the suffering of the desire realm is called the fulfillment of medium patience; there is only one mode of practice and one moment of mind.
Contemplating the suffering of the desire realm is called "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*); within this stage of patience,
it is before the path has been diminished.
Although the aspects of the practice have been reduced,
because one still contemplates the Path,
one is able to fully cultivate all four types of truths.
The verse states that "medium patience is the same as the Peak stage" (*mūrdhan*) regarding the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths;
this is said with reference to this point. Upon reaching the fulfillment of medium patience, one contemplates only a single truth.
It does not possess all four [aspects]. Furthermore, within that stage of patience (*kṣānti*),
while the path has not yet been diminished,
one cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
This term "cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers merely to the attainment of practice; although it arises as a single [moment], [it is so designated].
It is able to give rise to attainment;
because one cultivates those sixteen aspects (ākāra) under the four truths in the future,
it is said that "one cultivates" them.
The verse states that "middle patience" (*madhyā kṣānti*) is the same as the previous summit stage (*mūrdhan*) in cultivating the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
This refers to middle patience when it has not yet diminished the path (*mārga*). As for this middle patience:
When the Truth of the Path is being abandoned, one cultivates only twelve aspects, not sixteen aspects.
Since that path has been diminished,
the mind has no longing for it;
therefore, that path is inferior.
The four aspects are likewise cultivated through the attainment of non-arising. By this principle.
When the truth of cessation is being reduced, one cultivates only eight aspects;
that is, because one does not cultivate the four aspects each belonging to the truths of cessation and the path. When the truth of origination is being reduced...
One cultivates only four aspects;
that is, one cultivates only the four lower aspects of suffering. Therefore, within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), there is cultivation of sixteen or twelve aspects.
Regarding the eight aspects of the four truths: at the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
one also cultivates these four aspects,
yet gives rise to only a single aspect within a single momentary mind.
Because one contemplates suffering, one is able to give rise to attainment;
this refers to cultivating the four aspects of that [contemplation] regarding suffering.
Question: Regarding the stage of Superior Patience (adhimātra-kṣānti):
Regarding the reduction of those three practices:
for what reason does one cultivate those very practices that have been reduced?
Answer: Although those practices are reduced, [one still cultivates them].
Because they do not diminish the Truths,
a mind of aspiration and admiration arises; thus,
one is able to cultivate the aspects of those practices that are to be diminished.
Regarding the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) therein,
the practices to be diminished should be understood according to this principle.
Among the thirty-two modes of practice,
only one mode— the suffering of the desire realm— is retained,
as it is intended for entry into the path of seeing.
They must be retained.
The remaining thirty-one follow the order of their names.
Proceeding from the end toward the beginning,
eliminate them gradually; since the conditions are eliminated starting from the end, [the mind becomes purified].
The practice is also reduced from the end. Question: Regarding the single practice following "suffering" (duḥkha), which practice is retained?
Answer: For a person who has entered the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there are two practices.
The first is those of sharp faculties, namely those whose conduct is based on views. There are two types of those whose conduct is based on views:
those who are attached to a self, and...
Those who dwell in the practice of non-self are attached to "mine";

those who are thus attached immediately dwell in the practice of emptiness. Second, there are those of dull faculties; those of dull faculties are also of two types: those for whom the conceit of self is predominant.
One should apply the contemplation of impermanence;
for those in whom laziness increases, one should instead apply the contemplation of suffering. Furthermore, according to the master Guṇaprabha of the Western Tradition:
Regarding the practice of the "diminution of understanding":
one eliminates the four aspects of the suffering of desire starting from the last.
Just as impermanence remains,
those who enter the path of seeing first diminish the notion of non-self.
Next, one reduces the perception of space;
afterwards, one reduces the perception of suffering. If one persists in ascetic practices while entering the path of seeing, [one will not attain it].
First eliminate "not-self," next eliminate "emptiness," and finally eliminate "impermanence. If one leaves emptiness remaining:
For one who enters the path of vision,
first the notion of "non-self" is diminished,
and next, suffering is diminished.
Subsequently, one diminishes impermanence; if it remains, one considers it non-self.
For those who enter the path of vision, they first diminish emptiness.
Next, one diminishes suffering;
subsequently, one diminishes impermanence.
One diminishes the truth of suffering regarding desire.
Since the four aspects of the first truth are thus established, the same applies to the four aspects of the remaining seven truths;
that is, for the other seven truths.
Each has four aspects;
these are associated with the four aspects of the suffering of desire in the order they are named.
It is appropriate to explain it by way of its reduction; for instance,
consider one who enters the path of vision regarding impermanence.
Regarding the paths of the higher realms,
first one reduces emergence,
and next one reduces practice.
Next, one eliminates the aspect of suffering, and finally eliminates the aspect of the path,
because the path is subject to impermanence.
This refers to the subsequent reduction.
If one enters the path of vision (darśanamārga) by means of ascetic practices (duṣkaracaryā), [then...]
Regarding the paths of the higher realms,
first one eliminates the [defilements] of emergence, and subsequently eliminates those of practice.
Next is the reduction of the path.
As for the subsequent reduction, it is because "suchness" (tathatā) is subsumed under suffering; therefore, it is reduced last.
This applies if one proceeds by way of emptiness.
One who has entered the path of seeing first eliminates the [afflictions] of the higher realms through the path of emergence.
Next, the aspects are reduced;
next, the paths are reduced;
finally, the applications are reduced.
Because formations are subsumed under emptiness,
formations subsequently diminish. If one enters the path of vision by means of "non-self," [the same applies].
Regarding the paths of the higher realms,
first one reduces the practice,
and subsequently one reduces the mode.
Next, the path is eliminated;
finally, emergence is eliminated.
Because emergence belongs to the category of non-self, it is eliminated last. The remaining six truths are then eliminated.
Each has four aspects; these are explained according to what was stated previously.
This is for the purpose of summarizing the preceding meaning.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states in summary:
"That is to say, the yoga practitioner,
with respect to the form and formless [realms]..."

Regarding the antidote path and so forth, among the remaining seven truths, each noble truth has thirty-two aspects; the fact that the objects of focus for the latter seven truths gradually decrease and are abbreviated clarifies the meaning of "diminution" (*hāna*), until there remains only two moments of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Contemplating the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm—
up to this point— it is called the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*).
Immediately following this stage,
one gives rise to superior roots of goodness,
consisting of a single practice for a single moment.
This is called "superior patience.
Because these roots of goodness arise without continuity, it is explained thus.
There is only a single thought-moment;
therefore, there is no continuity.
The above is from the treatise.
The meaning is as previously explained. Regarding "the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is likewise":
immediately following the highest degree of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), the supreme mundane dharma arises without interval.
This Supreme Mundane Dharma takes only the suffering of the desire realm as its object;
it consists of only a single mode of activity and lasts for only a single moment of mind.
It is the same as the aforementioned "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti); therefore, it is said to be likewise.
This is because it is contaminated (sāsrava).
It is called "the world," because it is the most supreme among all worlds.
It is called the foremost;
it is the foremost in this world.
It possesses the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
Because it arises by departing from its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and induces the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
it is called "supreme" (*agra*). All are wisdom (*prajñā*), excluding the five [factors] such as acquisition (*prāpti*).
Regarding their essential nature: because these four foundations of mindfulness—such as heat and the others—are by nature wisdom, they all have wisdom as their essence.
If one includes their associated factors, [they consist of the five aggregates].
All these possess the nature of the five aggregates; that which includes the fixed and shared precepts is called the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
The remaining four [aggregates] may be understood accordingly. These four, beginning with "heat" (uṣmagata), are as follows.
There is an acquisition that acquires [the roots of goodness]; it is the acquisition within the substance of the auxiliary associates,
not the substance of the four roots of goodness such as "heat" (uṣmagata) and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that after emerging from the path of seeing, there is a subsequently attained cognition (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that excludes [the object].
Having attained this "warmth" and so forth, one attains that which is superior to warmth and so forth;
the appearance of the Noble One manifests.
If these levels of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth have "attainment" (*prāpti*) as their essence,
how could the wholesome roots of heat and so forth ever manifest again in an Arya?
This refers to the four stages, such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth,
which are the preparatory practices for the Noble Path;
once the fruit of the Noble [Path] has been attained.
Because it is logically inconsistent for them to arise [as such],
the essence of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and the other stages is not "attainment" (prāpti).
This is the second point.
Analysis by way of various categories.
The treatise states:
"The essential characteristics of the roots of goodness that have been produced have already been explained."
Now, the meaning of their distinctions should be clarified.
The verse says:
These factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—all four—are produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
In the sixth stage, two or seven [are acquired]; based on a body of the desire realm, nine;
for women and men, three and two respectively are acquired. In the fourth [stage], it is the same for women.
The noble ones lose them by losing their stage; ordinary beings lose them by death.
The first two are also abandoned through falling away; based on the fundamental [dhyāna], one must see the truths.
What is abandoned has not been previously attained. Regarding the nature of these two abandonments as non-possession (*aprāpti*), the commentary states:
The first phrase indicates the title;
the second phrase clarifies the cultivation and inclusion;
the third phrase clarifies the basis.
The fourth line clarifies the basis of the body;
the fifth and sixth lines clarify that both males and females obtain the two [precepts];
and the seventh, eighth, and ninth lines clarify the characteristics of relinquishment.
The tenth phrase clarifies the duration [of attainment];
the eleventh phrase clarifies that it is not prior;
the twelfth phrase clarifies the essence of relinquishment. These are the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
This is the summary.

These four, beginning with "Heat" (ūṣmagata), are called the "Aids to Penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya). [They lead to] the paths of seeing (darśana-mārga), cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), and no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-mārga).
The three types of noble paths are all termed "decisive analysis" (nirṇaya).
"Decisive" (ni) means "to sever" (chid).
Because it is able to sever doubt.
"Discernment" (vicaya) means analytical discernment;
that is, because it is able to differentiate the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. Thus, the Path of Seeing is called the Stage of Decisive Discernment (nirvedha-bhāgīya).
This is because they constitute a portion of the *viniścaya* (ascertainment).
These four— Heat and so forth—
induce the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

That which is able to conform to those [noble paths] is called the "Aids to Penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya). Regarding the statement that "all four are produced by cultivation": these four, beginning with Heat (uṣmagata), are all accomplished through meditative cultivation.

Because it relies on the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), it is subsumed under that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*). Regarding the "six stages," this refers to the classification according to the stages upon which they rely.
The four wholesome states, beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata),
universally rely upon six stages; namely,
the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the four dhyānas.
It does not exist within the desire realm because that is not a stage of meditative concentration;
it also does not exist in the formless realm.
This refers to the four [stages] beginning with "heat" (ūṣmagata),
which are the attendants of the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Since there is no path of seeing in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
the stages such as "heat" do not exist there either.
"Two or seven": "two" refers to *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*;
the word "or" indicates the teaching of the master Subhūtiśrī.
That [text] states that the levels of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan) apply generally to all seven stages;
regarding the first six stages:
Furthermore, regarding the desire realm:
"based on the body of the desire realm" refers to the door of the body.
These four stages, beginning with "heat" (uṣmagata),
arise only within the bodies of humans and devas in the desire realm,
excluding those of Uttarakuru.
It arises among the three continents of the human realm and the six heavens of the desire realm;
it originates from bodies in these nine locations.
Only those who rely on the desire realm can develop loathing for suffering; thus, the first three roots of goodness initially arise in the three continents.
In subsequent births within the six heavens,
the fourth root of goodness likewise continues to manifest before one.
The heavens also first arise;
that is to say, the fourth dhyāna,
because it consists of only a single moment of thought.
Those who have gone to the heavenly realms all attain the first [attainment];
the three types of women and men attain two.
These four roots of goodness depend exclusively upon males and females,
and not upon those who are *śaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and so forth.
Regarding the first three roots of goodness,
both men and women attain two.
As for the case where a man attains two:
That is to say, a male attains the wholesome roots of a male as well as those of a female;
a female likewise attains both.
This means that a woman attains the roots of goodness of a woman and attains the roots of goodness of a man; therefore,
it is called "attaining both."
This is because, through the three stages beginning with *ūṣmagata*,
one whose male appearance transforms into female,
or one whose female appearance transforms into male, [is established].
Regarding the three [levels] beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata), both women and men attain two;
for the fourth [level], it is the same for women as well.
Regarding the fourth root of goodness,
women attain two types,
as previously described for *uṣmagata* and the others.
Thus, the same applies to speech:
it means that a woman attains the wholesome roots of a woman and also attains the wholesome roots of a man.
Because a woman’s form is transformed into that of a man,
if it is the fourth root of goodness,
a man obtains only one.
This means that a male obtains only the roots of goodness of a male body and does not obtain those of a female body,
because he has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body.
That "the noble ones [lose them] by losing their stage" and "ordinary beings [lose them] by the end of life" clarifies the meaning of relinquishment.
This refers to the noble ones relinquishing the four roots of goodness, such as *ūṣmagata* and the others.
It is abandoned through the loss of the stage;
that is to say, one abandons these roots of goodness based on whichever stage they were acquired.
If one migrates to a higher stage,
this stage is then lost; at the time of losing this stage, [the corresponding attainment is relinquished].
Only when the roots of goodness are relinquished will one die in this stage and be reborn again in this stage.
Because they do not lose the stage [of the path], they do not relinquish the levels of Heat and so forth;
whereas an ordinary person relinquishes them solely through death.
For ordinary beings,
whether [the roots] are lost or not lost depends solely upon the time of death.
One must necessarily abandon "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and the other stages;
that is to say, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack the provisions for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
they abandon them at the end of life.
Regarding "the first two are also abandoned through falling away":
this means that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), at the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*,
also abandon them through falling away, as they are not noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary beings also do not undergo retrogression or relinquishment regarding the stages of Patience and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas;
as long as they rely on these, they will inevitably perceive the Truths.
If ordinary beings,
relying on the four fundamental dhyānas,
give rise to the stages of "heat" and so forth.
In this life, he will certainly enter the path of vision and develop a mind of revulsion toward birth and death.
Because it is extremely intense.
"Having abandoned, one obtains what was not previously possessed" means that after having abandoned [the stages of] heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth.

If one later regains [the roots of goodness] through renewed cultivation, what is obtained must necessarily not be that which was previously abandoned; rather, only that which was previously unobtained is obtained. This is because [the roots of goodness such as] *uṣmagata* and so forth are wholesome.
Because it has not been previously cultivated to maturity,
it must be attained through extensive preparatory application before it can be cultivated.
Therefore, that which is attained for the first time is not something previously abandoned; this refers, for instance,
to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth.
Because one has passed through births,
[the roots] are abandoned; however, upon encountering a Dharma teacher who clearly explains the stages,
one then gives rise to the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) and so forth.
If one does not encounter [the conditions] again, one attains it once more from the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).
Regarding the two types of non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of the nature of equanimity (*upekṣā*):
The two types of relinquishment— loss and regression—
have non-possession as their essence, because they consist in the abandonment [of attainment].
From this second [section] onward,
the excellence of the roots of goodness is clarified.
The treatise states:
What are the benefits of attaining these roots of goodness?
The verse says:
The "Heat" stage necessarily leads to Nirvana; the "Summit" stage never severs the roots of goodness;
the "Patience" stage does not fall into the evil destinies; and the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" enters into the state free from birth.
The commentary says:
Although one may fall back from the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), lose their roots of goodness,
commit an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma),
or fall into the three evil destinies;
And because there will be no prolonged wandering [in saṃsāra],
one will certainly reach nirvāṇa. This is because if one attains the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan),...
Although there may be regression and so forth,
one will certainly not sever the roots of goodness if one attains the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Although they relinquish it at the end of life,
there is no regression,
and they do not fall into the evil destinies.
If one is at the stage of inferior patience,
one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the two evil destinies.
If one reaches the stage of supreme patience (adhimātra-kṣānti), one will not be reborn among those born from eggs or moisture,
nor among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
Uttarakuru, Mahābrahmā’s abode, and the Śaṇḍhas.
Pandaakas, those with dual sexual organs,
and those in their eighth existence, and so forth.
Regarding the afflictions abandoned by seeing:
within this place of birth, among those afflictions present in the body,
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Having reached the stage of supreme patience,
one will necessarily enter the path of vision and attain the fruit of an Arya.
Therefore, regarding the egg-born and other [modes of birth],
one attains non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) if the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-kleśa) [are eliminated].
Although it has not yet been severed,
because it will certainly not arise again,
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Although the Supreme Mundane Dharmas belong to ordinary beings,
they are capable of giving rise to the Uninterrupted Path.
One enters the state of correct determination and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*). "Correct determination and departure from birth" is a name for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
From this fourth [section], the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) of the three vehicles is elucidated.
The treatise states:
These four roots of goodness each have three grades,
due to the distinctions in lineage among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.
Whichever lineage [a person] may follow,
once roots of goodness have already arisen,
can they be shifted or redirected toward another vehicle?
The verse says:
Those of the śrāvaka lineage may transform; two [types] attain Buddhahood, while the third remains otherwise.
The rhinoceros-like buddhas do not transform, because they attain awakening in a single sitting.
The commentary states:
Regarding the lineage of the śrāvakas,
[this applies] to the two stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
They may still turn toward Buddhahood; however,
if they attain the stage of patience (kṣānti),
there is no principle for them to achieve Buddhahood.
When a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings,
they must go to the evil realms;
yet through patience, they transcend those evil realms.
Therefore, they do not attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the phrase "the three remaining," "remaining" refers to the Pratyekabuddhas.
Because they are outside of the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna),
they are called "the rest" (śeṣa).
This refers to those of the śrāvaka lineage (gotra).
The three stages of Heat, Peak,
and Patience are called "the remaining three" because they can still be transformed into the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.
The rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha and the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
[attain] the stages of "heat" and so forth.
Their nature is necessarily without transition;
that is to say, these two types of noble ones rely upon the fourth dhyāna.
Since awakening is achieved in a single sitting,
there is no possibility of turning back.
In Sanskrit, this is called *bodhi*.
This is translated as "awakening" (bodhi).
The bodhi of the three vehicles all take the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising as their essence.
Regarding the phrase "a single seat":
it begins from the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and ends with the attainment of *bodhi* (Enlightenment).
Without rising from his seat,
he entered the fourth dhyāna,
which is unshakable.
Because it is an extremely intense samādhi,
it is capable of serving as the basis for both the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas] and the Buddhas.
From this, the fifth [section] clarifies the duration and proximity of attaining the fruit.
The treatise states:

Is it possible that one who begins to practice preparatory application (*prayoga*) in this very life will, in that same life, give rise to the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)? No; why is this so?
The verse says:
The preceding *mokṣabhāgīya* (aids to liberation) leads to liberation within three lifetimes at most;
it is accomplished through hearing and reflection, and constitutes the three types of karma. It is planted by humans in the three continents.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that arise in this life,
