they must necessarily have been preceded by the arising of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in a previous life.
Those who first cultivate the factors conducive to liberation attain liberation at the utmost speed within three lifetimes;
that is to say, in the first life they give rise to the factors conducive to liberation.
In the second life, one gives rise to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and only in the third life does one enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*),
up until the attainment of arhatship; this is the swiftest possible case for a śrāvaka.
The maximum duration for a Pratyekabuddha is sixty kalpas;
the minimum duration for a Pratyekabuddha is three births.
The four types of birth take at most one hundred kalpas [to reach] the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
These are produced through hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*), as they exist only on the level of the distracted (*vikṣipta-bhūmi*).
Taking the three types of action as its substance, it plants the factors conducive to liberation;
this occurs only among humans in the three continents,
and not in the three miserable realms.
Because they lack prajñā,
the various devas do not exist either;
because they lack revulsion toward suffering.

As for why it does not exist in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), it is because of their lack of a sense of weariness [with suffering] and their [lack of] *prajñā*. Furthermore, they give but a single meal.
Maintaining even a single precept and so forth,
they deeply delight in liberation and turn their aspiration toward seeking bodhi.
Sustained by the power of aspiration,
this is termed "planting the factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
This concludes the third major section from here.
Distinguishing individuals by way of the three paths,
there are three parts therein.
First, the establishment of the three paths is explained.
Second, the seven types of noble persons (āryapudgala) are clarified;
third, the completion of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is clarified, established by way of the three paths.
The middle two [sections] consist of:
first, an explanation in terms of the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*);
second, an explanation in terms of the cultivation of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Regarding the explanation of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the sixteen moments of mind;
second, the establishment [of the stages] according to their positions. Regarding the explanation of the sixteen moments of mind, there are four parts.
First, a clear exposition of the sixteen moments of mind;
second, an exposition of the stages upon which the sixteen moments of mind depend;
third, an exposition of the sequence of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The fourth [section] clarifies the distinction between the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. First, regarding the sixteen moments of mind, the treatise states:
"Within this, the various paths of preparation have already been explained."
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) constitute its final limit;
it should be stated that [the Path of Seeing] proceeds from these.
Furthermore, into which realm is one reborn?
The verse says:
Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object.
The patience regarding the outflow-free dharma arises; following this patience, the dharma-knowledge arises.
Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as its object, the subsequent patience and subsequent knowledge arise.
Taking the truths of origin, cessation, and the path as their respective objects, four [moments] of each likewise arise.
These sixteen moments of mind are called the "clear realization of the noble truths" (*āryasatyābhisamaya*).
This is summarized as being of three types, namely: the vision [of the truths], the object, and the particulars. Regarding the explanation of these distinctions:
Immediately following the "supreme mundane roots of goodness" (laukikāgradharma),
one gives rise to untainted dharmas (anāsravadharma) that take as their object the Noble Truth of Suffering within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).

This is called the "receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti). Immediately following this receptivity to suffering, taking the truth of suffering in the desire realm as its object,
there subsequently arises the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).
This is called the "Dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*).

Immediately following this knowledge, there arises a "subsequent-knowledge-acceptance" (*anvaya-jñānakṣānti*) which takes as its object the Noble Truth of Suffering within the remaining two higher realms.
This is called the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*).
Immediately following this receptivity, there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that takes this same object as its domain.

This is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). Just as there are these four minds taking the truth of suffering as their object, so too [there are four] taking the truths of origin,
cessation, and the path as their objects.
Each likewise gives rise to four.
That is to say, following the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna), one takes the truth of origin (samudaya-satya) of the desire realm as its object.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the origin arises; immediately following this patience, the dharma-knowledge of the origin arises;
immediately following this knowledge, [the subsequent-knowledge of the origin arises].
Taking the truth of origin (samudaya-satya) of the upper realms as its object,
there arises the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origin (samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti). Immediately following this receptivity, [the subsequent knowledge of origin arises].
The subsequent knowledge of the origin of suffering arises;
immediately following this knowledge, one takes the truth of cessation in the desire realm as its object.
The patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of arising and ceasing;
immediately following this patience,
there arises the knowledge of the dharma of arising and ceasing.
Immediately after this knowledge,
taking the cessation of the higher realms as its object, there arises the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
Immediately after this patience,
there arises the subsequent knowledge of cessation; immediately after this knowledge, one takes the truth of the path regarding the desire realm as its object.
The patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path arises; immediately following this patience, the dharma-knowledge of the path arises;
immediately following this knowledge, [the subsequent knowledge arises].
Taking the Path Truth of the higher realms as its object,
the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñānakṣānti) arises; immediately following this receptivity, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) arises.
Therefore, regarding the Four Noble Truths,
there are four moments of mind for each,
constituting sixteen moments of mind. As for the "receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):
The dharma of suffering is the dharma of the truth of suffering.
Patience that takes the dharma of suffering as its object is called "patience with the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).
Wisdom is the fruit of patience;
it is a fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Wisdom is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
To demonstrate that this patience (*kṣānti*) is likewise exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*),
the subsequent outflow (*niṣyanda*) is cited as its distinguishing characteristic.
Therefore, patience is designated as "the wise" because it is named after its fruit,
just as a tree is called a "flower-tree" or a "fruit-tree."
It is not that they are flowers or fruits; rather, because they produce flowers and fruits,
they are called "flower-fruit trees."
Patience (*kṣānti*) is also like this.

Because it gives rise to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it is called the patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*). As for the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*): [it is the subsequent realization].
Because it takes the phenomena of suffering as its object, it is called "knowledge of the phenomena of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna).
The preceding "patience" (kṣānti) eliminates the afflictions.
The path of uninterrupted transition is so named;
the subsequent knowledge that realizes cessation is called the path of liberation.
The receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of suffering—
this object and this knowledge are similar to the preceding ones.
Therefore, the name "category" (jāti) is established.
Thus, the treatise says:
"It is the initial realization and knowledge of the true principle of all phenomena."
Therefore it is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna).
This subsequent object-knowledge is similar to the former.
Therefore, the designation "category" (jāti) is established.
Just as it is with suffering, so it is with the remaining [truths]: origin, cessation, and the path.
Each has four minds. One may understand this by reflecting upon it according to this principle.
These sixteen moments of mind are collectively termed the "clear realization of the noble truths" (āryasatyābhisamaya),
meaning that they are present before one.
Regarding the contemplation of the noble truths, there are three types.
The first is the clear realization through vision (*darśana-abhisamaya*), which consists solely of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*).
Because the truths are seen with clarity,
it is called the "clear-seeing clear-comprehension" (*darśana-abhisamaya*). Second is the "object-condition clear-comprehension" (*ālambana-abhisamaya*).
This untainted wisdom, along with the mind associated with that wisdom and its mental factors,
share a single object of cognition.
This is called the clear realization of the object-condition (ālambana-abhisamaya). It is the clear realization of the three factors,
which refers to the aforementioned association (samprayoga).

Furthermore, that which co-exists with others and shares the same activity is called the "actualization of the task" (*vastv-abhisamaya*). "Co-existing with others" refers to the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*).
Furthermore, because they are co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) with the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*),
they are called "co-existent" (*sahabhū*). Moreover, the treatise clarifies the attainment of the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
This is called "entering the state of rightness and departure from birth.
The afflictions to be abandoned through seeing cause sentient beings to fall into the evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings.
It is called "birth" (jāti) because it is like raw food within the body of a sentient being,
causing suffering and affliction;
or it is so called by virtue of the delusions of view.
Because it prevents various roots of goodness from reaching full maturity,
it is called "birth.
The Path of Seeing is able to transcend it.
Therefore, it is called "born of separation.
As for the term "right state" (samyaktva),
it refers to nirvāṇa.
The path of seeing is able to realize it;
this is called "entry into the state of correctness and freedom from birth" (samyaktva-nyāma). It is the freedom from birth within the state of correctness.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
Alternatively, this path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is itself termed "right nature" (*samyaktva*).
Because it is the noble rightness (*āryasamyaktva*).
Rightness is itself the state of departure from birth (*niyāma*);
this is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*).
Furthermore, this path of seeing is also called "certainty in the right nature" (*samyaktva-niyāma*),
because it resolutely grasps for *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, it is called "definitive" because it definitively discerns the characteristics of the truths.
If the true nature is nirvana, [it is definitive].
This is the determination of the state of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
If it is the state of correctness, it refers to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
"Right nature" (*samyaktva*) means "certainty.
Both interpretations are the same as before.
It refers to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
It is called "entry" because it is the initial entry; therefore,
it receives the name "entry."
Second, this clarifies the basis upon which [the path] relies.
The treatise states:
Having already established that clear realization consists of sixteen moments of mind,
upon which stages do these sixteen moments of mind depend?
The verse says:
"All are based on the same stage as the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
The commentary explains:
Because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) induce the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga),
the sixteen moments of mind are [identical] to those Supreme Mundane Dharmas.
They rely on the same stage.
Since it was previously stated that the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) relies on six stages,
the path of seeing (darśanamārga) likewise relies only on these six stages.
Third, this clarifies the sequence of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The treatise states:
For what reason must such patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) necessarily arise in this sequence, alternating one after another?
The verse says:
"Patience and knowledge are, respectively, the path of uninterrupted continuity and the path of liberation.
The commentary explains:
Patience (*kṣānti*) is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*). With respect to the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions,
it is not obstructed or hindered by the attainment of those afflictions.
Therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. Wisdom is the path of liberation;
it has already liberated one from the acquisition of afflictions and is further conjoined with the acquisition of dissociation.
Because they arise simultaneously,
it is called "liberation. This refers to the sequence of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
This must logically be so;
it is just as in the world, where one drives out thieves and closes the door—
patience is like driving out the thieves.
Wisdom is like closing a door.
From this fourth [stage] onward,
the distinction between the path of seeing and the path of cultivation is clarified.
The treatise states:
These sixteen moments of mind all perceive the principle of the Truths.
Is everything that can be spoken subsumed under the path of seeing? No; how so?
The verse says:
The first fifteen [moments] constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what has never been seen before.
The commentary states:
this excludes the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
The first fifteen moments of mind are called the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
What was not previously seen is now seen;
because one sees what has never been seen before,
it receives the name "seeing."
Regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna),
there is not a single principle of any truth that was previously unseen and is now seen;
it is as if one were practicing upon what has already been seen.
Therefore, it is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Question: If the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) is the principle of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), then what of this subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)?
Regarding the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*): within the patience of the subsequent knowledge of the path,
that which was not previously seen is now seen.
Why is the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) not subsumed within the path of seeing (darśanamārga)?
Answer: Because this [classification] is based on the truths (satya).
This does not refer to a single moment;
for although one has not yet seen what is now being seen during the single-moment mind of the path-knowledge-acceptance (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti), [the statement applies].
Since one has already previously seen all eight truths of the higher and lower realms,
it is therefore subsumed under the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
It is like a field of rice that has been harvested;
if only a single stalk remains,
one cannot say that the field has not been harvested.
Question: Regarding the principle of the Truths,
that which was previously unseen and is now seen may be called the Path of Seeing.
Regarding the seven intermediate knowledges:
they have already seen and are currently seeing.
For what reason are there seven knowledges?
It is also subsumed under the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga).
Answer: Because it arises in the interim while the knowledge of the Truths (satya) is not yet complete.
It is also subsumed within the Path of Seeing.
Following this, secondly,
[the path] is established according to the stages.
Within this, there are two [types]: first, based on the fifteen moments of mind;
second, based on the sixteenth moment of mind.
For now, regarding that which is based on the fifteen moments of mind:
The treatise states:
For now, the various noble ones (ārya) are established based on the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Regarding the distinctions,
the verse says:
They are called followers by faith and followers by dharma, distinguished by the dullness or sharpness of their faculties.
One who possesses the full afflictions and has abandoned from one up to five [categories] is a candidate for the first fruit;
one who has abandoned the next three is a candidate for the second; and one who has abandoned the eighth category is a candidate for the third. Commentary:
Regarding the distinction between those who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma based on the difference between dull and sharp faculties:
among the noble ones in the stage of the path of seeing,
there are two types.
First, those who follow by faith;
second, those who follow by dharma. These distinctions arise from the dullness or sharpness of their faculties.
These two names are established as follows:
if one is of dull faculties,
they are called a "follower by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
Because in the past,
he practiced for the sake of the meaning by following the words of others out of faith.
If one possesses sharp faculties,
they are called a "Dharma-follower" (dharmānusārī);
such a person, at a previous time, [was a stream-enterer].
Because they personally study and contemplate the Dharma of the sūtras and so forth,

and practice in accordance with their meaning, those who have fully cultivated the abandonment of one to five grades of afflictions and are heading toward the first fruit are the two aforementioned noble ones.
Within the stage of the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
three types of candidates (pratipannaka) are established;
this verse refers to the first candidate.
This means that at a previous time,
one who has not yet abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation by means of the mundane path is said to "possess the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation."
This refers to a person bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*). As for those who have abandoned from one up to five [categories of defilements] and are "candidates" (*pratipannaka*),
this means that while previously in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they used the path with outflows (*sāsravamārga*).
Those who have abandoned from one up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation constitute these five types of persons;
when combined with the previously mentioned "fully bound" individuals, they form six.
These are six types of persons.
When these six reach the stage of the Path of Seeing, they are called those "approaching the first fruit" (prathamaphalapratipannaka).
Because of proceeding toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), "the second [candidate] who abandons the next three" refers to the second candidate; that is,
while still at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
To abandon the sixth grade, or the seventh and eighth grades,
is called "abandoning the next three," namely, the first five grades.
Because of the three subsequent categories,
there are three types of persons here;
these are the three persons who abandon [the defilements] subsequently.
Upon reaching the path of seeing,

There are four types of those who practice the formless realm (*ārūpya*). Regarding "attaining parinirvāṇa while dwelling here," the commentary says:
This refers to the non-returner (anāgāmin).
Generally speaking, there are seven types. The first is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
This refers to passing away from the desire realm and attaining parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the form realm.
The second is "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin), because one attains parinirvāṇa after having been born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
This refers to one who possesses both the path of diligent cultivation and the path of swift progress;
such a person is an "attainer of parinirvāṇa through exertion" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) after being born in the realm of form.
Only after long-term application does one enter parinirvāṇa;
such is the diligent practice.
There is no path of rapid progress.
There are four types of those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Having been born for a long time,
one's application becomes lax, and one enters into effortless practice (*anābhoga-prayoga*).
Because they have entered parinirvāṇa,
their diligent cultivation proceeds swiftly;
thus, both paths are deficient.
Furthermore, the Sautrāntika interpretation is accepted by the Master;
thus, the treatise states:
In the sūtras, non-practice is taught first,
and practice is taught afterward.
In this sequential manner,
in accordance with principle,
there is the path of swift progress.
Because one attains parinirvāṇa without relying on effort,
it is called "without activity" (anabhisamskāra).
Because there is no path of rapid progress,
and because one attains parinirvāṇa through practice involving effort.
That which is called "with practice" (sābhisamskāra) refers to those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas);
this means they proceed upward,
specifically within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
One must be reborn in the higher realms before attaining parinirvāṇa.
There are two types of those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).
First is that which involves mixed cultivation, namely the delight in wisdom (*prajñā*).
Second is that which involves unmixed cultivation, namely the delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Those who practice mixed cultivation are born in Akaniṣṭha.
Those who do not practice mixed cultivation can go to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
The verse states: "Others can go to the Peak of Existence."
The others are those who do not practice mixed cultivation.
Within mixed cultivation,
there are furthermore three types.
First, the "complete leap" (sakalābhisamkrama); second, the "partial leap" (ardhapluta);
third, the "universal immersion" (sarvasthānacyuta). Now, this is based on the sixteen heavens within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
To distinguish these three types:
that which is called "complete transcendence" refers to one who is in the desire realm.
Having already mastered the mixed cultivation within the four dhyānas,
he encounters conditions that cause him to fall away from the upper three dhyānas.
He relishes only the first dhyāna;
having passed away from there, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Brahma-People (Brahmapārṣadya) by the power of his prior habituation.
Furthermore, he is able to practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna;
passing away from the Brahmakāyika heaven,
he is reborn in Akaniṣṭha.
Because one suddenly transcends the intermediate stages,
it is called "complete leaping" (*aśakṣepa*). As for "half-leaping," it refers to passing away from the Brahmakāyika heaven.
One is born in Akaniṣṭha;
there are fourteen intermediate heavens where one takes birth in gradual succession.
Or, skipping one heaven,
they are later reborn in Akaniṣṭha;
or, skipping two heavens.
Thereafter, one is reborn in Akaniṣṭha,
or even transcending thirteen celestial realms,
until finally attaining ultimate birth.
All are called "half-leapers" because their leaping is not complete;
thus they are named half-leapers.
One who transgresses against one heavenly realm undergoes fifteen births;
one who transgresses against two heavenly realms...
One undergoes fourteen births;
however, for one who transcends thirteen heavens,
one undergoes only three births.
By means of this "half-leaper," at most there are fifteen births,
and at least only three births.
Reflect upon this according to reason as to how much [of a difference there is] in the interim.
A noble one (*ārya*) will certainly not be reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā.
That is to say, when Mahābrahmā says, "I have brought forth this world," it is the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa),
because it is a locus of perverse views. As for the term "pervasive submergence" (vyāpya-samvarta):
Because one undergoes rebirth throughout all sixteen heavens,
it is called "universal dissolution" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).
Those who do not practice mixed cultivation are born throughout the form realm,
but they alone cannot go to the five Pure Abodes.
Passing away from the Bṛhatphala Heaven,
they are reborn in the three formless realms,
and subsequently are reborn in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, within the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
in the eleven lower heavens,
there were those possessing blissful concentration and blissful wisdom.
They both attain rebirth in the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala),
where they then diverge into two paths.
Those who delight in wisdom are reborn in the five Pure Abodes; those who delight in meditative concentration [are reborn in the form realm].
Those born in the formless realm— these five are called those who have practiced in the realm of form.
The *anāgāmin* who delights in meditative concentration,
although born in the formless realm, [is included among them].
Because it arises from form,
it is subsumed under the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). As for those who practice the formless (*ārūpya*),
there are four distinctions.
Excluding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state— since there is no intermediate existence for them—
they pass away from the desire realm.
They are born directly into the formless realm;
there are four types of non-returners (anāgāmin), such as those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth and so forth.
These are collectively termed "formless-realm non-returners."
With the preceding, there are six types. Alternatively, there are those who are not born in the form realm or the formless realm,
but attain parinirvāṇa solely within the desire realm.
He is called a "present-time Anāgāmin" because he attains nirvāṇa within his current body.
The verse states that "one who attains parinirvāṇa while dwelling here" refers to one who dwells in this realm of desire;
this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life."
This, together with the preceding six,
constitutes the seven types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
From this second [category],...
This clarifies the nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
The treatise states:
"Among those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are five types of non-returners."
Furthermore, there is another method for clarifying their distinctions.
The verse says:

There are nine [types of] rebirth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), namely, three [categories], each divided into three, due to differences in karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*). Thus, they constitute the distinction of three times nine.
The commentary states:
Practicing within the realm of form,
the five types of Anāgāmins are divided into nine types.
Furthermore, these are summarized into three types:
first, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); second, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin).
The three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards): those with exertion (*sābhisamskāra*) and those without exertion (*anabhisamskāra*).
Having been born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), they all attain parinirvāṇa.
All are included within birth-attainment (upapadya-parinirvāyin);
these three each have three types, thus forming nine kinds. As for the three types of intermediate-attainment (antarā-parinirvāyin):
1. One who attains parinirvāṇa swiftly;
2. one who attains parinirvāṇa without being swift;
3. one who attains parinirvāṇa after a long duration.

Because they are illustrated by the three similes of firebrands: regarding the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), first, the "rebirth-attainer" is established in reference to speed;
second, the "attainer through exertion" (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) is established in reference to non-speed.
The three types of *anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin* are established based on duration; as for the three types of *ūrdhvasrotas*,
the first is the "complete leaper," established based on speed,
and the second is the "half-leaper," established based on what is not speedy.
Third, "universal submergence" is established by way of duration. Thus, these three types,
as well as the nine types,
all depend upon whether they are swift, not swift, or long-lasting.
They attain parinirvāṇa; thus,
in relation to one another,
there is no confusion or error among these three types.
And there are nine types;
these all arise due to differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties.
There are those who are swift and those who are not swift, differing in the duration [of their attainment] due to three types of karma:
by performing karma conducive to arising,
one becomes an antarāparinirvāyin.
They create karma conducive to rebirth in the next life, because they achieve birth-attainment (upapadya-parinirvāṇa);
they also create karma conducive to subsequent lives.
Because they achieve the state of an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), there are three types of afflictions:
those who manifest lower-grade afflictions pass away in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); those with middle-grade afflictions [pass away in the higher realms].

The manifestation of the highest grade of afflictions pertains to those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*). The manifestation [of afflictions] by way of the three grades of faculties pertains to those who ascend to the higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*):

those with superior faculties attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those with middling faculties attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, and those with inferior faculties ascend to the higher realms. This applies to both those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Each is divided into three types solely because there are distinctions among the afflictions and the faculties; thus,
they are classified into three kinds.
It is not due to differences in karma;
that is to say, the three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) arise from the same karmic undertaking.
If one is born in the three types of *upapadya-parinirvāyin*,
it is because their karma for birth is identical;
therefore, their karma is not different.
The upward-streaming [attainment] is divided into three types based on differences in afflictions, faculties,
and karma. Regarding the distinctions in karma:
This refers to karma that ripens in subsequent lives,
because there is a distinction;
namely, it refers to "leap-over" (atyantābhisamdhika) karma.
And because of the karma of "half-leaping" and the karma of "complete sinking," these nine are non-returners (anāgāmin).
This can be understood by reflecting upon the distinctions among the afflictions and faculties.
This concludes the third [section].
This clarifies the seven destinations of superior persons (*saptasatpuruṣagati*). The treatise says: "If that is so..."
For what reason?
Because in the various sūtras,
the Buddha has taught that there are only seven destinations for superior persons (saptasatpuruṣagati).
The verse says:
Seven destinations of the virtuous are established based on the distinction between those who go upstream and those who do not;
because of the presence or absence of wholesome and unwholesome conduct, and because there is going forth without returning.
The commentary states:
There are three types each for those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state and those who attain it upon rebirth; there is one type for those who go upstream.
Based on this, the Sūtra establishes seven destinations for superior persons (*saptasatpuruṣagati*).
The "one who flows upward" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is so called because he moves in the same direction as those above.
Taken together, they are established as one.
Question: Why must these two fruits be established, rather than establishing them by the name of the "seven noble destinies" (*saptasatpuruṣagati*)?
Answer: "Gati" (destiny) has the meaning of "going.
Only these seven types all perform wholesome karma.
One who does not perform evil karma [attains] the two fruits of *sūksma*; one who performs a mixture of good and evil deeds [attains the fruit of] *sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*.
Furthermore, these seven types all ascend to the higher realms and do not return again.
The two fruits of the *srotāpanna* and *sakṛdāgāmin* involve returning after having gone; therefore,
there are only these seven types.
The designation "destiny of the virtuous" (satpuruṣagati) is established.
From this fourth [section],
it is clarified that one does not take birth in the higher realms.
The treatise states:
"Those who are in the stages of the noble ones (ārya) and have previously undergone birth."
Are there also such distinctions among them?
No; why is this so? The verse says:
One who has attained the state of a noble one (ārya) by being born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) does not go to be born in another realm;
rather, they are born here [in the desire realm] again or are born in the higher realms. There is no refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) nor any falling away (parihāṇi).
Thus it is explained.
If one is in the stage of a noble being (ārya) and has undergone births in the desire realm,
they become weary of those births in the desire realm.
With a mind of intense revulsion,
he will certainly not ascend to the higher realms of the form or formless worlds;
having realized the state of a non-returner, he remains here.
Because they will attain parinirvāṇa in their present body; this applies to noble ones who have undergone rebirth in the form realm.
It is possible for there to be rebirth in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
because in the form realm (rūpadhātu) there is no suffering,
and thus the mind of revulsion is weak.
They may be born in the formless heavens.
This sutra refers to noble ones born in the desire realm as well as noble ones who have been reborn in the higher realms.
There is certainly no refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), nor is there any falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Question: For what reason do noble ones (*ārya*) undergo rebirth?

Furthermore, for those who have been reborn in higher realms or are noble ones (ārya), there is necessarily no refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) nor any falling away (parihāṇi). Answer: This refers to those who have cultivated their faculties through successive births.
Because it is utterly matured and because one has attained a superior basis; previously, while in an ordinary body,
the attainment of the Path was not yet called a "superior basis."
Those who undergo rebirth do so only within the bodies of noble ones (ārya),
which is what is meant by "excellent.
Therefore, they neither refine their faculties nor undergo retrogression.
Fifth from here, the mixed cultivation of dhyāna is explained.
The treatise says:
It was previously stated that the practice of meditative absorption through intermingling (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) serves as the cause for ascending to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
This raises the first question: which meditative absorptions should one first practice by way of intermingling?
By which stage is it known that the mixed cultivation has been accomplished? This is the first question. Furthermore, for what reason [is this so]? This is the second question.
There are three questions regarding the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
The verse says:
First, one mixes the fourth [dhyāna]; its accomplishment arises from a single moment of mixing.
"For the sake of taking birth, manifesting pleasure, and preventing decline through afflictions.
The commentary states:
The first phrase answers the first question.
The second phrase answers the second question,
and the following two phrases answer the third question.
First, regarding "those who practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth [dhyāna]":
Now, one who wishes to practice the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas must first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna,
because the fourth dhyāna is the most capable. Its accomplishment through a single moment of mixed cultivation is as follows:
The meditative absorption of mixed cultivation is accomplished through the mixing of a single moment;
this refers to the Arhat.
Alternatively, it may be a non-returner (anāgāmin).
Such a person must first enter the fourth dhyāna for many moments of outflow-free (anāsrava) consciousness.
It manifests in a continuous succession;
from this, many moments of outflowing (sāsrava) states are induced,
followed again by many subsequent moments.
The untainted [states] manifest.
Thus they revolve and return,
gradually diminishing in each subsequent stage.
Finally, at the very end,
two moments of outflow-free [consciousness] are followed by two moments of outflowing [consciousness].
Immediately following the present [moment],
two subsequent moments of untainted consciousness arise;
this is called the meditative concentration of mixed cultivation.
When the preparatory application is perfected, there is next again a single moment of untainted (anāsrava) [consciousness];
then, one further arouses a single moment of tainted (sāsrava) [consciousness],
immediately followed by the arising of a single moment of untainted [consciousness].
The middle portion consists of outflows (sāsrava),
while the preceding and succeeding portions are without outflows (anāsrava); thus, they are interspersed with one another.
Therefore, it is called "mixed cultivation.
This single moment of mixing is termed the "accomplishment of the fundamental [attainment]."
Having cultivated the fourth dhyāna,
one can also, by means of this power,
practice the mixed cultivation of the three lower dhyānas; this is the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas.
In total, there are three conditions.
The first is for the sake of taking birth,
because one is born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Second, it is for the sake of manifest happiness,
because one experiences the joy of the Dharma.
Third, it is for the purpose of preventing the arising of afflictions and subsequent regression.
If it is not cultivated by a non-returner,
it is due to the first three conditions;
if it is cultivated by an arhat, [it is due to all four].
Excluding one [of the heavens] where beings are born by transformation, from this sixth [point],
it is clarified that the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) consist of only five.
The treatise asks:
For what reason are there only five Pure Abodes?
The verse says:
Through the five grades of mixed cultivation, there arise the five Pure Abodes.
The commentary says:
Because there are five grades of the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna,
there are only five Pure Abodes.
First, the inferior grade;
second, the middling grade;
third, the superior grade.
Fourth is the superior grade;
fifth is the supreme grade.
The first grade has three [subdivisions].
This refers to three moments of mind:
first, one arises that is untainted (anāsrava);
next, one arises that is tainted (sāsrava).
Subsequently, one untainted [moment] arises;
in the second category, there are six, namely,
three further moments together with the preceding ones, making six in total.
The third category consists of nine:
that is, three further moments of mind,
which together with the preceding ones constitute nine.
The fourth category consists of twelve [minds]:
namely, the three further minds together with the preceding nine minds.
Thus, twelve [minds] are established.
In the fifth category, fifteen [minds] arise,
further giving rise to three minds.
Together with the previous twelve,
they thus constitute fifteen.
Such are the five categories.
In their respective order,
they bring about rebirth in the five Pure Abodes;
this should be understood therein.
The power of the untainted (anāsrava) perfumes and cultivates the tainted (sāsrava),
causing one to be reborn in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
It is not the case that the untainted [attainments] can induce rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
because they involve aversion toward and rejection of existence (*bhava*). From this seventh [point],...
Regarding the "clearly realized body" (kāyasākṣin) non-returner,
the treatise states:
"The Sūtra speaks of the non-returner."
There is that which is called "attainment through bodily witness" (kāyasākṣin). Based on what superior quality is the name "bodily witness" established?
The verse says:
One who has attained the absorption of cessation and is a non-returner is designated by the name "Body-Witness" (kāyasākṣin).
The commentary says:
If one who has attained the fruit of non-returning further cultivates and realizes the meditative attainment of cessation,
they are re-designated as a "body-witness."
The attainment of cessation is mindless;
because it is realized through the body,
it is called "bodily realization."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are two kinds of fields of merit;
namely, the eighteen [qualities] of those in training (śaikṣa)."
There are nine for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The commentary explains:
as for the statement that there are eighteen for those in training (*śaikṣa*), [it refers to the following:]...
Among those in training (śaikṣa),
there are four paths and three fruits, which constitute seven,
along with the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin).
The follower by faith, the one resolved through faith,
and the one who has attained vision.
The family-to-family,
the one-interval,
and the five types of non-returners (anāgāmin).
Thus, eighteen [types] are established.
Regarding the nine types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa): first is the one subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman).
Second, guarding the Dharma;
third, contemplating the Dharma;
fourth, abiding securely in the Dharma.
Fifth, the one capable of penetration;
sixth, the immovable;
seventh, the non-retrogressive.
Eight: liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Nine: both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukti*).
Question: By what cause is there bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*)?
It is not included in that number.
The answer is: the three trainings without outflows are the causes of the noble ones.
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is nirvāṇa;
it is the fruit of the noble ones. The meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is with outflows (sāsrava).
It is not based on causes;
because it lacks a basis in causes,
it is not included among their number.
From this fourth section onward,
the stages leading toward and attaining the fruit of arhatship are clarified;
within this, five parts are distinguished.
First, clarifying the distinctions regarding the fruits of the path;
second, clarifying the path of cultivation through inquiry;
third, clarifying the knowledge of exhaustion and subsequent knowledge.
The fourth clarifies the fruits of the path;
the fifth clarifies the six lineages.
Now, regarding the first, which clarifies those directed toward the fruit:
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished the differences between the third path and its fruit,
one should next establish the fourth path and its fruit.
The verse says:

Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, from the abandonment of the first level’s first grade up to the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence, all are candidates for Arhatship.
The ninth path of immediate succession is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

At the moment of its exhaustion, the attainment of exhaustion (*kṣaya-prāpti*) arises together with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), whereby one becomes an adept (*aśaikṣa*) and attains the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]
Regarding those who attain the state of non-returner (anāgāmin):
it begins from the abandonment of the first category of the first dhyāna and concludes with the abandonment of the eighth category of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
This is called "one who is heading toward arhatship," because they are proceeding toward the fruit of arhatship.
Within this very stage of heading toward it:

The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth category of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
This concentration can destroy all afflictions,
just as a vajra can crush all things; therefore,
it is called the "Vajra-like Concentration" (vajropama-samādhi).
Although this meditative concentration possesses the power to destroy all other afflictions, those others have already been severed previously;
therefore, it now severs only the ninth grade of affliction. Since this concentration can sever the ninth grade of affliction of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), [it is called the "unshakeable"].
It is able to induce the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that functions simultaneously with the complete attainment of the exhaustion of these afflictions;
this very knowledge of exhaustion is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
This path of liberation arises simultaneously with the initial attainment of the destruction of the outflows.
Therefore, it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna).
When the verse says "co-arising with the attainment of exhaustion," this refers to the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-prāpti).
Both are termed the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Once the knowledge of exhaustion has arisen,
one attains the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*).
Because there is nothing further to be learned,
they are also called "Worthy Ones" (arhat), that is to say, Arhats.
This is translated as "the worthy" (*arhat*),
because they are worthy of receiving vast offerings from humans and devas.
Following this, secondly, the treatise clarifies the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Among these, there are five [points]:
first, clarifying that detachment from defilement occurs through the path; second, clarifying that the path brings about the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*);
third, clarifying the specific and general applications of the path for detachment from the stages (*bhūmi*).
The fourth clarifies the paths of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*); the fifth clarifies the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) that takes conditioned phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, regarding how the stages (*bhūmi*) are freed from defilement by means of the path:
The treatise asks:
By means of which path does one become detached from the defilements of which stage?
The verse says:
"The Peak of Existence [is abandoned] by the untainted; the rest by both. The commentary explains: "Detachment from the defilements [is achieved] through these two."
Regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) being abandoned by the untainted (*anāsrava*):
the defilements of the Peak of Existence are severed solely by the untainted path.
It is not by means of the contaminated path;
for the contaminated path involves rejoicing in what is above and feeling aversion toward what is below,
[which cannot occur] regarding the stage of the Peak of Existence.
Because there is nothing unsurpassed to be delighted in,
the path with outflows does not sever the Peak of Existence.
"Others [attain it] through two ways by means of detachment from defilement.
"Others" refers to the remaining eight stages; this means they detach from the defilements of those eight stages.
It is attained through two paths:
the path with outflows and the path without outflows,
for both are capable of bringing about detachment.
Second, this clarifies how the path leads to the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
The treatise states:
Since both [paths] serve as the means of transcendence,
how many kinds of acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) are there for each when one becomes free from the defilements of the eight stages?
The verse says:

"The two noble [paths] abandon eight through cultivation; each has two acquisitions of disconnection. The commentary says: [This refers to the fact that] for each [of the two noble paths], there are two types of acquisition of disconnection.
When noble beings in training,
by means of both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths,
abandon the defilements to be eliminated through cultivation across the eight stages.
Each is capable of inducing two acquisitions of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*):

the latter is "liberated unconditionally" (asamayavimukta), arising from the previous "those who have attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
The commentary states:
The sūtras speak of six types of arhats. The first is the one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman).
The first is the one who regresses upon encountering even slight conditions.
The second is the one who contemplates the Dharma (cintāmayī),
who, fearing regression and loss, constantly contemplates self-harm.
Third is the protection of the Dharma,
which means personally guarding the Dharma previously attained.
Fourth is the abiding in the Dharma.
There are no conditions for defeat or regression;
thus, even without self-protection,
one is still able not to regress.
There is no superior application,
nor is there further progress. These are the five types of those capable of reaching penetration (*abhisamaya*).
That is to say, one who is by nature capable and delights in cultivating the faculties of the senses (indriya-saṃvara) will swiftly attain the unshakable state; this is the sixth,
the quality of being unshakable (akopyadharman).
Because they are not shaken or regressed by afflictions, the first five types of lineage arise from the stage of "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*) during the prior stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
These five are collectively termed "those liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*).
In short, one must wait for the proper time before being able to enter meditative concentration and achieve liberation of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "waiting for the proper time," there are six such times.
The first is obtaining fine robes.
Second, obtaining excellent food;
third, obtaining excellent bedding and seating;
fourth, obtaining an excellent dwelling place.
Fifth, one obtains excellent teachers of the Dharma;
sixth, one obtains excellent fellow students. Subsequently, those of the immovable lineage (akopya-gotra) become those liberated at any time (asamayavimukta).
This refers to those of sharp faculties,
who are able to enter meditative concentration and achieve liberation of mind without depending on time.
This arises from the nature of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) during the stage of prior training (*śaikṣa*).
This is the second [section],
clarifying the sequence of the six natures.
The treatise says:
Regarding the spiritual lineages (gotra) of the six types of arhats.
This is a question asking whether [the Buddha] existed prior [to enlightenment] or attained it subsequently;
it is not answered categorically.
What is the proof?
The verse says:
Some possess this innate lineage; others acquire it through the refinement of their faculties.
The commentary states:
The lineage of those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) must necessarily have existed previously.
The five [mental factors] beginning with attention (manasikāra) also possess subsequent attainment (pṛṣṭhalabdha);
that is to say, they have existed from the outset.
These are those of the *cetana-dharman* lineage.
Or there may be those who, having fallen back, refine their faculties (*indriya*) to become *cetana-dharman*, and so on up to the *akopya-dharman* (immovable type);
they are explained in the same manner as the *cetana-dharman*.
Among these, one of the nature of falling away does not necessarily fall away,
up to and including one who is capable of reaching the goal.
It is not necessarily that they can reach it;
rather, this name is established based on the possibility of its occurrence.
Therefore, the six types of arhats exist throughout all three realms.
This is also the case for those who fall away from meditative concentration.
The "capable of penetration" and the "penetrated" constitute the upper realm;
therein there are only two types: abiding and immovable.
The remaining four are excluded because,
in those higher realms,
there is no falling away, no self-harm, no self-protection, and no refinement of the faculties.
Therefore, there are no other four [types of falling away].
Following this third point,
it clarifies falling away from the fruit by way of lineage.
The treatise says:
Regarding these six types [of persons],
who regresses from what, and by virtue of what lineage or fruit?
The verse says:
Four [types of persons] fall away from their lineage; five fall away from the fruit, but not from what preceded it.
The commentary explains:
Regarding the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*),
there is absolutely no possibility of regression.
As for the aforementioned five types [of lineages]:
Only the one of the "nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman) necessarily does not fall back from their lineage;
this is because they occupy the lowest [position].
Only those of the four types beginning with the *cetanādharman* may fall away from their lineage; that is, one may fall away from the state of being a *cetanādharman*.

One may regress from the stage of one who abides in the dharma to enter the stage of one who regresses from the dharma; or, from the stage of one who protects the dharma, one may regress to enter the stage of one who contemplates the dharma.
Either from the stage of one who abides securely,
they regress and enter the stage of one who protects the Dharma;
or from the stage of one capable of reaching perfection.
To retreat and then re-enter abiding is called "retrogression by lineage. Fifth, "from the fruit,
not from the prior" refers to those who have attained the fruit but not its preceding stage.
The five types, beginning with those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), all possess the quality of falling away from their fruit;
that is to say, they may fall away from the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the four types beginning with those who fall away from reflection (cintāmayī), some may fall away from their lineage (gotra) and some may fall away from their fruit (phala).
Although both possess retrogression,
they are not alike; "prior" refers to the prior stage,
namely the stage of training (śaikṣa).
Abiding in the four [factors] beginning with reflection,
one attains the state of no-more-learning.
These four factors, beginning with reflection—
Regarding the lineage and the fruit,
there is necessarily no possibility of regression;
this refers to those in training and those beyond training.
Because that which is accomplished through the Path is firm; thus, for those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) who belong to the lineage of those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman),
there is the cultivation and accomplishment of volition (cetanā) and so forth.
Regarding the four types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*),
this name was not given previously;
it is one in which falling back (*parihāṇi*) is possible.

Because it is accomplished solely by the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is exclusively the "one liable to fall" (parihāṇadharman) who possesses the possibility of falling away from the fruit;
for such a person's spiritual lineage (gotra) is that of one liable to fall.
Therefore, the verse states that those of the "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman) are not included among those who have not yet attained [the fruit]. According to the Sarvāstivāda school,
only the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) is necessarily free from falling away.
Because the delusions regarding the principles of the path of seeing have been severed, the reality of the truths is authentic,
definitively established, and reliable;
it has already been realized by noble wisdom.
There is certainly no possibility of falling back from these;
however, regarding the latter three fruits,
it is admitted that there can be a falling away from the fruit.
Because the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation are delusions regarding phenomena;
the characteristics of phenomena are superficial and deceptive.
There is no fixed basis upon which to rely;
one may lose mindfulness and regress by severing the delusions that obscure that [basis]. This is the view of the Mahāsāṃghika school.
According to the Sautrāntika school, there is falling away from the fruit of stream-entry, but no falling away from arhatship.
Those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) or arhatship (arhat) will certainly not fall away from their respective fruits,
because they have realized them through the Noble Path (āryamārga). This does not apply to the two intermediate fruits.
Since it is admitted that one realizes the path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga),
there is the possibility of falling away.
This applies if one has transcended two or three fruits.
Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika school,
there are six types of Arhatship, none of which involve falling back.
Regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life,
there is falling away and non-falling away;
this does not refer to falling away from the fruit.
If one attains the lineage of the fruit,
all are termed "unshakable" (akopya) and there are no six types.
Abiding in happiness in the present life refers to the four dhyānas with outflows;
one may fall away from these dhyānas.
One who is named "of the nature of falling back" (parihāṇadharman) contemplates this dhyāna; one who is named "of the nature of reflecting" (cetana-dharman) likewise contemplates it.
To protect this meditative concentration is called "protecting the Dharma";
it is to abide securely in meditative concentration.
That which is called "abiding in the dharma" is the state of being capable of attaining meditative absorption;
this is termed "capable-of-attainment dharma."
Non-retrogression from meditative absorption is called the "dharma of non-retrogression," with respect to dwelling in happiness in the present life.
This divides the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) into six types.
From this fourth [section],
the lineage of ordinary persons who train is explained.
The treatise says:
"Only the lineage of the Arhat is of six types.
Are there also six types of lineage for others?"
If there are those who can all cultivate and refine their faculties, the verse says:
Learners and worldlings also have six; refining the faculties does not occur during the path of seeing.
The commentary states:
Both those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) possess six types of spiritual lineage (gotra).
Based on the six types of fruition,
there are six lineages (gotra) due to the distinction between those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Therefore, among those beyond training (aśaikṣa),
there are six types; however, in the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there is necessarily no refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
Because the path of seeing is so rapid,
there is no opportunity to initiate the preparatory application for the refinement of faculties; therefore,
this is the fifth [point] from here.
This clarifies the three types of regression.
The treatise states:
"As it is said in the Sūtra."
I say that by means of this, there may be a falling away from any one of the four kinds of higher mental states (adhicitta) through which one dwells in happiness in the present life.
Having attained the unshakable liberation of mind and realized it through direct bodily witness,
I declare with certainty that there is no cause or condition for falling back from this state.
How does one who possesses the quality of being unshakable (akopyadharman) fall away from the blissful abiding in the present life?
The verse says:
It should be known that there are three types of falling away: from what has already been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
Among these, Buddhas possess only the last; those of medium capacity possess the middle and the last; and those of dull capacity possess all three.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
There are three types of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
The first is "falling away from what has already been attained," which refers to falling away from the superior qualities and dharmas that have already been acquired.
Second is "retrogression from what has not yet been attained," which refers to retrogression in the sense that one has not yet attained superior qualities.
Thus it is called retrogression.
Third is the decline of enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*),
which refers to when one has already attained spiritual qualities but fails to enjoy them at the time of their utilization.
That which does not manifest before one is called "retrogression. Regarding the Buddha, there is only the last:
the Buddha possesses only the final type of retrogression, namely, retrogression from enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*).
Because, although they possess all virtues,
it is impossible for them to manifest simultaneously; thus,
those with sharp faculties attain the latter two [results] later.
"Advantage" refers to the immovable arhat (*akopya-arhan*).
There are two types of falling away among those who possess [defilements]: the latter two; "the middle" refers to falling away from what has not yet been attained (*aprāpti-parihāṇi*).
The latter refers to the regression from enjoyment;
because of their sharp faculties, they do not undergo regression from what has already been attained.
Regarding the three types of dullness:
"dullness" refers to the five [faculties] beginning with the dharma of regression.
These possess all three kinds of regression.
When the Sūtra speaks of "one of immovable dharma" who "retrogresses from the dwelling in happiness in the present life," this refers to retrogression regarding enjoyment.
It is not the case that there is falling away from the other two; therefore,
there is no falling away from this sixth [state].
This clarifies the characteristics of falling back from the fruit. The treatise states: "All Arhats..."
Since it has been admitted that one may fall from the fruit,
does one arise [from that state] again?
During the time one abides in the fruit...
Regarding actions not performed:
at the time of retreat, one does not act; this is not a matter of questioning, nor is it a matter of answering otherwise.
For what reason is this questioned?
The verse says:
"All who fall away from fruition will certainly attain [it] again before they die."
"One does not do what is not done by one abiding in the fruit; because of the increase of shame, one does not act [in such a way].
The commentary explains:
"All those who have fallen away from the fruit..."
One will certainly obtain it within a brief moment;
there is no one who dies without obtaining it. As for those who do die, [they shall obtain it].
The fruit of practicing the holy life would not be secure or a state worthy of trust.
Furthermore, regarding actions not performed while abiding in the state of fruition, [the retribution for them arises] at the time of falling away from that fruition.
Because shame and remorse have increased,
they will certainly not commit [such acts] either;
they are like a mighty warrior.
Though they stumble, they do not fall.
From this point, the seventh section clarifies the differences in the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The treatise states:
As explained above, there are those who attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) or the state of learning (śaikṣa) through the refinement of their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra).
At the time of correctly refining the faculties (*indriya*),
how many paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and how many paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there for each? This is the first question.
The second question concerns what nature [it] comprises;
the third question concerns what its basis is.
The verse says:

In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) consists of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because these have been practiced for a long time. In the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*), there is only one [path]. The untainted (*anāsrava*) [refinement] relies on three types of persons;
the [refinement of] those beyond learning relies on nine stages (*bhūmi*). Those still in training rely only on six stages.
"Abandoning the path of the fruit and the superior fruit, because one attains only the path of the fruit.
Commentary: The first three phrases answer the first question.
The two characters "anāsrava" (untainted) in the fourth line answer the second question.
From "based on the three [types of persons]" onwards answers the third question.

Regarding the statement that "in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are due to long-standing cultivation," this refers to the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

This clarifies the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). There are five types, beginning with those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
Each transformation of the individual natures consists of nine uninterrupted paths and nine paths of liberation.
It is like first attaining the fruit of arhatship by means of the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation;
such is the nature of one with dull faculties.
Because of long-standing habituation,
nine uninterrupted paths and nine paths of liberation are required for the paths of training and no-more-training.
Because that which has been accomplished is firm, it is called "long-cultivated. Regarding "training in one":
this refers to the stage of training (śaikṣa).
One transforms the single nature;
each has one path of uninterrupted realization and one path of liberation.
This is because it has not been practiced for long;

it is like first attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), which consists of one path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) and its corresponding patience (*kṣānti*), and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and its corresponding knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*). These are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The path for clarifying the faculties (*indriya*) is exclusively of an untainted nature (*anāsrava*),
because it is superior. Regarding "based on the three persons," this refers to the door of the physical body (*kāya*).
Only humans in the three continents are able to cultivate the refinement of the faculties;
this does not exist within the heavenly realms.
This means that because there is no falling back, those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) rely upon nine stages;
this refers to the gate of the stages. That is to say, it concerns the refinement of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) by those in the stage of no-more-learning.
It relies on the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*). As for those in training (*śaikṣa*), they rely on only six;
when those in training refine their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they rely exclusively on these six stages.
Regarding the preceding nine stages,
the final three are excluded. As for the statement, "Abandoning the path of the fruit and the path of superior fruit,
one attains only the path of the fruit," this clarifies the reason why those in training (śaikṣa) rely upon the six stages.

Now, regarding the transformation of the sexual organ (*vyañjanaparivṛtti*): it involves the relinquishing of the path of fruition (*phalamārga*), the path superior to fruition (*viśeṣamārga*), and the path of application (*prayogamārga*).
What is attained is exclusively the path of fruition.
This is not directed toward the path;
it must be the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*) subsumed under the formless realm (*ārūpya-bhūmi*). Therefore, one refines the faculties while still a learner (*śaikṣa*).
This is based solely on the six stages;
from this eighth [stage] onward,
the nine types of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are clarified.
The treatise says:
"In total, how many kinds of those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are there?"
By what distinction?
The verse says:
Seven śrāvakas and two Buddhas; their distinction is due to nine faculties.
The commentary states:
There are nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
namely, the seven śrāvakas.
The five types, beginning with those subject to regression,
and the immovable type, which is divided into two:
the first is called "non-regressing," because they possess sharp faculties from the outset.
The second is called "Immovable" because it is attained through subsequent cultivation.
Regarding the "two Buddhas," this refers to the Pratyekabuddha and the Mahābuddha.
These distinctions among the noble ones arise from the differences in the nine grades of faculties, such as the lowest-of-the-low and so forth;
thus, there are nine types of noble ones.
From this point, the second major section clarifies the seven types of noble beings (*āryapudgala*).
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the establishment of the seven noble ones;
second, the clarification of those liberated through wisdom and those liberated through both [wisdom and concentration].
Regarding the first, the seven noble ones:
The treatise states:
Within the stages of training and beyond training,
there are seven noble beings (ārya-pudgala).
All noble beings (ārya) are subsumed within this; first,
those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin).
2. Those who follow by means of the Dharma (dharmānusārin);
3. those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta); 4. those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Fifth, the body-witness;
sixth, the one liberated by wisdom;
seventh, the one liberated both ways.
Based on what are the seven established? This is the first question.
How many distinct entities are there? This is the second question.
The verse says:
The preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the faculties (*indriya*), the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*) constitute seven [categories].
However, as for the specific entities (*vastu*), there are only six, because each of the three paths (*mārga*) contains two [of these categories]. Commentary:
[This is explained as follows:]...
The first two lines answer the first question;
the following two lines answer the second question,
based on the difference in preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The first two noble ones are established as those who previously engaged in preparatory practice:

namely, the follower by faith through the words of others (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma through their own [investigation] (*dharmānusārin*). This distinction is based on the difference in their faculties (*indriya*).

Next, two types are established: those of dull faculties are called "those liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta), and those of sharp faculties are called "those who have attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). Based on the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), the name "bodily witness" (kāyasākṣin) is established; these distinctions are based on the difference in liberation.
The latter two types of noble beings are established;
that is to say, by the power of wisdom,
they are freed from the afflictive obstructions.
They are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
When they also attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), they are liberated from the hindrance to liberation, which is precisely the hindrance to the absorption of cessation.
It is called the "hindrance to liberation.
Its essence is undefiled ignorance.
It is termed "liberation from both."
Being free from the obstacles to meditative concentration and wisdom is called "conjunction.
Although these names are seven, [they refer to the same state].
The essential categories are only six,
because each of the three paths has two [aspects].
First, two are established for the path of seeing.

That is to say, two types are established on the path of cultivation: those who attain through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta). Two types are established on the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga):
namely, those liberated by time (samayavimukta).
Because they are not liberated at any time, there are three paths;
in terms of the actual entities, there are only six.
This is the second [section].
Regarding the establishment of those liberated through both [tranquility and insight] and those liberated through wisdom,
the treatise asks:
"What are those termed 'liberated through both' and 'liberated through wisdom'?"
The verse says:
"Both [attain it] through the attainment of the cessation-concentration; the others are called 'liberated by wisdom'.
The commentary says:
Among the six types of arhats,
those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation are called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
First, by the power of wisdom,
one is liberated from the obstacle of afflictions and further attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Because they are liberated from the hindrances to concentration, they are called "both-liberated" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta);
others are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta).
The others— namely, those Arhats who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation—
are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
It is solely by the power of wisdom that one attains liberation from the hindrance of afflictions.
Since they have not yet abandoned the hindrances to meditative concentration, they cannot be said to be "conjoined.
This concludes the third major section.
Regarding the fulfillment of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*):
the treatise says,
"As the Blessed One has taught."
The abandonment of the five afflictions refers to the abandonment of the five lower fetters by an Anāgāmin.
"Unshakeable" means not being led astray by the delusions of desire.
This concludes the preceding scriptural passage concerning those who have not yet been designated as "perfected learners."
The following is based on a scriptural inquiry:
By how many causes does each of the stages of training (śaikṣa) and beyond-training (aśaikṣa) arise?
Among those of equal status,
it alone is called "fulfilled.
The verse says:
The learner is called "perfected" by means of three factors: faculties, fruits, and meditative attainments;
the non-learner obtains the name "perfected" by means of two: faculties and meditative attainments.
The commentary states:
The designation "one whose training is fulfilled" (śaikṣa-paripūrṇa) is established by three causes.
First, by the fulfillment of the faculties (indriya).
That is to say, they possess sharp faculties;
second, by the fulfillment of the fruit,
meaning they have attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin).
Third, by the fulfillment of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*),

which refers to attaining the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). There are also learners (*śaikṣa*) who possess fulfillment solely by way of their faculties (*indriya*), namely those who have attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
One who has not yet abandoned the defilements of desire is called "perfected in faculties" by virtue of having attained through vision.
Because they have not yet abandoned desire,
there are no others who are complete; there are those in training (śaikṣa) who are complete solely by virtue of the fruit.
This refers to one who is liberated through faith, a non-returner who has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation;
because they are a non-returner,
they are said to have "perfected the fruit."
This refers to one who possesses faith and understanding but is not said to have perfected the faculties;
such a person has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
It is not that they are fully perfected in concentration; there are those in training who,
by virtue of their faculties and fruits,
also receive the designation "perfected."
This refers to a non-returner who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) but has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
By virtue of being a non-returner who has attained vision...
Therefore, it is called the fulfillment of the faculties and the fruits;
however, one who has not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is not said to have fulfilled concentration. There are those who are still in training (śaikṣa).
Because their fruition is certain,
they also receive the name "fulfilled," namely,
those who are resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).

One who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) but is not one who has reached through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) is not said to have perfected the faculties (indriya-paripūrṇa). There is such a person among those in training (śaikṣa).
It is due to the fulfillment of three factors:
namely, being one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and having attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation is necessarily a non-returner;
thus, they possess three fulfillments. One who is beyond training is called "fulfilled."
It is solely due to two causes:
first, the perfection of the faculties;
