they may remain as a skeletal frame until the era of Maitreya, becoming nothing but a solid, enduring substance, just as Mahākāśyapa left behind his skeleton.
It can remain for a long time;
that is, the body as a skeleton is what is called "solid and substantial."
This means excluding meat and so forth.
Regarding the statement by others that there is no sense of "keeping" (storing), other masters say:
There is no such thing as maintaining the body until after death.
As for those whom Kāśyapa maintains,
they are supported by celestial deities.
This is not due to the power of a vow.
As for the statement that "initially, many minds transform into one to complete this," it refers to the initial arising of the transformative act.
Through many transformation-minds,
one is only then able to manifest a single transformed object;
subsequently, if it reaches completion.
The opposite of this is that a single transformative mind alone is capable of producing numerous transformative manifestations.
Regarding those acquired through cultivation that are comprised within the indeterminate:
these are the fourteen aforementioned minds capable of transformation.

It arises from cultivation within meditative concentration and is subsumed under the indeterminate nature. Among the four types of indeterminate states, it belongs to the category of the unmanifest (avijñapti).
The result-of-attainment [attainments] are neutral (avyākṛta).
As for the others that can pertain to all three natures,
these are the innate [attainments] and so forth.
The mind capable of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta) can correspond to all three moral natures; for example, the transformative minds of spirits, ghosts,
and the like may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
Or it may be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
From this fifth [section],
the eye and ear are explained separately.
The treatise asks:
Regarding the terms "divine eye" and "divine ear," what do they signify?
The verse says:

The divine eye and ear are faculties; they consist of pure matter belonging to the stage of meditative concentration, are always of the same class (sabhāga), and are without defect; they perceive what is obstructed, subtle, distant, and so forth.
The commentary states:
"The divine eye and ear" refers to the supernormal powers of the eye and the ear.
The pure matter produced by relying on the four dhyānas,
namely the two faculties of the eye and the ear.
Seeing forms and hearing sounds are called the "divine eye" and "divine ear.
As for the term "divine" (deva) used here:
Because it is comprised within the stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi), the divine eye is of three kinds.
The first is that acquired through birth (upapattipratilambhika), which refers to those born among the gods.
The second is that attained through cultivation, which is as previously described.
The third is that resembling a deva, which is acquired through karma,
such as the case of universal monarchs (cakravartin) or ghosts and spirits.
Furthermore, those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and others possess only the divine eyes and ears acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*),
which are always of the nature of being "functioning" (*sabhāga*).
Furthermore, it is unimpaired and capable of apprehending subtle, distant, and obstructed forms,
sounds, and so forth in all directions.
Thus, there is a verse that says: "The physical eye, regarding all directions, Lacks the functional power to see Obscured, subtle, or distant forms; The divine eye sees them without exception.
This concludes the sixth [chapter].
This clarifies the varieties of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
The treatise states:
"As previously explained, there are differences such as those acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*) regarding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*)."
Is there also a difference regarding the five [supernormal powers], such as the power of the divine realm?
This is the question. There is also an answer. How is it demonstrated?
The verse says:
The supernormal power of the base (ṛddhi) is fivefold—attained through cultivation, birth, spells, medicine, and action.
The knowledge of others' minds is attained through cultivation, birth, and spells; furthermore, it includes attainment through divination and signs.

The three [types of knowledge] arise through cultivation; the karma-born [knowledge] is accomplished. Excluding those born of cultivation, all are of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). Humans alone possess that which is acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*); those in hell can know it only at the very beginning. Commentary: The three types of knowledge—conventional (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), dharma (*dharma-jñāna*), and subsequent (*anvaya-jñāna*)—arise through cultivation. The knowledge born of karma is accomplished through the power of past actions. Excluding the knowledge born of cultivation, all other types of knowledge pertain to the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral). Among these, only humans possess the type acquired at birth; those in the hells can only know it at the very beginning of their existence.
The first five phrases clarify the common categories;
the next single phrase distinguishes the three natures;
and the final two phrases concern the universality or restriction regarding the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
The supernormal power of the divine realm (ṛddhividhi-jñāna) generally comprises five types:
first, that acquired through cultivation;
second, that acquired at birth.
Third, obtained through incantations;
fourth, obtained through medicine;
fifth, obtained through karma.
The supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds has four types:
first, that acquired through cultivation;
second, that acquired at birth.
Third is obtaining it through incantations;
fourth is through divining signs.
As for the remaining types of divine eye:
The three supernormal knowledges— divine ear, recollection of past lives,
and [the knowledge of others' minds]— possess only three types [of objects].
That is to say: cultivation, birth,
and karma— among these five supernormal powers (abhijñā).
The three beginning with the supernormal power of the divine realm (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna), if acquired through cultivation,
are exclusively of a wholesome nature.
The divine eye and the divine ear are of indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*),
with the exception of those obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
The others, such as those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) and so forth, all pertain to the three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*).
Among humans, there are none who possess superknowledges (*abhijñā*) acquired at birth.
The others may all exist;
however, this is the case at the moment of first taking birth within the hell realm.
There are those who, from birth, possess the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of past lives;
having known the past and so forth,
they are then oppressed by painful sensations.
There is nothing further to be known.
If one cultivates and attains the supernormal powers (abhijñā),
they pertain only to the realms of humans and devas.
Because it is capable of entering meditative concentration,
it excludes those born with [attainment] and extends to the other four destinies.
All possess both innate and acquired [powers], consisting of two types: spells and medicinal herbs;
these apply to humans, devas, and the realm of ghosts.
Divination and physiognomy apply only to humans.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā, Main Text, Fascicle 27 [and] 28.
Commentary states: One-pointedness of mind is termed "concentration" (*samādhi*). This chapter explains it extensively; therefore, it is named...
Analysis: Within this chapter, there are three general sections: first, an explanation of the merits of meditative concentration;
second, an explanation of the duration of the True Dharma in the world;
and third, an explanation of the fundamental purpose of composing this treatise.
This section clarifies two aspects within meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
first, the various concentrations that serve as the basis;
second, the spiritual qualities that depend upon them.
This section on the elucidation of the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) is divided into four parts:
first, the elucidation of the four dhyānas;
second, the elucidation of the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
The three knowledges and the eight attainments;
the four knowledges clarify the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Below this, first, the four dhyānas are clarified.
The treatise says:
The meritorious qualities accomplished by the various types of knowledge have already been explained;
as for the remaining meritorious qualities of nature...
This shall now be analyzed.
Among these, first the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis will be analyzed.
Furthermore, what are the dhyānas among the various concentrations?
The verse says:

There are four dhyānas, each having two types. Among these, that which has already been explained as "concentration" (samādhi) is wholesome one-pointedness of mind; together with its attendants, it is of the nature of the five aggregates.
"Initially possessing investigation, joy, and bliss; later, gradually abandoning the preceding factors.
The commentary states:
"The four dhyānas each have two [aspects]."
The four types of dhyāna each have two kinds:
first, the dhyāna of birth.
Regarding the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti-dhyāna*):
as for that which has been explained regarding birth within them,
it refers to the fourfold essence of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) within those two absorptions.
The Chapter on the World has already been explained;
that is to say, in the Chapter on the World,
it was stated that there are seventeen heavens in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This is the dhyāna of arising. "Concentration" (samādhi) refers to that which has the nature of the five aggregates, including their attendants, being virtuous and one-pointed;
this is the essence of concentration-dhyāna.
That is to say, its nature is exclusively virtuous.
Regarding one-pointedness of mind:
to speak of its essential nature,
it consists of wholesome meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because it is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If one includes the associated factors (*sahāya*), the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute its essence; therein, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) refers specifically to the *saṃvara-śīla* (the discipline of restraint). Question: What is meant by "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*)?
Answer: It is that which enables the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object.
Question: What is called dhyāna? Answer: It is so named because of its tranquility through concentration.
Because it is capable of deliberation,
and the essence of deliberation is wisdom (*prajñā*);
concentration possesses the function of stillness.

Furthermore, because it gives rise to wisdom and reflection, it is called "meditative absorption" (dhyāna). Question: The meditative concentrations of the formless realm (ārūpya-samādhi) are also capable of such quiet contemplation.
It should be called "dhyāna" (meditative absorption).
Answer: The meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the formless realm are not called "dhyāna."
This means that the name "dhyāna" is established from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
for the meditative concentrations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are preeminent.
It is called *dhyāna* alone,
just as in the world one speaks of the sun by the name "Radiant One," whereas although fireflies and candles emit light, they cannot be called the sun.
Question: For what reason is the dhyāna of the form realm alone designated as "supreme"?
Answer: First, because among all forms of meditative concentration (samādhi), [it is the most excellent].
It subsumes the eighteen mental factors;
it is the balanced practice of both tranquility and insight,
and is most capable of thorough deliberation.
The third is called dwelling in happiness in the present life;
the fourth is called the pleasant path of practice.
Therefore, these constitute the form realm concentrations.
"Only [the meditative absorptions] are called *dhyāna*. Question: How can the defiled concentrations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) receive this name?
Answer: Because they, too, are capable of false deliberation (*vitarka*).
The Blessed One has also spoken of "unwholesome meditative absorption" (akuśala-dhyāna).
It is asked: is one-pointedness of mind the essential nature of meditative absorption?
Based on what characteristics are the first, second, third, and fourth [dhyānas] established?
The verse answers: "The first possesses vicāra, prīti, and sukha; the subsequent ones gradually abandon the preceding factors.
This refers to the internal state of the first dhyāna.
Possessing investigation, joy, and bliss,
it is called the first dhyāna.
As for the latter three concentrations:
The first factor is gradually abandoned;
that is to say, there is only the factor of joy and bliss, while applied thought (*vitarka*) is absent.
Establishing the second dhyāna,
if one is free from vicāra and prīti,
there is only the factor of sukha.
The third dhyāna is established as being endowed with the abandonment of three types [of suffering]. The fourth dhyāna is established [as being endowed with the abandonment of all suffering].
Therefore, one-pointedness of mind is divided into four types.
This is the second [section].
Explaining the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
The treatise says:
"The dhyānas have already been analyzed."
What are the formless [attainments]?
The verse says:
The formless are likewise; they consist of four aggregates and are free from the lower stages.
Together with the three aforementioned preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*),
these are collectively termed "formless" (*ārūpya*) because they are devoid of the perception of form. The subsequent arising of form from the mind— namely,
the three [realms] beginning with Infinite Space— is designated by names established according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*).
"Neither-perception-nor-non-perception": it is so named because of its dullness and inferiority.
The commentary states:
"The formless [attainments] are also like this."
The essence of the formless attainments consists of four,
each having two types: those that constitute birth in the formless realm and those that constitute meditative attainment.
The World Chapter has already explained that meditative absorption (samādhi) lacks a material form and is also subsumed under the nature of the wholesome (kuśala).
One-pointedness of mind is described as being "thus" because it is identical to that of the form realm.
As for the four aggregates:
However, the nature of its accompanying factors consists of only four aggregates,
because it lacks form.
"Excluding the aggregate of form" means that it is distinct from the lower stages;
this clarifies the differentiation.
Although their essential nature and characteristics as one-pointedness are without distinction,
they are divided into four types because they arise free from the lower stages.
Detached from the fourth dhyāna,
one is established in the designation "the sphere of infinite space. Detached from the sphere of space, one is established in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
One establishes the sphere of infinite consciousness,
arising from the departure from the sphere of consciousness;
one establishes the sphere of nothingness.

Having emerged from the sphere of nothingness, one establishes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; together with the three upper access concentrations (sāmantaka), these are collectively termed "those who have eliminated the perception of form.
These refer to the four fundamental [dhyānas].
The formless [attainments],
together with the three higher formless [attainments] and their preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
These seven are collectively termed the "accessory stage of the sphere of infinite space" (ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka), excluding the perception of form;
they have not yet attained this name because they take the forms of the lower stages as their object.
Because there is the perception of form,
"formless" refers to that which is without form;
this occurs within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
It is called "formless" (ārūpya) because it lacks form;
this is established according to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
The Mahīśāsaka school and others maintain that there are material phenomena within the formless realm.
Because form is subtle, the name "formless" (*ārūpya*) is established.
Question: For many eons in the formless realm, [how is it that...]?
When the continuity of form is severed and one subsequently passes away to be reborn below,
from what does form arise?
The verse replies that "subsequent matter arises from the mind," meaning that it arises from the maturation cause (vipāka-hetu) of matter produced in the past.
The habitual tendencies reside in the mind;
their functional capacity now ripens.
Therefore, the present form arises from that mind.

This arising is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation based on the Sautrāntika school. Regarding the statement that the three names, such as "Infinite Space," are established according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*):
this refers to the stage of preparatory application prior to cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Because of weariness with the sphere of visible forms,
one forms a resolute perception;
when the preparatory application for "unbounded space" is accomplished, [the sphere of infinite space arises].
It is called the Sphere of Infinite Space; furthermore, during the stage of preparatory application,
one becomes weary of infinite space and gives rise to the perception of resolute conviction.
When the preparatory application for contemplating infinite consciousness is perfected,
it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Furthermore, within that preparatory application...
Becoming weary of infinite consciousness,
one gives rise to the perception of resolute conviction and relinquishes all that exists.
Abiding in silence, when the preparatory application is perfected,
it is called the Sphere of Nothingness. As for the establishment of the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception," it is because [that state] is dull and inferior.
The fourth name is established because perception is dull and inferior; that is to say,
there is no superior perception of clear wisdom belonging to the lower stages.

It receives the name "Non-perception" because it possesses a dull and inferior perception; it is named "Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception" because that perception is so faint as to be indistinguishable from its absence.
Therefore, because the perception (*saṃjñā*) in that realm is dull and inferior,
the name "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is established based on its essential nature.
The first three formless attainments are established by way of their preparatory application;
the fourth is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Established according to their essential nature,
this third section clarifies the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation;
second, a detailed explanation.
Furthermore, to explain the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in general, the treatise says:
"The formless realms have already been analyzed; what, then, are the meditative attainments?"
The verse says:
These fundamental attainments are eight; the first seven each have three types—namely, the relishing, the pure, and the untainted; the last has two types—the relishing and the pure.
"Flavoring" refers to that which is associated with craving;
"pure" refers to mundane wholesomeness, which is precisely what is relished; and "untainted" refers to the supramundane.
The commentary states:
These eight fundamental attainments consist of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
The fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) comprise eight types in total.
Of these, each of the first seven has three varieties: namely, those characterized by attachment (*āsvādanasamprayukta*), those that are pure (*śuddha*), and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
In each of the preceding seven stages,
there are three types of one-flavor meditative attainment (*ekarasa-samāpatti*).
This refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because craving is able to relish and become attached,
it is called "savoring" (*āsvāda*).
Because that meditative absorption is associated with craving,
it receives the name "tasting" (āsvādana).
The other two are the pure attainments (śuddha-samāpatti).
This refers to mundane wholesome concentration,
which arises in association with various pure and white dharmas such as non-attachment and so forth.
The "attainment of purity" refers to the three untainted meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*), namely,
supramundane concentration (*lokottara-samādhi*). As for the subsequent two types— tasting (*āsvādana*) and pure (*śuddha*)— they are as follows:
The subsequent stage is the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
There are two kinds of meditative attainments there, namely, those characterized by relish and those that are pure; this is because [the former] are dull and inferior in their conceptualization.
There is no untainted [state] here.
"Savoring" refers to that which is associated with craving;
this explains the concentration of savoring.
Craving is called "taste.
Since meditative absorption is associated with craving,
it is therefore termed "absorption of taste" (*āsvādanā-samādhi*).
"Purity" refers to mundane wholesomeness;
this explains "pure concentration.
This is precisely that which is relished and clung to.
This pure attainment is the object of relish for the preceding relishing meditative concentration.

That is to say, when a pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) arises by extinguishing a relishing concentration (*āsvādana-samādhi*), one develops a deep attachment toward that pure concentration which has already arisen and is now being experienced.
The untainted (anāsrava) is said to be supramundane because craving does not take it as its object; thus,
it is not something to be relished.
From this fourth [section] onward,
the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are explained individually; therein are two parts.
First, the factors of dhyāna are explained;
second, the pure attainments (śuddha-samāpatti) are explained.
Within the former, there are six divisions.
First, clarifying the number of dhyāna factors;
second, clarifying the essential nature of the factors;
third, clarifying that defiled states lack these factors.
The fourth clarifies that it is called "immovable";
the fifth clarifies that there are differences in the arising and experiencing [of results];
the sixth clarifies the arousal of a humble mind.
Furthermore, regarding the first clarification on the number of factors of dhyāna,
the treatise states:
"In the four dhyānas..."
How many factors does each [dhyāna] possess?
The verse says:
The first dhyāna has five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi.
The second [dhyāna] has four factors; the third dhyāna, characterized by inner purity, joy, bliss, and concentration, possesses five factors;
the fourth [dhyāna], characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and concentration, has four factors;
and the [formless] concentration characterized by equanimity and neutral feeling.
The commentary states:
It is exclusively pure and untainted within the four dhyānas.
There are eighteen factors. Within the first dhyāna, there are five factors:
first, vitarka (applied thought).
2. Investigation; 3. Joy; 4. Bliss.
Regarding the five types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the second dhyāna consists of only four factors:
first, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*);
second, joy (*prīti*).
The third dhyāna possesses five factors: the three kinds of bliss and equanimity. The fourth dhyāna possesses five factors.
The third dhyāna is endowed with five branches.
The commentary on "equanimity of application" states:
because it is equanimity within the great wholesome ground (*mahābhūmika*), it is called "equanimity of application. Second is right mindfulness.
Third is right wisdom;
fourth is pleasant feeling;

fifth is meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Of these, the first two are the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), while this pleasant feeling is the bliss [of the fourth dhyāna]. This is the fourth dhyāna.
There are only four factors:
first, the purification of equanimity through practice;
second, the purification of mindfulness, which is free from the eight calamities.
It receives the name "pure.
This is the explanation found in the subsequent text. Third, regarding the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant:
this refers to the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) mentioned in the verse. Question: For what reason are pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth established in the first two dhyānas?
Equanimity of application is not established in the first dhyāna; it is established in the latter two dhyānas,
whereas pliancy is not so established.
Answer: In the third dhyāna, one abandons extreme joy;
in the fourth dhyāna, one abandons extreme pleasure;
therefore, equanimity (upekṣā) is established.
Since the first two [stages] do not establish the application of equanimity (praśrabdhi), they establish pliancy (praśrabdhi).
Question: Does faith (śraddhā) pervade all stages?
Why is it that confidence alone is established as a factor only in the second dhyāna?
Answer: Because it arises in accordance with superior, pure confidence.
It must rely on great joy,
because the second dhyāna possesses superior joy.
The factor of internal clarity is established.
Question: Since wisdom permeates all stages, why is it [specifically] mentioned in the third dhyāna?
Wisdom is established as a factor [of enlightenment].
The answer is: because they possess pleasant feeling, they become attached to this pleasure.
One does not take delight in the higher stages; to counteract this,
the factor of right wisdom is established.
Question: Since mindfulness (smṛti) is present throughout all stages (bhūmi),
why is it established as a distinct factor (aṅga) only in the third and fourth dhyānas?
Answer: This third dhyāna is [so called] because it is overwhelmed by the superior joy of the second dhyāna; as for the fourth dhyāna, [it is so called because it is free from that].
It acts as an obstacle to the superior bliss of the third dhyāna;
because it is obstructed by the lower stage,
one remains defiled within one's own stage.
One cannot achieve liberation [thereby].
For this reason, the Blessed One exhorted one to abide in right mindfulness.
Question: Why [are these] the first three dhyānas?
The [first] four dhyānas each possess five factors;
the [last] two dhyānas each possess four factors.
Answer: Because the various evils of the desire realm are difficult to sever,
difficult to destroy, and difficult to transcend.
The first dhyāna must possess five factors.
In the second dhyāna, there is an extremely heavy joy (*prīti*) that is difficult to sever,
difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
The third dhyāna is established with five factors;
the first and the third [dhyānas] do not possess such [factors].
Therefore, [these factors exist] in the second and the fourth.
Only four factors are established.
Furthermore, it is explained that this is for the sake of conforming to the method of transcending meditative absorption;
that is, one transcends from a five-factored absorption and enters another five-factored absorption.
Furthermore, from a four-limbed concentration,
one transcends into a four-limbed concentration;
this is because the limbs are equal.
It is easy to transcend.
From this second [section] onward,
the nature of the constituent members is clarified.
The treatise says:
Since there are eighteen names for the factors of dhyāna,
how many distinct entities are there in total among them?
The verse says:
These are eleven real entities; the first two are bliss and pliancy;
inner serenity is itself the faculty of faith; and joy is the feeling of joy.
The commentary states:
Although there are eighteen names,
the actual entities are eleven.
That is to say, the first [dhyāna] has five factors,
which are five real entities;
as for the second dhyāna:
The three branches are the same as before;
adding one internal purity makes six in total.
In the third dhyāna, the factors of concentration are the same as before,
with four additional factors added.
With the aforementioned [three] factors,
these total ten. In the fourth dhyāna,
three factors are the same as before, with the addition of the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
With the addition of the [previous] two, there are eleven.
Question: Why are the first two already said to possess the factor of joy (*sukha*)?
Why is it that the third [dhyāna] is said to have an increase in pleasant feeling?
The verse answers: "In the first two, pleasure is pliancy."

This means that because it has already been abandoned,
it cannot sever itself;
for it is bound by itself.
One cannot abandon the higher [stages],
because they have already been transcended;
the intermediate dhyāna is pure.
Furthermore, it does not abandon the afflictions;
therefore, it is called a "preparatory stage" (*sāmantaka*).
From this, the eighth [stage] follows.
This clarifies the distinctions among the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The treatise asks:
"How many preparatory stages are there?"

The first question concerns which feelings (*vedanā*) are associated [with the dhyānas]. The second question concerns whether [the factors] such as "tasting" (*āsvādana*) are all fully present [in each]. Regarding the third question, the verse says: "The eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) possess equanimity and are pure;

the first is also noble (*ārya*), or else three. The commentary explains: [The eight preparatory stages are associated with the feeling of equanimity and are exclusively pure. The first [preparatory stage] is also noble, or else [it may be associated with three types of feeling].
Regarding the "eight preparatory stages":
the answer to the first question concerns the four fundamental dhyānas.
The four formless [attainments] each have their own preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), which together with the eight fundamental [formless attainments] constitute [the eighteen].
For the sake of entering [the main stages],
the one who abandons [the lower] answers the second question:
these are the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Because all [mental states] are associated with relinquishment and function through deliberate effort,
there is no joy or bliss.
"Pure syllables and the first are also noble, or else three":
this answers the third question.
"Pure" refers to the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
All are subsumed under pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*).
The first is also that of the noble ones (*ārya*).
It is the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna.
They also include the untainted (*anāsrava*).
These eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are all entirely free from attachment (*asvāda*).
Because it is the path of detachment from passion.
"Or three" means that the word "or" indicates that there is another distinct explanation.
At first, in the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-samādhi), there is an attainment with relish (sāsvāda-samāpatti),
but the fundamental [dhyāna] has not yet arisen.
Because they also crave this,
they have not yet reached the three types of meditative attainments (samāpatti) that are fully present therein.
From this ninth [section] onward,
the differences among the meditative concentrations (samādhi) are clarified.
The verse says:
The intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka; it possesses [the other factors] and consists solely of the feeling of equanimity.
Explanation: This refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
Without vitarka and with only vicāra,
it possesses all three meditative attainments (samāpatti) and is associated exclusively with equanimity (upekṣā).
What is called "the intermediate" refers to the first dhyāna,
which is associated with vitarka and vicāra.
From the second dhyāna upward,
there is neither vitarka nor vicāra;
this applies to all except for the intermediate dhyāna.
Because it possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka, it is superior to the first [dhyāna] but has not yet reached the second;
it is on the basis of this meaning that [it is so designated].
The intermediate name is established;
this concentration can bring about the fruit of the Great Brahma realm for those who practice it extensively.
For the sake of the Great Brahmā,
following this fourth [section],
the various samādhis are elucidated.
Among these, first, the three beginning with vitarka and vicāra are clarified;
second, the three beginning with simple emptiness (śūnyatā) are clarified; third, the three beginning with the "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) are clarified.

The fourth [section] explains the cultivation of the four meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Regarding the first concentration, which consists of the triad of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth,
the treatise states:
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) have already been explained. What, then, are the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*)?
The Sūtra speaks of meditative concentration.
In total, there are three types:
first, with vitarka and vicāra;
second, without vitarka and with vicāra only.
Third is that which is without vitarka and without vicāra. What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The first [dhyāna] has both vitarka and vicāra; the middle [dhyānas] have only vicāra; the higher [dhyānas] have neither.
Regarding the commentary:
"The first has both vitarka and vicāra."
"Initial" refers to the first dhyāna;
"lower" refers to the threshold (anāgamya).
This [state] possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
This means that because it is associated with both vitarka and vicāra;
"only vicāra" refers to the intermediate dhyāna.
It is the samādhi that is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra.
Regarding the phrase "above there is none":
From the second dhyāna upwards,
up to the peak of existence,
there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
This is called the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*).
Following this second [section],
there is the clarification of the three types of emptiness and so forth taken individually.
The treatise says:
The sūtras further speak of three kinds of samādhi:
first, emptiness;...
Second is wishlessness;
third is signlessness.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Emptiness refers to emptiness and non-self; signlessness refers to the cessation [of suffering];
wishlessness refers to the remaining ten aspects associated with the aspects of the Truths.
This [insight] is both pure and untainted. Regarding the statement that the untainted constitutes the three gates of liberation:
"emptiness" refers to emptiness and non-self.
The concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) associated with emptiness and non-self.
Emptiness is the emptiness of "mine";
it is not that "I" empty my self.
Therefore, there are these two aspects of practice.
Both are designated as "emptiness.
Regarding "signlessness," it refers to the signless samādhi, which is the cessation of the four [marks].
It refers to the meditative concentration associated with the four modes of activity that take the Truth of Cessation as their object.
Nirvana is free from the ten marks;
therefore, it is called "signless.
Concentration takes this signlessness as its object.
It receives the name "signless" (animitta).
As for the "ten signs," they refer to the five [objects] beginning with form (rūpa) and so forth.
Regarding the two types [of persons], male and female,

the "wishless" (*apraṇihita*) refers to those associated with the ten aspects of the remaining truths, excluding the aspect of duration (*sthiti*) among the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
This explains the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
This refers to the meditative concentration associated with ten modes of activity that take other truths as their object.
As for the "remaining truths," this refers to the remaining truth of suffering,
which has the characteristic of impermanence and suffering.
Under the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), there are four: cause (hetu), origination (samudaya), production (jāti), and condition (pratyaya).
Under the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), there are four.
The Path is like proceeding forth.
These are called the ten aspects of the remaining Truths:
impermanence and suffering.
Furthermore, because the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) and the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*)— by virtue of these two truths— are objects to be reviled and abandoned;
and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) is like a boat or a raft.
Because one must necessarily relinquish them,
the contemplation of those truths receives the name "wishless" (apraṇihita).
Because there is no longing or delight,
it is called "wishless" (apraṇihita);
that is to say, this transcends all that is currently confronted.
Because the truths of the origin and the path are to be reviled and abandoned,
[the investigation] regarding the truth of suffering is as follows:
Emptiness does not have the characteristic of self;
it is not something to be weary of or abandoned,
because its characteristics are similar to those of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement "this [samādhi] is common to both the pure and the untainted":
these aforementioned superior concentrations each pertain to both types.
The second refers to the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*),
distinguished by their respective mundane (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*) meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Regarding the three untainted gates of liberation:
only those that are exclusively untainted are called the three gates of liberation.
Because it serves as the gateway to liberation and nirvāṇa,
this is the third [section].
This clarifies the three types of emptiness, etc.
The treatise states:
"The sūtras further speak of three kinds of samādhi."
First, the emptiness of emptiness;
second, the wishlessness of wishlessness;
third, the signlessness of signlessness.
What are its characteristics? The verse says: It is twofold;
it takes as its objects the two [truths] that are beyond training, and it has emptiness and impermanence as its characteristics.
Subsequently, one takes the concentration on the signless as its object; it is [the attainment of] non-analytical cessation, which is tranquil.
For those with outflows, it is not occasional. This refers to the separation from the seven upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The commentary says:
"Reiterating the second" refers to the heading of the name.
"Based on those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) below," etc.
This is the correct explanation.
Because they are both equally empty,
they are called the "double two."
Conditioned by the syllables of one beyond training,
they flow into the lower three phrases; therein,
one grasps the characteristics of emptiness and impermanence.
First, grasping at the characteristic of emptiness;
second, grasping at the characteristic of impermanence.
Regarding grasping at the characteristic of emptiness:
This explains "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
The meditative concentration of the emptiness of emptiness takes as its object the previously mentioned unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) emptiness-trance (*śūnya-samādhi*).
One grasps that mark of emptiness;
the mark of emptiness accords with revulsion because it is superior to non-self.
One grasps only the characteristic of emptiness and does not grasp non-self;
one grasps emptiness within emptiness.
Therefore it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
It is like burning a corpse and turning it over with a staff.
Once the corpse has been completely consumed,
the staff should also be burned,
because it was previously characterized by emptiness.
Having burned away the afflictions,
one subsequently gives rise to the concentration on emptiness and, through weariness, relinquishes the preceding emptiness.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
To grasp at the characteristic of non-permanence is to explain the "wishlessness of wishlessness."
The wishless-without-wish takes as its object the preceding wishless meditative concentration of one beyond training,
apprehending it through the aspect of impermanence.
Contemplating the wishless in what precedes,
one forms the perception of impermanence; then, one becomes weary of and relinquishes the wishless.
There is no aspiration and no delight.
To speak again of "no aspiration":
it means not grasping at the characteristics of suffering, nor its causes, origins, or conditions.
Because these five are not the characteristics of the untainted (*anāsrava*),
they do not apprehend the Path and so forth.
As for the four aspects of activity (*ākāra*):
It is for the sake of wearying of and relinquishing;
that is to say, this wishlessness does not aspire to the noble path.
By forming conceptions such as the characteristics of the Path,
one takes delight in the Path; because of this inability to feel weary [of saṃsāra], [one does not attain liberation].

Regarding the statement that "the subsequent concentration on signlessness takes non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object of tranquility," this explains the "repeated signlessness. It is the signlessness of signlessness (*animittānimitta*).
It takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the signless samādhi (animitta-samādhi) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
because there is no analytical cessation for untainted phenomena (anāsrava-dharma).
Because one contemplates that the signless is non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
there is further signlessness upon the signless.
It is called "signless-signless" because it contemplates non-analytical cessation,
grasping only its aspect of stillness.
It is not a cessation that is sublime, free from confusion, or characterized by permanence;
nor does it constitute the characteristic of cessation, because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
It does not produce excellent marks;
it is not a fruit of disjunction;
it does not produce the characteristic of disjunction.
Regarding those with outflows (sāsrava) who are not occasional (asamayavimukta):
their three types of meditative concentration (samādhi) are exclusively with outflows.
Because they are weary of the Noble Path,
these are exclusively humans of the three continents who are non-learner (aśaikṣa) and not subject to fixed times (akālika).
The statement that "one can give rise to this meditative absorption, being free from the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) above" clarifies that the three absorptions—
namely the "further emptiness" (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth— arise based on eleven stages.
That is to say: the desire realm,
the threshold concentration, and the intermediate concentration.
The four fundamental dhyānas and the four fundamental formless attainments;
these are from the first dhyāna upward.
Regarding the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka-bhūmi*):
because they lack the three [samādhis] such as the profound emptiness (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*) and so forth, they are said to be "detached" (*viveka*).
From this fourth [stage],...
This clarifies the cultivation of the four meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
The treatise states:
"The sūtras further speak of four kinds of meditative concentration."
First, for dwelling in happiness in the present life;
second, for attaining superior knowledge and vision;
third, for attaining analytical wisdom.
Fourth, for the sake of the permanent exhaustion of all outflows,
one cultivates samādhi.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
To attain happiness in the present life, one cultivates all wholesome meditative absorptions;
to attain superior knowledge and vision, one cultivates the pure supernormal power of the divine eye.
In order to attain the wisdom of discernment, one cultivates various preparatory virtues;
in order to attain the exhaustion of all outflows, one cultivates the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). Commentary:
For those who cultivate various wholesome meditative absorptions (dhyāna) in order to attain happiness in the present life,
the term "wholesome" comprehensively includes both the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava),
as they cultivate these various wholesome meditative absorptions.
Because they have attained abiding in the happiness of the present life,
they cultivate the pure divine eye and attain superior knowledge and vision.
Knowledge and vision are precisely the wisdom associated with the pure visual consciousness.
If one cultivates the various preparatory virtues of the three realms as well as untainted virtue,
one attains analytical wisdom.
Cultivating the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi),
one attains the eternal exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava). *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 28.
27. Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa, Treatise Volume Twenty-nine.
This second section elucidates the qualities that depend [upon the meditative absorptions]. It contains six parts: first, the elucidation of the four immeasurables;
second, the elucidation of the eight liberations; third, the elucidation of the eight bases of mastery; and fourth, the elucidation of the ten spheres of totality.
The fifth clarifies the physical basis upon which they depend;
the sixth clarifies the objects for arising from meditative absorption.
First, regarding the first clarification, the four immeasurables:
The treatise says:
Having thus explained the meditative concentrations that serve as the basis,
one should now distinguish the virtues produced by relying upon those concentrations.
Among all the various merits,
the immeasurables are first distinguished.
The verse says:

The immeasurables are of four kinds; because they are the antidotes to hatred and so forth, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) have the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Joy (*muditā*) has the nature of joy, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) has the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*).
Their aspects (*ākāra*) are, respectively, the wish to bestow happiness and the wish to remove suffering.
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) takes sentient beings as its object; it arises in the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.
The other six [immeasurables] consist of either five or ten [types];
they cannot sever any afflictions. When arising in the human realm, they become threefold through meditative absorption.
The commentary states:
The first phrase provides a general indication;
the next phrase clarifies that there are only four.
The next two lines set forth its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The next three lines clarify its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
The final line clarifies its object of focus (*ālambana*).
The next two lines clarify the basis upon which it relies;
the next line clarifies the non-interruption of afflictions;
and the final line clarifies the location and its accomplishment.
The four kinds of immeasurables are:
first, loving-kindness;
second, compassion.
Third is sympathetic joy;
fourth is equanimity.
As for the term "immeasurable":
Because it takes immeasurable sentient beings as its object,
because it draws forth immeasurable merit,
and because it brings about immeasurable results.
Question: For what reason are there only these four types? Answer:
The verse states "because they counteract hatred and so forth"; the phrase "and so forth" includes the three obstacles such as harmfulness. Thus, there are these four obstacles.
First, anger;
second, harmfulness;
third, lack of joy.
The four [immeasurables] are loving-kindness and the others; they are established as antidotes to these four predominant obstacles of sensual desire and ill will.
Compassion (maitrī) and loving-kindness (karuṇā) are non-aversion;
their essential nature consists of joy, equanimity, and non-greed.
There are two types of compassion.
Its essence is non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
According to the Master [Vasubandhu], the function of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-hatred,
while compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).
Joy is the feeling of joy;
equanimity is non-attachment.
These are loving-kindness and the others.
If taken together with its retinue, its substance consists of the five aggregates. Question: If it has the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*), how can it counteract hatred (*dveṣa*)?
Answer: This [affliction] is hatred, which is the object to be counteracted;
for it is induced by craving.
This is according to the Master of the Treatise.
The essence of equanimity consists of the two dharmas of non-attachment and non-hatred.
Its mental aspect (*ākāra*) is clarified by the description: "bestowing happiness, removing suffering, and gladdening sentient beings."
Bestowing happiness is loving-kindness (*maitrī*);
removing suffering is compassion (*karuṇā*);
and sympathetic joy is rejoicing (*muditā*).
Sentient beings and so forth are the object of equanimity;
that is, being equal toward enemies and kin,
one abandons enmity and abandons attachment.
This is called equanimity.
May all sentient beings attain such happiness.
Reflecting in this way,
one enters the meditative attainment of loving-kindness,
making this aspiration for all sentient beings:
Contemplating, "May they be free from such suffering," one enters the meditative attainment of compassion (*karuṇā-samāpatti*).
How joyful it would be if all sentient beings were to obtain happiness and be free from suffering!
Reflecting in this way, one enters the meditative attainment of joy.
All classes of sentient beings are equal and impartial.
Thinking thus, "There is neither enemy nor relative," one enters the meditative attainment of equanimity (*upekṣā-samāpatti*), taking sentient beings of the desire realm as its object.
This clarifies the objective referents:
these four immeasurables universally take all sentient beings of the desire realm as their object.
Regarding "not taking the upper realms as an object":
this means that [the lower wholesome roots] can counteract hindrances such as hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth,
whereas hatred and the like do not exist in the upper realms.

"It does not take the upper realms as its object" means that the immeasurable joy (*muditā*) takes the first two dhyānas as its basis; "the remaining six, or five, or ten" clarifies the basis of the other immeasurables.
This explains the basis (*āśraya*). As for the immeasurable joy: [it is based on the first two dhyānas].
"Established only based on the first two dhyānas; the remaining six" refers to the other three immeasurables,
which rely upon six stages.
That is to say: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), and the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara).
"Or five": some masters say that it relies solely upon the five stages.
Excluding the stage of "not yet arrived" (anāgamya),
that is, the cultivation of the immeasurables (apramāṇa),
constitutes the stage of leisurely progression (sa-vicāra).
Because only those who have already abandoned desire are able to cultivate them,
the *anāgamya* stage is excluded. Alternatively, some maintain that these four immeasurables...
It generally relies upon the ten stages,
namely: the desire realm and the four fundamental dhyānas.
And the preparatory stages of the four dhyānas,
as well as the intermediate stage;
this is intended to include both the concentrated and non-concentrated states.
The fundamental and preparatory practices are all subsumed within the immeasurables; therefore,
they pertain to all ten stages.
Regarding those who cannot sever the various afflictions:
these four immeasurables are incapable of severing the afflictions.
This refers to three meanings.

First, because it is subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas with outflows, the previous text has already explained that these fundamental states do not sever the afflictions. Second, it refers to attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).
Because it arises in association [with other mental factors],
the abandonment of afflictions requires genuine attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*); since this [present state] is merely resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), [it cannot effect such abandonment].
It cannot sever [the afflictions],
because it takes all sentient beings as its object three times over.
To sever the delusions, one must necessarily attend to mental objects (dharma-manasikāra).
Because this takes sentient beings as its object, it does not sever the afflictions.
As for the statement in the preceding text that "this remedies the four obstacles": [it refers to this very practice].
In the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), it subdues anger and the like;
alternatively, because it can cause these [defilements] to be severed and further distanced,
it was previously stated that this serves as the antidote to the four obstacles.
If one relies on the four immeasurables in their fundamental form,
they do not actually sever the afflictions.
Question: At the stage of initial training, how does one cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables]?
Answer: It means first reflecting upon the happiness that one has personally experienced.
Then he formed this thought:
"May all sentient beings equally experience such happiness as this.
If they were originally..."
When afflictions increase and flourish,
one is unable to direct the mind with such equanimity;
one should instead divide sentient beings into three categories.
Regarding those who are friends, neutral parties, or enemies: friends are further divided into three types—superior, middling, and inferior.
As for superior friends:
This refers to the arising of the Dharma-body.
As for the "intimate friend" therein,
it refers to the intersection of wealth and Dharma.
Regarding "inferior friends," this refers to those who associate solely for the sake of wealth; "neutral persons" constitute one category;
and "enemies" are further divided into three types; as for "superior enemies," they are those who harbor deep-seated hostility.
This refers to those who seize one's reputation, life, and kinsmen, or act as enemies among friends;
it refers to those who seize one's own life, its conditions, and requisites—
these are the inferior enemies.
That is to say, seizing one's relatives and friends,
as well as the conditions for life and essential requisites;
these together constitute seven categories.
The Chapter on Discrimination is concluded.
First, one should arouse genuine sincerity toward those who are superior.
Having formed the resolute conviction of bestowing happiness, once this vow is accomplished,
[it extends] toward those who are middling and inferior relatives.
One also gradually cultivates such resolute conviction;
having attained equanimity toward the three categories of relatives, one proceeds.
Next, regarding those who are neutral,
and those who are inferior, middling, or superior enemies,
one should likewise gradually cultivate such resolute conviction (adhimukti).
Through the power of repeated practice,
one is able to give rise to the aspiration for others' happiness even toward those who have been superior enemies.
Together with one's parents and others,
one cultivates this resolute conviction until it becomes irreversible.
Next, regarding the object of focus,
one gradually cultivates it to become expansive;
that is, one gradually extends the mental image.
Contemplate a single village,
a single country,
or a single region.
To cause all worlds to be filled with happiness is what constitutes cultivation.
The immeasurable state of loving-kindness is accomplished by one who cultivates the dharma of compassion;
that is to say, they contemplate sentient beings submerged in the ocean of manifold sufferings.
One then makes the aspiration that they all may attain liberation.
As for the cultivation of the dharma of sympathetic joy (*muditā*),
it means conceiving the thought that sentient beings obtain happiness and are freed from suffering.
This brings deep joy and consolation; it is truly blissful!
The cultivation of equanimity (upekṣā) first arises from the state of neutrality, and proceeds gradually until—
To be able to give rise to a mind of equanimity toward one's superiors,
and to achieve the three qualities together with those of middle status— this is [the third].
These four immeasurables arise in human beings and not in others;
one attains them at any given time.
These must necessarily be of three kinds.
Following this second [section],
the eight liberations are explained.
The treatise says:
Having already distinguished the immeasurables,
we shall next distinguish the liberations.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of liberation; the first three have non-attachment as their nature;
they occur in pairs, one by one, and in the dhyānas; the four formless absorptions are wholesome.
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception arises immediately after the "subtle-subtle" state (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*).
It emerges from a pure mind of its own level or from an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind of a lower level.
It has three objects: the desire realm, the visible [form], and the path belonging to the category of the form realm. It possesses four objects: the same three plus the untainted. It is the path.
"From the beginning, suffering, its origin, and its cessation; non-analytical cessation and space.
Commentary: The first phrase provides a general indication.
The next two lines specifically clarify the first three liberations;
the fourth line specifically clarifies the subsequent four liberations;
and the second verse-line specifically clarifies the eighth liberation.
The final verse generally clarifies the objects of focus.
Regarding the eight kinds of liberation:
the first is that which possesses the perception of internal form.
The liberation by contemplating external forms refers to the presence of desire for the perception of form within one's own internal body.
To eliminate this craving,
one contemplates external impurities,
such as the color of a livid corpse and so forth.
Because it causes greed not to arise,
it is called liberation.
Second is the internal perception of formlessness.
The liberation by contemplating external forms:
that is, being without the perception of form or craving regarding one's own internal body.
Although greed has already been eliminated,
one contemplates external impurities, such as the color of a livid corpse, for the sake of making it firm and stable.
Causing greed not to arise is called liberation.
This is the third pure liberation.
One dwells having personally realized it through direct experience;
that is, by contemplating pure form,
one prevents lust from arising.
This is called the "pure liberation.
Regarding the contemplation of pure form,
it reveals that the contemplation becomes increasingly superior.
This is realized within the body through this pure liberation;
it is called "bodily realization," which is fully perfected and complete.
Abiding in this concentration is called "abiding fully endowed with" the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*),
which constitute the next four liberations (*vimokṣa*).
These four liberations are each called "liberations" because they are able to relinquish the craving for the lower stages.
The eighth liberation is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
having realized it through the body and dwelling therein,
one turns away from and abandons feeling and the other aggregates.
It is called "liberation" (vimukti).
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
this is translated as "liberation."
This means the sense of turning away and abandoning.
Regarding the first three having non-attachment as their nature:
these refer to the first three liberations.
It has non-attachment as its essence because it directly counteracts attachment. Among the three [types of concentration],
the first two operate through the aspect of impurity.
Because it forms the various mental images (*saṃjñā*) such as the livid corpse and so forth,
the third liberation proceeds with the aspect of purity.
Because they function as the modes of activity that produce pure, radiant,
and fresh manifestations, these three assistants are all of the nature of the five aggregates.
Regarding "the two-by-two fixed [attainments]":
this refers to the two-by-two fixed attainments and the one-by-one fixed attainment.
The "upper two" refer to the first two liberations;
the "lower two" refer to the first two dhyānas.
Because the first two liberations rely upon the first two dhyānas,
they are designated as the "two pairs of concentrations."
Regarding "one by one":
"one" refers to the third liberation;
this refers to that single liberation.
It arises based solely on the fourth dhyāna;
this is called "one by one dhyāna.
This is because of the fourth dhyāna.
Because the mind is pure and free from the eight afflictions,
there is the "pure liberation."
Regarding the wholesome states of the four formless absorptions:
the four formless liberations have wholesome meditative concentration as their essence.
It is neither indeterminate nor defiled,
because it is not liberation;
nor is it mundane wholesome [virtue].
Because their nature is weak and inferior.
As for non-material wholesome states that are dispersed,
they are like the mind at the moment of death.

Regarding the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) arising immediately after the subtle-subtle state: this is the liberation of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti-vimokṣa*).
It is that which involves the revulsion toward and turning away from feeling and perception.
Some explain it as being weary of and turning away from all minds that have an object;
others explain it as liberation from the hindrances to meditative concentration (samādhi-āvaraṇa), and thus it is called "liberation" (vimokṣa).
Following the subtle mind, this meditative absorption manifests; the mind that enters the attainment of cessation is, in total, of three kinds.
The first is the perceiving mind.
The second is the subtle mind;
the third is the extremely subtle mind.
These are contrasted with the preceding conceptual mind.
That which has already been called "subtle" is further refined; therefore,
it is named "ultra-subtle."
From the extremely subtle mind,
one enters the meditative attainment of cessation by means of the pure [mind] of its own level.

"Mind and the subsequent outflow-free [mind] that emerges" clarifies the mind that emerges from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This refers to the mind emerging from the absorption of cessation.
Either one gives rise to a pure mind of the Peak of Existence,
or one gives rise to an untainted mind of the lower Sphere of Nothingness.
Thus, the mind that enters [the meditative attainment] is exclusively impure (*sāsrava*).
It emerges from both impure and pure (*anāsrava*) minds.
Regarding the three objects, those visible in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are as follows:
The first three liberations take only the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) of the desire realm as their object.
As for the distinction [between them]:
The objects of the first two [knowledges] are loathsome;
the object of the third is desirable.
Regarding the fourth, its category consists of the path and the suffering, origin, and cessation of its own stage and the stages above it.
The four formless liberations each take as their objects the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation pertaining to their own level and the higher levels.
Furthermore, the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the nine stages serve as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).
As for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*), [they are not so].
The formless liberations also take as their objects the truths of suffering and origin belonging to their own level,
as well as the non-analytical cessation of the levels above.

Furthermore, they take as their objects the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) pertaining to the nine stages, the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the higher realms, and space (ākāśa). [Question: Regarding the third dhyāna...
"Is it not rather that there is no liberation?
The answer is: within the third dhyāna, there is nothing induced by visual consciousness.
Because of attachment to manifest colors,
and because of being agitated by the exquisite pleasures of one's own level.
Therefore, there is no liberation. Question: For what reason does the practitioner cultivate the pure liberation?
Answer: It is because he desires to inspire delight.
One cultivates the pure liberation;
the preceding contemplation of impurity causes the mind to become depressed and sorrowful.
Now, one cultivates the meditation on purity to stimulate and inspire joy; or,
it may be for the purpose of thoroughly knowing one's own capability.
That is to say: whether or not the previously cultivated liberation through the contemplation of impurity has been accomplished.
If one contemplates the aspect of purity,
