Question: For what reason are only the third and eighth liberations among those taught in the sūtras designated by the term "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*),
and not the other six?
The answer is: because among the eight [realms],
these two are superior, and because they are the limits of the two realms.
The third liberation, which receives the name "bodily realization," takes up only the aspect of purity.
Causing delusions not to arise is called the "excellent" eighth liberation.
Because it is without mind,
it is called "excellent.
The third liberation is situated at the limit of the form realm.
The eighth liberation is at the limit of the formless realm;
it follows from this third.
Explaining the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The treatise says:
"The liberations (*vimokṣa*) have already been analyzed."
Next, the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are explained.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of spheres of mastery; two are like the first liberation.
The next two are as in the second [section], and the final four are as in the third.
The commentary states:
There are eight kinds of spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
First, having the perception of internal forms,
one perceives external forms as limited.
Second, having the perception of internal forms...
One contemplates external forms as manifold;
third, being without internal perception of form,
one contemplates external forms as few.
Fourth, having no perception of internal forms,
one perceives external forms as manifold;
this is "having no perception of internal forms."
Contemplating external blue, yellow, red,
and white constitutes the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); together with the preceding [four], they form eight.
Among the eight [liberations], the first two are like the first liberation;
the next two are like the second liberation.
The latter four are like the third liberation.
When practicing the former liberations,
one is only able to abandon and turn away from a mind of craving.
One cannot control the objects;
subsequently, one cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
which can control the focal objects.
As one observes according to what is appropriate,
delusions will ultimately not arise;
one is thus able to subdue the objects of perception.
Because the mind excels over the objects,
they are called "mastery objects" (abhibhvāyatana). From this fourth [stage]...
Explaining the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The treatise says:
"The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) have already been analyzed."
Next, the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are distinguished.
The verse says:
There are ten kinds of spheres of totality; Eight are like the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa).
The latter two are pure and formless, taking the four aggregates of their own level as objects.
The commentary states:
There are ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
That is to say: one pervasively contemplates earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, as well as space and consciousness, and the two spheres of the infinite.
In all places, he observes them pervasively,
without any interval.
Therefore, they are called "totalities" (kṛtsnāyatana).
Among the ten, the first eight are like the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa).
That is to say, the eight intrinsic natures are all non-attachment;
this is so whether they are taken together with their associated factors.
All have the nature of the five aggregates;
they rely on the fourth dhyāna and take as their object visible forms of the desire realm.
The latter two spheres of totality correspond respectively to the formless attainments of infinite space and infinite consciousness; they are wholesome.
These constitute their intrinsic nature.
Each takes the four aggregates of its own level as its object.
It should be understood that herein, the practitioner who cultivates meditation...
From the various liberations,
one enters the various spheres of mastery;
from the various spheres of mastery...
One enters the various spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
because each subsequent one arises as superior to each preceding one;
that is to say, one cultivates the liberations (*vimokṣa*).
However, regarding the object of focus,
one grasps it only as a general mark of purity,
without yet being able to distinguish between blue, yellow, red, or white.
Although the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) can distinguish blue, yellow, red, and white,
they are not yet able to produce the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of "boundlessness."
Regarding the first four bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*):
one contemplates each [color], such as blue, as being boundless;
furthermore, one reflects upon what these blues and so forth depend upon.
Knowing that [the body] depends upon the great elements (mahābhūta),
one next contemplates each of the elements, such as earth, as being boundless.
One then further reflects upon this perceived form (rūpa).
By what is it vast? It is known to be so by virtue of space.
Next, one contemplates the sphere of infinite space.
He further reflects on what this consciousness that can awaken depends upon;
knowing it depends on the vast consciousness,
he contemplates the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Because this consciousness which serves as the basis has no separate basis,
one does not further cultivate it separately as a universal base (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
From this, the fifth [section] clarifies the physical basis upon which [the practitioner] relies.
The treatise states:
Regarding these three gateways of merit, such as liberation and so forth:
by what means are they attained? This is the first question.
Based on which body do these two questions arise?
The verse says:
Regarding the attainment of cessation, as previously explained; for all others, both types of acquisition apply.
The formless [attainments] depend on the three realms; the others arise only in the human realm.
Commentary: This refers to the deliverances of the meditative absorption of cessation.
The Chapter on Faculties has already been explained.
As for the remaining [states], such as the liberations and so forth,
they are all acquired through both types of attainment.
If it has been previously cultivated,
it is acquired through the abandonment of defilements; if it has not been previously practiced, [it is acquired through effort].
They are acquired through preparatory application:
the four formless liberations and the two universal bases of space and consciousness.
Each [of these] arises based on bodies within the three realms; the others arise only among humans due to the power of the teaching.
This applies to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
All of these can be manifested.
Following this, the sixth [section] clarifies the conditions for arising from meditative absorption.
The treatise says:
"All those born in the form and formless realms give rise to dhyāna and the formless attainments."
By what specific conditions?
The verse says:
Through the two realms, by means of causes and karma, one is able to give rise to the formless attainments.
The arising of dhyāna in the form realm is also due to the power of *dharmatā*.
Commentary: This refers to being born in the two higher realms.
It is entirely due to three conditions.
First, by the power of the cause;
that is to say, at a previous time.
Proximity and repeated practice serve as the causes for origination;
secondly, it is due to the power of karma.
This refers to karma previously created that brings about birth in a higher realm and is to be experienced in a subsequent life;
the maturation of that karma is now about to arise and manifest.
The power of influence can cause one to enter that meditative absorption;
third is the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*),
namely, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
When it is about to be destroyed,
sentient beings of the lower realms naturally become able to give rise to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the higher realms.
Born in the two higher realms,
they give rise to formless attainments through the power of causes and karma.
It is not by the power of natural law;
for in the heavens such as Anabhraka (Cloudless),
there is no destruction by calamity.
When one born in the realm of form gives rise to meditative absorption,
it occurs by virtue of the two aforementioned conditions as well as the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
If one is born in the desire realm and gives rise to a higher meditative absorption,
regarding the three aforementioned conditions:
Furthermore, by the power of the teaching,
from this second major section,
it clarifies the duration of the True Dharma remaining in the world.
If we clarify the meaning according to the three divisions,
what follows below constitutes the *pariṇāmanā* (concluding) section.
The treatise states:
The various dharma-gates previously analyzed were all for the purpose of widely upholding the World-Honored One’s teaching.
What is the single question regarding the True Dharma?
Regarding the two questions concerning how long [the Dharma] shall remain,
the verse says:
The Buddha’s True Dharma is twofold, Having the teachings and the realization as its essence.
"There are those who uphold, explain, and practice [this]—they shall abide in the world. Commentary:
The first two lines answer the initial question.
The final two lines answer the second question.
There are two aspects of the True Dharma (*saddharma*):
first, the teaching (*śāsana*).
Second, the proof by means of scripture refers to the sūtras,
the vinaya, and the abhidharma.
"Realization" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of the three vehicles.
When there are those who can uphold and correctly expound them,
the teaching remains in the world.
If there are those who are able to practice correctly according to the teaching,
the Buddha’s Dharma of realization will indeed abide in the world.
The Way relies on people for its propagation;
the Dharma depends on people for its endurance.
When people exist, the Dharma exists.
When the person perishes, the Dharma perishes.
Therefore, Vasubandhu said:
"Thus, it lasts for as long as those three persons remain in the world."
One should know that worldly phenomena abide for such a duration;
this is the general statement of the Noble Teaching.
The Śākya who realized the Dharma will remain for only a thousand years.
The duration of the Dharma’s abiding exceeds even this;
from this third [period]...
The fundamental tenets of the *Abhidharma-kośa* are divided into two parts:
first, the explicit exposition of the fundamental tenets.
Second, the lamentation and exhortation to study.
Now, to clarify the primary tenet:
the treatise states:
This treatise relies upon the Abhidharma.
By what principle does it explain the Abhidharma?
The verse says:
The principles established by the scholars of Kaśmīra are what I have mostly relied upon in my commentary on the Abhidharma;
any slight devaluation thereof is my own fault. It is the Muni who has determined the correct principles of the Dharma.
Thus he said.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra deliberate upon the principles of the Abhidharma.
It is well-established;
I have relied extensively upon it to explain the Abhidharmakośa.
To disparage even slightly [another] is my own fault;
it is for you to judge the correct principles of the Dharma.
This exists only in the World-Honored One and all Tathāgatas,
as well as among the great holy disciples;
this is the second [point] from here.
Expressing lamentation and exhorting to study;
this section is divided into two parts.
First, lamenting over people.
Second, the method of exhorting to study.
This is divided into two parts concerning those who lament:
first, the actual lamentation for such people.
The second part provides a double explanation of the lamentation.
Regarding the primary section on praising those among humans, it is divided into two:
first, the lamentation for those possessed of virtue.
Second, the arising of lamentation over loss.
First, regarding the lamentation for those who possess virtue,
the verse says:
The Great Master, the Eye of the World, has long since closed; those capable of serving as witnesses have for the most part perished.
[Commentary:
The Great Master of the three realms...
As the eyes of the world,
he has been in nirvana for a long time;
thus it is said that they are already closed.
Śāriputra and others,
who were worthy of being witnesses,
followed the Buddha into parinirvāṇa.
This is called "the extensive dispersal and extinction.
Following this second [section],
there is the lamentation arising from loss.
The verse says:
Those who do not perceive the True Reality and lack self-restraint, through their base discursive thoughts, disturb the Holy Teaching.
The commentary says:
Having already lost the Great Master,
and furthermore lacking Dharmakṣema,
all ordinary beings [are left without refuge].
Consequently, one lacks the eye of wisdom,
fails to perceive the ultimate truth,
and is unable to exercise self-restraint.
To give rise to evil discursive thoughts and to bring disorder and confusion to the holy teachings—
these are grave transgressions.
From this second section,
the re-explanation of the lamentation is divided into two parts.
First, the re-explanation of those possessing virtue.
This provides a double explanation to resolve potential objections.
First, regarding the double explanation of those who possess virtue,
the verse says:
"Having personally realized and returned to supreme tranquility, those who uphold his teachings have for the most part passed away.
Commentary: The Buddha is called "Self-Awakened" (Svayambhū).
Because he attained awakening without a teacher,
his nirvana has long since occurred;
his name has already returned to stillness.
Śāriputra and others who upheld those teachings have now also passed away. Following this,
the second section provides a further explanation regarding the arising of faults, with the verse stating:
The world is without refuge; it has lost its manifold virtues; there is no hook to restrain it, so that delusion turns according to its will. Commentary:
"The world is without refuge."
Because the Tathāgata and the assembly of great disciples— who possessed such virtues— have passed away,
these sentient beings lack the hook of the True Dharma to restrain the elephants of their afflictions; thus,
they give rise to attachments according to their own whims.
From this, the second [section]:
Exhortation to Study the Dharma.
The verse says:

Having known that the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is gradually perishing like [water] reaching the throat, when the power of these afflictions increases, one should seek liberation and not be negligent.

Commentary: This means that because the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is now being exhausted, it is like water reaching the throat; at such a time, when the power of the various afflictions increases, one must strive for liberation and not be lax.
Nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Vasubandhu composed various treatises.
The lifespan of the True Dharma gradually fades away and perishes,
like a person about to die whose breath reaches the throat.
In a mere moment they die; during this time,
their afflictions increase.
All wise persons should seek liberation;
do not allow negligence to give rise to afflictions.
Chapter One: Refuting the Self. Now, when clouds part and the moon appears, the obstruction vanishes and the sky becomes clear;
likewise, if one does not demolish the heterodox, [the truth cannot be revealed].
How, then, can the correct [teaching] be revealed?
There is indeed a profound reason for the intent behind the arrival of this chapter:
there are guests who are obstructed by appearances and children who are lost as to their direction.
Phenomena have no sovereign;
yet one arbitrarily gives rise to the grasping at a self.
Once the view of a self-body arises, [suffering follows].
Various afflictions arise accordingly,
causing one to drown in the river of the three realms of existence and turn one's back on the Eightfold Noble Path.
That such a transgression should occur— how tragic it is!
It is as if a master of debate were about to love only one child.
With sincere emotion, I have restrained my mind;
moved by sorrow and compassion for them,
I have therefore composed this treatise.
There are three types of adherents who hold differing views regarding the self (*ātman*).
The first is the Vātsīputrīya school.
Second, the Sāṃkhya school;
third, the Vaiśeṣika school.
These three views are refuted.
As explained at length in the prose commentary (*śāstra*), I shall now only explain the verses (*kārikā*).
It is impossible to present everything in detail;
I shall briefly set forth the essential framework.
This is considered the origin [of the name].
The Vātsīputrīya school is one of the eighteen schools.
During the time when the Buddha was in the world,
there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Vatsīputra.
Since this school’s tenets are identical to those of these non-Buddhists,
it is designated by their name.
This is for the purpose of refuting them within this chapter.
First he refutes the Vātsīputrīyas;
next he refutes the Sāṃkhyas;
finally he refutes the Vaiśeṣikas.
It is precisely because this school views its own disciples as being the same as non-Buddhists that it is utterly improper; therefore,
I shall first refute it.
Now, wishing to refute that [position], one first examines their reasoning. The *Śāstra* says:
"However, the Vātsīputrīya school maintains that the *pudgala* exists."
Its essence is neither identical to nor different from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The commentary explains:
they postulate a true self (*ātman*) called the *pudgala*.
This is called the "person" (pudgala).
Since the aggregates (skandhas) perish moment by moment,
they lack the capacity for transition [to another life].
However, because I am able to relinquish these aggregates and continue other aggregates as one who undergoes rebirth through various destinies,
I grasp at a real self-essence and name it the *pudgala*.
I reckon that the self and the aggregates are neither identical nor different,
and are neither annihilated nor eternal.
If one were to say that the aggregates are identical [to the self],...
If one says that with the cessation of the aggregates the self ceases, this constitutes the view of annihilationism. If, on the other hand,
one says that the aggregates are different [from the self]...
To think, "I exist when the aggregates have ceased," is the view of eternalism;
both [of these] fall into extremes.
Therefore, it is known that this self and the phenomena of the five aggregates are neither identical nor different, and neither annihilated nor eternal.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying:
"Is the self you grasp as real or as provisional?"
If it were said to be real,
it would have to be distinct from the aggregates (skandhas),
because it would possess a separate nature.
Just as form (rūpa) and so forth are truly distinct from sensation (vedanā) and so forth,
and possess substantial reality,
they must necessarily have causes.
Just as the five aggregates truly arise from causes,
if one reckons them as arising from causes,
they are therefore impermanent.
This would contradict your own tenet that "I am not impermanent.
If there were a substantial entity,
it would not arise from causes.
It must be causeless, which would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, your conception of the self is not unconditioned.
If it were neither produced by causes nor unconditioned,
then the self you maintain would be rendered useless.
If the self were merely conventional,
it would be the same as my own position,
because there is no real self. Furthermore, that school’s doctrine consists of five dharma-piṭakas.
The three periods of time constitute three;
the unconditioned constitutes the fourth;
and the self constitutes the fifth, the unspeakable treasury.
While I am in saṃsāra,
it cannot be said that I am either identical to or different from the three periods of time;
this remains the case even when I enter nirvāṇa.
It cannot be said whether the inexpressible and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are identical or different;
therefore, this self is established as the "inexpressible treasury" (*avaktavyakośa*). [The opponent] refutes this, saying:
"The self and the four preceding dharma-treasuries..."
If it cannot be said to be different [from the other four],
then one should not say that it is a fifth Dharma-piṭaka distinct from the preceding four.
If it cannot be said to be one,
then it cannot be said to be not the fifth.
That which is not the fifth—
These are precisely the aforementioned four dharma-piṭakas.
Since the fifth is neither the fifth nor can it be described as such,
one should establish only the four preceding dharma-piṭakas.
The above constitutes the refutation by means of reasoning; below follows the proof by means of scripture.
The treatise states:
The Bhagavān addressed the brahmin, saying:
I say that all that exists is subsumed solely within the twelve bases (āyatana).
As for the person (pudgala), [it is likewise so].

If it were not included within the categories of existence, its lack of intrinsic nature would be logically established; however, if it were included within the categories of existence, [its lack of intrinsic nature would be undermined].
Then one should not say that this is "inexpressible.
Furthermore, the sūtras recited by your own school also state:
"Whatever eyes there may be..."
"Whatever forms there are—
expounded at length, up to and including:
'Bhikṣus, you should know.'"
It is up to this point that the Tathāgata establishes all things and institutes all things.
There are dharmas that possess substantial reality; yet within these, there is no *pudgala*.
How, then, can it be said that the latter possesses substantial reality?
The Piṇḍola-sūtra also states:
"In this, there is no nature of self or what belongs to self;
there is only the substantial reality of all phenomena of suffering."
"Regarding that which has already arisen," and so forth, as explained at length;
this is based on the aforementioned principles and teachings.
Since there is no self-nature whatsoever,
how could the Vātsīputrīyas perversely conceive of and cling to a self? From this point,
the Master of the Treatise cites a verse to provide proof and refute [their position].
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the actual refutation;
second, the dissemination of the teaching.
The first seventeen verses constitute the actual refutation;
the final three verses are supplementary.
This is the dissemination.
Within the initial section on the correct refutation,
it is condensed into six parts.
The first part explicitly reveals the division on true emptiness;
the second clarifies the division on the Buddha’s universal knowledge;
and the third constitutes the division on answering questions for the benefit of sentient beings.
The fourth is the section on the unmeasurability of causal characteristics;
the fifth is the section on the sequence of the arising of results;
and the sixth is the section on the difficulty of knowing karmic retribution.
Within the section that correctly reveals the true emptiness,
the first part is spoken by the Arhatī,
and the subsequent part is spoken by the World-Honored One.
Now this is the first instance.
The treatise states: "There was an Arhatī."
This was spoken by Mañjuśrī—here called "Small Mountain"—to the Māra King:
"You have fallen into an evil view; within this collection of empty formations, you falsely cling to the existence of a sentient being. The wise realize that it does not exist."
Just as one gathers various parts and conventionally establishes them as a "chariot," so too,
one should know that by gathering the aggregates (skandhas), a "sentient being" is established. Commentary:
"You who have fallen into an evil course of views"—
this indicates the fault of Māra.
"You, this King Māra, have fallen into an evil course of views."
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is called evil;
first, it obstructs the Noble Path,
and second, it is shrouded by delusion.
Third, it serves as the cause of delusion;
thus it is called "evil," for it leads one toward birth and death.
It is the cause of saṃsāra;
it is the cause of the realms of existence (gati).
Wrong views themselves are the realms of existence.

This is called a "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi-gati*); it refers specifically to the wrong view of falsely clinging to the existence of a sentient being within the collection of empty formations (*śūnya-saṃskāra-rāśi*).
It is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that are in combination.
It is called a collection of formations;
being entirely devoid of an agent, it is termed "empty."
To grasp at sentient beings as real is a false view; for the wise to realize they do not exist is to manifest true emptiness.
Sentient beings are provisional;
the noble ones realize they do not exist.
Since the grasping at a self has been eliminated, [one is liberated].

Therefore, it reveals the true emptiness. As for the passage from "likewise gathering the various parts" up to "gathering the various aggregates," this is an explanation established through the use of metaphors;
the former serves as the metaphorical illustration.
Subsequently, it is logically consistent that by gathering the rim and other components, the chariot is formed;

Because of mastery over wisdom regarding all phenomena,
there is a verse that says:
"Within a single eye of a peacock feather, The causal characteristics of every kind [are present]."
"It is not the domain of other forms of knowledge; it is known only by the Omniscient One. Commentary:
The peacock’s eye-pattern possesses all distinctions, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
By what cause is this [result] produced in all its aspects?
Such characteristics of the cause are not within the sphere of others;
only a Buddha can know them.
The causes for the differentiation of form are already difficult to comprehend;
how much more so the distinctions among the causes and conditions of the various formless phenomena— the mind and mental factors—
how could these be easily understood?
From this point, the fifth [section] concerns the prior and subsequent parts of the arising of karma;
the former is difficult and the latter is clarified.
Next, the Vaiśeṣika school is refuted.
The Vaiśeṣika raises an objection, saying:
"If there is truly no self,
then once karma has already perished and been destroyed..."
"How, then, can it produce future results?
The Master of the Treatise answers:
"It does not arise from the destruction of karma."
When the future fruit arises,
although the karma has already perished,
the seed still remains.
However, it is solely from the functional capacity of the transformation and differentiation within the continuity of the karmic seed that future fruits arise,
just as worldly fruits arise from seeds.
However, the fruit does not arise from a seed that has already perished,
nor does it arise immediately after the seed. Rather,
the fruit arises only from a specific functional capacity resulting from the transformation of the continuity of the seed.
That is to say: from the seed the sprout arises;
from the sprout the stalk arises;
from the stalk the leaf arises.
Leaves grow from flowers;
the flower is the final stage that leads to the production of fruit.
The Vaiśeṣika school further objects:
If that is so, why say that the fruit arises from the seed?
The author of the treatise answers:
In reality, the fruit’s efficacy belongs solely to the flower.
Through the successive causation of prior seeds,
the capacity to produce fruit within the flower is induced;
it is with reference to this successive causation that one says "the seed produces the fruit."
Therefore, the capacity for this flower to produce fruit arises from the successive induction of its prior seed;
thus, the characteristics of the produced fruit resemble the seed.
Now, the production of fruit by karma is likewise like that of external seeds.
With karma as the precursor, seeds are perfumed;
through the transformation of the continuum, a specific result arises.
The Vaiśeṣika asks:
What is meant by "the differentiation of the transformation of the continuum"?
The Master of the Treatise answers:
it is preceded by karma.
Within form and mind, seeds are repeatedly formed;
this uninterrupted continuity within these very seeds is called "succession" (*saṃtati*).
This very continuity arises in each successive moment as something different from the preceding moments;
therefore, it is called "transformation.
This very transformation possesses a superior functional capacity.
Because it produces its final fruit and excels other transformations,
it is called "distinctive" (viśeṣa).
Therefore, this dialogue clarifies the prior fruit;

it corresponds to the fifth section. For example, at the time of death, although the consciousness-mind carries within it many seeds capable of producing fruits in the future, [it does not yet manifest them].
However, these karmic seeds are briefly of three types that can first project a fruit:
the first is the extremely heavy.
For example, as when those with debts are dragged forward by the stronger first;
second, it is like "proximate action," where at the time of death, the wholesome or unwholesome states arising upon encountering a virtuous or evil friend first draw forth their fruit.
Third is that which is frequently performed;
this refers to karma accumulated throughout one's life that is capable of projecting its fruit first.
Therefore, the Sautrāntika masters have this verse:
"Karma that is extremely heavy, that which arises proximately, that which is habitually practiced,
and that which was performed first— these, in their respective order, lead one to revolve in saṃsāra."
The commentary states:
First, there is karma that is extremely heavy,
which first brings about its maturation (*vipāka*).
Second, karma that arises proximately brings its maturation first; third, karma that is frequently performed [brings its maturation first].
If karma is heavy, it brings about maturation first;
if karma is light and so forth, it brings about later maturation.
By the power of this karma, one revolves through birth and death.

From this sixth section, "The Difficulty of Knowing Karmic Retribution," the author of the treatise defers to the Blessed One regarding the transformation of the continuum through the seeds perfumed by karma.
That various fruits arise at their respective stages is realized only by the Buddha;
it is not within the domain of others.
Therefore, the Sautrāntika masters have this verse:
"This karma, this perfuming, reaching this time, yielding its fruit—
the fixed principle of all these aspects no one can know except the Buddha."
The commentary states:
At the time when karma arises,
it necessarily perfumes and forms seeds.
That this karma, as this seed, can yield its fruit at this particular time is a fixed principle of seeds that only a Buddha can know.
The above six sections of the main body of the teaching have now concluded.
From here begins the second part, the Propagation,
which consists of three sections.
First, praising the Path and exhorting renunciation;
second, praising the Path and not beholding [the world];
third, briefly revealing and exhorting study.
Now this is the beginning.
The verse says:
This path of the cause of purity has been well expounded— Namely, the Buddha’s ultimate words on the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
One should abandon the blind darkness of all external attachments and the deeds of evil views in order to seek the eye of wisdom.
Commentary: This path of the cause of purification has already been well explained.
This praises the Path.
Nirvana is called purity;
this is the path of non-self.
That which is able to realize nirvana is called the path of the pure cause;
once the grasping at a self has been shattered.
The principle of selflessness is established;
this is called "well-spoken. That is to say, "the Buddha’s ultimate words are the true nature of phenomena" explains the preceding heading.
The teaching of non-self is the supreme word of the Buddha;
the principle of non-self is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Both this teaching and this principle are causes for nirvana.
This is the path of the cause of purification; it is for those who seek the eye of wisdom to abandon the various external attachments and evil views born of darkness and blindness.
This is an exhortation to renounce them.
The dogmatic attachments of non-Buddhists are called "evil views," and being devoid of the eye of wisdom, they are termed "dark and blind."
To turn one's back on the path of cessation and instead take it as a cause for the cycle of existence—
even to abandon it— is regrettable.
From this, secondly, we praise the path and do not behold [the cycle].
The verse says:
This single broad path to the palace of nirvāṇa, Traversed by thousands of sages, is the nature of selflessness;
Illumined by the light of the words of the sun-like Buddhas, Though the eyes of the ignorant are opened, they cannot behold it.
The commentary states:
The principle of selflessness leads toward the palace of nirvāṇa;
this broad path is traversed by the thousands of noble ones.
The teaching of selflessness is the speech of the sun-like Buddhas;
that teaching destroys darkness,
just like the blazing sun.
Relying on the teaching to manifest the principle is called "that which is illuminated by light";
this is the merit of the Path.
The evil eyes of the non-Buddhists are called "blinded eyes"; how could they possibly behold the sun of selflessness?
From this point, the third section briefly clarifies the exhortation to those who study.
The verse says:
In this direction, I have already spoken briefly, To open for the wise the gateway of the poison of their own intellect;
May each, according to their own capacity and power, Universally realize all that is to be known and accomplish the supreme task.
The commentary states:
I have already briefly explained the absence of self and spatial directions in order to open the gateway to the wisdom that neutralizes the poison for those of intelligence.
Just as when a small wound on the body is treated with a small amount of poison,
the toxic vapors will in an instant pervade the entire body,
so too is it with this treatise.
It opens the gate of limited wisdom;
those with true intelligence who can deeply awaken to and enter it call it the "gate of wisdom-poison."
This is the gateway to the wisdom-antidote;
I universally exhort people to practice it,
so that each may, according to their own capacity within the three vehicles, attain their respective goals.
Having fully awakened to all that is knowable,
one will necessarily accomplish supreme deeds;
since its merit is thus, [it is unsurpassed].
"Is it not that peace is not practiced?
This concludes the thirtieth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*. The manuscript states:

'On the twenty-first day of the month of Jyeṣṭha in the second year of Kwansei (the Xin-si year), this was transcribed from the original copy held at Ryūzan-ji; furthermore, it was collated with the copy held at Kakurin-ji using the diligent efforts of Jun.'"
The manuscript written by Mitsui Norushige states:

"On the third day of the third month of spring in the second year of Ōnin (the *mushi* year), I finished copying this from the aforementioned original and concealed it within my window; let it remain so, never to be brought outside the room."
The Great Sōjū Zen-tsu raised the following objection: "If this was an interpretation by En-ei, why did E-ei not interpret it? How can one say such things?
Regarding the manuscript, he noted:
"On the seventh day of the third month of that year, while I was reviewing it, the characters were incorrect; how can one say such things? etc.

The manuscript states: On the eleventh day of the ninth month of the seventh year [1379], while serving as *sōjō* (Chief Abbot) for the late [Emperor] Kōkō, and concurrently holding the office of *chūnagon* (Junior General) of the *Hei-Sō* (Central Wing), I completed this transcription at the age of thirty-two on the sixteenth night of the first month of winter in the third year of En’ō (*sin-hai*, 1391) at Ōtani-in, Jōdai-ji. On the first day of the latter part of the first month of autumn in the first year of Eishō (*ka-shi*, 1504), I finished a single reading. At that time, in the inner quarters of Hōsen-bō at Sanmi-ji, on the north window, I completed the transcription from the aforementioned original on the tenth day of the seventh month of the seventh year of Bun’ei (*tei-hai*, 1270).
